children.translated_text: Chapter 1
Chapter 1, Section 1
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 1
Because of the capacity for activity upon the apprehension of an object through a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), the <s>pramāṇa</s> is meaningful.

children.text: pramāṇam antareṇa nārthapratipattiḥ, nārhtapratipattim antareṇa pravṛttisāmarthyam/ pramāṇena khalv ayaṃ jñātārtham abhīpsati jihāsati vā/ tasyepsājihāsāprayuktasya samīhā pravṛttir ity ucyate/ sāmrthyaṃ punar asyāḥ phalenābhisambandhaḥ/ samīhamānas tam artham abhīpsan jihāsan vā tam artham āpnoti jahāti vā/ arthas tu sukhaṃ sukhahetuś ca, duḥkhaṃ duḥkhahetuś ca/
children.translated_text: Without a <s>pramāṇa</s> there is no apprehension of an object; without the apprehension of an object there is no capacity for activity. For it is through a <s>pramāṇa</s> that a person, having known an object, desires or avoids it. The endeavor of one impelled by desire and aversion is called activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>). Its capacity, moreover, is its connection with a result. One who is endeavoring — whether desiring or avoiding that object — attains or abandons that object. And the object is pleasure and the cause of pleasure, [or] pain and the cause of pain.

children.text: so 'yaṃ pramāṇārtho 'parisaṅkhyeyaḥ, prāṇabhṛdbhedasyāparisaṅkhyeyatvāt/ arthavati ca pramāṇe pramātā prameyaṃ pramitir ity arthavanti bhavanti/ kasmāt? anyatamāpāye 'rthasyānupapatteḥ/
children.translated_text: This scope of <s>pramāṇa</s> is innumerable, because the distinctions among living beings are innumerable. And when the <s>pramāṇa</s> is meaningful, the knower (<s>pramātā</s>), the knowable (<s>prameya</s>), and the resultant knowledge (<s>pramiti</s>) become meaningful. Why? Because if any one of them is absent, the [whole] purpose does not obtain.

children.text:
tatra yasyepsājihāsāprayuktasya pravṛttiḥ sa pramātā, sa yenārthaṃ pramiṇoti tat pramāṇam, yo 'rthaḥ pramīyate tat prameyam, yad arthavijñānaṃ sā pramitiḥ, catasṛṣu caivaṃvidhāsv arthatattvaṃ parisamāpyate/
kiṃ punas tattvam? sataś ca sadbhāvo 'sataśüEcāsadbhāvaḥ/ sat sad iti gṛhyamāṇaṃ yathābhūtam aviparītaṃ tattvaṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text:
Of these, the one whose activity is impelled by desire and aversion is the knower (<s>pramātā</s>); that by which he ascertains an object is the <s>pramāṇa</s>; the object that is ascertained is the <s>prameya</s> (knowable); the cognition of the object is the <s>pramiti</s> (resultant knowledge); and in these four, the reality of an object is fully comprehended.
What, then, is reality (<s>tattva</s>)? The being of what exists and the non-being of what does not exist. What exists, when grasped as existing, is reality — as it truly is, without distortion.

children.text: asac cāsad iti gṛhyamāṇaṃ yathābhūtam aviparītaṃ tattvaṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: And what does not exist, when grasped as non-existing, is reality — as it truly is, without distortion.

children.text: katham uttarasya pramāṇenopalabdhir iti? saty upalabhyamāne tadanupalabdheḥ pradīpavat/ yathā darśakena dīpena dṛśye gṛhyamāṇe tad iva yan na gṛhyate, tan nāsti/ yady abhaviṣyad idam iva vyajñāsyata, vijñānābhāvān nāstīti/ evaṃ pramāṇena sati gṛhyamāṇe tad iva yan na gṛhyate,
children.translated_text: How is the apprehension of the latter [i.e., the non-existent] by a <s>pramāṇa</s> possible? When an existent is being apprehended, the non-apprehension of that [putative object] is like a lamp. Just as, when visible objects are being grasped by a revealing lamp, that which is not grasped in the same manner does not exist — if it had existed, it would have been known just like these; from the absence of cognition, it does not exist. Similarly, when existents are being grasped by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, that which is not grasped in the same manner

children.text: tan nāsti/ yady abhaviṣyad idam iva vyajñāsyata, vijñānābhāvān nāstīti/ tad evaṃ sataḥ prakāśakaṃ pramāṇam asad api prakāśayatīti/
children.translated_text: does not exist. If it had existed, it would have been known just like these; from the absence of cognition, it does not exist. Thus, the <s>pramāṇa</s>, which illuminates what exists, illuminates the non-existent as well.

children.text: sac ca khalu ṣoḍaśadhā vyūḍham upadekṣyate/ tāsāṃ khalv āsāṃ sadvidhānām—
children.translated_text: And that which exists will be taught as classified in sixteen ways. Of these sixteen categories —

From the true knowledge of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), <s>prameya</s> (objects of knowledge), <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt), <s>prayojana</s> (purpose), <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine), <s>avayava</s> (members of a syllogism), <s>tarka</s> (suppositional reasoning), <s>nirṇaya</s> (ascertainment), <s>vāda</s> (debate), <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling), <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil), <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reasons), <s>chala</s> (quibbling), <s>jāti</s> (futile objections), and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat), there is the attainment of the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>). // 1.1.1 //

children.text: nirdeśe yathāvacanaṃ vigrahaḥ/ cārthe dvandvasamāsaḥ/ pramāṇādīnāṃ tattvam iti śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī/
children.translated_text: In the exposition, the analysis [of the compound] follows the order of words. The word 'ca' (and) forms a <s>dvandva</s> compound. The genitive in '<s>pramāṇa</s> etc.' with 'reality' is a pertaining-to genitive (<s>śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī</s>).

children.text: tattvasya jñānaṃ niḥśreyasasyādhigama iti karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhau/ ta etāvanto vidyamānārthāḥ, yeṣām aviparītajñānārtham ihopadeśaḥ/
children.translated_text: The genitives in 'knowledge of reality' and 'attainment of the highest good' are objective genitives. These are so many real entities, for the correct knowledge of which this instruction is [given] here.

children.text:
% vidyamānārthā, ...] p/32
so 'yam anavayavena tantrārtha uddiṣṭo veditavyaḥ/ ātmādeḥ khalu prameyasya tattvajñānān niḥśreyasādhigamaḥ/
children.translated_text: This, then, is the content of the <s>tantra</s> (system), which has been stated in summary and is to be understood. For it is from the true knowledge of <s>prameya</s> (the knowable), beginning with the <s>Ātman</s> (Self), that there is attainment of the highest good.

children.text: tac caitad uttarasūtreṇānūdyata iti/ heyam, tasya nirvartakaṃ hānam ātyantikam, tasyopāyo 'dhigantavya ity etāni catvāry arthapadāni samyag buddhvā niḥśreyasam adhigacchati/
children.translated_text: And this is taken up again by the subsequent <s>sūtra</s>. That which is to be abandoned [i.e., suffering]; its complete cessation, which is the means of its removal; that cessation being absolute; the means to it, which is to be comprehended — having rightly understood these four items of meaning, one attains the highest good.

children.text: tatra saṃśayādīnāṃ pṛthagvacanam anarthakam — saṃśayādayo yathāsambhavaṃ pramāṇeṣu prameyeṣu cāntarbhavanto na vyatiricyanta iti? satyam etat, imās tu catasro vidyāḥ pṛthakprasthānāḥ prāṇabhṛtām anugrahāyopadiśyante, yāsāṃ caturthīyam ānvīkṣikī nyāyavidyā/
children.translated_text: In this regard, [the objection is:] the separate mention of doubt and the rest is purposeless — for doubt and the rest, as they properly belong, are subsumed under <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s> and are not distinct [categories]? That is true, but these four sciences (<s>vidyās</s>), having separate fields of inquiry, are taught for the benefit of living beings, of which this <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (science of inquiry), the science of <s>Nyāya</s>, is the fourth.

children.text: tasyāḥ pṛthakprasthānāḥ saṃśayādayaḥ padārthāḥ/ teṣāṃ pṛthagvacanam antareṇādhyātmavidyāmātram iyaṃ syāt, yathopaniṣadaḥ/ tasmāt saṃśayādibhiḥ padārthaiḥ pṛthak prasthāpyate/ tatra nānupalabdhe na nirṇīte 'rthe nyāyaḥ pravartate, kiṃ tarhi? saṃśayite 'rthe/ yathoktaṃ —
children.translated_text: Its separate fields of inquiry are the categories beginning with doubt. Without their separate mention, this [science] would be merely <s>Adhyātmavidyā</s> (spiritual knowledge), like the <s>Upaniṣads</s>. Therefore, it is given a separate field by the categories beginning with doubt. Therein, <s>Nyāya</s> does not operate with respect to an object that is either unapprehended or already ascertained; rather, [it operates] with respect to an object that is in doubt. As it has been said —
'Ascertainment (<s>nirṇaya</s>) is the determination of an object, after deliberation, by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis.'

children.text: iti/ vimarśaḥ — saṃśayaḥ/ pakṣapratipakṣau — nyāyapravṛttiḥ/ arthāvadhāraṇaṃ — nirṇayas tattvajñānam iti/ sa ca
children.translated_text: Deliberation is doubt. The thesis and counter-thesis constitute the operation of <s>Nyāya</s>. The determination of the object is ascertainment — that is, true knowledge. And
'What is this?'

children.text: iti vastuvimarśamātram anavadhāraṇaṃ jñānaṃ saṃśayaḥ, prameye 'ntarbhavann evam arthaṃ pṛthag ucyate/
children.translated_text: — such mere wondering about a thing, an indeterminate cognition, is doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>), which, though subsumed under <s>prameya</s>, is stated separately for this purpose.

children.text: atha prayojanam — yena prayuktaḥ pravartate, tat prayojanam/ yam artham abhīpsan jihāsan vā karmārabhate,
children.translated_text: Now, purpose (<s>prayojana</s>) — that which impels one to act is purpose. The object which, desiring or avoiding, one undertakes action for —

children.text: tenānena sarve prāṇinaḥ sarvāṇi karmāṇi sarvāś ca vidyā vyāptāḥ, tadāśrayaś ca nyāyaḥ pravartate/ kaḥ punar ayaṃ nyāyaḥ? pramāṇair arthaparīkṣaṇaṃ nyāyaḥ/
children.translated_text: by this, all living beings, all actions, and all sciences are pervaded; and <s>Nyāya</s>, resting upon it, operates. What then is this <s>Nyāya</s>? <s>Nyāya</s> is the examination of objects by means of <s>pramāṇas</s>.

children.text: pratyakṣāgamāśritam anumānam, sānvīkṣā/ pratyakṣāgamābhyām īkṣitasyānvīkṣaṇam anvīkṣā/ tayā pravarttata ity ānvīkṣikī — nyāyavidyā — nyāyaśāstram/ yat punar anumānaṃ pratyakṣāgamaviruddhaṃ nyāyābhāsaḥ sa iti/
children.translated_text: Inference resting upon perception and <s>āgama</s> (scriptural testimony) — that is investigation (<s>anvīkṣā</s>). The re-examination of what has been examined by perception and <s>āgama</s> is <s>anvīkṣā</s>. That which proceeds by it is <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> — the science of <s>Nyāya</s> — the <s>Nyāyaśāstra</s>. Inference that is contrary to perception and <s>āgama</s>, however, is a semblance of <s>Nyāya</s> (<s>nyāyābhāsa</s>).

children.text:
tatra vādajalpau saprayojanau/ vitaṇḍā tu parīkṣyate/ vitaṇḍayā pravartamāno vaitaṇḍikaḥ/ sa prayojanam anuyukto yadi pratipadyate so 'sya pakṣaḥ so 'sya siddhānta iti, vaitaṇḍikatvaṃ jahāti/ atha na pratipadyate nāyaṃ laukiko na parīkṣaka ity āpadyate/ athāpi parapakṣapratiṣedhajñāpanaṃ prayojanaṃ bravīti, etad api tādṛg eva/ yo jñāpayati yo jānāti yena jñāpyate yac ca jñāpyate etac ca pratipadyate yadi, tadā vaitaṇḍikatvaṃ jahāti/ atha na pratipadyate, parapakṣapratiṣedhajñāpanaṃ prayojanam ity etad asya vākyam anarthakaṃ bhavati/ vākyasamūhaś ca sthāpanāhīno vitaṇḍā, tasya yady abhidheyaṃ pratipadyate, so 'sya pakṣaḥ sthāpanīyo bhavati/ atha na pratipadyate, pralāpamātram anarthakaṃ bhavati, vitaṇḍātvaṃ nivartata iti/
atha dṛṣṭāntaḥ pratyakṣaviṣayo 'rthaḥ, yatra laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ darśanaṃ na vyāhanyate/
children.translated_text:
Of these, debate (<s>vāda</s>) and wrangling (<s>jalpa</s>) have a purpose. But cavil (<s>vitaṇḍā</s>) is to be examined. One who engages in <s>vitaṇḍā</s> is a caviler (<s>vaitaṇḍika</s>). If, when questioned about his purpose, he accepts — 'this is my thesis, this is my <s>siddhānta</s>' — he ceases to be a caviler. But if he does not accept, then he falls into [the position of] being neither a common person nor an examiner. And if he claims that the demonstration of the refutation of the opponent's thesis is his purpose, even that is the same. If he accepts the one who demonstrates, the one who knows, that by which [it is] demonstrated, and that which is demonstrated — then he ceases to be a caviler. But if he does not accept, then his statement 'the demonstration of the refutation of the opponent's thesis is the purpose' becomes meaningless. And a collection of statements devoid of a positive position (<s>sthāpanā</s>) is <s>vitaṇḍā</s>; if he accepts its content, then he has a thesis to establish. If he does not accept it, it becomes mere babble, meaningless, and the status of <s>vitaṇḍā</s> ceases.
Now, example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) is an object that falls within the range of perception, where the view of common people and examiners is not contradicted.

children.text: sa ca prameyam/ tasya pṛthagvacanaṃ ca tadāśrayāv anumānāgamau, tasmin sati syātām anumānāgamau asati ca na syātām/ tadāśrayā ca nyāyapravṛttiḥ/ dṛṣṭāntavirodhena ca parapakṣapratiṣedho vacanīyo bhavati, dṛṣṭāntasamādhinā ca svapakṣaḥ sādhanīyo bhavati/ nāstikaś ca dṛṣṭāntam abhyupagacchann āstikatvaṃ jahāti/ anabhyupagacchan kiṃsādhanaḥ param upālabheteti/ niruktena ca dṛṣṭāntena śakyam abhidhātuṃ
children.translated_text: And it is a <s>prameya</s> (knowable). Its separate mention [is justified] because inference and <s>āgama</s> depend upon it — with it, inference and <s>āgama</s> would exist; without it, they would not. The operation of <s>Nyāya</s> also depends upon it. By contradiction of the example, the refutation of the opponent's thesis is to be stated; and by the proper application of the example, one's own thesis is to be established. And a skeptic (<s>nāstika</s>) who accepts the example thereby abandons his skepticism. If he does not accept it, on what basis would he challenge another? And with a properly stated example, it is possible to formulate
'An example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>) is that which, because of sharing the properties of the provable, possesses those properties, [and is cited] for illustration'
'the contrary being from the opposite [i.e., dissimilarity]'
— thus.

children.text: asty ayam ity anujñāyamāno 'rthaḥ siddhāntaḥ/ sa ca prameyam/ tasya pṛthagvacanaṃ satsu siddhāntabhedeṣu vādajalpavitaṇḍāḥ pravartante, nāto 'nyatheti/
children.translated_text: An object that is acknowledged as 'this exists' is a <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine). And it is a <s>prameya</s>. Its separate mention [is justified] because it is on the basis of distinctions among <s>siddhāntas</s> that debate, wrangling, and cavil operate, and not otherwise.

children.text: sādhanīyārthasya yāvati śabdasamūhe siddhiḥ parisamāpyate tasya pañcāvayavāḥ pratijñādayaḥ, samūham apekṣyāvayavā ucyante/
children.translated_text: The five members (<s>avayavas</s>), beginning with the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>), [constitute] the aggregate of words in which the establishment of the object to be proved is fully accomplished; they are called 'members' in relation to the aggregate.

children.text: teṣu pramāṇasamavāyaḥ, āgamaḥ pratijñā/ hetur anumānam/
children.translated_text: Among them, the combination with <s>pramāṇa</s> [in the syllogism is as follows]: <s>āgama</s> (scriptural testimony) is the thesis. The reason (<s>hetu</s>) is inference.
The example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>) is perception. The application (<s>upanayana</s>) is analogy (<s>upamāna</s>).

children.text: sarveṣām ekārthasamavāye sāmarthyapradarśanaṃ nigamanam iti/ so 'yaṃ paramo nyāya iti/ etena vādajalpavitaṇḍāḥ pravartante nāto 'nyatheti/
children.translated_text: The demonstration of efficacy when all [members] converge upon a single meaning is the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>). This is the supreme <s>Nyāya</s>. By this, debate, wrangling, and cavil operate, and not otherwise.

children.text:
tadāśrayā ca tattvavyavasthā/ te caite 'vayavāḥ śabdaviśeṣāḥ santaḥ prameye 'ntarbhūtā evamarthaṃ pṛthag ucyanta iti/
tarko na pramāṇasaṃgṛhīto, na pramāṇāntaram, pramāṇānām anugrāhakas tattvajñānāya kalpate/ tasyodāharaṇam — kim idaṃ janma kṛtakena hetunā nirvartyate, āhosvid akṛtakena, athākasmikam iti?
children.translated_text:
The determination of reality depends upon it. And these members, being particular words that are subsumed under <s>prameya</s>, are stated separately for this purpose.
<s>Tarka</s> (suppositional reasoning) is not included among the <s>pramāṇas</s>, nor is it an additional <s>pramāṇa</s>; [rather,] it serves to assist the <s>pramāṇas</s> for the sake of true knowledge. An illustration of it: Is this birth brought about by a created cause, or by an uncreated cause, or is it causeless?

children.text: evam avijñāte 'rthe kāraṇopapattyā ūhaḥ pravarttate — yadi kṛtakena hetunā nirvartyate, hetūcchedād upapanno 'yaṃ janmocchedaḥ/ athākṛtakena hetunā, tato hetūcchedasyāśakyatvād anupapanno janmocchedaḥ/ athākasmikam, ato 'kasmān nirvartyamānaṃ na punar nivartsyatīti nivṛttikāraṇaṃ nopapadyate, tena janmānuccheda iti/ etasmiṃs tarkaviṣaye karmanimittaṃ janmeti pramāṇāni pravarttamānāni tarkeṇānugṛhante,
children.translated_text: Thus, when the object is unknown, deliberation proceeds through the propriety of causes — if [birth] is brought about by a created cause, then the cessation of birth is tenable through the destruction of the cause. But if by an uncreated cause, then since the destruction of the cause is impossible, the cessation of birth is untenable. But if it is causeless, then since what is produced without a cause will not [necessarily] cease again, the ground for cessation does not obtain, and therefore there is non-cessation of birth. In this domain of <s>tarka</s>, the <s>pramāṇas</s> that operate [to establish] 'birth is caused by <s>karma</s> (action)' are assisted by <s>tarka</s>,

children.text: tattvajñānaviṣayasya vibhāgāt tattvajñānāya kalpate tarka iti/ so 'yam itthambhūtas tarkaḥ pramāṇasahito vāde sādhanāyopālambhāya cārthasya bhavatīty evam arthaṃ pṛghag ucyate prameyāntarbhūto 'pīti/
children.translated_text: and because of the differentiation within the domain of true knowledge, <s>tarka</s> serves the purpose of true knowledge. This kind of <s>tarka</s>, combined with <s>pramāṇa</s>, functions in debate both for the establishment and the refutation of an object — and for this purpose it is stated separately, even though it is subsumed under <s>prameya</s>.

children.text: nirṇayas tattvajñānaṃ pramāṇānāṃ phalam, tadavasāno vādaḥ, tasya pālanārthaṃ jalpaviṭaṇḍe/ tāv etau tarkanirṇayau lokayātrāṃ vahata iti/ so 'yaṃ nirṇayaḥ prameyāntarbhūta evamarthaṃ pṛthag uddīṣṭa iti/
children.translated_text: Ascertainment (<s>nirṇaya</s>) is true knowledge, the result of the <s>pramāṇas</s>; debate ends with it; and wrangling and cavil exist for the sake of protecting it. These two — <s>tarka</s> and <s>nirṇaya</s> — sustain the conduct of the world. Thus this <s>nirṇaya</s>, though subsumed under <s>prameya</s>, is stated separately for this purpose.
Debate (<s>vāda</s>) is indeed an aggregate of statements [proceeding] from multiple speakers, establishing the thesis of each side, ending with the ascertainment of one or the other side.

children.text: pṛthag uddiṣṭa upalakṣaṇārtham/ upalakṣitena vyavahāras tattvajñānāya bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: It is stated separately for the purpose of characterization. Conduct characterized [by these categories] serves for the attainment of true knowledge.
Wrangling (<s>jalpa</s>) and cavil (<s>vitaṇḍā</s>) are two varieties of that, for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality —
as stated.

children.text: nigrahasthānebhyaḥ pṛthag uddhiṣṭā hetvābhāsā vāde codanīyā bhaviṣyantīti/
children.translated_text: The <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons), stated separately from the <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat), are to be challenged in [proper] debate.
But in wrangling and cavil, the <s>nigrahasthānas</s> [apply].

children.text: chalajātinigrahasthānānāṃ pṛthagupadeśa upalakṣaṇārtham iti/ upalakṣitānāṃ svavākye parivarjanam, chalajātinigrahasthānānāṃ paravākye paryanuyogaḥ/ jāteś ca pareṇa prayujyamānāyāḥ sulabhaḥ samādhiḥ, svayaṃ ca sukaraḥ prayoga iti/
children.translated_text: The separate instruction on <s>chala</s> (quibbling), <s>jāti</s> (futile objections), and <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) is for the purpose of characterization. [Practically:] the avoidance of the characterized [fallacies] in one's own speech, and the challenging of <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthānas</s> in the opponent's speech. And a <s>jāti</s> employed by the opponent is easily answered, while its own employment is easily performed.

children.text:
seyam ānvīkṣikī pramāṇādibhiḥ padārthair vibhajyamānā —
pradīpaḥ sarvavidyānām upāyaḥ sarvakarmaṇām/
āśrayaḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ vidyoddeśe prakīrtitā//
children.translated_text:
This <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (science of inquiry), being analyzed through the categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> —
is a lamp for all sciences, a means for all actions,
a foundation for all <s>dharmas</s> — thus it is celebrated in the teaching of sciences.

children.text: tad idaṃ tattvajñānaṃ niḥśreyasādhigamārthaṃ yathāvidyaṃ veditavyam/ iha tv adhyātmavidyāyām ātmādijñānaṃ tattvajñānam/ niḥśreyasādhigamo 'pavargaprāptiḥ//1//
children.translated_text: This true knowledge, for the sake of attaining the highest good, is to be understood according to the [respective] science. But here, in the science of the Self (<s>Adhyātmavidyā</s>), the knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s> (Self) and the rest is true knowledge. The attainment of the highest good is the reaching of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 1 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 2

children.text: tat khalu niḥśreyasaṃ kiṃ tattvajñānāntaram eva bhavati? nety ucyate/ kiṃ tarhi? tattvajñānāt —
children.translated_text: Now, does that highest good occur immediately after true knowledge? No, it is said. What then? From true knowledge —

From the successive removal of false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>), defects (<s>doṣa</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), birth (<s>janma</s>), and suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), each following upon the removal of the one immediately preceding it, there is liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). // 1.1.2 //
There, concerning the <s>prameya</s> (knowable) ranging from the <s>Ātman</s> (Self) to <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>) operates in many forms.

children.text: ātmani tāvan nāstīti, anātmani ātmeti duḥkhe sukham iti anitye nityam ity atrāṇe trāṇam iti,
children.translated_text: Regarding the <s>Ātman</s>, first: '[the Self] does not exist'; regarding the non-Self, '[this is] the Self'; regarding suffering, '[this is] pleasure'; regarding the impermanent, '[this is] permanent'; regarding what offers no refuge, '[this is] a refuge' —

children.text:
sabhaye nirbhayam iti, jugupsite 'bhimatam iti, hātavye apratihātavyam iti, pravṛttau nāsti karma, nāsti karmaphalam iti, doṣeṣu nāyaṃ doṣanimittaḥ saṃsāra iti, pretyabhāve nāsti jantur jīvo vā sattva ātmā vā, yaḥ preyāt, pretya ca bhaved iti, animittaṃ janma, animitto janmoparama ity ādimān pretyabhāvaḥ, anantaś ceti, naimittikaḥ sann akarmanimittaḥ pretyabhāva iti, dehendriyabuddhivedanāsantānocchedapratisandhānābhyāṃ nirātmakaḥ pretyabhāva iti/ apavarge bhīṣmaḥ khalv ayaṃ sarvakāyoparamaḥ, sarvaviprayoge 'pavarge bahu ca bhadrakaṃ lupyata iti kathaṃ buddhimān sarvasukhocchedam acaitanyam amum apavargaṃ rocayed iti/
etasmān mithyājñānād anukūleṣu rāgaḥ, pratikūleṣu dveṣaḥ/ rāgadveṣādhikārāc cāsatyerṣyamāyālobhādayo doṣā bhavanti/ doṣaiḥ prayuktaḥ śarīreṇa pravarttamāno hiṃsāsteyapratiṣiddhamaithunāny ācarati, vācānṛtaparuṣasūcanāsambaddhāni, manasā paradrohaṃ paradravyābhīpsāṃ nāstikyaṃ ceti/ seyaṃ pāpātmikā pravṛttir adharmāya/
atha śubhā — śarīreṇa dānaṃ paritrāṇaṃ paricaraṇaṃ ca, vācā satyaṃ hitaṃ priyaṃ svādhyāyaṃ ceti, manasā dayām aspṛhāṃ śraddhāṃ ceti/ seyaṃ dharmāya/
atra pravṛttisādhanau dharmādharmau pravṛttiśabdenoktau, yathānnasādhanāḥ prāṇāḥ
children.translated_text: [False knowledge holds:] 'the fearless in what is fearful,' 'the desirable in what is loathsome,' 'what should not be abandoned in what should be abandoned,' 'in activity — there is no action, there is no fruit of action,' 'in the defects — this <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of rebirth) is not caused by defects,' 'regarding post-mortem existence — there is no living being, no soul or sentient being or <s>ātman</s> (self), who, having died, would come into being again,' 'birth is without cause, the cessation of birth is without cause' — thus is <s>pretyabhāva</s> (post-mortem existence) beginningless and endless; or 'though caused, post-mortem existence is not caused by action'; or 'post-mortem existence is without a self, operating through the severance and reconnection of the continuum of body, senses, intellect, and sensation.' Regarding <s>apavarga</s> (liberation): 'terrifying indeed is this cessation of all bodily activity; in liberation, which is the separation from everything, much good is lost — so how would a wise person desire this liberation, which is the annihilation of all pleasure and mere unconsciousness?' From this false knowledge arise attachment toward the agreeable and aversion toward the disagreeable. From the dominion of attachment and aversion arise the defects of falsehood, envy, deceit, greed, and the like. Impelled by defects, one acting through the body commits violence, theft, and prohibited sexual conduct; through speech — falsehood, harshness, slander, and incoherent talk; through the mind — malice toward others, coveting others' property, and nihilism. This is sinful activity leading to <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness). Now the virtuous [activity]: through the body — giving, protecting, and serving; through speech — truth, beneficial words, pleasant words, and <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study); through the mind — compassion, non-covetousness, and faith. This leads to <s>dharma</s> (righteousness). Here, <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, being the means of activity, are denoted by the word 'activity,' just as the means of sustaining life (<s>prāṇa</s>) are called <s>prāṇa</s> —
'Food indeed is the life-breath of living beings'
— thus.

children.text: seyaṃ pravṛttiḥ kutsitasyābhipūjitasya ca janmanaḥ kāraṇam/ janma punaḥ śarīrendriyabuddhīnāṃ nikāyaviśiṣṭaḥ prādurbhāvaḥ, tasmin sati duḥkham/ tat punaḥ pratikūlavedanīyaṃ bādhanā pīḍā tāpa iti/ ta ime mithyājñānādayo duḥkhāntā dharmā avicchedenaiva pravartamānāḥ saṃsāra iti/
children.translated_text: This activity is the cause of both despicable and honored birth. Birth, in turn, is the manifestation of body, senses, and intellect in a particular class of beings; when that exists, there is suffering. That [suffering] is the experience of what is adverse — affliction, distress, torment. These phenomena beginning with false knowledge and ending in suffering, proceeding in an unbroken succession, constitute <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth).

children.text: yadā tu tattvajñānān mithyājñānam apaiti, tadā mithyājñānāpāye doṣā apayanti, doṣāpāye pravṛttir apaiti,
children.translated_text: But when, through the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), false knowledge departs, then with the departure of false knowledge the defects depart; with the departure of defects, activity departs;

children.text: pravṛttyapāye janmāpaiti, janmāpāye duḥkham apaiti, duḥkhāpāye ca ātyantiko 'pavargo niḥśreyasam iti/
children.translated_text: with the departure of activity, birth departs; with the departure of birth, suffering departs; and with the departure of suffering, there is absolute <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) — the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>).

children.text: tattvajñānaṃ tu khalu mithyājñānaviparyayeṇa vyākhyātam/ ātmani — tāvad astīti, anātmani — anātmeti, evaṃ duḥkhe 'nitye 'trāṇe sabhaye jugupsite hātavye ca yathāviṣayaṃ veditavyam, pravṛttau — asti karma, asti karmaphalam iti, doṣeṣu — doṣanimitto 'yaṃ saṃsāra iti, pretyabhāve khalu — asti jantur jīvaḥ sattva ātmā vā, yaḥ pretya bhaved iti, nimittavaj janma, nimittavān janmoparama ity anādiḥ pretyabhāvo 'pavargānta iti, naimittikaḥ san pretyabhāvaḥ pravṛttinimitta iti, sātmakaḥ san dehendriyabuddhivedanāsantānocchedapratisandhānābhyāṃ pravarttata iti, apavarge śāntaḥ khalv ayaṃ sarvaviprayogaḥ sarvoparamo 'pavargaḥ, bahu ca kṛcchaṃ ghoraṃ pāpakaṃ lupyata iti kathaṃ buddhimān sarvaduḥkhocchedaṃ sarvaduḥkhāsaṃvidam apavargaṃ na rocayed iti,
children.translated_text: The knowledge of reality is explained as the opposite of false knowledge. Regarding the <s>ātman</s> (self) — first, 'it exists'; regarding the non-self — 'it is non-self'; likewise regarding suffering, impermanence, lack of protection, what is fearful, what is loathsome, and what is to be abandoned — each is to be known according to its proper object. Regarding activity — 'there is action, there is the fruit of action'; regarding defects — 'this <s>saṃsāra</s> is caused by defects'; regarding post-mortem existence — 'there is indeed a living being, a soul, a sentient being, or an <s>ātman</s>, who, having died, comes into being again'; 'birth has a cause, the cessation of birth has a cause' — thus post-mortem existence is beginningless but ends in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation); 'being caused, post-mortem existence is caused by activity'; 'being endowed with a self, it proceeds through the severance and reconnection of the continuum of body, senses, intellect, and sensation.' Regarding liberation: 'peaceful indeed is this separation from everything, this complete cessation that is liberation; much that is painful, terrible, and sinful is destroyed — so how would a wise person not desire this liberation, which is the cessation of all suffering, the non-experience of all suffering?'

children.text: tad yathā madhuviṣasampṛktānnam anādeyam iti, evaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhānuṣaktam anādeyam iti//2//
children.translated_text: Just as food mixed with honey and poison is not to be accepted, so too pleasure, being associated with suffering, is not to be accepted. // 2 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 3

children.text: trividhā cāsya śāstrasya pravṛttiḥ, — uddeśo lakṣaṇaṃ parīkṣā ceti/ tatra nāmadheyena padārthamātrasyābhidhānam uddśaḥ/
children.translated_text: The procedure of this <s>śāstra</s> (science) is threefold: <s>uddeśa</s> (enumeration), <s>lakṣaṇa</s> (definition), and <s>parīkṣā</s> (examination). Of these, <s>uddeśa</s> is the mere designation of a category by name.

children.text: tatroddiṣṭasya tattvavyavacchedako dharmao lakṣaṇam/ lakṣitasya yathālakṣaṇam upapadyate na veti pramāṇair avadhāraṇaṃ parīkṣā/ tatroddiṣṭasya pravibhaktasya lakṣaṇam ucyate,
children.translated_text: The <s>lakṣaṇa</s> (definition) of what has been enumerated is the attribute that distinguishes its true nature. <s>Parīkṣā</s> (examination) is the ascertainment through <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) of whether what has been defined conforms to its definition or not. Of these, the definition of what has been enumerated and classified is stated,

children.text: yathā — pramāṇānāṃ prameyasya ca/ uddhiṣṭasya lakṣitasya ca vibhāgavacanam, yathā — chalasya
children.translated_text: as for instance, that of the <s>pramāṇas</s> and of <s>prameya</s> (the knowable). The statement of division of what has been enumerated and defined — as for instance, that of <s>chala</s> (quibble):
'<s>Chala</s> (quibble) is the frustration of [an opponent's] statement through a distortion of meaning'
'it is of three kinds'
— thus. Now the statement of division of what has been enumerated:
<s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>upamāna</s> (comparison), and <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) are the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge). // 1.1.3 //

children.text: akṣasyākṣasya prativiṣayaṃ vṛttiḥ pratyakṣam/ vṛttis tu — sannikarṣaḥ, jñānaṃ vā/
children.translated_text: <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is the functioning of each sense organ with respect to its own object. 'Functioning' means either contact or cognition.

children.text: yadā sannikarṣas tadā jñānaṃ pramitiḥ, yadā jñānam, tadā hānopādānopekṣābuddhayaḥ phalam/
children.translated_text: When [it means] contact, then cognition — valid knowledge — [is the result]; when [it means] cognition, then the apprehensions of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference are the fruit.

children.text: anumānaṃ — mitena liṅgena liṅgino 'rthasya paścān mānam anumānam/
children.translated_text: <s>Anumāna</s> (inference) — is the subsequent cognition (<s>māna</s>) of the thing possessing the mark (<s>liṅgin</s>) by means of a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) that has been [previously] ascertained.

children.text: upamānaṃ — sāmīpyajñānaṃ — yathā gaur evaṃ gavaya iti/ sāmīpyaṃ tu sāmānyayogaḥ/ śabdaḥ — śabdyate 'nenārtha ity abhidhīyate jñāpyate/
children.translated_text: <s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) — is knowledge based on similarity — as in 'a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is like a cow.' Similarity here means the possession of common properties. <s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) — is that by which a meaning is expressed, i.e., made known or cognized.

children.text:
upalabdhisādhanāni pramāṇāni samākhyānirvacanasāmarthyāt boddhavyam/ pramīyate 'neneti karaṇārthābhidhāno hi pramāṇaśabdaḥ/ tadviśeṣasamākhyāyā api tathaiva vyākhyānam/
kiṃ punaḥ pramāṇāni prameyam abhisaṃplavante? atha pratiprameyaṃ vyavatiṣṭhanta iti?
children.translated_text: That the <s>pramāṇas</s> are the means of apprehension (<s>upalabdhi</s>) should be understood from the force of the etymological analysis of the term. The word <s>pramāṇa</s> denotes 'that by which something is measured/known' — it has the sense of an instrument. The explanation of the specific names [of each <s>pramāṇa</s>] follows the same pattern. Now, do the <s>pramāṇas</s> converge upon [a single] <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge)? Or do they stand separately for each <s>prameya</s>?
Both cases are observed.
'The <s>ātman</s> (self) exists'
— this is known from the instruction of a trustworthy authority (<s>āptopadeśa</s>). In that case, <s>anumāna</s> (inference) [also applies] —
'Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the <s>ātman</s>'
— thus. And <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) — that born of <s>yogasamādhi</s> (meditative concentration) in one who is practicing <s>yoga</s>:
'The <s>ātman</s> is perceptible through a special connection of the <s>ātman</s> and the mind'
— thus. Fire is known from the instruction of a trustworthy authority:
'There is fire here'

children.text: iti, pratyāsīdatā dhūmadarśanenānumīyate, pratyāsannena ca pratyakṣata upalabhyate/ vyavasthā punaḥ —
children.translated_text: — thus. By one approaching, it is inferred through the sight of smoke; and by one who has come near, it is apprehended directly through perception. The distinction, however, [is as follows] —
'One who desires heaven should perform the <s>Agnihotra</s> (fire-sacrifice)'

children.text:
iti, laukikasya svarge na liṅgadarśanam, na pratyakṣam/ stanayitnuśabde śrūyamāṇe śabdahetor anumānam, tatra na pratyakṣam, nāgamaḥ/ pāṇau pratyakṣata upalabhyamāne nānumānam, nāgama iti/
sā ceyaṃ pramitiḥ pratyakṣaparā/ jijñāsitam artham āptopadeśāt pratipadyamāno liṅgadarśanenāpi bubhutsate,
children.translated_text: — here, for one in the ordinary world, there is neither the observation of a mark for heaven nor perception [of it]. Upon hearing the sound of thunder, there is inference from the auditory cause; there, neither perception nor scripture [applies]. When something is apprehended directly in the hand through perception, neither inference nor scripture [applies]. And this valid cognition ultimately rests on perception. One who learns of a desired object from authoritative instruction also wishes to ascertain it through the observation of a mark;

children.text: liṅgadarśanānumitaṃ ca pratyakṣato didṛkṣate, upalabdhe 'rthe jijñāsā nivarttate/ pūrvoktam udāharaṇam
children.translated_text: and what has been inferred through the observation of a mark, one wishes to see directly through perception. When the object is [directly] apprehended, inquiry ceases. The previously stated example is
'fire'

children.text:
iti/ pramātuḥ pramāṇānāṃ sambhavo 'bhisaṃplavaḥ, asambhavo vyavastheti//3//
iti trisūtrībhāṣyam/
children.translated_text: — thus. The convergence of <s>pramāṇas</s> is their [simultaneous] applicability to a single knower; the non-convergence is [their separate] distribution. // 3 // Thus ends the commentary on the three <s>sūtras</s>.
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 4
Now the statement of definitions of what has been classified:

children.text: indriyārthasannikarṣottpannaṃ jñānam avyapadeśyam avyabhicāri vyavasāyātmakaṃ pratyakṣam // 1.1.4 //
children.translated_text: <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is cognition that arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object, that is non-verbal, non-deviating, and of the nature of determinate ascertainment. // 1.1.4 //

children.text: indriyasyārthena sannikarṣād utpadyate yaj jñānaṃ tat pratyakṣam/
children.translated_text: The cognition that arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object — that is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception).

children.text: na tarhīdānīm idaṃ bhavati, ātmā manasā saṃyujyate, mana indriyeṇa, indriyam artheneti?
children.translated_text: But then, does not [the following] also hold: the <s>ātman</s> is conjoined with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object?

children.text:
nedaṃ kāraṇāvadhāraṇam — etāvat pratyakṣe kāraṇam iti, kiṃ tu viśiṣṭakāraṇavacanam iti/ yat pratyakṣajñānasya viśiṣṭakāraṇaṃ tad ucyate, yat tu samānam anumānādijñānasya, na tannivarttata iti/
manasas tarhīndriyeṇa saṃyogo vaktavyaḥ?
children.translated_text: This is not a restrictive statement of causes — that only this much is the cause of perception; rather, it is a statement of the distinguishing cause. What is stated is the distinguishing cause of perceptual cognition; that which is common [also] to inferential and other cognitions is not thereby excluded. Then should the conjunction of the mind with the sense organ be stated?

children.text: bhidyamānasya pratyakṣajñānasya nāyaṃ bhidyata iti samānatvān nokta iti/
children.translated_text: Since this [conjunction of mind] does not vary when perceptual cognition varies, it is not stated, being common [to all cognitions].

children.text: yāvad arthaṃ vai nāmadheyaśabdās tair arthasampratyayaḥ, arthasampratyayāc ca vyavahāraḥ/ tatredam indriyārthasannikarṣād utpannam arthajñānaṃ
children.translated_text: Name-words serve their purposes [of referring to objects]; from them arises the comprehension of objects, and from the comprehension of objects comes practical activity. Now, this cognition of an object arising from sense-object contact [may take the form]
'color'
or
'taste'

children.text: ity evaṃ vā bhavati, rūparasaśabdāś ca viṣayanāmadheyam/ tena vyapadiśyate jñānaṃ — rūpam iti jānīte, rasa iti jānīte/ nāmadheyaśabdena vyapadiśyamānaṃ sat śābdaṃ prasajyate, ata āha — avyapadeśyam iti/
children.translated_text: — and so on. 'Color,' 'taste,' and such words are the names of the sense-objects. Cognition is verbally designated by these — 'one knows color,' 'one knows taste.' But since what is designated by a name-word would become verbal [cognition], therefore [the sūtra] says — 'non-verbal' (<s>avyapadeśya</s>).

children.text: yad idam anupayukte śabdārthasanbandhe 'rthajñānam, na tat nāmadheyaśabdena vyapadiśyate, gṛhīte 'pi ca śabdārthasambandhe 'syārthasyāyaṃ śabdo nāmadheyam iti/ yadā tu so 'rtho gṛhyate,
children.translated_text: This cognition of an object, when the word-object relation has not been employed, is not designated by a name-word; even when the word-object relation has been grasped — 'this word is the name of this object' — when that object is apprehended,

children.text: tadā tat pūrvasmād arthajñānān na viśiṣyate, tad arthavijñānaṃ tādṛg eva bhavati/ tasya tv arthajñānasyānyaḥ samākhyāśabdo nāstīti, yena pratīyamānaṃ vyavahārāya lakpeta/ na cāpratīyamānena vyavahāraḥ/ tasmāj jñeyasyārthasya saṃjñāśabdenetikaraṇayuktena nirdiśyate — rūpam iti jñānam, rasa iti jñānam iti/ tad evam arthajñānakāle sa na samākhyāśabdo vyāpriyate, vyavahārakāle tu vyāpriyate/ tasmād aśābdam arthajñānam indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam iti/
children.translated_text: then that [cognition] is not different from the prior cognition of the object; the cognition of the object is of the very same kind. But there is no other designating word for that cognition of the object by which, when apprehended, it could be employed for practical activity. And without apprehension there is no practical activity. Therefore, the cognition of an object is indicated by the conventional name-word of the thing to be known, used in an 'in-this-manner' fashion — 'the cognition that is [of] color,' 'the cognition that is [of] taste.' Thus, at the time of object-cognition, the designating word does not function; but at the time of practical activity, it functions. Therefore, object-cognition arising from sense-object contact is non-verbal.

children.text: grīṣme marīcayo bhaumenoṣmaṇā saṃsṛṣṭāḥ spandamānā dūrasthasya cakṣuṣā sannikṛṣyante,
children.translated_text: In summer, mirages, mixed with the heat rising from the ground, flickering, are apprehended by the eye of one standing at a distance;

children.text: tatrendriyārthasannikarṣād udakam iti jñānam utpadyate, tac ca pratyakṣaṃ prasajyata ity ata āha — avyabhicārīti/ yad atasmiṃs tad iti tad vyabhicāri pratyakṣam iti/
children.translated_text: there, from the contact of sense and object, a cognition arises — 'this is water' — and that would qualify as perception. Therefore [the sūtra] says — 'non-deviating' (<s>avyabhicāri</s>). That which [apprehends] what is not there as being there — that is deviating, [and is] not [valid] perception.

children.text: dūrāc cakṣuṣā hy ayam arthaṃ paśyan nāvadhārayati dhūma iti vā reṇur iti vā/ tad etad indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam anavadhāraṇajñānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ prasajyata ity ata āha — vyavasāyātmakam iti/ na caitan mantavyam — ātmamanaḥsannikarṣajam evānavadhāraṇajñānam iti/ cakṣuṣā hy ayam arthaṃ paśyan nāvadhārayati,
children.translated_text: One seeing an object from afar with the eye cannot determine whether it is smoke or dust. This cognition, which arises from sense-object contact but is indeterminate, would qualify as perception. Therefore [the sūtra] says — 'of the nature of determinate ascertainment' (<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>). And one should not think that indeterminate cognition arises only from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind [without sense involvement]; for it is through the eye that one sees the object without determining it,

children.text: yathā cendriyeṇopalabdham arthaṃ manasopalabhate, evam indriyeṇānavadhārayan manasā nāvadhārayati/ yac ca tadindriyānavadhāraṇapūrvakaṃ manasānavadhāraṇaṃ tad viśeṣāpekṣaṃ vimarśamātraṃ saṃśayaḥ, na pūrvam iti/ sarvatra pratyakṣaviṣaye jñātur indriyeṇa vyavasāyaḥ,
children.translated_text: and just as the mind apprehends an object apprehended by a sense organ, so too when a sense organ fails to determine, the mind also fails to determine. That indetermination of the mind which is preceded by the sense organ's indetermination is mere deliberation dependent on specific features — it is doubt, not [something] prior [to perception]. In every case within the domain of perception, the knower's determinate ascertainment is first through the sense organ,

children.text:
paścān manasāanuvyavasāyaḥ, upahatendriyāṇām anuvyavasāyābhāvād iti/
ātmādiṣu sukhādiṣu ca pratyakṣalakṣaṇaṃ vaktavyam, anindriyārthasannikarṣajaṃ hi tad iti/ indriyasya vai sato manasa indriyebhyaḥ pṛthagupadeśo dharmabhedāt, bhautikānīndriyāṇi niyataviṣayāṇi,
children.translated_text: and subsequently the mind's re-ascertainment follows; for those with impaired sense organs, there is no re-ascertainment. The definition of perception must be stated for the <s>ātman</s> and for pleasure and the like, for that [cognition of them] does not arise from sense-object contact. The mind, though a sense organ, is taught as distinct from the [other] sense organs because of its difference in properties: the material sense organs have restricted objects,

children.text: saguṇānāṃ caiṣām indriyabhāva iti, manas tv abhautikaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ ca, nāsya saguṇasyendriyabhāva iti/ sati cendriyārthasannikarṣe sannidhim asannidhiṃ cāsya yugapajjñānānutpattikāraṇaṃ vakṣyāmaḥ iti/
children.translated_text: and it is those possessing qualities that have the nature of sense organs; but the mind is non-material and has all objects as its domain — it, possessing [different] qualities, does not have the nature of [the other] sense organs. And when sense-object contact does exist, we shall explain the [mind's] presence and absence as the cause of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions.

children.text: manasaś cendriyabhāvān na vācyaṃ lakṣaṇāntaram iti/ tantrāntarasamācārāc caitat pratyetavyam iti/ paramatam apratiṣiddham anumatam iti hi tantrayuktiḥ/ vyākhyātaṃ pratyakṣam//4//
children.translated_text: Since the mind has the nature of a sense organ, a separate definition need not be stated. This should be understood from the practice of other systems. For it is a principle of systematic exposition that what is not rejected from another's view is [implicitly] accepted. <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) has been explained. // 4 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 5

children.text: atha tatpūrvakaṃ trividham anumānaṃ pūrvavac cheṣavat sāmānyato dṛṣṭaṃ ca // 1.1.5 //
children.translated_text: Now, <s>anumāna</s> (inference), which is preceded by that [perception], is threefold: <s>pūrvavat</s> (from cause to effect), <s>śeṣavat</s> (from effect to cause), and <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> (from commonly observed [correlation]). // 1.1.5 //

children.text: tatpūrvakam ity anena liṅgaliṅginoḥ sambandhadarśanaṃ liṅgadarśanaṃ cābhisambadhyate/
children.translated_text: By [the phrase] 'preceded by that,' the observation of the relation between the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and the thing possessing the mark (<s>liṅgin</s>), as well as the observation of the mark [itself], are connected [as prerequisites].

children.text:
liṅgaliṅginoḥ sambaddhayor darśanena liṅgasmṛtir abhisambadhyate/ smṛtyā liṅgadarśanena cāpratyakṣo 'rtho 'numīyate/
pūrvavad iti — yatra kāraṇena kāryam anumīyate, yathā meghonnatyā bhaviṣyati vṛṣṭir iti/
children.translated_text: When two things that are related as <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark) and <s>liṅgin</s> (the thing marked) are seen together, the memory of the mark is connected [with its possessor]. Through memory and the perception of the mark, an imperceptible object is inferred. '<s>Pūrvavat</s>' (effect-based inference) — this is where the effect is inferred from the cause, as when from the rising of clouds one infers that there will be rain.

children.text: śeṣavat tad — yatra kāryeṇa kāraṇam anumīyate, pūrvodakaviparītam udakaṃ nadyāḥ pūrṇatvaṃ śīghratvañ ca dṛṣṭvā srotaso 'numīyate bhūtā vṛṣṭir iti/ sāmānyatodṛṣṭam — vrajyāpūrvakam anyatra dṛṣṭasya ṇyatra darśanam iti,
children.translated_text: '<s>Śeṣavat</s>' (cause-based inference) — this is where the cause is inferred from the effect; seeing the river's water flowing in a direction opposite to before, and its fullness and swiftness, one infers from the current that rain has occurred. '<s>Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>' (inference from general observation) — the perception elsewhere of something previously seen in one place through locomotion;

children.text: tathā cādityasya, tasmād asty apratyakṣāpy ādityasya vrajyeti/
children.translated_text: so too with the sun; therefore, though imperceptible, the locomotion of the sun exists.

children.text: atha vā pūrvavad iti — yatra yathāpūrvaṃ pratyakṣabhūtayor anyataradarśanenānyatarasyānumānam,
children.translated_text: Alternatively, '<s>pūrvavat</s>' — where from previous direct perception of two things together, by seeing one, the other is inferred,

children.text: 'pratyakṣasyānumānam, yathā dhūmenāgnir iti/ śeṣavan nāma pariśeṣaḥ, sa ca prasaktapratiṣedhe ṇyatrāprasaṅgāc chiṣyamāṇe sampratyayaḥ, yathā sad anityam evamādinā dravyaguṇakarmaṇām aviśeṣeṇa sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyebhyo vibhaktasya śabdasya, tasmin dravyakarmaguṇasaṃśaye, na dravyam, ekadravyatvāt, na karma, śabdāntarahetutvāt, yas tu śiṣyate so .yam iti śabdasya guṇatvapratipattiḥ/
children.translated_text: that is, the inference of something previously perceived, as fire is inferred from smoke. '<s>Śeṣavat</s>' means elimination by remainder (<s>pariśeṣa</s>): when there is a general negation and the application [of the negation] does not hold in a remaining case, there is certainty regarding that remainder. For example, by [the reasoning] 'it exists, it is non-eternal,' and so forth, when <s>śabda</s> (word/sound) has been distinguished from <s>dravya</s> (substance), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and <s>karma</s> (action) without distinction from <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), and when there is doubt whether sound is a substance, action, or quality — it is not a substance, because it inheres in a single substance; it is not an action, because it is the cause of another sound; and what remains — that is, the ascertainment that sound is a quality.

children.text: sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ nāma — yatrāpratyakṣe liṅgaliṅginoḥ sambandhe kenacid arthena liṅgasya sāmānyād apratyakṣo liṅgī gamyate, yathecchādibhir ātmā, icchādayo guṇāḥ,
children.translated_text: '<s>Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>' (inference from general observation) — where the relation of mark and marked is imperceptible, an imperceptible marked entity is cognized through some commonality with the mark; just as the <s>ātman</s> (self) is inferred from desire and the like: desire and the rest are qualities,

children.text:
guṇāś ca dravyasaṃsthānāḥ, tad tad eṣāṃ sthānaṃ sa ātmeti/
vibhāgavacanād eva trividham iti siddhe trividhavacanaṃ mahato mahāviṣayasya nyāyasya laghīyasā sūtreṇopadeśāt paraṃ vākyalāghavaṃ manyamānasyānyasmin vākyalāghave 'nādaraḥ/ tathā cāyam itthaṃbhūtena vākyavikalpena pravṛttaḥ siddhānte chale śabdādiṣu ca bahulaṃ samācāraḥ śāstra iti/
children.translated_text: and qualities reside in substances; therefore, that in which they reside — that is the <s>ātman</s> (self). Since the threefold division is already established by the statement of distinction, the explicit mention of 'threefold' is because the author, considering supreme verbal economy in teaching a great subject of wide scope through a concise <s>sūtra</s>, is unconcerned about verbal economy elsewhere. And thus, this kind of procedure — employing various formulations of sentences — is found abundantly throughout the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise), in <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine), <s>chala</s> (equivocation), and matters of words and the like.

children.text: sadviṣayaṃ ca pratyakṣaṃ sadasadviṣayaṃ cānumānam/ kasmāt?/ traikālyagrahaṇāt —
children.translated_text: Perception has existing things as its object, while inference has both existing and non-existing things as its object. Why? Because it grasps [objects in] all three times —

children.text: trikālayuktā arthā anumānena gṛhyante, bhaviṣyatīty anumīyate, bhavatīti, cābhūd iti ca, asac ca khalv attam anāgataṃ ceti//5//
children.translated_text: Objects connected with the three times are grasped by inference: 'it will be' is inferred, 'it is,' and 'it was'; and the non-existent [here means] what is past and what is yet to come. // 5 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 6
Now, <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) —
<s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) is the means of establishing what is to be proved through its similarity with something well-known. // 1.1.6 //

children.text: prajñātena sāmānyāt prajñāpanīyasya prajñāpanam upamānam iti/ yathā gaur evaṃ gavaya iti/
children.translated_text: <s>Upamāna</s> is the cognition of what is to be made known through its commonality with what is already known. For example: 'A <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is like a cow.'

children.text: kiṃ punar atropamānena kriyate? yadā khalv ayaṃ gavā samānadharmaṃ pratipadyate tadā pratyakṣatas tam arthaṃ pratipadyata iti, samākhyāsambandhapratipattir upamānārtha ity āha/ yathā gaur evaṃ gavaya ity upamāne prayukte gavā samānadharmam artham indriyārthasannikarṣād upalabhamāno 'sya gavayaśabdaḥ saṃjñeti saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandhaṃ pratipadyata iti/
children.translated_text: What then is accomplished by this <s>upamāna</s>? When one apprehends that this [animal] has qualities in common with a cow, then one apprehends that object through direct perception — and the comprehension of the relation between a name and its referent is the purpose of <s>upamāna</s>, he says. For example, when the comparison 'a <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow' is applied, one who perceives through sense-contact an object having qualities in common with a cow understands that this word '<s>gavaya</s>' is a designation — and thus comprehends the relation between the designation and the designated.
Just as a <s>mudga</s> (mung bean), so is a <s>mudgaparṇī</s> (a plant resembling the mung bean);

children.text: yathā māṣas tathā māṣaparṇīty upamāne prayukte upamānāt saṃjñāsaṃjñisanbandhaṃ pratipadyamānas tām oṣadhīṃ bhaiṣajyāyāharati/
children.translated_text: just as a <s>māṣa</s> (black gram), so is a <s>māṣaparṇī</s> (a plant resembling black gram) — when comparison is thus employed, one who comprehends through <s>upamāna</s> the relation between the designation and the designated gathers that herb for medicinal use.

children.text: evam anyo 'py upamānasya loke viṣayo bubhutsitavya iti//6//
children.translated_text: Thus other applications of <s>upamāna</s> in the world should also be investigated. // 6 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 7
Now, <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) —
<s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is the instruction of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>). // 1.1.7 //

children.text: āptaḥ khalu sākṣātkṛtadharmā yathādṛṣṭasyārthasya cikhyāpayiṣayā prayukta upadeṣṭā/
children.translated_text: An <s>āpta</s> (trustworthy person) is indeed one who has directly realized <s>dharma</s>, and who instructs with the desire to communicate an object as it has been perceived.

children.text: sākṣātkaraṇam arthasyāptiḥ, tayā pravartata ity āptaḥ/ ṛṣyāryamlecchānāṃ samānaṃ lakṣaṇam/
children.translated_text: The direct realization of an object is <s>āpti</s> (attainment); one who acts from that is an <s>āpta</s>. The definition is the same for <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages), <s>āryas</s> (civilized people), and <s>mlecchas</s> (foreigners).

children.text: tathā ca sarveṣāṃ vyavahārāḥ pravarttanta iti/ evam ebhiḥ pramāṇair devamanuṣyatiraścāṃ vyavahārāḥ prakalpante, nāto 'nyatheti//7//
children.translated_text: And thus the transactions of all [these people] proceed. In this way, through these <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), the transactions of gods, humans, and animals are established — and not otherwise. // 7 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
That [verbal testimony] is of two kinds, because it pertains to objects seen and unseen. // 1.1.8 //

children.text: yasyeha dṛśyate 'rthaḥ sa dṛṣṭārthaḥ/ yasyāmutra pratīyate so 'dṛṣṭārthaḥ/ evam ṛṣilaukikavākyānāṃ vibhāga iti/ kimarthaṃ punar idam ucyate? sa na manyeta dṛṣṭārtha evāptopadeśaḥ pramāṇam, arthasyāvadhāraṇād iti, adṛṣṭārtho 'pi pramāṇam arthasyānumānād iti//8//
children.translated_text: That whose object is seen here [in this world] is <s>dṛṣṭārtha</s> (pertaining to seen objects). That whose object is understood in the other world is <s>adṛṣṭārtha</s> (pertaining to unseen objects). Thus is the division of the statements of <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages) and ordinary people. Now why is this said? Lest one think that only verbal testimony about seen objects is a valid means of knowledge, since the object can be ascertained [by other means]; [it is stated that] testimony about unseen objects is also a valid means of knowledge, since the object is [known] by inference. // 8 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 9

children.text: kiṃ punar anena pramāṇenārthajātaṃ pramātavyam iti? —
children.translated_text: What then is the class of objects to be known by this means of knowledge?

<s>Ātman</s> (self), body, sense-organs, objects, <s>buddhi</s> (cognition), <s>manas</s> (mind), activity, defects, rebirth, fruits [of action], suffering, and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) — these are the objects of valid knowledge (<s>prameya</s>). // 1.1.9 //

children.text: tatrātmā sarvasya draṣṭā sarvasya bhoktā sarvajñaḥ sarvānubhāvī/ tasya bhogāyatanaṃ śarīram/ bhogasādhanānīndriyāṇi/ bhoktavyā indriyārthāḥ/ bhogo buddhiḥ/ sarvārthopalabdhau nendriyāṇi prabhavantīti sarvaviṣayam antaḥkaraṇaṃ manaḥ/ śarīrendriyārthabuddhisukhavedanānāṃ nivṛttikāraṇaṃ pravṛttiḥ, doṣāś ca/ nāsyedaṃ śarīram apūrvam anuttaraṃ ca, pūrvaśarīrāṇām ādir nāsti, uttareṣām apavargo 'nta iti pretyabhāvaḥ/ sasādhanasukhaduḥkhopabhogaḥ phalam/ duḥkham iti nedam anukūlavedanīyasya sukhasya pratīteḥ pratyākhyānam/ kiṃ tarhi? janmana evedaṃ sasukhasādhanasya duḥkhānuṣaṅgāt duḥkhenāviprayogād vividhabādhanāyogād duḥkham iti samādhibhāvanam upadiśyate/
children.translated_text: Among these, the <s>ātman</s> (self) is the seer of all, the experiencer of all, the knower of all, the one who perceives all. The body is the seat of its experience. The sense-organs are the instruments of experience. The sense-objects are what is to be experienced. <s>Buddhi</s> (cognition) is experience itself. Since the sense-organs are not capable of apprehending all objects, <s>manas</s> (mind) is the inner instrument that has all objects as its domain. Activity and defects are the causes of the cessation of body, sense-organs, objects, cognition, and the experience of pleasure. This body of his is neither without a predecessor nor without a successor; there is no beginning of prior bodies, and liberation is the end of future ones — this is <s>pretyabhāva</s> (rebirth/transmigration). The experience of pleasure and suffering along with their means is the fruit. 'Suffering' — this is not a denial of pleasure, which is experienced as agreeable. Rather, it teaches the meditative realization that birth itself, being inseparably accompanied by suffering even when it includes the means of pleasure, being never free from suffering, being subject to various afflictions — is suffering.

children.text: samāhito bhāvayati, bhāvayan nirvidyate, nirviṇṇasya vairāgyam, viraktasyāpavarga iti/ janmamaraṇaprabandhocchedaḥ sarvaduḥkhaprahāṇam apavarga iti/ asty anyad api dravyaguṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyāḥ prameyam, tadbhedena cāparisaṅkhyeyam; asya tu tattvajñānād apavargo mithyājñānāt saṃsāra ity ata etad upadiṣṭaṃ viśeṣeṇeti//9//
children.translated_text: The concentrated one contemplates; contemplating, he becomes disenchanted; from the disenchantment of the disenchanted comes dispassion; from the dispassionate comes liberation. The cutting off of the continuous chain of birth and death, the abandonment of all suffering — that is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). There are also other objects of valid knowledge — <s>dravya</s> (substance), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) — and their subdivisions are innumerable. But because from true knowledge of these [twelve categories] comes liberation, and from false knowledge comes <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly bondage), these have been taught specifically. // 9 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 10

children.text: tatrātmā tāvat pratyakṣato na gṛhyate/ sa kim āptopadeśamātrād eva pratipadyata iti? nety ucyate/ anumānāc ca pratipattavya iti/ katham?
children.translated_text: Among these, the <s>ātman</s> (self) is not grasped by direct perception. Is it then known only from the verbal testimony of a trustworthy person? No, it is said; it is also to be known through inference. How?
Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, suffering, and cognition are the marks of the <s>ātman</s> (self). // 1.1.10 //

children.text: yajjātīyasyārthasya sannikarṣāt sukham ātmopalabdhavān, tajjātīyam evārthaṃ paśyann upādātum icchati, seyam ādātum icchā ekasyānekārthadarśino darśanapratisandhānād bhavati liṅgam ātmanaḥ/ niyataviṣaye hi buddhibhedamātre na sambhavati, dehāntaravad iti/ evam ekasyānekārthadarśino darśanapratisandhānāt duḥkhahetau dveṣaḥ,
children.translated_text: One who has experienced pleasure through contact with a certain type of object, upon seeing an object of the same type, desires to take it. This desire to take — arising from the connecting of perceptions in one who perceives many objects — is a mark of the <s>ātman</s>. For in a mere difference of cognitions with fixed objects, it would not be possible [without a unifying self], just as in different bodies. Similarly, from the connecting of perceptions in one who perceives many objects, there is aversion toward the cause of suffering.

children.text: yajjātīyo 'syārthaḥ sukhahetuḥ prasiddhas tajjātīyam arthaṃ paśyann ādātuṃ prayatate/ ekam anekārthadarśinaṃ darśanapratisandhātāram antareṇa na syāt/ niyataviṣaye buddhimātre na sambhavati, dehāntaravad iti/ etena duḥkhahetau prayatno vyākhyātaḥ/ sukhaduḥkhasmṛtyā cāyaṃ tatsādhanam ādadānaḥ sukham upalabhate duḥkham upalabhate, sukhaduḥkhe vedayate/ pūrvokta eva hetuḥ/ bubhutsamānaḥ khalv ayaṃ vimṛśati kiṃsvid iti, vimṛśaṃś ca jānīte idam iti, tad idaṃ jñānaṃ bubhutsāvimarśābhyām abhinnakartṛkaṃ gṛhyamāṇam ātmaliṅgam/ pūrvokta eva hetur iti/ tatra dehāntaravad iti vibhajyate yathānātmavādino dehāntareṣu niyataviṣayā buddhibhedā na pratisandhīyante tathaikadehaviṣayā api na pratisandhīyeran, aviśeṣāt/
children.translated_text: One whose experience of a certain type of object as the cause of pleasure is well-established, upon seeing an object of the same type, makes effort to take it. Without a single entity that perceives many objects and connects perceptions, this would not be possible; in a mere cognition with fixed objects it would not be possible, just as in different bodies. By this, the effort toward the cause of suffering is also explained. And by the memory of pleasure and suffering, this one who takes their means experiences pleasure and experiences suffering — he feels pleasure and suffering. The reason is as stated before. When one wishes to know, one deliberates 'what is this?'; and deliberating, one knows 'this is such.' This cognition, grasped as having the same agent as the desire to know and the deliberation, is a mark of the <s>ātman</s>. The reason is as stated before. Here, 'just as in different bodies' is explained thus: just as for those who deny the self, cognitions with fixed objects in different bodies are not connected, so too cognitions within a single body would not be connected, there being no difference.

children.text: so 'yam ekasattvasya samācāraḥ svayaṃdṛṣṭasya smaraṇam, nānyaddṛṣṭasya, nādṛṣṭasyeti/ evaṃ khalu nānāsattvānāṃ samācāro 'nyadṛṣṭam anyo na smaratīti/ tad etad ubyayam aśakyam anātmavādinā vyavasthāpayitum ity evam upapannam asty ātmeti//10//
children.translated_text: This practice of a single being — the remembering of what was seen by oneself, not of what was seen by another, not of what was not seen — is thus. And similarly, the practice of different beings is that one does not remember what was seen by another. Both of these cannot be established by one who denies the <s>ātman</s> (self); therefore it is established that the <s>ātman</s> exists. // 10 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
Its seat of experience is —
The body is the locus of effort, sense-organs, and objects. // 1.1.11 //

children.text: kathaṃ ceṣṭāśrayaḥ? īpsitaṃ jihāsitaṃ vārtham adhikṛtyepsājihāsāprayuktasya tadupāyānuṣṭhānalakṣaṇā samīhā ceṣṭā, sā yatra varttate tac charīram/
children.translated_text: How is it the locus of effort? With regard to an object to be obtained or to be avoided, the activity characterized by the undertaking of means for obtaining or avoiding, impelled by the desire to obtain or avoid — that is effort (<s>ceṣṭā</s>); and that in which it occurs is the body.

children.text: katham indriyāśrayaḥ? yasyānugraheṇānugṛhītāni upaghāte copahatāni svaviṣayeṣu sādhvasādhuṣu vartante sa eṣām āśrayaḥ tac charīram/ katham arthāśrayaḥ/
children.translated_text: How is it the locus of the sense-organs? That by whose support the sense-organs, when aided, function well, and when impaired, function poorly, with respect to their respective objects, good or bad — that is their locus, that is the body. How is it the locus of objects?

children.text: yasminn āyatane indriyārthasannikarṣād utpannayoḥ sukhaduḥkhayoḥ pratisaṃvedanaṃ pravartate sa eṣām āśrayaḥ,
children.translated_text: That seat in which the experiencing of pleasure and suffering, arisen from the contact of sense-organs and objects, proceeds — that is their locus,
that is the body. // 11 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 12
The instruments of experience are —
Nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear are the sense-organs; [they arise] from the elements. // 1.1.12 //

children.text: jighraty aneneti ghrāṇaṃ gandhaṃ gṛhṇātīti/ rasayaty aneneti rasanaṃ rasaṃ gṛhṇātīti/ caṣṭe 'neneti cakṣū rūpaṃ paśyatīti/ tvaksthānam indriyaṃ tvak/ tadupacāraḥ sthānād iti/
children.translated_text: 'That by which one smells' is the nose — it grasps odor. 'That by which one tastes' is the tongue — it grasps flavor. 'That by which one sees' is the eye — it perceives form. The sense-organ located at the skin is 'skin'; this is a figurative usage, [naming the organ] after its location.

children.text: śṛṇoty aneneti śrotraṃ śabdaṃ gṛhṇātīti/ evaṃ samākhyānirvacanasāmarthyād bodhyaṃ svaviṣayagrahaṇalakṣaṇānīndriyāṇīti/
children.translated_text: 'That by which one hears' is the ear — it grasps sound. Thus, by the force of the etymological explanation of their names, it should be understood that the sense-organs are characterized by the grasping of their respective objects.

children.text: bhūtebhya iti/ nānāprakṛtīnām eṣāṃ satāṃ viṣayaniyamaḥ, naikaprakṛtīnām/ sati ca viṣayaniyame svaviṣayagrahaṇalakṣaṇatvaṃ bhavatīti//12//
children.translated_text: 'From the elements' — when these [sense-organs] are of diverse material natures, there is a restriction of their objects; not when they are of a single material nature. And when there is a restriction of objects, the characterization as grasping their respective objects obtains. // 12 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
What then are the causes of the sense-organs?

children.text: pṛthivy āpas tejo vāyur ākāśam iti bhūtāni // 1.1.13 //
children.translated_text: Earth, water, fire, air, and <s>ākāśa</s> (space) — these are the elements. // 1.1.13 //

children.text: saṃjñāśabdaiḥ pṛthagupadeśo bhūtānāṃ vibhaktānāṃ suvacaṃ kāryaṃ bhaviṣyatīti//13//
children.translated_text: The separate teaching of the elements through distinct designating words will make the exposition of their effects easy. // 13 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 14
Now these —

children.text:
gandharasarūpasparśaśabdāḥ pṛthivyādiguṇās tadarthāḥ //
pṛthivyādīnāṃ yathāviniyogaṃ guṇā indriyāṇāṃ yathākramam arthā viṣayā iti // 1.1.14 //
children.translated_text: Odor, flavor, form, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the rest respectively, and are the objects of those [sense-organs]. The qualities of earth etc. are assigned accordingly, and the objects of the sense-organs are their respective domains. // 1.1.14 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 15

children.text: acetanasya karaṇasya buddher jñānaṃ vṛttiḥ cetanasyākartur upalabdhir iti yuktiviruddham arthaṃ pratyācakṣāṇaka ivedam āha —
children.translated_text: As if rejecting an interpretation that contradicts reason — namely, that cognition is the function of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), which is an unconscious instrument, and that apprehension belongs to a conscious [self] that is not an agent — he says this:
<s>Buddhi</s> (intellect), apprehension, and cognition are not different in meaning. // 1.1.15 //

children.text: nācetanasya karaṇasya buddher jñānaṃ bhavitum arhati, tad dhi cetanaṃ syāt, ekaś cāyaṃ cetano dehendriyasaṃghātavyatirikta iti/
children.translated_text: Cognition cannot belong to <s>buddhi</s> as an unconscious instrument, for then it would be conscious; and this one conscious entity is distinct from the aggregate of body and sense-organs.
The illumination of a meaning different from the literal meaning of a sentence whose purpose is to define the objects of valid knowledge is due to the force of reasoning. // 15 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 16

children.text: smṛtyanumānāgamasaṃśayapratibhāsvapnajñānohāḥ sukhādipratyakṣam icchādayaś ca manaso liṅgāni/ teṣu satsv ayam api —
children.translated_text: Memory, inference, <s>āgama</s> (scripture), doubt, intuition, dream, cognition, and reasoning; the perception of pleasure and the like; and desire and the rest — these are the marks of <s>manas</s> (mind). Among these, this too —
The non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is the mark of <s>manas</s> (mind). // 1.1.16 //

children.text: anindriyanimittāḥ smṛtyādayaḥ karaṇāntaranimittā bhavitum arhantīti/ yugapac ca khalu ghrāṇādīnāṃ gandhādīnāṃ ca sannikarṣeṣu satsu yugapaj jñānāni notpadyante,
children.translated_text: Memories and other (cognitions) that do not arise from the sense-organs must have some other instrument as their cause. And indeed, even when the contacts of the olfactory organ and other senses with odors and other objects are simultaneously present, cognitions do not arise simultaneously;

children.text: tenānumīyate, asti tat tad indriyasaṃyogi sahakāri nimittāntaram avyāpi, yasyāsannidher notpadyate jñānaṃ sannidheś cotpadyata iti/
children.translated_text: therefore it is inferred that there exists some other auxiliary cause connected with each sense-organ, which is non-pervasive, and from whose absence cognition does not arise, and from whose presence it does arise.

children.text: manaḥsaṃyogānapekṣasya hīndriyārthasannikarṣasya jñānahetutve yugapad uptadyeran jñānānīti//16//
children.translated_text: For if the contact of sense-organ and object were the cause of cognition without dependence on contact with <s>manas</s> (the mind), then cognitions would arise simultaneously. // 1.1.16 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 17
Next in order comes —
<s>Pravṛtti</s> (activity) is the commencement of speech, mind, and body. // 1.1.17 //

children.text: mano 'tra buddhir ity abhipretam, budhyate 'neneti buddhiḥ/ so 'yam ārambhaḥ śarīreṇa vācā manasā ca puṇyaḥ pāpaś ca daśavidhaḥ/ tad etat kṛtabhāṣyaṃ dvitīyasūtra iti//17//
children.translated_text: Here 'mind' is meant by <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) — '<s>buddhi</s>' is that by which one cognizes. This commencement, through body, speech, and mind, is tenfold — meritorious and sinful. This has already been commented upon in connection with the second <s>sūtra</s>. // 1.1.17 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 18
<s>Doṣāḥ</s> (faults) are characterized by incitement to activity. // 1.1.18 //

children.text: pravartanā pravṛttihetutvam, jñātāraṃ hi rāgādayaḥ pravartayanti puṇye pāpe vā/ yatra mithyājñānaṃ tatra rāgadveṣāv iti/ pratyātmavedanīyā hīme doṣāḥ kasmāl lakṣaṇato nirdiśyanta iti? karmalakṣaṇāḥ khalu raktadviṣṭamūḍhāḥ, rakto hi tat karma kurute yena karmaṇā sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ vā labhate, tathā dviṣṭas tathā mūḍha iti/ rāgadveṣamohā ity ucyamāne bahu noktaṃ bhavatīti//18//
children.translated_text: Incitement means being the cause of activity; for <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the other (faults) impel the knower toward meritorious or sinful activity. Where there is false knowledge, there arise attachment and aversion. Now, these faults are experienced by each person individually — why then are they defined by their characteristic? Because they are indeed characterized by their actions: the attached, the hateful, and the deluded (are known by their actions); for the attached person performs that action by which he obtains pleasure or pain, and likewise the hateful and the deluded. If one merely said '<s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion),' not much would have been stated. // 1.1.18 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 19
<s>Pretyabhāva</s> (rebirth) is re-birth after death. // 1.1.19 //

children.text: utpannasya kvacit sattvanikāye mṛtvā yā punarutpattiḥ sa pretyabhāvaḥ/ utpannasya — sambaddhasya/ sambandhas tu dehendriyamanobuddhivedanābhiḥ/ punarutpattiḥ — punar dehādibhiḥ sambandhaḥ/ punar ity abhyāsābhidhānam/ yatra kvacit prāṇabhṛnnikāye vartamānaḥ pūrvopāttān dehādīn jahāti tat praiti/
children.translated_text: The re-birth of one who has been born, after dying, in some class of living beings — that is <s>pretyabhāva</s>. 'Of one who has been born' means of one who is conjoined. The conjunction is with body, sense-organs, <s>manas</s>, intellect, and sensations. 'Re-birth' means conjunction again with body and the rest. 'Again' denotes repetition. One who exists in some class of living beings abandons the previously acquired body and the rest — that is 'departing' (<s>praiti</s>);

children.text: yat tatrānyatra vā dehādīn anyān upādatte tad bhavati/ pretyabhāvaḥ — mṛtvā punarjanma, so 'yaṃ janmamaraṇaprabandhābhyāso 'nādir apavargāntaḥ pretyabhāvo veditavya iti//19//
children.translated_text: and when, there or elsewhere, he takes up other bodies and the rest — that is 'coming into being' (<s>bhavati</s>). <s>Pretyabhāva</s> — dying and being born again — this continuous cycle of birth and death, beginningless and ending only with <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), should be understood as <s>pretyabhāva</s>. // 1.1.19 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 20
<s>Phala</s> (fruit) is the result produced by activity and faults. // 1.1.20 //

children.text: sukhaduḥkhasaṃvedanaṃ phalam/ sukhavipākaṃ karma duḥkhavipākaṃ ca/ tat punar dehendriyaviṣayabuddhiṣu satīṣu bhavatīti saha dehādibhiḥ phalam abhipretam/ tathā hi pravṛttidoṣajanito 'rthaḥ phalam etat sarvaṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: The experience of pleasure and pain is the fruit. Action has either a pleasurable or a painful ripening. And that occurs when body, sense-organs, objects, and intellect are present — thus the fruit is understood together with the body and the rest. For indeed, the result produced by activity and faults — all of this constitutes the fruit.

children.text: tad etat phalam upātam upātaṃ heyam, tyaktaṃ tyaktam upādeyam iti nāsya hānopādānayor niṣṭhā paryavasānaṃ vāsti, sa khalv ayaṃ phalasya hānopādānasrotasohyate loka iti//20//
children.translated_text: This fruit, each time it is taken up, is to be abandoned, and each time it is abandoned, is to be taken up again — thus there is no finality or conclusion to its abandonment and acquisition. Indeed, this world is carried along in the stream of the acquisition and abandonment of fruit. // 1.1.20 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
Now, this itself —
<s>Duḥkha</s> (suffering) is characterized by affliction. // 1.1.21 //

children.text: bādhanā pīḍā tāpa iti/ tayānuviddham anuṣaktam avinirbhāgena vartamānaṃ duḥkhayogād duḥkham iti/ so 'yaṃ sarvaṃ duḥkhenānuviddham iti paśyan duḥkhaṃ jihāsur janmani duḥkhadarśī nirvidyate, nirviṇṇo virajyate, virakto vimucyate//21//
children.translated_text: 'Affliction' means torment, pain. That which is pervaded by it, conjoined with it, existing inseparably from it — because of its connection with suffering, it is called <s>duḥkha</s>. Thus, one who sees that everything is pervaded by suffering, desiring to abandon suffering, and perceiving suffering in birth, becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, he becomes liberated. // 1.1.21 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 22

children.text: yatra tu niṣṭhā yatra tu paryavasānaṃ so .yam —
children.translated_text: But where there is finality, where there is conclusion — that is —
The absolute release from that (<s>duḥkha</s>) is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 1.1.22 //

children.text: tena — duḥkhena janmanā atyantaṃ vimuktir apavargaḥ/ katham? upāttasya janmano hānam, anyasya cānupādānam/ etām avasthām aparyantam apavargaṃ vedayante 'pavargavidaḥ/ tad abhayam ajaram amṛtyupadaṃ brahma kṣemaprāptir iti/
children.translated_text: Absolute release from that — from suffering and birth — is <s>apavarga</s>. How? The cessation of acquired birth, and the non-acquisition of another. This state, without end, is known as <s>apavarga</s> by those who know liberation. That is described as fearless, ageless, the state free from death, <s>Brahman</s>, the attainment of security.

children.text:
nityaṃ sukham ātmano mahattvavan mokṣe vyajyate, yenābhivyaktenātyantaṃ vimuktaḥ sukhī bhātīti kecin manyante/ teṣāṃ pramāṇābhāvād anupapattiḥ/ na pratyakṣaṃ nānumānaṃ nāgamo vā vidyate nityaṃ sukham ātmano mahattvavan mokṣe 'bhivyajyata iti/
nityasyābhivyaktiḥ — saṃvedanam, tasya hetuvacanam/ nityasyābhivyaktiḥ —saṃvedanam — jñānam iti, tasya hetur vācyo yatas tad utpadyata iti/
children.translated_text: Some hold that eternal bliss, like the greatness of the <s>ātman</s>, is manifested in <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), and that the one in whom it is thus manifested is absolutely released and appears as happy. Their position is untenable due to the absence of proof. There is no perception, no inference, nor scripture establishing that eternal bliss, like the greatness of the <s>ātman</s>, is manifested in liberation. The manifestation of what is eternal is its being experienced; and the cause of that must be stated — the manifestation of what is eternal is its experience, i.e., cognition, and the cause from which it arises must be specified.

children.text: sukhavan nityam iti cet? saṃsārasthasya muktenāviśeṣaḥ/ yathā muktaḥ sukhena tatsaṃvedanena ca sannityenopapannas tathā saṃsārastho 'pi prasajyata iti, ubhayasya nityatvāt/
children.translated_text: If it be said that it is eternal like bliss? Then there would be no difference between one in <s>saṃsāra</s> and one who is liberated. Just as the liberated one is endowed with eternal bliss and the eternal experience of it, so too the one in <s>saṃsāra</s> would be — since both are eternal.

children.text:
abhyanujñāne ca dharmādharmaphalena sāhacaryaṃ yaugapadyaṃ gṛhyeta/ yad idam utpattisthāneṣu dharmādharmaphalaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ vā saṃvedyate paryāyeṇa, tasya ca nityasaṃvedanasya ca sahabhāvo yaugapadyaṃ gṛhyeta, na sukhābhāvo nānabhivyaktir asti, ubhayasya nityatvāt/
anityatve hetuvacanam/ atha mokṣe nityasya sukhasya saṃvedanam anityam? yata utpadyate sa hetur vācyaḥ/
ātmamanaḥsaṃyogasya nimittāntarasahitasya hetutvam/ ātmamanaḥsaṃyogo hetur iti cet? evam api tasya sahakāri nimittāntaraṃ vacanīyam iti/
dharmasya kāraṇavacanam/ yadi dharmo nimittāntaram? tasya hetur vācyo yataḥ utpadyata iti/ yogasamādhijasya kāryāvasāyavirodhāt prakṣaye saṃvedananivṛttiḥ/ yadi yogasamādhijo dharmo hetuḥ?
children.translated_text: And if this is accepted, then co-existence with the fruit of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — i.e., simultaneity — would have to be admitted. The pleasure or pain that is experienced successively as the fruit of merit and demerit in the places of birth, and the eternal experience — the co-existence and simultaneity of these two would have to be admitted. There can be neither the absence of bliss nor its non-manifestation, since both are eternal. If the experience of the eternal bliss in liberation is non-eternal, then the cause from which it arises must be stated. If the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> together with some other auxiliary cause is the cause — if the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is said to be the cause, then even so its auxiliary co-cause must be specified.
