If <s>dharma</s> is the auxiliary cause? Then its cause must be stated, from which it arises. If the <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>-<s>samādhi</s> is the cause?

children.text:
tasya kāryāvasāyavirodhāt prakṣaye saṃvedanam atyantaṃ nivartate/
asaṃvedane cāvidyamānenāviśeṣaḥ/ yadi dharmakṣayāt saṃvedanoparamo nityaṃ sukhaṃ na saṃvedyata iti? kiṃ vidyamānaṃ na saṃvedyate, athāvidyamānam iti nānumānaṃ viśiṣṭe 'stīti/
aprakṣayaś ca dharmasya niranumānam utpattidharmakatvāt/ yogasamādhijo dharmo na kṣīyata iti nāsty anumānam/ utpattidharmakam anityam iti viparyayasya tv anumānam/ yasya tu saṃvedanoparamo nāsti tena saṃvedanahetur nitya ity anumeyam/
nitye ca muktasaṃsārasthayor aviśeṣa ity uktam/ yathā muktasya nityaṃ sukhaṃ tatsaṃvedanahetuś ca, saṃvedanasya tūparamo nāsti, kāraṇasya nityatvāt, tathā saṃsārasthasyāpīti/ evaṃ ca sati dharmādharmaphalena sukhaduḥkhasaṃvedanena sāhacaryaṃ gṛhyeteti/
śarīrādisambandhaḥ pratibandhahetur iti cet? na, śarīrādīnām upabhogārthatvāt viparyayasya cānanumānāt/
children.translated_text: Upon its exhaustion, the experience would absolutely cease, since it contradicts the fulfillment of purpose. If the experience ceases upon the exhaustion of <s>dharma</s> and the eternal bliss is not experienced — is it existent but not experienced, or non-existent? There is no inference that something distinctive exists. And that the <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>-<s>samādhi</s> does not perish — there is no inference for this, because what has the character of origination is impermanent. But for that whose experience does not cease, it should be inferred that the cause of experience is eternal. And if it is eternal, there is no difference between the liberated and the one in <s>saṃsāra</s> — as has been stated. Just as the liberated one has eternal bliss and the cause of its experience, and the experience does not cease because the cause is eternal, so too for the one in <s>saṃsāra</s>. And this being so, co-existence with the experience of pleasure and pain as the fruit of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> would have to be admitted. If it be said that connection with body and the rest is the obstructing cause — no, because body and the rest are for the purpose of enjoyment, and there is no inference for the contrary.

children.text: syān matam — saṃsārāvasthasya śarīrādisambandho nityasukhasaṃvedanahetoḥ pratibandhakaḥ, tenāviśeṣo nāstīti/ etac cāyuktam, śarīrādayaḥ upabhogārthās te bhogapratibandhaṃ kariṣyantīty anupapannam; na cāsty anumānam aśarīrasyātmano bhogaḥ kaścid astīti/
children.translated_text: One might think: the connection with body and the rest obstructs the cause of the experience of eternal bliss for one in the state of <s>saṃsāra</s>, and therefore there is no lack of distinction. But this is untenable — the body and the rest are for the purpose of enjoyment; that they should obstruct enjoyment is illogical; nor is there any inference that the <s>ātman</s> without a body has any enjoyment whatsoever.

children.text:
iṣṭādhigamārthā pravṛttir iti cet? na, aniṣṭoparamārthatvāt/ idam anumānam — iṣṭādhigamārtho mokṣopadeśaḥ pravṛttiś ca mumukṣūṇām, nobhayam anarthakam iti/ etac cāyuktam, aniṣṭoparamārtho mokṣopadeśaḥ pravṛttiś ca mumukṣūṇām iti/ neṣṭam aniṣṭenānanuviddhaṃ sambhavatīti iṣṭam apy aniṣṭaṃ sampadyate, aniṣṭahānāya ghaṭamāna iṣṭam api jahāti, vivekahānasyāśakyatvād iti/
dṛṣṭātikramaś ca dehādiṣu tulyaḥ/ yathā dṛṣṭam anityaṃ sukhaṃ parityajya nityaṃ sukhaṃ kāmayate, evaṃ dehendriyabuddhīr anityā dṛṣṭā atikramya muktasya nityā dehendriyabuddhayaḥ kalpayitavyāḥ, sādhīyaś caivaṃ muktasya caikātmyaṃ kalpitaṃ bhavatīti/
upapattiviruddham iti cet? samānam/ dehādīnāṃ nityatvaṃ pramāṇaviruddhaṃ kalpayitum aśakyam iti? samānaṃ sukhasyāpi nityatvaṃ pramāṇaviruddhaṃ kalpayitum aśakyam iti/
ātyantike ca saṃsāraduḥkhābhāve sukhavacanād āgame 'pi saty avirodhaḥ/ yady api kaścid āgamaḥ syāt muktasyātyantikaṃ sukham iti?
children.translated_text: If it be said that activity is for the purpose of attaining what is desired? No, because it is for the purpose of cessation of the undesired. The inference would be: the teaching of <s>mokṣa</s> and the striving of those who seek liberation are for the purpose of attaining what is desired, and neither of the two is purposeless. But this is untenable — the teaching of <s>mokṣa</s> and the striving of those who seek liberation are for the purpose of cessation of the undesired. What is desired, not pervaded by the undesired, is impossible — thus even what is desired turns out to be undesired; one who strives to abandon the undesired abandons even the desired, because the separation of the two is impossible. And the transgression of what is observed is equally applicable to body and the rest. Just as one abandons observed non-eternal pleasure and desires eternal pleasure, so too, having observed body, sense-organs, and intellect to be non-eternal, one should, transgressing this, postulate that the liberated one has eternal body, sense-organs, and intellect — and thus the unity of the liberated one would be even more strongly established. If it be said that this contradicts reason — the same applies: just as it is impossible to postulate the eternality of body and the rest in contradiction to the evidence, equally it is impossible to postulate the eternality of pleasure in contradiction to the evidence. And even if there is some scripture stating that the liberated one has absolute bliss,

children.text:
sukhaśabda ātyantike duḥkhābhāve prayukta ity evam upapadyate, dṛṣṭo hi duḥkhābhāve sukhaśabdaprayogo bahulaṃ loka iti/
nityasukharāgasyāprahāṇe mokṣādhigamābhāvaḥ, rāgasya bandhanasamājñānāt/ yady ayaṃ mokṣo nityaṃ sukham abhivyajyata iti, nityasukharāgeṇa mokṣāya ghaṭamāno na mokṣam adhigacchet, nādhigantum arhatīti/ bandhanasamājñāto hi rāgaḥ/ na ca bandhane saty api kaścin mukta ity upapadyata iti/
prahīṇanityasukharāgasyāpratikūlatvam/ athāsya nityasukharāgaḥ prahīyate, tasmin prahīṇe nāsya nityasukharāgaḥ pratikūlo bhavati? yady evam, muktasya nityaṃ sukhaṃ bhavati, athāpi na bhavati, nāsyobhayoḥ pakṣayor mokṣādhigamo vikalpyate iti//22//
children.translated_text: the word 'bliss' is used in the sense of the absolute absence of the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s> — and thus it is explained. For the use of the word 'bliss' for the absence of suffering is frequently observed in the world. Without the abandonment of the craving for eternal bliss, there is no attainment of <s>mokṣa</s>, since craving is recognized as bondage. If this <s>mokṣa</s> is the manifestation of eternal bliss, then one who strives for liberation out of craving for eternal bliss would not attain liberation, nor would he deserve to attain it. For craving is recognized as bondage, and it is untenable that anyone is liberated while bondage still exists. If the craving for eternal bliss is abandoned, then there is no aversion to it. And if his craving for eternal bliss is abandoned, then the eternal bliss is not averse to him. If so, whether the liberated one has eternal bliss or does not have it — in neither case is the attainment of liberation to be disputed. // 1.1.22 //
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 23

children.text: sthānavata eva tarhi saṃśayasya lakṣaṇaṃ vācyam iti tad ucyate —
children.translated_text: Since doubt has a proper place, its definition should be stated — and so it is said:

children.text: samānānekadharmopapatter vipratipatter upalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthātaś ca viśeṣāpekṣo vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ // 1.1.23 //
children.translated_text: <s>Saṃśaya</s> (doubt) is an inquiry that depends on a distinguishing feature, arising from the apprehension of common and multiple properties, from conflicting claims, and from the irregularity of perception and non-perception. // 1.1.23 //

children.text:
samānadharmopapatter viśeṣāpekṣo vimarśaḥ saṃśaya iti/ sthāṇupuruṣayoḥ samānaṃ dharmam ārohapariṇāhau paśyan pūrvadṛṣṭaṃ ca tayor viśeṣam bubhutsamānaḥ kiṃsvid ity anyataraṃ nāvadhārayati, tadanavadhāraṇaṃ jñānaṃ saṃśayaḥ/ samānam anayor dharmam upalabhe viśeṣam anyatarasya nopalabha ity eṣā buddhir apekṣā —
% nopalabha ity eṣā buddhir apekṣā —]

saṃśayasya pravṛttikā vartate, tena viśeṣāpekṣo vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ/
anekadharmopapatter iti/ samānajātīyam asamānajātīyaṃ cānekam/ tasyānekasya dharmopapatteḥ —
children.translated_text: that serves as the occasion for <s>saṃśaya</s>. Therefore, <s>saṃśaya</s> is an inquiry that depends on a distinguishing feature. 'Arising from the apprehension of multiple properties' — 'multiple' means both of the same class and of a different class. From the apprehension of the properties of this multiplicity —

An inquiry that depends on a distinguishing feature, arising from the apprehension of common properties — that is <s>saṃśaya</s>. Seeing the common properties of height and girth in a post and a person, and wishing to ascertain the distinguishing feature previously observed between them, one does not determine either one, thinking 'What is this?' — that non-determination, that cognition, is <s>saṃśaya</s>. 'I apprehend their common property but do not apprehend the distinguishing feature of either' — this cognition is the expectation —

children.text: viśeṣasyobayathā dṛṣṭatvāt/ samānajātīyebhyo 'samānajātīyebyaś cārthā viśiṣyante, gandhavattvāt pṛthivy abādhibyo viśiṣyate guṇakarmabhyaś ca / asti ca śabde vibhāgajanyatvaṃ viśeṣaḥ/ tasmin dravyaṃ guṇaḥ karma veti sandehaḥ, viśeṣasyobayathā dṛṣṭatvāt/
children.translated_text: because the distinguishing feature has been observed in both ways: things are distinguished from things of the same class and things of a different class. Earth is distinguished from other (substances) by possessing odor, and from qualities and actions. And in sound there exists the distinguishing feature of being produced by separation. Regarding it, the doubt arises: 'Is it a substance, a quality, or an action?' — because the distinguishing feature has been observed in both ways.

children.text:
kiṃ dravyasya sato guṇakarmabhyo viśeṣaḥ, āhosvid guṇasya sata iti, atha karmaṇaḥ sata iti? viśeṣāpekṣā — anyatamasya vyavasthāpakaṃ dharma nopalaba iti buddhir iti/
vipratipatter iti/ vyāhatam ekārthadarśanaṃ vipratipattiḥ, vyāghātaḥ — virodho 'sahabhāva iti/ asty ātmety ekaṃ darśanam, nāsty ātmety aparam, na ca sadbhāvāsadbhāvau sahaikatra sambhavataḥ, na cānyatarasādhako hetur upalabhyate, tatra tattvānavadhāraṇaṃ saṃśaya iti/
upalabdhyavayavasthātaḥ khalv api sac codakam upalabhyate taḍāgādiṣu, marīciṣu cāvidyamānam udakam iti, ataḥ kvacid upalabhyamāne tattvavyavasthāpakasya pramāṇasyānupalabdheḥ kiṃ sad upalabhyate 'thāsad iti saṃśayo bhavati/
anupalabdhyavyavasthātaḥ/ sac ca nopalabyate mūlakīlakodakādi, asac cānutpannaṃ niruddhaṃ vā,
children.translated_text:
Is there a distinction of an existing substance from qualities and actions, or of an existing quality [from them], or of an existing action [from them]? The expectation of a specific [distinguishing property] — the cognition that 'no property establishing either one is perceived.'
'From conflicting opinions' — a contradictory perception of the same object is conflicting opinion (<s>vipratipattiḥ</s>); the contradiction is incompatibility, non-coexistence. 'There is a self' is one view; 'there is no self' is another; and existence and non-existence cannot both obtain in one and the same [thing]; and no reason establishing either is perceived — therein, the non-ascertainment of the truth is doubt.
'From the indeterminacy of perception' — water is indeed perceived in ponds and such; and in mirages, non-existent water [appears]; therefore, when something is perceived somewhere, since no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that would establish the truth is perceived, there is doubt: 'is what is perceived real or unreal?'
'From the indeterminacy of non-perception' — what exists is also sometimes not perceived, such as water in a root-cavity or stake-hole; and what does not exist [is also not perceived] — what has not yet arisen, or what has ceased,

children.text:
tataḥ kvacid anupalabhyamāne saṃśayaḥ, kiṃ san nopalabyate utāsad iti saṃśayo bhavati/ viśeṣāpekṣā pūrvavat/
pūrvaḥ samāno 'nekaś ca dharmo jñeyasthaḥ, upalabdhyanupalabdhī punar jñātṛsthe, etāvatā viśeṣeṇa punarvacanam/
children.translated_text:
therefore, when something is not perceived somewhere, there is doubt: 'is it that something real is not perceived, or that something unreal [is not perceived]?' The expectation of a specific [distinguishing property] is as before.
The former properties — common, multiple — belong to the object of knowledge; perception and non-perception, however, belong to the knower. With this distinction, there is a restatement.

From the ascertainment of common properties, from the applicability of common properties, there is deliberation (<s>vimarśa</s>) in expectation of the recollection of a specific [distinguishing property]. //23//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
The definition is the same for those that have [their own] place [in the system].

children.text: yam arhtam adhikṛtya pravartate tat prayojanam // 1.1.24 //
children.translated_text: That object with reference to which one acts is <s>prayojana</s> (purpose). // 1.1.24 //

children.text: yam artham āptavyaṃ hātavyaṃ vā vyavasāya tadāptihānopāyam anutiṣṭhati, prayojanaṃ tad veditavyam, pravṛttihetutvāt/ imam artham āpsyāmi hāsyāmi veti vyavasāyo 'rthasyādhikāraḥ, evaṃ vyavasīyamāno 'rtho 'dhikriyata iti//24//
children.translated_text: That object which one determines to be attainable or avoidable, and in accordance with which one adopts the means of attainment or avoidance — that should be known as <s>prayojana</s> (purpose), because it is the cause of activity. 'I shall obtain this object' or 'I shall avoid this' — [such] determination is the taking up (<s>adhikāra</s>) of the object; an object being thus determined is taken up. //24//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 25

children.text: laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ yasminn arthe buddhisāmyaṃ sa dṛṣṭānataḥ // 1.1.25 //
children.translated_text: That regarding which the cognitions of ordinary people and critical examiners are the same — that is a <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example). // 1.1.25 //

children.text: lokasāmānyam anatītā laukikā naisargikaṃ vainayikaṃ buddhyatiśayam aprāptāḥ/ tadviparītāḥ parīkṣakāḥ/ tarkeṇa pramāṇair arthaṃ parīkṣitum arhantīti/ yathā yam arthaṃ laukikā budhyante tathā parīkṣakā api,
children.translated_text: Those who have not transcended ordinary knowledge are 'ordinary people' (<s>laukika</s>), who have not attained a superior intellect, whether natural or acquired through training. The opposite of them are 'critical examiners' (<s>parīkṣaka</s>) — those who are capable of examining an object through reasoning and means of valid knowledge. The object that ordinary people understand in a certain way,

children.text: so 'rtho dṛṣṭāntaḥ/ dṛṣṭāntavirodhena hi pratipakṣāḥ pratiṣeddhavyā bhavantīti, dṛṣṭāntasamādhinā ca svapakṣāḥ sthāpanīyā bhavantīti, avayaveṣu codāharaṇāya kalpata iti//25//
children.translated_text: and critical examiners also [understand] in that same way — that object is a <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example). For opposing views must be refuted through contradiction with the example, and one's own positions must be established through agreement with the example; and among the members [of a syllogism], it serves as the illustration (<s>udāharaṇa</s>). //25//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 26

children.text:
atha siddhāntaḥ, idam itthambhūtañ cety abhyanujñāyamānam arthajātaṃ siddham, siddhasya saṃsthitiḥ siddhāntaḥ, saṃsthitir itthambhāvavyavasthā dharmaniyamaḥ/
sa khalv ayam —
children.translated_text:
Now, <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine): the totality of objects that is acknowledged as 'this is of such a nature' is 'established' (<s>siddha</s>); the firm standing (<s>saṃsthiti</s>) of what is established is <s>siddhānta</s>; firm standing means the definite determination of having such a nature — the fixation of a property.
That indeed is —
The firm standing based on a <s>tantra</s> (system), a topic (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>), or a provisional acceptance (<s>abhyupagama</s>) is <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine). // 1.1.26 //

children.text: tantrārthasaṃsthitiḥ tantrasaṃsthitiḥ, tantram itaretarābhisambaddhasyārthasamūhasyopadeśaḥ śāstram/ adhikaraṇānuṣaktārthasaṃsthitir adhikaraṇasaṃsthitiḥ, abhyupagamasaṃsthitir anavadhāritārthaparigrahaḥ, tadviśeṣaparīkṣaṇāyābhyupagamasiddhāntaḥ/
children.translated_text: The firm standing of the meaning of a system is the system-based firm standing; a <s>tantra</s> is a teaching (<s>śāstra</s>) — the instruction of a body of interconnected meanings. The firm standing of a meaning connected with a topic is the topic-based firm standing. The firm standing based on provisional acceptance is the adoption of an undetermined meaning, [done] for the purpose of examining its particular [character] — that is the <s>abhyupagama-siddhānta</s> (provisionally accepted doctrine).
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
But due to the division of systems —

It is fourfold, because of the distinct natures of <s>sarvatantra</s> (universally accepted), <s>pratitantra</s> (system-specific), <s>adhikaraṇa</s> (topic-based), and <s>abhyupagama</s> (provisionally accepted) firm standings. // 1.1.27 //
Among those, these four firm standings are distinct in their objects. //27//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
Among those —
A meaning that is taken up in one's own system and is not contradicted by any system is a <s>sarvatantra-siddhānta</s> (universally accepted doctrine). // 1.1.28 //

children.text: yathā ghrāṇādīnīnindriyāṇi gandhādaya indriyārhāḥ pṛthivyādīni bhūtāni pramāṇair arthasya grahaṇam iti//28//
children.translated_text: Such as: the sense-organs — smell and the rest; the sense-objects — odor and the rest; the elements — earth and the rest; the apprehension of objects through means of valid knowledge. //28//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 29
What is established in one's own system but not established in a similar system is a <s>pratitantra-siddhānta</s> (system-specific doctrine). // 1.1.29 //

children.text: yathā nāsata ātmalābhaḥ, na sata ātmahānam, niratiśayāś cetanāḥ dehendriyamanaḥsu viṣayeṣu tattatkāraṇeṣu ca viśeṣa iti sāṅkhyānām, puruṣakarmādinimitto bhūtasargaḥ, karmahetavo doṣāḥ pravṛttiś ca, svaguṇaviśiṣṭāś cetanāḥ, asad utpadyate utpannaṃ nirudhyata iti yogānām//29//
children.translated_text: For example, [the tenets] of the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s>: there is no origination from non-existence; there is no destruction of what exists; consciousnesses are unsurpassed [in their essential nature]; there is a specific [distinction] in body, sense-organs, mind, objects, and their respective causes. [And the tenets] of the <s>Yogas</s>: the creation of beings is caused by individual <s>karma</s> and so forth; the defects (<s>doṣas</s>) and activity are the causes of <s>karma</s>; consciousnesses are qualified by their own specific qualities; what does not exist originates; what has originated ceases. //29//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
That whose establishment [leads to] the establishment of another topic — that is an <s>adhikaraṇa-siddhānta</s> (topic-based doctrine). // 1.1.30 //

children.text: yasyārhtasya siddhāv anye 'rthā anuṣajyante, na tair vinā so 'rthaḥ sidhyati te 'rthā yadadhiṣṭhānāḥ so 'dhikaraṇasiddhāntaḥ,
children.translated_text: That meaning whose establishment is followed by other meanings, and without which that meaning cannot be established — those meanings, which have it as their foundation, constitute the <s>adhikaraṇa-siddhānta</s>,
for example: 'the knower is different from body and sense-organs' —
'because of the grasping of a single object through seeing and touching' —

children.text: iti atrānuṣaṅgiṇo 'rthā indriyanānātvaṃ niyataviṣayāṇīndriyāṇi svaviṣayagrahaṇaliṅgāni jñātur jñānasādhanāni, gandhādiguṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyaṃ guṇādhikaraṇam aniyataviṣayāś cetanā iti pūrvārthasiddhāv ete 'rhāḥ sidhyanti na tair vinā so 'rthaḥ sambhavatīti//30//
children.translated_text: herein, the connected meanings are: the multiplicity of sense-organs; sense-organs have fixed [specific] objects; sense-organs are characterized by the apprehension of their own objects; [sense-organs] are the instruments of knowledge for the knower; substance, being different from qualities such as odor and the rest, is the substratum of qualities; consciousnesses have unfixed [unlimited] objects. Upon the establishment of the former meaning, these meanings are established; without them, that meaning is not possible. //30//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 31
The examination of a particular [aspect] of something accepted without examination is an <s>abhyupagama-siddhānta</s> (provisionally accepted doctrine). // 1.1.31 //

children.text: yatra kiñcid arthajātam aparīkṣitam abhyupagamyate, astu dravyaṃ śabdaḥ sa tu nityo 'thānitya iti? dravyasya sato nityatānityatā vā tadviśeṣaḥ parīkṣyate, so 'bhyupagamasiddhāntaḥ svabuddhyatiśayacikhyāpayiṣayā parabuddhyavajñānāc ca pravartata iti//31//
children.translated_text: Where a certain class of objects is accepted without examination — for instance, 'let substance exist; [let] sound [be a substance]; but is it eternal or non-eternal?' — the eternality or non-eternality of the accepted substance, being its particular [aspect], is examined; that is the <s>abhyupagama-siddhānta</s>. It is undertaken out of a desire to display the superiority of one's own intellect and out of disregard for the intellect of another. //31//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 32
Now, the members (<s>avayavas</s>) —
Thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>), reason (<s>hetu</s>), example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>), application (<s>upanaya</s>), and conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>) are the members. // 1.1.32 //

children.text: daśāvayavān eke naiyāyikā vākye sañcakṣate, jijñāsā saṃśayaḥ śakyaprāptiḥ prayojanaṃ saṃśayavyudāsa iti, te kasmān nocyanta iti/ tatrāpratīyamāne 'rthe pratyayārthasya pravartikā jijñāsā/
children.translated_text: Some <s>Naiyāyikas</s> enumerate ten members in a [syllogistic] statement: desire to know (<s>jijñāsā</s>), doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>), possibility of attainment (<s>śakyaprāpti</s>), purpose (<s>prayojana</s>), and removal of doubt (<s>saṃśayavyudāsa</s>). Why are these not included? Among those, <s>jijñāsā</s> (desire to know) is [that which,] when an object is not [yet] understood, prompts [one] toward the understanding of the object.

children.text: apratīyamānam arthaṃ kasmāj jijñāsate? taṃ tattvato jñātaṃ hāsyāmi vopādāsya upekṣiṣye veti/ tā etā hānopādānopekṣābuddhayas tattvajñānasyārthaṣ tadartham(corr.; -rthaḥ, stadartham, ed.) ayaṃ jijñāsate/ sā khalv ayam asādhanam arthasyeti/ jijñāsādhiṣṭhānaṃ saṃśayaś ca vyāhatadharmopasaṅghātāt tattvajñāne pratyāsannaḥ, vyāhatayor hi dharmayor anyataratattvaṃ bhavitum arhatīti/ sa pṛthag upadiṣṭo 'py asādhanam arthasyeti/ pramātuḥ pramāṇāni prameyādhigamārthāni, sā śakyaprāptir na sādhakasya vākyasya bhāgena yujyate pratijñādivad iti/ prayojanaṃ tattvāvadhāraṇam arthasādhakasya vākyasya phalaṃ naikadeśa iti/ saṃśayavyudāsaḥ pratipakṣopavarṇanaṃ tatpratiṣedhena tattvajñānābhyanujñānārtham, na tv ayaṃ sādhakavākyaikadeśa iti/ prakaraṇe tu jijñāsādayaḥ samarthā avadhāraṇīyārthopakārāt/
children.translated_text: Why does one who does not understand an object desire to know it? [Thinking:] 'Having truly known it, I shall either abandon it, adopt it, or disregard it.' These cognitions of abandonment, adoption, and disregard are the purpose of true knowledge; for their sake, one desires to know. That [desire to know], however, is not a means for [establishing] the object. Doubt, which is the basis of the desire to know, being a conjunction of contradictory properties, is close to true knowledge — for the truth of either of the two contradictory properties is possible. Though separately taught, it too is not a means for [establishing] the object. The means of valid knowledge belonging to the knower serve the purpose of ascertaining the object to be known; that possibility of attainment (<s>śakyaprāpti</s>) does not function as a part of the probative statement, like the thesis and so forth. <s>Prayojana</s> (purpose) is the ascertainment of truth — the fruit of the probative statement, not a constituent part. The removal of doubt (<s>saṃśayavyudāsa</s>) is the description of the opposing view for the purpose of sanctioning true knowledge through its refutation; but this [too] is not a constituent part of the probative statement. In a topic [of debate], however, the desire to know and the rest are efficacious, because of their usefulness for the object to be ascertained.
[p. break]

children.text: tattvārthasādhakabhāvāt tu pratijñādayaḥ sādhakavākyasya bhāgā ekadeśā avayavā iti// 32 //
children.translated_text: But the thesis and the rest, because of their nature as that which establishes the truth of an object, are portions — constituent parts — members of the probative statement. //32//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 33
Now, as these are severally distinguished —
The statement of what is to be proved is the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>). // 1.1.33 //

children.text: prajñāpanīyena dharmeṇa dharmiṇo viśiṣṭasya parigrahavacanaṃ pratijñā sādhyanirdeśaḥ anityaḥ śabda iti//33//
children.translated_text: A statement of acceptance (<s>parigrahavacana</s>) of the property-possessor (<s>dharmin</s>) qualified by the property to be made known (<s>prajñāpanīya dharma</s>) is the thesis — the statement of what is to be proved: 'Sound is non-eternal.' //33//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 34
That which proves what is to be proved, by virtue of similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) with the example, is the reason (<s>hetu</s>). // 1.1.34 //

children.text: udāharaṇena sāmānyāt sādhyasya dharmasya sādhanaṃ prajñāpanaṃ hetuḥ, sādhye pratisandhāya dharmam udāharaṇe ca pratisandhāya tasya sādhanatāvacanaṃ hetuḥ utpattidharmakatvād iti/
children.translated_text: The proof (<s>sādhana</s>) — the making known (<s>prajñāpana</s>) — of the property to be proved, through the commonality with the example, is the reason. Connecting the property with what is to be proved and also connecting it with the example — the statement of its being a proof is the reason: 'because of having the nature of being originated.'
[p. break]
What has the nature of origination has been seen to be non-eternal. //34//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 35

children.text: kim etāvad dhetulakṣaṇam iti? nety ucyate/ kiṃ tarhi?
children.translated_text: Is this the entire definition of the reason? No, it is said. What then?
Likewise through dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>). // 1.1.35 //

children.text: udāharaṇavaidharmyāc ca sādhyasādhanaṃ hetuḥ/ katham? anityaḥ śabda utpattidharmakatvāt, anutpattidharmakaṃ nityaṃ yathātmādidravyam iti//35//
children.translated_text: The proof of what is to be proved through dissimilarity with the example is also the reason. How? 'Sound is non-eternal, because of having the nature of origination; what does not have the nature of origination is eternal, like the self and other [eternal] substances.' //35//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 36
A well-known instance (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) that, because of similarity with what is to be proved, possesses its properties — that is the example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>). // 1.1.36 //

children.text: sādhyena sādharmyaṃ samānadharmatā/ sādhyasādharmyāt kāraṇāt taddharmabhāvī dṛṣṭānta iti/
children.translated_text: Similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) with what is to be proved is having a common property (<s>samānadharmatā</s>). Because of similarity with what is to be proved, the well-known instance possessing its property is the example.

children.text: tasya dharmas taddharmaḥ, tasya — sādhyasya/ sādhyaṃ ca dvividhaṃ dharmiviśiṣṭo vā dharmaḥ śabdasyānityatvam, dharmaviśiṣṭo vā dharmy anityaḥ śabda iti/ ihottaraṃ tadgrahaṇena gṛhyata iti/ kasmāt? pṛthagdharmavacanāt/ tasya dharmas taddharmas tasya bhāvas taddharmabhāvaḥ sa yasmin dṛṣṭānte vartate sa dṛṣṭāntaḥ sādhyasādharmyād utpattidharmakatvat taddharmabhāvī bhavati, sa codāharaṇam iṣyate/ tatra yad utpadyate tad utpattidharmakam/ tac ca bhūtvā na bhavati ātmānaṃ jahāti nirudhyata ity anityam/ evam utpattidharmakatvaṃ sādhanam anityatvaṃ sādhyam/
children.translated_text: Its property is 'taddharma' — 'its' refers to: what is to be proved. And what is to be proved is twofold: either the property qualified by the property-possessor — the non-eternality of sound; or the property-possessor qualified by the property — 'non-eternal sound.' Here, the latter is taken by the pronoun 'tat.' Why? Because of the separate mention of 'property.' Its property is <s>taddharma</s>; its state (<s>bhāva</s>) is <s>taddharmabhāva</s>; that in which this [state] obtains is the well-known instance (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>); that instance, because of similarity with what is to be proved — namely, because of having the nature of being originated — possesses its property, and it is accepted as the example. Therein, what is originated has the nature of origination. And that, having come into being, ceases to be — it abandons itself, it ceases — [and so] is non-eternal. Thus, having the nature of origination is the proof (<s>sādhana</s>); non-eternality is what is to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>).

children.text: so 'yam ekasmin dvayor dharmayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvaḥ sādharmyād vyavasthita upalabhyate, taṃ dṛṣṭānta upalabhamānaḥ śabde 'py anuminoti — śabdo 'py utpattidharmakatvād anityaḥ sthālyādivad iti, udāhriyate 'nena dharmayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāva ity udāharaṇam//36//
children.translated_text: This relation of being that which is to be proved and its proof, [pertaining to] two properties in one [thing], is seen to be established through similarity in the example; and perceiving this in the example, one infers also in [the case of] sound — 'Sound too is non-eternal because of having the nature of origination, like a pot and so forth.' It is through this that the relation of the two properties — what is to be proved and its proof — is illustrated; hence it is the example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>). //36//
Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
Or the reverse of that, through contrariety. // 1.1.37 //

children.text: dṛṣṭānta udāharaṇam iti prakṛtam/ sādhyavaidharmyād ataddharmabhāvī dṛṣṭānta udāharaṇam iti/ anityaḥ śabda utpattidharmakatvāt anutpattidharmakaṃ nityam ātmādi, so 'yam ātmādir dṛṭṣṭāntaḥ sādhyavaidharmyād anutpattidharmakatvād ataddharmabhāvī — yo 'sau sādhyasya dharmo 'nityatvaṃ sa tasmin na bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: 'A well-known instance is an example' is the subject at hand. A well-known instance that, because of dissimilarity with what is to be proved, does not possess its properties — that is the [negative] example. 'Sound is non-eternal, because of having the nature of origination; what does not have the nature of origination is eternal, like the self and other substances.' This self and so forth is the example; because of dissimilarity with what is to be proved — because of not having the nature of origination — it does not possess its property: the property of what is to be proved, namely non-eternality, does not obtain in it.

children.text: atrātmādau dṛṣṭānta utpattidharmakatvasyābhāvād anityatvaṃ na bhavatīty upalabhamānaḥ śabde viparyayam anuminoty utpattidharmakatvasya bhāvād anityaḥ śabda iti/ sādharmyoktasya hetoḥ sādhyasādharmyāt taddharmabhāvī dṛṣṭānta udāharaṇam/ vaidharmyoktasya hetoḥ sādhyavaidharmyād ataddharmabhāvī dṛṣṭānta udāharaṇam/
children.translated_text: Here, perceiving in the self and so forth — the example — that due to the absence of the nature of origination, non-eternality does not obtain, one infers the contrary in sound: because of the presence of the nature of origination, sound is non-eternal. For a reason stated through similarity, the example is a well-known instance that, because of similarity with what is to be proved, possesses its properties. For a reason stated through dissimilarity, the example is a well-known instance that, because of dissimilarity with what is to be proved, does not possess its properties.

children.text: pūrvasmin dṛṣṭānte yau tau dharmau sādhyasādhanabhūtau paśyati sādhye 'pi tayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvam anuminoti/ uttarasmin dṛṣṭānte tayor dharmayor ekasyābhāvād itarasyābhāvaṃ paśyati tayor ekasya bhāvād itarasya bhāvaṃ sādhye 'numinotīti/ tad etad dhetuvābhāseṣu na sambhavatīty ahetavo hetvābhāsāḥ/
children.translated_text: In the affirmative <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), one observes the two properties that constitute the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) and <s>sādhana</s> (probans), and infers their relationship of probandum-and-probans in the <s>sādhya</s> as well. In the negative <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, one observes that from the absence of one of those two properties follows the absence of the other, and infers in the <s>sādhya</s> that from the presence of the one follows the presence of the other. This does not obtain in the case of <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons) — therefore the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are pseudo-reasons.

children.text: tad idaṃ hetūdāharaṇayoḥ sāmarthyaṃ paramasūkṣmaṃ duḥkhabodhaṃ paṇḍitarūpavedanīyam iti//37//
children.translated_text: This capacity of the <s>hetu</s> (reason) and <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example) is supremely subtle, difficult to comprehend, and to be understood only by the wise.
[Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 38]

children.text: udāharaṇāpekṣas tathety upasaṃhāro na tatheti vā sādhyasyopanayaḥ // 1.1.38 //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.38: The application (<s>upanaya</s>) of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is the corroborative restatement dependent on the example, as 'so it is' or 'it is not so.'

children.text: udāharaṇāpekṣa udāharaṇatantra udāharaṇavaśaḥ/ vaśaḥ sāmarthyam/ sādhyasādharmyayukte udāharaṇe sthālyādi dravyam utpattidharmakam anityaṃ dṛṣṭam, tathā śabda utpattidharmaka iti sādhyasya śabdasyotpattidharmakatvam upasaṃhriyate/
children.translated_text: 'Dependent on the example' means governed by the example, subject to the capacity of the example. When the example is conjoined with similarity to the <s>sādhya</s>: a substance such as a pot is seen to possess the property of being produced and to be impermanent; similarly, sound possesses the property of being produced — thus the property of being produced is applied to sound, which is the <s>sādhya</s>.

children.text: sādhyavaidharmyayukte punar udāharaṇa ātmādi dravyam anutpattidharmakaṃ nityaṃ dṛṣṭam, na ca tathā śabda iti, anutpattidharmakatvasyopasaṃhārarapratiṣedhenotpattidharmakatvam upasaṃhriyate/ tad idam upasaṃhāradvaitam udāharaṇadvaitād bhavati/ upasaṃhriyate 'neneti copasaṃhāro veditavya iti//38//
children.translated_text: When the example is conjoined with dissimilarity from the <s>sādhya</s>: a substance such as the <s>ātman</s> (self) is seen to be without the property of being produced and to be permanent; but sound is not like that — by the negation of the application of the property of not-being-produced, the property of being produced is applied. Thus this twofold application arises from the twofold example. And <s>upasaṃhāra</s> (application) should be understood as 'that by which one applies.'
[Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 39]

children.text: dvividhasya punar hetor dvividhasya codāharaṇasyopasaṃhāradvaite ca samānam —
children.translated_text: And given the twofold <s>hetu</s> (reason) and twofold <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example), and the twofold application, the same holds —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.39: The restatement of the <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis) on the basis of the <s>hetu</s> (reason) is <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion).

children.text: sādharmyokte vā vaidharmyokte vā yathodāharaṇam upasaṃhriyate, tasmād utpattidharmakatvād anityaḥ śabda iti nigamanam — nigamyante 'neneti pratijñāhetūdāharaṇopanayā ekatreti nigamanam/ nigamyante — samarthyante — sambadhyante/ tatra sādharmokte tāvad dhetau vākyam anityaḥ śabda iti pratijñā/ utpattidharmakatvād iti hetuḥ/ utpattidharmakaṃ sthālyādi dravyam anityam ity udāharaṇam/ tathā cotpattidharmakaḥ śabda ity upanayaḥ/ tasmād utpattidharmakatvād anityaḥ śabda iti nigamanam/ vaidharmyokte 'py anityaḥ śabda utpattidharmakatvāt,
children.translated_text: Whether the application is made in accordance with the example stated by similarity or by dissimilarity — 'therefore, because of possessing the property of being produced, sound is impermanent' — this is <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion). 'That by which they are concluded' — the <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis), <s>hetu</s> (reason), <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example), and <s>upanaya</s> (application) are brought together into one — this is <s>nigamana</s>. 'Concluded' means: established, connected. Now, in the case where the reason is stated by similarity, the statement is: 'Sound is impermanent' — this is the <s>pratijñā</s>. 'Because of possessing the property of being produced' — this is the <s>hetu</s>. 'A substance such as a pot, possessing the property of being produced, is impermanent' — this is the <s>udāharaṇa</s>. 'And sound likewise possesses the property of being produced' — this is the <s>upanaya</s>. 'Therefore, because of possessing the property of being produced, sound is impermanent' — this is the <s>nigamana</s>. In the case stated by dissimilarity too: 'Sound is impermanent, because of possessing the property of being produced;

children.text:
anutpattidharmakam ātmādi dravyaṃ nityaṃ dṛṣṭam, na ca tathānutpattidharmakaḥ śabdaḥ tasmād utpattidharmakatvād anityaḥ śabda iti/
avayavasamudāye ca vākye sambhūyetaretarābhisambandhāt pramāṇāny arthān sādhayantīti/ sambhavas tāvat śabdaviṣayā pratijñā, āptopadeśasya pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ pratisandhānād anṛṣeś ca svātantryānupapatteḥ/ anumānaṃ hetuḥ, udāharaṇe sādṛśyapratipatteḥ/ tac codāharaṇabhāṣye vyākhyātam/ pratyakṣaviṣayam udāharaṇaṃ dṛṣṭenādṛṣṭasiddheḥ/ upamānam upanayaḥ tathety upasaṃhārāt, na ca tatheti vopamānadharmapratiṣedehe viparītadharmopasaṃhārasiddheḥ/ sarveṣām ekārthapratipattau sāmarthyapradarśanaṃ nigamanam iti/
itaretarābhisambandho 'pi — asatyāṃ pratijñāyām anāśrayā hetvādayo na pravarteran/
children.translated_text:
a substance such as the <s>ātman</s>, not possessing the property of being produced, is seen to be permanent; but sound is not likewise without the property of being produced — therefore, because of possessing the property of being produced, sound is impermanent.'
And when the members are combined in a single statement, the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) establish their objects through mutual connection. Thus: the <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis) has <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) as its domain, because <s>āptopadeśa</s> (authoritative instruction) is corroborated by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference), and because an unreliable person cannot have independence. <s>Anumāna</s> (inference) is the <s>hetu</s> (reason). The <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example) involves perception of similarity, and that has been explained in the commentary on the example. <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is the domain of the <s>udāharaṇa</s>, since the unseen is established through the seen. <s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) is the <s>upanaya</s> (application), because of the corroborative restatement 'so it is,' and because in the negation of the property of comparison with 'it is not so,' the application of the opposite property is established. The <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion) demonstrates the capacity of all members for the cognition of a single object.
The mutual connection is also this: without the <s>pratijñā</s>, the <s>hetu</s> and the rest, having no foundation, would not operate.

children.text:
asati hetau kasya sādhanabhāvaḥ pradarśyeta/ udāharaṇe sādhye ca kasyopasaṃhāraḥ syāt kasya cāpadeśāt pratijñāyāḥ punarvacanaṃ nigamanaṃ syād iti/ asaty udāharaṇe kena sādharmyaṃ vaidharmyaṃ vā sādhyasādhanam upādīyeta, kasya vā sādharmyavaśād upasaṃhāraḥ pravarteta/ upanayaṃ cāntareṇa sādhye 'nupasaṃhṛtaḥ sādhako dharmo nārthaṃ sādhayet/ nigamanābhāve cānabhiyuktasambandhānāṃ pratijñādīnām ekārthena pravartanaṃ tatheti pratipādanaṃ kasyeti/
athāvayavārthaḥ — sādhyasya dharmasya dharmiṇā sambandhopādānaṃ pratijñārthaḥ/ udāharaṇena samānasya viparītasya vā sādhyasya dharmasya sādhakabhāvavacanaṃ hetvarthaḥ/ dharmayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvapradarśanam ekatrodāharaṇārthaḥ/ sādhanabhūtasya dharmasya sādhyena dharmeṇa sāmānādhikaraṇyopapādanam upanayārthaḥ/ udāharaṇasthayor dharmayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvopapattau sādhye viparītaprasaṅgapratiṣedhārthaṃ nigamanam/ nacaitasyāṃ hetūdāharaṇapariśuddhau satyāṃ sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ pratyavasthānasya vikalyāj jātinigrahasthānabahutvaṃ prakramate/ avyavasthāpya khalu dharmayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvam udāharaṇe jātivādī pratyavatiṣṭhate/ vyavasthite tu khalu dharmayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāve dṛṣṭāntasthe gṛhyamāṇe sādhanabhūtasya dharmasya hetutvenopādānaṃ na sādharmyamātrasya na vaidharmyamātrasya veti// 39 //
children.translated_text:
Without the <s>hetu</s> (reason), whose status as a means of proof would be demonstrated? Without the <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example) and the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum), of what would there be application, and on the basis of what would there be the restatement of the <s>pratijñā</s> as <s>nigamana</s>? Without the <s>udāharaṇa</s>, by what would similarity or dissimilarity with the probandum-and-probans be established, or by virtue of what similarity would the application proceed? And without the <s>upanaya</s> (application), the probative property, not having been applied to the <s>sādhya</s>, would not prove the object. And in the absence of <s>nigamana</s>, how would the uncoordinated <s>pratijñā</s> and the rest be directed toward a single object and established as 'so it is'?
Now the meaning of the members: the purpose of the <s>pratijñā</s> is to predicate the connection of a property with a property-bearer that is to be proved. The purpose of the <s>hetu</s> is to state the probative character of a property that is the same as or opposite to the <s>sādhya</s> by means of the example. The purpose of the <s>udāharaṇa</s> is to demonstrate in one place the relationship of probandum and probans between the two properties. The purpose of the <s>upanaya</s> is to establish the co-location of the probative property with the property that is the probandum. The <s>nigamana</s> serves to preclude the contingency of the opposite when the probandum-probans relationship between the two properties in the example is established. And when there is this purity of <s>hetu</s> and <s>udāharaṇa</s> through both similarity and dissimilarity, the failure to maintain one's position does not give rise to the multiplicity of <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinders) and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat). For it is only when the probandum-probans relationship of the properties has not been established in the example that the <s>jāti</s>-debater objects. But when the probandum-probans relationship of the properties has been established and is grasped as residing in the example, one employs the probative property as a <s>hetu</s>, not mere similarity alone nor mere dissimilarity alone.
[Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 40]

children.text: ata ūrdhvaṃ tarko lakṣaṇīya ity athedam ucyate —
children.translated_text: Next, <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) is to be defined — and so this is stated:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.40: <s>Tarka</s> (reasoning) is deliberation (<s>ūha</s>) for the purpose of knowing reality, regarding an object whose true nature is not known, through the cogency of reasons.

children.text: avijñāyamānatattve 'rthe jijñāsā tāvaj jāyate jānīyemam artham iti/ atha jijñāsitasya vastuno vyāhatau dharmau vibhāgena vimṛśati —
children.translated_text: When the true nature of an object is not known, there arises first the desire to know: 'I should know this object.' Then, regarding the object one desires to know, one separately examines its two contradictory properties —

children.text:
kiṃsvid ittham āhosvin nettham iti/ vimṛśyamānayor dharmayor ekaṃ kāraṇopapattyānujānāti, sambhavaty asmin kāraṇaṃ pramāṇaṃ hetur iti kāraṇopapattyā syād evam etan netarad iti/
tatra nidarśanam — yo 'yaṃ jñātā jñātavyam arthaṃ jānīte taṃ tattvato jānīyeti jijñāsā/ sa kim utpattidharmako 'thānutpattidharmaka iti vimarśaḥ/ vimṛśyamāne 'vijñātatatte 'rthe yasya dharmasyābhyanujñākāraṇam upapadyate tam anujānāti/ yady ayam anutpattidharmakaḥ, tataḥ svakṛtasya karmaṇaḥ phalam anubhavati jñātā, duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣamithyājñānānām uttaram uttaraṃ pūrvasya pūrvasya kāraṇam, uttarottarāpāye tadanantarāpāyād apavarga iti syātāṃ saṃsārāpavargau/
children.translated_text:
'Is it thus, or is it not thus?' Of the two properties being examined, one approves one through the cogency of reasons — 'a reason, that is, a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) or cause, is applicable here' — and through that cogency of reasons concludes 'it must be thus and not otherwise.'
Here is an illustration: regarding the knower who knows the object to be known, there arises the desire to know: 'I should know him as he truly is.' 'Is he produced or unproduced?' — this is the examination. When the true nature of the object being examined is not known, one approves that property for which there is a supporting reason. If this knower is unproduced, then the knower experiences the fruit of his own actions; suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge — each successive one is the cause of the preceding one; and through the cessation of each successive one, the cessation of the one immediately preceding follows, leading to <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) — thus both <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) and <s>apavarga</s> would be possible.

children.text:
utpattidharmake jñātari punar na syātām/ utpannaḥ khalu jñātā dehendriyabuddhivedanābhiḥ sambadhyata iti nāsyedaṃ svakṛtasya karmaṇaḥ phalam utpannaś ca bhūtvā na bhavatīti tasyāvidyamānasya niruddhasya vā svakṛtakarmaṇaḥ phalopabhogo nāsti/ tad evam ekasyānekaśarīrayogaḥ śarīraviyogaś cātyantaṃ na syād iti yatra kāraṇam anupapadyamānaṃ paśyati tan nānujānāti/ so 'yam evaṃlakṣaṇa ūhas tarka ity ucyate/
kathaṃ punar ayaṃ tattvajñānārtho na tattvajñānam eveti? anavadhāraṇāt/ anujānāty ayam ekataraṃ dharmaṃ kāraṇopapattyā, na tv avadhārayati na vyavasyati na niścinoti evam evedam iti/ kathaṃ tattvajñānārtha iti? tattvajñānaviṣayābhyanujñālakṣaṇānugrahabhāvitāt prasannād anatarapramāṇasāmarthyāt tattvajñānam utpadyata ity evaṃ tattvajñānārtha iti/
so 'yaṃ tarkaḥ pramāṇāni pratisandadhānaḥ pramāṇābhyanujñānāt pramāṇasahito vāde 'padiṣṭa ity avijñātatattvam anujānāti/
children.translated_text:
But if the knower is produced, these two would not be possible. For a produced knower becomes connected with body, senses, intellect, and sensations — thus 'this is the fruit of his own actions' would not hold; and being produced, he ceases to exist — therefore for such a non-existent or ceased being, there is no experience of the fruit of his own actions. Thus the conjunction of one self with many bodies and the separation from the body would ultimately not be possible — where one sees that the reason does not apply, one does not approve that. This deliberation of such character is called <s>tarka</s> (reasoning).
But how is this 'for the purpose of knowing reality' rather than being knowledge of reality itself? Because it does not determine with certainty. It approves one property through the cogency of reasons, but it does not determine, does not ascertain, does not conclude that 'it is definitely thus.' How then is it 'for the purpose of knowing reality'? Because knowledge of reality arises from the subsequent capacity of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that is facilitated by the approval, which has the character of favoring the object of true knowledge, thus it is 'for the purpose of knowing reality.'
This <s>tarka</s>, connecting with the <s>pramāṇas</s>, is sanctioned by the <s>pramāṇas</s> and has been taught as combined with <s>pramāṇa</s> in the context of <s>vāda</s> (debate), and thus it approves that whose true nature is unknown.

children.text: yathā so 'rho bhavati tasya tathābhāvaḥ tattvam, aviparyayo yāthātathyam//40//
children.translated_text: The true state of that object as it really is — that is <s>tattva</s> (reality); non-reversal, accuracy.
[Chapter 1, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 41]
And regarding this subject of <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.41: <s>Nirṇaya</s> (ascertainment) is the determination of an object through deliberation by means of the thesis and counter-thesis.

children.text:
sthāpanā sādhanam, pratiṣedha upālambhaḥ/ tau sādhanopālambhau pakṣapratipakṣāśrayau vyatiṣaktāv anubandhena pravartamānau pakṣapratipakṣāv ity ucyete/ tayor anyatarasya nivṛttir ekatarasyāvasthānam avaśyambhāvi, yasyāvasthānaṃ tasyārthāvadhāraṇaṃ nirṇayaḥ/
nedaṃ pakṣapratipakṣābhyām arthāvadhāraṇaṃ sambhavatīti — eko hi pratijñātam arthaṃ hetutaḥ sthāpayati pratiṣiddhaṃ coddharati dvitīyasya/ dvitīyena sthāpanāhetuḥ pratiṣidhyate tasyaiva pratiṣedhahetuś coddhriyate sa nivartate/
children.translated_text:
<s>Sthāpanā</s> (establishment) is proof; <s>pratiṣedha</s> (refutation) is objection. These two — proof and objection — resting on the thesis and counter-thesis, operating in continuous engagement, are called the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) and counter-thesis (<s>pratipakṣa</s>). The cessation of one and the standing of the other is inevitable; the determination of the object through that which stands is <s>nirṇaya</s> (ascertainment).
'This determination of an object through thesis and counter-thesis is not possible' — [one might object]. But one person establishes the proposed object on the basis of a reason and also refutes the reason of the second person's establishment. The second person's reason for establishment is refuted, and the reason for his own refutation is also overturned — he is defeated.

children.text:
tasya nivṛttau yo 'vatiṣṭhate tenārthāvadhāraṇaṃ nirṇayaḥ/
ubhābhyām evārthāvadhāraṇam ity āha/ kayā yuktyā? ekasya sambhavo dvitīyasyāsambhavaḥ/ tāv etau sambhavāsambhavau vimarśaṃ saha nivarttayataḥ — ubhayasambhave ubhayāsambhave vānivṛtto vimarśa iti/ vimṛśyeti vimarśaṃ kṛtvā/ so 'yaṃ vimarśaḥ pakṣapratipakṣāv avadyotya nyāyaṃ pravartayatīty upādīyata iti/ etac ca viruddhayor ekadharmisthayor boddhavyam/ yatra tu dharmisāmānyagatau viruddhau dharmau hetutaḥ sambhavataḥ tatra samuccayaḥ, hetuto 'rthasya tathābhāvopapatteḥ/ yathā — kriyāvad dravyam iti lakṣaṇavacane yasya dravyasya kriyāyogo hetutaḥ sambhavati tat kriyāvat, yasya na sambhavati tad akriyam iti/ ekadharmisthayoś ca viruddhayor dharmayor ayugapadbhāvinoḥ kālavikalpaḥ/ yathā — tad eva dravyaṃ kriyāyuktaṃ kriyāvat, anutpannoparatakriyaṃ punar akriyam iti/
na cāyaṃ nirṇaye niyamo vimṛśyaiva pakṣapratipakṣābhyām arthāvadhāraṇaṃ nirṇaya iti, kiṃ tv indriyārthasannikarṣotpannapratyakṣe 'rthāvadhāraṇaṃ nirṇaya iti, parīkṣāviṣaye tu vimṛśya pakṣapratipakṣābhyām arthāvadhāraṇaṃ nirṇayaḥ/ vāde śāstre ca vimarśavarjam// 41 //
children.translated_text:
Upon his defeat, the one who stands — through him the determination of the object is <s>nirṇaya</s> (ascertainment).
He says: the determination of the object is through both. By what logic? The possibility of one entails the impossibility of the other. These two — possibility and impossibility — together terminate the doubt; for if both were possible or both impossible, the doubt would not be resolved. 'Having deliberated' means having conducted the examination. This examination, illuminating both the thesis and counter-thesis, sets the <s>nyāya</s> (logical method) in motion — therefore it is employed. And this should be understood regarding two contradictory properties residing in a single subject. But where two contradictory properties belonging to a general class of subjects are both established through reasons, there is a combination, since the object's being so is established through reasons. For example, in the definitional statement 'a substance possesses activity,' whatever substance for which connection with activity is established through reasons is 'active,' and whatever substance for which it is not established is 'inactive.' And regarding two contradictory properties residing in a single subject that cannot coexist simultaneously, there is a temporal distinction. For example, the very same substance, when conjoined with activity, is 'active,' and when its activity has not yet arisen or has ceased, it is 'inactive.'
But <s>nirṇaya</s> is not restricted to this — that ascertainment is determination of an object only through deliberation by means of thesis and counter-thesis. Rather, in the case of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) arising from contact of the senses with the object, the determination of the object is also <s>nirṇaya</s>. But in matters requiring investigation, <s>nirṇaya</s> is determination through deliberation by means of thesis and counter-thesis. In <s>vāda</s> (debate) and in <s>śāstra</s> (treatise), it is without deliberation.
[Chapter 1, Section 2]
[Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 1]
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> of <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
Second section.

children.text: tisraḥ kathā bhavanti — vādo jalpo vitaṇḍā ceti/ tāsām —
children.translated_text: There are three kinds of discourse: <s>vāda</s> (debate), <s>jalpa</s> (disputation), and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil). Of these —

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.2.1: <s>Vāda</s> (debate) is the adoption of a thesis and counter-thesis that is supported by <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), <s>tarka</s> (reasoning), and proof and refutation, that is not contradictory to any established doctrine (<s>siddhānta</s>), and that is furnished with the five members (<s>pañcāvayava</s>).

children.text: ekādhikaraṇasthau viruddhau dharmau pakṣapratipakṣau pratyanīkabhāvāt, asty ātmā nāsty ātmeti/
children.translated_text: Two contradictory properties residing in a single subject are the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) and counter-thesis (<s>pratipakṣa</s>), because of their opposition — as in 'the <s>ātman</s> (self) exists' and 'the <s>ātman</s> does not exist.'

children.text: nānādhikaraṇasthau viruddhau na pakṣapratipakṣau, yathā — nitya ātmā anityā buddhir iti/ parigraho 'bhyupagamavyavasthā/ so 'yam pakṣapratipakṣaparigraho vādaḥ/ tasya viśeṣanaṃ pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambhaḥ, pramāṇais tarkeṇa ca sādhanam upālambhaś cāsmin kriyata iti/ sādhanaṃ sthāpanā/ upālambhaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ tau sādhanopālambhāv ubhayor api pakṣayor vyatiṣaktāv anubaddhau ca yāvad eko nivṛtta ekataro vyavasthita iti nivṛttasyopālambho vyavasthitasya sādhanam iti/
children.translated_text: Two contradictory (properties) residing in different substrates are not a <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis) and <s>pratipakṣa</s> (counter-thesis), as for example — 'the <s>ātman</s> (self) is eternal' and 'cognition is non-eternal.' <s>Parigraha</s> (acceptance) is the determination of commitment. This acceptance of thesis and counter-thesis constitutes <s>vāda</s> (debate). Its distinguishing feature is that proof and refutation are carried out by means of <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) and <s>tarka</s> (reasoning). <s>Sādhana</s> (proof) is establishment. <s>Upālambha</s> (refutation) is negation. These two — proof and refutation — are intertwined and connected with both theses, until one is abandoned and the other is established; then refutation belongs to the abandoned thesis and proof to the established one.

children.text: jalpe nigrahasthānaviniyogād vāde tatpratiṣedhaḥ/ pratiṣedhe kasyacid abhyanujñānārthaṃ siddhāntāviruddha iti vacanam/
children.translated_text: In <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling), there is application of <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat); in <s>vāda</s> (debate), that is prohibited. To indicate the permission of certain things, the expression 'not contradicting the <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine)' is used.
'Having accepted a <s>siddhānta</s>, that which contradicts it is <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory)' —

children.text: iti hetvābhāsasya nigrahasthānasyābhyanujñā vāde/ pañcāvayavopapanna iti
children.translated_text: this is the permission (in <s>vāda</s>) of (recognizing) a <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reason) as a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat). 'Equipped with five members' —
'deficient' means lacking even one member,
'excessive' means having more than the <s>hetu</s> (reason) and <s>udāharaṇa</s> (example) —

children.text: iti caitayor abhyanujñānārtham iti/ avayaveṣu pramānatarkāntarbhāve pṛthak pramāṇatarkagrahaṇaṃ sādhanopālambhavyatiṣaṅgajñāpanārtham/ anyathobhāv api pakṣau sthāpanāpravṛttau vāda iti syāt/
children.translated_text: these two are stated for the purpose of permitting them. When <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>tarka</s> are included within the members (of a syllogism), the separate mention of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>tarka</s> is for the purpose of indicating their interconnection with proof and refutation. Otherwise, both theses being engaged in establishment would constitute <s>vāda</s>.

children.text: antareṇāpi cāvayavasambandhaṃ pramāṇāny arthaṃ sādhayantīti dṛṣṭam, tenāpi kalpena sādhanopālambhau vāde bhavata iti jñāpayati/
children.translated_text: And it is observed that <s>pramāṇas</s> establish a matter even without the arrangement of formal members; by that method too, proof and refutation occur in <s>vāda</s> — this is what is indicated.
'<s>Jalpa</s> (wrangling) is proof and refutation by means of <s>chala</s> (quibble), <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinder), and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat)' —

children.text: iti vacanād vinigraho jalpa iti mā vijñāyi, chalajātinigrahasthānasādhanopālambha eva jalpaḥ pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambho vād eveti mā vijñāyīty evamarthaṃ pṛthak pramānatarkagrahaṇam iti// 1 //
children.translated_text: lest it be understood from this statement that <s>jalpa</s> is merely refutation, (the sūtra clarifies that) <s>jalpa</s> is specifically proof and refutation through <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>; and lest it be understood that proof and refutation through <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>tarka</s> constitutes only <s>vāda</s> — for this purpose, the separate mention of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>tarka</s> is made. // 1 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 2

<s>Jalpa</s> (wrangling) is that which, being equipped as described above, involves proof and refutation through <s>chala</s> (quibble), <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinder), and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat). // 1.2.2 //

children.text: yathoktopapanna iti, pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambhaḥ siddhāntāviruddhaḥ pañcāvayavopapannaḥ pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahaḥ/ chalajātinigrahasthānasādhanopālambha iti, chalajātinigrahasthānaiḥ sādhanam upālambhaś cāsmin kriyata iti evaṃviśeṣaṇo jalpaḥ/
children.translated_text: 'Equipped as described above' means: proof and refutation through <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>tarka</s>, not contradicting the <s>siddhānta</s>, equipped with five members, and involving the acceptance of thesis and counter-thesis. 'Proof and refutation through <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>' means: that in which proof and refutation are carried out by means of <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> — thus qualified, it is <s>jalpa</s>.

children.text: na khalu vai chalajātinigrahasthānaiḥ sādhanaṃ kasyacid arthasya sambhavati, pratiṣedhārthataivaiṣāṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇe viśeṣalakṣaṇe ca śrūyate —
children.translated_text: Indeed, proof of any matter is not possible through <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> alone; their purpose of negation is heard both in their general definition and in their specific definitions —
'<s>Chala</s> (quibble) is the obstruction of a statement through recourse to an alternative meaning' —
thus;
'<s>Jāti</s> (futile rejoinder) is a counter-argument based on similarity and dissimilarity' —
'Misunderstanding and non-understanding constitute <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat)' —
thus.

children.text:
viśeṣalakṣaṇeṣv api yathāsvam iti/ na caitad vijānīyāt pratiṣedhārthatayaivārthaṃ sādhayantīti, chalajātinigrahasthānopālambho jalpa ity evam apy ucyamāne vijñāyata etad iti/
pramāṇaiḥ sādhanopālambhayoś chalajātinigrahasthānānām aṅgabhāvaḥ svapakṣarakṣaṇārthatvāt/ na svatantrāṇāṃ sādhanabhāvaḥ — yat tat pramāṇair arthasya sādhanaṃ tatra chalajātinigrahasthānānām aṅgabhāvo rakṣaṇārthatvāt/ tāni hi prayujyamānāni parapakṣavighātena svapakṣaṃ rakṣanti/
children.translated_text: And in the specific definitions too, each respectively. One should not understand this as meaning that they prove a matter solely through the purpose of negation; even if it were said '<s>jalpa</s> is refutation through <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>,' this would still be understood. The subsidiary status of <s>chala</s>, <s>jāti</s>, and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> in relation to proof and refutation through <s>pramāṇas</s> is because they serve to protect one's own thesis. They do not independently constitute proof — the proof of a matter through <s>pramāṇas</s> is what they serve as subsidiaries to, because their purpose is protection. For when employed, they protect one's own thesis by obstructing the opponent's thesis.
And thus it has been said:
'<s>Jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> serve to protect the ascertainment of truth, like a fence of thorny branches that protects the growth of a seed' —

children.text: iti/ yaś cāsau pramāṇaiḥ pratipakṣasyopālambhas tasya caitāni prayujyamānāni pratiṣedhavighātāt sahakārīṇi bhavanti/ tad evam aṅgībhūtanāṃ chalādīnām upādānaṃ jalpe, na svatantrāṇāṃ sādhanabhāvaḥ/ upālambhe tu svātantryam apy astīti// 2 //
children.translated_text: thus. And the refutation of the opponent's thesis through <s>pramāṇas</s> — when these (<s>chala</s> etc.) are employed alongside it, they become auxiliaries by obstructing the counter-refutation. Thus the employment of <s>chala</s> and the rest in <s>jalpa</s> is in their subsidiary capacity, not as independent means of proof. In refutation, however, they do possess independence. // 2 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 3
That (i.e., <s>jalpa</s>), devoid of the establishment of a counter-thesis, is <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil). // 1.2.3 //

children.text: sa jalpo vitaṇḍā bhavati/ kiṃviśeṣaṇaḥ? pratipakṣasthāpanayā hīnaḥ/ yau tau samānādhikaraṇau viruddhau dharmau pakṣāv ity uktaṃ tayor ekataraṃ vaitaṇḍiko na sthāpayatīti prapakṣapratiṣedhenaiva pravartata iti/
children.translated_text: That <s>jalpa</s> becomes <s>vitaṇḍā</s>. With what distinguishing feature? Devoid of the establishment of a counter-thesis. It has been said that the two contradictory properties residing in the same substrate are the two theses; of these two, the caviler does not establish one, and thus proceeds solely by negating the opponent's thesis.

children.text: astu tarhi sa pratipakṣahīno vitaṇḍā? yad vai khalu tat parapratiṣedhalakṣaṇaṃ vākyaṃ sa vaitaṇḍikasya pakṣaḥ, na tv asau sādhyaṃ kañcid arthaṃ pratijñāya sthāpayatīti/ tasmād yathānyāsam evāstv iti// 3 //
children.translated_text: Then let it be: 'That which lacks a counter-thesis is <s>vitaṇḍā</s>'? Indeed, that statement whose defining characteristic is the negation of the opponent — that itself is the thesis of the caviler; but he does not establish (it) by asserting any matter to be proved. Therefore, let it stand as originally formulated. // 3 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 4

children.text: hetulakṣaṇābhāvād ahetavo hetusāmānyād dhetuvad ābhāsamānāḥ/ ta ime —
children.translated_text: Due to the absence of the defining characteristics of a <s>hetu</s> (reason), non-reasons (<s>ahetu</s>) appear as reasons due to their general resemblance to reasons. They are as follows —

<s>Hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons) are: <s>savyabhicāra</s> (the erratic), <s>viruddha</s> (the contradictory), <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (the equivalent to the question), <s>sādhyasama</s> (the equivalent to what is to be proved), and <s>kālātīta</s> (the mistimed). // 1.2.4 //
Of these —
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
<s>Savyabhicāra</s> (the erratic) is that which is non-conclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). // 1.2.5 //

children.text: vyabhicāra ekatrāvyavasthitiḥ/ sahavyabhicāreṇa vartata iti svayabhicāraḥ/
children.translated_text: <s>Vyabhicāra</s> (deviation) is non-fixity in a single (conclusion). That which operates with deviation is <s>savyabhicāra</s>.

children.text: nidarśanam — nityaḥ śabdo 'sparśatvāt, sparśavān kumbho 'nityo dṛṣṭaḥ na ca tathā sparśavān śabdas tasmād asparśatvān nityaḥ śabda iti/
children.translated_text: Illustration — 'Sound is eternal because it is intangible; a pot, which is tangible, is observed to be non-eternal; sound is not tangible like that; therefore, being intangible, sound is eternal.'

children.text: dṛṣṭānte sparśavattvam anityatvaṃ ca dharmau na sādhyasādhanabhūtau gṛhyete sparśavāṃś cāṇur nityaś ceti/ ātmādau ca dṛṣṭānte
children.translated_text: In the example, tangibility and non-eternality are the two properties, but they are not grasped as being in a proved-prover relationship, since an atom is tangible yet eternal. And in examples such as the <s>ātman</s> (self),
'A <s>hetu</s> (reason) establishes what is to be proved through similarity with the example' —

children.text:
ity asparśatvād iti hetur nityatvaṃ vyabhicarati, asparśā buddhir anityā ceti/ evaṃ dvividhe 'pi dṛṣṭānte vyabhicārāt sādhyasādhanabhāvo nāstīti lakṣaṇābhāvād ahetur iti/
nityatvam apy eko 'nto 'nityatvam apy eko ṇta ekasminn ante vidyata iti aikāntikaḥ viparyayād anaikāntika ubhayāntavyāpakatvād iti// 5 //
children.translated_text: the reason 'because of intangibility' deviates from eternality, since cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) is intangible yet non-eternal. Thus, due to deviation in both types of examples, the proved-prover relationship does not exist; due to the absence of the defining characteristic, it is a non-reason. Eternality is one extreme, non-eternality is another extreme; that which exists at one extreme is <s>aikāntika</s> (conclusive); its opposite, being pervaded by both extremes, is <s>anaikāntika</s> (non-conclusive). // 5 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 6
That which contradicts the <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine) that has been accepted is <s>viruddha</s> (the contradictory). // 1.2.6 //

children.text: taṃ viruṇaddhīti tadvirodhy abhyupetaṃ siddhāntaṃ vyāhantīti/ yathā so 'yaṃ vikāro vyakter apaiti nityatvapratiṣedhāt —
children.translated_text: It obstructs that — it is contradictory to it — it opposes the accepted <s>siddhānta</s>. For example: 'This modification (<s>vikāra</s>) departs from manifestation (<s>vyakti</s>) because eternality is negated' —

children.text: na nityo vikāra upapadyata apeto 'pi vikāro 'sti vināśapratiṣedhāt/ so 'yaṃ nityatvapratiṣedhād iti/ hetur vyakter apeto 'pi vikāro 'stīty anena svasiddhāntena virudhyate/ katham? vyaktir ātmalābhaḥ/ apāyaḥ pracyutiḥ/ yady ātmalābhāt pracyuto vikāro 'sti nityatvapratiṣedho nopapadyate/ yad vyakter apetasyāpi vikārasyāstitvaṃ tat khalu nityatvam iti/ nityatvapratiṣedho nāma vikārasyātmalābhāt pracyuter upapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: 'An eternal modification is not tenable; the modification exists even when departed (from manifestation) because destruction is negated.' Here, the reason 'because eternality is negated' contradicts one's own <s>siddhānta</s> that 'the modification exists even when departed from manifestation.' How so? <s>Vyakti</s> (manifestation) is the attainment of self-existence. <s>Apāya</s> (departure) is cessation. If a modification that has ceased from self-existence still exists, then the negation of eternality is not tenable. For the existence of a modification even when departed from manifestation — that is indeed eternality. The negation of eternality means the tenability of the modification's cessation from self-existence.

children.text: yad ātmalābhāt pracyavate tad anityaṃ dṛṣṭam, yad asti na tad ātmalābhāt pracyavate/ astitvaṃ cātmalābhāt pracyutir iti ca viruddhāv etau dharmau na saha sambhavata iti/ so 'yaṃ hetur yaṃ siddhāntam āśritya pravartate tam eva vyāhantīti// 6 //
children.translated_text: That which ceases from self-existence is observed to be non-eternal; that which exists does not cease from self-existence. Existence and cessation from self-existence — these two properties are contradictory and cannot coexist. Thus this reason undermines the very <s>siddhānta</s> on which it depends. // 6 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 7

children.text: yasmāt prakaraṇacintā sa nirṇayārtham apadiṣṭaḥ prakaraṇasamaḥ // 1.2.7 //
children.translated_text: That which is adduced for the purpose of settling the very question under deliberation (<s>prakaraṇa</s>) is <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (equivalent to the question). // 1.2.7 //

children.text: vimarśādhiṣṭhānau pakṣapratipakṣāv ubhāv anavasitau prakaraṇam, tasya cintā vimarśāt prabhṛti prāṅ nirṇayād yat samīkṣaṇam,
children.translated_text: The thesis and counter-thesis, both unsettled, which are the basis of deliberation, constitute the <s>prakaraṇa</s> (topic). Its deliberation is the examination from the point of inquiry up to but before the determination.

children.text:
sā jijñāsā yatkṛtā sa nirṇayārthaṃ prayukta ubhayapakṣasāmyāt prakaraṇam anativartamānaḥ prakaraṇasamo nirṇayāya na prakalpate/
prajñāpanaṃ tv anityaḥ śabdo nityadharmānupalabdher iti, anupalabhyamānan ity adharmakaṃ nityaṃ dṛṣṭam sthālyādi/ nityaḥ śabdo vānityadharmānupalabdheḥ anupalabhyamānānityadharmakaṃ nityaṃ dṛṣṭam ākāśādi/
yatra samāno dharmaḥ saṃśayakāraṇaṃ hetutvenopādīyate sa saṃśayasamaḥ savyabhicāra eva/
children.translated_text: That inquiry on account of which (the reason) is adduced for the purpose of determination — being equal to both theses and not surpassing the topic — it is <s>prakaraṇasama</s> and does not serve for determination. For instance: 'Sound is non-eternal because eternal properties are not perceived' — that whose eternal properties are not perceived is observed to be non-eternal, like a pot and so forth. Or: 'Sound is eternal because non-eternal properties are not perceived' — that whose non-eternal properties are not perceived is observed to be eternal, like space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and so forth. Where a common property that is the cause of doubt is adduced as a reason, that is <s>saṃśayasama</s> (equivalent to the doubt), which is simply a type of <s>savyabhicāra</s> (the erratic).

children.text: yā tu vimarśasya viśeṣāpekṣitā ubhayapakṣaviśeṣānupalabdhiś ca sā prakaraṇaṃ pravartayati/ yathā śabde nityadharmo nopalabhyata evam anityadharmo 'pi/ seyam ubhayapakṣaviśeṣānupalabdhiḥ prakaraṇacintāṃ pravartayati/
children.translated_text: But it is the need for a distinguishing factor in the inquiry and the non-perception of distinguishing features of both theses that sets the <s>prakaraṇa</s> (topic) in motion. Just as eternal properties are not perceived in sound, so too non-eternal properties are not perceived. This non-perception of distinguishing features of both theses sets the <s>prakaraṇa</s>-deliberation in motion.

children.text: katham? viparyaye hi prakaraṇanivṛtteḥ — yadi nityadharmaḥ śabde gṛhyeta na syāt prakaraṇam, yadi na syāt prakaraṇam, yadi vānityadharmo gṛhyeta evam api nivarteta prakaraṇam/ so 'yaṃ hetur ubhau pakṣau pravartayann anyatarasya nirṇayāya na prakalpate// 7 //
children.translated_text: How so? Because in the contrary case, the <s>prakaraṇa</s> would cease — if eternal properties were grasped in sound, there would be no <s>prakaraṇa</s>; if non-eternal properties were grasped, likewise the <s>prakaraṇa</s> would cease. Thus this reason, setting both theses in motion, does not serve for the determination of either one. // 7 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
That which is not distinct from what is to be proved, because it itself requires proof, is <s>sādhyasama</s> (equivalent to what is to be proved). // 1.2.8 //

children.text: dravyaṃ chāyeti sādhyam, gatimattvād iti hetuḥ sādhyenāviśiṣṭaḥ sādhanīyatvāt sādhyasamaḥ/
children.translated_text: 'A shadow is a substance' — this is what is to be proved. 'Because it possesses movement' — this is the reason. It is not distinct from what is to be proved because it itself requires establishment; hence it is <s>sādhyasama</s>.

children.text: ayam apy asiddhatvāt sādhyavat prajñāpayitavyaḥ/ sādhyaṃ tāvad etat kiṃ puruṣavac chāyāpi gacchaty āhosvid āvarakadravye saṃsarpaty āvaraṇasantānād asannidhisantāno 'yaṃ tejaso gṛhyata iti/
children.translated_text: This too, being unestablished, requires demonstration just like what is to be proved. The question is: does the shadow itself move like a person, or does it shift along the obstructing substance, and this continuity of non-presence of light is grasped as a succession of obstruction?

children.text: sarpatā khalu dravyeṇa yo yas tejobhāga āvriyate tasya tasyāsannidhir evāvicchinno gṛhyata iti/ āvaraṇaṃ tu prāptipratiṣedhaḥ// 8 //
children.translated_text: Indeed, as the obstructing substance moves, whichever portion of light is obstructed, the uninterrupted non-presence of that very (light) is what is grasped. And obstruction is the prevention of contact (of light). // 8 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 9
That which is adduced with a temporal discrepancy is <s>kālātīta</s> (the mistimed). // 1.2.9 //

children.text: kālātyayena yukto yasyārthaikadeśo 'padiśyamānasya sa kālātyayāpadiṣṭaḥ kālātīta ity ucyate/ nidarśanam — nityaḥ śabdaḥ saṃyogavyaṅgyatvād rūpavat/
children.translated_text: That whose one part of meaning, when being adduced, is combined with a temporal discrepancy — that is called <s>kālātīta</s> (the mistimed). Illustration — 'Sound is eternal because it is manifested by contact, like color.'

children.text: prāg ūrdhvaṃ ca vyakter avasthitaṃ rūpaṃ pradīpaghaṭasaṃyogena vyajyate, tathā ca śabdo 'py avasthito bherīdaṇḍasaṃyogena vyajyate dāruparaśusaṃyogena vā, tasmāt samyogavyaṅgyatvān nityaḥ śabda iti; ayam ahetuḥ kālātyayāpadeśāt/ vyañjakasya saṃyogasya kālaṃ na vyaṅgyasya rūpasya vyaktir atyeti/ sati pradīpasaṃyoge rūpasya grahaṇaṃ bhavati, na nivṛtte saṃyoge rūpaṃ gṛhyate/ nivṛtte dāruparaśusaṃyoge dūrasthena śabdaḥ śrūyate vibhāgakāle/ seyaṃ śabdasya vyaktiḥ saṃyogakālam atyetīti na saṃyoganirmitā bhavati/ kasmāt? kāraṇābhāvād dhi kāryābhāva iti/ evam udāharaṇasādharmyasyābhāvād asādhanam ayaṃ hetur hetvābhāsa iti/
children.translated_text: Color, existing prior to and after manifestation, is manifested by the contact of a lamp and a pot; similarly, sound too, (supposedly) existing (before), is manifested by the contact of a drum and a drumstick, or of wood and an axe; therefore, being manifested by contact, sound is eternal. This is a non-reason due to temporal discrepancy. The manifestation of color does not outlast the time of the contact that manifests it. When the lamp-contact exists, color is grasped; when the contact ceases, color is not grasped. But when the wood-axe contact has ceased, sound is heard by one standing far away, during the time of separation. This manifestation of sound outlasts the time of contact, and therefore is not produced by contact. Why? Because from the absence of a cause follows the absence of an effect. Thus, due to the absence of similarity with the example, this reason fails to prove and is a <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reason).
However, the statement about transposition of members is not the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. Why?

children.text:
yasya yenārthasambandho dūrasthasyāpi tasya saḥ/
arthato hy asamarthānām ānantaryam akāraṇam//
children.translated_text: 'The connection of meaning with that to which it pertains exists even when (the member) is distant;

children.text: ity etadvacanād viparyāsenokto hetur udāharaṇasādharmyāt tathā vaidharmyāt sādhyasādhanaṃ hetulakṣaṇaṃ na jahāti/ ajahaddhetulakṣaṇaṃ na hetvābhāso bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: mere (lack of) contiguity is not a cause for those that are meaningfully connected' — by this statement, a reason stated in transposed order does not lose the defining characteristic of a <s>hetu</s>, namely that it establishes what is to be proved through similarity and dissimilarity with the example. That which does not lose the defining characteristic of a <s>hetu</s> is not a <s>hetvābhāsa</s>.
'Statement with transposition of members is untimely' —

children.text: iti nigrahasthānam uktam, tad evedaṃ punar ucyata iti, atas tan na sūtrārthaḥ// 9 //
children.translated_text: this has been stated as a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat); since it is merely restated here, therefore that is not the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. // 9 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 10
Now, <s>chala</s> (quibble) —
<s>Chala</s> (quibble) is the obstruction of a statement through recourse to an alternative meaning. // 1.2.10 //

children.text: na sāmānyalakṣaṇe chalaṃ śakyam udāhartum, vibhāge tūdāharaṇāni// 10//
children.translated_text: It is not possible to give an example of <s>chala</s> (quibbling) in the general definition, but examples can be given in the classification. // 10 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 11
And the classification is —

children.text: tat trividhaṃ vākchalaṃ sāmānyacchalam upacāracchalam ceti // 1.2.11 //
children.translated_text: That [<s>chala</s>] is of three kinds: <s>vākchala</s> (verbal quibbling), <s>sāmānyacchala</s> (quibbling based on generality), and <s>upacāracchala</s> (quibbling based on figurative usage). // 1.2.11 //
Of these —
<s>Vākchala</s> (verbal quibbling) is the supposition of a different meaning, contrary to the speaker's intention, when the meaning expressed is not specific. // 1.2.12 //

children.text: navakambalo 'yaṃ māṇavaka iti prayogaḥ/ atra navaḥ kambalo 'syeti vaktur abhiprāyaḥ/ vigrahe tu viśeṣaḥ, na samāse/ tatrāyaṃ chalavādī vaktur abhiprāyād avivakṣitam anyam arthaṃ nava kambalā asyeti tāvad abhihitaṃ bhavateti kalpayati,
children.translated_text: The expression is 'this young man is navakambala (possessing a new blanket).' Here the speaker's intention is 'navaḥ kambalaḥ asya' (he has a new blanket). The distinction [of meaning] exists in the analytical form, not in the compound. There the quibbler, contrary to the speaker's intention, supposes another meaning not intended — 'nava kambalāḥ asya' (he has nine blankets) — and maintains 'that much has been stated by you,'

children.text:
kalpayitvā cāsambhavena pratiṣedhati eko 'sya kambalaḥ kuto nava kambalā iti/
tad idaṃ sāmānyaśabde vāci chalaṃ vākchalam iti/
asya pratyavasthānam — sāmānyaśabdasyānekārthatve 'nyatarābhidhānakalpanāyāṃ viśeṣavacanam/ navakambala ity anekārthābhidhānam, navaḥ kambalo 'syeti nava kambalā asyeti; etasmin prayukte yeyaṃ kalpanā nava kambalā asyety etadbhavatābhihitaṃ tac ca na sambhavatīti, etasyām anyatarābhidhānakalpanāyāṃ viśeṣo vaktavyaḥ/ yasmād viśeṣo 'rthaviśeṣeṣu vijñāyate 'yam artho 'nenābhihita iti/ sa ca viśeṣo nāsti/ tasmān mithyābhiyogamātram etad iti/
prasiddhaś ca loke śabdārthasambandho 'bhidhānābhidheyaniyamaniyogaḥ/ asyābhidhānasyāyam artho 'bhidheya iti samānaḥ sāmānyaśabdasya, viśeṣo viśiṣṭaśabdasya/ prayuktapūrvāś ceme śabdā arthe prayujyante nāprayuktapūrvāḥ/ prayogaś cārthasampratyayārthaḥ/ arthapratyayāc ca vyavahāra iti/
children.translated_text: and having supposed this, refutes it on grounds of impossibility: 'He has one blanket; where would nine blankets come from?' This is <s>vākchala</s> — quibbling on the word (<s>vāc</s>) when the general term is ambiguous. The counter-reply to this is: when a general word has multiple meanings, and one of the meanings is supposed [by the quibbler], a specific statement [is needed to settle it]. 'Navakambala' is an expression with multiple meanings: 'navaḥ kambalaḥ asya' (he has a new blanket) and 'nava kambalāḥ asya' (he has nine blankets).
