When this [expression] is used and the supposition is made — 'What you have stated is "he has nine blankets," and that is impossible' — in this supposition of one of the meanings, a specific [determining factor] must be stated. Since the specific [meaning] is known in particular contexts of meaning — 'this meaning is expressed by this [word]' — and since no such specific [indicator for nine blankets] exists, therefore this is merely a false charge. And the relation between word and meaning is well-established in the world as the fixed connection of expression and expressed. This [connection] is the same for the general word and specific for the qualified word. These words are used for meanings in which they have been previously used, not in meanings where they have not. And usage is for the purpose of conveying meaning. And from the cognition of meaning comes practical activity.

children.text: tatraivam arthagatyarthe śabdaprayoge sāmarthyāt sāmānyaśabdasya prayoganiyamaḥ/ ajāṃ grāmaṃ naya sarpir āhāra brāhmaṇaṃ bhojayeti sāmānyaśabdāḥ santo 'rthāvayaveṣu prayujyante sāmārthyat, yatrārthakriyācodanā sambhavati tatra pravartante nārthasāmānye, kriyādeśanāsambhavāt/ evam ayaṃ sāmānyaśabdo navakambala iti yo 'rthaḥ sambhavati navaḥ kambalo 'syeti tatra pravartate, yas tu na sambhavait nava kambalā asyeti tatra na pravartate/ so 'yam anupapadyamānārthakalpanayā paravākyopālambho na kalpata iti//12//
children.translated_text: Thus, when words are used for the purpose of conveying meaning, the rule of usage of general words is [determined] by capacity. General words such as 'lead the goat to the village,' 'bring ghee,' 'feed the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>' are used with reference to particular instances of the object by virtue of capacity — they apply where the injunction of purposive action is possible, not to the generality of the meaning, since direction of action [to a universal] is impossible. In the same way, this general word 'navakambala,' with regard to the meaning that is possible — 'navaḥ kambalaḥ asya' (he has a new blanket) — applies there, and with regard to the meaning that is impossible — 'nava kambalāḥ asya' (he has nine blankets) — does not apply there. Thus, the censuring of another's statement by supposing an untenable meaning is not valid. // 12 //
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 13
<s>Sāmānyacchala</s> (quibbling based on generality) is the supposition of a non-existent meaning by applying an excessive generality to a meaning that is feasible. // 1.2.13 //

children.text: aho khalv asau brāhmaṇo vidyācaraṇasampanna ity ukte kaścid āha sambhavati brāhmaṇe vidyācaraṇasampad iti/
children.translated_text: When it is said, 'Ah, that <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> is truly endowed with learning and conduct,' someone says, 'Learning and conduct are possible in a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> [in general].'

children.text:
asya vacanasya vighāto 'rthavikalpopapattyāsambhūtārthakalpanayā kriyate — yadi brāhmaṇe vidyācaraṃasampat sambhavati vrātye 'pi sambhavet, vrātyo 'pi brāhmaṇaḥ, so 'py astu vidyācaraṇasampanna iti/ yad vivakṣitam artham āpnoti cātyeti ca tad atisāmānyam/ yathā brāhmaṇatvaṃ vidyācaraṇasampadaṃ kvacid āpnoti kvacid atyeti/ sāmānyanimittaṃ chalaṃ sāmānyacchalam iti/
asya ca pratyavasthānam — avivakṣitahetukasya viṣayānuvādaḥ praśaṃsārthatvād vākyasya; tad atrāsambhūtārthakalpanānupapattiḥ/ yathā sambhavanty asmin kṣetre śālaya iti anirākṛtam avivakṣitaṃ ca bījajanma, pravṛttiviṣayas tu kṣetraṃ praśasyate; so 'yaṃ kṣetrānuvādaḥ nāsmin śālayo vidhīyanta iti; bījāt tu śālinirvṛttiḥ satī na vivakṣitā/ evaṃ sambhavati brāhmaṇe vidyācaraṇasampad iti sampadviṣayo brāhmaṇatvaṃ na sampaddhetuḥ/ na cātra hetur vivakṣitaḥ/ viṣayānuvādas tv ayaṃ praśaṃsārthatvād vākyasya, sati brāhmaṇatve sampaddhetuḥ samartha iti/ vis'yaṃ ca praśaṃsatā vākyena yathāhetutaḥ phalanirvṛttir na pratyākhyāyate/ tad evaṃ sati vacanavighāto 'sambhūtārthakalpanayā nopapadyata iti//
children.translated_text: The disruption of this statement is made through the supposition of a non-existent meaning by the applicability of an alternative construction of meaning — 'If learning and conduct are possible in a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, they should be possible in an outcast (<s>vrātya</s>) too, for the <s>vrātya</s> is also a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>; so let him too be endowed with learning and conduct.' That which reaches the intended meaning and also goes beyond it is excessive generality. Just as <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-hood sometimes reaches the possession of learning and conduct and sometimes goes beyond it. Quibbling based on generality is <s>sāmānyacchala</s>. The counter-reply to this is: [this is merely] the reiteration of the subject without an intended causal reason, since the statement is for the purpose of praise. Therefore, the supposition of a non-existent meaning is inapplicable here. Just as [in the statement] 'rice grows in this field,' the [role of] seed and birth is neither denied nor intended; the subject is the field being praised in relation to [its] productive capacity. This is the reiteration of the field [as subject]; rice is not being prescribed as originating in it — rather, the production of rice from seed, though actual, is not what is intended. Similarly, in 'learning and conduct are possible in a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>,' <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-hood is the domain of the endowment, not the cause of the endowment. And no cause is intended here. This is merely the reiteration of the subject, since the statement is for the purpose of praise — [meaning] that given <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-hood, the cause of endowment is effective. And a statement that praises the subject does not deny the production of the result from its [actual] cause. Therefore, the disruption of the statement through the supposition of a non-existent meaning is untenable.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 14
<s>Upacāracchala</s> (quibbling based on figurative usage) is the denial of the actual existence of a thing when a figurative expression of a property is indicated. // 1.2.14 //

children.text: abhidhānasya dharmo yathārthaprayogaḥ, dharmavikalpo 'nyatra dṛṣṭasyānyatra prayogaḥ, tasya nirdeśe dharmavikalpanirdeśe/ yathā mañcāḥ krośantīti arthasadbhāvena pratiṣedhaḥ,
children.translated_text: The property of an expression is its literal usage; a variant of property is the use elsewhere of what is observed in one place; when that is indicated — when a variant of property is indicated — for example, when it is said 'the platforms are shouting,' the denial is made on the basis of actual existence:

children.text:
mañcasthāḥ puruṣāḥ krośanti na tu mañcāḥ krośanti/
kā punar atrārthavikalpopapattiḥ? anyathā prayuktasyānyathārthakalpanam, bhaktyā prayoge prādhānyena kalpanam upacāraviṣayaṃ chalam upacāracchalam/ upacāro nītārthaḥ sahacaraṇādinimittena, atadbhāve tadvad abhidhānam upacāra iti/
atra samādhiḥ — prasiddhe prayoge vaktur yathābhiprāyaṃ śabdārthayor abhyanujñā pratiṣedhā vā na cchandataḥ/ pradhānabhūtasya śabdasya bhāktasya ca guṇabhūtasya prayoga ubhayor lokasiddhaḥ/ siddhe prayoge yathā vaktur abhiprāyas tathā śabdārthāv anujñeyau pratiṣedhyau vā na cchandataḥ/ yadi vaktā pradhānaśabdaṃ prayuṅkte yathābhūtasyābhyanujñā pratiṣedho vā, na cchandataḥ/ atha guṇabhūtam, tadā guṇabhūtasya/ yatra tu vaktā guṇabhūtaṃ śabdaṃ prayuṅkte pradhānabhūtam abhipretya paraḥ pratiṣedhati, svamanīṣayā pratiṣedho 'sau bhavati na paropālambha iti//
children.translated_text: 'The people on the platforms are shouting, not the platforms themselves.' Now, what is the applicability of the alternative construction of meaning here? It is the supposition of a meaning other than what was intended in the figurative usage — taking what is used figuratively as if used literally. The <s>upacāra</s>-based quibble is <s>upacāracchala</s>. <s>Upacāra</s> (figurative usage) is a transferred sense, occasioned by association and the like — the designation of something as being what it is not, in the absence of the [actual] thing. The resolution here is: in established usage, the acceptance or rejection of word and meaning should be according to the speaker's intention, not arbitrarily. The usage of both the primary word, which is principal, and the figurative word, which is secondary, is well-established in the world. In established usage, word and meaning should be accepted or rejected as the speaker intends, not arbitrarily. If the speaker uses the primary word, acceptance or rejection is of the thing as it actually is, not arbitrary. If [he uses] the secondary, then [the response pertains] to the secondary. But where the speaker uses the secondary word and the opponent rejects it by taking it as primary, that rejection is based on his own fancy, not a legitimate censure of the other.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 15
<s>Upacāracchala</s> is just <s>vākchala</s>, because there is no difference between them. // 1.2.15 //

children.text: na vākchalād upacāracchalaṃ bhidyate tasyāpy arthāntarakalpanāyā aviśeṣāt/ ihāpi sthānyartho guṇaśabdaḥ pradhānaśabdaḥ sthānārtha iti kalpayitvā pratiṣidhyata iti//
children.translated_text: <s>Upacāracchala</s> is not different from <s>vākchala</s>, since there is no difference in the supposition of a different meaning in this case too. Here too, the secondary word, which stands for the primary meaning, is supposed to be the primary word, which stands for the [secondary] meaning, and [then] is refuted.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 16
No, because that [denial of actual existence] is a different matter. // 1.2.16 //

children.text: na vākchalam evopacāracchalam, tasyārthasadbhāvapratiṣedhasyārthāntarabhāvāt/ kutaḥ? arthāntarakalpanātaḥ/ anyā hy arthāntarakalpanā, anyo 'rthasadbhāvapratiṣedha iti//
children.translated_text: <s>Upacāracchala</s> is not merely <s>vākchala</s>, because that denial of actual existence is a different matter. Why? Because of the supposition of a different meaning. For the supposition of a different meaning is one thing, and the denial of actual existence is another.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 17
Or, if there is no distinction, since there is some similarity, the consequence would be that there is only one [kind of] <s>chala</s>. // 1.2.17 //

children.text: chalasya dvitvam abhyanujñāya tritvaṃ pratiṣidhyate kiñcit sādharmyāt/ yathā cāyaṃ hetus tritvaṃ pratiṣedhati tathā dvitvam apy abhyanujñātaṃ pratiṣedhati, vidyate hi kiñcit sādharmyaṃ dvayor apīti/ atha dvitvaṃ kiñcitsādharmyān na nivartate, tritvam api na nivartsyati//
children.translated_text: Having accepted that <s>chala</s> is twofold, the threefold [classification] is being refuted on the ground of some similarity. But just as this reason refutes threefoldness, it also refutes the accepted twofoldness, for there is some similarity between the two as well. And if twofoldness is not overturned by some similarity, then threefoldness too will not be overturned.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 18
After the definition of <s>chala</s> —
A counter-argument based on similarity or dissimilarity is <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinder). // 1.2.18 //

children.text: prayukte hi hetau yaḥ prasaṅgo jāyate sa jātiḥ/ sa ca prasaṅgaḥ sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ pratyavasthānam upālambhaḥ pratiṣedha iti/
children.translated_text: When a reason is employed, the objection that arises is <s>jāti</s>. And that objection is a counter-argument — a censure, a refutation — based on similarity or dissimilarity.
'A reason is that which establishes the thing to be proved by similarity with the example'
— a counter-argument against this by dissimilarity with the example;
'A reason is that which establishes the thing to be proved by dissimilarity with the example'

children.text: ity asyodāharaṇasādharmyeṇa pratyavasthānam, pratyanīkabhāvāt/ jāyamāno 'rtho jātir iti//
children.translated_text: — a counter-argument against this by similarity with the example, because of opposition. What arises [as an objection] is <s>jāti</s>.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 19
Misapprehension and non-apprehension constitute <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat). // 1.2.19 //

children.text: viparītā vā kutsitā vā pratipattir vipratipattiḥ/ vipratipadyamānaḥ parājayaṃ prāpnoti/ nigrahasthānaṃ khalu parājayaprāptiḥ/ apratipattis tv ārambhaviṣaye anārambhaḥ/ pareṇa sthāpitaṃ vā na pratiṣedhati pratiṣedhaṃ vā noddharati/ asamāsāc ca naite eva nigrahasthāne iti//
children.translated_text: <s>Vipratipatti</s> (misapprehension) is a wrong or defective understanding. One who misapprehends meets with defeat. <s>Nigrahasthāna</s> is indeed the attainment of defeat. <s>Apratipatti</s> (non-apprehension) is the failure to begin what should be undertaken. Or [it is when] one does not refute what has been established by the opponent, or does not counter the refutation. And these are not the only points of defeat, since [the list] is not exhaustive.
Chapter 1, Section 2, Sūtra 20

children.text: kiṃ punar dṛṣṭāntavaj jātinigrahasthānayor abhedo 'tha siddhāntavad bheda ity ata āha —
children.translated_text: Now, is there no distinction between <s>jāti</s> and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>, as with examples, or is there a distinction, as with established doctrines? To this he says —
From the varieties of that [counter-argument], there is a multiplicity of <s>jāti</s> and <s>nigrahasthāna</s>. // 1.2.20 //

children.text: tasya sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ pratyavasthānasya vikalpāj jātibahutvam, tayoś ca vipratipattyapratipattyor vikalpān nigrahasthānabahutvam/ nānā kalpo vikalpaḥ, vividho vā kalpo vikalpaḥ/ tatra ananubhāṣaṇam ajñānam apratibhā vikṣepo matānujñā paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam ity apratipattir nigrasthānam/ śeṣas tu vipratipattir iti/
children.translated_text: From the varieties of that counter-argument based on similarity and dissimilarity, there is a multiplicity of <s>jāti</s>; and from the varieties of those two — misapprehension and non-apprehension — there is a multiplicity of <s>nigrahasthāna</s>. <s>Vikalpa</s> means manifold division, or diverse division. Among these, non-response, ignorance, absence of ready wit, distraction, assent [to the opponent's view], and overlooking what deserves censure — these constitute <s>apratipatti</s> as <s>nigrahasthāna</s>. The rest constitute <s>vipratipatti</s>.

children.text: ime pramāṇādayaḥ padārthā uddiṣṭāḥ, yathoddeśaṃ lakṣitāḥ, yathālakṣaṇaṃ parīkṣiṣyanta iti trividhā cāsya śāstrasya pravṛttir veditavyeti//
children.translated_text: These categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> have been enumerated, defined according to their enumeration, and will be examined according to their definitions — thus the threefold procedure of this <s>śāstra</s> should be understood.

children.text:
iti vātsyāyanīye nyāyabhāṣye prathamādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam/
samāptaś cāyaṃ prathamo 'dhyāyaḥ//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second section of the first chapter in the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> of <s>Vātsyāyana</s>. And thus the first chapter is complete.
Chapter 2
Chapter 2, Section 1
Chapter 2, Section 1, Sūtra 1
ascertainment of a matter by deliberating between thesis and counter-thesis is <s>nirṇaya</s> (determination)
— it is deliberation itself that is first to be examined.
Henceforth [begins] the examination of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest. And that [examination]—
Doubt does not arise from the apprehension of common properties alone or from the apprehension of multiple properties, or from the apprehension of one of the properties. // 2.1.1 //

children.text: samānasya dharmasyādhyavasāyāt saṃśayo na dharmamātrāt/ atha vā samānam anayor dharmam upalabha iti dharmadharmigrahaṇe saṃśayābhāva iti/
children.translated_text: Doubt arises from the apprehension of a common property, not from the property alone. Or: having apprehended a property common to these two, in the apprehension of property and property-bearer, there is no doubt.

children.text: atha vā samānadharmādhyavasāyād arthāntarabhūte dharmiṇi saṃśayo 'nupapannaḥ, na jātu rūpasyārthāntarabhūtasyādhyavasāyād arthāntarabhūte sparśe saṃśaya iti/ atha vā na adhyavasāyād arthāvadhāraṇād anavadhāraṇajñānaṃ saṃśaya upapadyate kāryakāraṇayoḥ sārūpyābhāvād iti/ etenānekadharmādhyavasāyād iti vyākhyātam/ anyataradharmādhyvasāyāc ca saṃśayo na bhavati, tato hy anyatarāvadhāraṇam eveti//
children.translated_text: Or: doubt regarding a property-bearer that is something different is untenable [merely] from the apprehension of a common property; for doubt about touch, which is something different, never arises from the apprehension of form, which is something different. Or: from apprehension, i.e., from the ascertainment of a matter, the cognition of non-ascertainment, which is doubt, is untenable, since there is no similarity between cause and effect. By this, [the phrase] 'from the apprehension of multiple properties' is also explained. And from the apprehension of one of the properties, doubt does not arise either, for from that arises only the ascertainment of one [alternative].
Chapter 2, Section 1, Sūtra 2
And [doubt arises] from conflicting views and from irregular apprehension. // 2.1.2 //

children.text: na vipratipattimātrād avyavasthāmātrād vā saṃśayaḥ/ kiṃ tarhi? vipratipattim upalabhamānasya saṃśayaḥ/ evam avyavasthāyām apīti/ atha vāsty ātmety eke nāsty ātmety apare manyanta ity upalabdheḥ kathaṃ saṃśayaḥ syād iti/ tathopalabdhir avyavasthitā anupalabdhiś cāvyavasthiteti vibhāgenādhyavasite saṃśayo nopapadyata iti//
children.translated_text: Doubt does not arise from mere conflicting views or from mere irregularity. Rather, doubt arises for one who perceives the conflict. Similarly with irregularity. Or: some hold 'the self exists' and others hold 'the self does not exist' — from [merely] perceiving [this disagreement], how can doubt arise? Similarly, when perception is irregular and non-perception is also irregular, when these are ascertained as distinct divisions, doubt is untenable.
Chapter 2, Section 1, Sūtra 3
And because of agreement amid disagreement. // 2.1.3 //

children.text: yāṃ ca vipratipattiṃ bhavān saṃśayahetuḥ manyate sā sampratipattiḥ, sā hi dvayoḥ pratyanīkadharmaviṣayā/ tatra yadi vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ, sampratipatter eva saṃśaya iti//
children.translated_text: And the conflicting views that you consider to be the cause of <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) are in fact agreements, for they concern two mutually contradictory properties in a single locus. If doubt arises from conflicting views, then it equally arises from agreement.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 4
And because the instability is established in its own nature, instability [does not lead to doubt]. // 2.1.4 //

children.text:
na saṃśayaḥ/ yadi tāvad iyam avyavasthā ātmani eva vyavasthitā, vyavasthānād avyavasthā na bhavatīty anupapannaḥ saṃśayaḥ/
atha avyavasthātmani na vyavasthitā, evam atādātmyād avyavasthā na bhavatīti saṃśayābhāva iti//
children.translated_text: There is no <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt). If this instability is established in its own nature, then since it is established, it is not instability — hence doubt is untenable. If, on the other hand, the instability is not established in its own nature, then since it does not have that nature, there is no instability, and hence no doubt.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt, because of the continuous presence of those properties. // 2.1.5 //

children.text: yena kalpena bhavān samānadharmopapatteḥ saṃśaya iti manyate, tena khalv atyantasaṃśayaḥ prasajyate/ samānadharmopapatter anucchedāt saṃśayānucchedaḥ/ na hy ayam ataddharmā dharmī vimṛśyamāṇo gṛhyate, satataṃ tu taddharmā bhavatīti//
children.translated_text: By the same reasoning through which you hold that doubt arises from the presence of common properties, perpetual doubt would follow — because there is no cessation of the presence of common properties, there is no cessation of doubt. For the subject being examined is never grasped as lacking those properties; rather, it continuously possesses them.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 6
The summary resolution of this elaborate refutation is:

children.text: yathoktādhyavasāyād eva tadaviśeṣāpekṣāt saṃśaye nāsaṃśayo nātyantasaṃśayo vā // 2.1.6 //
children.translated_text: From the ascertainment as described, which requires a distinguishing feature, there is neither absence of doubt nor perpetual doubt. // 2.1.6 //

children.text:
na saṃśayānutpattiḥ saṃśayānucchedaś ca prasajyate/ katham? yat tāvat samānadharmādhyavasāyaḥ saṃśayahetuḥ na samānadharmamātram iti, evam etat/ kasmād evaṃ nocyata iti? viśeṣāpekṣa iti vacanāt tatsiddheḥ — viśeṣasyāpekṣā ākaṅkṣā, sā cānupalabhyamāne viśeṣe samarthā, na coktaṃ samānadharmāpekṣa iti/ samāne ca dharme katham ākaṅkṣā na bhaved yady ayaṃ pratyakṣaḥ syāt/ etena sāmarthyena vijñāyate samānadharmādhyavasāyād iti/
upapattivacanād vā — samānadharmopapatter ity ucyate na cānyā sadbhāvasaṃvedanād ṛte samānadharmopapattir asti/ anupalabhyamānasadbhāvo hi samāno dharmo 'vidyamānavad bhavatīti/
viṣayaśabdena vā viṣayiṇaḥ pratyayasyābhidhānam — yathā loke dhūmenāgnir anumīyate ity ukte dhūmadarśanenāgnir anumīyata iti jñāyate/ katham? dṛṣṭvā hi dhūmam athāgnim anuminoti nādṛṣṭveti; na ca vākye darśanaśabdaḥ śrūyate, anujānāti ca vākyasyārthapratyāyakatvam; tena manyāmahe viṣayaśabdena viṣayiṇaḥ pratyayasyābhidhānaṃ boddhānujānāti/ evam ihāpi samānadharmaśabdena samānadharmādhyvasāyam āheti/
children.translated_text: Neither the non-arising of doubt nor the non-cessation of doubt follows. How? First, the cause of doubt is the ascertainment of common properties, not mere common properties — this is so. Why is it stated thus? Because it follows from the statement 'requiring a distinguishing feature' — the expectation (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>) of a distinguishing feature is effective when the distinguishing feature is not apprehended; and it is not said 'requiring common properties.' And regarding the common property, how could there be expectation if it were directly perceived? By this implication, it is understood that [doubt arises] from the ascertainment of common properties. Or from the word 'occurrence' (<s>upapatti</s>) — it is said 'from the occurrence of common properties,' and there is no occurrence of common properties apart from the awareness of their existence. For a common property whose existence is not apprehended is as good as non-existent. Or by the word 'object' (<s>viṣaya</s>), the cognition (<s>pratyaya</s>) which has it as its object is designated — just as in the world when it is said 'fire is inferred from smoke,' it is understood as 'fire is inferred from the seeing of smoke.' How? For one infers fire having seen smoke, not without seeing it; and the word 'seeing' does not appear in the sentence, yet one acknowledges the sentence's capacity to convey meaning. Therefore we hold that the knower acknowledges that by the word 'object,' the cognition having that object is designated. Similarly here too, by the word 'common property,' the ascertainment of common properties is meant.

children.text:
yathohitvā samānamanayor dharmam upalabha iti dharmadharmigrahaṇe saṃśayābhāva iti, pūrvadṛṣṭaviṣayam etat/ yāv aham arthau pūrvam adrākṣaṃ tayoḥ samānaṃ dharmam upalabhe viśeṣaṃ nopalabha iti, kathaṃ nu viśeṣaṃ paśyeyaṃ yenānyataram avadhārayeyam iti/ na caitat samānadharmopalabdhau dharmadharmigrahaṇamātreṇa nivartata iti/
yac coktaṃ nārthāntarādhyavasāyād anyatra saṃśaya iti, yo hy arthāntarādhyavasāyamātraṃ saṃśayahetum upādadīta sa evaṃ vācya iti/
yat punar etat kāryakāraṇayoḥ sārūpyābhāvād iti, kāraṇasya bhāvābhāvayoḥ kāryasya bhāvābhāvau kāryakāraṇayoḥ sārūpyam/
children.translated_text: As for [the objection] that when one grasps the common property and the property-bearer, there is no doubt — this pertains to what was previously seen. When I perceive the common property of the two objects I saw before but do not perceive the distinguishing feature, how shall I see the distinguishing feature by which I could determine one or the other? And this is not removed merely by grasping the property and property-bearer when common properties are apprehended. As for the statement that there is no doubt from the ascertainment of something different — whoever would take mere ascertainment of something different as the cause of doubt, to him this objection applies. As for the argument that there is no similarity between cause and effect, the similarity of cause and effect consists in this: the existence and non-existence of the effect follow the existence and non-existence of the cause.

children.text:
yasyotpādād yad utpadyate yasya cānutpādād yan notpadyate tat kāraṇaṃ kāryam itarad ity etat sārūpyam, asti ca saṃśayakāraṇe saṃśaye caitad iti/ etenānekadharmādhyavasāyād iti pratiṣedhaḥ parihṛta iti/
yat punar etad uktaṃ
children.translated_text: That upon whose arising something arises, and upon whose non-arising something does not arise — that is the cause, and the other is the effect: this is their similarity. And this similarity exists between the cause of doubt and doubt itself. By this, the objection 'not from the ascertainment of multiple properties' is also answered. As for what was further said —
there is no doubt from the ascertainment of conflicting views and instability

children.text: iti, pṛthakpravādayor vyāhatam artham upalabhe viśeṣaṃ ca na jānāmi nopalabhe yenānyataram avadhārayeyam,
children.translated_text: — I perceive the contradictory content of two opposing statements and do not know the distinguishing feature, nor do I perceive that by which I could determine one or the other.

children.text:
tat ko 'tra viśeṣaḥ syād yenaikataram avadhārayeyam iti saṃśayo vipratipattijanito 'yaṃ na śakyo vipratipattisampratipattimātreṇa nivartayitum iti/evam upalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthākṛte saṃśaye veditavyam iti/
yat punar etat vipratipattau ca sampratipatter iti, vipratipattiśabdasya yo 'rthaḥ tadadhyavasāyo viśeṣāpekṣaḥ saṃśayahetus tasya ca samākhyāntareṇa na nivṛttiḥ/ samāne 'dhikaraṇe vyāhatārthau pravādau vipratipattiśabdasyārthaḥ tadadhyavasāyaś ca viśeṣāpekṣaḥ saṃśayahetuḥ/ na cāsya sampratipattiśabde samākhyāntare yojyamāne saṃśayahetutuvaṃ nivartate/ tad idam akṛtabuddhisammohanam iti/
yat punaḥ
children.translated_text: What distinguishing feature could there be by which I could determine one or the other? This doubt born from conflicting views cannot be removed merely by conflicting views or agreement. The same is to be understood regarding doubt arising from the instability of apprehension and non-apprehension. As for the statement about conflicting views being agreement: the meaning of the word 'conflicting views' — the ascertainment of that, requiring a distinguishing feature, is the cause of doubt, and it is not removed by using a different name. Statements of contradictory import regarding the same subject — this is the meaning of the word 'conflicting views,' and the ascertainment of that, requiring a distinguishing feature, is the cause of doubt. And its nature as a cause of doubt is not removed by applying the different name 'agreement.' This is thus a mere confusion of the unintelligent. As for what was further said —
because instability is established in its own nature

children.text: iti, saṃśayahetor arthasyāpratiṣedhād avyavasthābhyanujñānāc ca nimittāntareṇa śabdāntarakalpanā vyarthā/ śabdāntarakalpanāvyavasthā khalv avyavasthā na bhavaty avyavasthātmani vyavasthitatvād iti/
children.translated_text: — since the real content that is the cause of doubt is not refuted, and since instability is thereby acknowledged, the mere invention of a different term is futile. The instability of inventing a different term indeed is not instability, because it is established in its own nature as instability.

children.text:
nānayor upalabdhyanupalabdhyoḥ sadasadviṣayatvaṃ viśeṣāpekṣaṃ saṃśayahetur na bhvatīti pratiṣidhyate yāvatā cāvyavasthātmani vyavasthitā na tāvatātmānaṃ jahāti, tāvatā hy anujñātāvyavasthā/ evam iyaṃ kriyamāṇāpi śabdāntarakalpanā nārthāntaraṃ sādhayatīti/
yat punar etat
children.translated_text: It is not the case that the property of having existent and non-existent objects, belonging to apprehension and non-apprehension, requiring a distinguishing feature, ceases to be the cause of doubt. And insofar as it is established in its own nature as instability, it does not thereby abandon itself; for to that extent, instability is acknowledged. Thus, even when this invention of a different term is carried out, it does not establish anything different. As for what was further said —
likewise, there would be perpetual doubt, because of the continuous presence of those properties

children.text:
iti, nāyaṃ samānadharmādibhya eva saṃśayaḥ/ kiṃ tarhi? tadviṣayādhyavasāyād viśeṣasmṛtisahitād ity ato nātyantasaṃśaya iti/
anyataradharmādhyavasāyād vā na saṃśaya iti, tan na yuktam; viśeṣāpekṣo vimarṣaḥ saṃśaya iti vacanāt/ viśeṣaś cānyataradharmo na tasminn adhyvasīyamāne viśeṣāpekṣā sambhavatīti//
children.translated_text: — doubt does not arise from common properties alone. Rather, it arises from the ascertainment of them accompanied by the recollection of a distinguishing feature; hence there is no perpetual doubt. [The objection] that there is no doubt from the ascertainment of one or the other property is also not correct, because of the statement that deliberation requiring a distinguishing feature is doubt. And the distinguishing feature is one or the other property — when that is ascertained, the expectation of a distinguishing feature is not possible.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 7
Wherever there is doubt, there in this manner the subsequent objections arise. // 2.1.7 //

children.text: yatra yatra saṃśayapūrvikā parīkṣā śāstre kathāyāṃ vā, tatra tatraivaṃ saṃśaye pareṇa pratiṣiddhe samādhir vācya iti/ ataḥ sarvaparīkṣāvyāpitvāt prathamaṃ saṃśayaḥ parīkṣita iti//
children.translated_text: Wherever in the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise) or in discussion there is inquiry preceded by doubt, there, when doubt is refuted by the opponent, a resolution must be stated. Therefore, since it pervades all inquiry, doubt has been examined first.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
Now, the examination of the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) —
The invalidity of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and the rest, because of the impossibility of [their relation to] the three times. // 2.1.8 //

children.text: pratyakṣādīnāṃ pramāṇatvaṃ nāsti traikālyāsiddheḥ pūrvāparasahabhāvānupapatter ity arthaḥ//
children.translated_text: The validity of <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the rest does not exist, because of the impossibility of the three times — the meaning is that the relations of priority, posteriority, and simultaneity are untenable.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 9
The division of the meaning of this general statement —
For if the <s>pramāṇa</s> is established first, then perception does not arise from the contact of sense organ and object. // 2.1.9 //

children.text: gandhādiviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ pratyakṣam, tad yadi pūrvam, paścād gandhādīnāṃ siddhiḥ, nedaṃ gandhādisannikarṣād utpadyata iti//
children.translated_text: Cognition of smell and other objects is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception). If that is established first, then the establishment of smell and the rest comes afterwards — hence it does not arise from the contact with smell and the rest.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 10
If established afterwards, the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is not established from the <s>pramāṇas</s>. // 2.1.10 //

children.text: asati pramāṇe kena pramīyamāṇo 'rthaḥ prameyaḥ syāt pramāṇena khalu pramīyamāṇo 'rthaḥ prameyam ity etat sidhyati//
children.translated_text: Without a <s>pramāṇa</s>, by what would the object being measured be a <s>prameya</s> (knowable)? For it is established that an object is <s>prameya</s> when it is being measured by a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
If established simultaneously, since cognitions are determined for each object, there would be no successive functioning of cognitions. // 2.1.11 //

children.text: yadi pramāṇaṃ prameyaṃ ca yugapadbhavataḥ, evam api gandhādiṣv indriyārtheṣu jñānāni pratyarthaniyatāni yugapatsambhavantīti jñānānāṃ pratyakṣaniyatatvāt kramavṛttitvābhāvaḥ/ yā imā buddhayaḥ krameṇārtheṣu varttante tāsāṃ kramavṛttitvaṃ na sambhavatīti/ vyāghātaś ca

children.translated_text: the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of mind (<s>manas</s>)

children.text:
iti/ etāvāṃś ca pramāṇaprameyayoḥ sadbhāvaviṣayaḥ sa cānupapanna iti/ tasmāt pratyakṣādīnāṃ pramāṇatvaṃ na sambhavatīti/
asya samādhiḥ — upalabdhihetor upalabdhiviṣayasya cārthasya pūrvāparasahabhāvāniyamād yathādarśanaṃ vibhāgavacanam/
children.translated_text: — and this is the extent of the content regarding the existence of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s>, and it is untenable. Therefore the validity of <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the rest is not possible. The resolution of this is: since there is no fixed rule of priority, posteriority, or simultaneity regarding the object that is the cause of apprehension and the object that is the content of apprehension, a distinction must be stated according to observation.

If <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s> exist simultaneously, then cognitions of smell and other sense objects, being determined for each object, would occur simultaneously — and since cognitions would be fixed to each perception, there would be no successive functioning. The successive functioning of these cognitions that operate upon objects in sequence would not be possible. And the contradiction would be —

children.text:
kavacid upalabdhihetuḥ, paścād upalabdhiviṣayaḥ, yathādityasya prakāśa utpadyamānānām/ kvacit pūrvam upalabdhiviṣayaḥ paścād upalabdhihetuḥ, yathāvasthitānāṃ pradīpaḥ/ kvacid upalabdhihetur upalabdhiviṣayaś ca saha bhvataḥ, yathā dhūmenāgner grahaṇam iti/ upalabdhihetuś ca pramāṇaṃ prameyaṃ tūpalabdhiviṣayaḥ/ evaṃ pramāṇaprameyayoḥ pūrvāparasahabhāve 'niyate yathārtho dṛśyate tathā vibhajya vacanīya iti tatraikāntena pratiṣedhānupapattiḥ, sāmānyena khalu vibhajya pratiṣedha ukta iti/
samākhyāhetos traikālyayogāt tathābhūtā samākhyā/ yat punar idaṃ paścāt siddhāv asati pramāṇe prameyaṃ na sidhyati, pramāṇena pramīyamāṇo 'rthaḥ prameyam iti vijñāyata iti/ pramāṇam ity etasyāḥ samākhyāyā upalabdhihetutvaṃ nimittam,
children.translated_text: In some cases, the cause of apprehension comes first and the object of apprehension afterwards, as the light of the sun for things coming into being. In some cases, the object of apprehension comes first and the cause of apprehension afterwards, as a lamp for things already present. In some cases, the cause and object of apprehension exist simultaneously, as the grasping of fire through smoke. The cause of apprehension is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, and the object of apprehension is the <s>prameya</s>. Thus, when there is no fixed rule regarding priority, posteriority, or simultaneity of <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s>, one must state distinctions according to how the object is seen — hence a blanket refutation is untenable, since the refutation was stated in general terms. Because of the applicability of the three times to the cause of designation, the designation is thus constituted. As for the argument that in the case of posteriority, without a <s>pramāṇa</s> the <s>prameya</s> is not established, and an object being measured by a <s>pramāṇa</s> is known as <s>prameya</s> — the basis for the designation '<s>pramāṇa</s>' is its being the cause of apprehension,

children.text: tasya traikālyayogaḥ/ upalabdhim akārṣīt, upalabdhiṃ karoti, upalabdhiṃ kariṣyatīti samākhyāhetos traikālyayogāt samākhyā tathābhūtā pramito 'nenārthaḥ pramīyate pramāsyata iti pramāṇam; pramitam, pramīyate, pramāsyate iti ca prameyam/ evaṃ sati bhaviṣyaty asmin hetuta upalabdhiḥ, pramāsyate 'yam arthaḥ prameyam idam ity etat sarvaṃ bhvatīti/ traikālyānabhyanujñāne ca vyavahārānupapattiḥ/ yaś caivaṃ nābhyanujānīyāt tasya pācakam ānaya pakṣyati lāvakam ānaya laviṣyatīti vyavahāro nopapadyata iti/
children.translated_text: and that has applicability to the three times. It made apprehension, it makes apprehension, it will make apprehension — because of the applicability of the three times to the cause of designation, the designation is thus constituted: that by which an object was measured, is measured, or will be measured is the <s>pramāṇa</s>; and that which was measured, is measured, or will be measured is the <s>prameya</s>. This being so, when this will be the cause of apprehension in the future — 'this object will be measured, this is the <s>prameya</s>' — all of this holds. And if the three times were not acknowledged, practical activity would be impossible. One who does not acknowledge this could not engage in such usage as 'bring the cook, he will cook' or 'bring the harvester, he will harvest.'
The invalidity of <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the rest, because of the impossibility of [their relation to] the three times

children.text: ity evamādi vākyaṃ pramāṇapratiṣedhaḥ/ tatrāyaṃ praṣṭavyaḥ, athānena pratiṣedhena bhavatā kiṃ kriyata iti? kiṃ sambhavo nivartyate athāsambhavo jñāpyate iti/
children.translated_text: — a statement of this kind is a refutation of the <s>pramāṇas</s>. Here one should ask: what does this refutation accomplish for you? Is a real possibility being negated, or is an impossibility being indicated?

children.text: tad yadi sambhavo nivartyate sati sambhave pratyakṣādīnāṃ pratiṣedhānupapattiḥ/ athāsambhavo jñāpyate, pramāṇalakṣaṇaṃ prāptas tarhi pratiṣedhaḥ pramāṇāsambhavasyopalabdhihetutvād iti//
children.translated_text: If a real possibility is being negated, then since <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the rest do exist, the refutation is untenable. If an impossibility is being indicated, then the refutation has attained the character of a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it is the cause of apprehension of the non-existence of <s>pramāṇas</s>.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 12
Moreover, what follows from this?
Because of the impossibility of [the relation to] the three times, the refutation is untenable. // 2.1.12 //

children.text: asya tu vibhāgaḥ/ pūrvaṃ hi pratiṣedhasiddhāv asati pratiṣedhye kim anena pratiṣidhyate paścāt siddhau pratiṣedhyāsiddhiḥ pratiṣedhābhāvād iti/ yugapatsiddhau pratiṣedhyasiddhyabhyanujñānād anarthakaḥ pratiṣedha iti/
children.translated_text: The analysis of this: If the refutation is established first, then since the object to be refuted does not yet exist, what is refuted by it? If established afterwards, then the object to be refuted is not established, since there is no refutation [at that point]. If established simultaneously, since the existence of the object to be refuted is acknowledged, the refutation is pointless.

children.text: pratiṣedhalakṣaṇe ca vākye 'nupapadyamāne siddhaṃ pratyakṣādīnāṃ pramāṇatvam iti//
children.translated_text: And when the statement having the character of a refutation is untenable, the validity of <s>pratyakṣa</s> and the rest as <s>pramāṇas</s> is established.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
How?
And because of the denial of all <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), the denial itself is untenable. // 2.1.13 //

children.text: traikālyāsiddher ity asya hetor yady udāharaṇam upādīyate hetvarthasya sādhakatvaṃ dṛṣṭānte darśayitavyam iti,
children.translated_text: If an example is adduced for the reason 'because of the non-establishment of the three times,' in order to show the probative force of the reason's meaning in the example,

children.text: na ca tarhi pratyakṣādīnām aprāmāṇyam/ atha pratyakṣādīnām aprāmāṇyam, upādīyamānam apy udāharaṇaṃ nārthaṃ sādhayiṣyatīti so 'yaṃ sarvapramāṇavyāhato hetur ahetuḥ;
children.translated_text: then indeed perception and the others are not invalid. On the other hand, if perception and the others are invalid, then even the example, though adduced, will not prove the thesis — thus this reason, being contradicted by all <s>pramāṇas</s>, is a non-reason;
'That which, having accepted a <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion), contradicts it, is <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory)'

children.text: iti/ vākyārtho hy asya siddhāntaḥ/ sa ca vākyārthaḥ pratyakṣādīni nārthaṃ sādhayantītīdaṃ cāvayavānām upādānam arthasya sādhanāyeti/ atha nopādīyate apradarśitaṃ hetvarthasya dṛṣṭāntena sādhakatvam iti niṣedho nopapadyate hetutvāsiddher iti//
children.translated_text: — thus. For the <s>siddhānta</s> here is the meaning of his own statement. And that meaning of the statement is: 'Perception and the others do not establish the object' — and [yet] this employment of the component parts [of inference] is for the establishment of an object. Now if [the example] is not adduced, then since the probative force of the reason's meaning has not been demonstrated through an example, the denial is untenable because the status of the reason is not established.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 14
Or, if those [means of knowledge] are valid, there is no contradiction of all <s>pramāṇas</s>. // 2.1.14 //

children.text: pratiṣedhalakṣaṇe svavākye teṣām avayavāśritānāṃ pratyakṣādīnāṃ prāmāṇye 'bhyanujñāyamāne paravākye 'py avayavāśritānāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ prasajyate 'viśeṣād iti/ evaṃ ca na sarvāṇi pramāṇāni pratiṣidhyanta iti/ vipratiṣedha iti vīty ayam upasargaḥ sampratipattyarthe, na vyāghāte 'rthābhāvād iti//
children.translated_text: If the validity of perception and the others — which are relied upon in the component parts of the opponent's own statement expressing denial — is conceded, then the validity of those relied upon in the component parts of another's statement also follows, since there is no difference. And thus not all <s>pramāṇas</s> are denied. [The word] '<s>vipratiṣedha</s>' — here the prefix 'vi' is used in the sense of agreement, not in the sense of contradiction, for [the latter] has no meaning [here].
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
And the non-denial of the three times, [is established] from sound, as in the case of the establishment of a musical instrument. // 2.1.15 //

children.text: kim arthaṃ punar idam ucyate? pūrvoktanibandhanārtham/ yat tāvat pūrvoktam upalabdhihetor upalabdhiviṣayasya cārthasya pūrvāparasahabhāvāniyamād yathādarśanaṃ vibhāgavacanam iti, tad itaḥ samutthānaṃ yathā vijñāyeta/ anityam adarśī khalv ayam ṛṣir niyamena pratiṣedhaṃ pratyācaṣṭe — traikālyasya cāyuktaḥ pratiṣedha iti/ tatraikāṃ vidhām udāharati śabdād ātodyasiddhivad iti/
children.translated_text: For what purpose is this stated again? For the purpose of [explaining] what was previously stated. That which was previously stated — 'since there is no fixed rule of temporal precedence, subsequence, or simultaneity between the cause of apprehension and the object of apprehension, the division is stated as observed' — this is stated so that one may understand its origin. This sage, who did not perceive impermanence, definitively rejects the denial — 'the denial of the three times is improper.' In this regard, he gives an example of one kind: 'from sound, as in the establishment of a musical instrument.'

children.text:
yathā paścāt siddhena śabdena pūrvasiddham ātodyam anumīyate, sādhyaṃ cātodyaṃ sādhanaṃ ca śabdaḥ, antarhite hy ātodye svanato 'numānaṃ bhavatīti vīṇā vādyate veṇuḥ pūryate iti svanaviśeṣeṇa ātodyaviśeṣaṃ pratipadyate; tathā pūrvasiddham upalabdhiviṣayaṃ paścāt siddhenopalabdhihetunā pratipadyata iti/ nidarśanārthatvāc cāsya śeṣayor vidhayor yathoktam udāharaṇaṃ veditavyam iti/
kasmāt punar iha tan nocyate? pūrvoktam upapādyata iti/ sarvathā tāvad ayam arthaḥ prakāśayitavyaḥ, sa iha vā prakāśyeta tatra vā, na kaścid viśeṣa iti//
children.translated_text:
Just as from sound, which is established later, a musical instrument established earlier is inferred — the instrument is what is to be proved and the sound is the means of proof, for when the instrument is hidden, inference proceeds from its sound, and one recognizes the specific instrument from the specific sound: 'a <s>vīṇā</s> is being played,' 'a flute is being blown' — so too, the object of apprehension, established earlier, is cognized through the cause of apprehension, established later. And since this serves as an illustration, the examples for the remaining two kinds should be understood as already stated.
Why then is that not stated here? Because what was previously stated is being substantiated. In any case, this meaning is to be made clear, whether it is elucidated here or there — there is no difference.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 16

children.text: pramāṇaṃ prameyam iti ca samākhyā samāveśena varttate samākhyānimittavaśāt/ samākhyānimittaṃ tūpalabdhisādhanaṃ pramāṇam upalabdhiviṣayaś ca prameyam iti/ yadā ca upalabdhiviṣayaḥ kvacid upalabdhisādhanaṃ bhavati tadā pramāṇaṃ prameyam iti caiko 'rtho 'bhidhīyate/ asyārthasyāvadyotanārtham idam ucyate —
children.translated_text: The designations '<s>pramāṇa</s>' (means of knowledge) and '<s>prameya</s>' (object of knowledge) operate by overlapping, due to the basis of the designations. The basis of the designation is: the means of apprehension is <s>pramāṇa</s> and the object of apprehension is <s>prameya</s>. And when the object of apprehension sometimes becomes the means of apprehension, then a single entity is designated as both <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s>. To illustrate this meaning, the following is stated —
And [the <s>pramāṇas</s>] are <s>prameya</s> (objects of knowledge), like the validity of a balance. // 2.1.16 //

children.text: gurutvaparimāṇajñānasādhanaṃ tulā pramāṇam, jñānaviṣayo guru dravyaṃ suvarṇādi prameyam/ yathā suvarṇādinā tulāntaraṃ vyavasthāpyate tadā tulāntarapratipattau suvarṇādi pramāṇam tulāntaraṃ prameyam iti/ evam anavayavena tantrārtha uddiṣṭo veditavyaḥ/ ātmā tāvad upalabdhiviṣayatvāt prameye paripaṭhitaḥ, upalabdhau svātantryāt pramātā/ buddhir upalabdhisādhanatvāt pramāṇam, upalabdhiviṣayatvāt prameyam; ubhayābhāvāt tu pramitiḥ/ evam arthaviśeṣe samākhyāsamāveśo yojyaḥ/ tathā ca kārakaśabdā nimittavaśāt samāveśena varttanta iti/
children.translated_text: A balance is a <s>pramāṇa</s> as the means of knowing weight and measure; the heavy substance such as gold etc. is the <s>prameya</s> as the object of knowledge. Just as when gold etc. is used to verify another balance, then in the cognition of the other balance, the gold etc. is the <s>pramāṇa</s> and the other balance is the <s>prameya</s>. Thus the teaching of the treatise should be understood without residue. The <s>ātman</s> (self), being an object of apprehension, is listed under <s>prameya</s>, [yet] being autonomous in apprehension, it is the knower. <s>Buddhi</s> (cognition), being a means of apprehension, is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, [yet] being an object of apprehension, it is <s>prameya</s>; but when both [functions] are absent, it is [simply] a cognition-event (<s>pramiti</s>). Thus the overlapping of designations should be applied to specific meanings. Likewise, <s>kāraka</s> (case-relation) words operate by overlapping due to the basis [of designation].

children.text: vṛkṣas tiṣṭhatīti svasthitau svātantryāt kartā/ vṛkṣaṃ paśyatīti darśanenāptum iṣyamāṇatamatvāt karma/
children.translated_text: 'A tree stands' — in standing on its own, due to its autonomy, it is the agent (<s>kartā</s>). 'He sees the tree' — since the tree is most desired to be attained through seeing, it is the object (<s>karma</s>).

children.text: vṛkṣeṇa candramasaṃ jñāpayatīti jñāpakasya sādhakatamatvāt karaṇam/
children.translated_text: 'He indicates the moon by means of the tree' — since the tree is most instrumental in indicating, it is the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>).

children.text: vṛkṣāyodakam āsiñcatīti āsicyamānenodakena vṛkṣam abhipraitīti sampradānam/ vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patatīti
children.translated_text: 'He pours water for the tree' — since he aims at the tree with the water being poured, it is the recipient (<s>sampradāna</s>). 'A leaf falls from the tree' —
'the fixed point in separation is <s>apādāna</s> (ablative source)'
— thus it is the <s>apādāna</s>. 'Birds are in the tree' —
'the support is <s>adhikaraṇa</s> (locative)'

children.text: ity adhikaraṇam/ evam ca sati na dravyamātraṃ kārakam, na kriyāmātram/ kiṃ tarhi? kriyāsādhanaṃ kriyāviśeṣayuktaṃ kārakam/ yat kriyāsādhanaṃ svatantram sa kartā, na dravyamātraṃ na kriyāmātram/ kriyayā vyāptum iṣyamāṇatamaṃ karma,
children.translated_text: — thus it is the <s>adhikaraṇa</s>. This being so, the <s>kāraka</s> is not mere substance, nor mere action. What then? A <s>kāraka</s> is that which is a means of accomplishing action and is qualified by a specific action. That which is an autonomous means of accomplishing action is the agent — neither mere substance nor mere action. The object is what is most desired to be attained through action,

children.text: na dravyamātraṃ na kryāmātram/ evaṃ sādhakatamādiṣv api/ evaṃ ca kārakānvākhyānaṃ yathaiva upapattita evaṃ lakṣaṇataḥ/ kārakānvākhyānam api na dravyamātre na kriyāyām vā/ kiṃ tarhi? kriyāsādhane kriyāviśeṣayukta iti/ kārakaśabdaś cāyaṃ pramāṇaṃ prameyam iti, sa ca kārakadharmaṃ na hātum arhati//16//
children.translated_text: neither mere substance nor mere action. The same applies to 'most instrumental' and the rest. And thus the analysis of <s>kārakas</s> applies equally from the standpoint of both logical reasoning and definition. The analysis of <s>kārakas</s> pertains neither to substance alone nor to action alone. What then? To the means of accomplishing action qualified by a specific action. And this <s>kāraka</s>-designation, [which is the same as] '<s>pramāṇa</s>' and '<s>prameya</s>,' should not abandon the nature of <s>kāraka</s>. // 16 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 17

children.text: asti bhoḥ kārakaśabdānāṃ nimittavaśāt samāveṣaḥ/ pratyakṣādīni ca pramāṇāni upalabdhihetutvāt, prameyaṃ copalabdhiviṣayatvāt/ saṃvedyāni ca pratyakṣādīni pramāṇāni, pratyakṣeṇopalabhe anumānenopalabhe upamānenopalabhe āgamenopalabhe/ pratyakṣaṃ me jñānam ānumānikaṃ me jñānam aupamānikaṃ me jñānam āgamikaṃ me jñānam iti viśeṣā gṛhyante/ lakṣaṇataś ca jñāpyamānāni jñāyante viśeṣeṇendriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānam ity evamādinā/
children.translated_text: Indeed, the <s>kāraka</s>-designations overlap due to the basis [of designation]. And perception and the others are <s>pramāṇas</s> because they are causes of apprehension, and [they are] <s>prameya</s> because they are objects of apprehension. And the <s>pramāṇas</s> — perception and the others — are knowable: apprehended through perception, apprehended through inference, apprehended through comparison, apprehended through verbal testimony. The specific cognitions are grasped: 'my knowledge is perceptual,' 'my knowledge is inferential,' 'my knowledge is analogical,' 'my knowledge is from scripture.' And they are known through their definitions — being made known through specifications such as 'cognition born of sense-object contact' and so on.

children.text: seyam upalabdhiḥ pratyakṣādiviṣayā kiṃ pramāṇāntarataḥ athāntareṇa pramāṇāntaram asādhaneti? kaś cātra viśeṣaḥ?
children.translated_text: Now, is this apprehension — which has perception and the others as its objects — from another <s>pramāṇa</s>, or without another <s>pramāṇa</s> and thus without proof? And what difference does it make?
If [the <s>pramāṇas</s>] are established through a [further] <s>pramāṇa</s>, then the consequence of [requiring] another <s>pramāṇa</s> for the <s>pramāṇas</s> [arises]. // 2.1.17 //

children.text: yadi pratyakṣādīni pramāṇenopalabhyante, yena pramāṇenopalabhyante tat pramāṇāntaram astīti pramāṇāntarasadbhāvaḥ prasajyata iti anavasthām āha tasyāpy anyena tasyāpy anyeneti/
children.translated_text: If perception and the others are apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, then another <s>pramāṇa</s> by which they are apprehended must exist — thus the existence of another <s>pramāṇa</s> follows. And he states the infinite regress: that [further <s>pramāṇa</s>] too by another, and that too by another.
And an infinite regress cannot be accepted, since it is untenable.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 18
Then let [the <s>pramāṇas</s> be] without proof, without another <s>pramāṇa</s>? —
Or, from the cessation of that [regress], the establishment of <s>prameya</s> (objects of knowledge) would be like the establishment of <s>pramāṇa</s>. // 2.1.18 //

children.text: yadi pratyakṣādyupalabdhau pramāṇāntaraṃ nivarttane ātmādyupalabdhāv api pramāṇāntaraṃ nivartsyaty aviśeṣāt//
children.translated_text: If another <s>pramāṇa</s> ceases [to be required] in the apprehension of perception and the others, then another <s>pramāṇa</s> will also cease [to be required] in the apprehension of the <s>ātman</s> and the rest, since there is no difference.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 19

children.text: evaṃ ca sarvapramāṇavilopa ity ata āha —
children.translated_text: And thus there would be the destruction of all <s>pramāṇas</s> — therefore he says —
Not so, because of [their] establishment like the illumination of a lamp. // 2.1.19 //

children.text: yathā pradīpaprakāśaḥ pratyakṣāṅgatvād dṛśyadarśane pramāṇam, sa ca pratyakṣāntareṇa cakṣuṣaḥ sannikarṣeṇa gṛhyate; pradīpabhāvābhāvayor darśanasya tathābhāvād darśanahetur anumīyate, tamasi pradīpam upādadīthā ity āptopadeśenāpi pratipadyate; evaṃ pratyakṣādīnāṃ yathādarśanaṃ pratyakṣādibhir evopalabdhiḥ/ indriyāṇi tāvat svaviṣayagrahaṇenaivānumīyante/ arthāḥ pratyakṣato gṛhyante/ indriyārthasannikarṣās tv āvaraṇena liṅgenānumīyante/
children.translated_text: Just as the light of a lamp, being a component of perception, is a <s>pramāṇa</s> for seeing the visible, and it is grasped by another perception through the contact of the eye; and since seeing obtains or does not obtain according to the presence or absence of the lamp, the lamp is inferred as the cause of seeing; and through the instruction of a reliable authority — 'bring a lamp in the darkness' — it is also known [through verbal testimony]; so too, the apprehension of perception and the others is through perception and the others themselves, according to what is observed. The sense organs, for their part, are inferred through the very grasping of their own objects. Objects are grasped through direct perception. And the contacts of sense organs and objects are inferred through the mark of obstruction.

children.text:
indriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānam ātmamanasoḥ saṃyogaviśeṣād ātmasamavayāc ca sukhādivad gṛhyate/ evaṃ pramāṇaviśeṣo vibhajya vacanīyaḥ/ yathā ca dṛśyaḥ san pradīpaprakāśo dṛśyāntarāṇāṃ darśanahetur iti dṛśyadarśanavyavasthāṃ labhate, evaṃ prameyaṃ sat kiñcid arthajātam upalabdhihetutvāt pramāṇaprameyavyvasthāṃ labhate/ seyaṃ pratyakṣādibhir eva pratyakṣādīnāṃ yathādarśanam upalabdhir na pramāṇāntarataḥ, na ca pramāṇam antareṇa niḥsādhaneti/
tenaiva tasyāgrahaṇam iti cet, na; arthabhedasya lakṣaṇasāmānyāt — pratyakṣādīnāṃ pratyakṣādibhir eva grahaṇam ity ayuktam, anyena hy anyasya grahaṇaṃ dṛṣṭam iti/ na, arthabhedasya lakṣaṇasāmānyāt — pratyakṣalakṣaṇenāneko 'rthaḥ saṃgṛhītas tatra kenacit kasyacid grahaṇam ity adoṣaḥ/ evam anumānādiṣv apīti/ yatoddhṛtenodakenāśayasthasya grahaṇam iti/
children.translated_text:
Cognition born of sense-object contact is grasped — like pleasure and the like — through a special conjunction of the <s>ātman</s> and the mind, and through inherence in the <s>ātman</s>. Thus the specific <s>pramāṇa</s> should be stated with discrimination. And just as the light of a lamp, being itself visible, is the cause of seeing other visible things, and thereby obtains the status of both visible and cause-of-seeing — so too, a certain class of objects, being <s>prameya</s> (knowable), obtains the status of both <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>prameya</s> because it is a cause of apprehension. Thus this apprehension of perception and the others is through perception and the others themselves as observed — not from another <s>pramāṇa</s>, and not without a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
If [one objects:] 'by the very same [<s>pramāṇa</s>], the non-grasping of it [itself would follow]' — No; because of the commonality of the definition despite the difference of objects. 'The grasping of perception and the others by perception and the others themselves is improper, for it is seen that one thing is grasped by another' — No; because of the commonality of the definition despite the difference of objects. Multiple objects are encompassed under the definition of perception; among them, one [instance] grasps another — there is no fault. The same applies to inference and the rest. Just as water drawn up [from a well] grasps [i.e., ascertains] the water remaining in the reservoir.

children.text: jñātṛmanasoś ca darśanāt — ahaṃ sukhī ahaṃ duḥkhī ceti tenaiva jñātrā tasyaiva grahaṇaṃ dṛśyate/
children.translated_text: And from the observation of the knower and the mind — 'I am happy,' 'I am unhappy' — by that very knower, the grasping of that very [self] is observed.
'The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind'

children.text:
iti ca tenaiva manasā tasyaivānumānaṃ dṛśyate, jñātur jñeyasya cābhedo grahaṇasya grāhyasya cābheda iti/
nimittabhedo 'treti cet samānam — na nimittāntareṇa vinā jñātā ātmānaṃ jānīte, na ca nimittāntareṇa vinā manasā mano gṛhyata iti samānam etat, pratyakṣādbhiḥ pratyakṣādīnāṃ grahaṃam ity atrāpy arthabhedo na gṛhyata iti/
pratyakṣādīnāṃ cāviṣayasyānupapatteḥ — yadi syāt kiṃcid arthajātaṃ pratyakṣādīnām aviṣayaḥ yat pratyakṣādibhir na śakyaṃ grahītum, tasya grahaṇāya pramāṇāntaram upādīyeta, tat tu na śakyaṃ kenacid upapādayitum iti/ pratyakṣādīnāṃ yathādarśanam evedaṃ sac cāsac ca sarvaṃ viṣaya iti//
children.translated_text:
— and thus by that very mind, the inference of that very [mind] is observed, since there is no difference between the knower and the known, nor between the grasper and the grasped.
If [one says] 'there is a difference of basis here' — the same [applies]: the knower does not know himself without another basis, nor is the mind grasped by the mind without another basis — this is the same [situation], so even in the case of 'perception and the others grasping perception and the others,' the difference of objects is not grasped.
And since [an object] outside the domain of perception and the others is untenable — if there were some class of objects that was not within the domain of perception and the others, that could not be grasped by perception and the others, then another <s>pramāṇa</s> would be needed for its grasping; but no one can demonstrate such [an object]. For perception and the others have as their domain everything that exists and does not exist, as observed.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 20

children.text: kvacin nivṛttidarśanād anivṛttidarśanāc ca kvacid anekāntaḥ // 2.1.20 //
children.translated_text: Because cessation is seen in some cases and non-cessation in other cases, [the argument is] inconclusive (<s>anekānta</s>). // 2.1.20 //

children.text:
kecit tu dṛṣṭāntam aparigṛhītaṃ hetunā viśeṣahetum antareṇa sādhyasādhanāyopādadate; yathā pradīpaprakāśaḥ pradīpāntaraprakāśam antareṇa gṛhyate tathā pramāṇāni pramāṇāntaram antareṇa gṛhyata iti/ sa cāyam —
yathā cāyaṃ prasaṅgo nivṛttidarśanāt pramāṇasādhāyopādīyate/ evaṃ prameyasādhanāyāpy upādeyo 'viśeṣahetutvāt — yathā ca sthālyādirūpagrahaṇe pradīpaprakāśaḥ prameyasādhanāyopādīyate,
children.translated_text:
However, some adduce an example without accepting it [properly] with the reason — without a specific differentiating reason — for proving the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved): 'Just as the light of a lamp is grasped without the light of another lamp, so too the <s>pramāṇas</s> are grasped without another <s>pramāṇa</s>.' And this —
just as this [lamp] analogy is adduced from the observation of cessation to prove [the self-sufficiency of] <s>pramāṇa</s>, so too it should be adduced to prove [the self-sufficiency of] <s>prameya</s>, since there is no differentiating reason — and just as the light of a lamp is adduced as a means of proving <s>prameya</s> in the grasping of the form of a pot and the like,

children.text: evaṃ pramāṇasādhāyāpy upādeyo viśeṣahetvabhāvāt, so 'yaṃ viśeṣahetuparigraham antareṇa dṛṣṭānta ekasmin pakṣe upādeyo na pratipakṣa ity anekāntaḥ/ ekasmiṃś ca pakṣe dṛṣṭānta ity anekānto viśeṣahetvabhāvād iti/
children.translated_text: so too it should be adduced for proving <s>pramāṇa</s>, since there is no differentiating reason. Thus this example, without accepting a differentiating reason, being adducible for one side and not the other, is inconclusive. And being an example for [only] one side, it is inconclusive due to the absence of a differentiating reason.

children.text:
viśeṣahetuparigrahe sati upasaṃhārābhyanujñānād apratiṣedhaḥ — viśeṣahetuparigṛhītas tu dṛṣṭānta ekasmin pakṣe upasaṃhriyamāṇo na śakyo 'nujñātum/ evaṃ ca saty anekānta ity ayaṃ pratiṣedho na bhavati/
pratyakṣādīnāṃ pratyakṣādibhir upalabdhāv anavastheti ced, na saṃvidviṣayanimittānām upalabdhyā vyavahāropapatteḥ — pratyakṣeṇārtham upalabhe, anumānenārtham upalabhe, upamānenārtham upalabhe, āgamenārtham upalabhe iti, pratyakṣaṃ me jñānam, ānumānikaṃ me jñānam, aupamānikaṃ me jñānam, āgamikaṃ me jñānam iti saṃvidviṣayaṃ saṃvinnimittaṃ copalabhamānasya dharmārthasukhāpavargaprayojanas tatpratyanīkaparivarjanaprayojanaś ca vyavahāra upapadyate, so 'yaṃ tāvaty eva nivartate/
% tāvaty eva nivartate]
children.translated_text: When a particular reason has been accepted, the non-prohibition [of the general thesis] follows from the admission of the restriction — but a particular reason that has been accepted, when restricted to one instance, cannot be admitted [as universal]. And when this is the case, the objection 'this is inconclusive' does not arise. If [it is objected that] the apprehension of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and the rest by [other instances of] perception and the rest leads to an infinite regress — no, because practical activity is established through the apprehension of that whose objects are cognitions and whose causes are cognitions. 'I apprehend the object through perception,' 'I apprehend the object through inference,' 'I apprehend the object through comparison,' 'I apprehend the object through verbal testimony'; 'my knowledge is perceptual,' 'my knowledge is inferential,' 'my knowledge is comparative,' 'my knowledge is from testimony' — for one who apprehends both the object of cognition and the cause of cognition, practical activity aimed at <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s> (wealth), <s>sukha</s> (pleasure), and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), as well as the avoidance of their opposites, is established; and this [process] terminates at just that point.

children.text: na cāsti vyavahārāntaram anavasthāsādhanīyaṃ yena pratyuktānavasthām upādadīteti//20//
children.translated_text: There is no further practical activity that requires an infinite regress, by means of which one could posit the [alleged] infinite regress as unanswered. // 20 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 21

children.text: sāmānyena pramāṇāni parīkṣya viśeṣeṇa parīkṣyante/ tatra —
children.translated_text: Having examined the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) in general, they are now examined in particular. Of these —
The definition of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is inapplicable because the statement [of the definition] is incomplete. // 2.1.21 //
For the contact of <s>ātman</s> (self) and <s>manas</s> (mind) — another causal condition — has not been stated. // 21 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 22

children.text: na cāsaṃyukte dravye saṃyogajanyasya guṇasyotpattir iti jñānotpattidarśanād ātmamanaḥsannikarṣaḥ kāraṇam/
children.translated_text: And since a quality born from conjunction cannot arise in a substance that is not in conjunction, from the observed arising of cognition, the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is [indeed] a cause.

children.text: manaḥsannikarṣānapekṣasya cendriyārthasannikarṣasya jñānakāraṇatve yugapad utpadyeran buddhaya iti manaḥsannikarṣo 'pi kāraṇam/ tad idaṃ sūtraṃ purastāt kṛtabhāṣyam/
children.translated_text: And if the contact of sense-organ and object were the cause of cognition without depending on the contact with <s>manas</s>, cognitions would arise simultaneously — therefore the contact with <s>manas</s> is also a cause. This <s>sūtra</s> has been commented upon earlier.
Without the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, perception does not arise. // 2.1.22 //

children.text: ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣābhāve notpadyate pratyakṣam indriyārthasannikarṣābhāvavad iti//22//
children.translated_text: Without the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, perception does not arise — just as [it does not arise] without the contact of sense-organ and object. // 22 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 23
To one who claims causal status [for sense-object contact] on the ground that cognition is observed to arise when sense-object contact exists —
The same consequence applies to direction, place, time, and <s>ākāśa</s> (space) as well. // 2.1.23 //

children.text: digādiṣu satsu jñānabhāvāt tāny api kāraṇānīti? akāraṇabhāve 'pi jñānotpattir digādisannidher avarjanīyatvāt — yadāpy akāraṇaṃ digādīni jñānotpattau, tadāpi satsu digādiṣu jñānena bhavitavyam,
children.translated_text: Since cognition exists when direction and the rest exist, are they too causes? Even if they are not causes, cognition arises — because the presence of direction and the rest is unavoidable. Even when direction and the rest are not causes of the arising of cognition, cognition must occur when direction and the rest are present,

children.text: na hi digādīnāṃ sannidhiḥ śakyaḥ parivarjayitum iti/ tatra kāraṇabhāve hetuvacanam, etasmād dhetor digādīni jñānakāraṇānīti//23//
children.translated_text: for the presence of direction and the rest cannot be avoided. In this regard, the statement of the reason [is as follows:] 'by this reason, direction and the rest are causes of cognition.' // 23 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 24

children.text: ātmamanaḥsannikarṣas tarhy upasaṅkhyeya iti/ tatredam ucyate —
children.translated_text: Then the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> should be additionally enumerated [in the definition]. To this it is said —
Because cognition is a mark of the <s>ātman</s>, there is no exclusion [of ātman-manas contact]. // 2.1.24 //

children.text: jñānam ātmaliṅgaṃ tadguṇatvāt/ na cāsaṃyukte dravye saṃyogajasya guṇasyotpattir astīti//24//
children.translated_text: Cognition is a mark of the <s>ātman</s> because it is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. And a quality born of conjunction cannot arise in a substance that is not in conjunction. // 24 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 25
And because the non-simultaneous arising [of cognitions] is a mark of <s>manas</s>, there is no [exclusion] of <s>manas</s> either. // 2.1.25 //

children.text: anavarodha iti varttate/ yugapaj jñānānutpattir manaso liṅgam ity ucyamāne sidhyaty eva manaḥsannikarṣāpekṣa indriyārthasannikarṣo jñānakāraṇam iti//25//
children.translated_text: 'No exclusion' continues [from the previous sūtra]. When it is said that the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of <s>manas</s>, it is thereby established that the contact of sense-organ and object, as dependent on the contact with <s>manas</s>, is the cause of cognition. // 25 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 26
And because [sense-object contact] is the specific cause of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), it is stated by its own term. // 2.1.26 //

children.text: pratyakṣānumānopamānaśabdānāṃ nimittam ātmamanaḥsannikarṣaḥ, pratyakṣasyaivendriyārthasannikarṣa ity asamānaḥ, asamānatvāt tasya grahaṇam//26//
children.translated_text: The contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is the cause of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>upamāna</s> (comparison), and <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) [alike]; but the contact of sense-organ and object is [the specific cause] of perception alone — it is non-common. Because of its non-common nature, it is mentioned [in the definition]. // 26 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
And because [sense-object contact] is the cause [of cognition] even for those who are asleep or whose minds are engaged [elsewhere]. // 2.1.27 //

children.text:
indriyārthasannikarṣasya grahaṇaṃ nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasyeti/ ekadā khalv ayaṃ prabodhakālaṃ praṇidhāya suptaḥ praṇidhānavaśāt prabudhyate/ yadā tu tīvrau dhvanisparśau prabodhakāraṇaṃ bhavatas tadā prasuptasyendriyasannikarṣanimittaṃ prabodhajñānam utpadyate/ tatra na jñātur manasaś ca sannikarṣasya prādhānyaṃ bhavati/ kiṃ tarhi? indriyārthayoḥ sannikarṣasya/ na hy ātmā jijñāsamānaḥ prayatnena manas tadā prerayatīti/
ekadā khalv ayaṃ viṣayāntarāsaktamanāḥ saṅkalpavaśād viṣayāntaraṃ jijñāsamānaḥ prayatnapreritena manasā indriyaṃ saṃyojya tad viṣayāntaraṃ jānīte/ yadā tu khalv asya niḥsaṅkalpasya nirjijñāsasya ca vyāsaktamanaso bāhyaviṣayopanipātanāj jñānam utpadyate tadendriyārthasannikarṣasya prādhānyam/
children.translated_text: The mention [in the definition] is of the contact of sense-organ and object, not of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>. Now, sometimes a person, having fixed upon a time of awakening, sleeps and wakes by the force of that resolution. But when intense sound or touch becomes the cause of awakening, then for the sleeping person, a cognition of awakening arises caused by the contact of the sense-organ [with its object]. In that case, the predominance does not belong to the contact of the knower with <s>manas</s>; rather, [it belongs] to the contact of sense-organ and object. For the <s>ātman</s>, desiring to know, does not at that time impel the <s>manas</s> through effort. Sometimes, when the mind is engaged with another object, the person, desiring to know yet another object through volition, connects the sense-organ with that other object by means of <s>manas</s> impelled by effort and thereby knows it. But when, for one without volition, without desire to know, and with mind engaged [elsewhere], cognition arises from the intrusion of an external object — then the predominance belongs to the contact of sense-organ and object.

children.text: na hy atrāsau jijñāsamānaḥ prayatnena manaḥ prerayatīti/ prādhānyāc cendriyārthasannikarṣasya grahaṇaṃ kāryaṃ guṇatvād nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasyeti//27//
children.translated_text: For in this case, he does not impel the <s>manas</s> through effort with a desire to know. And because of the predominance of sense-object contact, its mention [in the definition] is required; the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, being subsidiary, [need not be mentioned]. // 27 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
And there is another reason for the predominance [of sense-object contact] —
And it is by those [sense-organs and objects] that particular cognitions are designated. // 2.1.28 //

children.text: tair indriyair arthaiś ca vyapadiśyante jñānaviśeṣāḥ/ katham? ghrāṇena jighrati, cakṣuṣā paśyati, rasanayā rasayatīti, ghrāṇavijñānaṃ cakṣurvijñānaṃ rasanāvijñānaṃ gandhavijñānaṃ rūpavijñānaṃ rasavijñānam iti ca/ indriyaviṣayaviśeṣāc ca pañcadhā buddhir bhavati/ ataḥ prādhānyam indriyārthasannikarṣasyeti//28//
children.translated_text: Particular cognitions are designated by those sense-organs and objects. How? 'One smells with the nose,' 'one sees with the eye,' 'one tastes with the tongue'; 'olfactory cognition,' 'visual cognition,' 'gustatory cognition,' 'cognition of odor,' 'cognition of form,' 'cognition of taste' — thus. And because of the differentiation of sense-organs and objects, cognition is fivefold. Therefore, the contact of sense-organ and object is predominant. // 28 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 29

children.text: yad uktam indriyārthasannikarṣagrahaṇaṃ kāryam, nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasyeti, kasmāt? suptavyāsaktamanasām indriyārthayoḥ sannikarṣasya jñānanimittatvād iti/ so 'yam —
children.translated_text: It was said that the mention [in the definition] should be of sense-object contact, not of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>. Why? Because for those who are asleep or whose minds are engaged [elsewhere], the contact of sense-organ and object is the cause of cognition. Now this [argument] —
Is not a [valid] reason, because it is self-contradictory. // 2.1.29 //

children.text: yadi tāvat kvacid ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasya jñānakāraṇatvaṃ neṣyate, tadā

children.translated_text: 'the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of <s>manas</s>'

children.text: iti vyāhanyeta/ nedānīṃ manasaḥ sannikarṣam indriyārthasannikarṣo 'pekṣate/
children.translated_text: — this would be contradicted. The contact of sense-organ and object would then not depend on the contact of <s>manas</s>.
If the causal nature of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> for cognition is denied in some cases, then
[Variant reading: '...the contact of sense-organ and object does not depend [on manas].']

children.text: manaḥsaṃyogānapekṣāyāṃ ca yugapajjñānotpattiprasaṅgaḥ/ atha mā bhūd vyāghāta iti sarvavijñānānām ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣaḥ kāraṇam iṣyate, tadavastham evedaṃ bhavati; jñānakāraṇatvād ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasya grahaṇaṃ kāryam iti//29//
children.translated_text: And if the dependence on the conjunction with <s>manas</s> is denied, the consequence would be the simultaneous arising of cognitions. But if, to avoid the contradiction, the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is accepted as the cause of all cognitions, then the situation remains the same: because the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is a cause of cognition, its mention [in the definition] should be required. // 29 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
[There is] no [self-contradiction], because of the predominance of particular objects. // 2.1.30 //

children.text: nāsti vyāghātaḥ, na hy ātmamanaḥsannikarṣasya jñānakāraṇatvaṃ vyabhicarati/ indriyārthasannikarṣasya prādhānyam upādīyate/ arthaviśeṣaprābalyād dhi suptavyāsaktamanasāṃ jñānotpattir ekadā bhavati/ arthaviśeṣaḥ kaścid evendriyārthaḥ, tasya prābalyaṃ tīvratāpaṭute/ tac cārthaviśeṣaprābalyam indriyārthasannikarṣaviṣayaṃ nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣaviṣayam, tasmād indriyārthasannikarṣaḥ pradhānam iti/
children.translated_text: There is no self-contradiction, for the causal nature of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> for cognition is not deviated from. The predominance of sense-object contact is what is maintained. For it is due to the predominance of a particular object that cognition sometimes arises for those who are asleep or whose minds are engaged. A 'particular object' is a certain sense-object; its 'predominance' is its intensity and acuteness. And that predominance of the particular object pertains to the domain of sense-object contact, not to the domain of <s>ātman</s>-<s>manas</s> contact. Therefore, the contact of sense-organ and object is predominant.

children.text:
asati praṇidhāne saṅkalpe cāsati suptavyāsaktamanasāṃ yad indriyārthasannikarṣād utpadyate jñānam, tatra manaḥsaṃyogo 'pi kāraṇam iti manasi kriyākāraṇaṃ vācyam iti/
yathaiva jñātuḥ khalv ayam icchājanitaḥ prayatno manasaḥ preraka ātmaguṇaḥ, evam ātmani guṇāntaraṃ sarvasya sādhakaṃ pravṛttidoṣajanitam asti, yena preritaṃ mana indriyeṇa sambadhyate/ tena hy apreryamāṇe manasi saṃyogābhāvāj jñānānutpattau sarvārthatāsya nivarttate/ eṣitavyaṃ cāsya guṇāntarasya dravyaguṇakarmakāraṇatvam, anyathā hi caturvidhānām aṇūnāṃ bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṃ manasāṃ ca tato 'nyasya kriyāhetor asambhavāt śarīrendriyaviṣayāṇām anutpattiprasaṅgaḥ//30//
children.translated_text: When, in the absence of resolution or volition, cognition arises for those who are asleep or whose minds are engaged from the contact of sense-organ and object, even then the conjunction with <s>manas</s> is a cause — and thus the operative cause regarding <s>manas</s> must be stated. Just as the effort born of desire in the knower is a quality of the <s>ātman</s> that impels the <s>manas</s>, so too there exists in the <s>ātman</s> another quality, born of the defects that drive activity, which accomplishes all [this], and by which the impelled <s>manas</s> conjoins with the sense-organ. For when <s>manas</s> is not impelled, the non-arising of cognition due to the absence of conjunction would negate its all-object nature. And the capacity of this other quality to cause substance, quality, and action must be investigated; otherwise, given the impossibility of another cause of motion besides the four types of atoms, subtle elements, and minds, the consequence would be the non-arising of body, sense-organs, and objects. // 30 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 31
Perception is [really] inference, because apprehension is based on the grasping of one part only. // 2.1.31 //

children.text: yad idam indriyārthasannikarṣād utpadyate jñānaṃ vṛkṣa iti, etat kila pratyakṣam, tat khalv anumānam eva/ kasmāt? ekadeśagrahaṇād vṛkṣasyopalabdheḥ/ arvāgbhāgam ayaṃ gṛhītvā vṛkṣam upalabhate/ na caikadeśo vṛkṣaḥ/ tatra yathā dhūmaṃ gṛhītvā vahnim anuminoti tādṛg eva tad bhavati/
children.translated_text: This cognition 'it is a tree' that arises from the contact of sense-organ and object — this is supposedly perception. But it is really just inference. Why? Because the apprehension of the tree is based on the grasping of one part [only]. One grasps the front part and [then] apprehends the tree. But one part is not the tree [as a whole]. Therefore, just as one grasps smoke and infers fire, the case is exactly the same.

children.text: kiṃ punar gṛhyamāṇād ekadeśād arthāntaram anumeyaṃ manyase? avayavasamūhapakṣe avayavāntarāṇi dravyāntarotpattipakṣe tāni cāvavavī ceti/ avayavasamūhapakṣe tāvad ekadeśagrahaṇād vṛkṣabuddher abhāvaḥ, nāgṛhyamāṇam ekadeśāntaraṃ vṛkṣo gṛhyamāṇaikadeśavad iti/
children.translated_text: Do you then think that what is to be inferred is something other than the part being grasped? On the view that [the whole] is a collection of parts, [the inference would be of] the other parts; on the view that a new substance arises [from the parts], [the inference would be of] those [parts] as well as the whole. On the collection-of-parts view, then, since one part alone does not give rise to the cognition 'tree,' the other part that is not grasped is not [apprehended] in the same way as the part being grasped.

children.text: athaikadeśagrahaṇād ekadeśāntarānumāne samudāyapratisandhānāt tatra vṛkṣabuddhiḥ? na tarhi vṛkṣabuddhir anumānam evaṃ sati bhavitum arhatīti/
children.translated_text: But if from the grasping of one part, the other parts are inferred, and from the mental synthesis of the collection the cognition 'tree' arises — then the cognition 'tree' cannot, under this scenario, be [merely] inference.

children.text: dravyāntarotpattipakṣe nāvayavyanumeyaḥ, asyaikadeśasambaddhasyāgrahaṇāt grahaṇe cāviśeṣād anumeyatvābhāvaḥ/ tasmād vṛkṣabuddhir anumānaṃ na bhavati//31//
children.translated_text: On the view that a new substance arises [from parts], the whole is not inferred, because [the whole] is connected with the one part [being grasped] and its non-grasping [would mean that] if it were grasped there would be no distinction — hence no inferability. Therefore, the cognition 'tree' is not inference. // 31 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 32

children.text: ekadeśagrahaṇam āśritya pratyakṣasyānumānatvam upapādyate/ tac ca —
children.translated_text: Relying on the grasping of one part, the status of perception as inference is being argued. But that —

children.text: na, pratyakṣeṇa yāvat tāvad apy upalambhāt // 2.1.32 //
children.translated_text: No, because there is apprehension by perception of as much as [is grasped]. // 2.1.32 //

children.text:
na pratyakṣam anumānam, kasmāt? pratyakṣeṇaivopalambhāt/ yat tadekadeśagrahaṇam āśrīyate pratyakṣeṇāsāv upalambhaḥ/ na copalambho nirviṣayo 'sti/ yāvac cārthajātaṃ tasya viṣayas tāvad abhyupajñāyamānaṃ pratyakṣavyavasthāpakaṃ bhavati/
kiṃ punas tato 'nyad arthajātam, avayavī samudāyo vā? na caikadeśagrahaṇam anumānaṃ bhāvayituṃ śakyaṃ hetvabhāvād iti/
