children.translated_text: Perception is not inference. Why? Because apprehension is by perception itself. That grasping of one part which is relied upon — that apprehension is by perception. And apprehension is not without an object. And whatever class of objects constitutes its domain — that, when acknowledged, establishes the status of perception. Now, is there some other class of objects — either a whole or a collection — [beyond what is grasped]? The grasping of one part cannot be made into inference, because there is no [inferential] reason.

children.text: anyathāpi ca pratyakṣasya nānumānatvaprasaṅgas tatpūrvakatvāt — pratyakṣapūrvakam anumānam, sambaddhāv agnidhūmau pratyakṣato dṛṣṭavato dhūmapratyakṣadarśanād agnāv anumānaṃ bhavati/ yac ca sambaddhayor liṅgaliṅginoḥ pratyakṣam, yac ca liṅgamātrapratyakṣagrahaṇam, naitad antareṇa anumānasya pravṛttir asti; na tv etad anumānam indriyārthasannikarṣajatvāt/ na cānumeyasyendriyeṇa sannikarṣād anumānaṃ bhavati/ so 'ya. pratyakṣānumānayor lakṣaṇabhedo mahān āśrayitavya iti/
children.translated_text: And there is yet another reason why perception cannot have the status of inference — because [inference] is preceded by that [perception]. Inference is preceded by perception: one who has seen the connection of fire and smoke through perception, upon perceiving smoke, makes an inference about fire. Both the perception of the connected mark and thing-possessing-the-mark, and the perceptual grasping of the mark alone — without these, inference cannot proceed. But this [grasping] is not inference, because it arises from the contact of sense-organ and object. And inference does not arise from the contact of the sense-organ with the thing to be inferred. This great distinction in the definitions of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference) must be maintained.

children.text:
na caikadeśopalabdhir avayavisadbhāvāt/ na caikadeśopalabdhimātram/ kiṃ tarhi? ekadeśopalabdhiḥ tatsahacaritāvayavyupalabdhiś ca/ kasmāt? avayavisadbhāvāt/ asti hy ayam ekadeśavyatirikto 'vayavī tasyāvayavasthānasyopalabdhikāraṇaprāptasyaikadeśopalabdhāv anupalabdhir anupapanneti/
akṛtsnagrahaṇād iti cet, na kāraṇato 'nyasyaikadeśasyābhāvāt — na cāvayavāḥ kṛtsnā gṛhyante avayavair evāvayavāntaravyavadhānāt,
children.translated_text:
Nor is it merely the perception of one part. What then? It is the perception of one part accompanied by the perception of the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) that coexists with it. Why? Because the composite whole exists. For this composite whole, which is different from the part and which has met the conditions for perception at that place of the parts, its non-perception when the part is perceived would be untenable.
If [one objects] that it is due to incomplete apprehension — no, because apart from the causes [of perception], there is no other 'part' of the composite. Nor are the parts completely apprehended, since parts are separated from other parts by intervening parts,

children.text:
nāvayavī kṛtsno gṛhyata iti, nāyaṃ gṛhyamnāṇeṣv avayaveṣu parisamāpta iti, seyam ekaddeśopalabdhir anivṛttaiveti/
kṛtsnam iti vai khalv aśeṣatāyāṃ satyāṃ bhavati, akṛtsnam iti śeṣe sati, tac caitad avayaveṣu bahuṣv asti avyavadhāne grahaṇād vyavadhāne cāgrahaṇād iti/ aṅga tu bhavān pṛṣṭo vyācaṣṭāṃ gṛhyamāṇasyāvayavinaḥ kim agṛhītaṃ manyate?
children.translated_text:
nor is the composite whole completely apprehended — so it has not been exhausted among the parts being apprehended, and thus this is just the perception of one part, unresolved.
Now, 'complete' applies when there is totality, and 'incomplete' when there is a remainder; and this obtains among the many parts — some being apprehended because they are not obscured, and others not apprehended because they are obscured. But let your honor, when asked, explain — of the composite whole being apprehended, what does he consider not apprehended

children.text: yenaikadeśopalabdhiḥ syād iti/ na hy asya kāraṇebhyo 'nye ekadeśā bhavantīti tatrāvayavavṛttaṃ nopapadyata iti/
children.translated_text: such that there would be the perception of merely one part? For the composite has no parts other than its causes; therefore, being located in the parts cannot be maintained for it.

children.text: idaṃ tasya vṛttam — yeṣām indriyasannikarṣād grahaṇam avayavānāṃ taiḥ saha gṛhyate, yeṣām avayavānāṃ vyavadhānād agrahaṇaṃ taiḥ saha na gṛhyate/ na caitatkṛto 'sti bheda iti/
children.translated_text: This is its mode of being located: it is apprehended together with those parts that are apprehended through sense-contact, and it is not apprehended together with those parts that are not apprehended because of obstruction. And this does not create a difference [in the composite itself].

children.text: samudāyaśeṣatā vā samudāyo vṛkṣaḥ syāt tatprāptir vā, ubhayathā grahaṇābhāvaḥ/ mūlaskandhaśākhāpalāśādīnām aśeṣatā vā samudāyo vṛkṣa iti syāt prāptir vā samudāyinām iti, ubhayathā samudāyabhūtasya vṛkṣasya grahaṇaṃ nopapadyata iti/ avayavais tāvad avayavāntarasya vyavadhānād aśeṣagrahaṇaṃ nopapadyate/ prāptigrahaṇam api nopapadyate prāptimatām agrahaṇāt/ seyam ekadeśagrahaṇasahacaritā vṛkṣavuddhir dravyāntarotpattau kalpate na samudayamātre iti//32//
children.translated_text: Either the aggregate is the totality or the aggregate is [identical with] the tree, or else the aggregate is a relation [to the parts] — in both ways, there is no apprehension [of the tree]. Whether the tree is the totality of roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and the like, or a relation among the members of the aggregate — in both cases, the apprehension of the tree as the aggregate is untenable. For the complete apprehension of parts is untenable, since some parts are obscured by others. The apprehension of the relation is also untenable, since the relata themselves are not [all] apprehended. Therefore this cognition of the tree, accompanied by the perception of one part [only], is appropriate if there is the origination of a distinct substance, not if there is a mere aggregate. //32//
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 33
Because [the existence of] the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is what is to be proved, there is doubt. // 2.1.33 //

children.text: yad uktam avayavisadhbāvād iti, ayam ahetuḥ sādhyatvāt/ sādhyaṃ tāvad etat kāraṇebhyo dravyāntaram utpadyata iti, anupapāditam etat/ evaṃ ca sati vipratipattimātraṃ bhavati vipratipatteś cāvayavini saṃśaya iti//33//
children.translated_text: The statement 'because the composite whole exists' — this is not a valid reason, because it is what is to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>). For this — that a distinct substance is produced from its causes — is precisely what is to be established, and it has not been demonstrated. This being so, there is merely a disagreement, and from the disagreement there is doubt regarding the composite whole. //33//
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 34
If the composite whole does not exist, nothing at all can be apprehended. // 2.1.34 //

children.text: yady avayavī nāsti sarvasya grahaṇaṃ nopapadyate/ kiṃ tat sarvam? dravyaguṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyāḥ/ kathaṃ kṛtvā? paramāṇusamavasthānaṃ tāvad darśanaviṣayo na bhavaty atīndriyatvād aṇūnām, dravyāntarañ cāvayavibhūtaṃ darśanaviṣayo nāsti, darśanaviṣayasthāś ceme dravyādayo gṛhante te niradhiṣṭhānā na gṛhyeran/ gṛhyante tu kumbho 'yaṃ śyāma eko mahān saṃyuktaḥ spandate asti mṛnmayaś ceti, santi ceme guṇādayo dharmā iti/ tena sarvasya grahaṇāt paśyāmo 'sti dravyāntarabhūto .vayavīti//34//
children.translated_text: If the composite whole does not exist, the apprehension of anything is untenable. What is this 'anything'? <s>Dravya</s> (substance), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence). How so? First, the configuration of atoms is not an object of sight, because atoms are beyond the senses. Nor is a distinct substance, being a composite whole, an object of sight [if the composite is denied]. And these substances and the rest that are objects of sight are apprehended [only as residing in a substratum]; if they had no substratum, they would not be apprehended. But they are apprehended — 'this is a pot, dark, one, large, conjoined, it moves, it exists, it is made of clay' — and these are qualities and other properties. Therefore, from the apprehension of everything, we see that the composite whole exists as a distinct substance. //34//
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 35
And because of the tenable explanation of holding (<s>dhāraṇa</s>) and pulling (<s>ākarṣaṇa</s>). // 2.1.35 //

children.text:
avayavy arthāntarabhūta iti/
saṅgrahakārite vai dhāraṇākarṣaṇe/ saṃgraho nāma saṃyogasahacaritaṃ guṇāntaraṃ snehadravatvakāritam, apāṃ saṃyogād āme kumbhe, agnisaṃyogāt pakve/ yadi tv avayavikārite abhaviṣyatāṃ pāṃśurāśiprabhṛtiśv apy ajñāsyetām/ dravyāntarānutpattau ca tṛṇopalakāṣṭhādiṣu jatusaṃgṛhīteṣv api nābhāviṣyatām iti/
children.translated_text:
The composite whole is a distinct entity.
Holding and pulling are indeed caused by cohesion (<s>saṃgraha</s>). Cohesion is a quality other [than conjunction], accompanied by conjunction, caused by viscosity and fluidity — [it occurs] in a raw pot through contact with water, and in a baked one through contact with fire. If, however, these were caused by the composite whole, they should also be known in heaps of sand and the like. And if no distinct substance is produced, they would not exist even in sticks, stones, and wood held together by lac.

children.text: athāvayavinaṃ pratyācakṣāṇako mā bhūt pratyakṣalopa ity aṇusañcayaṃ darśanaviṣayaṃ pratijānānaḥ kim anuyoktavya iti/ ekam idaṃ dravyam ity ekavuddher viṣayaṃ paryanuyojyaḥ — kim ekabuddhir abhinnārthaviṣayeti āhosvit bhinnārthaviṣayeti/ abhinnārthaviṣayeti cet —
children.translated_text: Moreover, one who denies the composite whole, while asserting that the aggregate of atoms is the object of sight — lest direct perception be lost — should be questioned as follows regarding the object of the cognition 'this is one substance': Is the cognition of oneness directed at an undifferentiated object, or at a differentiated object? If directed at an undifferentiated object —

children.text: arthāntarānujñānād avayavavisiddhiḥ/ nānārthaviṣayeti cet — bhinneṣv ekadarśanānupapattiḥ anekasminn eka iti vyāhatā buddhir na dṛśyata iti//35//
children.translated_text: then by acknowledging a distinct entity, the composite whole is established. If directed at a differentiated object — then the cognition of one in many is contradictory and is not observed, for the cognition 'one in many' is self-contradictory. //35//
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 36

children.text: senāvanavat grahaṇam iti cen nātīndriyatvād aṇūnām // 2.1.36 //
children.translated_text: If it is said that apprehension is like that of an army or a forest — no, because atoms are beyond the senses. // 2.1.36 //

children.text: yathā senāṅgeṣu vanāṅgeṣu ca dūrād agṛhyamāṇapṛthaktveṣv ekam idam ity upapadyate buddhiḥ evam aṇuṣu sañciteṣv agṛhyamāṇapṛthaktveṣv ekam idam ity upapadyate buddhir iti/ yathā gṛhyamāṇapṛthaktvānāṃ senāvanāṅgānām ārāt kāraṇāntarataḥ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇam,
children.translated_text: Just as, when the separateness of the members of an army or forest is not apprehended from a distance, the cognition 'this is one' is reasonable, so too, when the separateness of aggregated atoms is not apprehended, the cognition 'this is one' is reasonable — so the objection. [The reply:] Just as for the members of an army or forest, whose separateness is [in principle] apprehensible, the non-apprehension of separateness from afar is due to another cause [namely distance],

children.text: yathā gṛhyamāṇajātīnāṃ palāśa iti vā khadira iti vā nārāj jātigrahaṇaṃ bhavati/ yathā gṛhyamāṇapraspandānāṃ nārāt spandagrahaṇam, gṛhyamāṇe cārthajāte pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād ekam iti bhāktaḥ pratyayo bhavati, na tv aṇūnāṃ gṛhyamāṇapṛthaktvānāṃ kāraṇataḥ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād bhākta ekapratyayaḥ, atīndriyatvād aṇūnām iti/
children.translated_text: just as for trees whose class is apprehensible — whether <s>palāśa</s> or <s>khadira</s> — the apprehension of their class does not occur from a distance; just as for things whose motion is apprehensible, the apprehension of motion does not occur from afar; and because the separateness is not apprehended even though the objects are apprehended, the cognition 'one' is figurative — but it is not the case that for atoms whose separateness is [in principle] apprehensible, the non-apprehension of separateness is due to another cause and hence the 'one' cognition is figurative — because atoms are beyond the senses.

children.text:
idam eva ca parīkṣyate kim ekapratyayo ṇusañcayaviṣaya āhosvit neti, aṇusañcaya eva senāvanāṅāni/ na ca parīkṣyamāṇam udāharaṇam iti yuktaṃ sādhyatvād iti/
dṛṣṭam iti cen na tadviṣayasya parīkṣopapatteḥ/ yad api manyeta dṛṣṭam idaṃ senāvanāṅgānāṃ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād abhedenaikam iti grahaṇam, na ca dṛṣṭaṃ śakyaṃ pratyākhyātum iti, tac ca naivam, tadviṣayasya parīkṣopapatteḥ — darśanaviṣaya evāyaṃ parīkṣyate yo 'yam ekam iti pratyayo dṛśyate, sa parīkṣyate kiṃ dravyāntaraviṣayo vā athāṇusañcayaviṣaya iti/ atra darśanam anyatarasya sādhakaṃ na bhavati/ nānābhāve cāṇūnāṃ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād abhedenaikam iti grahaṇam atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayaḥ, yathā sthāṇau puruṣa iti/ tataḥ kim?
children.translated_text:
And this is precisely what is being examined: whether the cognition of 'one' has the aggregate of atoms as its object or not; the aggregate of atoms is [analogous to] the members of an army or forest. And it is not proper to use what is under examination as an example, since it is what is to be proved.
If [one says] 'it is observed' — no, because it is possible to examine the object of that [observation]. Even if one thinks it is observed that, due to the non-apprehension of the separateness of army or forest members, there is the apprehension as one through non-differentiation, and that what is observed cannot be denied — that is not so, because it is possible to examine the object of that [observation]: this very observable thing is being examined — this cognition of 'one' that is seen — whether its object is a distinct substance or an aggregate of atoms. Here, observation does not establish either one. And when atoms are many, the apprehension as one through the non-apprehension of separateness is a cognition of 'that where it is not' — like [the cognition of] a person in a post. What follows from this?

children.text: atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayasya pradhānāpekṣitvāt pradhānasiddhiḥ/ sthāṇau puruṣa iti pratyayasya kiṃ pradhānam? so 'sau puruṣe puruṣapratyayaḥ, tasmin sati puruṣasāmānyagrahaṇāt sthāṇau puruṣo .yam iti/ evaṃ nānābhūteṣv ekam iti sāmānyagrahaṇāt pradhāne sati bhavitum arhati/ pradhānaṃ ca sarvasyāgrahaṇād iti nopapadyate/ tasmād abhinna evāyam abhedapratyaya ekam iti/
children.translated_text: Since the cognition 'that where it is not' requires a primary [instance], the existence of a primary is established. What is the primary for the cognition 'this is a person' in a post? It is the cognition of person in an actual person. When that [primary] exists — because of the apprehension of the universal 'person' in that — there arises [the erroneous cognition] 'this is a person' in the post. Similarly, the cognition 'one' regarding what is in fact many should be possible when there is a primary, due to the apprehension of the universal [oneness]. And [if you say] the primary does not exist because nothing at all [i.e., no composite] is apprehended — that is untenable. Therefore, this cognition of non-difference 'one' is indeed directed at something that is undifferentiated.

children.text: indriyāntaraviṣayeṣv abhedapratyayaḥ pradhānam iti ced, na viśeṣahetvabhāvād dṛṣṭāntāvyavasthā — śrotrādiviṣayeṣu śabdādiṣv abhinneṣv ekapratyayaḥ pradhānam anekasminn ekapratyayasyeti/ evaṃ ca sati dṛṣṭāntopādānaṃ na vyavatiṣṭhate viśeṣahetvabhāvāt/ aṇuṣu saṃśiteṣv ekapratyayaḥ kim atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayaḥ sthāṇau puruṣapratyayavat, athārthasya tathābhāvāt tasmiṃs tad iti pratyayaḥ yathā śabdasyaikatvād ekaḥ śabda iti viśeṣahetuparigrahaṇam antareṇa dṛṣṭāntau saṃśayam āpādayata iti/ kumbhavatsañcayamātraṃ gandhādayo 'pīty anudāharaṇaṃ gandhādaya iti/
children.translated_text: If [one says] the cognition of non-difference regarding objects of other sense-organs is the primary — no, because in the absence of a distinguishing reason, the example is unstable. [That is:] If the cognition of 'one' regarding the undifferentiated objects of hearing and the like — sounds and the like — is the primary for the cognition of 'one in many' — then the adoption of the example [of army/forest] is unstable, because there is no distinguishing reason. Is the cognition of 'one' regarding aggregated atoms a cognition of 'that where it is not' like the cognition of a person in a post, or is it a cognition of 'that in what is truly such' because the object is actually so, like [the cognition] 'one sound' due to the actual oneness of a sound? Without the adoption of a distinguishing reason, both examples generate doubt.

children.text:
evaṃ parimāṇasaṃyogaspandajātiviśeṣapratyayān apy anuyoktavyaḥ, teṣu caivaṃ prasaṅga iti/
ekatvabuddhis tasmiṃs tad iti pratyaya iti viśeṣahetur mahad iti pratyayena sāmānādhikaraṇyāt — ekam idaṃ mahac ceti ekaviṣayau pratyayau samānādhikaraṇau bhavataḥ tena vijñāyate yan mahat tad ekam iti/ aṇusamūhātiśayagrahaṇaṃ mahatpratyaya iti cet so .yam amahatsu aṇuṣu mahatpratyayo 'tasmiṃs tad iti pratyayo bhavatīti/ kiṃ cātaḥ? atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayasya pradhānāpekṣitvāt pradhānasiddhir iti bhavitavyaṃ mahaty eva mahatpratyayeneti/
children.translated_text:
Similarly, he should be questioned about the cognitions of magnitude, duality, the substrate of conjunction, motion, and universal-particular — and in those cases too, the same consequence applies.
The cognition of oneness is the distinguishing reason that the cognition is of 'that in what is truly such,' because of its co-referentiality with the cognition of 'large': 'this is one' and 'this is large' are two cognitions with the same referent. From this we understand that what is large is one. If [one says] the cognition of 'large' is the apprehension of a surplus over the aggregate of atoms — then this cognition of 'large' regarding atoms that are not [individually] large is a cognition of 'that where it is not.' What follows? Since the cognition of 'that where it is not' requires a primary, the primary is established — thus there must be a cognition of 'large' regarding something that is truly large.

children.text: aṇuḥ śabdo mahān iti ca vyavasāyāt pradhānasiddhir iti cet, na mandatīvratāgrahaṇam iyattānavadhāraṇāt — yathā dravye aṇuḥ śabdo 'lpo manda ity etasya grahaṇaṃ mahan śabdaḥ paṭus tīvra ity etasya grahaṇam/ kasmāt? iyattānavadhāraṇāt/ na hy ayaṃ mahān śabda iti vyavasyann iyān ayam ity avadhārayati, yathā badarāmalakabilvādīni/
children.translated_text: If [one says] the primary is established from the determination 'a small sound, a large [sound]' — no, because the apprehension of softness and loudness does not involve the determination of quantity. Just as regarding a substance, there is the apprehension of 'small sound, slight, soft' and 'large sound, sharp, loud' — why? Because there is no determination of quantity. For one who determines 'this is a large sound' does not ascertain 'this is of such-and-such magnitude,' as one does with jujubes, myrobalans, wood-apples, and the like.

children.text:
saṃyukte ime iti ca dvitvasamānāśrayaprāptigrahaṇam — dvau samudāyāv āśrayaḥ saṃyogasyeti cet ko 'yaṃ samudāyaḥ? prāptir anekasyānekā vā prāptir ekasya samudāya iti cet prāpter agrahaṇaṃ prāptyāśritāyāḥ/ saṃyukte ime vastunī iti nātra dve prāptī saṃyukte gṛhyete/
anekasamūhaḥ samudāya iti cet, na dvitvena samānādhikaraṇasya grahaṇāt/ dvāv imau saṃyuktāv arthāv iti grahaṇe sati nānekasamūhāśrayaḥ saṃyogo gṛhyate/ na ca dvayor aṇvor grahaṇam asti/ tasmān mahatī dvitvāśrayabhūte dravye saṃyogasya sthānam iti/
children.translated_text:
And the apprehension of duality in 'these are conjoined' [requires] the apprehension of the substrate sharing duality — if [one says] two aggregates are the substrate of conjunction, then what is this 'aggregate'? If [one says] the aggregate is the relation of many, or the multiple relations of one — then the non-apprehension of the relation [itself] undermines what is based on the relation. 'These two things are conjoined' — here two relations as conjoined are not apprehended.
If [one says] the aggregate is a collection of many — no, because of the apprehension of what is co-referential with duality. When there is the apprehension 'these two conjoined objects,' the conjunction is not apprehended as based on a collection of many. Nor is there apprehension of two atoms [as such]. Therefore, conjunction has its locus in substances that are large and serve as the substrates of duality.

children.text: pratyāsattiḥ pratīghātāvasānā saṃyogo nārthāntaram iti cet, nārthāntarahetutvāt saṃyogasya/ śabdarūpādispandānāṃ hetuḥ saṃyogaḥ/ na ca dravyayor guṇāntaropajananam antareṇa śabde rūpādiṣu spande ca kāraṇatvaṃ gṛhyate, tasmād guṇāntaram/ pratyayaviṣayaś cārthāntaraṃ tatpratiṣedho vā, kuṇḍalī gurur akuṇḍalaś chātra iti/ saṃyogabuddheś ca yady arthāntaraṃ na viṣayaḥ arthāntarapratiṣedhas tarhi viṣayaḥ, tatra pratiṣidhyamānavacanam — saṃyukte dravye iti yad arthāntaram anyatra dṛṣṭam iha pratiṣidhyate tadvaktavyam iti/ dvayor mahator āśritasya grahaṇān nāṇvāśraya iti/
children.translated_text: If [one says] proximity and the cessation of resistance constitute conjunction, and conjunction is not a distinct entity — no, because conjunction is the cause of a distinct entity. Conjunction is the cause of sounds, forms, and motions. And without the generation of a distinct quality [in the substrates], conjunction is not apprehended as a cause of sound, form, and motion. Therefore, it is a distinct quality. And the object of a cognition is either a distinct entity or the negation of a distinct entity — 'the one with earrings is the teacher, the one without earrings is the student.' And if the cognition of conjunction does not have a distinct entity as its object, then its object is the negation of a distinct entity; in that case, one should state what distinct entity observed elsewhere is being negated here in 'conjoined substances.' From the apprehension of [conjunction] based on two large [substances], it is not based on atoms.

children.text: jātiviśeṣasya pratyayānuvṛttiliṅgasyāpratyākhyānam, pratyākhyāne vā pratyayavyavasthānupapattiḥ/ vyadhikaraṇasyānabhivyakter adhikaraṇavacanam/ aṇusamavasthānaṃ viṣaya iti cet prāptāprāptasāmarthyavacanam — kim aprāpte aṇusamavasthāne tadāśrayo jātiviśeṣo gṛhyate atha prāpte iti/ aprāpte grahaṇam iti cet vyavahitasyāṇusamavasthānasyāpy upalabdhiprasaṅgaḥ, vyavahite 'ṇsamavasthāne tadāśrayo jātiviśeṣo gṛhyeta/ prāpte grahaṇam iti cet,
children.translated_text: The non-rejection of class-particular (<s>jātiviśeṣa</s>), whose mark is the recurrence of cognition; or if rejected, the impossibility of the regularity of cognitions. The mention of a substrate is because [a class-particular] that is in a different substrate is not manifested [without its own substrate]. If [one says] the configuration of atoms is the object — the statement of the capacity of the reached and unreached: is the class-particular based on the configuration of atoms apprehended when the configuration is not reached [by the senses], or when it is reached? If [one says] apprehension occurs when it is not reached — then there would follow the apprehension of even a concealed configuration of atoms, [and] the class-particular based on a concealed configuration of atoms would be apprehended. If [one says] apprehension occurs when it is reached —

children.text: madhyaparabhāgayor aprāptāv anabhivyaktiḥ/ yāvat prāptaṃ bhavati tāvaty abhivyaktir iti cet, tāvato 'dhikaraṇatvam aṇusamavasthānasya/ yāvati prāpte jātiviśeṣe gṛhyate tāvad asyādhikaraṇam iti prāptaṃ bhavati/ tatraikasamudāye pratīyamāne 'rthabhedaḥ/ evaṃ ca sati yo 'yam aṇusamudāyo vṛkṣa iti pratīyate tatra vṛkṣabahutvaṃ pratīyeta, yatra yatra hy aṇusamudāyasya bhāge vṛkṣatvaṃ gṛhyate sa sa vṛkṣa iti/ tasmāt samuditāṇusamavasthānasyārthāntarasya jātiviśeṣābhivyaktiviṣayatvād avayavyarthāntarabhūta iti//39//
children.translated_text: When the middle and final parts have not reached [the sense-organ], there is no manifestation. If one says that manifestation occurs only when [the universal] has reached [the sense-organ], then that much constitutes the substratum of the atomic configuration. The substratum of this [universal] is as much as is required for the particular universal to be grasped when reached. Then, when a single collection is perceived, there is a distinction of objects. And if this is so, then in this collection of atoms that is perceived as 'a tree,' the multiplicity of trees should be perceived, since wherever the tree-nature is grasped in a part of the atomic collection, that is a tree. Therefore, because the configuration of aggregated atoms, which is a distinct entity, is the domain of the manifestation of a particular universal, the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is a distinct entity. // 39 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
Perception has been examined. Inference is now examined —
Inference is not a valid means of knowledge, because of deviation due to obstruction, damage, and resemblance. // 2.1.37 //

children.text: apramāṇam iti ekadāpy arthasya na pratipādakam iti/ rodhād api nadī pūrṇā gṛhyate, tadā copariṣṭād vṛṣṭo deva iti mithyānumānam/ nīḍopaghātād api pipīlikāṇḍasañcāro bhavati, tadā ca bhaviṣyati vṛṣṭir iti mithyānumānam iti/ puruṣo 'pi mayūravāśitam anukaroti tadā 'pi śabdasādṛśyān mithyānumānaṃ bhavati//37//
children.translated_text: 'Not a valid means of knowledge' means that it does not ever establish an object. Even from obstruction, a river is seen to be full, and then one falsely infers 'it has rained upstream.' Even from damage to an anthill, the movement of ant eggs occurs, and then one falsely infers 'it will rain.' A person may also imitate the cry of a peacock, and then, due to resemblance of sound, a false inference arises. // 37 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 38
Because of the difference of the objects from [cases of] partial [resemblance], obstruction, and resemblance, [they are not genuine instances of inference]. // 2.1.38 //

children.text: nāyam anumānavyabhicāraḥ, ananumāne tu khalv ayam anumānābhimānaḥ/ katham? nāviśiṣṭo liṅgaṃ bhavitum arhati/ pūrvodakaviśiṣṭaṃ khalu varṣodakaṃ śīgrataratvaṃ srātaso bahutaraphenaphalaparṇakāṣṭhādivahanaṃ copalabhamānaḥ pūrṇatvena nadyā upari vṛṣṭo deva ity anuminoti nodakavṛddhimātreṇa/ pipīlikāprāyasyāṇḍasañcāre bhaviṣyati vṛṣṭir ity anumīyate na kāsāñcid iti/ nedaṃ mayūravāśitaṃ tatsadṛśo 'yaṃ śabda iti viśeṣāparijñānān mithyānumānam iti/ yas tu sadṛśād viśiṣṭāc chabdād viśisṭamayūravāśitaṃ gṛhṇāti tasya viśiṣṭo 'rtho gṛhyamāṇo liṅgam, yathā sarpādīnām iti/ so 'yam anumātur aparādho nānumānasya, yo 'rthaviśeṣeṇānumeyam artham aviśiṣṭārthadarśanena bubhutsata iti//38//
children.translated_text: This is not a deviation of inference; rather, it is a mistaken belief that something which is not inference is inference. How so? What is undistinguished cannot be a <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark). One who observes that rainwater, distinguished from prior water, has greater speed and carries more foam, fruits, leaves, wood, etc. in the current, infers 'it has rained upstream' on the basis of the river's fullness — not merely from the increase of water. It is inferred 'it will rain' when most of the ants move their eggs, not when just some do. 'This is not the cry of a peacock; this sound is similar to it' — due to failure to discern the distinction, it is a false inference. But one who grasps the distinct peacock cry from a distinguished sound has a distinguished object as the <s>liṅga</s>, as in the case of serpents and the like. This is the fault of the inferrer, not of inference — the one who wishes to know the object to be inferred through the perception of an undistinguished object. // 38 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 39

children.text: trikālaviṣayam anumānaṃ traikālyagrahaṇād ity uktam/ ata ca —
children.translated_text: It has been stated that inference has the three times as its domain, because of the apprehension of the three times. And therefore —
The present does not exist, because of the applicability of the past and future times to what is falling. // 2.1.39 //

children.text: vṛntāt pracyutasya phalasya bhūmau pratyāsīdato yadūrdhvaṃ sa patito 'dhvā tatsaṃyuktaḥ kālaḥ patitakālaḥ, yo 'dhastāt sa patitavyo 'dhvā, tatsaṃyuktaḥ kālaḥ patitavyakālaḥ/ nedānīṃ tṛtīyo 'dhvā vidyate yatra patatīti vartamānaḥ kālo gṛhyeta/ tasmād vartamānaḥ kālo na vidyata iti//39//
children.translated_text: When a fruit that has detached from its stalk is approaching the ground, the path above is the 'fallen' course, and the time connected with it is the past time (<s>patitakāla</s>); the path below is the 'yet-to-fall' course, and the time connected with it is the future time (<s>patitavyakāla</s>). There is now no third course where 'it is falling,' so that the present time could be grasped. Therefore, the present time does not exist. // 39 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 40
The non-existence of those two also [follows] from the non-existence of the present, since they are dependent on it. // 2.1.40 //

children.text: nādhvavyaṅgyaḥ kālaḥ/ kiṃ tarhi? kriyāvyaṅgyaḥ patatīti/ yadā patanakriyā vyuparatā bhavati sa kālaḥ patitakālaḥ/ yadotpatsyate sa patitavyakālaḥ/
children.translated_text: Time is not indicated by a spatial path. What then? It is indicated by action — 'it is falling.' When the falling action has ceased, that is the past time — 'it fell.' When it is about to arise, that is the future time — 'it will fall.'

children.text: yadā dravye vartamānā kriyā gṛhyate sa vartamānaḥ kālaḥ/ yadi cāyaṃ dravye vartamānaṃ patanaṃ na gṛhṇāti kasyoparamam utpatsyamānatāṃ vā pratipadyate/ patitaḥ kāla iti bhūtā kriyā, patitavyaḥ kāla iti cotpatsyamānā kriyā, ubhayoḥ kālayoḥ kriyāhīnaṃ dravyam; adhaḥ patatīti kriyāsambaddham/ so 'yaṃ kriyādravyayoḥ sambandhaṃ gṛhṇātīti vartamānaḥ kālaḥ, tadāśrayau cetarau kālau tadahāve na syātām iti//40//
children.translated_text: When a present action is grasped in a substance, that is the present time. And if one does not grasp the present falling in the substance, whose cessation or future arising would one apprehend? 'The past time' means a past action; 'the future time' means a future action; in both times the substance is devoid of action; 'it is falling downward' means connected with action. Thus this one grasps the connection of action and substance, and that is the present time; and the other two times depend on it — in its absence, they would not exist. // 40 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 41
Moreover —
The past and future are not established through mutual dependence on each other. // 2.1.41 //

children.text: yady atītānāgatāv itaretarāpekṣau sidhyetāṃ pratipadyemahi vartamānavilopam/ nātītāpekṣānāgatasiddhiḥ nāpy anāgatāpekṣātītasiddhiḥ/ kayā yuktyā? kena kalpenātītaḥ katham atītāpekṣānāgatasiddhiḥ, kena ca kalpenānāgata iti naitac chakyaṃ nirvaktum avyākaraṇīyam etad vartamānalopa iti/ yac ca manyeta hrasvadīrghayoḥ sthalanimnayoś chāyātapayoś ca yathetaretarāpekṣayā siddhir evam atītānāgatayor iti, tan nopapadyate viśeṣahetvabhāvāt/ dṛṣṭāntavat pratidṛṣṭānto 'pi prasajyate, yathā rūpasparśau gandharasau netaretarāpekṣau siddhyataḥ evam atītānāgatāv iti netaretarāpekṣā kasyacit siddhir iti/
children.translated_text: If the past and future were established through mutual dependence, we would accept the elimination of the present. But the future is not established in dependence on the past, nor is the past established in dependence on the future. By what reasoning? By what account is something past? How is the future established in dependence on the past? And by what account is something future? This cannot be explained — it is inexplicable — this elimination of the present. And one might think that just as short and long, highland and lowland, shade and sunlight are established through mutual dependence, so too past and future — but that is not tenable, due to the absence of a distinguishing reason. A counter-example can be adduced against the example: just as form and touch, smell and taste, are not established through mutual dependence on each other, so too past and future — thus nothing is established through mutual dependence.

children.text: yasmād ekābhāve ṇyatarābhāvād ubhayābhāvaḥ — yady ekasyānyatarāpekṣā siddhir anyatarasyedānīṃ kim apekṣā? yady anyatarasyaikāpekṣā siddhir ekasyedānīṃ kim apekṣā? evam ekasyābhāve anyataran na sidhyatīty ubhayābhāvaḥ prasajyate//41//
children.translated_text: Since in the absence of one, the absence of the other follows, and thus the absence of both — if one is established in dependence on the other, what is the other then dependent on? If the other is established in dependence on the one, what is the one then dependent on? Thus, in the absence of one, the other is not established, and the absence of both follows. // 41 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 42

children.text: arthasadbhāvavyaṅgyaś cāyaṃ vartamānaḥ kālaḥ, vidyate dravyaṃ vidyate guṇaḥ vidyate karmeti/ yasya cāyaṃ nāsti, tasya —
children.translated_text: And this present time is indicated by the existence of objects — 'the substance exists,' 'the quality exists,' 'the action exists.' And for one who denies this —
In the absence of the present, there would be no apprehension of anything, because perception would be impossible. // 2.1.42 //

children.text: pratyakṣam indriyārthasannikarṣajam, na cāvidyamānam asad indriyeṇa sannikṛṣyate/ nacāyaṃ vidyamānaṃ sat kiñcid anujānāti/ pratyakṣanimittaṃ pratyakṣaviṣayaḥ pratyakṣajñānaṃ sarvaṃ nopapadyate, pratyakṣānupapattau tatpūrvakatvād anumānāgamayor anupapattiḥ/ sarvapramāṇavilope sarvagrahaṇaṃ na bhavatīti//42//
children.translated_text: Perception arises from the contact of sense-organ and object; what is non-existent and unreal is not contacted by a sense-organ. And this one does not admit that anything existing and real exists. The object of perception, the occasion of perception, perceptual cognition — none of these would be possible. When perception is impossible, inference and verbal testimony are also impossible, since they presuppose perception. When all means of valid knowledge are destroyed, no apprehension of anything occurs. // 42 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 43

children.text:
ubhayathā ca vartamānaḥ kālo gṛhyate kvacid arthasadbhāvavyaṅgyaḥ yathāsti dravyam iti/ kvacit kriyāsantānavyaṅgyaḥ yathā pacati chinattīti/ nānāvidhā caikārthā kriyā kriyāsantānaḥ kriyābhyāsaś ca/ nānāvidhā caikārthā kriyā pacatīti sthālyadhiśrayaṇam udakāsecanaṃ taṇḍulāvapanam edho'pasarpaṇam agnyabhijvālanaṃ darvīghaṭṭanaṃ maṇḍasrāvaṇam adho'vatāraṇam iti/
chinattīti kriyābhyāsa udyamyodyamya paraśuṃ dāruṇi nipātayan chinattīty ucyate/
children.translated_text: The present time is grasped in two ways: sometimes as indicated by the existence of an object, such as 'the substance exists'; sometimes as indicated by the continuity of action, such as 'he cooks' or 'he cuts.' A series of diverse but single-purposed actions is the continuity of action, and the repetition of action. The diverse but single-purposed action of 'he cooks' involves placing the pot, pouring water, adding rice, bringing fuel, kindling the fire, stirring with the ladle, draining the starch, and taking down [the pot]. 'He cuts' is a repetition of action — raising the axe again and again and striking the wood, one is said to cut.

children.text: yac cedaṃ pacyamānaṃ chidyamānaṃ ca tat kriyamāṇam, tasmin kriyamāṇe —
children.translated_text: And what is being cooked and being cut is being acted upon; while it is being acted upon —
Because of the applicability of 'done-ness' and 'to-be-done-ness,' apprehension is in both ways. // 2.1.43 //

children.text: kriyāsantāno ṇārabdhaś cikīrṣito .āgataḥ kālaḥ pakṣyatīti/ prayojanāvasānaḥ kriyāsantānoparamaḥ atītaḥ kālaḥ apākṣīd iti/
children.translated_text: The continuity of action not yet begun but intended — that is the future time: 'he will cook.' The cessation of the continuity of action upon completion of purpose — that is the past time: 'he cooked.'

children.text: ārabdhakriyāsantāno vartamānaḥ kālaḥ pacatīti/ tatra yā uparatā sā kṛtatā/ yā cikīrṣitā sā kartavyatā/ yā vidyamānā sā kriyamāṇatā/ tad evaṃ kriyāsantānasthas traikālyasamāhāraḥ pacati pacyata iti vartamānagrahaṇena gṛhyate, kriyāsantānasya hy atrāvicchedo 'bhidhīyate nārambho noparama iti/ so 'yam ubhayathā vartamāno gṛhyate apavṛkto vyapavṛktaś cātītānāgatābhyām/ sthitivyaṅgyaḥ — vidyate dravyam iti/ kriyāsantānāvicchedābhidhāyī ca traikālyānvitaḥ — pacati chinattīti/ anyaś ca pratyāsattiprabhṛter arthasya vivakṣāyāṃ tadabhidhāyī bahuprakāro lokeṣu utprekṣitavyaḥ/ tasmād asti vartamānaḥ kāla iti//43//
children.translated_text: The continuity of action that has begun — that is the present time: 'he cooks.' Therein, what has ceased is 'done-ness'; what is intended is 'to-be-done-ness'; what is presently occurring is 'being-done-ness.' Thus the aggregate of three times situated within the continuity of action is grasped by the present-tense expression 'he cooks' or 'it is being cooked,' for what is denoted here is the uninterrupted continuity of action, not its beginning or its cessation. Thus the present is grasped in both ways — distinguished and separated from the past and the future: as indicated by persistence — 'the substance exists'; and as denoting the uninterrupted continuity of action, conjoined with the three times — 'he cooks,' 'he cuts.' And other expressions denoting the object from proximity onward should be investigated in their many forms in worldly usage. Therefore, the present time exists. // 43 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 44
Comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) is established through complete, predominant, or partial similarity. // 2.1.44 //

children.text: atyantasādharmyād upamānaṃ na sidhyati/ na caivaṃ bhavati yathā gaur evaṃ gaur iti/
children.translated_text: Comparison is not established through complete similarity, for one does not say 'as a cow, so is a cow.'

children.text: prāyaḥsādharmyād upamānaṃ na sidhyati, na hi bhavati yathānaḍvān evaṃ mahiṣa iti/ ekadeśasādharmyād upamānaṃ na sidhyati, na hi sarveṇa sarvam upamīyata iti//44//
children.translated_text: Comparison is not established through predominant similarity, for one does not say 'as a bull, so is a buffalo.' Comparison is not established through partial similarity, for not everything is compared with everything in all respects. // 44 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 45
Because comparison is established through well-known similarity, the stated faults do not apply. // 2.1.45 //

children.text: na sādharmyasya kṛtsnaprāyālpabhāvam āśrityopamānaṃ pravartate/ kiṃ tarhi?
children.translated_text: Comparison does not operate by relying on the complete, predominant, or partial character of similarity. What then?

children.text: prasiddhasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanabhāvam āśritya pravartate/ yatra caitad asti na tatropamānaṃ pratiṣeddhuṃ śakyam/ tasmād yathoktadoṣo nopapadyata iti//45//
children.translated_text: It operates by relying on well-known similarity in the relation of what is to be established and the means of establishment. And where this obtains, comparison cannot be denied. Therefore, the stated fault does not apply. // 45 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 46
Let comparison then be [a form of] inference —
Because the imperceptible is established through the perceptible. // 2.1.46 //

children.text: yathā dhūmena pratyakṣeṇāpratyakṣasya vahner grahaṇam anumānam, evaṃ gavā pratyakṣeṇāpratyakṣasya gavayasya grahaṇam iti nedam anumānād viśiṣyate//46//
children.translated_text: Just as inference is the apprehension of imperceptible fire through perceptible smoke, so is the apprehension of the imperceptible <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) through the perceptible cow — thus this is not different from inference. // 46 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 47
It is different, he says. By what reasoning?
We do not see the purpose of comparison as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) with respect to the unperceived <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox). // 2.1.47 //

children.text: yadā hy ayam upayuktopamāno godarśī gavayasamānam arthaṃ paśyati tadāyaṃ gavaya ity asya saṃjñāśabdasya vyavasthāṃ pratipadyate na caivam anumānam iti/ parārthaṃ copamānam — yasya hy upamānam aprasiddhaṃ tadarthaṃ prasiddhobhayena kriyata iti parārtham upamānam iti cet; na,
children.translated_text: For when this person, equipped with the comparison, sees a cow and perceives an object similar to a <s>gavaya</s>, he then apprehends the conventional assignment of the designating word 'this is a <s>gavaya</s>' — and this is not inference. And if one says comparison is for another's benefit — for one to whom the comparison is not known, it is made by one to whom both are known, and hence comparison is for another's benefit — no,

children.text: svayam adhyavasāyāt — bhavati ca bhoḥ svayam adhyavasāyaḥ yathā gaur evaṃ gavaya iti/ nādhyavasāyaḥ pratiṣidhyate upamānaṃ tu tan na bhavati
children.translated_text: because of one's own ascertainment — for there is indeed one's own ascertainment: 'as a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s>.' It is not the ascertainment that is denied, but rather that it constitutes comparison.
Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be established through well-known similarity.

children.text: / na ca yasyobhayaṃ prasiddhaṃ taṃ prati sādhyasādhanabhāavo vidyata iti//47//
children.translated_text: And for one to whom both are well-known, the relation of what is to be established and the means of establishment does not exist. // 47 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 48
Moreover —
Because comparison is established through the subsumption 'so [it is],' there is no non-distinction [from inference]. // 2.1.48 //

children.text: tatheti samānadharmopasaṃhārād upamānaṃ sidhyati nānumānam/ ayaṃ cānayor viśeṣa iti//48//
children.translated_text: Comparison is established through the subsumption of a common property — 'so [it is]' — not inference. And this is the distinction between the two. // 48 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 49
Verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is inference, because its object is not perceived and hence is to be inferred. // 2.1.49 //

children.text: śabdo 'numānam, na pramāṇāntaram/ kasmāt? śabdārthasyānumeyatvāt/ katham anumeyatvam? pratyakṣato 'nupalabdheḥ/ yathānupalabhyamāno liṅgī mitena liṅgena paścān mīyata iti anumānam/ evaṃ mitena śabdena paścān mīyate artho 'nupalabhyamāna ity anumānaṃ śabdaḥ//
children.translated_text: Verbal testimony is inference, not a separate means of valid knowledge. Why? Because the object of verbal testimony is to be inferred. How is it to be inferred? Because it is not perceived directly. Just as the possessor of the mark (<s>liṅgin</s>), not being perceived, is subsequently measured by the perceived mark — that is inference — so too the object, not being perceived, is subsequently measured by the perceived word — thus verbal testimony is inference.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 50
And for this further reason verbal testimony is inference:
Because cognition does not operate in two [distinct] ways. // 2.1.50 //

children.text: pramāṇāntarabhāve dvipravṛttir upalabdhiḥ, anyathā hy upalabdhir anumāne anyathopamāne tad vyākhyātam/ śabdānumānayos tūpalabdhir advipravṛttiḥ yathānumāne tathā śabde 'pi/ viśeṣābhāvād anumānaṃ śabda iti//
children.translated_text: When there is a separate means of valid knowledge, cognition operates in two ways — it operates one way in inference and another way in comparison; that has been explained. But in the case of verbal testimony and inference, cognition does not operate in two ways — it operates in verbal testimony just as in inference. Due to the absence of distinction, verbal testimony is inference.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 51
And because of the relation. // 2.1.51 //

children.text: śabdo 'numānam iti vartate/ sambaddhayoś ca śabdārthayoḥ sambandhaprasiddhau śabdopalabdher arthagrahaṇaṃ yathā sambaddhayor liṅgaliṅinoḥ sambandhapratītau liṅgopalabdhau liṅgigrahaṇam iti//
children.translated_text: The topic continues: '<s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is [merely] inference.' And when two related things — word and meaning — are known in their relation, the grasping of the meaning from the apprehension of the word is just like the grasping of the marked entity from the apprehension of the mark, when the relation between mark and marked is known.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 52

children.text: yat tāvad arthasyānumeyatvād iti tan na—
children.translated_text: Now, as for [the objection] that the meaning is to be inferred — that is not so:
The cognition of the meaning from <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) arises from the authority of a trustworthy person's instruction. // 2.1.52 //

children.text: svargaḥ apsarasaḥ uttarāḥ kuravaḥ sapta dvīpāḥ samudro lokasanniveśa ity evamāder apratyakṣasyārthasya ca śabdamātrāt pratyayaḥ, kiṃ tarhi? āptair ayam uktāḥ śabda ity ataḥ sampratyayaḥ viparyayeṇa sampratyayābhāvāt; na tv evam anumānam iti/
children.translated_text: The cognition of imperceptible objects such as heaven, <s>apsarases</s> (celestial nymphs), the <s>Uttarakurus</s> (northern continent), the seven continents, the ocean, and the arrangement of the worlds does not arise from the word alone; rather, the cognition arises because 'this word was uttered by trustworthy persons' — the proof being that in the contrary case there would be no cognition. Thus it is not inference.

children.text: yat punar upalabdher advipravṛttitvād iti, ayam eva śabdānumānayor upalabdheḥ pravṛttibhedaḥ; tatra viśeṣe saty ahetur viśeṣābhāvād iti/
children.translated_text: As for [the objection] that apprehension does not proceed in two different ways — this itself is the difference in the functioning of apprehension between verbal testimony and inference; and where a specific difference exists, to say there is no reason [for distinction] due to the absence of difference is [circular].

children.text: yat punar idaṃ sambandhāc ceti, asti ca śabdārthayoḥ sambandho 'nujñātaḥ, asti ca pratiṣiddhaḥ/ asyedam iti ṣaṣṭhīviśiṣṭasya vākyasyārthaviśeṣo 'nujñātaḥ, prāptilakṣaṇas tu śabdārthayoḥ sambandhaḥ pratiṣiddhaḥ/ kasmāt? pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ—pratyakṣatas tāvac chabdārthaprāpter nopalabdhir atīndriyatvāt/ yenendriyeṇa gṛhyate śabdas tasya viṣayabhāvam ativṛtto 'rtho na gṛhyate/ asti cātīndriyaviṣayabhūto 'py arthaḥ samānena cendriyeṇa gṛhyamāṇayoḥ prāptir gṛhyata iti//
children.translated_text: As for [the argument] 'because of the relation' — there is indeed an accepted relation between word and meaning, and there is also a denied one. The meaning of the sentence qualified by the genitive case 'this belongs to that' is the accepted [conventional] relation; but a relation between word and meaning characterized by physical contact is denied. Why? Because it is not apprehended by any means of valid knowledge. First, physical contact between word and meaning is not perceived, because it is beyond the senses. The sense-organ by which the word is grasped cannot grasp the meaning, which transcends the domain of that sense. However, even an object that is beyond the senses — if grasped by the same sense-organ — the contact between [word and meaning] could be grasped.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 53
Because filling, burning, and splitting are not observed, there is no [physical] relation. // 2.1.53 //

children.text:
prāptilakṣaṇe ca gṛhyamāṇe sambandhe śabdārthayoḥ śabdāntike vārthaḥ syāt, arthāntike vā śabdaḥ syāt, ubhayaṃ vobhayatra/ atha khalv ubhayam?
sthānakaraṇābhāvād iti cārthaḥ/ na cāyam anumānato 'py upalabhyate śabdāntike 'rtha iti/ etasmin pakṣe 'py āsyasthānakaraṇoccāraṇīyaḥ śabdas tadantike 'rtha ity annāgnyasiśabdoccāraṇe pūraṇapāhapāṭanāni gṛhyeran, na ca gṛhyante; agrahaṇāt nānumeyaḥ prāptilakṣaṇaḥ sambandhaḥ/
children.translated_text: If a relation characterized by physical contact between word and meaning were grasped, then either the meaning would be near the word, or the word near the meaning, or both would be in both places. Now, if both? The point about the absence of place and instrument [applies]. Nor is this inferred — that the meaning is near the word. In this case too, since the word is to be uttered with a place and instrument of articulation [in the mouth], and if the meaning were near it, then upon uttering the words 'food,' 'fire,' and 'sword,' filling, burning, and splitting would be grasped — but they are not grasped. Since they are not grasped, a relation characterized by physical contact is not to be inferred.

children.text: arthāntike śabda iti sthānakaraṇāsambhavād anuccāraṇam—sthānaṃ kaṇṭhādayaḥ, karaṇaṃ prayatnaviśeṣaḥ, tasyārthāntike 'nupapattir iti/ ubhayapratiṣedhāc ca nobhayam/ tasmān na śabdenārthaḥ prāpta iti//
children.translated_text: As for 'the word is near the meaning' — that is impossible due to the impossibility of the place and instrument [of articulation being near the meaning]. The place is the throat and so forth; the instrument is a particular effort [of articulation]; and its being near the meaning is untenable. And by the negation of both, neither can both [be the case]. Therefore the meaning is not physically reached by the word.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 54
Because of the fixed correspondence between word and meaning, [the relation] is not denied. // 2.1.54 //

children.text: śabdād arthapratyayasya vyavasthādarśanād anumīyata asti śabdārthasambandho vyavasthākāraṇam/ asambandhe hi śabdamātrād arthamātre pratyayaprasaṅgaḥ/ tasmād apratiṣedhaḥ sambandhasyeti//
children.translated_text: Since a fixed correspondence is observed between the cognition of meaning and the word, it is inferred that there exists a word-meaning relation that is the cause of this fixed correspondence. For in the absence of a relation, there would be the absurd consequence that any word whatsoever would produce cognition of any meaning whatsoever. Therefore the relation is not denied.
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 55
Here is the resolution —
No, because the cognition of meaning from words is conventional. // 2.1.55 //

children.text: na sambandhakāritaṃ śabdārthavyavasthānam/ kiṃ tarhi? samayakāritam/ yat tad avocāma asyedam iti ṣaṣṭhīviśiṣṭasya vākyasyārthaviśeṣo 'nujñātaḥ śabdārthayoḥ sambandha iti samayaṃ tam avocāma iti/ kaḥ punar ayaṃ samayaḥ? asya śabdasyedam arthajātam abhidheyam ity abhidhānābhidheyaniyamaniyogaḥ/ tasminn upayukte śabdād arthasampratyayo bhavati/ viparyaye hi śabdaśravaṇa 'pi pratyayābhāvaḥ/ sambandhavādino 'pi cāyam avarjanīya iti/
children.translated_text: The fixed correspondence between word and meaning is not produced by an [inherent] relation. What then? It is produced by convention (<s>samaya</s>). What we stated — that the meaning of the genitive sentence 'this belongs to that' is the accepted relation of word and meaning — that we called a convention. What then is this convention? It is the fixed assignment: 'this class of meanings is to be denoted by this word' — a binding regulation of <s>abhidhāna</s> (expression) and <s>abhidheya</s> (what is expressed). When that [convention] is operative, the cognition of meaning from words arises. In the contrary case, even upon hearing a word, there is no cognition. And this [convention] is unavoidable even for those who advocate an [inherent] relation.

children.text: prayujyamānagrahaṇāc ca samayopayogo laukikānām/ samayaparipālanārthaṃ cedaṃ padalakṣaṇāyā vācānvākhyānaṃ vyākaraṇam vākyalakṣaṇāyā vāco 'rthalakṣaṇam,
children.translated_text: The employment of convention by ordinary people is [known] from their learning [words] through usage. And for the purpose of preserving convention, there is <s>vyākaraṇa</s> (grammar) — which is the explanation of speech for the definition of words and the determination of meaning for the definition of sentences;

children.text: padasamūho vākyam arthaparisamāprāv iti/ tad evaṃ prāptilakṣaṇasya śabdārthasambandhasyārthatuṣo 'pi anumānahetur na bhavatīti//55//
children.translated_text: a sentence is a collection of words that completes a meaning. Thus, even the satisfaction of purpose does not become a reason for inferring a relation between word and meaning characterized by physical contact. // 55 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 56
And because there is no restriction to particular species. // 2.1.56 //

children.text: sāmāyikaḥ śabdād arthasampratyayo na svābhāvikaḥ/ ṛṣyāryamlecchānāṃ yathākāmaṃ śabdaviniyogo 'rthapratyāyanāya pravartate/ svābhāvike hi śabdasyārthapratyāyakatve yathākāmaṃ na syād yathā taijasasya prakāśasya rūpapratyayahetutvaṃ na jātiviśeṣe vyabhicaratīti//56//
children.translated_text: The cognition of meaning from words is conventional, not natural. Among <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages), <s>āryas</s> (civilized people), and <s>mlecchas</s> (foreigners), the assignment of words to convey meaning proceeds according to their wish. For if the capacity of words to convey meaning were natural, it would not be according to wish — just as the capacity of luminous fire to cause the cognition of form does not vary by species. // 56 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 57
Regarding the <s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s> (sacrifice for obtaining a son), the <s>havana</s> (oblation), and repetition —
Its invalidity [is argued] on the grounds of the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and redundancy. // 2.1.57 //

children.text: tasyeti śabdaviśeṣam evādhikurute bhagavān ṛṣiḥ/ śabdasya pramāṇatvaṃ na sambhavati/ kasmāt? anṛtadoṣāt—putrakameṣṭau

children.translated_text: 'One who desires a son should sacrifice with the <s>putreṣṭi</s> (son-sacrifice).'

children.text: iti; neṣṭau saṃsthitāyāṃ putrajanma dṛśyate/ dṛṣṭārthasya vākyasyānṛtatvād adṛṣṭārtham api vākyam
children.translated_text: Yet when the sacrifice is completed, no birth of a son is observed. Since the statement about a visible object is false, the statement about an invisible object too —
'One who desires heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s> (fire-oblation)'
— and the like are known to be false.

By 'its,' the venerable sage specifically addresses a particular kind of <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) [i.e., Vedic injunctions]. The validity of [such] verbal testimony is impossible. Why? Because of the defect of falsehood — in the <s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s>:
And because of the defect of contradiction in what is enjoined — in the <s>havana</s> (oblation):

children.text: udite hotavyam anudite hotavyam samayādhyuṣite hotavyam
children.translated_text: 'One should offer when [the sun] has risen; one should offer when [the sun] has not risen; one should offer when twilight has come' —
having thus enjoined, [the Veda] contradicts what it enjoined:

children.text: śyāvo 'syāhutim abhyavaharati ya udite juhoti, śabalo 'syāhutim abhyavaharati yo 'nudite juhoti śyāvaśabalau vāsyāhutim abhyavaharato yaḥ samayādhyuṣite juhoti
children.translated_text: 'A dark [demon] devours the oblation of one who offers when the sun has risen; a spotted [demon] devours the oblation of one who offers when the sun has not risen; a dark-and-spotted [demon] devours the oblation of one who offers at twilight.'
And because of this contradiction, one of the two [statements] is false.
And because of the defect of redundancy — when repetition is being taught:
'He recites the first [verse] thrice, and the last thrice'

children.text: iti punaruktadoṣo bhavati/ punaruktaṃ ca pramattavākyam iti/ tasmād apramāṇaṃ śabdo 'nṛtavyāghātapunaruktadoṣebhya iti//57//
children.translated_text: — this constitutes the defect of redundancy. And redundancy is the speech of one who is careless. Therefore <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is not a valid means of knowledge, due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and redundancy. // 57 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 58
No, because of defects in the action, the agent, or the instruments. // 2.1.58 //

children.text: nānṛtadoṣaḥ putrakāmeṣṭiau/ kasmāt? karmakartṛsādhanavaiguṇyāt/ iṣṭyā pitarau saṃyujyamānau putraṃ janayata iti/ iṣṭeḥ karaṇaṃ sādhanam, pitarau kartārau, saṃyogaḥ karma, trayāṇāṃ guṇayogāt putrajanma, vaiguṇyād viparyayaḥ/ iṣṭyāśrayaṃ tāvad karmavaiguṇyaṃ samīhābhreṣaḥ, kartṛvaiguṇyam avidvān prayoktā kapūyācaraṇaś ca/
children.translated_text: There is no defect of falsehood in the <s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s>. Why? Because of defects in the action, the agent, or the instruments. The sacrifice brings together the parents, who produce a son. The sacrifice is the instrument (<s>sādhana</s>), the parents are the agents, the union is the action — from the proper combination of all three comes the birth of a son, and from their deficiency comes the contrary result. The defect of action pertaining to the sacrifice is the failure of proper procedure; the defect of the agent is an ignorant or sinfully behaving performer;

children.text: sādhanavaiguṇyaṃ havir asaṃkṛtam upahatam iti, mantrā nyūnādhikāḥ svaravarṇahīnā iti, dakṣiṇā durāgatā hīnā ninditā ceti/ athopajanāśrayaṃ karmavaiguṇyaṃ mithyāsamprayogaḥ, kartṛvaiguṇyaṃ yonivyāpado bījopaghātaś ceti/ sādhanavaiguṇyam iṣṭāv abhihitam/ loke ca
children.translated_text: the defect of instruments is that the oblation material is improperly prepared or spoiled; the <s>mantras</s> are deficient or excessive, lacking proper accent or phonemes; the <s>dakṣiṇā</s> (ritual fee) is ill-gotten, insufficient, or condemned. Then, regarding the defect of action pertaining to conception: it is improper intercourse; the defect of the agent is defects of the womb and damage to the seed. The defect of instruments has been stated with regard to the sacrifice. In worldly life too,
'One who desires fire should churn the fire-sticks' —

children.text: iti vidhivākyam, tatra karmavaiguṇyaṃ mithyābhimanthanam, kartṛvaiguṇyaṃ prajñāprayatnataḥ pramādaḥ, sādhanavaiguṇyam ārdraṃ suṣiraṃ dāviti, tatra phalaṃ na niṣpadyata iti nānṛtadoṣaḥ, guṇayogena phalaniṣpattidarśanāt/ na cedaṃ laukikād bhidyate
children.translated_text: this is an injunctive statement. There, the defect of action is improper churning; the defect of the agent is carelessness arising from lack of intelligence and effort; the defect of instruments is that the wood is moist, hollow, or [too] dry. In that case, the result is not produced — yet there is no defect of falsehood, because the production of the result is seen when the [conditions] are properly combined. And this [Vedic injunction] is no different from the worldly [case] —
'One who desires a son should sacrifice with the <s>putreṣṭi</s>.'
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 59
Because the fault is stated when there is deviation from the accepted time. // 2.1.59 //

children.text: na vyāghāto havana ity anuvartate/ yo 'bhyupagataṃ havanakālaṃ bhinatti tato 'nyatra juhoti tatrāyam abhyupagatakālabhede doṣa ucyate

children.translated_text: 'A dark [demon] devours the oblation of one who offers when the sun has risen.'
This is a censure-statement for deviation from the [proper] injunction. // 59 //

The topic continues: there is no contradiction in the <s>havana</s> (oblation). One who deviates from the accepted time of oblation and offers at another time — the fault is stated for that deviation from the accepted time:
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 60
And because [repetition] can be explained as reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>). // 2.1.60 //

children.text:
punaruktadoṣo 'bhyāse neti prakṛtam/
anarthako 'bhyāsaḥ punaruktam, arthavān abhyāso 'nuvādaḥ/ yo 'yam abhyāsaḥ

children.translated_text: 'He recites the first thrice and the last thrice' —

children.text: ity anuvāda upapadyate arthavattvāt/ trirvacanena hi prathamottamayoḥ pañcadaśatvaṃ sāmidhenīnāṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: is properly explained as reiteration, because it serves a purpose. For by the triple recitation, the first and last <s>sāmidhenī</s> (kindling verses) become fifteen in number.
The topic continues: there is no defect of redundancy in repetition. Purposeless repetition is redundancy; purposeful repetition is <s>anuvāda</s> (reiteration). The repetition here —
And there is the <s>mantra</s> invocation:

children.text: idam ahaṃ bhrātṛvyaṃ pañcadaśāvareṇa vāgvajreṇāvabodhe yo 'smān dveṣṭi yaṃ ca vayaṃ dviṣma
children.translated_text: 'With this, I strike down the rival with the fifteen-fold thunder-weapon of speech — whoever hates us and whomever we hate.'

children.text: iti pañcadaśa sāmidhenīr vajramantro 'bhivadati tad abhyāsam antareṇa na syād iti//60//
children.translated_text: This [invocation of] fifteen <s>sāmidhenīs</s> as a thunder-<s>mantra</s> would not be possible without the repetition. // 60 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 61
And because meaning is grasped from the division of sentences. // 2.1.61 //
<s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is a valid means of knowledge, just as in the world. // 61 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 62
And the division of <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> statements is threefold —
Because of the application [of statements] as injunction (<s>vidhi</s>), explanatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>), and reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>). // 2.1.62 //

children.text: tridhā khalu brāhmaṇavākyāni viniyuktāni—vidhivacanāny arthavādavacanāni anuvādavacanānīti//62//
children.translated_text: <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> statements are indeed applied in three ways: as injunctive statements, as explanatory statements, and as reiterative statements. // 62 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 63
Among these —

children.text:
vidhir vidhāyakaḥ //
                yad vākyaṃ vidhāyakaṃ codakaṃ sa vidhiḥ/ vidhis tu niyogo 'nujñā vā/ yathā

children.translated_text: 'One who desires heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s>'
and so forth. // 2.1.63 //

<s>Vidhi</s> (injunction) is that which enjoins. A statement that enjoins, that impels — that is <s>vidhi</s>. <s>Vidhi</s> is either a binding obligation (<s>niyoga</s>) or a permission (<s>anujñā</s>). For example:
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 64

children.text: stutir nindā parakṛtiḥ purākalpa ity arthavādaḥ // 2.1.64 //
children.translated_text: Praise, blame, precedent from others, and ancient practice — these constitute <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage). // 2.1.64 //

children.text: vidheḥ phalavādalakṣaṇā yā praśaṃsā sā stutiḥ sampratyayārthā, stūyamānaṃ śraddadhīteti, pravartikā ca, phalaśravaṇāt pravartate—
sarvajitā vai devāḥ sarvam ajayan sarvasyāptyai sarvasya jityai sarvam evaitenāptenāpnoti sarvaṃ jayati
children.translated_text: 'By the <s>Sarvajit</s> (all-conquering sacrifice), the gods conquered all. For the attainment of all, for the conquest of all — by this [sacrifice] one attains all, one conquers all.'

children.text: iti evamādi/ aniṣṭaphalavādo nindā varjanārthā ninditaṃ na samācared iti
children.translated_text: Such and the like. Blame is the description of undesirable results, meant to cause avoidance — 'one should not do what is condemned':

Praise is the commendation that describes the result of an injunction; its purpose is to produce conviction — 'one would believe in what is praised' — and it is also motivating, since one acts upon hearing the result:

children.text:
sa eṣa vāva prathamo yajño yajñānāṃ yaj jotiṣṭomo ya etenādiṣṭvānyana yajate garttapatyam eva taj jīyate vā pramīyate vā ity evamādiḥ/
anyakartṛkasya vyāhatasya vidher vādaḥ parakṛtiḥ
children.translated_text: 'This indeed is the first sacrifice among sacrifices, namely the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>. He who, having performed this, sacrifices with another [first], falls into a pit, or is killed' — and so forth. <s>Parakṛti</s> (precedent from others) is the citation of an injunction performed by another that is at variance [with the present one]:

children.text: hutvā vapām evāgre 'bhighārayanti atha pṛṣad ājyaṃ taduha carakādhvaryavaḥ pṛṣadājyam evāgre 'bhidhārayanti agneḥ prāṇāḥ pṛṣadājyastomam ity evam abhidadhati
children.translated_text: 'Having offered the <s>vapā</s> (omentum), they first pour ghee; then [they pour] curd-mixed ghee. But the <s>Caraka</s> <s>Adhvaryus</s> first pour curd-mixed ghee, saying: the <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths) of <s>Agni</s> are the curd-mixed-ghee <s>stoma</s> (hymn-arrangement).'

children.text:
ity evamādi/
aitihyasamācarito vidhiḥ purākalpa iti/ ``tasmād vā etena brāhmaṇā bahiṣ pavamānaṃ sāmastomama stoṣan yone yajñaṃ pratanavāmahe ity evamādi/
kathaṃ purākṛtipurākalpāv arthavādāv iti? stutinindāvākyenābhisambandhād vidhyāśrayasya kasyacid arthasya dyotanād arthavāda iti//64//
children.translated_text: And so forth. An injunction practiced in accordance with tradition is <s>purākalpa</s> (ancient practice). 'Therefore <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> with this <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> <s>sāmastoma</s> will chant: we extend the sacrifice from the source' — and so forth. How are <s>parakṛti</s> and <s>purākalpa</s> explanatory passages? Because they illuminate some point that depends on an injunction, by being connected with statements of praise or blame — hence they are <s>arthavāda</s>. // 64 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 65
<s>Anuvāda</s> (reiteration) is the re-statement of what has been enjoined. // 2.1.65 //

children.text: vidhyanuvacanaṃ cānuvādo vihitānuvacanaṃ ca/ pūrvaḥ śabdānuvādo 'paro 'rthānuvādaḥ/ yathā punaruktaṃ dvividham evam anuvādo 'pi/ kimarthaṃ punar vihitam anūdyate? adhikārārtham; vihitam adhikṛtya stutir bodhyate nindā vā, vidhiśeṣo vābhidhīyate/
children.translated_text: Reiteration of an injunction is <s>anuvāda</s>, and also the re-statement of what has been enjoined. The former is verbal reiteration, the latter is reiteration of meaning. Just as redundancy is of two kinds, so too is <s>anuvāda</s>. For what purpose then is what has been enjoined restated? For the purpose of introducing a topic: having introduced what was enjoined, praise or blame is conveyed, or a supplementary injunction is stated.

children.text:
vihitānantarārtho 'pi cānuvādā bhavati/ evam anyad apy utprekṣaṇīyam/
loke 'pi ca vidhir arthavādo 'nuvāda iti ca trividhaṃ vākyam/ odanaṃ paced iti vidhivākyam/ arthavādavākyam—āyurvarco balaṃ sukhaṃ pratibhānaṃ cānne pratiṣṭhitam/ anuvādaḥ—pacatu pacatu bhavān ity abhyāsaḥ, kṣipraṃ pacyatām iti vā; aṅga pacyatām ity adhyeṣaṇārtham, pacyatām eveti cāvadhāraṇārtham/
yathā laukike vākye vibhāgenārthagrahaṇāt pramāṇatvam evam vedavākyānām api vibhāgenārthagrahaṇāt pramāṇatvaṃ bhavitum arhatīti//65//
children.translated_text:
And even what follows upon an injunction can be an <s>anuvāda</s> (re-statement). Other cases too should be considered in this way.
In worldly discourse also, statements are threefold: <s>vidhi</s> (injunction), <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory praise), and <s>anuvāda</s> (re-statement). "One should cook rice" is an injunctive statement. An <s>arthavāda</s> statement is: "Longevity, splendor, strength, happiness, and intelligence are established in food." An <s>anuvāda</s> is: "Cook, do cook, sir!" — which is repetition; or "Let it be cooked quickly!" — which expresses urgency; or "Please, let it be cooked!" — which serves as a request; or "Let it indeed be cooked!" — which serves as emphatic determination.
Just as in worldly statements, authoritative validity arises from grasping the meaning through differentiation, so too for Vedic statements, authoritative validity can arise from grasping the meaning through differentiation. // 65 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 66
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.66: There is no distinction between <s>anuvāda</s> (re-statement) and <s>punarukta</s> (mere repetition), since the repetition of words is possible in both cases. // 2.1.66 //

children.text: punaruktam asādhu sādhur anuvāda iti ayaṃ viśeṣo nopapadyate/ kasmāt? ubhayatra hi pratītārthaḥ śabdo 'bhyasyate caritārthasya śabdasyābhyāsād ubhayam asādhv iti//66//
children.translated_text: The distinction that <s>punarukta</s> (repetition) is faulty while <s>anuvāda</s> (re-statement) is correct does not hold. Why? Because in both cases, a word whose meaning is already understood is repeated; and since what has already served its purpose is being repeated, both are equally faulty. // 66 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 67
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.67: There is no lack of distinction, because repetition can have purpose, like the instruction "go faster and faster." // 2.1.67 //

children.text: nānuvādapunaruktayor aviśeṣaḥ/ kasmāt? arthavato 'bhyāsasyānuvādabhāvāt/ arthavān abhyāso 'nuvādaḥ, śīghrataragamanopadeśavat/ śīghraṃ śīghraṃ gamyatām iti kriyātiśayo 'bhyāsenaivocyate/
children.translated_text: There is no lack of distinction between <s>anuvāda</s> and <s>punarukta</s>. Why? Because purposeful repetition constitutes <s>anuvāda</s>. Meaningful repetition is <s>anuvāda</s>, like the instruction to go faster and faster. "Go quickly, quickly!" — here an intensification of the action is expressed through repetition itself.

children.text: udāharaṇārthaṃ cedam/ evam anyo 'py abhyāsaḥ pacati pacatīti kriyānuparamaḥ/ grāmo grāmo ramanīya iti vyāptiḥ/ pari pari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo deva iti parivarjanam/ adhy adhi kuḍyaṃ niṣaṇṇam iti sāmīpyam/ tiktaṃ tiktam iti prakāraḥ/ evam anuvādasya stutinindāśeṣavidhiṣv adhikārārthatā vihitānantarārthatā ceti//67//
children.translated_text: This is given by way of illustration. Similarly, other repetitions too have purpose: "He cooks, he cooks" expresses continuity of action; "Village after village is delightful" expresses pervasiveness; "Away, away from the <s>Trigartas</s> the god has rained" expresses avoidance; "Right up against the wall it sat" expresses proximity; "Bitter, bitter" expresses the degree of a quality. Thus <s>anuvāda</s> serves the purposes of praise, blame, supplementary injunction, and expressing what follows upon an injunction. // 67 //
Chapter 2, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 68

children.text: kiṃ punaḥ pratiṣedhahetūddhārād eva śabdasya pramāṇatvaṃ sidhyati? na, ataś ca—
children.translated_text: But does the authoritative validity of <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) become established merely by refuting the grounds for its denial? No, and therefore —

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.68: Its authoritative validity is like the authoritative validity of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>, since it derives from the trustworthiness of reliable persons (<s>āptaprāmāṇya</s>). // 2.1.68 //

children.text: kiṃ punar āyurvedasya prāmāṇyam? yat tad āyurvedenopadiśyate idaṃ kṛtveṣṭam adhigacchati, idaṃ varjayitvāniṣṭaṃ jahāti, tasyānuṣṭhīyamānasya tathābhāvaḥ satyārthatāviparyayaḥ/ mantrapadānāṃ ca viṣayabhūtāśanipratiṣedhārthānāṃ prayoge 'rthasya tathābhāva etatprāmāṇyam/ kiṃkṛtam etat? āptaprāmāṇyakṛtam/ kiṃ punar āptānāṃ prāmāṇyam? sākṣātkṛtadharmatā bhūtadayā yathābhūtārthacikhyāpayiṣeti/
children.translated_text: What then is the authoritative validity of <s>Āyurveda</s>? That which is taught by <s>Āyurveda</s> — "by doing this one attains what is desired, by avoiding that one escapes what is undesired" — when practiced accordingly, the result corresponds to the teaching, and the meaning proves true without deviation. And regarding <s>mantra</s> words whose purpose is the counteraction of poison, fire, demons, and lightning, the correspondence of results upon their application constitutes their authoritative validity. What is the basis of this? It is based on <s>āptaprāmāṇya</s> (the trustworthiness of reliable persons). And what is the trustworthiness of the <s>āptas</s> (reliable persons)? It consists in their having directly realized <s>dharma</s>, their compassion for living beings, and their desire to communicate things as they truly are.

children.text: āptāḥ khalu sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇaḥ idaṃ hātavyam idam asya hānihetur idam asyādhigantavyam idam asyādhigamahetuḥ iti bhūtāny anukampante/ teṣāṃ khalu vai prāṇabhṛtāṃ svayam anavabudhyamānānāṃ nānyad upadeśād avabodhakāraṇam asti/%vai prāṇabhṛtāṃ svayam anavabudhyamānānāṃ nānyad upadeśād avabodhakāraṇam asti/]
children.translated_text: Indeed, the <s>āptas</s>, having directly realized <s>dharma</s>, feel compassion for living beings, thinking: "This is to be abandoned, this is the cause of its abandonment; this is to be attained, this is the means of its attainment." For those living beings who do not understand by themselves, there is no other cause of understanding than instruction. [Note: variant reading — "vai prāṇabhṛtāṃ svayam anavabudhyamānānāṃ nānyad upadeśād avabodhakāraṇam asti"]

children.text:
na cānavabodhe samīhā varjanaṃ vā, na vākṛtvā svastibhāvaḥ, nāpy asyānya upakārako 'py asti/ hanta vayam ebhyo yathādarśanaṃ yathābhūtam upadiśyāmaḥ ta ime śrutvā pratipadyamānā heyaṃ hāsyanty adhigantavyam evādhigamiṣyantīti/ evam āptopadeśaḥ etena trividhenāptaprāmāṇyena parigṛhīto 'nuṣṭhīyamāno 'rthasya sādhako bhavati; evam āptopadeśaḥ pramāṇam/ evam āptāḥ pramāṇam/
dṛṣṭārthenāptopadeśenāyurvedenādṛṣṭārtho vedabhāgo 'numātavyaḥ pramāṇam ity āptaprāmāṇyasya hetoḥ samānatvād iti/ asyāpi caikadeśo
children.translated_text:
Without understanding, there is neither purposeful activity nor avoidance, and without performing these there is no well-being, nor is there any other helper for such a person. "Come, let us instruct these beings according to what we have seen, as things truly are; having heard this, they will act accordingly — they will abandon what is to be abandoned and attain what is to be attained." Thus, the instruction of <s>āptas</s>, encompassed by this threefold <s>āptaprāmāṇya</s> (trustworthiness of reliable persons), when practiced, becomes the means of accomplishing one's purpose; thus the instruction of <s>āptas</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge); thus <s>āptas</s> are authoritative.
By the instruction of <s>āptas</s> whose results are seen, such as <s>Āyurveda</s>, the portion of the <s>Veda</s> dealing with unseen results is to be inferred as authoritative, since the basis — namely <s>āptaprāmāṇya</s> — is the same. And even of this, one part,
"One who desires a village should perform a sacrifice,"

children.text:
ity evamādir dṛṣṭārthaḥ, tenānumātavyam iti/
loke ca bhūyān upadeśāśrayo vyavahāraḥ/ laukikasyāpy upadeṣṭur upadeṣṭavyārthajñānena parānujighṛkṣayā yathābhūtārthacikhyāpayiṣayā ca prāmāṇyam,
children.translated_text:
and such statements have visible results, by which the rest is to be inferred.
In the world too, the greater part of practical activity depends on instruction. Even a worldly instructor has authoritative validity by virtue of knowledge of what is to be taught, the desire to benefit others, and the wish to communicate things as they truly are.

children.text:
tatparigrahād āptopadeśaḥ pramāṇam iti/
draṣṭṛpravaktṛsāmānyāc cānumānam/ ya evāptā vedārthānāṃ draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca ta evāyurvedaprabhṛtīnām ity āyurvedaprāmāṇyavad vedaprāmāṇyam anumātavyam iti/
nityatvād vedavākyānāṃ pramāṇatve tatprāmāṇyam āptaprāmāṇyād ity ayuktam/ śabdasya vācakatvād arthapratipattau pramāṇatvaṃ na nityatvād/ nityatve hi sarvasya sarveṇa vacanāc chabdārthavyavasthānupapattiḥ/ nānityatve vācakatvam iti ced na, laukikeṣv adarśanāt/ te 'pi nityā iti cet na, anāptopadeśād arthavisaṃvādo 'nupapannaḥ/ nityatvād dhi śabdaḥ pramāṇam iti/
children.translated_text:
Because of being so characterized, the instruction of <s>āptas</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And the inference is based on the commonality between the seers and speakers — those very <s>āptas</s> who are the seers and speakers of Vedic meanings are the same for <s>Āyurveda</s> and the like; therefore the authoritative validity of the <s>Veda</s> is to be inferred in the same way as that of <s>Āyurveda</s>.
[Objection:] If the authoritative validity of Vedic statements is due to their eternality, then it is inappropriate to say that their validity comes from <s>āptaprāmāṇya</s>. [Reply:] The validity of <s>śabda</s> (word) as a <s>pramāṇa</s> lies in its capacity to signify meaning, not in its eternality. For if everything were eternal, everything would express everything, and the fixed relation between word and meaning would be impossible. [Objection:] If it is said that the capacity to signify does not exist in what is non-eternal — [Reply:] No, because this is not observed in worldly words. [Objection:] If it is said that worldly words too are eternal — [Reply:] No, because then the deviation of meaning from the instruction of unreliable persons would be inexplicable. For, [on your view,] it is because of eternality that <s>śabda</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text: anityaḥ sa iti cet? aviśeṣavacanam/ anāptopadeśo laukiko na nitya iti kāraṇaṃ vācyam iti/ yathāyogaṃ cārthasya pratyāyanād nāmadheyaśabdānāṃ loke prāmāṇyaṃ nityatvāt prāmāṇyānupapattiḥ/ yatrārthe nāmadheyaśabdo niyujyate loke tasya niyogasāmarthyāt pratyāyako bhavati, na nityatvāt/ manvantarayugāntantareṣu cātītānāgateṣu sampradāyābhyāsaprayogāvicchedo vedānāṃ nityatvam,
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If it is said that worldly speech is non-eternal? [Reply:] This is a statement without distinction. One must state the reason why worldly speech, being the instruction of non-<s>āptas</s>, is not eternal. And since <s>nāmadheya</s> (naming) words in the world convey their meanings as appropriate, it is impossible that their authoritative validity derives from eternality. A naming word, when applied to a particular meaning in the world, becomes capable of conveying it by the force of that conventional assignment, not by eternality. The eternality of the <s>Vedas</s> consists in the unbroken continuity of tradition, practice, and usage across <s>manvantaras</s> (cosmic epochs) and <s>yugāntas</s> (ends of ages), past and future,

children.text: āptaprāmāṇyāc ca prāmāṇyam; laukikeṣu śabdeṣu caitat samānam iti//68//
children.translated_text: and their authoritative validity comes from <s>āptaprāmāṇya</s>; and this is the same for worldly words as well. // 68 //
Thus ends the first section of the second chapter in <s>Vātsyāyana's</s> <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>.
Chapter 2, Section 2
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 1

children.text:
atha dvitīyādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam
ayathārthaḥ pramāṇoddeśa iti matvāha—
children.translated_text:
Now begins the second section of the second chapter.
Thinking that the enumeration of <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) is incorrect, [the opponent] says —

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.1: The number is not [limited to] four, because of the authoritative validity of <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>sambhava</s> (subsumption), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence). // 2.2.1 //

children.text: na catvāry eva pramāṇāni/ kiṃ tarhi? aitihyam arthāpattiḥ sambhavo 'bhāva ity etāny api pramāṇāni,
children.translated_text: The <s>pramāṇas</s> are not only four. What then? <s>Aitihya</s> (tradition), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>sambhava</s> (subsumption), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) — these too are <s>pramāṇas</s>.

children.text: tāni kasmān noktāni/ itihocur ity anirdiṣṭapravaktṛkam pravādapāramparyam aitihyam/ arthād āpattir arthāpattiḥ/ āpattiḥ prāptiḥ prasaṅgaḥ/ yatrābhidhīyamāne 'rthe yo 'nyo 'rthaḥ prasajyate so 'rthāpattiḥ/ yathā megheṣv asatsu vṛṣṭir na bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: Why were they not mentioned? "Thus they say" — a tradition of teaching without a specified original speaker is <s>aitihya</s>. <s>Arthāpatti</s> is the obtaining of a meaning from another meaning — <s>āpatti</s> means arrival, occurrence, or implication.
