When, upon a certain meaning being stated, another meaning necessarily follows, that is <s>arthāpatti</s>. For example: "When there are no clouds, rain does not occur."

children.text: kim atra prasajyate? satsu bhavatīti/ sambhavo nāmāvinābhāvino 'rthasya sattāgrahaṇād anyasya sattāgrahaṇam/ yathā droṇasya sattāgrahaṇād āḍhakasya sattāgrahaṇam, āḍakasya sattāgrahaṇāt prasthasyeti/ abhāvo virodhy abhūtaṃ bhūtasya, avidyamānaṃ varṣakarma vidyamānasya vāyvabhrasaṃyogasya pratipādakam, vidhārake hi vāyvabhrasaṃyoge gurutvād apāṃ patanakarma na bhavatīti//1//
children.translated_text: What is implied here? "When they are present, it does occur." <s>Sambhava</s> (subsumption) means the cognition of the existence of one thing from the cognition of the existence of another thing that is inseparably connected with it. For example, from the cognition of the existence of a <s>droṇa</s> measure, one cognizes the existence of an <s>āḍhaka</s> measure; from the cognition of an <s>āḍhaka</s>, that of a <s>prastha</s>. <s>Abhāva</s> (non-existence): what is contrary, what has not come into being, indicates that which has come into being — the non-existence of the action of rain indicates the existence of the conjunction of wind and clouds that prevents it; for when the sustaining conjunction of wind and clouds exists, the falling of water does not occur due to its heaviness. // 1 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 2

children.text: satyam etāni pramāṇāni, na tu pramāṇāntarāṇi/ pramāṇāntaraṃ ca manyamānena pratiṣedha ucyate/ so 'yam—
children.translated_text: It is true that these are <s>pramāṇas</s>, but they are not separate <s>pramāṇas</s>. The denial is stated by one who considers them to be separate <s>pramāṇas</s>. This is as follows —

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.2: There is no refutation, because <s>aitihya</s> (tradition) is not different from <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony), and <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>sambhava</s> (subsumption), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) are not different from <s>anumāna</s> (inference). // 2.2.2 //
"<s>Śabda</s> is the instruction of <s>āptas</s>"

children.text: iti/ na ca śabdalakṣaṇam aitihyād vyāvartate; so 'yaṃ bhedaḥ sāmānyāt saṃgṛhyata iti/ pratyakṣeṇāpratyakṣasya sambaddhasya pratipattir anumānam/
children.translated_text: — thus defined. And the definition of <s>śabda</s> does not exclude <s>aitihya</s>; this distinction is subsumed under the general category. <s>Anumāna</s> (inference) is the cognition of something not directly perceived through its connection with what is perceived.
The refutation is untenable. How so?

children.text: tathā cārthāpattisambhavābhāvaḥ/ vākyārthasampratyayenānabhihitasyārthasya pratyanīkabhāvād grahaṇam arthāpattir anumānam eva/ avinābhāvavṛttyā ca sambaddhayoḥ samudāyasamudāyinoḥ samudāyenetarasya grahaṇaṃ sambhavaḥ,
children.translated_text: And so too with <s>arthāpatti</s>, <s>sambhava</s>, and <s>abhāva</s>. <s>Arthāpatti</s> — the cognition of an unstated meaning through the understanding of a stated meaning, by way of its contradictory opposite — is nothing but <s>anumāna</s>. And <s>sambhava</s> — the cognition of one from the other in the case of a whole and its parts that exist in an inseparable relation —

children.text: tad apy anumānam eva/ asmin satīdaṃ nopapadyata iti virodhitve prasiddhe kāryānupapattyā kāraṇasya pratibandhakam anumīyate/ so 'yaṃ yathārtha eva pramāṇoddeśa iti//2//
children.translated_text: that too is nothing but <s>anumāna</s>. When, given that something exists, something else is impossible, and when this incompatibility is established, the obstruction of the cause is inferred from the non-occurrence of the effect. Thus the enumeration of <s>pramāṇas</s> is exactly correct. // 2 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 3

children.text: satyam etāni pramāṇāni na tu pramāṇāntarāṇīty uktam, atrārthāpatteḥ pramāṇabhāvābhyanujñā nopapadyate/ tathā hīyam—
children.translated_text: It was said that these are indeed <s>pramāṇas</s> but not separate ones; however, the concession that <s>arthāpatti</s> has <s>pramāṇa</s> status is untenable. For indeed —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.3: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). // 2.2.3 //

children.text: asatsu megheṣu vṛṣṭir na bhavatīti satsu bhavatīty etad arthād āpadyate, satsv api caikadā na bhavati/ seyam arthāpattir apramāṇam iti//3//
children.translated_text: "When there are no clouds, rain does not occur" — from this it is presumed that "when they are present, it does occur." But even when they are present, sometimes it does not occur. Therefore this <s>arthāpatti</s> is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. // 3 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 4
<s>Arthāpatti</s> is not inconclusive —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.4: Because what is imagined to be <s>arthāpatti</s> is in fact a case of non-<s>arthāpatti</s>. // 2.2.4 //

children.text:
asati kāraṇe kāryaṃ notpadyata iti vākyāt pratyanīkabhūto 'rthaḥ sati kāraṇe kāryam utpadyata ity arthād āpadyate/ abhāvasya hi bhāvaḥ pratyanīka iti/ so 'yaṃ kāryotpādaḥ sati kāraṇe 'rthād āpadyamāno na kāraṇasya sattāṃ vyabhicarati/ na khalv asati kāraṇe kāryam utpadyate tasmān nānaikāntikī/
yat tu sati kāraṇe nimittapratibandāt kāryaṃ notpadyata iti kāraṇadharmo 'sau na tv arthāpatteḥ prameyam/ kiṃ tarhy asyāḥ prameyam? sati kāraṇe kāryam utpadyata iti yo 'sau kāryotpādaḥ kāraṇasya sattāṃ na vyabhicatati tad asyāḥ prameyam/ evaṃ tu saty anarthāpattāv arthāpattyabhimānaṃ kṛtvā pratiṣedha ucyata iti/
children.translated_text:
From the statement that "when the cause is absent, the effect does not arise," the contradictory meaning — "when the cause is present, the effect arises" — is obtained by <s>arthāpatti</s>. For the contradictory opposite of absence is presence. Now, this arising of the effect when the cause is present, being obtained by <s>arthāpatti</s>, does not deviate from the existence of the cause. For it is never the case that the effect arises when the cause is absent; therefore <s>arthāpatti</s> is not inconclusive.
As for the case where the effect does not arise even when the cause is present due to obstruction by an interfering factor — that is a property of the cause, not a subject matter of <s>arthāpatti</s>. What then is its subject matter? That the arising of the effect when the cause is present does not deviate from the existence of the cause — that is its subject matter. Thus, having mistakenly attributed <s>arthāpatti</s> to what is in fact a case of non-<s>arthāpatti</s>, the refutation is offered.
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.5: And the refutation itself lacks authoritative validity, because it too is inconclusive. // 2.2.5 //

children.text: arthāpattir na pramāṇam anaikāntikatvād iti vākyaṃ pratiṣedhaḥ/ tenānenārthāpatteḥ pramāṇatvaṃ pratiṣidhyate na sadbhāvaḥ, evam anaikāntiko bhavati/ anaikāntikatvād apramāṇenānena na kaścid arthaḥ pratiṣidhyata iti//5//
children.translated_text: The statement "<s>arthāpatti</s> is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> because it is inconclusive" is itself a refutation. By this, only the <s>pramāṇa</s> status of <s>arthāpatti</s> is denied, not its existence; thus it is equally inconclusive. Since it is inconclusive and not a valid <s>pramāṇa</s>, nothing is actually refuted by it. // 5 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 6

children.text: atha manyase niyataviṣayeṣv artheṣu svaviṣaye vyabhicāro bhavati, na ca pratiṣedhasya sadbhāvo viṣayaḥ? evaṃ tarhi—
children.translated_text: Now, if you think that things with fixed domains may deviate in their own domain, but the existence [of the subject] is not the domain of refutation — then in that case —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.6: Or, if the refutation is valid, then <s>arthāpatti</s> is not without authoritative validity. // 2.2.6 //

children.text: arthāpatter api kāryotpādena kāraṇasattāyā avyabhicāro viṣayaḥ/ na ca kāraṇadharmo nimittapratibandhāt kāryānutpādakatvam iti//6//
children.translated_text: For <s>arthāpatti</s> too has as its domain the non-deviation of the existence of the cause from the arising of the effect. And the non-production of the effect due to obstruction by an interfering factor is a property of the cause, [not of <s>arthāpatti</s>]. // 6 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 7

children.text: abhāvasya tarhi pramāṇabhāvābhyanujñā nopapadyate/ katham iti?
children.translated_text: However, the concession that <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) has <s>pramāṇa</s> status is untenable. How so?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.7: <s>Abhāva</s> (non-existence) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because its object is not established. // 2.2.7 //

children.text: abhāvasya bhūyasi prameye lokasiddhe vaiyātyād ucyate nābhāvaprāmāṇyaṃ prameyāsiddher iti//7//
children.translated_text: Since the objects to be known by <s>abhāva</s> are for the most part already well-established in common experience, it is said that <s>abhāva</s> is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> because its object [as distinct from other <s>pramāṇas</s>] is not established, due to the inconsistency [of its proposed scope]. // 7 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
Now, due to the multiplicity of objects, one particular case is cited as an example —

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.8: Among things that are characterized, because what is uncharacterized is known through the characterized, the objects of <s>abhāva</s> are established [by other <s>pramāṇas</s>]. // 2.2.8 //

children.text: tasyābhāvasya sidhyati prameyam/ katham? lakṣiteṣu vāsaḥsu anupādeyeṣv upādeyānām alakṣitānām alakṣaṇalakṣitatvād lakṣaṇābhāvena lakṣitatvād iti/ ubhayasannidhāv alakṣitāni vāsāṃsy ānayeti prayukto yeṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣaṇāni na bhavanti tāni lakṣaṇābhāvena pratipadyate, pratipadya cānayati, pratipattihetuś ca pramāṇam iti//8//
children.translated_text: The <s>prameya</s> (object of valid cognition) of that absence is established. How? Among marked garments that are not to be taken, the unmarked ones that are to be taken are recognized by the absence of marks — that is, they are recognized through the absence of distinguishing marks. When both [marked and unmarked garments] are present, and one is told 'bring the unmarked garments,' one recognizes those garments in which marks do not exist through the absence of marks, and having recognized them, brings them. And the means of recognition is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). // 8 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 9

children.text: asaty arthe nābhāva iti cen nānyalakṣaṇopapatteḥ // 2.2.9 //
children.translated_text: If it is objected that there is no absence when the thing never existed — no, because of the applicability of the characteristic of the other. // 2.2.9 //

children.text: yatra bhūtvā kiñcin na bhavati tatra tasyābhāva upapadyate/ na cālakṣiteṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣitāni bhūtvā na bhavanti, tasmāt teṣu lakṣaṇābhāvo 'nupapanna iti/
children.translated_text: Where something, having existed, ceases to exist — there its absence is tenable. But marks, having never existed in the unmarked garments, do not then cease to exist; therefore the absence of marks in them is untenable — so the objection goes.

children.text: nānyalakṣaṇopapatteḥ—yathāyam anyeṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣaṇānām upapattiṃ paśyati naivam alakṣiteṣu/ so 'yaṃ lakṣaṇābhāvaṃ paśyann abhāvenārthaṃ pratipadyata iti//9//
children.translated_text: 'Because of the applicability of the characteristic of the other' — just as one sees the occurrence of marks in other garments, one does not see this in the unmarked ones. Seeing this absence of marks, one cognizes the object through absence. // 9 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 10
Because of their being established in marked ones, this is a non-reason for the unmarked ones. // 2.2.10 //

children.text: teṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣiteṣu siddhir vidhyamānatā yeṣāṃ bhavati na teṣām abhāvo lakṣaṇānām/ yāni ca lakṣiteṣu vidyante lakṣaṇāni teṣām alakṣiteṣv abhāva ity ahetuḥ/ yāni khalu bhavanti teṣām abhāvo vyāhata iti//10//
children.translated_text: The marks whose existence — that is, presence — is established in the marked garments, of those [marks] there is no absence. And those marks that exist in the marked ones — their absence in the unmarked ones is a non-reason. For the absence of things that do exist is contradictory. // 10 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
No, because the cognition depends on marks being present [in some] and absent [in others]. // 2.2.11 //

children.text: na brūmo yāni lakṣaṇāni bhavanti teṣām abhāva iti, kin tu keṣucil lakṣaṇāny avasthitāni anavasthitāni keṣucit, apekṣamāṇo yeṣu lakṣaṇānāṃ bhāvaṃ na paśyati tāni lakṣaṇābhāvena pratipadyata iti//11//
children.translated_text: We are not saying that there is absence of marks that do exist. Rather, marks are present in some [garments] and not present in others; one who, looking [at those in which marks are absent], does not see the presence of marks, cognizes them through the absence of marks. // 11 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 12
And because absence is tenable prior to origination as well. // 2.2.12 //

children.text: abhāvadvaitaṃ khalu bhavati prāk cotpatter avidyamānatā, utpannasya cātmano hānād avidyamānatā/ tatrālakṣiteṣu vāsaḥsu prāg utpatter avidyamānatālakṣaṇo lakṣaṇānām abhāvo netara iti//12//
children.translated_text: Absence is indeed twofold: the non-existence prior to origination, and the non-existence due to the destruction of what has come into being. Of these, the absence of marks in the unmarked garments is the absence characterized by non-existence prior to origination — not the other kind. // 12 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
'<s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is the instruction of a trustworthy person' —

children.text:
iti pramāṇabhāve viśeṣaṇaṃ bruvatā nānāprakāraḥ śabda iti jñāpyate/ tasmin sāmanyena vicāraḥ—kiṃ nityo 'thānitya iti/
vimarśahetvanuyoge ca vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ/ ākāśaguṇaḥ śabdao vibhur nityo 'bhivyaktidharmaka ity eke/
children.translated_text: by stating a qualification regarding the status of being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, it is indicated that <s>śabda</s> (word/sound) is of various kinds. Regarding it, there is a general inquiry: is it eternal or non-eternal? And when the grounds for investigation are examined, there is doubt due to conflicting views. Some say: '<s>Śabda</s> is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> (space), all-pervading, eternal, and subject to manifestation.'

children.text:
gandhādisahavṛttir dravyeṣu sanniviṣṭo gandhādivad avasthito 'bhivyaktidharmaka ity apare/
ākāśaguṇaḥ śabda utpattinirodhadharmako buddhivad ity apare/
mahābhūtasaṃkṣobhajaḥ śabdo 'nāśrita utpattidharmako nirodhadharmaka ity anye/ ataḥ saṃśayaḥ kim atra tattvam iti//
children.translated_text: Others say: 'It coexists with smell and the like, is situated in substances, is stationary like smell and the like, and is subject to manifestation.' Yet others say: '<s>Śabda</s> is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s>, subject to origination and cessation, like cognition.' And still others say: '<s>Śabda</s> is born from the agitation of the great elements, is without a substrate, is subject to origination and cessation.' Hence the doubt: what is the truth here?
The answer is: <s>śabda</s> (sound) is non-eternal. How?
Because it has an origin, because it is sense-perceptible, because it is used figuratively like a produced thing, and [for other reasons]. // 2.2.13 //

children.text:
ādir yoniḥ kāraṇam ādīyate asmād iti/ kāraṇavad anityaṃ dṛṣṭam/ saṃyogavibhāgajaś ca śabdaḥ kāraṇavattvād anitya iti/ kā punar iyam arthadeśanā kāraṇavattvād iti? utpattidharmakatvāt; anityaḥ śabda iti—bhūtvā na bhavati vināśadharmaka iti/
sāṃśayikam etat—kim utpattikāraṇaṃ saṃyogavibhāgau śabdasya, āhosvid abhivyaktikāraṇam ity ata āha—aindriyakatvāt/ indriyapratyāsattigrāhya aindriyakaḥ/
kim ayaṃ vyañjakena samānadeśo 'bhivyajyate rūpādivat atha saṃyogajāc chabdāc chabdasantāne sati śrotrapratyāsanno gṛhyata iti? saṃyoganivṛttau śabdagrahaṇāt na vyañjakena samānadeśasya grahaṇam—dāruvraścane dāruparaśusaṃyoganivṛttau dūrasthena śabdo gṛhyate/ na ca vyañjakābhāve vyaṅgyagrahaṇaṃ bhavati,
children.translated_text: <s>Ādi</s> (origin) means source, cause — 'that from which it originates.' What has a cause is observed to be non-eternal. And <s>śabda</s>, born from conjunction and disjunction, is non-eternal because it has a cause. What then is the meaning of this teaching 'because it has a cause'? Because it has the nature of origination — <s>śabda</s> is non-eternal means: having come into being, it ceases to be, i.e., it has the nature of destruction. This raises a doubt: are conjunction and disjunction the cause of the origination of <s>śabda</s>, or the cause of its manifestation? Therefore he says: 'because it is sense-perceptible.' <s>Aindriyaka</s> (sense-perceptible) means graspable through proximity to a sense-organ. Is this [sound] manifested while occupying the same location as the manifester, like color and such? Or does sound, originating from conjunction, exist in a continuum and is grasped when proximate to the ear? Since sound is grasped even after the conjunction has ceased, the grasping is not of something in the same location as the manifester — when wood is being cut, after the conjunction of wood and axe has ceased, sound is heard by one standing far away. And there is no grasping of the manifestable in the absence of the manifester.

children.text: tasmān na vyañjakaḥ saṃyogaḥ, utpādake tu saṃyoge saṃyogajāc chabdāc chabdasantāne sati śrotrapratyāsannasya grahaṇam iti yuktaṃ saṃyoganivṛttau śabdasya grahaṇam iti/
children.translated_text: Therefore conjunction is not a manifester; rather, with conjunction as the producer, the grasping of that which is proximate to the ear, in the presence of a sound-continuum produced from conjunction, is reasonable — it is reasonable that sound is grasped even after conjunction has ceased.

children.text: itaś ca śabda utpadyate nābhivyajyate—kṛtakavad upacārāt/ tīvraṃ mandam iti kṛtakam upacaryate, tīvraṃ sukhaṃ mandaṃ sukhaṃ tīvraṃ duḥkhaṃ mandaṃ duḥkham iti, upacaryate ca tīvraḥ śabdo mandaḥ śabda iti/
children.translated_text: Moreover, sound is produced, not manifested — because of figurative usage like that of produced things. What is produced is figuratively described as 'intense' and 'faint': 'intense pleasure,' 'faint pleasure,' 'intense pain,' 'faint pain' — and similarly it is said: 'intense sound,' 'faint sound.'

children.text: vyañjakasya tathābhāvād grahaṇasya tīvramandatā rūpavad iti ced na abhibhavopapatteḥ—saṃyogasya vyañjakasya tīvramandatayā śabdagrahaṇasya tīvramandatā bhavati na tu śabdo bhidyate yathā prakāśasya tīvramandatayā rūpagrahaṇasyeti, tac ca na, evam abhibhavopapatteḥ—tīvro bherīśabdo mandaṃ tantrīśabdam abhibhavati na mandaḥ/ na ca śabdagrahaṇam abhibhāvakam, śabdaś ca na bhidyate, śabde tu bhidyamāne yukto 'bhibhavaḥ/ tasmād utpadyate śabdo nābhivyajyata iti/
children.translated_text: If it be objected that the intensity and faintness of perception is due to the nature of the manifester, like color — [the reply is:] no, because overpowering is tenable. Due to the intensity and faintness of conjunction (the manifester), there would be intensity and faintness of sound-perception, but sound itself would not differ — just as due to the intensity and faintness of light, there is intensity and faintness of color-perception. But this is not so, because overpowering is tenable: an intense drum-sound overpowers a faint lute-sound, but a faint one does not. It is not the perception of sound that overpowers; rather, sound itself [does], and [if] sound does not differ, overpowering cannot be explained. But if sound itself differs, overpowering is tenable. Therefore sound is produced, not manifested.

children.text: abhibhavānupapattiś ca vyañjakasamānadeśasyābhivyaktau prāptyabhāvāt—vyañjakena samānadeśe 'bhivyajyate śabda ity etasmin pakṣe nopapadyate 'bhibhavaḥ/ na hi bherīśabdena tantrīsvanaḥ prāpta iti/
children.translated_text: And overpowering is untenable if manifestation occurs in the same location as the manifester — on the view that sound is manifested at the same location as its manifester, overpowering is untenable. For a drum-sound does not reach a lute-sound.

children.text: aprāpte 'bhibhava iti cet śabdamātrābhibhavaprasaṅgaḥ—atha manyeta asatyām prāptāv abhibhavo bhavatīti, evaṃ sati yathā bherīśabdaḥ kañcit tantrīsvanam abhibhavati evam antikasthopādānam iva davīyaḥstho pādānān api tantrīsvanān abhibhaved aprāpter aviśeṣāt/ tatra kvacid eva bheryāṃ praṇāditāyāṃ sarvalokeṣu samānakālās tantrīsvanā na śrūyeran iti/ nānābhūteṣu śabdasantāneṣu satsu śrotrapratyāsattibhāvena kasyacic chabdasya tīvreṇa mandasyābhibhavo yukta iti/
children.translated_text: If it be said that overpowering occurs without reaching — if one thinks that overpowering occurs even without reaching, then, since there is no difference in the absence of reaching, the consequence would be that any given sound overpowers all sounds — just as a drum-sound overpowers some nearby lute-sound, so too it should overpower even distant lute-sounds, since there is no difference in the absence of reaching. In that case, whenever a drum is sounded anywhere, all contemporaneous lute-sounds in all regions would not be heard. But when there are multiple distinct sound-continua, due to the proximity of one to the ear, the overpowering of a faint sound by an intense one is tenable.

children.text: kaḥ punar ayam abhibhavo nāma? grāhyasamānajātīyagrahaṇakṛtam agrahaṇam abhibhavaḥ; yatholkāprakāśasya grahaṇārhasyādityaprakāśeneti//13//
children.translated_text: What then is this 'overpowering'? Overpowering is the non-grasping caused by the grasping of something of the same kind as the graspable — as when the light of a torch, though worthy of being grasped, is [overpowered] by sunlight. // 13 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 14

children.text: na ghaṭābhāvasāmānyanityatvān nityeṣv apy anityavad upacārāc ca // 2.2.14 //
children.translated_text: Not so, because absence of a pot and universals are eternal; and because figurative usage occurs with eternal things too, as with non-eternal things. // 2.2.14 //

children.text: na khalu ādimattvād anityaḥ śabdaḥ/ kasmāt? vyabhicārāt/ ādimataḥ khalu ghaṭābhāvasya dṛṣṭaṃ nityatvam/ katham ādimān? kāraṇavibhāgebhyo hi ghaṭo na bhavati/ katham asya nityatvam? yo 'sau kāraṇavibhāgebhyo na bhavati na tasyābhāvo bhāvena kadācin nivartyata iti/ yad apy aindriyakatvāt, tad api vyabhicarati, aindriyakaṃ ca sāmānyaṃ nityaṃ ceti/ yad api kṛtakavad upacārād iti, etad api vyabhicarati; nityeṣv anityavad upacāro dṛṣṭaḥ—tathā hi bhavati vṛkṣasya pradeśaḥ kambalasya pradeśaḥ evam ākāśasya pradeśaḥ ātmanaḥ pradeśa iti bhavatīti//14//
children.translated_text: Sound is not non-eternal merely because it has an origin. Why? Because of deviation. The absence of a pot, which has an origin, is observed to be eternal. How does it have an origin? Because from the disjunction of causes, the pot ceases to exist. How is its [absence's] eternality? That which ceases to exist due to the disjunction of causes — its absence is never annulled by any positive existence. As for 'because it is sense-perceptible,' that too deviates, since the <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) is sense-perceptible yet eternal. As for 'because of figurative usage like a produced thing,' that too deviates, since figurative usage as with non-eternal things is observed for eternal things too — for instance, one says 'a portion of a tree,' 'a portion of a blanket,' and likewise 'a portion of space,' 'a portion of the self.' // 14 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
There is no deviation, because of the distinction between the literal and the figurative. // 2.2.15 //

children.text: nityam ity atra kiṃ tāvat tattvam? arthāntarasyānutpattidharmakasyātmahānānupapattir nityatvam, tac cābhāve nopapadyate/ bhāktaṃ tu bhavati yat tatrātmānam ahāsīd yad bhūtvā na bhavati na jātu tat punar bhavati, tatra nitya iva nityo ghaṭābhāva ity ayaṃ padārtha iti/ tatra yathājātīyakaḥ śabdo na tathājātīyakaṃ kāryaṃ kiṃcin nityaṃ dṛśyata ity avyabhicāraḥ//
children.translated_text: Regarding 'eternal' — what is the literal meaning here? Eternality is the impossibility of the destruction of the very nature of a real entity that is not subject to origination. And this does not apply to absence. But the figurative [usage] is: 'that whose own nature has never been destroyed, which, having come into being, does not exist [again] and will never come into being again — about that, [one says] the absence of the pot is eternal as if it were [truly] eternal' — this is the meaning. In that case, nothing of the same kind as sound is observed to be eternal in its effect — hence there is no deviation.
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 16

children.text: yad api sāmānyanityatvād itīndriyapratyāsattigrāhyam aindriyakam iti—
children.translated_text: And as for the [objection] that because universals are eternal and sense-perceptible —
Because of the qualification through the inference of a continuum. // 2.2.16 //

children.text: nityeṣv avyabhicāra iti prakṛtam/ nendriyagrahaṇasāmarthyāc chabdasyānityatvam/ kiṃ tarhi indriyapratyāsattigrāhyatvāt santānānumānaṃ tenānityatvam iti //
children.translated_text: The topic is: there is no deviation in the case of eternal things. The non-eternality of sound is not merely from its being graspable by the senses. Rather, because it is graspable through proximity to a sense-organ, a continuum is inferred, and from that, non-eternality [follows].
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 17

children.text: yad api nityeṣv apy anityavad upacārād iti/ na—
children.translated_text: And as for the [objection] that figurative usage occurs with eternal things too, as with non-eternal things — no,
because the word 'portion' refers to the causal substance. // 2.2.17 //

children.text:
nityeṣv apy avyabhicāra iti/ evam ākāśapradeśaḥ ātmapradeśa iti nātrākāśātmanoḥ kāraṇadravyam abhidhīyate yathā kṛtakasya/ kathaṃ hy avidyamānam abhidhīyate,
avidyamānatā ca pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ/ kiṃ tarhi tatrābhidhīyate? saṃyogasyāvyāpyavṛttitvam—paricchinnena dravyenākāśasya saṃyogo nākāśaṃ vyāpnoti avyāpya vartata iti, tad asy kṛtakena dravyeṇa sāmānyam/ na hy āmalakayoḥ saṃyoga āśrayaṃ vyāpnoti/ sāmānyakṛtā ca bhaktir ākāśasya pradeśa iti/ anenātmapradeśo vyākhyātaḥ/ saṃyogavac ca śabdabuddhyādīnām avyāpyavṛttitvam iti/ parīkṣitā ca tīvramandatā śabdatattvaṃ na bhaktikṛteti/
children.translated_text: There is no deviation in the case of eternal things either. When one says 'a portion of space,' 'a portion of the self,' the causal substance of space and the self is not what is denoted, as it is for a produced thing. For how can what does not exist be denoted? And non-existence is [established] from non-apprehension by a <s>pramāṇa</s>. What then is denoted there? The non-pervading nature of conjunction — the conjunction of space with a delimited substance does not pervade [all of] space; it operates without pervading. That is its commonality with a produced substance. For the conjunction of two myrobalan fruits does not pervade its substrate. And the figurative attribution of 'a portion of space' is based on this commonality. By this, 'a portion of the self' is also explained. And like conjunction, the cognitions, volitions, and the like of [the self] also operate without pervading. And the intensity and faintness [of sound] has been examined — it pertains to the real nature of sound, not to figurative attribution.

children.text: kasmāt punaḥ sūtrakārasyāsminn arthe sūtraṃ na śrūyata iti? śīlam idaṃ bhavgavataḥ sūtrakārasya bahuṣv adhikaraṇeṣu dvau pakṣau na vyavasthāpayati tatra śāstrasiddhāntāt tattvāvadhāraṇaṃ pratipattum arhatīti manyate/ śāstrasiddhāntas tu nyāyasamākhyātam anumataṃ bahuśākham anumānam iti//17//
children.translated_text: Why then is there no <s>sūtra</s> of the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (aphorist) heard on this matter? This is the style of the blessed <s>sūtrakāra</s>: in many topics he does not set forth both positions, considering that from the established doctrine of the <s>śāstra</s>, one should be able to ascertain the truth. And the established doctrine of the <s>śāstra</s> is the inference sanctioned by <s>nyāya</s> (logic), which has many branches. // 17 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 18

children.text: athāpi khalv idam asti idaṃ nāstīti kuta etat pratipattavyam iti? pramāṇata upalabdher anupalabdheś ceti/ avidyamānas tarhi śabdaḥ—
children.translated_text: Now, if one asks: 'this exists,' 'this does not exist' — how is this to be known? Through a <s>pramāṇa</s> — from apprehension and non-apprehension. Therefore, sound is non-existent [before utterance] —
Because of non-apprehension prior to utterance, and because of non-apprehension through obstruction and the like. // 2.2.18 //

children.text: prāg uccāraṇān nāsti śabdaḥ/ kasmāt? anupalabdheḥ/

children.translated_text: [Objection:] The non-apprehension of an existent thing is due to obstruction and the like —

children.text: etan nopapadyate/ kasmāt? āvaraṇādīnām anupalabdhikāraṇānām agrahaṇāt—anenāvṛtaḥ śabdo nopalabhyata asannikṛṣṭaś cendriyavyavadhānād ity evamādi anupalabdhikāraṇaṃ na gṛhyata iti so 'yam anuccārito nāstīti/ uccāraṇam asya vyañjakaṃ tadabhāvād prāg uccāraṇād anupalabdhir iti/ kim idam uccāraṇaṃ nāmeti? vivakṣājanitena prayatnena koṣṭhyasya vāyoḥ preritasya kaṇṭhatālvādipratighātaḥ,
children.translated_text: This is untenable. Why? Because no cause of non-apprehension such as obstruction is grasped — one cannot say: 'Sound is not apprehended because it is covered by this,' or 'because it is not in proximity [to the sense organ] and there is an obstruction of the sense organ' — no such cause of non-apprehension is grasped. Therefore, when unuttered, it does not exist. [Objection:] Utterance is its manifester, and due to its absence, there is non-apprehension prior to utterance. What then is this 'utterance'? It is the striking against the throat, palate, and other locations by the air in the chest, propelled by effort born of the desire to speak.
Prior to utterance, sound does not exist. Why? Because of non-apprehension.

children.text: yathāsthānaṃ pratighātād varṇābhivyaktir iti/ saṃyogaviśeṣo vai pratighātaḥ, pratiṣiddhaṃ ca saṃyogasya vyañjakatvam, tasmān na vyañjakābhāvād agrahaṇam, api tv abhāvād eveti/ so 'yam uccāryamāṇaḥ śrūyate śrūyamāṇaś cābhūtvā bhavatīti anumīyate/ ūrdhvaṃ coccāraṇān na śrūyate sa bhūtvā na bhavati abhāvān na śrūyata iti/ katham? āvaraṇādyanupalabdher ity uktam/ tasmād utpattitirobhāvadharmakaḥ śabda iti//18//
children.translated_text: From the striking at the appropriate location, the manifestation of phonemes occurs. But the striking is a particular kind of conjunction, and the manifesting nature of conjunction has been refuted. Therefore, it is not that non-grasping is due to the absence of a manifester; rather, it is simply due to non-existence. And when being uttered, [sound] is heard; and when it is heard, it is inferred that it has come into being without having existed before. And after utterance, it is not heard — having existed, it ceases to exist; it is not heard because of non-existence. How [is this known]? It has been said: because of non-apprehension of obstruction and the like. Therefore, sound has the nature of origination and cessation. // 18 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 19

children.text: evaṃ ca sati tattvaṃ pāṃśubhir ivāvakirann idam āha—
children.translated_text: This being so, as though scattering dust on the truth, he says:
From the non-apprehension of that, and from non-apprehension [in general], the tenability of obstruction [follows]. // 2.2.19 //

children.text: yady anupalambhād āvaraṇaṃ nāsti, āvaraṇānupalabdhir api tarhy anupalambhāt nāstīti tasyā abhāvād apratiṣiddham āvaraṇam iti/ kathaṃ punar jānīte bhavān nāvaraṇānupalabdhir upalabhyata iti?
children.translated_text: If obstruction does not exist because of non-apprehension, then the non-apprehension of obstruction also does not exist because of non-apprehension; and from the absence of that [non-apprehension of obstruction], obstruction is not refuted. But how does your honor know that the non-apprehension of obstruction is not apprehended?

children.text: kim atra jñeyaṃ pratyātmavedanīyatvāt samānam—ayaṃ khalv āvaraṇam anupalambhamānaḥ pratyātmam eva saṃvedayate nāvaraṇam upalabha iti, yathā kuḍyenāvṛtasyāvaraṇam upalabhamānaḥ pratyātmam eva saṃvedayate/ seyam āvaraṇopalabdhivad āvaraṇānupalabdhir api saṃvedyaiveti/ evaṃ ca saty apahṛtaviṣayam uttaravākyam astīti//16//
children.translated_text: What need be known here? It is the same, since it is known through individual self-awareness. For one who does not apprehend obstruction is aware within oneself "I do not apprehend obstruction," just as one who is enclosed by a wall and apprehends obstruction is aware within oneself. Thus this non-apprehension of obstruction, like the apprehension of obstruction, is indeed experienced. And this being so, the counter-statement has its subject matter removed. // 16 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 20
The <s>jātivādin</s> (proponent of the universal) now speaks by way of concession:
Because of the existence of non-apprehension even from non-apprehension, the untenability of obstruction does not follow from non-apprehension. // 2.2.20 //

children.text: yathānupalambhamānāpy āvaraṇānupalabdhir asti evam anupalabhyamānam apy āvaraṇam astīti yady abhyanujānāti bhavān anupalabhyamānāvaraṇānupalabdhir astīti abhyanujñāya ca vadati nāsty āvaraṇam anupalambhād iti, etasminn apy abhyanujñāvāde pratipattiniyamo nopapadyata iti//20//
children.translated_text: Just as the non-apprehension of obstruction exists even though not being apprehended, so too obstruction can exist even though not being apprehended. If your honor concedes that the non-apprehension of obstruction exists even while not being apprehended, and having conceded says "obstruction does not exist because of non-apprehension," then even in this argument by concession, the restriction of conclusion is untenable. // 20 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
Non-apprehension, being of the nature of non-apprehension, is a non-reason. // 2.2.21 //

children.text: yad upalabhyate tad asti, yan nopalabhyate tan nāsti, ity anupalambhātmakam asad iti vyavasthitam/ upalabdhyabhāvaś cānupalabdhir iti seyam abhāvatvān nopalabhyate/ sac ca khalv āvaraṇaṃ tasyopalabdhyā bhavitavyaṃ na copalabhyate tasmān nāstīti/
children.translated_text: What is apprehended exists; what is not apprehended does not exist — thus non-existence is established as having the nature of non-apprehension. And non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension — since it is an absence, it is not apprehended. But if obstruction exists, it must be apprehended, and it is not apprehended; therefore it does not exist.

children.text: tatra yad uktaṃ nāvaraṇānupapattir anupalambhād ity ayuktam iti//21//
children.translated_text: Therefore what was said — "the untenability of obstruction does not follow from non-apprehension" — that is untenable. // 21 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 22

children.text: atha śabdasya nityatvaṃ pratijānānaḥ kasmād dhetoḥ pratijānīte—
children.translated_text: Now, one who claims the eternality of sound — on what ground does he make this claim?
Because of intangibility. // 2.2.22 //

children.text: asparśam ākāśaṃ nityaṃ dṛṣṭam iti tathā ca śabda iti//22//
children.translated_text: Space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is intangible and observed to be eternal; and sound is likewise [intangible], therefore [it is eternal]. // 22 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 23

children.text:
so 'yam ubhayataḥ savyabhicāraḥ—sparśavāṃś cāṇur nityaḥ, asparśaṃ ca karmānityaṃ dṛṣṭam/
asparśatvād ity etasya sādhyasādharmyeṇodāharaṇam—
children.translated_text: This [reason] deviates in both directions — an atom is tangible yet eternal, and <s>karma</s> (motion) is intangible yet non-eternal. The example by similarity with what is to be proved, for "because of intangibility," is:
Not so, because <s>karma</s> (motion) is non-eternal. // 2.2.23 //
The example by dissimilarity with what is to be proved is:
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
Not so, because the atom is eternal. // 2.2.24 //
Due to deviation in both examples, it is not a [valid] reason. // 24 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 25
Then let this be the reason:
Because of transmission. // 2.2.25 //

children.text: sampradīyamānam avasthitaṃ dṛṣṭam, sampradīyate ca śabda ācaryeṇāntevāsane, tasmād avasthita iti//25//
children.translated_text: What is transmitted is observed to be persistent — and sound is transmitted from teacher to pupil; therefore it is persistent. // 25 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 26
Because the non-apprehension of [sound] in the interval [makes this] a non-reason. // 2.2.26 //

children.text: yena sampradīyate yasmai ca, tayor antarāle 'vasthānam asya kena liṅgenopalabhyate/ sampradīyamāno 'hy avasthitaḥ sampradātur apaiti sampradānaṃ ca prāpnotīty avarjanīyam etat//26//
children.translated_text: Between the one who transmits and the one to whom it is transmitted, by what mark is its persistence in the interval apprehended? For what is being transmitted, being persistent, would have to depart from the transmitter and reach the recipient — this is unavoidable. // 26 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
From teaching, there is no refutation. // 2.2.27 //

children.text: adhyayanaṃ liṅgam, asati sampradāne 'dhyāpanaṃ na syād iti//27//
children.translated_text: Teaching is the mark [of transmission]; without transmission, teaching would not occur. // 27 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
Since teaching exists for either thesis, there is no refutation. // 2.2.28 //

children.text: samānam adhyāpanam ubhayoḥ pakṣayoḥ saṃśayānivṛtteḥ, kim ācāryasthaḥ śabdo 'ntevāsinam āpadyate tad adhyāpanam,
children.translated_text: Teaching is common to both theses, and does not resolve the doubt: Is it that the sound residing in the teacher reaches the pupil, and that constitutes teaching?

children.text: āhosvin nṛtyopadeśavad gṛhītasyānukaraṇam adhyāpanam iti/ evam adhyāpanam aliṅgaṃ sampradānasyeti//28//
children.translated_text: Or is teaching the imitation of what has been grasped, like instruction in dancing? Thus teaching is not a mark of transmission. // 28 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 29
Then let this be the reason:
Because of repetition. // 2.2.29 //

children.text:
abhyasyamānam avasthitaṃ dṛṣṭam/
pañcakṛtvaḥ paśyatīti rūpam avasthitaṃ punaḥ punar dṛśyate/ bhavati ca śabde 'bhyāsaḥ—daśakṭtvo 'dhīto 'nuvāko viṃśatikṛtvo 'dhīta iti/ tasmād avasthitasya punaḥ punar uccāraṇam abhyāsa iti//29//
children.translated_text: What is repeated is observed to be persistent. Form is persistent and is seen again and again — "one sees five times." And there is repetition of sound — "the lesson was recited ten times, recited twenty times." Therefore, the repeated utterance is of something persistent. // 29 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
Not so, because the term "repetition" is used figuratively even when there is difference. // 2.2.30 //

children.text: anavasthāne 'py abhyāsasyābhidhānaṃ bhavati dvir nṛtyatu bhavān trir nṛtyatu bhavān iti, dvir anṛtyat trir anṛtyad dvir agnihotraṃ juhoti dvir bhuṅkte//30//
children.translated_text: Even when there is no persistence, the expression of repetition occurs: "Let your honor dance twice, let your honor dance thrice"; "he danced twice, he danced thrice"; "he performs the <s>agnihotra</s> twice"; "he eats twice." // 30 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 31

children.text: evaṃ vyabhicārāt pratiṣiddhahetāv anyaśabdasya prayogaḥ pratiṣidhyate—
children.translated_text: When the reason has been refuted through this deviation, the use of the word "other" is rejected:

children.text: anyad anyasmād ananyatvād ananyad ity anyatābhāvaḥ // 2.2.31 //
children.translated_text: What is other is not other than itself, due to non-difference from itself — thus there is the absence of otherness. // 2.2.31 //

children.text: yad idam anyad iti manyase tat svārthenānanyatvād anyan na bhavati, evam anyatāyā abhāvaḥ/ tatra yad uktam anyatve 'py abhyāsopacārād iti etad ayuktam iti//31//
children.translated_text: What you consider "other" is not other because it is non-different from its own nature. Thus otherness is absent. Therefore what was said — "because the term repetition is used figuratively even when there is difference" — that is untenable. // 31 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 32
In refuting the use of one word, the use of another word is refuted:
In the absence of that [otherness], non-otherness does not exist either, since the two are established in mutual dependence. // 2.2.32 //

children.text: anyasmād ananyatām upapādayati bhavān, upapādya cānyat pratyācaṣṭe ananyad iti ca śabdam anujānāti, prayuṅkte cānanyad ity etat samāsapadam, anyaśadbo 'yaṃ pratiṣedhena saha samasyate/ yadi cātrottaraṃ padaṃ nāsti kasyāyaṃ pratiṣedhena saha samāsaḥ? tasmāt tayor anyānanyaśabdayor itaro 'nanyaśabda itaram anyaśabdam apekṣamāṇaḥ sidhyatīti tatra yad uktam anyatāyā abhāva iti etad ayuktam iti//32//
children.translated_text: Your honor establishes non-otherness from what is other, and having established it, rejects "other" and accepts the word "non-other" and employs it. But "non-other" is a compound word — the word "other" is compounded with negation. If the latter element does not exist here, with what does the negation form a compound? Therefore, of these two words "other" and "non-other," each is established in dependence on the other. Thus what was said — "there is an absence of otherness" — that is untenable. // 32 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 33
Then let it be that sound is eternal:
Because of the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction. // 2.2.33 //

children.text: yad anityaṃ tasya vināśaḥ kāraṇād bhavati yathā loṣṭasya kāraṇadravyavibhāgāt/ śabdaś ced anityas tasya vināśo yasmāt kāraṇād bhavati tad upalabhyeta, na copalabhyate tasmān nitya iti//33//
children.translated_text: What is non-eternal is destroyed by a cause, as a clod of earth is destroyed by the separation of its constituent substances. If sound is non-eternal, the cause by which it is destroyed should be apprehended, but it is not apprehended; therefore it is eternal. // 33 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 34
From the non-apprehension of a cause of non-hearing, the absurd consequence of perpetual hearing [follows]. // 2.2.34 //

children.text: yathā vināśakāraṇānupalabdher avināśaprasaṅga evam aśravaṇakāraṇānupalabdheḥ satataṃ śravaṇaprasaṅgaḥ/ vyañjakābhāvād aśravaṇam iti cet? pratiṣiddhaṃ vyañjakam/ atha vidyamānasya nirnimittam aśravanam iti vidyamānasya nirnimitto vināśa iti/ samānaś ca dṛṣṭavirodho nimittam antareṇa vināśe cāśravaṇe ceti//34//
children.translated_text: Just as from the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction there follows the absurd consequence of non-destruction, so too from the non-apprehension of a cause of non-hearing there follows the absurd consequence of perpetual hearing. If it be said that non-hearing is due to the absence of a manifester — the manifester has been refuted. And if there is non-hearing of something that exists without a cause, then there can also be destruction of something that exists without a cause. And the observed contradiction is the same whether destruction or non-hearing is causeless. // 34 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 35
When the cause of destruction is being apprehended, the non-apprehension [claim] is groundless because of its non-existence, and [therefore] an unfounded assertion. // 2.2.35 //

children.text: anumānāc copalabhyamāne śabdasya vināśakāraṇe vināśakāraṇānupalabdher asattvād ity anapadeśaḥ, yathā yasmād viṣāṇī tasmād aśva iti/ kim anumānam iti cet? santānopapattiḥ/ upapāditaḥ śabdasantānaḥ saṃyogavibhāgajāc chabdāc chabdāntaraṃ tato 'ntat tato 'py anyad iti/ tatra kāryaḥ śabdaḥ kāraṇaśabdaṃ niruṇaddhi pratighātidravyasaṃyogas tv antyasya śabdasya nirodhakaḥ/
children.translated_text: Since the cause of destruction of sound is being apprehended through inference, the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction is non-existent — hence it is an unfounded assertion, like saying "because it has horns, therefore it is a horse." What is the inference? The tenability of a sound-series. The sound-series has been demonstrated: from the sound produced by conjunction and disjunction, another sound arises, from that yet another, and from that still another. There the effect-sound obstructs the cause-sound, while the conjunction of a repelling substance stops the final sound.

children.text: dṛṣṭaṃ hi tiraḥpratikuḍyam antikasthenāpy aśravaṇaṃ śabdasya śravaṇaṃ dūrasthenāpy asati vyavadhāne iti/
children.translated_text: For it is observed that behind a wall, even one standing nearby does not hear the sound, while one standing far away hears the sound when there is no obstruction.

children.text: ghaṇṭāyām abhihanyamānāyāṃ tāras tārataro mando mandatara iti śrutibhedān nānāśabdasantāno 'vicchedena śrūyate/ tatra nitye śabde ghaṇṭāstham anyagataṃ vāvasthitaṃ santānavṛtti vābhivyaktikāraṇaṃ vācyam,
children.translated_text: When a bell is being struck, a sound-series consisting of successive sounds — sharp, sharper, soft, softer — is heard without interruption, due to the differences in auditory quality. If sound is eternal, one must explain the cause of manifestation, whether it resides in the bell, elsewhere, or operates through a series,

children.text: yena śrutisantāno bhavatīti śabdabhede vāsati śrutibheda upapādayitavya iti/ anitye tu śabde ghaṇṭāsthaṃ santānavṛtti saṃyogasahakāri nimittāntaraṃ saṃskārabhūtaṃ paṭu mandam anuvartate tastānuvṛttyā śabdasantānānuvṛttiḥ, paṭumandabhāvāc ca tīvramandatā śabdasya, tatkṛtaś ca śrutibheda iti//35//
children.translated_text: by which the auditory series occurs — or else one must explain the difference in auditory quality when there is no difference in sound. But if sound is non-eternal, an additional factor in the form of an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>), residing in the bell and operating in a series, cooperating with conjunction, follows the intensity and weakness — and through its continuity, the continuity of the sound-series follows; and from the state of intensity and weakness, the sharp and soft quality of the sound follows; and from that, the difference in auditory quality. // 35 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 36

children.text: na vai nimittāntaraṃ saṃskāra upalabhyate/ anupalabdher nāstīti?
children.translated_text: Indeed, no additional factor in the form of an impression is apprehended. Is it non-existent because of non-apprehension?
Due to the joining of the hand, and from the absence of sound, there is no non-apprehension [of the impression]. // 2.2.36 //

children.text: pāṇikarmaṇā pāṇighaṇṭāpraśleṣo bhavati tasmiṃś ca sati śabdasantāno notpadyate ataḥ śravaṇānupapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: Through the action of the hand, a joining of the hand to the bell occurs, and when that happens, the sound-series is not produced — hence the non-occurrence of hearing.

children.text: tatra pratighātidravyasaṃyogaḥ śabdasya nimittāntaraṃ saṃskārabhūtaṃ niruṇaddhīty anumīyate; tasya ca nirodhāc chabdasantāno notpadyate/ anutpattau śrutivicchedo yathā pratighātidravyasaṃyogād iṣoḥ kriyāhetau saṃskāre niruddhe gamanābhāva iti/ kampasantānasya sparśanendriyagrāhyasya coparamaḥ/ kāṃsyapātrādiṣu pāṇisaṃśleṣo liṅgaṃ saṃskārasantānasyeti/ tasmān nimittāntarasya saṃskārabhūtasya nānupalabdhir iti//36//
children.translated_text: It is inferred that the conjunction of a repelling substance stops the additional factor, the impression; and from its cessation, the sound-series is not produced. When it is not produced, the auditory sequence is interrupted — just as when the impression that is the cause of the arrow's motion is stopped by the conjunction of a repelling substance, movement ceases. The cessation of the vibration-series, which is graspable by the sense of touch, also occurs. The joining of the hand to bronze vessels and the like is the mark of the impression-series. Therefore there is no non-apprehension of the additional factor in the form of an impression. // 36 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
And if persistence [follows] from the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction, the absurd consequence of its eternality [follows]. // 2.2.37 //

children.text: yadi yasya vināśakāraṇaṃ nopalabhyate tad avatiṣṭhate, avasthānāc ca tasya nityatvaṃ prasajyate; evaṃ yāni khalv imāni śabdaśravaṇāni śabdābhivyaktaya iti matam, na teṣāṃ vināśakāraṇaṃ bhavatopapādyate, anupapādanād avasthānam avasthānāt teṣāṃ nityatvaṃ prasajyata iti/ atha naivam, na tarhi vināśakāraṇānupalabdheḥ śabdasyāvasthānān nityatvam iti//37//
children.translated_text: If that whose cause of destruction is not apprehended persists, and from persistence its eternality follows — then those very sound-hearings which are considered to be manifestations of sound, for them no cause of destruction is demonstrated by you; from the failure to demonstrate, they persist; from persistence, the absurd consequence of their eternality follows. But if this is not so, then sound's eternality does not follow merely from persistence due to the non-apprehension of a cause of destruction. // 37 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 38

children.text: kampasamānāśrayasyānunādasya pāṇipraśleṣāt kampavat kāraṇoparamād abhāvaḥ/ vaiyadhikaraṇye hi pratighātidravyapraśleṣāt samānādhikaraṇasyaivoparamaḥ syād iti—
children.translated_text: The resonance (<s>anunāda</s>), which shares the same substrate as the vibration, ceases when the hand is joined [to the bell], just as the vibration ceases due to the cessation of its cause. If there were a difference in substrate, the joining of a repelling substance would only stop what shares the same substrate —
Because of intangibility, there is no refutation. // 2.2.38 //

children.text: yad idaṃ nākāśaguṇaḥ śabda iti pratiṣidhyate ayam anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, asparśatvāc chabdāśrayasya/ rūpādisamānadeśasyāgrahaṇe śabdasantānopapatter asparśavyāpidravyāśrayaḥ śabda iti jñāyate na kampasamānāśraya iti//38//
children.translated_text: This denial that sound is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> (space) is untenable, because the substrate of sound is intangible. Since the tenability of a sound-series [can be explained] without apprehending [a substrate] in the same location as form, etc., it is known that sound has an intangible substance as its substrate, and does not share the same substrate as vibration. // 38 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 39

children.text: pratidravyaṃ rūpādibhiḥ saha sanniviṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ samānadeśo vyajyata iti nopapadyate/ katham?—
children.translated_text: That sound is located together with form, etc., in each substance and is manifested in the same location — this is untenable. How?
Because of the tenability of a different case-ending in a compound. // 2.2.39 //

children.text: santānopapatteś ceti cārthaḥ/ tad vyākhyātam/ yadi rūpādayaḥ śabdāś ca pratidravyaṃ samastāḥ samuditāḥ samuditās tasmin samāse samudāye yo yathājātīyakaḥ sanniviṣṭas tasya tathā jātīyasyaiva grahaṇena bhavitavyaṃ śabde rūpādivat/ tatra yo 'yaṃ vibhāga ekadravye nānārūpā bhinnaśrutayo vidharmāṇaḥ śabdā abhivyajyamānāḥ śrūyante yac ca vibhāgāntaraṃ sarūpāḥ samānaśrutayaḥ sadharmāṇaḥ śabdās tīvramandadharmatayā bhinnāḥ śrūyante tad ubhayaṃ nopapadyate, nānābhūtānām utpadyamānānām ayaṃ dharmo naikasya vyajyamānasyeti/
children.translated_text: And the word 'ca' conveys the meaning 'because a continuous series is tenable.' This has been explained: if colors and other (qualities) and sounds in each substance are all combined together in that aggregate, then in that combination whichever (quality) is of a particular class, only that class should be apprehended — in the case of sound, as with color and the rest. Now, the distinction here is twofold: first, in a single substance, sounds of diverse forms, different in auditory aspect and dissimilar in properties, are heard as being manifested; and second, sounds of similar form, same in auditory aspect and similar in properties, are heard as differing in the properties of intensity and softness — neither of these can be explained if different things are being produced, as this is the property of multiple things arising, not of a single thing being manifested.

children.text: asti cāyaṃ vibhāgo vibhāgāntaraṃ ca, tena vibhāgopapatter manyāmahe na pratidravyaṃ rūpādibhiḥ saha śabdaḥ sanniviṣṭo vyajyata iti//39//
children.translated_text: And this distinction, as well as the other distinction, exists; therefore, because this distinction is tenable, we hold that sound is not manifested as being embedded together with colors and the rest in each substance. // 2.2.39 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 40

children.text: dvividhaś cāyaṃ śabdo varṇātmako dhvanimātraś ca/ tatra varṇātmani tāvat—
children.translated_text: And this sound is of two kinds: consisting of <s>varṇas</s> (phonemes), and consisting of mere <s>dhvani</s> (sound). Of these, regarding that which consists of phonemes —
Doubt arises from the teaching of modification and substitution. // 2.2.40 //

children.text: dadhy atreti kecit ikāra itvaṃ hitvā yatvam āpadyata iti vikāraṃ manyante/ kecid ikārasya prayoge viṣayakṛte yad ikāraḥ sthānaṃ jahāti tatra yakārasya prayogaṃ bruvate/ saṃhitāyāṃ viṣaye ikāro na prayujyate tasya sthāne yakāraḥ prayujyate sa ādeśa iti ubhayam idam upadiśyate/ tatra na jñāyate kiṃ tattvam iti/
children.translated_text: In '<s>dadhy atra</s>' (yogurt here), some hold that the <s>i</s>-vowel undergoes <s>vikāra</s> (modification), abandoning its <s>i</s>-nature and assuming <s>y</s>-nature. Others state that when the <s>i</s>-vowel, in the domain of its use, vacates its position, the <s>y</s>-consonant is employed in its place. Both things are taught — that in the domain of <s>saṃhitā</s> (juncture), the <s>i</s>-vowel is not employed and the <s>y</s>-consonant is employed in its place: this is an <s>ādeśa</s> (substitution). And here, the true nature of the matter is not known.

children.text:
ādeśopadeśas tattvam/ vikāropadeśe hy anvayasyāgrahaṇād vikārānanumānam—saty anvaye kiñcin nivartate kiñcid upajāyata iti śakyeta vikāro 'numātum/ na cānvayo gṛhyate tasmād vikāro nāstīti/
bhinnakaraṇayoś ca varṇayor aprayoge prayogopapattiḥ—vivṛtakaraṇa ikāra īṣatspṛṣṭakaraṇo yakāraḥ, tāv imau pṛthakkaraṇākhyena prayatnenoccāraṇīyau, tayor ekasyāprayoge 'nyasya prayoga upapanna iti/
avikāre cāviśeṣaḥ/ yatremāv ikārayakārau na vikārabhūtau—yatate, yacchati, prāyaṃsta, iti, ikāra idam iti ca, yatra ca vikārabhūtau iṣṭyā dadhy āhareti, ubhayatra prayoktur aviśeṣo yatnaḥ śrotuś ca śrutir ity ādeśopapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: The teaching of substitution is the truth. For in the teaching of modification, since continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) is not grasped, modification cannot be inferred — only when there is continuity, and something ceases while something else arises, can modification be inferred. But continuity is not grasped; therefore modification does not exist. And the tenability of the employment of one when the other, having a different articulatory organ, is not employed — the <s>i</s>-vowel has an open articulation and the <s>y</s>-consonant has a slightly-touching articulation; these two are to be pronounced with the effort called 'having separate articulations'; when one is not employed, the employment of the other is tenable. And when there is no modification, there is no difference: where these <s>i</s>-vowel and <s>y</s>-consonant are not in a relation of modification — in '<s>yatate</s>' (he strives), '<s>yacchati</s>' (he restrains), '<s>prāyaṃsta</s>,' '<s>iti</s>,' '<s>ikāra</s>,' '<s>idam</s>' (this) — and where they are in a modification-relation as in '<s>iṣṭyā dadhy āhara</s>' — in both cases, the effort of the speaker is the same and the hearer's perception is the same; therefore substitution is tenable.

children.text:
prayujyamānāgrahaṇāc ca/ na khalv ikāraḥ prayujyamāno yakāratām āpadyamāno gṛhyate/ kiṃ tarhi? ikārasya prayoge yakāraḥ prayujyate, tasmād avikāra iti/
avikāre ca na śabdānvākhyānalopaḥ/ na vikriyante varṇā iti/ na caitasmin pakṣe śabdānvākhyānasyāsambhave yena varṇavikāraṃ pratipadyemahīti/
na khalv varṇasya varṇāntaraṃ kāryam, na hi ikārād yakāra utpadyate yakārād vā ikāraḥ/ pṛthaksthānaprayatnotpādyā hīme varṇāḥ teṣām anyonyasya sthāne prayujyata iti yuktam/ etāvac caitat pariṇāmo vā vikāraḥ syāt kāryakāraṇabhāvo vā/ ubhayaṃ ca nāsti tasmāt na santi varṇavikārāḥ/
varṇasamudāyavikārānupapattivac ca varṇavikārānupapattiḥ—
children.translated_text: And because the one being employed is not grasped as transforming: the <s>i</s>-vowel is not grasped as being employed while turning into a <s>y</s>-consonant. Rather, when the <s>i</s>-vowel is not employed, the <s>y</s>-consonant is employed; therefore it is not a modification. And when there is no modification, there is no loss of etymological explanation of the word. Phonemes do not undergo modification — and in this position, since the impossibility of etymological explanation does not arise, we do not accept phoneme-modification.
'<s>aster bhūḥ</s>'
'<s>bruvo vaciḥ</s>'

children.text: iti yathā varṇasamudāyasya dhātulakṣaṇasya kvacid viṣaye varṇāntarasamudāyo na pariṇāmo na kāryaṃ śabdāntarasya sthāne śabdāntaraṃ prayujyate tathā varṇasya varṇānataram iti//40//
children.translated_text: — just as a combination of phonemes constituting a verbal root, in certain domains, is replaced by a different combination of phonemes which is neither a transformation nor an effect — one word is employed in place of another — so too with a phoneme (being replaced by) another phoneme. // 2.2.40 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 41
And for this further reason, phoneme-modifications do not exist —
If the base (<s>prakṛti</s>) increases, the modification (<s>vikāra</s>) increases. // 2.2.41 //

children.text: prakṛtyanuvidhānaṃ vikāreṣu dṛṣṭam, yakāre hrasvadīrghānuvidhānaṃ nāsti yena vikāratvam anumīyata iti//41//
children.translated_text: Conformity of modifications to their bases is observed: in the case of the <s>y</s>-consonant, conformity with the short and long (vowels) does not exist — therefore modification cannot be inferred from this. // 2.2.41 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 42
Not a reason, because modifications are observed as lesser, equal, or greater. // 2.2.42 //

children.text: dravyavikārā nyūnāḥ samāḥ adhikāś ca gṛhyante/ tadvad ayaṃ vikāro nyūnaḥ syād iti//42//
children.translated_text: Modifications of substances are grasped as lesser, equal, and greater. Accordingly, this modification too could be lesser. // 2.2.42 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 43
The example is inconclusive, because both types of reasons are absent. // 2.2.43 //

children.text:
atra nodāharaṇasādharmyād dhetur asti na vaidharmyāt/ anupasaṃhṛtaś ca hetunā dṛṣṭānto na sādhaka iti/
pratidṛṣṭānte cāniyamaḥ prasajyeta/ yathānuḍuhaḥ sthāne 'śvo voḍhuṃ niyukto na tadvikāro bhavati evam ivarṇasya sthāne yakāraḥ prayukto na vikāra iti/ na cātra niyamahetur asti—dṛṣṭāntaḥ sādhako na pratidṛṣṭānta iti//43//
children.translated_text: Here there is no reason based on similarity with the example, nor on dissimilarity; and an example not connected with a reason does not prove (anything). And if a counter-example were admitted, indeterminacy would follow: just as a horse, employed in place of a bull to draw (a cart), does not become a modification of that (bull), so too the <s>y</s>-consonant employed in place of the <s>i</s>-vowel is not a modification. But there is no reason establishing the determinacy here — that the example proves but the counter-example does not. // 2.2.43 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 44
And regarding the example of substance-modification —
Not so, because of the alternative application of modifications among things of dissimilar nature. // 2.2.44 //

children.text: atulyānāṃ dravyāṇāṃ prakṛtibhāvo vikalpate vikārāś ca prakṛtīr anuvidhīyante/ na tv ivarṇam anuvidhīyate yakāraḥ/ tasmād anudāharaṇaṃ dravyavikāra iti//44//
children.translated_text: The relation of being the base is distributed variably among substances of dissimilar nature, and modifications conform to their bases. But the <s>y</s>-consonant does not conform to the <s>i</s>-vowel. Therefore, substance-modification is not a valid example. // 2.2.44 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 45
The alternative applicability of phoneme-modifications, like the variability of substance-modifications. // 2.2.45 //

children.text: yathā dravyabhāvena tulyāyāḥ prakṛter vikāravaiṣamyam, evaṃ varṇābhāvena tulyāyāḥ prakṛter vikāravikalpa iti//45//
children.translated_text: Just as there is variability of modifications from a base that is similar in being a substance, so too there is alternative applicability of modifications from a base that is similar in being a phoneme. // 2.2.45 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 46
No, because the properties of modification are not tenable. // 2.2.46 //

children.text: ayaṃ vikāradharmā dravyasāmānye, yadātmakaṃ dravyaṃ mṛd vā suvarṇaṃ vā tasyātmano 'nvaye pūrvo vyūho nivartate, vyūhāntaraṃ copajāyate; taṃ vikāram ācaṣṭe/ na varṇasāmānye kaścic chabdātmā 'nvayī ya itthaṃ jahāti yatvaṃ cāpadyate/ tatra yathā sati dravyabhāve vikāravaiṣamye nānaḍuho 'śvo vikāro vikāradharmānupapatteḥ, evam ivarṇasya na yakāro vikāro vikāradharmānupapatter iti//46//
children.translated_text: This is the property of modification in the general category of substance: that substance — whether clay or gold — whose essential nature (<s>ātman</s>) persists continuously, the previous configuration ceases and a new configuration arises; this is called modification. But in the general category of phonemes, there is no phoneme-essence that persists continuously, abandoning <s>i</s>-nature and assuming <s>y</s>-nature. Therefore, just as among substances, despite the variability of modifications, a horse is not a modification of a bull because the properties of modification are not tenable, so too the <s>y</s>-consonant is not a modification of the <s>i</s>-vowel because the properties of modification are not tenable. // 2.2.46 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 47
And for this further reason, phoneme-modifications do not exist —
Because things that have undergone modification do not revert. // 2.2.47 //

children.text: anupapannā punarāpattiḥ/ katham? punarāpatter ananumānād iti/ ikāro yakāratvam āpannaḥ punar ikāro bhavati, na punar ikārasya sthāne yakārasya prayogo 'prayogaś cety atrānumānaṃ nāsti//47//
children.translated_text: Reversion is untenable. How? Because there is no inference for reversion. The <s>i</s>-vowel, having assumed <s>y</s>-nature, again becomes an <s>i</s>-vowel — but there is no inference here that the <s>y</s>-consonant's employment and non-employment in place of the <s>i</s>-vowel (constitutes reversion). // 2.2.47 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 48

children.text: ananumānād iti na/ idaṃ hy anumānam—
children.translated_text: 'Because there is no inference' — this is not so. For here is the inference:
Not a reason, because of the reversion of gold and the like. // 2.2.48 //

children.text: suvarṇaṃ kuṇḍalatvaṃ hitvā rucakatvam āpadyate rucakatvaṃ hitvā punaḥ kuṇḍalatvam āpadyate, evam ikāro 'pi yakāratvam āpannaḥ punar ikāro bhavatīti//48//
children.translated_text: Gold, abandoning the form of a bracelet, assumes the form of a neck-ornament; abandoning the neck-ornament form, it again assumes the bracelet form. Similarly, the <s>i</s>-vowel too, having assumed <s>y</s>-nature, again becomes an <s>i</s>-vowel. // 2.2.48 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 49

children.text: vyabhicārād ananumānam yathā payo dadhibhāvam āpannaṃ punaḥ na payo bhavati kim evaṃ varṇānāṃ na punarāpattiḥ, atha suvarṇavat punarāpattir iti suvarṇodāharaṇopapattiś ca—
children.translated_text: Due to deviation, there is no inference — just as milk, having become curd, does not again become milk, so do phonemes not revert? Or is there reversion as with gold? And the tenability of the gold-example is (addressed) —
Not so, because the modifications of that (gold) do not deviate from the gold-nature. // 2.2.49 //

children.text: avasthitaṃ suvarṇaṃ hīyamānena dharmeṇa upajāyamānena ca dharmi bhavati, naivaṃ kaścic chabdātmā hīyamānena itvenopajāyamānena yatvena dharmī gṛhyate, tasmāt suvarṇodāharaṇaṃ nopapadyata iti//
children.translated_text: Gold, which is stable, becomes a substratum of properties through properties that cease and properties that arise; but no phoneme-essence is grasped as a substratum possessing a property that ceases, namely <s>i</s>-nature, and a property that arises, namely <s>y</s>-nature. Therefore, the gold-example is not tenable.

children.text:
varṇatvāvyatirekād varṇavikārāṇām apratiṣedhaḥ/ varṇavikārā api varṇatvaṃ na vyabhicaranti yathā suvarṇavikāraḥ suvarṇatvam iti/
sāmānyavato dharmayogo na sāmānyasya/ kuṇḍalarucakau suvarṇasya dharmau na suvarṇatvasya, evam ikārayakārau kasya varṇātmano dharmau? varṇatvaṃ sāmānyaṃ na tasyemau dharmau bhavitum arhati/ na ca nivartamāno dharma upajāyamānasya prakṛtis tatra nivartamāna ikāro na yakārasyopajāyamānasya prakṛtir iti//49//
children.translated_text: Phoneme-modifications are not refuted because they do not deviate from phoneme-hood. Even phoneme-modifications do not deviate from the nature of being phonemes, just as gold-modifications do not deviate from gold-nature. (Reply:) Properties belong to a thing possessing the universal, not to the universal itself. Bracelet and neck-ornament are properties of gold, not of gold-ness. Similarly, the <s>i</s>-vowel and <s>y</s>-consonant — of which phoneme-essence are they properties? Phoneme-hood is the universal; these two cannot be its properties. And a property that ceases is not the base of that which arises — the ceasing <s>i</s>-vowel is not the base of the arising <s>y</s>-consonant. // 2.2.49 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 50
And for this further reason, phoneme-modification is untenable —
If (phonemes are) eternal, because of the impossibility of modification; if non-eternal, because of the impossibility of persistence. // 2.2.50 //

children.text: nityā varṇā ity etasmin pakṣe ikārayakārau varṇau ity ubhayor nityatvād vikārānupapattiḥ, nityatve 'vināśitvāt kaḥ kasya vikāra iti/ athānityā varṇā iti pakṣaḥ,
children.translated_text: In the position that phonemes are eternal: the <s>i</s>-vowel and the <s>y</s>-consonant are both phonemes, and since both are eternal, modification is untenable — if they are eternal and imperishable, which could be the modification of which? And if the position is that phonemes are non-eternal,

children.text: evam apy anavasthānaṃ varṇānām/ kim idam anavasthānaṃ varṇānām? utpadya nirodhaḥ/ utpadya niruddhe ikāre yakāra utpadyate yakāre cotpadya niruddhe ikāra utpadyata iti kaḥ kasya vikāraḥ? tad etad avagṛhya sandhāne sandhāya cāvagrahe veditavyam iti//50//
children.translated_text: even so, there is no persistence of phonemes. What is this non-persistence of phonemes? Arising and then ceasing. When the <s>i</s>-vowel, having arisen, has ceased, the <s>y</s>-consonant arises; and when the <s>y</s>-consonant, having arisen, has ceased, the <s>i</s>-vowel arises — so which is the modification of which? This should be understood in the context of both disjunction (<s>avagraha</s>) and conjunction (<s>sandhāna</s>). // 2.2.50 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 51
Now, regarding the response in the position of eternality —

children.text: nityānām atīndriyatvāt taddharmavikalpāc ca varṇavikārāṇām apratiṣedhaḥ // 2.2.51 //
children.translated_text: Phoneme-modifications are not refuted, because eternal things are supersensible, and because of the alternative applicability of their properties. // 2.2.51 //

children.text: nityā varṇā na vikalpanta iti vipratiṣedhaḥ/ yathā nityatve sati kiñcid atīndriyaṃ kiñcid indriyagrāhyam, indriyagrāhyāś ca varṇāḥ, evaṃ nityatve sati kiñcin na vikriyate, varṇās tu vikriyanta iti/
children.translated_text: That eternal phonemes do not undergo modification is a contradiction. Just as, despite being eternal, some things are supersensible while some are graspable by the senses — and phonemes are graspable by the senses — so too, despite being eternal, some things do not undergo modification, but phonemes do undergo modification.

children.text: virodhād ahetus taddharmavikalpaḥ/ nityaṃ nopajāyate nāpaity anupajanāpāyadharmakaṃ nityam anityaṃ punar upajanāpāyayuktam, na cāntareṇopajanāpāyau vikāraḥ sambhavati/ tad yadi varṇā vikriyante, nityatvam eṣāṃ nivartate/ atha nityāḥ, vikāradharmatvam eṣāṃ nivartate/ so 'yaṃ viruddho hetvābhāso dharmavikalpa iti//51//
children.translated_text: The alternative applicability of their properties is not a reason, due to contradiction. What is eternal does not arise and does not pass away — what is eternal has the character of not arising and not passing away; the non-eternal, on the other hand, is subject to arising and passing away. And without arising and passing away, modification is not possible. Therefore, if phonemes undergo modification, their eternality is negated. And if they are eternal, their property of being modifiable is negated. This is a contradictory <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reason) — the alternative applicability of properties. // 2.2.51 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 52
The response in the position of non-eternality —
Even if there is no persistence, just as the perception of phonemes is possible, so too is the arising of their modification. // 2.2.52 //

children.text:
yathānavasthāyināṃ varṇānāṃ śravaṇaṃ bhavaty evam eṣāṃ vikāro bhavati/
asambandhād asamarthā arthapratipādikā varṇopalabdhiḥ na vikāreṇa sambandhād asamarthā yā gṛhyamāṇā varṇavikāram anumāpayed iti/ tatra yādṛg idaṃ yathā gandhaguṇā pṛthivy evaṃ śabdasukhādiguṇāpīti, tādṛg etad bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: Just as hearing of non-persisting phonemes occurs, so too their modification occurs. (Reply:) The perception of phonemes, which is unconnected (with modification), is incapable of establishing the point — it is not incapable because of connection with modification, such that when grasped it could lead one to infer phoneme-modification. In this matter, as with the argument 'just as earth has the quality of odor, so too does it have the qualities of sound, pleasure, and the rest' — so too this becomes.

children.text: na ca varṇopalabdhir varṇanivṛttau varṇāntaraprayogasya nivartikā/ yo 'yam ivarṇanivṛttau yakārasya prayogo yady ayaṃ varṇopalabdhyā nivartate tadā tatropalabhyamānā ivarṇo yatvam āpadyate iti gṛhyeta/ tasmād varṇopalabdhir ahetur varṇavikārasyeti//52//
children.translated_text: And the perception of phonemes does not prevent the employment of another phoneme when one phoneme ceases. If this employment of the <s>y</s>-consonant upon the cessation of the <s>i</s>-vowel were prevented by the perception of phonemes, then in that context, what is perceived — that the <s>i</s>-vowel is assuming <s>y</s>-nature — would be grasped. Therefore, the perception of phonemes is not a reason for phoneme-modification. // 2.2.52 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 53
Phoneme-modifications are not refuted, because if they have the property of being modifiable, eternality is absent, and because at a different time, modification is tenable. // 2.2.53 //

children.text: taddharmavikalpād iti na yuktaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ na khalv vikāradharmakaṃ kiñcin nityam upalabhyata iti varṇopalabdhivad iti na yuktaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ avagrahe hi dadhi atreti prayujya ciraṃ sthitvā tataḥ saṃhitāyāṃ prayuṅkte dadhy atreti/
children.translated_text: The refutation 'because of the alternative applicability of their properties' is not valid. For nothing that has the property of being modifiable is observed to be eternal — therefore, the refutation through 'like the perception of phonemes' is not valid. For in disjunction, one first uses '<s>dadhi atra</s>' (yogurt here), and after standing for a while, then in <s>saṃhitā</s> (juncture), one uses '<s>dadhy atra</s>'.

children.text: ciranivṛtte cāyam ivarṇe yakāraḥ prayujyamānaḥ kasya vikāra iti pratīyate, kāraṇābhāvāt kāryābhāva iti anuyogaḥ prasajyata iti//53//
children.translated_text: And when the <s>i</s>-vowel has long since ceased, this <s>y</s>-consonant that is being employed — of what is it a modification? This is understood (as a difficulty), and the objection follows: from the absence of a cause follows the absence of an effect. // 2.2.53 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 54
And for the following further reason, the modification of phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>) is untenable —
Because there is no fixed material cause (<s>prakṛti</s>). // 2.2.54 //

children.text: ikārasthāne yakāraḥ śrūyate yakārasthāne khalv ikāro vidhīyate vidhyatīti/ tad yadi syāt prakṛtivikārabhāvā varṇānām, tasya prakṛtiniyamaḥ syāt/ dṛṣṭo vikāradharmitve prakṛtiniyama iti//54//
children.translated_text: In place of the vowel 'i,' the semivowel 'y' is heard; in place of 'y,' the vowel 'i' is prescribed — it is substituted. If there were a material-cause-and-modification relationship among phonemes, there would be a fixed material cause for it. A fixed material cause is observed in cases where something has the property of being a modification. // 54 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 55
Where there is non-fixity, the fixity (shows that) there is no non-fixity. // 2.2.55 //

children.text: yo 'yaṃ prakṛter aniyama uktaḥ sa niyato yathāviṣayaṃ vyavasthito niyatatvān niyama iti bhavati, evaṃ saty aniyamo nāsti, tatra yad uktaṃ prakṛtyaniyamād iti, etad ayuktam iti//55//
children.translated_text: This non-fixity of the material cause that has been stated is itself fixed — established in its respective domain — and being fixed, it constitutes fixity. This being so, there is no non-fixity. Therefore, what was stated as 'because there is no fixed material cause' is not valid. // 55 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 56
Due to the contradiction between fixity and non-fixity, there is no refutation of non-fixity through fixity. // 2.2.56 //

children.text: niyama ity atrārthābhyanujñā, aniyama iti tasya pratiṣedhaḥ/ anujñātaniṣiddhayoś ca vyāghātād anarthāntaratvaṃ na bhavati/ aniyamaś ca niyatatvāt niyamo na bhavatīti nātrārthasya tathābhāvaḥ pratiṣidhyate/ kiṃ tarhi? tathābhūtasyārthasya niyamaśabdenābhidhīyamānasya niyatatvān niyamaśabda evopapadyate/ so 'yaṃ niyamād aniyame pratiṣedho na bhavatīti//56//
children.translated_text: 'Fixity' — here there is acceptance of a meaning; 'non-fixity' is its negation. Since what is accepted and what is negated are contradictory, they do not amount to the same thing. And the non-fixity does not become fixity merely because of being fixed — the actual nature of the thing is not what is being negated here. Rather, the thing being of such a nature, being designated by the word 'fixity' — because of its being fixed, only the word 'fixity' is applicable. This refutation of non-fixity through fixity does not hold. // 56 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 57

children.text: na ceyaṃ varṇavikāropapattiḥ pariṇāmāt kāryakāraṇabhāvād vā/ kiṃ tarhi?
children.translated_text: And this tenability of phonemic modification is not due to transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) or to a cause-and-effect relationship. What then?
Phonemic modifications are tenable on account of the acquisition of another quality, obliteration, contraction, extension, abbreviation, and coalescence. // 2.2.57 //

children.text: sthānyādeśabhāvād aprayogo vikāraśabdārthaḥ, sa bhidyate/ guṇāntarāpattiḥ udāttasyānudātta ity evamādiḥ/ upamardo nāma ekarūpanivṛttau rūpāntaropajanaḥ/ hrāso dīrghasya hrasvaḥ/ vṛddhir hrasvasya dīrghaḥ, tayor vā plutaḥ/ leśo lāghavam, sta ity aster vikāraḥ/ śleṣa āgamaḥ, prakṛteḥ pratyayasya vā/ eta eva viśeṣā vikārā iti/ eta evādeśāḥ, ete ced vikārā upapadyante tarhi varṇavikārā iti//57//
children.translated_text: The meaning of the word 'modification' is non-use due to the relationship of the original form (<s>sthānin</s>) and substitute (<s>ādeśa</s>); it is of various kinds. Acquisition of another quality is such as an <s>udātta</s> (high-pitched accent) becoming <s>anudātta</s> (low-pitched) and so forth. Obliteration is the production of another form upon the cessation of one form. Contraction is the shortening of a long (vowel). Extension is the lengthening of a short (vowel), or the <s>pluta</s> (prolated vowel) of either. Abbreviation is reduction — 'sta' is a modification of 'asti' (the verb 'to be'). Coalescence is augment (<s>āgama</s>), either of the base or the suffix. These specific types are the modifications. These are the substitutes; if these modifications are tenable, then phonemic modifications exist. // 57 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 58
Those (phonemes), ending in case-endings, constitute a <s>pada</s> (word). // 2.2.58 //

children.text: yathādarśanaṃ vikṛtā varṇā vibhaktyantāḥ padasaṃjñā bhavanti/ vibhaktir dvayī—nāmiky ākhyātikī ca, brāhmaṇaḥ pacatīty udāharaṇam/
children.translated_text: Phonemes modified as observed, when ending in case-endings, receive the designation <s>pada</s> (word). Case-ending is of two kinds — nominal and verbal; the illustration is '<s>brāhmaṇaḥ</s> <s>pacati</s>' ('the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> cooks').

children.text: upasarganipātās tarhi na padasaṃjñāḥ lakṣaṇāntaraṃ vācyam iti; śiṣyate ca khalu nāmikyā vibhakter avyayāl lopaḥ tayoḥ padasaṃjñārtham iti//58//
children.translated_text: Then prefixes (<s>upasarga</s>) and particles (<s>nipāta</s>) would not have the designation <s>pada</s>, and a separate definition would need to be stated. But it is maintained that the elision of the nominal case-ending from indeclinables (<s>avyaya</s>) serves the purpose of giving them the designation <s>pada</s>. // 58 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 59

children.text: padenārthasampratyaya iti prayojanam, nāmapadaṃ cādhikṛtya parīkṣā, gaur iti padaṃ khalv idam udāharaṇaṃ tadarthe —
children.translated_text: The purpose is the comprehension of meaning through a word. The examination concerns the noun-word. 'Cow' (<s>go</s>) is the word used as an example. Regarding its meaning —
There is doubt due to secondary usage (<s>upacāra</s>) when particular (<s>vyakti</s>), configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>), and universal (<s>jāti</s>) are co-present. // 2.2.59 //

children.text: avinābhāvavṛttiḥ sannidhiḥ/ avinābhāvena vartamānāsu vyaktyākṛtijātiṣu gaur iti prayujyate, tatra na jñāyate kim anyatamaḥ padārthaḥ utaitat sarvam iti//
children.translated_text: Co-presence (<s>sannidhi</s>) is the relation of invariable concomitance. When particular, configuration, and universal are invariably co-present, the word 'cow' is used; and there it is not known whether any one of these is the word-meaning, or all of them together.
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 60
The determination of word-meaning is from the capacity of the usage of the word. Therefore —

The particular (<s>vyakti</s>) is (the word-meaning), because of the secondary usage of the relative pronoun, collective, abandonment, possession, number, growth, diminution, color, compound, and continuity with reference to the particular. // 2.2.60 //

children.text: vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ/ kasmāt? yāśabdaprabhṛtīnāṃ vyaktāv upacārāt/ upacāraḥ prayogaḥ/ yā gaus tiṣṭhati yā gaur niṣaṇṇeiti, nedaṃ vākyaṃ jāter abhidhāyakam abhedāt, bhedāt tu dravyābhidhāyakam/
children.translated_text: The particular is the word-meaning. Why? Because of the usage of the relative pronoun and the rest with reference to the particular. Usage means employment.
