'Which cow is standing, which cow is sitting' — this sentence does not denote the universal, because there is no difference (in the universal); but it denotes substance, because there is difference (among substances).

children.text: gavāṃ samūha iti bhedād dravyābhidhānaṃ na jāter abhedāt/ vaidyāya gāṃ dadatīti dravyasya tyāgo na jāter amūrtatvāt pratikramānukramānupapatteeś ca/ parigrahaḥ svatvenābhisambandhaḥ, kauṇḍinyasya gaur brāhmaṇasya gaur iti; dravyābhidhāne dravyabhedāt sambandhabheda ity upapannam, abhinnā tu jātir iti/ saṅkhyā — daśa gāvo viṃśatir gāva iti bhinnaṃ dravyaṃ saṅkhyāyate, na jātir abhedād iti/ vṛddhiḥ kāraṇavato dravyasyāvayavopacayaḥ avardhata gaur iti; niravayavā tu jātir iti/ etenāpacayo vyākhyātaḥ/ varṇaḥ — śuklā gauḥ kapilā gaur iti; dravyasya guṇayogo na sāmānyasya/ samāsaḥ — gohitaṃ gosukham iti, dravyasya sukhādiyogo na jāter iti/ anubandhaḥ — sarūpaprajananasantāno gaur gāṃ janayatīti, tadutpattidharmatvād dravye yuktaṃ na jātau viparyayād iti/ dravyaṃ vyaktir iti hi nārthāntaram//60//
children.translated_text: 'A herd of cows' — denoting substance because of difference, not the universal because of non-difference. 'One gives a cow to the physician' — it is the abandonment of a substance, not of the universal, because the universal is incorporeal and because approach and withdrawal are inapplicable. Possession is the relation of ownership — '<s>Kauṇḍinya</s>'s cow,' 'the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>'s cow'; in the denotation of substance, the difference of relation is tenable because of the difference of substances, but the universal is undifferentiated. Number — 'ten cows,' 'twenty cows' — it is differentiated substance that is counted, not the universal, because of non-difference. Growth is the increase of parts of a substance that has a cause — 'the cow has grown'; but the universal is partless. By this, diminution is also explained. Color — 'a white cow,' 'a tawny cow'; it is substance that has conjunction with qualities, not the universal. Compound — 'cow-welfare,' 'cow-happiness'; it is substance that has conjunction with happiness and the like, not the universal. Continuity is the succession of producing offspring of the same form — 'the cow begets a cow'; since this is a property of that which is born, it is applicable to substance, not to the universal, because the reverse (holds for the universal). Substance and particular are indeed not different things. // 60 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 61
The refutation of this —
Not so, because of non-fixity (of the particular). // 2.2.61 //

children.text: na vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ/ kasmāt? anavasthānāt/ yāśabdaprabhṛtibhir yo viśeṣyate sa gośabdārtho yā gaus tiṣṭhati yā gaur niṣaṇṇeti, na dravyamātram aviśiṣṭaṃ jātyā vinābhidhīyate/ kiṃ tarhi? jātiviśiṣṭam/ tasmān na vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ / evaṃ samūhādiṣu draṣṭavyam//61//
children.translated_text: The particular is not the word-meaning. Why? Because of non-fixity. That which is qualified by the relative pronoun and the rest — that is the meaning of the word 'cow' — 'which cow is standing, which cow is sitting' — mere substance without qualification is not denoted without the universal. Rather, it is qualified by the universal. Therefore, the particular is not the word-meaning. The same is to be seen in the case of collection and the rest. // 61 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 62

children.text: yadi na vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ kathaṃ tarhi vyaktāv upacāra iti? nimittād atadbhāve 'pi tadupacāraḥ/ dṛśyate khalu —
children.translated_text: If the particular is not the word-meaning, then how is there usage with reference to the particular? Due to a ground (<s>nimitta</s>), there is usage of that (term) even when the thing is not actually that. Indeed, it is observed —

There is usage of a term even when the thing is not actually that, due to association, location, purpose, conduct, measure, support, proximity, connection, instrumentality, and lordship — as in (the cases of) the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, the cot, the mat, the king, the flour, the sandalwood, the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, the garment, the food, and the person. // 2.2.62 //

children.text: atadbhāve 'pi tadupacāra iti atacchabdasya tena śabdenābhidhānam iti/ sahacaraṇād — yaṣṭikāṃ bhojayeti, yaṣtikāsahacarito brāhmaṇo 'bhidhīyata iti/
children.translated_text: 'Usage of a term even when the thing is not actually that' means: the designation of what is not that thing by the word for that thing. Due to association — 'Feed the staffs' means the <s>brāhmaṇas</s> accompanied by staffs are denoted.

children.text: sthānāt — mañcāḥ krośantīti mañcasthāḥ puruṣā abhidhīyante/ tādarthyāt — kaṭārtheṣu vīraṇeṣu vyuhyamāneṣu kaṭaṃ karotīti bhavati/ vṛtāt — yamo rājā kubero rājeti tadvadvartata iti/ mānāt — āḍhakena mitāḥ saktavaḥ āḍhakasaktava iti/ dhāraṇāt — tulāyāṃ dhṛtaṃ candanaṃ tulācandanam iti/ sāmīpyāt — gaṅgāyāṃ gāvaś carantīti deśo 'bhidhīyate sannikṛṣṭaḥ/ yogāt — kṛṣṇena rāgeṇa yuktaḥ śāṭakaḥ kṛṣṇa ity abhidhīyate/ sādhanāt — annaṃ prāṇā iti/ ādhipatyāt — ayaṃ puruṣaḥ kulam ayaṃ gotram iti/ tatrāyaṃ sahacaraṇād yogād vā jātiśabdo vyaktau prayjyata iti//62//
children.translated_text: Due to location — 'The cots are crying' means the people on the cots are denoted. Due to purpose — when reeds intended for a mat are being gathered, it is said 'he is making a mat.' Due to conduct — '<s>Yama</s> is a king,' '<s>Kubera</s> is a king,' because he conducts himself like one. Due to measure — flour measured by an <s>āḍhaka</s> (measure) is called '<s>āḍhaka</s>-flour.' Due to support — sandalwood weighed on a balance is called 'balance-sandalwood.' Due to proximity — 'the cows are grazing on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>' denotes a place nearby. Due to connection — a garment connected with the color black is called 'black.' Due to instrumentality — 'food is life.' Due to lordship — 'this person is the family,' 'this one is the lineage.' In this context, the word for the universal is used for the particular due to association or connection. // 62 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 63

children.text: yadi gaur ity asya padasya na vyaktir arthaḥ, astu tarhi —
children.translated_text: If the particular is not the meaning of the word 'cow,' then let it be —
Configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) is (the word-meaning), because the establishment of the identity of beings depends on it. // 2.2.63 //

children.text: ākṛtiḥ padārthaḥ/ kasmāt? tadapekṣatvāt sattvavyavasthānisiddheḥ/ sattvāvayavānāṃ tadavayavānāṃ ca niyato vyūha ākṛtiḥ, tasyāṃ gṛhyamāṇāyāṃ sattvavyavasthānaṃ sidhyaty ayam gaur ayaṃ aśva iti, nāgṛhyamāṇāyām/ yasya grahaṇāt sattvavyavasthānaṃ sidhyati taṃ śabdo 'bhidhātum arhati so 'syārtha iti//63//
children.translated_text: Configuration is the word-meaning. Why? Because the establishment of the identity of beings depends on it. The fixed arrangement of the parts of a living being and of their sub-parts is the configuration; when it is grasped, the identification of beings is accomplished — 'this is a cow,' 'this is a horse' — but not when it is not grasped. That whose grasping accomplishes the identification of beings — that is what the word deserves to denote, and that is its meaning. // 63 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 64

children.text: tad upapadyate yasya jātyā yogas tad atra jātiviśiṣṭam abhidhīyate gaur iti/na
children.translated_text: That is tenable which has conjunction with the universal; and what is denoted here, qualified by the universal, is 'cow.' But

children.text:
cāvayavavyūhasya jātyā yogaḥ/ kasya tarhi? niyatāvayavavyūhasya dravyasya/tasmān nākṛtiḥ padārthaḥ/
astu tarhi jātiḥ padārthaḥ —
children.translated_text: it is not the arrangement of parts that has conjunction with the universal. What then? A substance with a fixed arrangement of parts. Therefore, configuration is not the word-meaning. Then let the universal be the word-meaning —
The universal (<s>jāti</s>) is (the word-meaning), because sprinkling and other (ritual actions) are inapplicable to a clay cow, even though it possesses particular and configuration. // 2.2.64 //

children.text: jātiḥ padārthaḥ/ kasmāt? vyaktyākṛtiyukte 'pi mṛdgavake prokṣaṇādīnām aprasaṅgād iti/ gāṃ prokṣaya gām ānaya gāṃ dehīti naitāni mṛdgavake prayujyante/ kasmāt? jāter abhāvāt/
children.translated_text: The universal is the word-meaning. Why? Because sprinkling and other actions are inapplicable to a clay cow even though it possesses particular and configuration. 'Sprinkle the cow,' 'bring the cow,' 'give the cow' — these are not used with reference to a clay cow. Why? Because of the absence of the universal.

children.text: asti hi tatra vyaktiḥ asty ākṛtiḥ yadabhāvāt tatrāsampratyayaḥ sa padārtha iti//64//
children.translated_text: There exists in it both particular and configuration; that whose absence causes non-comprehension there — that is the word-meaning. // 64 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 65
Not so, because the manifestation of the universal depends on configuration and particular. // 2.2.65 //

children.text: jāter abhivyaktir ākṛtivyaktī apekṣate, nāgṛhyamāṇāyām ākṛtau vyaktau ca jātimātraṃ śuddhaṃ gṛhyate; tasmān na jātiḥ padārtha iti//65//
children.translated_text: The manifestation of the universal depends on configuration and particular; when configuration and particular are not grasped, the universal alone in its purity is not grasped. Therefore, the universal is not the word-meaning. // 65 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 66

children.text: na vai padārthena na bhavituṃ śakyam, kaḥ khalv idānīṃ padārtha iti?
children.translated_text: It is not possible for there to be no word-meaning at all; what then is the word-meaning?
Rather, particular, configuration, and universal (together) are the word-meaning. // 2.2.66 //

children.text: tuśabdo viśeṣaṇārthaḥ/ kiṃ viśiṣyate? pradhānāṅgabhāvasyāniyamena padārthatvam iti/ yadā hi bhedavivakṣā viśeṣagatiś ca tadā vyaktiḥ pradhānam aṅgaṃ tu jātyākṛtī/ yadā tu bhedo 'vivakṣitaḥ sāmānyagatiś ca, tadā jātiḥ pradhānam aṅgaṃ tu vyaktyākṛtī/ tad etad bahulaṃ prayogeṣu/ ākṛtes tu pradhānabhāva utprekṣitavyaḥ//66//
children.translated_text: The word 'tu' (rather) is for the purpose of qualification. What is being qualified? That word-meaning-hood is not restricted to the relationship of principal and subordinate. For when there is an intention to express difference and the cognition is of the specific, then the particular is principal and the universal and configuration are subordinate. But when difference is not intended and the cognition is of the general, then the universal is principal and the particular and configuration are subordinate. This is abundantly (seen) in usage. The principal status of configuration, however, must be inferred. // 66 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 67

children.text: kathaṃ punar jñāyate nānā vyaktyākṛtijātaya iti? lakṣaṇabhedāt/ tatra tāvat —
children.translated_text: But how is it known that particular, configuration, and universal are distinct? Due to the difference in their defining characteristics. Of these, first —
A particular (<s>vyakti</s>) is a corporeal entity (<s>mūrti</s>) that is the substratum of specific qualities. // 2.2.67 //

children.text: vyajyata iti vyaktir indriyagrāhyeti na sarvaṃ dravyaṃ vyaktiḥ/ yo guṇaviśeṣāṇāṃ sparśāntānāṃ gurutvaghanatvadravatvasaṃskārāṇām avyāpinaḥ parimāṇasyāśrayo yathāsambhavaṃ tad dravyaṃ mūrtiḥ mūrcchitāvayavatvād iti//67//
children.translated_text: That which is manifested — <s>vyakti</s> — means perceptible to the senses; hence not every substance is a particular. That substance which is the substratum, as applicable, of specific qualities ending with touch — gravity, solidity, fluidity, and <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent tendency) — and of non-pervading magnitude, that is <s>mūrti</s> (corporeal entity), because it has compacted parts. // 67 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 68
Configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) is that which is called the mark of the universal (<s>jātiliṅga</s>). // 2.2.68 //

children.text: yayā jātir jātiliṅgāni ca prakhyāyante tām ākṛtiṃ vidyāt/ sā ca nānyā sattvāvayavānāṃ tadavayavānāṃ ca niyatād vyūhād iti/
children.translated_text: That through which the universal and the marks of the universal become manifest — know that to be configuration. And it is nothing other than the fixed arrangement of the parts of a living being and of their sub-parts.

children.text: niyatāvayavavyūhāḥ khalu sattvāvayavā jātiliṅgam, śirasā pādena gām anuminvanti/ niyate ca sattvāvayavānāṃ vyūhe sati gotvaṃ prakhyāyata iti/ anākṛtivyaṅgyāyāṃ jātau mṛtsuvarṇaṃ rajatam ity evamādiṣv ākṛtir nivartate jahāti padārthatvam iti//68//
children.translated_text: Indeed, the fixed arrangements of the parts of a living being are the marks of the universal — they infer a cow from its head or foot. And when there is a fixed arrangement of the parts of a living being, cowness (<s>gotva</s>) becomes manifest. In cases where the universal is not manifested through configuration — such as clay, gold, silver, and the like — configuration withdraws and relinquishes its word-meaning-hood. // 68 //
Chapter 2, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 69
A universal (<s>jāti</s>) is that whose nature is to produce the same cognition. // 2.2.69 //

children.text: yā samānaṃ buddhiṃ prasūte bhinneṣv adhikaraṇeṣu, yayā bahūnīteretarato na vyāvartante yo 'rtho 'nekatra pratyayānuvṛttinimittaṃ tat sāmānyam/ yac ca keṣāñcid abhedaṃ kutaścid bhedaṃ karoti tat sāmānyaviśeṣo jātir iti//69//
children.translated_text: That which produces the same cognition in different substrates, by which many things are not differentiated from one another, that entity which is the ground for the recurrence of cognition in multiple (things) — that is the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>). And that which creates non-difference among some things and difference from others — that universal-cum-particular is <s>jāti</s> (universal). // 69 //

children.text:
iti vātsyāyanīye nyāyabhāṣye dvitīyādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam//
samāptaś cāyaṃ dvitīyo 'dhyāyaḥ//2//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second section of the second chapter in <s>Vātsyāyana</s>'s <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>. And thus the second chapter is complete. // 2 //
Third Chapter, First Section.
Chapter 3
Chapter 3, Section 1
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 1

children.text: parīkṣitāni pramāṇāni, prameyam idānīṃ parīkṣyate/ tac cātmādīty ātmā vivicyate, kiṃ dehendriyamanobuddhivedanāsaṅghātamātram ātmā āhosvit tadvayatirikta iti /
children.translated_text: The <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) have been examined; the <s>prameya</s> (objects of knowledge) are now examined. And since that begins with the <s>ātman</s> (self), the <s>ātman</s> is investigated: is the <s>ātman</s> merely the aggregate of body, sense-organs, mind, intellect, and sensation, or is it distinct from them?

children.text: kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ vyapadeśyobhayathā siddheḥ/ kriyākaraṇayoḥ kartrā sambandhasyābhidhānaṃ vyapadeśaḥ/
children.translated_text: Whence the doubt? Because of the dual establishment of designation. Designation (<s>vyapadeśa</s>) is the statement of the relation of an agent with action and instrument.

children.text: sa dvividhaḥ, avayavena samudāyasya — mūlair vṛkṣas tiṣṭhati, stambhaiḥ prāsādo dhriyata iti/ anyenānyasya vyapadeśaḥ — paraśunā vṛścati, pradīpena paśyati/ asti cāyaṃ vyapadeśaḥ cakṣuṣā paśyati manasā vijānāti buddhyā vicārayati śarīreṇa sukhaduḥkham anubhavatīti / tatra nāvadhāryate kim avayavena samudāyasya dehādisaṅghātasya, athānyenānyasya tadvyatiriktasya veti//
children.translated_text: That [designation] is of two kinds: [first,] the designation of a whole by its part — 'the tree stands by its roots,' 'the palace is supported by its pillars'; [second,] the designation of one thing by another — 'he cuts with an axe,' 'he sees with a lamp.' And there is this designation: 'he sees with the eye, he knows with <s>manas</s> (mind), he deliberates with <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), he experiences pleasure and pain with the body.' In this regard, it is not determined whether this is a designation of the whole by its part — that is, of the aggregate (<s>saṅghāta</s>) of body and so forth — or of one thing by another, that is, of something distinct from that [aggregate].
This is the designation of one thing by another. Why?
Because a single object is grasped by sight and touch. // 3.1.1 //

children.text: darśanena kaścid artho gṛhītaḥ sparśanenāpi so 'rtho gṛhyate — yam aham adrākṣaṃ cakṣuṣā taṃ sparśanenāpi spṛśāmīti, yaṃ cāspārkṣaṃ sparśanena taṃ cakṣuṣā paśyāmīti/ ekaviṣayau cemau pratyayāv ekakartṛkau pratisandhīyete,
children.translated_text: An object grasped by sight is also grasped by touch — 'that which I saw with the eye, I also touch with the sense of touch,' and 'that which I touched with the sense of touch, I now see with the eye.' And these two cognitions, having a single object, are connected together as having a single agent,

children.text: na ca saṅghātakartṛkau, nendriyeṇaikakartṛkau/ tad yo 'sau cakṣuṣā tvagindriyeṇa caikārthasya grahītā bhinnanimittāv anyakartṛkau pratyayau samānaviṣayau pratisandadhāti so 'rthāntarabhūta ātmā/
children.translated_text: and they do not have the aggregate as their agent, nor do they have a single sense-organ as their agent. Therefore, he who grasps a single object through the eye and the tactile sense-organ, and who connects together two cognitions that have different causes, different agents, yet the same object — that is the <s>ātman</s> (self), which is a different entity [from the aggregate].

children.text: kathaṃ punar nendriyeṇaikakartṛkau? indriyaṃ khalu svasvaviṣayagrahaṇam ananyakartṛkaṃ pratisandhātum arhati nendriyāntarasya viṣayāntaragrahaṇam iti/ kathaṃ na saṅghātakartṛkau? ekaḥ khalv ayaṃ bhinnanimittau svātmakartṛkau paryayau pratisaṃhitau vedayate na saṅghātaḥ/ kasmāt? anivṛttaṃ hi saṅghāte pratyekaṃ viṣayāntaragrahaṇasyāpratisandhānam indriyāntareṇeveti//1//
children.translated_text: But how do they not have a single sense-organ as their agent? A sense-organ, being the grasper of only its own specific object, can connect its own grasp but not the grasp of another object by another sense-organ. And how do they not have the aggregate as their agent? For it is a single [entity] that experiences two cognitions, having different causes and having itself as their agent, connected together — not the aggregate. Why? Because in the aggregate, the non-connection of the grasp of another object by each [component] individually remains unresolved, just as with another sense-organ. // 1 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 2]
Not so, because of the fixed domain [of each sense-organ]. // 3.1.2 //

children.text: na dehādisaṅghātād anyaś cetanaḥ/ kasmāt? viṣayavyavasthānāt/ vyavasthitaviṣayāṇīndriyāṇi, cakṣuṣy asati rūpaṃ na gṛhyate sati ca gṛhyate/ yac ca yasminn asati na bhavati sati bhavati tasya tad iti vijñāyate/
children.translated_text: [Objection:] There is no conscious entity other than the aggregate of body and so forth. Why? Because of the fixed domain [of the sense-organs]. The sense-organs have fixed domains: when the eye is absent, form is not grasped, and when it is present, form is grasped. And that which does not occur when something is absent but occurs when it is present is understood to belong to that [thing].

children.text:
tasmād rūpagrahaṇaṃ cakṣuṣaḥ, cakṣū rūpaṃ paśyati/ evaṃ ghrāṇādiṣv apīti/ tānīndriyāṇīmāni svasvaviṣayagrahaṇāc cetanāni indriyāṇāṃ bhāvābhāvayor viṣayagrahaṇasya tathābhāvāt/ evaṃ sati kim anyena cetanena?
sandhigdhatvād ahetuḥ — yo 'yam indriyāṇāṃ bhāvābhāvayor viṣayagrahaṇasya tathābhāvaḥ, sa kiṃ cetanatvāt, āhosvic cetanopakaraṇānāṃ grahaṇanimittatvād iti sandihyate/ cetanopakaraṇatve 'pīndriyāṇāṃ grahaṇanimittatvād bhavitum arhati//2//
children.translated_text:
Therefore, the grasping of form belongs to the eye; the eye sees form. Likewise for the nose and the other [sense-organs]. These sense-organs are conscious, because each grasps its own specific object, and because the grasping of objects corresponds to the presence and absence of the sense-organs. This being so, what need is there for another conscious entity?
[Reply:] This is inconclusive because it is doubtful — this correspondence of object-grasping with the presence and absence of the sense-organs: is it because [the sense-organs] are conscious, or is it because they are instruments of a conscious [entity] and serve as causes of grasping? This is doubtful. Even if the sense-organs are instruments of a conscious entity, their being causes of grasping can still obtain. // 2 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 3]
And as to what was said — 'because of the fixed domain [of sense-organs]' —
Precisely because of that fixed domain, the existence of the <s>ātman</s> (self) is not refuted. // 3.1.3 //

children.text: yadi khalv ekam indriyam avyavasthitaviṣayaṃ sarvajñaṃ sarvaviṣayagrāhi cetanaṃ syāt kas tato 'nyaṃ cetanam anumātuṃ śaknuyāt? yasmāt tu vyavasthitaviṣayāṇīndriyāṇi tasmāt tebhyo 'nyaś cetanaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvaviṣayagrāhī viṣayavyavasthitam atīto 'numīyate/ tatredam abhijñānam apratyākhyeyaṃ cetanavṛttam udāhriyate/ rūpadarśī khalv ayaṃ rasaṃ gandhaṃ vā pūrvagṛītam anuminoti/ gandhapratisaṃvedī ca rūparasāv anuminoti/ evaṃ viṣayaśeṣe 'pi vācyam/ rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā (emend.; dṛṣṭā, ed.) gandhaṃ jighrati, ghrātvā ca gandhaṃ rūpaṃ paśyati/ tad evam aniyataparyāyaṃ sarvaviṣayagrahaṇam ekacetanādhikaraṇam ananyakartṛkaṃ pratisandhatte,
children.translated_text: If a single sense-organ were omniscient, grasping all objects, conscious, and without a fixed domain, who could then infer another conscious entity beyond it? But since the sense-organs have fixed domains, a conscious entity other than them — omniscient, grasping all objects, transcending the fixed domain of [each sense-organ] — is inferred. Here, this sign [of such an entity], which cannot be denied, is cited as evidence of conscious activity: one who sees form infers a previously grasped taste or smell; one who perceives smell infers form and taste; and the same should be stated for the remaining sense-objects. Having seen form, one smells an odor; and having smelled an odor, one sees form. Thus, this grasping of all objects, occurring in no fixed sequence, having a single conscious entity as its locus, and having no other agent, is connected together,

children.text: pratyakṣānumānāgamasaṃśayān pratyayāṃś ca nānāviṣayān svātmakartṛkān pratisandhāya vedayate, sarvaviṣayaṃ ca śāstraṃ pratipadyate, artham aviṣayabhūtaṃ śrotrasya kramabhāvino varṇān śrutvā padavākyabhāvena pratisandhāya śabdārthavyavasthāṃ ca budhyamāno 'nekaviṣayam arthajātam agrahaṇīyam ekaikenendriyeṇa gṛhṇāti/ seyaṃ sarvajñasya jñeyāvyavasthānupadaṃ na śakyā parikramitum/ ākṛtimātraṃ tūdāhṛtam/ tatra yad uktam indriyacaitanye sati kim aneya cetanena tad ayuktaṃ bhavati //3//
children.translated_text: and [this entity] connects together and experiences cognitions of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>āgama</s> (scripture), and <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt) — cognitions having diverse objects and having itself as their agent — and comprehends the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise) which encompasses all objects; and, hearing the phonemes which arise in sequence and which are not objects of the ear [as meaningful wholes], connecting them in the form of words and sentences, and understanding the determination of word-meaning, it grasps the manifold collection of objects that cannot be grasped by any single sense-organ. This [capacity] of the omniscient [self], following upon the non-fixity of objects to be known, cannot be fully traversed; only a sketch has been presented. Therefore, what was said — 'if the sense-organs are conscious, what need is there for another conscious entity' — that is untenable. // 3 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 4]

children.text: itaś ca dehādivyatirikta ātmā, na dehādisaṅghātamātram
children.translated_text: And for this further reason the <s>ātman</s> (self) is distinct from body and so forth; it is not merely the aggregate of body and so forth —
Because there would be no sin in burning the body. // 3.1.4 //

children.text: śarīragrahaṇena śarīrendriyabuddhivedanāsaṅghātaḥ prāṇibhūto gṛhyate/ prāṇibhūtaṃ śarīraṃ dahataḥ prāṇihiṃsākṛtapāpaṃ pātakam ity ucyate; tasyābhāvaḥ, tatphalena kartur asambandhāt, akartuś ca sambandhāt/ śarīrendriyabuddhivedanāprabandhe khalv anyaḥ saṅghāta utpadyate anyo nirudhyate,
children.translated_text: By the word 'body' is meant the aggregate of body, sense-organs, <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), and sensation, which constitutes a living being. The sin that arises from the act of killing a living being by burning its body is called <s>pātaka</s> (a grievous sin); and its absence [would follow], because the doer would have no connection with its result, while one who is not the doer would have a connection. For in the continuum of body, sense-organs, <s>buddhi</s>, and sensation, one aggregate arises and another ceases,

children.text: utpādanirodhasantatibhūtaḥ prabandho nānyatvaṃ bādhate dehādisaṅghātasyānyatvādhiṣṭhānatvāt/ anyatvādhiṣṭhāno hy asau prakhyāyata iti/ evaṃ ca sati yo dehādisaṅghātaḥ prāṇibhūto hiṃsāṃ karoti nāsau hiṃsāphalena sambadhyate, yaś ca sambadhyate na tena hiṃsā kṛtā/ tad evaṃ sattvabhede kṛtahānam akṛtābhyāgamaḥ prasajyate/ sati ca sattvotpāde sattvanirodhe cākarmanimittaḥ sattvasarsargaḥ prāpnoti, tatra muktyartho brahmacaryavāso na syāt/ tad yadi dehādisaṅghātamātraṃ sattvaṃ syāt śarīradāhe pātakaṃ na bhavet, aniṣṭaṃ caitat/ tasmād dehādisaṅghātavyatirikta ātmā nitya iti//4//
children.translated_text: but the continuum, consisting of a series of originations and cessations, does not preclude otherness, because the aggregate of body and so forth is the locus of otherness. For it is manifest that [each successive aggregate] is different. This being so, the aggregate of body and so forth that constitutes a living being and commits the act of killing is not connected with the result of that killing, and the one that is connected with it did not commit the killing. Thus, if the living being [at each moment] is different, [the faults of] loss of what was done and arrival of what was not done would follow. And if there is origination and cessation of the living being, a conjunction of beings without any karmic cause would result; in that case, the celibate life for the sake of liberation would be pointless. Therefore, if the living being were merely the aggregate of body and so forth, there would be no sin in burning the body — and this is unacceptable. Hence the <s>ātman</s> (self) is distinct from the aggregate of body and so forth, and is permanent. // 4 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 5]
That absence [of sin] would apply even when burning a body that has a [permanent] self, because of its permanence. // 3.1.5 //

children.text: yasyāpi nityenātmanā sātmakaṃ śarīraṃ dahyate tasyāpi śarīradāhe pātakaṃ na bhaved dagdhuḥ/
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Even for one who holds that the body possessing a permanent <s>ātman</s> (self) is burned, there would be no sin in burning the body for the burner.

children.text: kasmāt? nityatvād ātmanaḥ; na jātu kaścin nityaṃ hiṃsitum arhati/ atha hiṃsyate, nityatvam asya na bhavati/ seyam ekasmin pakṣe hiṃsā niṣphalā anyasmiṃs tv anupapanneti//5//
children.translated_text: Why? Because of the permanence of the <s>ātman</s>; no one can ever kill what is permanent. And if it is killed, then its permanence does not hold. Thus, on one view the killing is fruitless, and on the other it is impossible. // 5 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 6]
Not so, because killing consists in the destruction of the locus of function and the agent [of experience]. // 3.1.6 //

children.text: na brūmo nityasya sattvasya badho hiṃsā, api tv anucchittidharmakasya sattvasya kāryāśrayasya śarīrasya svaviṣayopalabdheś ca kartṛṇām indriyāṇām upaghātaḥ pīḍā vaikalyalakṣaṇaḥ prabandhocchedo vā pramāpaṇalakṣaṇo vā vadho hiṃseti/ kāryaṃ tu sukhaduḥkhasaṃvedanaṃ tasyāyatanam adhiṣṭhānam āśrayaḥ śarīram,
children.translated_text: [Reply:] We do not say that killing is the destruction of a permanent being. Rather, for a being that is not subject to annihilation, killing (<s>hiṃsā</s>) is the injury to the body — which is the locus of function — and to the sense-organs — which are the agents of apprehending their respective objects — [and this injury is] characterized as affliction, impairment, or the cutting off of the continuum, which is characterized as slaying. And the function is the experience of pleasure and pain; its receptacle, support, and locus is the body,

children.text: kāryāśrayasya śarīrasya svaviṣayopalabdheś ca kartṛṇām indriyāṇāṃ badho hiṃsā, na nityasyātmanaḥ/ tatra yad uktam —
children.translated_text: killing (<s>hiṃsā</s>) is the destruction of the body, which is the locus of function, and of the sense-organs, which are the agents of apprehending their respective objects — not the destruction of the permanent <s>ātman</s>. Against this, what was said —
'That absence [of sin] would apply even when burning a body that has a [permanent] self, because of its permanence' —

children.text:
ity etad ayuktam/ yasya sattvocchedo hiṃsā tasya kṛtahānam akṛtābhyāgamaś ceti doṣaḥ/ etāvac caitat syāt — sattvocchedo vā hiṃsā, anucchittidharmakasya sattvasya kāryāśrayakartṛvadho vā; na kalpāntaram asti/ sattvocchedaś ca pratiṣiddhaḥ, tatra kim anyat? śeṣaṃ yathābhūtam iti/
atha vā kāryāśrayakartṛvadhād iti, kāryāśrayo dehendriyabuddhisaṅghātaḥ, nityasyātmanas tatra sukhaduḥkhapratisaṃvedanam, tasyādhiṣṭhānam āśrayaḥ tadāyatanaṃ tad bhavati na tato 'nyad iti sa eva kartā/ tannimittā hi sukhaduḥkhasaṃvedanasya nivṛttiḥ na tam antareṇeti/ tasya vadha upaghātaḥ pīḍā pramāpaṇam vā hiṃsā na nityatvenātmocchedaḥ/ tatra yad uktam —
children.translated_text:
that is untenable. The fault of loss of what was done and arrival of what was not done applies to one for whom killing is the annihilation of the being. And this much is the extent [of the alternatives]: either killing is the annihilation of the being, or it is the destruction of the locus of function and the agent [of experience] for a being not subject to annihilation; there is no third alternative. And annihilation of the being has been refuted; so what else [remains]? The remainder stands as established.
Alternatively, 'because killing consists in the destruction of the locus of function and the agent': the locus of function is the aggregate of body, sense-organs, and <s>buddhi</s> (intellect); the experience of pleasure and pain by the permanent <s>ātman</s> occurs therein; that [aggregate] is its support, locus, and receptacle — it [the experience] exists there and not apart from it — so that [aggregate] itself is the agent. For the cessation of the experience of pleasure and pain is caused by it [the aggregate] and does not occur without it. Its destruction — injury, affliction, or slaying — is killing (<s>hiṃsā</s>), not the annihilation of the <s>ātman</s> by virtue of its permanence. Against this, what was said —
'That absence [of sin] would apply even when burning a body that has a [permanent] self, because of its permanence' —
that is not so. // 6 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 7]
And for this further reason the <s>ātman</s> (self) is distinct from body and so forth —
Because of recognition by one eye of what was seen by the other. // 3.1.7 //

children.text: pūrvaparayor vijñānayor ekaviṣaye pratisandhijñānaṃ pratyabhijñānam — tam evaitarhi paśyāmi yam ajñāsiṣam sa evāyam artha iti savyena cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭasyetareṇāpi cakṣuṣā pratyabhijñānād yam adrākṣaṃ tam evaitarhi paśyāmīti/
children.translated_text: Recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) is the connecting cognition regarding a single object between an earlier and a later cognition — 'I now see the very same [object] that I knew before; this is that same object.' Because what was seen by the left eye is recognized also by the other eye — 'that which I saw [before], I now see the very same [thing]' —

children.text: indriyacaitanye tu nānyadṛṣṭam anyaḥ pratyabhijānātīti pratyabhijñānupapattiḥ/ asti tv idaṃ pratyabhijñanam tasmād indriyavyatiriktaś cetanaḥ//7//
children.translated_text: but if consciousness belonged to the sense-organs, one [eye] would not recognize what was seen by another, and so recognition would be impossible. Yet this recognition exists; therefore there is a conscious entity distinct from the sense-organs. // 7 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 8]
Not so, because there is no apprehension of duality in what is single and separated by the nasal bone. // 3.1.8 //

children.text: ekam idaṃ cakṣur madhye nāsāsthivyavahitaṃ tasyāntau gṛhyamāṇau dvitvābhimānaṃ prayojayato madhyavyavahitasya dīrghasyeva
children.translated_text: [Objection:] This is a single eye, separated in the middle by the nasal bone, whose two ends, when apprehended [separately], give rise to the apprehension of duality, just as something long that is separated in the middle [appears as two].
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 9]
Because when one is destroyed the second is not destroyed, they are not one. // 3.1.9 //

children.text: ekasminn upahate coddhṛte vā cakṣuṣi dvitīyam avatiṣṭhate cakṣuḥviṣayagrahaṇaliṅgam, tasmād ekasya vyavadhānānupapattiḥ//9//
children.translated_text: [Reply:] When one eye is impaired or removed, the second persists — as indicated by its grasping of visual objects. Therefore, the obstruction of a single [organ] is impossible [to explain duality]. // 9 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 10]
This is inconclusive, because the composite whole is perceived even when a part is destroyed. // 3.1.10 //

children.text: ekavināśe dvitīyāvināśād ity ahetuḥ/ kasmāt? vṛkṣasya hi kāsucic chākhāsu chinnāsūpalabhyate eva vṛkṣaḥ//10//
children.translated_text: [Objection:] 'Because when one is destroyed the second is not destroyed' — this is inconclusive. Why? Because even when some branches of a tree are cut off, the tree is still perceived. // 10 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 11]
There is no refutation, because [that reasoning] contradicts the example. // 3.1.11 //

children.text:
na kāraṇadravyasya vibhāge kāryadravyam avatiṣṭate nityatvaprasaṅgāt/ bahuṣv avayaviṣu yasya kāraṇāni vibhaktāni tasya vināśaḥ, yeṣāṃ kāraṇāny avibhaktāni tāni avatiṣṭhante/
atha vā dṛśyamānārthavirodho dṛṣṭāntavirodhaḥ/ mṛtasya hi śiraḥkapāle dvāv avaṭau nāsāsthivyavahitau cakṣuṣaḥ sthāne bhedena gṛhyete na caitad ekasmin nāsāsthivyavahite sambhavati/
atha vā ekavināśasyāniyamād dvāv imāv arthau, tau ca pṛthagāvaraṇopaghātau anumīyete vibhinnav iti/
children.translated_text:
[Reply:] When the causal substance is divided, the effect-substance does not persist, for [otherwise] permanence would follow. When the causes of something that has many parts are divided, it is destroyed; those whose causes are not divided persist.
Alternatively, 'contradiction of the example' means contradiction with what is directly observed. For in the skull of a dead person, two cavities separated by the nasal bone are perceived as distinct — the locations of the eyes — and this is not possible if it were a single [organ] separated by the nasal bone.
Or again, since the destruction of one [eye] is not invariably [connected with the destruction of the other], these two entities, being subject to separate obstruction and impairment, are inferred to be distinct.

children.text: avapīḍanāc caikasya cakṣuṣo raśmiviṣayasannikarṣasya bhedād dṛśyabheda iva gṛhyate; tac caikatve virudhyate; avapīḍananivṛttau cābhinnapratisandhānam iti/ tasmād ekasya vyavadhānānupapattiḥ//11//
children.translated_text: And by pressing one eye, because the contact of the ray with the object of that [eye] is altered, there arises what appears to be a difference in the seen [object]; and that is inconsistent with [the eye being] a single [organ]; and when the pressing ceases, there is an unbroken reconnection [of the visual image]. Therefore, the obstruction of a single [organ] is impossible [to explain this]. // 11 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 12]
And this conscious entity distinct from the aggregate of body and so forth is inferred [as follows] —
Because of a modification in another sense-organ. // 3.1.12 //

children.text: kasyacid amlaphalasya gṛhītatadrasasāhacarye rūpe gandhe vā kenacid indriyeṇa gṛhyamāṇe rasanasyendriyāntarasya vikāraḥ rasānusmṛtau rasagardhivartito dantodakasaṃplavabhūto gṛhyate/ tasyendriyacaitanye 'nupapattiḥ, nānyadṛṣṭam anyaḥ smarati//12//
children.translated_text: When the form or smell of a certain sour fruit — whose taste has been previously experienced — is being grasped by some sense-organ, a modification of the tongue, which is another sense-organ, is perceived: one arising from the recollection of the taste, produced by craving for the taste, and taking the form of salivation. This is impossible if consciousness belongs to the sense-organs, for one [sense-organ] does not remember what was experienced by another. // 12 //
[Chapter 3, Section 1, Sutra 13]
Not so, because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered. // 3.1.13 //

children.text: smṛtir nāma dharmo nimittād utpadyate, tasyāḥ smartavyo viṣayaḥ, tatkṛta indriyāntaravikāro nātmakṛta iti//13//
children.translated_text: Memory is a <s>dharma</s> (attribute) that arises from a cause; its object is what is to be remembered. The modification of another sense organ caused by it is not caused by the self. // 13 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 14
Because of its actual existence as an attribute of the self, there is no refutation [of the self]. // 3.1.14 //

children.text: tasyā ātmaguṇatve sati sadbhāvād apratiṣedha ātmanaḥ/ yadi smṛtir ātmaguṇaḥ, evaṃ sati smṛtir upapadyate nānyad dṛṣṭam anyaḥ samaratīti/ indriyacaitanye tu nānākartṛkāṇāṃ viṣayagrahaṇānām apratisandhānam, pratisandhāne vā viṣayavyavasthānupapattiḥ/ ekas tu cetano 'nekārthadarśī bhinnanimittaḥ pūrvadṛṣṭam artham smaratīti ekasyānekārthadarśino darśanapratisandhānāt smṛter ātmaguṇatve sati sadbhāvaḥ viparyaye cānupapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: Since memory is an attribute of the self, because of its actual existence, there is no refutation of the self. If memory is an attribute of the self, then memory is accounted for — it is not the case that one [entity] sees and another remembers. But if consciousness belonged to the sense organs, there would be no coordination of the perceptions of different objects made by different agents; or if there were coordination, the determination of distinct objects would be untenable. But a single conscious entity, seeing multiple objects, having different causes [for cognition], remembers a previously seen object — thus, because of the coordination of the perceptions of a single entity that sees multiple objects, when memory is an attribute of the self, its actual existence [is established], and in the contrary case, [memory] is untenable.

children.text:
smṛtyāśrayāḥ prāṇabhṛtāṃ sarve vyavahārāḥ/ ātmaliṅgam udāharaṇamātram indriyāntaravikāra iti/
aparisaṅkhyānāś ca smṛtiviṣayasya — aparisaṅghyāya ca smṛtiviṣayam idam ucyate
children.translated_text: All activities of living beings depend on memory. The modification of another sense organ is merely an example serving as a mark of the self. And the enumeration of the objects of memory is not limited — regarding this unlimited scope of memory's objects, the following is stated:
Not [to be refuted] because of memory having what-is-to-be-remembered as its object.

children.text: iti/ yeyaṃ smṛtir agṛhyamāṇe 'rthe ajñāsiṣam aham amum artham iti, etasyā jñātṛjñānaviśiṣṭaḥ pūrvajñāto 'rtho viṣayo nārthamātram, jñātavān aham amum artham,
children.translated_text: This memory, [arising] when the object is not being perceived — 'I knew this object' — its object is not merely the object, but the object as qualified by the knower and knowledge, i.e., the previously known object. 'I knew this object,'

children.text: asav artho mayā jñataḥ, asminn arthe mama jñānam abhūd iti caturvidham etadvākyaṃ smṛtiviṣayajñāpakaṃ samānārtham/ sarvatra khalu jñātā jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ ca gṛhyate/ atha pratyakṣe 'rthe yā smṛtis tayā trīṇi jñānāni ekasminn arthe pratisandhīyante samānakartṛkāṇi, na nānākartṛkāṇi nākartṛkāṇi/ kiṃ tarhi? ekakartṛkāṇi/ adrākṣam amum arthaṃ yam evaitarhi paśyāmi/ adrākṣam iti darśanaṃ darśanasaṃvic ca, na khalv asaṃvidite sve darśane syād etad adrakṣam iti/ te khalv ete dve jñāne, yam evaitarhi paśyāmīti tṛtīyaṃ jñānam, evam eko 'rthas tribhir jñānair yujyamāno nākartṛko na nānākartṛkaḥ kiṃ tarhi?
children.translated_text: 'this object was known by me,' 'I had knowledge of this object' — this fourfold expression, conveying the same meaning, reveals the object of memory. In every case, the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable are apprehended. Now, regarding a directly perceived object, the memory coordinates three cognitions concerning a single object as having the same agent — not different agents, not without an agent. Rather, they have a single agent. 'I saw this very object that I now see.' 'I saw' involves both the seeing and the awareness of seeing — for one whose own seeing was unperceived could not [say] 'I saw.' These indeed are two cognitions; 'which I now see' is the third cognition. Thus a single object, connected with three cognitions, is not without an agent, nor has different agents — rather,

children.text: ekakartṛka iti/ so 'yaṃ smṛtiviṣayo 'parisaṅkhyāyamāno vidyamānaḥ prajñāto 'rthaḥ pratiṣidhyate — nāsty ātmā smṛteḥ smartavyaviṣayatvād iti/ na cedaṃ smṛtimātraṃ smartavyamātraviṣayam vā idaṃ khalu jñānapratisandhānavat smṛtipratisandhānam ekasya sarvaviṣayatvāt/ eko 'yaṃ jñātā sarvaviṣayaḥ svāni jñānāni pratisandhatte amum arthaṃ jñāsyāmi amum artham vijānāmy amum artham ajñāsiṣam amum arthaṃ jijñāsamānaś ciram ajñātvādhyavasyaty ajñāsiṣam iti/ evaṃ smṛtim api trikālaviśiṣṭāṃ suṣmūrṣāviśiṣṭāṃ ca pratisandhatte/ saṃskārasantatimātre tu sattve utpadyotpadya saṃskārās tirobhavanti/ sa nāsty eko 'pi saṃskāro yas trikālaviśiṣṭaṃ jñānaṃ smṛtiṃ cānubhavet/ na cānubhavam antareṇa jñānasya smṛteś ca pratisandhānam ahaṃ mameti cotpadyate dehāntaravat/ ato 'numīyate asty ekaḥ sarvaviṣayaḥ pratidehaṃ svajñānaprabandhaṃ smṛtiprabandhaṃ ca pratisandhatta iti, yasya dehāntareṣu vṛtter abhāvān na pratisandhānaṃ bhavatīti//14//
children.translated_text: it has a single agent. This object of memory, which when not limited is an existent, well-known thing, is [sought to be] refuted — 'There is no self, because memory has what-is-to-be-remembered as its object.' But this is not merely memory having merely what-is-to-be-remembered as its object. Rather, this is the coordination of memory, like the coordination of knowledge, because a single [knower] has all objects as domain. This single knower, having all objects as domain, coordinates his own cognitions: 'I will know this object,' 'I know this object,' 'I knew this object,' and 'having desired to know this object for a long time without knowing it, he determines: I knew it.' Similarly, he coordinates memory too, as qualified by the three times and as qualified by desire to remember. But if only a continuum of <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) exists, the impressions arise and then disappear. There is not a single impression that could experience cognition and memory as qualified by the three times. And without experience, there is no coordination of cognition and memory, and [the notions] 'I' and 'mine' arise [without basis], as in a different body. Therefore it is inferred: there exists a single [entity] having all objects as domain, which in each body coordinates its own stream of cognitions and stream of memories — and due to the absence of its functioning in other bodies, there is no coordination [with them]. // 14 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 15
Not [established], because the reasons for apprehending the self are possible in the mind. // 3.1.15 //

children.text: na dehādisaṅghātavyatirikta ātmā/ kasmāt? ātmapratipattihetūnāṃ manasi sambhavāt —

children.translated_text: from the grasping of a single object by sight and touch

children.text: ity evamādīnām ātmapratipādakānāṃ hetūnāṃ manasi sambhavo yataḥ, mano hi sarvaviṣayam iti/ tasmān na śarīrendriyamanobuddhisaṅghātavyatirikta ātmeti//15//
children.translated_text: — and so forth. The reasons that demonstrate the self are possible in the mind, since the mind has all objects as its domain. Therefore there is no self distinct from the aggregate of body, sense organs, mind, and intellect. // 15 //
There is no self distinct from the aggregate of body and the rest. Why? Because the reasons for apprehending the self are possible in the mind —
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 16
Since the instruments of knowledge are applicable to the knower, it is merely a difference in designation. // 3.1.16 //

children.text: jñātuḥ khalu jñānasādhanāny upapadyante — cakṣuṣā paśyati ghrāṇena jighrati sparśanena spṛśati, evaṃ mantuḥ sarvaviṣayasya matisādhanam antaḥkaraṇabhūtaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ vidyate yenāyaṃ manyata iti/ evaṃ sati jñātary ātmasaṃjñā na mṛṣyate manaḥsaṃjñābhyanujñāyate/ manasi ca manaḥsaṃjñā na mṛṣyate matisādhanaṃ tv abhyanujñāyate/ tad idaṃ saṃjñābhedamātraṃ nārthe vivāda iti/
children.translated_text: The instruments of knowledge are indeed applicable to the knower — he sees with the eye, smells with the nose, touches with the organ of touch. Likewise, for the thinker who has all objects as domain, there exists an internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) that has all objects as domain, which serves as the instrument of thought, by which he thinks. This being so, the designation '<s>ātman</s>' (self) for the knower is not accepted, while the designation '<s>manas</s>' (mind) is accepted. And for the mind, the designation 'mind' is not accepted, while [the designation] 'instrument of thought' is accepted. This is merely a difference in designation, not a dispute about the matter itself.

children.text: pratyākhyāne vā sarvendriyavilopaprasaṅaḥ/ atha mantuḥ sarvaviṣayasya matisādhanaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ pratyākhyāyate nāstīti, evaṃ rūpādiviṣayagrahaṇasādhanāny api na santīti sarvendriyavilopaḥ prasajyata iti//16//
children.translated_text: Or, if [the mind as all-knowing] is rejected, the consequence would be the negation of all sense organs. If the instrument of thought having all objects as domain is rejected for the thinker who has all objects as domain — [saying] 'it does not exist' — then the instruments for grasping form and the rest also do not exist, and the consequence would be the negation of all sense organs. // 16 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 17
And the restriction is without inference. // 3.1.17 //

children.text:
yo 'yam niyama iṣyate, rūpādigrahaṇasādhanāny asya santi, matisādhanaṃ sarvaviṣayaṃ nāstīti, ayaṃ niyamo niranumānaḥ/ nātrānumānam asti yena niyamaṃ pratipadyāmaha iti/
rūpādibhyaś ca viṣayāntaraṃ sukhādayas tadupalabdhau karaṇāntarasadbhāvaḥ/ yathā cakṣuṣā gandho na gṛhyata iti karaṇāntaraṃ ghrāṇam evaṃ cakṣur ghrāṇābhyāṃ raso na gṛhyata iti karaṇāntaraṃ rasanam/ evaṃ śeṣeṣv api/ tathā cakṣurādibhiḥ sukhādayo na gṛhyanta iti karaṇāntareṇa bhavitavyam/
children.translated_text: The restriction that is maintained — that this [entity] has instruments for grasping form and the rest but does not have an instrument of thought with all objects as domain — this restriction is without inference. There is no inference by which we could accept this restriction. And since pleasure and the rest are objects different from form and the rest, there must be a different instrument for apprehending them. Just as color is not grasped by the eye [alone without the nose grasping smell], hence a different instrument, the nose [exists]; and just as taste is not grasped by the eye or nose, hence a different instrument, the tongue [exists]; similarly for the rest. Likewise, since pleasure and the rest are not grasped by the eye and other [sense organs], there must be a different instrument.

children.text: tac ca jñānāyaugapadyaliṅgam/ yac ca sukhādyupalabdhau karaṇaṃ tac ca jñānāyaugaoadyaliṅgaṃ tasyendriyam indriyaṃ prati sannidher asannidheḥ ca na yugapaj jñānāny utpadyanta iti/ tatra yad uktam
children.translated_text: And that [instrument] is marked by the non-simultaneity of cognitions. The instrument for apprehending pleasure and the rest is also marked by the non-simultaneity of cognitions; that is a sense organ — cognitions do not arise simultaneously because of the proximity or non-proximity of each sense organ to [its object]. Therefore what was stated —
'because the reasons for apprehending the self are possible in the mind'
— that is untenable. // 17 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 18

children.text: kiṃ punar ayaṃ dehādisaṅghātād anyo nityaḥ utānitya iti/ kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ? ubhayathā dṛṣṭatvāt saṃśayaḥ/ vidyamānam ubhayathā bhavati nityam anityaṃ ca/ pratipādite ca ātmasadbhāve saṃśayānivṛttir iti/
children.translated_text: Now, is this [self], being different from the aggregate of body and the rest, permanent or impermanent? Whence the doubt? The doubt arises because both are observed. What exists can be either permanent or impermanent. And since the existence of the self has been established, the doubt has not been resolved.

children.text: ātmasadbhāvahetubhir evāsya prāg dehabhedād avasthānaṃ siddham ūrddhvam api dehabhedād avatiṣṭhate/ kutaḥ?
children.translated_text: By the very reasons that prove the existence of the self, its continued existence prior to the destruction of the body is established. [The question is whether] it also continues after the destruction of the body. Why [should it]?
Because a newborn [child] apprehends joy, fear, and sorrow, through the connection with memory based on previous habituation. // 3.1.18 //

children.text: jātaḥ khalv ayaṃ kumārako 'smin janmany agṛhīteṣu harṣabhayaśokahetuṣu harṣabhayaśokān pratipadyate liṅgānumeyān/ te ca smṛtyanubandhād utpadyante nānyathā/ smṛtyanubandhaś ca pūrvābhyāsam antareṇa na bhavati/ pūrvābhyāsaś ca pūrvajanmani sati, nānyatheti sidhyaty etat avatiṣṭhate 'yam ūrdhvaṃ śarīrabhedād iti//18//
children.translated_text: This newborn infant, in this birth, without having grasped the causes of joy, fear, and sorrow, apprehends joy, fear, and sorrow — [these are] inferable from their signs. And these arise from the connection with memory, not otherwise. And the connection with memory does not occur without previous habituation. And previous habituation [requires] a previous birth — not otherwise. Thus it is established that [the self] continues after the destruction of the body. // 18 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 19
Like the modifications of opening and closing in lotuses and the like, so is that modification [of the self]. // 3.1.19 //

children.text:
yathā padmādiṣv anityeṣu prabodhaḥ sammīlanaṃ vikāro bhavati evam anityasyātmano harṣabhayaśokasampratipattir vikāraḥ syāt/
hetvabhāvād ayuktam — anena hetunā padmādiṣu prabodhasammīlanavikāravad anityasyātmano harṣādisampratipattir iti nātrodāharaṇasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanaṃ hetur na vaidharmyād asti hetvabhāvāt asambaddhārthakam apārthakam ucyata iti/
children.translated_text: Just as in impermanent lotuses and the like there are modifications of opening and closing, so too the apprehension of joy, fear, and sorrow would be a modification of an impermanent self. [Reply:] This is untenable due to the absence of a reason — by this reason, [the claim that] the apprehension of joy and the rest of an impermanent self is like the modification of opening and closing in lotuses and the like — here there is no reason establishing the thing to be proved through similarity with the example, nor through dissimilarity. Due to the absence of a reason, what is said is unconnected and meaningless.

children.text: dṛṣṭāntāc ca harṣādinimittasyānivṛttiḥ — yā ceyam āseviteṣu viṣayeṣu harṣādisampratipattiḥ smṛtyanubandhakṛtā pratyātmanaṃ gṛhyate seyaṃ padmādisammīlanadṛṣṭāntena na nivartate/ yathā ceyaṃ na nivarttate tathā jātasyāpīti/ kriyājātau ca parṇavibhāgasaṃyogau prabodhasammīlane, kriyāhetuś ca kriyānumeyaḥ/ evaṃ ca sati kiṃ dṛṣṭāntena pratiṣidhyate//19//
children.translated_text: And from the example, the cause of joy and the rest is not negated — this apprehension of joy and the rest regarding experienced objects, produced by the connection with memory, which is grasped for each individual self, is not negated by the example of the closing of lotuses and the like. And just as this [example] does not negate [it for the experienced], so too for the newborn. And in the class of actions, the separation and conjunction of petals constitute opening and closing; and the cause of an action is inferred from the action. This being so, what is refuted by the example? // 19 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 20

children.text: atha nirnimittaḥ padmādiṣu prabodhasammīlanavikāra iti matam evam ātmano 'pi harṣādisampratipattir iti/ tac ca —
children.translated_text: Now, if it is held that the modification of opening and closing in lotuses and the like is without a cause, then the apprehension of joy and the rest of the self is also [without a cause]. And that —
No, because of [the modifications] of entities composed of five elements being caused by the seasons of heat, cold, and rain. // 3.1.20 //

children.text: uṣṇādiṣu satsu bhāvād asatsv abhāvāt tannimittāḥ pañcabhūtānugraheṇa nivṛttānāṃ padmādīnāṃ prabodhasammīlanavikārā iti na nirnimittāḥ/ evaṃ harṣādayo 'pi vikārā nimittad bhavitum arhanti na nimittam antareṇa/
children.translated_text: Since they exist when heat and the rest are present and are absent when they are absent, the modifications of opening and closing of lotuses and the like, which have ceased through the influence of the five elements, are caused by those [seasonal factors] — they are not without a cause. Similarly, joy and other modifications too ought to have a cause, not [arise] without a cause.

children.text: na cānyat pūrvābhyastasmṛtyanubandhān nimittam astīti/ na cotpattitirodhakāraṇānumānam ātmano dṛṣṭāntāt, na harṣādīnāṃ nimittam antareṇotpattiḥ, noṣṇādivan nimittāntaropādānaṃ harṣādīnām, tasmād ayuktam etat//20//
children.translated_text: And there is no other cause than the connection with memory based on previous habituation. And the inference regarding the cause of origination and disappearance of the self from the example [does not hold] — there is no arising of joy and the rest without a cause; nor is there the adoption of another cause, like heat and the rest, for joy and the rest. Therefore this is untenable. // 20 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 21
And for this [further] reason the self is permanent —
Because of the desire for milk, which is caused by the habituation to food after death [and rebirth]. // 3.1.21 //

children.text: jātamātrasya vatsasya pravṛttiliṅgaḥ stanyābhilāṣo gṛhyate/ sa ca nāntareṇāhārābhyāsam/ kayā yuktyā? dṛśyate hi śarīriṇāṃ kṣudhā pīḍyamānānām āhārābhyāsakṛtāt smaraṇānubandhād āhārābhilāṣaḥ/ na ca pūrvaśarīrābhyāsam antareṇāsau jātamātrasyopapadyate/
children.translated_text: In a newborn calf, the desire for milk is observed as marked by [purposeful] activity. And that [desire] does not [arise] without habituation to food. By what reasoning? For it is observed that in embodied beings afflicted by hunger, the desire for food [arises] from the connection with remembrance caused by habituation to food. And that [desire] is not possible for a newborn without habituation in a previous body.

children.text: tenānumīyate bhūtapūrvaṃ śarīraṃ yatrānenāhāro 'bhyasta iti/ sa khalv ayam ātmā pūrvaśarīrāt pretya śarīrāntaram āpannaḥ kṣutpīḍitaḥ pūrvābhyastam āhāram anusmaran stanyam abhilaṣati/ tasmān na dehabhedād ātmā bhidyate bhavaty evorddhvaṃ dehabhedād iti//21//
children.translated_text: Therefore it is inferred that there was a previous body in which it was habituated to food. This self, having departed from the previous body and obtained another body, being afflicted by hunger and remembering the previously habituated food, desires milk. Therefore the self is not destroyed with the destruction of the body; it exists even after the destruction of the body. // 21 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 22
Like the movement of iron toward a magnet, so is its approach [to milk]. // 3.1.22 //

children.text: yathā khalv ayo 'bhyāsam antareṇāyaskāntam upasarpati, evam āhārābhyāsam antareṇa bālaḥ stanyam abhilaṣati//22//
children.translated_text: Just as iron approaches a magnet without [previous] habituation, so too the infant desires milk without habituation to food. // 22 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, Sūtra 23

children.text: kim idam ayaso 'yaskāntābhisarpaṇaṃ nirnimittam atha nimittād iti? nirnimittaṃ tāvat —
children.translated_text: Is this movement of iron toward a magnet without a cause, or is it from a cause? First, [if] without a cause —
No, because of the absence of such activity in other things. // 3.1.23 //

children.text: yadi nirnimittam, loṣṭādayo 'py ayaskāntam upasarpeyuḥ/ na jātu niyame kāraṇam astīti/ atha nimittāt, tat kenopalabhyate iti/ kriyāliṅgaḥ kriyāhetuḥ, kriyāniyamaliṅgaś ca kriyāhetuniyamaḥ, tenānyatra pravṛttyabhāvaḥ, bālasyāpi niyatam upasarpaṇakriyopalabhyate/ na ca stanyābhilāṣaliṅgam anyad āhārābhyāsakṛtāt smaraṇāubandhāt/ nimittaṃ dṛṣṭāntenopapādyate,
children.translated_text: If it were without a cause, then clods of earth and the like too would approach a magnet. There is never a restriction without a reason. If [it is] from a cause, then by what is that [cause] apprehended? The cause of an action is marked by the action, and the restriction of the cause of an action is marked by the restriction of the action. Therefore there is the absence of such activity in other things. In the infant too, a definite activity of approaching is observed. And there is no other mark of the desire for milk than the connection with remembrance caused by habituation to food. The cause is established by the example.

children.text:
na cāsati nimitte kasyacid utpattiḥ/ na ca dṛṣṭānto dṛṣṭam abhilāṣahetuṃ bādhate/ tasmād ayaso 'yaskāntābhigamanam adṛṣṭānta iti/
ayasaḥ khalv api nānyatra pravṛttir bhavati, na jātv ayo loṣṭam upasarpati, kiṃkṛito 'sya niyama iti? yadi kāraṇaniyamāt, sa ca kriyāniyamaliṅgaḥ/ evaṃ bālasyāpi niyataviṣayo 'bhilāṣaḥ kāraṇaniyamād bhavitum arhati/ tac ca kāraṇam abhyastasmaraṇam anyad veti dṛṣṭena viśiṣyate/ dṛṣṭo hi śarīriṇām abhastasmaraṇād āhārābhilāṣa iti//23//
children.translated_text:
And without a cause, nothing comes into being. Nor does an observed example refute an observed cause of desire. Therefore, the movement of iron toward a lodestone is not a counter-example.
Moreover, iron too does not move toward anything else — iron never approaches a clod of earth. What accounts for this restriction? If it is due to restriction of causes, that is indicated by the restriction of activity. Likewise, the desire of an infant, being directed toward a specific object, may arise from a restriction of causes. And whether that cause is the memory of past experience or something else is distinguished by what is observed. For it is observed that among embodied beings, the desire for food arises from the memory of past experience.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 24]
Moreover, the <s>ātman</s> (self) is permanent. Why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.24: Because birth without attachment (<s>vītarāga</s>) is not observed.

children.text: sarāgo jāyata ity arthād āpadyate/ ayaṃ jāyamāno rāgānubhaddho jāyate, rāgasya pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanaṃ yoniḥ, pūrvānubhavaś ca viṣayāṇām anyasmin janmani śarīram antareṇa nopapadyate/
children.translated_text: The implication is that one is born with attachment (<s>sarāga</s>). This being who is born is born bound by attachment (<s>rāga</s>); the source of attachment is the contemplation of objects previously experienced; and the previous experience of objects is not possible in another birth without a body.

children.text: so 'yam ātmā pūrvaśarīrānubhūtān viṣayān anusmaran teṣu teṣu rajyate, tathā cāyaṃ dvayor janmanoḥ pratisandhiḥ/ evaṃ pūrvaśarīrasya pūrvatareṇa pūrvatarasya pūrvatamenetyādinānādiś cetanasya śarīrayogaḥ, anādiś ca rāgānubandha iti siddhaṃ nityatvam iti//24//
children.translated_text: This <s>ātman</s>, remembering the objects experienced in a former body, becomes attached to those various objects — and thus there is a continuity (<s>pratisandhi</s>) between two births. In the same way, the former body is preceded by an earlier one, and that by a still earlier one — thus the connection of the conscious being with bodies is beginningless, and the bond of attachment is beginningless. Therefore, permanence is established.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 25]

children.text: kathaṃ punar jñāyate pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanajanito jātasya rāgaḥ, na punaḥ —
children.translated_text: But how is it known that the attachment of the newborn arises from contemplation of previously experienced objects, and not —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.25: Its origination is like the origination of a substance possessing qualities.

children.text: athotpattidharmakasya dravyasya guṇāḥ kāraṇata utpadyante tathotpattidharmakasyātmano rāgaḥ kutaścid utpadyate/ atrāyam uditānuvādo nidarśanārthaḥ//25//
children.translated_text: Just as the qualities of a substance that is subject to origination arise from a cause, so too the attachment of the <s>ātman</s>, if it were subject to origination, would arise from some cause. Here this stated view is recapitulated for the purpose of illustration.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 26]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.26: No, because <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the rest have volition (<s>saṅkalpa</s>) as their cause.

children.text: na khalu saguṇadravyotpattivad utpattir ātmano rāgasya ca/ kasmāt? saṅkalpanimittatvād rāgādīnām/ ayaṃ khalu prāṇināṃ viṣayān āsevamānānāṃ saṅkalpajanito rāgo gṛhyate, saṅkalpaś ca pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanayoniḥ/ tenānumīyate jātasyāpi pūrvānubhūtārthacintanakṛto rāga iti/ ātmotpādādhikaraṇāt tu rāgotpattir bhavantī saṅkalpād anyasmin rāgakāraṇe sati vācyā kāryadravyaguṇavat/ na cātmotpādaḥ siddho nāpi saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇam asti/
children.translated_text: The origination of the <s>ātman</s> and of its attachment is not like the origination of a substance possessing qualities. Why? Because <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the rest have <s>saṅkalpa</s> (volition) as their cause. For it is observed that among living beings who engage with objects, attachment arises from volition, and volition has its source in the contemplation of previously experienced objects. Therefore it is inferred that even in the newborn, attachment is produced by the contemplation of previously experienced objects. But the origination of attachment from the origination of the <s>ātman</s> — if there were a cause of attachment other than volition — could be stated as analogous to the qualities of a produced substance. But neither is the origination of the <s>ātman</s> established, nor is there a cause of attachment other than volition.

children.text:
tasmād ayuktaṃ saguṇadravyotpattivat tayor utpattir iti/
athāpi saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇaṃ dharmādharmalakṣaṇam adṛṣṭam upādīyate, tathāpi pūrvaśarīrayogo 'pratyākhyeyaḥ/ tatra hi tasya nirvṛttiḥ nāsmin janmani/
tanmayatvād rāga iti/ viṣayābhyāsaḥ khalv ayaṃ bhāvanāhetuḥ tanmayatvam ucyate iti/ jātiviśeṣāc ca rāgaviśeṣa iti/ karma khalv idaṃ jātiviśeṣanirvartakaṃ tādarthyāt tācchabdyaṃ vijñāyate/ tasmād anupapannaṃ saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇam iti//26//
children.translated_text:
Therefore it is inappropriate to say that the origination of both is like the origination of a substance possessing qualities.
Even if an unseen force (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) characterized as <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) is adduced as a cause of attachment other than volition, even so the connection with a former body is not refutable — for it is in that former body that the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> is produced, not in this present birth.
As for the argument 'because of being pervaded by that' (<s>tanmayatvāt</s>) — the habitual engagement with objects is called <s>bhāvanā</s> (cultivation), and that is said to be 'pervadedness by that.' And as for 'attachment varies according to the specific birth' — this <s>karma</s> (action) that produces specific types of birth is understood to be designated thus because of its purposive relation. Therefore it is untenable that there is a cause of attachment other than volition.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 27]

children.text: anādiś cetanasya śarīrayoga ity uktam, svakṛtakarmanimittaṃ cāsya śarīraṃ sukhaduḥkhādhiṣṭhānam/ tat parīkṣyate — kiṃ ghrāṇādivad ekaprakṛtikam uta nānāprakṛtīti/ kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ? vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ/ pṛthivyādīni bhūtāni saṅkhyāvikalpena śarīraprakṛtir iti pratijānata iti/ kiṃ tatra tattvam?
children.translated_text: It has been stated that the connection of the conscious being with bodies is beginningless, and that the body, which is the basis of pleasure and pain, is caused by one's own actions. Now this is examined: Is the body of a single material nature, like the nose and other sense organs, or of multiple material natures? What is the source of doubt? The doubt arises from conflicting views — because those who assert that elements beginning with earth are the material cause of the body disagree about the number of elements. What is the truth here?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.27: [The body is] composed of earth, because of the perception of distinctive qualities.

children.text: tatra mānuṣaṃ pārthivam/ kasmāt? guṇāntaropalabdheḥ/ gandhavatī pṛthivī gandhavac ca śarīram/ abādīnām agandhatvāt tatprakṛtyagandhaṃ syāt/ na tv idam abādibhir asampṛktayā pṛthivyārabdhaṃ ceṣṭendriyārthāśrayabhāvena kalpate ity ataḥ pañcānāṃ bhūtānāṃ saṃyoge sati śarīraṃ bhavati/ bhūtasaṃyogo hi mithaḥ pañcānāṃ na niṣiddha iti/ āpyataijasavāyavyāni lokāntare śarīrāṇi teṣv api bhūtasaṃyogaḥ puruṣārthatantra iti/ sthālyādidravyaniṣpattāv api niḥsaṃśayo nābādisaṃyogam antarena niṣpattir iti//27//
children.translated_text: Here, the human body is composed of earth. Why? Because of the perception of distinctive qualities — earth possesses smell, and the body possesses smell. Since water and the rest lack smell, a body made of their nature would be without smell. But this body, being produced by earth alone unmixed with water and the rest, would not function as the basis of movement, sense organs, and objects — therefore the body arises when all five elements are combined. For the mutual combination of the five elements is not prohibited. Bodies in other worlds that are composed of water, fire, or air also involve the combination of elements, which is governed by the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person). And in the production of substances such as pots, there is no doubt that production does not occur without the combination of water and the rest.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.28: [The body is] composed of earth, water, and fire, because of the perception of their respective qualities.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.29: [The body is] composed of four elements, because of the perception of inhalation and exhalation.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.30: [The body is] composed of five elements, because of smell, moisture, heat, spatial arrangement, and the provision of space.

children.text: ta ime sandigdhā hetava ity upekṣitavān sūtrakāraḥ/ kathaṃ sandigdhāḥ? sati ca prakṛtibhāve bhūtānāṃ dharmopalabdhir asati ca saṃyogāpratiṣedhāt sannihitānām iti, yathā sthālyām udakatejovāyvākāśānām iti/ tad idam anekabhūtaprakṛti śarīram agandham arasam arūpam asparśaṃ ca prakṛtyanuvidhānāt syāt,
children.translated_text: These are doubtful reasons, and therefore the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras) has set them aside. How are they doubtful? Because the perception of the properties of elements is possible both when they are the material cause and, since the proximity of combined elements is not denied, when they are merely present — as water, fire, air, and space are present in a pot. Thus, this body having multiple elements as its material cause would be without smell, taste, color, and touch, following the nature of its material cause.
But the body is not like this. Therefore,
[the body is] composed of earth, because of the perception of distinctive qualities.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 31]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.31: And because of the authority of scripture (<s>śruti</s>).
'Let your eye go to the sun'
— in this <s>mantra</s>,
'Let your body [go] to earth'

children.text: iti śrūyate/ tad idaṃ prakrtau vikārasya pralayābhidhānam iti/
children.translated_text: is heard. This is a statement of the dissolution of the effect into its material cause.
'I offer your eye to the sun'
— in this other <s>mantra</s>,
'I offer your body to earth'

children.text: śrūyate/ seyaṃ kāraṇād vikārasya spṛtir abhidhīyata iti/ sthālyādiṣu ca tulyajātīyānām ekakāryārambhadarśanād bhinnajātīyānām ekakāryārambhānupapattiḥ//31//
children.translated_text: is heard. This refers to the nourishment of the effect by the cause. And since in the case of pots and the like, it is observed that things of the same class combine to produce a single effect, the production of a single effect by things of different classes is untenable.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 32]

children.text: athedānīm indriyāṇi prameyakrameṇa vicāryante — kim āvyaktikāny āhosvid bhautikānīti/
children.translated_text: Now the sense organs are examined in the order of the <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) — are they products of the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>) or are they elemental (<s>bhautika</s>)?
What is the source of doubt?

children.text: kṛṣṇasāre saty upalambhād vyatiricya copalambhāt saṃśayaḥ // 3.1.32 //
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.32: Doubt arises because of perception when the sense organ is present, and perception even in its absence.

children.text: kṛṣṇasāraṃ bhautikam, tasminn anupahate rūpopalabdhiḥ upahate cānupalabdhir iti/ vyatiricya kṛṣṇasāram avasthitasya viṣayasya upalambho na kṛṣṇasāraprāptasya/ na cāprāpyakāritvam indriyāṇām, tad idam abhautikatve vibhutvāt sambhavati/ evam ubhayadharmopalabdheḥ saṃśayaḥ//32//
children.translated_text: The sense organ (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>, i.e. the pupil) is elemental. When it is unimpaired, there is perception of form; when impaired, there is non-perception. But there is also perception of an existing object apart from the sense organ — of an object not reached by the sense organ. And the sense organs do not function without contact — but this [distant perception] is possible if they are non-elemental, due to their all-pervasiveness. Thus, from the perception of properties of both kinds, there is doubt.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 33]
They are non-elemental, he says. Why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.33: Because of the apprehension of the large and the small.

children.text: mahad iti mahattaraṃ mahattamaṃ copalabhyate yathā nyagrodhaparvatādi/ aṇv iti aṇutaram aṇutamaṃ ca gṛhyate yathā nyagrodhadhānādi/ tadubhayam upalabhyamānaṃ cakṣuṣo bhautikatvaṃ bādhate/ bhautikaṃ hi yāvat tāvad eva vyāpnoti/ abhautikaṃ tu vibhutvāt sarvavyāpakam iti//33//
children.translated_text: 'Large' — the very large and the largest are perceived, such as a banyan tree or a mountain. 'Small' — the very small and the smallest are apprehended, such as a banyan seed and the like. The perception of both these contradicts the elemental nature of the eye. For what is elemental extends only so far as its size. But what is non-elemental, being all-pervasive due to its pervasiveness, pervades everything.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 34]

children.text: na mahadaṇugrahaṇamātrād abhautikatvaṃ vibhutvaṃ cendriyāṇāṃ śakyaṃ pratipattum/ idaṃ khalu —
children.translated_text: The non-elemental nature and all-pervasiveness of the sense organs cannot be established merely from the apprehension of the large and the small. Indeed —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.34: The apprehension of those is due to the specific contact between the visual ray and the object.

children.text: tayor mahadaṇvor grahaṇaṃ cakṣūraśmer arthasya ca sannikarṣaviśeṣād bhavati yathā pradīparaśmer arthasya ceti/
children.translated_text: The apprehension of both the large and the small occurs due to the specific contact between the visual ray of the eye and the object, just as with the ray of a lamp and the object.

children.text: raśmyarthasannikarṣaś cāvaraṇaliṅgaḥ/ cākṣuṣo hi raśmiḥ kuḍyādibhir āvṛtam arthaṃ na prakāśayati yathā pradīparaśmir iti//34//
children.translated_text: The contact between the ray and the object is indicated by obstruction. For the visual ray does not illuminate an object obstructed by a wall and the like, just as the ray of a lamp does not.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 35]
If obstruction is to be inferred, this is stated —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.35: This is not a valid reason, because of the non-perception of that [visual ray].

children.text: rūpasparśavad dhi tejaḥ, mahattvād anekadravyavattvād rūpavattvāc copalabdhir iti pradīpavat pratyakṣata upalabhyeta cākṣuṣo raśmir yadi syād iti//35//
children.translated_text: For fire possesses form and touch; being large, consisting of many substances, and possessing form, it is perceived — thus the visual ray, if it existed, would be directly perceived like a lamp. [But it is not perceived.]
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 36]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.36: The non-perception of what is inferred through a mark is not a reason for its non-existence.

children.text: sannikarṣapratiṣedhārthenāvaraṇena liṅgenānumīyamānasya raśmer yā pratyakṣato 'nupalabdhir nāsāv abhāvaṃ pratipādayati yathā candramasaḥ parabhāgasya prthivyāś cādhobhāgasya//36//
children.translated_text: The non-perception through direct observation of the visual ray, which is inferred through the inferential mark of obstruction — which serves to negate contact — does not establish its non-existence, just as with the far side of the moon and the underside of the earth.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 37]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.37: And the restriction of perception is due to the distinction between the properties of substance and quality.

children.text: bhinnaḥ khalv ayaṃ dravyadharmo guṇadharmaś ca, mahadanekadravyavac ca viṣaktāvayavam āpyaṃ dravyaṃ pratyakṣato nopalabhyate sparśas tu śīto gṛhyate/ tasya dravyasyānubandhād hemantaśiśirau kalpyete tathāvidham eva ca taijasaṃ dravyam anudbhūtarūpaṃ saha rūpeṇa nopalabhyate,
children.translated_text: The property of substance and the property of quality are indeed different. Water, which is a substance that is large, consists of many substances, and has connected parts, is not directly perceived, yet its quality — cold touch — is apprehended. From the persistence of that substance, the seasons of <s>hemanta</s> (early winter) and <s>śiśira</s> (late winter) are recognized. Likewise, fire as a substance whose form has not become manifest is not perceived together with its form,

children.text: sparśas tv asyoṣṇa upalabhyate tasya dravyasyānubandhād grīṣmavasantau kalpyete//37//
children.translated_text: yet its quality — hot touch — is perceived. From the persistence of that substance, the seasons of <s>grīṣma</s> (summer) and <s>vasanta</s> (spring) are recognized.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 38]
But where this [perception] does occur —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.38: The perception of form is due to inherence in many substances and due to a specific form.

children.text: tatra rūpaṃ ca dravyaṃ ca tadāśrayaḥ pratyakṣata upalabhyate/ rūpaviśeṣas tu yadbhāvāt kvacid rūpopalabdhiḥ yadabhāvāc ca dravyasya kvacid anupalabdhiḥ sa rūpadharmo 'yam udbhava samākhyāta iti/ anudbhūtarūpaś cāyaṃ nāyano raśmiḥ, tasmāt pratyakṣato nopalabhyata iti/
children.translated_text: In that case, both the form and the substance that is its substrate are directly perceived. The specific form — whose presence causes the perception of form in some cases and whose absence causes the non-perception of the substance in other cases — this property of form is called 'manifestation' (<s>udbhava</s>). And this visual ray has unmanifested form, and therefore it is not directly perceived.

children.text: dṛṣṭaś ca tejaso dharmabhedaḥ, udbhūtarūpasparśaṃ pratyakṣaṃ tejo yathā ādityaraśmayaḥ/ udbhūtarūpam anudbhūtasparśaṃ ca pratyakṣaṃ yathā pradīparaśmayaḥ/ udbhūtasparśam anudbhūtarūpam apratyakṣaṃ yathābādisaṃyuktaṃ tejaḥ/ anudbhūtarūpasparśo 'pratyakṣaś cākṣuṣo raśmir iti//38//
children.translated_text: And the distinction in the properties of fire is observed: fire with manifest form and touch is directly perceived, such as the rays of the sun. Fire with manifest form but unmanifest touch is directly perceived, such as the rays of a lamp. Fire with manifest touch but unmanifest form is not directly perceived, such as fire combined with water and the rest. The visual ray, having unmanifest form and touch, is not directly perceived.
[Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 39]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.39: And the arrangement of the sense organs, brought about by <s>karma</s> (action), is governed by the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person).

children.text: yathā cetanasyārtho viṣayopalabdhibhūtaḥ sukhaduḥkhopalabdhibhūtaś ca kalpyate tathendriyāṇi vyūḍhāni, viṣayaprāptyarthaś ca raśmeś cākṣuṣasya vyūhaḥ/ rūpasparśānabhivyaktiś ca vyavahāraprakḷptyarthā, dravyaviśeṣe ca pratīghātād āvaraṇopapattir vyavahārārthā/ sarvadravyāṇāṃ viśvarūpo vyūha indriyavat karmakāritaḥ puruṣārthatantraḥ/ karma tu dharmādharmabhūtaṃ cetanasyopabhogārtham iti/
children.translated_text: Just as the purpose of the conscious being is conceived as consisting in the experience of objects and the experience of pleasure and pain, so the sense organs are arranged accordingly; and the arrangement of the visual ray is for the purpose of reaching objects. The non-manifestation of form and touch serves the purpose of practical functioning, and the obstruction by specific substances, establishing the occurrence of obstruction, serves practical purposes. The multiform arrangement of all substances, like that of the sense organs, is brought about by <s>karma</s> and governed by the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s>. And <s>karma</s>, consisting of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), is for the experience of the conscious being.

children.text:
avyabhicārāc ca pratīghāto bhautikadharmaḥ/ yaś cātvaraṇopalambhād indriyasya dravyaviśeṣe pratighātaḥ sa bhautikadharmo na bhūtāni vyabhicarati, nābautikaṃ pratighātadharmakaṃ dṛṣṭam iti/ apratighātas tu vyabhicārī bhautikābhautikayoḥ samānatvād iti/
yad api manyeta pratighātād bhautikānīndriyāṇi, apratighātād abhautikānīti prāptam? dṛṣṭaś cāpratighātaḥ kācābhrapaṭalasphaṭikāntaritopalabdheḥ/ tan na yuktam/ kasmāt? yasmād bhautikam api na pratihanyate, kācābhrapaṭalasphaṭikāntaritaprakāśāt pradīparaśmīnām, sthālyādiṣu pācakasya tejaso 'pratighātaḥ//39//
children.translated_text:
And obstruction is an elemental property, because of its invariability. The obstruction of the sense organ by a specific substance, indicated by the non-perception due to covering, is an elemental property — it does not deviate from elements, and nothing non-elemental possessing the property of obstruction has been observed. Non-obstruction, however, is variable, being common to both the elemental and the non-elemental.
Even if one were to think 'the sense organs are elemental because of obstruction, and non-elemental because of non-obstruction' — the conclusion would follow? But non-obstruction is also observed in the case of perception through glass, clouds, crystal, and the like. This is not tenable. Why? Because even what is elemental is not obstructed — as seen from the light of lamp rays passing through glass, clouds, crystal, and the like, and from the non-obstruction of the fire that cooks in pots and similar vessels.
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 40
And non-apprehension is established due to difference of causes —
