Its non-apprehension is like the non-apprehension of the light of a firebrand at midday. // 3.1.40 //
apprehension occurs due to inherence in many substances and due to a specific form,

children.text: iti saty upalabdhikāraṇe madhyandinolkāprakāśo nopakabhyate ādityaprakāśenābhibhūtaḥ, evaṃ mahadanekadravyavattvād rūpaviśeṣāc copalabhir iti saty upalabdhikāraṇe cākṣuṣo raśmir nopalabhyate nimittāntarataḥ// tac ca vyākhyātam anudbhūtarūpasparśasya dravyasya pratyakṣato 'nupalabdhir iti//40//
children.translated_text: and when the cause of apprehension exists, the light of a firebrand at midday is not apprehended because it is overwhelmed by the light of the sun — similarly, though apprehension occurs because of possessing many substances of great magnitude and a specific form, and though the cause of apprehension exists, the visual ray is not apprehended due to another cause. And this has been explained: 'The non-apprehension through perception of a substance whose form and touch are not manifest.' // 40 //
Just as
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 41

children.text: atyantānupalabdhiś cābhāvakāraṇam/ yo hi bravīti loṣṭaprakāśo madhyandine ādityaprakāśābhibhavān nopalabhyata iti, tasyaitat syāt?
children.translated_text: And absolute non-apprehension is the cause of non-existence. For one who says that the light of a clod is not apprehended at midday because it is overwhelmed by the light of the sun — would this apply to his case?
No, because it is not apprehended even at night. // 3.1.41 //

children.text: apy anumānato 'nupalabdher iti/ evam atyantānupalabdher loṣṭaprakāśo nāsti, na tv evaṃ cakṣuṣo raśmir iti//41//
children.translated_text: Also because of non-apprehension even through inference. Thus, from absolute non-apprehension, the light of a clod does not exist; but the visual ray is not like that. // 41 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 42
And this has a well-established form —
Non-apprehension due to non-manifestation, since the apprehension of objects depends on external light. // 3.1.42 //

children.text: bāhyena prakāśenānugṛhītaṃ cakṣuḥ viṣayagrāhakaṃ tadabhāve 'nupalabdhiḥ/ sati ca prakāśānugrahe śītasparśopalabdhau ca satyāṃ tadāśrayasya dravyasya cakṣuṣā 'grahaṇaṃ rūpasyānudbhūtatvāt,
children.translated_text: The eye, when assisted by external light, grasps objects; in the absence of that, there is non-apprehension. And when there is the assistance of light and when there is the apprehension of cold touch, the non-grasping by the eye of the substance that is its substratum is due to the non-manifestation of its form.

children.text: seyaṃ rūpānabhivyaktito rūpāśrayasya dravyasyānupalabdhir dṛṣṭā/ tatra yad uktaṃ
children.translated_text: This non-apprehension of the substance that is the substratum of form, due to non-manifestation of form, has been observed. Therefore, what was said —
its non-apprehension is not a valid reason [against its existence]
— is incorrect. // 42 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 43

children.text: kasmāt punar abhibhavo 'nupalabdhikāraṇaṃ cākṣuṣasya raśmer nocyata iti?
children.translated_text: Why then is overwhelming not stated as the cause of non-apprehension of the visual ray?
And because in manifestation there is no overwhelming. // 3.1.43 //

children.text: bāhyaprakāśānugrahanirapekṣatāyāṃ ceti cārthaḥ/ yad rūpam abhivyaktam udbhūtaṃ bāhyaprakāśānugrahaṃ ca nāpekṣate tadviṣayo 'bhibhavaḥ, viparyaye 'bhibhavābhāvāt/ anudbhūtarūpatvāc cānupalabhyamānaṃ bāhyaprakāśānugrahāc copalabhyamānaṃ nābhibhūyata iti/
children.translated_text: The meaning is: 'and' means 'in the condition of not depending on the assistance of external light.' Overwhelming applies to a form that is manifest and fully arisen and does not require the assistance of external light; in the opposite case, there is no overwhelming. And what is not apprehended due to non-manifestation of form and is apprehended through the assistance of external light — that is not overwhelmed.

children.text: evam upapannam asti cākṣuṣo raśmir iti//43//
children.translated_text: Thus it is established that the visual ray exists. // 43 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 44
And from seeing the eye-rays of nocturnal creatures. // 3.1.44 //

children.text: dṛśyante hi naktaṃ nayanaraśmayo naktañcarāṇāṃ vṛṣadaṃśaprabhṛtīnām, tena śeṣasyānumānam iti/ jātibhedavad indriyabheda iti cet? dharmabhedamātraṃ cānupapannam āvaraṇasya prātipratiṣedhārthasya darśanād iti//44//
children.translated_text: For the eye-rays of nocturnal creatures such as bulls and gadflies are seen at night; from this, the rest is inferred. If one objects that the difference in sense organs is like the difference in species — a mere difference in properties is untenable, since a screen is seen to counteract [the visual ray of all species alike]. // 44 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 45
The untenable character of sense-object contact as the cause of cognition — why?
Grasping without contact, because of apprehension through an intervening glass, cloud-layer, or crystal. // 3.1.45 //

children.text: tṛṇādi sarpad dravyaṃ kāce abhrapaṭale vā pratihataṃ dṛṣt'm, avyavahitena sannikṛṣyate vyāhanyate vai prāptir vyavadhāneneti/ yadi ca raśmyarthasannikarṣo grahaṇahetuḥ syāt na vyavahitasya sannikarṣa ity agrahaṇaṃ syāt/ asti ceyaṃ kācābhrapaṭalasphaṭikāntaritopalabdhiḥ sā jñāpayati aprāpyakārīṇīndriyāṇi ata evābhautikāni, prāpyakāritvaṃ hi bhautikadharma iti//45//
children.translated_text: A moving substance such as grass is seen to be blocked by glass or a cloud-layer; one comes into contact with what is unobstructed, but contact is prevented by obstruction. If the contact of the ray with the object were the cause of grasping, then there would be no contact with something obstructed, and hence no grasping. But this apprehension through an intervening glass, cloud-layer, or crystal does exist — this shows that the sense organs act without contact and are therefore non-material, for acting through contact is a property of material things. // 45 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 46
The non-apprehension of what is behind a wall does not refute this. // 3.1.46 //
If the sense organs acted without contact, there would be no non-apprehension of what is behind a wall. // 46 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 47
But even if they act through contact, there should be no apprehension through an intervening glass, cloud-layer, or crystal.
Contact is possible because there is no obstruction. // 3.1.47 //

children.text: na ca kāco 'bhrapaṭalaṃ vā nayanaraśmiṃ viṣṭabhnāti so 'pratihanyamānaḥ sannikṛṣyata iti//47//
children.translated_text: Neither glass nor a cloud-layer obstructs the visual ray — being unobstructed, it makes contact. // 47 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 48

children.text: yaś ca manyate na bhautikasyāpratighāta iti tan na —
children.translated_text: And as for one who thinks that what is material cannot be unobstructed — that is not so:
Because of the non-obstruction of sunlight even when there is an intervening crystal, and its action on combustible objects. // 3.1.48 //

children.text: ādityaraśmer avighātāt sphaṭikāntarite 'py avighātāt, dāhye 'vighātāt/ avighātād iti ca padābhisambandhād vākyabheda iti/ prativākyaṃ cārthabheda iti/ ādityaraśmiḥ kumbhādiṣu na pratihanyate, avighātāt kumbhastham udakaṃ tapati/ prāptau hi dravyāntaraguṇasya uṣṇasya sparśasya grahaṇaṃ tena ca śītasparśābhibhava iti/ sphaṭikāntarite 'pi prakāśanīye pradīparaśmīnām apratighātaḥ, apratighātāt prāptasya grahaṇam iti/ bharjanakapālādisthaṃ ca dravyam āgneyena tejasā dahyate tatrāvighātāt prāptiḥ, prāptau tu dāho nāprāpyakāri teja iti/
children.translated_text: From the non-obstruction of sunlight, even through crystal, and from its action on combustible objects — and because 'non-obstruction' connects with each clause, making separate sentences with different meanings in each. Sunlight is not blocked by pots and the like; because of non-obstruction, it heats water inside the pot. For upon contact, there is the grasping of heat, a quality belonging to another substance, and thereby the cold touch is overwhelmed. Even when there is an intervening crystal before what is to be illuminated, the rays of a lamp are not obstructed; because of non-obstruction, what has arrived is grasped. And a substance placed on a roasting pan is burned by fire-heat; there, because of non-obstruction, there is contact; upon contact there is burning — fire does not act without contact.

children.text: avighātād iti ca kevalaṃ padam upādīyate, ko 'yam avighāto nāma? avyuhyamānāvayavena vyavadhāyena dravyeṇa sarvato dravyasyāviṣṭhmbhaḥ kriyāhetor apratibandhaḥ prāpter apratiṣedha iti/ dṛṣṭaṃ hi kalaśaniṣaktānām apāṃ bahiḥ śītasparśasya grahaṇam/ na cendriyeṇāsannikṛṣṭasya dravyasya sparśopalabdhiḥ/ dṛṣṭau ca praspandaparisravau/ tatra kācābhrapaṭalādibhir nayanaraśmer apratighātād vibhidyārthena saha sannikarṣād upapannaṃ grahaṇam iti//48//
children.translated_text: The word 'non-obstruction' is taken independently — what is this non-obstruction? It is the non-blocking of a substance from all sides by an intervening substance whose parts are not displaced; it is the non-prevention of the cause of action; it is the non-negation of contact. For the grasping of cold touch of water adhering to a pot on the outside has been observed. And without contact of the sense organ, there is no apprehension of touch of a substance. And vibration and seepage are observed. In this matter, the grasping [of an object through glass etc.] is established because the visual ray is not obstructed by glass, cloud-layer, and the like, and because, penetrating through, it comes into contact with the object. // 48 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 49
Because of the mutual transfer of properties. // 3.1.49 //

children.text: kācābhrapaṭalādivad vā kuḍyādibhir apratighātaḥ, kuḍyādivad vā kācābhrapaṭalādibhiḥ pratighāta iti prasajyate, niyame kāraṇaṃ vācyam iti//49//
children.translated_text: It could equally be argued that walls and the like do not obstruct, just like glass and cloud-layers; or that glass and cloud-layers obstruct, just like walls. A reason must be given for the restriction. // 49 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 50
Just as the apprehension of form in a mirror and water is due to their natural transparency, so is that apprehension. // 3.1.50 //

children.text: ādarśodakayoḥ prasādo rūpaviśeṣaḥ svo dharmo niyamadarśanāt, prasādasya vā svo dharmo rūpopalambhanam/ yathā ādarśapratihatasya parāvṛttasya nayanaraśmeḥ svena mukhena sannikarṣe sati svamukhopalambhanaṃ pratibimbagrahaṇākhyam ādarśarūpānugrahāt tannimittaṃ bhavati,
children.translated_text: The transparency of a mirror and water is a specific form, their own property, as observed from regularity. Or alternatively, the apprehension of form is the inherent property of transparency. Just as when the visual ray, reflected back after striking a mirror, comes into contact with one's own face, the apprehension of one's own face — called the grasping of a reflection — occurs due to the assistance of the mirror's form,

children.text: ādarśarūpopaghāte tadabhāvāt, kuḍyādiṣu ca pratibimbagrahaṇaṃ na bhavati evaṃ kācābhrapaṭalādibhir avighātaś cakṣūraśmeḥ kuḍyādibhiś ca pratighāto dravyasvabhāvaniyamād iti//50//
children.translated_text: and in the absence of that quality of the mirror's form, it does not occur, and reflection-grasping does not occur in walls and the like — similarly, the non-obstruction of the visual ray by glass, cloud-layers, and the like, and its obstruction by walls and the like, is due to the fixed nature of substances. // 50 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 51
For it is impossible to command or prohibit things that are seen and inferred. // 3.1.51 //

children.text: pramāṇasya tattvaviṣayatvāt/ na khalu bhoḥ parīkṣamāṇena dṛṣṭānumitā arthāḥ śakyā niyoktum evaṃ bhavateti,
children.translated_text: Because a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) has reality as its object. Indeed, sir, one who examines cannot command things that are seen and inferred, saying 'let them be thus,'

children.text: nāpi pratiṣeddhum evaṃ na bhavateti/ na hīdam upapadyate rūpavad gandho 'pi cākṣuṣo bhavatv iti, gandhavad vā rūpaṃ cākṣuṣaṃ mā bhūd iti, agnipratipattivat dhūmenodakapratipattir api bhavatv iti, udakāpratipattivad vā dhūmenāgnipratipattir api mā bhūd iti/ kiṃ kāraṇam? yathā khalv arthā bhavanti ya eṣāṃ svo bhāvaḥ svo dharma iti tathābhūtāḥ pramāṇena pratipadyanta iti/ tathābhūtaviṣayakaṃ hi pramāṇam iti/ imau khalu niyogapratiṣedhau bhavatā deśitau kācābhrapaṭalādivad vā kuḍyādibhir apratighāto bhavatu kuḍyādivad vā kācābhrapaṭalādibhir apratighāto mā bhūd iti/ na, dṛṣṭānumitāḥ khalv ime dravyadharmāḥ, pratighātāpratighātayor hy upalabdhī vyavasthāpike/ vyavahitānupalabdhyānumīyate kuḍyādibhiḥ pratighātaḥ, vyavahitopalabdhyānumīyate kācābhrapaṭalādibhir apratighāta iti//51//
children.translated_text: nor prohibit them, saying 'let them not be thus.' For this is untenable: 'let smell also be visual like form,' or 'let form not be visual like smell,' or 'let there be cognition of water from smoke as there is cognition of fire,' or 'let there not be cognition of fire from smoke as there is no cognition of water.' Why? Because things are as they are — whatever is their own nature, their own property — and they are apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s> as they truly are. For a <s>pramāṇa</s> has things as they truly are for its object. Now, you have taught these two commands and prohibitions: 'let there be non-obstruction by walls just as by glass and cloud-layers,' and 'let there not be non-obstruction by glass and cloud-layers just as by walls.' No — these are indeed properties of substances that are seen and inferred. For the two experiences of obstruction and non-obstruction are what establish them. Non-apprehension of what is screened leads to the inference of obstruction by walls and the like; apprehension of what is screened leads to the inference of non-obstruction by glass, cloud-layers, and the like. // 51 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 52

children.text: athāpi khalv ekam idam indriyaṃ bahūnīndriyāṇi vā? kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ?
children.translated_text: Now then, is this one sense organ or many? What is the source of doubt?
The doubt arises because multiple things occupy different locations, and because a whole can occupy different locations. // 3.1.52 //

children.text: bahūni dravyāṇi nānāsthānāni dṛśyante, nānāsthānaś ca sann eko 'vayavī ceti/ tenendriyeṣu bhinnasthāneṣu saṃśaya iti//52//
children.translated_text: Many substances are seen to occupy different locations; and a single whole occupying different locations is also [observed]. Therefore, there is doubt regarding the sense organs that occupy different locations. // 52 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 53
There is one sense organ —
Skin, because of non-difference. // 3.1.53 //

children.text:
tvag ekam indriyam ity āha/ kasmāt? avyatirekāt/ na tvacā kiñcid indriyādhiṣṭhānaṃ na prāptam, na cāsatyāṃ tvaci kiñcid viṣayagrahaṇaṃ bhavati, yayā satvendriyasthānāni vyāptāni yasyāṃ ca satyāṃ viṣayagrahaṇaṃ bhavati sā tvag ekam indriyam iti/
nendriyāntarārthānupalabdheḥ/ sparśopalabdhilakṣaṇāyāṃ satyāṃ tvaci gṛhyamāṇe tvagindriyeṇa sparśe indriyāntarārthā rūpādayo na gṛhyante andhādibhiḥ/ na sparśagrāhakāt indriyād indriyāntaram astīti sparśavad andhādibhir gṛhyeran rūpādayaḥ, na ca gṛhyante tasmān naikam indriyaṃ tvag iti/
children.translated_text: Skin is the one sense organ, he says. Why? Because of non-difference. There is no location of a sense organ that skin does not pervade, and without skin there is no grasping of any object. Since the locations of the sense organs are pervaded by it when it exists, and grasping of objects occurs when it exists — skin is the one sense organ. [Objection:] Because objects of other senses are not apprehended [through skin]. When skin is being grasped by the sense of touch — characterized by the apprehension of touch — the objects of other senses such as form are not grasped by blind persons and the like. There is no other sense organ besides the touch-grasping one, so that form and the like could be grasped by the blind — and they are not grasped. Therefore, skin is not the one sense organ.

children.text: tvagavayavaviśeṣeṇa dhūmopalabdhivat tadupalabdhiḥ/ yathā tvaco 'vayavaviśeṣaḥ kaścic cakṣuṣi sannikṛṣṭo dhūmasparśaṃ gṛhṇāti nānyaḥ, evaṃ tvaco 'vayavaviśeṣā rūpādigrāhakās teṣām upaghātād andhādibhir na gṛhyante rūpādaya iti/ vyāhatatvād ahetuḥ/ tvagavyatirekād ekam indriyam ity uktvā
children.translated_text: [Response:] The apprehension of those [other objects] is like the apprehension of smoke through a specific part of the skin. Just as a specific part of the skin connected to the eye grasps the touch of smoke but another part does not, similarly specific parts of the skin are the graspers of form and the like — and because of their impairment, form and the like are not grasped by the blind and such. [Reply:] This is no valid reason, because it is self-contradictory. Having said 'skin is the one sense organ because of non-difference,'
one then says 'the apprehension of form and the like is through a specific part of skin, like the apprehension of smoke.'

children.text:
ity ucyate/ evaṃ ca sati nānābhūtāni viṣayagrāhakāṇi viṣayavyavasthānāt tadbhāve viṣayagrahaṇasya bhāvāt tadupaghāte cābhāvāt, tathā ca pūrvo vāda uttareṇa vādeṇa vyāhanyata iti/
sandigdhaś cāvyatirekaḥ/ pṛthivyādibhir api bhūtair indriyādhiṣṭhānāni vyāptāni, na ca teṣv asatsu viṣayagrahaṇaṃ bhavatīti/ tasmān na tvag anyad vā sarvaviṣayam ekam indriyam iti//53//
children.translated_text: This being so, the graspers of objects are of many kinds, due to the differentiation of objects — because when they exist, the grasping of objects exists, and when they are impaired, it does not. And thus the earlier thesis is contradicted by the later one. Moreover, the non-difference is doubtful, for the locations of sense organs are also pervaded by the elements earth and the like, and without them too, no grasping of objects occurs. Therefore, neither skin nor anything else is a single all-encompassing sense organ. // 53 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 54
Because objects are not apprehended simultaneously. // 3.1.54 //

children.text: ātmā manasā sambadhyate, mana indriyeṇa, indriyaṃ sarvārthaiḥ sannikṛṣṭam iti, ātmendriyamanorthasannikarṣebhyo yugapad grahaṇāni syuḥ/ na ca yugapad rūpādayo gṛhyante tasmān naikam indriyaṃ sarvaviṣayam astīti/ asāhacaryāc ca viṣayagrahaṇānāṃ naikam indriyaṃ sarvaviṣayakam, sāhacarye hi viṣayagrahaṇānām andhādyanupapattir iti//54//
children.translated_text: The self is connected with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ is in contact with all objects — so there should be simultaneous grasping from the contact of self, sense organ, mind, and object. But form and the like are not grasped simultaneously; therefore there is no single sense organ encompassing all objects. And because the graspings of objects do not co-occur, there is no single all-encompassing sense organ, for if they co-occurred, the conditions of blindness and the like would be inexplicable. // 54 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 55
And because of contradiction, skin is not the one [sense organ]. // 3.1.55 //

children.text: na khalu tvag ekam indriyaṃ vyāghātāt — tvacā rūpāṇy aprāptāni gṛhyanta ity aprāpyakāritve sparśādiṣv apy evaṃ prasaṅgaḥ/ sparśādīnāṃ ca prāptānāṃ grahaṇād rūpādīnāṃ prāptānāṃ grahaṇam iti prāptam/
children.translated_text: Skin is indeed not the one sense organ, because of contradiction — if forms not in contact are grasped by the skin, then in the case of touch and the like too, the same consequence of grasping without contact would follow. And since touch and the like are grasped through contact, the grasping of form and the like should also require contact.

children.text: prāpyāprāpyakāritvam iti cet? āvaraṇānupapatter viṣayamātrasya grahaṇam/ athāpi manyeta prāptāḥ sparśādayas tvacā gṛhyante rūpāṇi tv aprāptānīti? evaṃ sati nāsty āvaraṇam, āvaraṇānupapatteś ca rūpamātrasya grahaṇaṃ vyavahitasya cāvyavahitasya ceti/ dūrāntikānuvidhānaṃ ca rūpopalabdhyanupalabdhyor na syāt/ aprāptaṃ tvacā gṛhyate rūpam iti dūre rūpasyāgrahaṇam antike ca grahaṇam ity etan na syād iti//55//
children.translated_text: If [you say it is] by the distinction of acting-upon-contact and acting-without-contact? [We reply:] because obstruction is untenable, only form alone is grasped. Or even if one were to think that touch and the like, being contacted, are grasped by the skin, while forms are grasped without contact — in that case there would be no obstruction, and because obstruction is untenable, form alone would be grasped, both occluded and unoccluded. And the correspondence of the apprehension and non-apprehension of form with distance and proximity would not obtain. If form is grasped by the skin without contact, then the non-grasping of form at a distance and its grasping at proximity — this would not be the case. // 55 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 56

children.text: pratiṣedhāc ca nānātvasiddhau sthāpanāhetur apy upādīyate —
children.translated_text: After the refutation, for the establishment of plurality, a positive reason is also adduced —
Because of the fivefold nature of the objects of the sense organs. // 3.1.56 //

children.text: arthaḥ prayojanam, tat pañcavidham indriyāṇām, sparśanenendriyeṇa sparśagrahaṇe sati na tenaiva rūpaṃ gṛhyata iti rūpagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ cakṣur anumīyate/
children.translated_text: The 'objects' here means purposes; and those are fivefold for the sense organs. When the organ of touch grasps touch, form is not grasped by that same organ — hence the eye is inferred as having the purpose of grasping form.

children.text: sparśarūpagrahaṇe ca tābhyām eva na gandho gṛhyata iti gandhagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ ghrāṇam anumīyate/ trayāṇāṃ grahaṇe na tair eva raso gṛhyata iti rasagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ rasanam anumīyate/ na ca caturṇāṃ grahaṇe tair eva śabdaḥ śrūyata iti śabdagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ śrotram anumīyate/ evam indriyaprayojanasyānitaretarasādhanasādhyatvāt pañcaivendriyāṇi//56//
children.translated_text: And when touch and form are grasped, smell is not grasped by those same [organs] — hence the organ of smell is inferred as having the purpose of grasping smell. When three [qualities] are grasped, taste is not grasped by those same — hence the tongue is inferred as having the purpose of grasping taste. And when four are grasped, sound is not heard by those same — hence the ear is inferred as having the purpose of grasping sound. Thus, since the purposes of the sense organs are not mutually interchangeable as means and ends, the sense organs are five and only five. // 56 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 57
No, because of the multiplicity of those objects. // 3.1.57 //

children.text: na khalv indriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇīti sidhyati/ kasmāt? teṣām arthānāṃ bahutvāt/ bahavaḥ khalv ime indriyārthāḥ, sparśās tāvat śītoṣnānuṣṇāśītā iti/ rūpāṇi śuklaharitādīni/ gandhā iṣṭāniṣṭopekṣaṇīyāḥ/ rasāḥ kaṭukādayaḥ, śabdā varṇātmāno dhvanimātrāś ca bhinnāḥ/ tad yasyendriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇi tasyendriyārthabahutvād bahūni indriyāṇi prasajyanta iti//57//
children.translated_text: It is not established that the sense organs are five merely because the sense-objects are fivefold. Why? Because those objects are many. These sense-objects are indeed numerous: touches, for instance, are cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold. Forms are white, green, and so on. Smells are pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral. Tastes are pungent and so on. Sounds are of the nature of phonemes, mere noises, and others. Therefore, for one who holds that the sense organs are five because the sense-objects are five, it would follow that the sense organs are many because the sense-objects are many. // 57 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 58
Because there is no differentiation of smell-ness and the like, there is no denial of smell and the rest. // 3.1.58 //

children.text: gandhatvādibhiḥ svasāmānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthānāṃ gandhādīnāṃ yāni gandhādigrahaṇāni tāny asamānasādhanasādhyatvād grāhakāntarāṇi na prayojayanti/ arthasamūho 'numānamukto nārthaikadeśaḥ/
children.translated_text: The grasping of smell and the rest — which are established in their respective categories by their own universals such as smell-ness — does not require different sense organs, since they are not mutually different as means and ends. It is the totality of objects that is freed from inference, not a part of the objects.

children.text:
arthaikadeśaṃ cāśritya viṣayapañcatvamātraṃ bhavān pratiṣedhati tasmād ayukto 'yaṃ pratiṣedha iti/
kathaṃ punar gandhatvādibhiḥ svasāmānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthā gandhādaya iti? sparśaḥ khalv ayaṃ trividhaḥ śīta uṣṇo 'nuṣṇāśītaś ca sparśatvena svasāmānyena saṃgṛhītaḥ/ gṛhyamāṇe ca śītasparśe noṣṇasyānuṣṇāśītasya vā sparśasya grahaṇaṃ grāhakāntaraṃ prayojayati sparśabhedānām ekasādhanasādhyatvād yenaiva śītasparśo gṛhyate tenaivetarāv apīti/ evaṃ gandhatvena gandhānām, rūpatvena rūpāṇām, rasatvena rasānām, śabdatvena śabdānām iti/ gandhādigrahaṇāni punar asamānasādhanasādhyatvād grāhakāntarāṇāṃ prayojakāni/ tasmād upapannam indriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇīti//58//
children.translated_text:
And you deny merely the fivefold nature of objects by resorting to a part of the objects — therefore this denial is improper.
But how are smell and the rest established in their respective categories by their own universals such as smell-ness? Touch is of three kinds — cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold — and is unified by its own universal, touch-ness. And when cold touch is grasped, the non-grasping of hot or neither-hot-nor-cold touch does not require a different sense organ, since the varieties of touch are mutually interchangeable as means and ends — for that by which cold touch is grasped, by that very same the other two are also grasped. Likewise, smells [are unified] by smell-ness, forms by form-ness, tastes by taste-ness, sounds by sound-ness. However, the grasping of smell and the rest [of different categories], since they are not mutually interchangeable as means and ends, does require different sense organs. Therefore, it is established that the sense organs are five because the objects of the sense organs are fivefold. // 58 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 59
If the universal is what unifies, then it follows for the sense organs —
There would be oneness, because there is no differentiation of object-ness. // 3.1.59 //

children.text: viṣayatvena hi sāmānyena gandhādayaḥ saṅgṛhītā iti//59//
children.translated_text: For smell and the rest are unified by the universal 'object-ness.' // 59 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 60
No, because of the fivefold nature of cognition-as-mark, locus, mode-of-operation, form, and origin. // 3.1.60 //

children.text:
na khalu viṣayatvena sāmānyena kṛtavyavasthā viṣayā grāhakāntaranirapekṣā ekasādhanagrāhyā anumīyante, anumīyante ca pañca gandhādayo gandhatvādibhiḥ svasāmānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthā indriyāntaragrāhyāḥ, tasmād asambaddham etat/ ayam eva cārtho 'nūdyate buddhilakṣaṇapañcatvād iti/
buddhaya eva lakṣaṇāni viṣayagrahaṇaliṅgatvāt indriyāṇām, tad etat

children.translated_text: already been commented upon in the <s>sūtra</s> 'because of the fivefold nature of the objects of the sense organs.'

children.text: ity etasmin sūtre kṛtabhāṣyam iti/ tasmād buddhilakṣaṇapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇi/
children.translated_text: Therefore, the sense organs are five because of the fivefold nature of cognitions-as-marks.

Objects that are established in their categories by the universal 'object-ness' are not inferred as graspable by a single sense organ without regard for different sense organs; rather, the five — smell and the rest — are inferred as established in their categories by their own universals such as smell-ness and as graspable by different sense organs. Therefore this [objection] is irrelevant. This very meaning is restated [by the phrase] 'because of the fivefold nature of cognition-as-mark.'
Cognitions themselves are the marks — since they serve as the inferential signs of the sense organs through their character of grasping objects. This has

children.text:
adhiṣṭhānāny api khalu pañcendriyāṇām, sarvaśarīrādhiṣṭhānaṃ sparśanaṃ sparśagrahaṇaliṅgam, kṛṣṇasārādhiṣṭhānaṃ cakṣuḥ bahirniḥsṛtaṃ rūpagrahaṇaliṅgam, nāsādhiṣṭhānaṃ ghrāṇam, jihvādhiṣṭhānaṃ rasanam, karṇacchidrādhiṣṭhānaṃ śrotram, gandharasarūpasparśaśabdagrahaṇaliṅgatvād iti/
gatibhedād apīndriyabhedaḥ/ kṛṣṇasāropanibaddhaṃ cakṣur bahirniḥsṛtya rūpādhikaraṇāni dravyāṇi prāpnoti/ sparśanādīni tv indriyāṇi viṣayā evāśrayopasarpaṇāt pratyāsīdanti/ santānavṛttyā śabdasya śrotrapratyāsattir iti/
ākṛtiḥ khalu parimāṇam iyattā sā pañcadhā/ svasthānamātrāṇi ghrāṇarasanasparśanāni viṣayagrahaṇenānumeyāni/ cakṣuḥ kṛṣṇasārāśrayaṃ bahirniḥsṛtaṃ viṣayavyāpi/ śrotraṃ nānyad ākāśāt, tac ca vibhu śabdamātrānubhavānumeyaṃ puruṣasaṃskāropagrahaṇāc cādhiṣṭhānaniyamena śabdasya vyañjakam iti/
children.translated_text:
The loci too of the five sense organs [are distinct]: the organ of touch, indicated by the grasping of touch, has the entire body as its locus; the eye, indicated by the grasping of form, has the pupil as its locus and extends outward; the organ of smell has the nose as its locus; the tongue has the tongue as its locus; the ear has the ear-cavity as its locus — since these are indicated by the grasping of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound respectively.
From the difference in mode-of-operation also, there is a difference of sense organs. The eye, bound to the pupil, extends outward and reaches the substances that are the substrata of form. The organs of touch and the rest, however — the objects themselves approach [them] because of the proximity of the support. The proximity of sound to the ear is through the continuous propagation [of sound].
Form (<s>ākṛti</s>) here means magnitude or extent, and it is fivefold. The organs of smell, taste, and touch are confined to their own locations and are to be inferred from object-grasping. The eye, based in the pupil, extends outward and pervades its objects. The ear is nothing other than <s>ākāśa</s> (space) — it is all-pervasive and is to be inferred from the experience of all sounds; and because it receives the impressions of the person, it manifests sound according to the restriction of its locus.

children.text: jātir iti yoniṃ pracakṣate/ pañca khalv indriyayonayaḥ pṛthivyādīni bhūtāni, tasmāt prakṛtipañcatvād api pañcendriyāṇīti siddham//60//
children.translated_text: Origin (<s>jāti</s>) here refers to the source. The five sources of the sense organs are the five elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) beginning with earth. Therefore, from the fivefold nature of their material sources too, it is established that the sense organs are five. // 60 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 61
But how is it known that the sense organs have the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) as their material source and not the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest [of Sāṅkhya])?
Because of the apprehension of specific elemental qualities, [the sense organs] are identical [with the elements]. // 3.1.61 //

children.text: dṛṣṭo hi vāyvādīnāṃ bhūtānāṃ guṇaviśeṣābhivyaktiniyamaḥ/ vāyuḥ sparśavyañjakaḥ, āpo rasavyañjikāḥ, tejo rūpavyañjakam, pārthivaṃ kiñcid dravyaṃ kasyacid dravyasya gandhavyañjakam/ asti cāyam indriyāṇāṃ bhūtaguṇaviśeṣopalabdhiniyamaḥ tena bhūtaguṇaviśeṣopalabdher manyāmahe bhūtaprakṛtīnīndriyāṇi nāvyaktaprakṛtīnīti//61//
children.translated_text: For a fixed rule is observed in the manifestation of the specific qualities of the elements such as wind and the rest. Wind manifests touch; water manifests taste; fire manifests form; a certain earthy substance manifests the smell of some [other] substance. And there is this fixed rule that sense organs apprehend specific elemental qualities. Therefore, from the apprehension of specific elemental qualities, we hold that the sense organs have the elements as their material source, not the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest). // 61 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 62

children.text: gandhādayaḥ pṛthivyādiguṇā ity uddiṣṭam uddeśaś ca pṛthivyādīnām ekaguṇatve cānekaguṇatve ca samāna ity ata āha —
children.translated_text: It has been stated that smell and the rest are qualities of earth and the rest. And the enumeration of earth and the rest is the same whether they have one quality or many qualities — therefore he says —
Of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound, earth has [all five] up to and including touch. // 3.1.62 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 63
Of water, fire, and wind, [each has the qualities] by removing the preceding ones; and space has the last one. // 3.1.63 //

children.text: sparśaparyantānām iti vibhaktivipariṇāmaḥ/ ākāśasyottaraḥ śabdaḥ sparśaparyantebhya iti/
children.translated_text: 'Up to and including touch' — this involves a change of case-ending. 'Space has the last one' — that is, sound, after those up to and including touch.

children.text: kathaṃ tarhi tarabnirdeśaḥ? svatantraviniyogasāmarthyāt/ tenottaraśabdasya parārthābhidhānaṃ vijñāyate/ uddeśasūtre hi sparśaparyantebhyaḥ paraḥ śabda iti/ tantraṃ vā sparśasya vivakṣitatvāt — sparśaparyanteṣu niyukteṣu yo 'nyas taduttaraḥ śabda iti//62-63//
children.translated_text: How then is the comparative reference [to be explained]? By the power of the independent syntactic construction. Thus the word 'last' (<s>uttara</s>) is understood as referring to the other. For in the enumeration <s>sūtra</s>, the meaning is: 'sound is beyond those ending with touch.' Or, the syntactic construction [is explained by the fact that] touch is what is intended to be expressed — when those ending with touch are assigned, what is different from them, that is the last one, namely sound. // 62-63 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 64
No, because not all qualities are apprehended. // 3.1.64 //

children.text: nāyaṃ guṇaniyogaḥ sādhuḥ/ kasmāt? yasya bhūtasya ye guṇā na te tadātmakenendriyeṇa sarve upalabhyante/ pārthivena hi ghrāṇena sparśaparyantā na gṛhyante gandha eva eko gṛhyate evaṃ śeṣeṣv apīti//64//
children.translated_text: This assignment of qualities is not correct. Why? Because the qualities that belong to an element are not all apprehended by the sense organ that is of the same nature as that element. For by the earthen organ of smell, the [qualities] up to and including touch are not grasped — only smell alone is grasped. The same applies to the rest. // 64 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 65
How then should these qualities be assigned?
Because of the successive presence of additional qualities one by one, [there is] non-apprehension of those [additional qualities] by the successively [higher elements]. // 3.1.65 //

children.text: gandhādīnām ekaiko yathākramaṃ pṛthivyādīnām ekaikasya guṇaḥ, ataḥ

children.translated_text: 'the non-apprehension of those' —
the non-apprehension of those, of those two, and of that one —
Of smell and the rest, each one in order is a quality of each one of earth and the rest. Therefore,

children.text:
ghrāṇena rasarūpasparśānāṃ rasanena rūpasparśayoḥ cakṣuṣā sparśasyeti/
kathaṃ tarhy anekaguṇāni bhūtāni gṛhyanta iti?
saṃsargāc cānekaguṇagrahaṇam/ abādisaṃsargāc ca pṛthivyāṃ rasādayo gṛhyante evaṃ śeṣeṣv apīti//65//
children.translated_text:
by the organ of smell, of taste, form, and touch; by the tongue, of form and touch; by the eye, of touch.
But how then are elements with many qualities grasped?
And the grasping of many qualities is through combination. Through combination with water and the rest, taste and the other [qualities] are grasped in earth; and the same applies to the rest. // 65 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 66

children.text: niyamas tarhi na prāpnoti saṃsargasyāniyamāt caturguṇā pṛthivī triguṇā āpo dviguṇaṃ teja ekaguṇo vāyur iti/ niyamaś copapadyate/ katham?
children.translated_text: Then no fixed rule would follow, since there is no fixed rule of combination — 'earth has four qualities, water three, fire two, wind one.' But a fixed rule is indeed tenable. How?
For the preceding [element] is pervaded by each successive one. // 3.1.66 //

children.text: pṛthivyādīnāṃ pūrvapūrvam uttareṇottareṇa viṣṭam ataḥ saṃsarganiyama iti/ tac caitad bhūtasṛṣṭau veditavyaṃ naitarhīti//66//
children.translated_text: Of earth and the rest, each preceding one is pervaded by each successive one — hence the fixed rule of combination. And this is to be understood [as applying] at the time of the creation of the elements, not at present. // 66 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 67
No, because of the perceptibility of earthen and watery [substances]. // 3.1.67 //

children.text: neti trisūtrīṃ pratyācaṣṭe/ kasmāt? pārthivasya dravyasyāpy asya ca pratyakṣaṭvāt/ mahatvānekadravyatvād rūpāc copalabdhir iti taijasam eva dravyaṃ pratyakṣaṃ syāt na pārthivam āpyaṃ vā rūpābhāvāt/ taijasavat tu pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt na saṃsargād anekaguṇagrahaṇaṃ bhūtānām iti/ bhūtāntararūpakṛtaṃ ca pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvaṃ bruvataḥ pratyakṣo vāyuḥ prasajyate niyame vā kāraṇam ucyatām iti/
children.translated_text: 'No' — he rejects the [preceding] three <s>sūtras</s>. Why? Because earthen and watery substances are perceptible. Since apprehension is [said to be] due to magnitude, multi-substanceness, and form — only fiery substances would be perceptible, not earthen or watery ones, since they [supposedly] lack [their own] form. But since earthen and watery substances are perceptible just like fiery ones, the grasping of many qualities of the elements is not due to combination. And for one who maintains that the perceptibility of earthen and watery substances is due to the form of another element, the consequence would be that wind too is perceptible — or let a reason be stated for the restriction.

children.text:
rasayor vā pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt — pārthivo rasaḥ ṣaḍvidhaḥ, āpyo madhura eva; na caitat saṃsargād bhavtitum arhati/ rūpayor vā pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt taijasarūpānugṛhītayoḥ, saṃsarge hi vyañjakam eva rūpaṃ na vyaṅgyam astīti/ ekānekavidhatve ca pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvād rūpayoḥ/ pārthivaṃ haritalohitapītādyanekavidhaṃ rūpam, āpyaṃ tu śuklam aprakāśakam, na caitad ekaguṇānāṃ saṃsarge saty upapadyata iti/ udāharaṇamātraṃ caitat, ataḥ paraṃ prapañcaḥ /
sparśayor vā pārthivataijasayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt/ pārthivo 'nuṣnāśītaḥ sparśaḥ, uṣṇas taijasaḥ pratyakṣaḥ, na caitad ekaguṇānām anuṣṇāśītasparśena vāyunā saṃsargeṇopapadyata iti/
atha vā pārthivāpyayor dravyayor vyvasthitaguṇayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt/ caturguṇaṃ pārthivaṃ dravyaṃ triguṇam āpyaṃ pratyakṣam, tena tatkāraṇam anumīyate tathābhūtam iti/ tasya kāryaṃ liṅgaṃ kāraṇabhāvād dhi kāryabhāva iti/ evaṃ taijasavāyavyayor dravyayoḥ pratyakṣatvād guṇavyavasthāyāḥ tatkāraṇe dravye vyavasthānumānam iti/
dṛṣṭaś ca vivekaḥ pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt/ pārthivaṃ dravyam abādibhir viyuktaṃ pratyakṣato gṛhyate,
children.translated_text:
Or, from the perceptibility of the tastes of earthen and watery [substances] — earthen taste is of six kinds, while watery taste is sweet alone; and this cannot be due to combination. Or, from the perceptibility of the forms of earthen and watery [substances], which are assisted by fiery form — for in combination, only the manifesting form exists, not the manifested. And from the perceptibility of the forms of earthen and watery substances being single and manifold — earthen form is manifold, being green, red, yellow, and so on, while watery form is white and non-luminous, and this is not tenable when single-qualitied [elements] are combined. This is merely an illustration; beyond this is elaboration.
Or, from the perceptibility of the touches of earthen and fiery [substances] — earthen touch is neither-hot-nor-cold, while fiery touch is hot and perceptible, and this is not tenable through combination with wind, which has neither-hot-nor-cold touch.
Alternatively, from the perceptibility of earthen and watery substances as having established [multiple] qualities — earthen substance has four qualities and watery substance has three qualities and they are perceptible; thereby their cause is inferred to be of the same nature, for the nature of the effect is due to the nature of the cause. Similarly, from the perceptibility of fiery and aerial substances, the establishment of qualities in their causal substances is inferred.
And differentiation is observed from the perceptibility of earthen and watery [substances] — an earthen substance is perceived as separate from water and the rest,

children.text: āpyaṃ ca parābhyām, taijasaṃ ca vāyunā, na caikaikaguṇaṃ gṛhyata iti/ niranumānaṃ tu
children.translated_text: and a watery substance [as separate] from the other two, and a fiery substance [as separate] from wind — and none is perceived as having only a single quality. But without inference,
'the preceding [element] is pervaded by each successive one'

children.text:
ity etad iti/ nātra liṅgam anumāpakaṃ gṛhyata iti yenaitad evaṃ pratipadyemahi/
yac coktaṃ viṣṭaṃ hy aparaṃ pareṇeti bhūtasṛṣṭau veditavyaṃ na sāmpratam iti niyamakāraṇābhāvād ayuktam/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca sāmpratam aparaṃ pareṇa viṣṭam iti, vāyunā ca viṣṭaṃ teja iti/ viṣṭatvaṃ saṃyogaḥ, sa ca dvayoḥ samānaḥ, vāyunā ca viṣṭatvāt sparśavat tejo na tu tejasā viṣṭatvād rūpavān vāyur iti niyamakāraṇaṃ nāstīti/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca taijasena sparśena vāyavyasya sparśasyābhibhavād agrahaṇam iti, na ca tenaiva tasyābhibhava iti//67//
children.translated_text: — thus. No inferential mark is grasped here by which we would ascertain this. And what was said — 'for one is pervaded by another' should be understood with reference to the creation of elements, not to the present state — this is untenable because there is no reason for such restriction. And we observe in the present that one is pervaded by another — fire is pervaded by wind. 'Pervadedness' means conjunction, and that is the same for both [pairs]. And there is no reason for the restriction that fire has touch because it is pervaded by wind, but wind does not have form because it is pervaded by fire. And we observe that the touch of wind is not grasped due to being overwhelmed by the touch of fire — but it does not follow that the latter is overwhelmed by the former. // 67 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 68
'because not all qualities are apprehended'
— the objection raised [earlier] is now resolved:
Having thus refuted the view that contradicts reason,
Because of the superiority of each preceding quality, that [sense-organ] has that [quality] as predominant. // 3.1.68 //

children.text:
tasmān na sarvaguṇopalabdhiḥ, ghrāṇādīnāṃ pūrvaṃ pūrvaṃ gandhāder guṇasyotkarṣāt tat tat pradhānam/ kā pradhānatā? viṣayagrāhakatvam/ ko guṇotkarṣaḥ? abhivyaktau samarthatvam/ yathā bāhyānāṃ pārthivāpyataijasānāṃ dravyāṇāṃ caturguṇatriguṇadviguṇānāṃ na sarvaguṇavyañjakatvaṃ gandharasarūpotkarṣāt tu yathākramaṃ gandharasarūpavyañjakatvam,
% bāhyānāṃ ...]

evaṃ ghrāṇa rasanacakṣuṣā.ṃ caturguṇatriguṇadviguṇānāṃ na sarvaguṇagrāhakatvam, gandharasarūpotkarṣāt tu yathākramaṃ gandharasarūpagrāhakatvam/ tasmād ghrāṇādibhir na sarveṣāṃ guṇānām upalabdhir iti/
yas tu pratijānīte gandhaguṇatvād ghrāṇaṃ gandhasya grāhakam evaṃ rasanādiṣv apīti, tasya yathāguṇayogaṃ ghrāṇādibhir guṇagrahaṇaṃ prasajyata iti//68//
children.translated_text: so too the nose, tongue, and eye, having four, three, and two qualities [respectively], do not grasp all qualities, but because of the superiority of odor, taste, and form [respectively], they grasp odor, taste, and form in that order. Therefore, not all qualities are apprehended by the nose and the rest. But one who claims that the nose grasps odor because it possesses the quality of odor, and similarly for the tongue and the rest — for such a person, the grasping of qualities by the nose and the rest in accordance with [all] their qualities would follow. // 68 //

Therefore, not all qualities are apprehended. For the nose and the rest, each preceding quality — odor and so forth — being superior, that [quality] is predominant for that [sense-organ]. What is predominance? The capacity to grasp its [specific] object. What is the superiority of a quality? The capacity for manifestation. Just as external substances — earthy, watery, and fiery — having four, three, and two qualities [respectively], do not manifest all qualities, but because of the superiority of odor, taste, and form [respectively], they manifest odor, taste, and form in that order;
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 69

children.text: kiṃkṛtaṃ punar vyavasthānam — kiñcit pārthivam indriyaṃ na sarvāṇi, kānicid āpyataijasavāyavyāni indriyāṇi na sarvāṇīti?
children.translated_text: What then determines the arrangement — that a certain sense-organ is earthy but not all of them, and that certain sense-organs are watery, fiery, or airy but not all of them?
That arrangement, however, is due to preponderance. // 3.1.69 //

children.text: arthanirvṛttisamarthasya pravibhaktasya dravyasya saṃsargaḥ puruṣasaṃskārakārito bhūyastvam/ dṛṣṭo hi prakarṣe bhūyastvaśabdaḥ, yathā prakṛṣṭo viṣayo bhūyān ity ucyate/ yathā pṛthagarthakriyāsamarthāni puruṣasaṃskāravaśād viṣauṣadhimaṇiprabhṛtīni dravyāṇi nirvartyante, na sarvaṃ sarvārtham; evaṃ pṛthagviṣayagrahaṇasamarthāni ghrāṇādīni nirvartyante na sarvaviṣayagrahaṇasamarthānīti//69//
children.translated_text: Preponderance is the combination of substance — which is differentiated and capable of producing its purpose — effected by the conditioning of the person (<s>puruṣa</s>). For the word 'preponderance' is observed [to denote] excellence, as when an excellent object is called 'preponderant.' Just as substances such as poisons, medicines, gems, and the like — each capable of distinct functions — are produced through the conditioning of the person and not everything [is produced] for every purpose; so too the nose and the rest, each capable of grasping distinct objects, are produced [through conditioning] and are not capable of grasping all objects. // 69 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 70

children.text: svaguṇān nopalabhanta indriyāṇi/ kasmād iti cet?
children.translated_text: The sense-organs do not apprehend their own qualities. Why?
Because their status as sense-organs exists together with their [own] qualities. // 3.1.70 //

children.text: svān gandhādīn nopalabhante ghrāṇādīni/ kena kāraṇeneti cet? svaguṇaiḥ saha ghrāṇādīnām indriyabhāvāt/ ghrāṇaṃ svena gandhena samānārthakāriṇā saha bāhyaṃ gandhaṃ gṛhṇāti tasya svagandhagrahaṇaṃ sahakārivaikalyān na bhavati, evaṃ śeṣāṇām api//70//
children.translated_text: The nose and the rest do not apprehend their own odors and the like. For what reason? Because the status of the nose and the rest as sense-organs exists together with their own qualities. The nose, together with its own odor which acts as a co-operative cause, grasps external odor; the grasping of its own odor does not occur due to the absence of a co-operative cause. The same applies to the rest. // 70 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 71

children.text: yadi punar gandhaḥ sahakārī ca syād ghrāṇasya grāhyaś cety ata āha —
children.translated_text: But if odor were both a co-operative cause of the nose and also to be grasped [by it], therefore he says —
And because of the non-grasping of that by that very [sense-organ]. // 3.1.71 //

children.text: na guṇopalabdhir indriyāṇām/ yo brūte — yathā bāhyaṃ dravyaṃ cakṣuṣā (corr.; cakṣaṣā, ed.) gṛhyate tathā tenaiva cakṣuṣā tad eva cakṣur gṛhyatām iti, tādṛṅ idam; tulyo hy ubhayatra pratipattihetvabhāva iti//71//
children.translated_text: The sense-organs do not apprehend their own qualities. One who says — 'just as an external substance is grasped by the eye, so let that very eye be grasped by that same eye' — this is of the same kind, for in both cases there is equally an absence of a reason for apprehension. // 71 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 72
No, because the quality of sound is apprehended [by its own sense-organ]. // 3.1.72 //

children.text: svaguṇān nopalabhanta indriyāṇīti etan na bhavati/ upalabhyate hi svaguṇaḥ śabdaḥ śrotreṇeti//72//
children.translated_text: 'The sense-organs do not apprehend their own qualities' — this does not hold. For the ear apprehends sound, which is its own quality. // 72 //
Chapter 3, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 73
That apprehension [of sound by the ear is possible] because of the dissimilarity between the qualities of different substances. // 3.1.73 //

children.text: na śabdena guṇena saguṇam ākāśam indriyaṃ bhavati/ na śabdaḥ śabdasya vyañjakaḥ, na ca ghrāṇādīnāṃ svaguṇagrahaṇaṃ pratyakṣam, nāpy anumīyate/ anumīyate tu śrotreṇākāśena śabdasya grahaṇam, śabdaguṇatvaṃ ca ākāśasyeti/ pariśeṣaś cānumānaṃ veditavyam/ ātmā tāvat śrotā na karaṇam, manasaḥ śrotratve badhiratvābhāvaḥ, pṛthivyādīnāṃ ghrāṇādibhāve sāmarthyam, śrotrabhāve cāsāmarthyam/
children.translated_text: <s>Ākāśa</s> (space), possessing the quality of sound, does not become a sense-organ [merely because of that quality]. Sound does not manifest [another] sound, nor is the grasping of their own qualities by the nose and the rest directly perceived, nor is it inferred. But it is inferred that the ear, being <s>ākāśa</s>, grasps sound, and that <s>ākāśa</s> possesses the quality of sound. And this [inference] should be understood as a process of elimination. The <s>ātman</s> (self) is the hearer, not the instrument; if <s>manas</s> (mind) were the ear, deafness would not exist; earth and the rest have the capacity [to function as] nose and the rest,

children.text: asti cedaṃ śrotram ākāśaṃ ca śiṣyate, pariśeṣād ākāśaṃ śrotram iti//73//
children.translated_text: but not the capacity [to function as] the ear. Since this ear exists and <s>ākāśa</s> remains [as the only candidate], by elimination, <s>ākāśa</s> is the ear. // 73 //
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter in the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> of the venerable <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
Now the second section of the third chapter.
Chapter 3, Section 2
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 1

children.text: parīkṣitānīndriyāṇy arthāś ca, buddher idānīṃ parīkṣākramaḥ, sā kim anityā nityā veti/ kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ?
children.translated_text: The sense-organs and objects have been examined. Now comes the order of examination of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect/cognition) — is it impermanent or permanent? Whence the doubt?
The doubt arises from the similarity [of buddhi] with <s>karma</s> (action) and <s>ākāśa</s> (space). // 3.2.1 //

children.text: asparśavattvaṃ tābhyāṃ samāno dharma upalabhyate buddhau, viśeṣaś copajanāpāyadharmavattvam, viparyayaś ca yathāsvam anityanityayos tasyāṃ buddau nopalabhyate, tena saṃśaya iti//1//
children.translated_text: The common property of being intangible is observed in <s>buddhi</s> in common with both [action and space]; the distinguishing feature is the possession of the property of arising and passing away; and the converse [permanence] — in that <s>buddhi</s>, the [distinguishing properties] of the impermanent and the permanent respectively are not [clearly] observed. Hence the doubt. // 1 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 2

children.text: anupapannarūpaḥ khalv ayaṃ saṃśayaḥ/ sarvaśarīriṇāṃ hi pratyātmavedanīyā anityā buddhiḥ sukhādivat/
children.translated_text: This doubt is, however, ill-formed. For <s>buddhi</s> is impermanent, being individually experienceable by every embodied being, like pleasure and the like.

children.text:
bhavati ca saṃvittiḥ — jñāsyāmi jānāmi ajñāsiṣam iti/ na copajanāpāyāv antareṇa traikālyavyāktiḥ, tataś ca traikālyavyakter anityā buddhir ity etat śiddham/ pramāṇasiddhaṃ cedaṃ śāstare 'py uktam — `indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam', `yugapaj jñānānutpattir manaso liṅgam ityevamādi/ tasmāt saṃśayaprakriyānupapattir iti/
dṛṣṭipravādopālambhārthan tu prakaraṇam/ evaṃ hi paśyantaḥ pravadanti sāṅkhyāḥ — puruṣasyāntaḥkaraṇabhūtā nityā buddhir iti/ sādhanaṃ ca pracakṣate —
children.translated_text: And there is awareness: 'I shall know,' 'I know,' 'I knew.' And the three-time manifestation is not possible without arising and passing away; and from the three-time manifestation, it is established that <s>buddhi</s> is impermanent. And this, being established by <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), is also stated in the <s>śāstra</s> — 'arising from the contact of sense-organ and object,' 'the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of <s>manas</s>' — and so on. Therefore, the formulation of the doubt is untenable. However, this section is for the purpose of criticizing the views of other schools. For the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s>, holding this view, declare: '<s>Buddhi</s> (intellect), being the inner instrument of <s>puruṣa</s> (the conscious self), is permanent.' And they cite the proof —
Because of the recognition of objects. // 3.2.2 //

children.text: kiṃ punar idaṃ pratyabhijñānam? yaṃ pūrvam ajñāsiṣam arthaṃ tam imaṃ jānāmīti jñānyoḥ samāne 'rthe pratisandhijñānaṃ pratyabhijñānam, etac cāvasthitāyā buddher upapannam/ nānātve tu buddhibhedeṣūtpannāpavargiṣu pratyabhijñānānupapattiḥ nānyajñātam anyaḥ pratyabhijānātīti//2//
children.translated_text: What then is this recognition? 'The object that I previously knew — I now know this same one' — this connective cognition regarding the same object between [two] cognitions is recognition. And this is tenable for a <s>buddhi</s> that persists. But if <s>buddhi</s> were manifold — cognitions arising and perishing — recognition would be untenable, for one [cognition] does not recognize what was known by another. // 2 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 3
[This is] not a [valid] reason, because it is on a par with what is to be proved. // 3.2.3 //

children.text: yathā khalu nityatvaṃ buddheḥ sādhyam evaṃ pratyabhijñānam apīti/ kiṃ kāraṇam? cetanadharmasya karaṇe 'nupapattiḥ/ puruṣadharmaḥ khalv ayaṃ jñānaṃ darśanam upalabdhir bodhaḥ pratyayaḥ adhyavasāya iti/
children.translated_text: Just as the permanence of <s>buddhi</s> is what is to be proved, so too is recognition. For what reason? Because a property of consciousness is untenable in an instrument. Cognition, seeing, apprehension, awareness, understanding, ascertainment — these are properties of <s>puruṣa</s> (the conscious self).

children.text:
cetano hi pūrvajñātam arthaṃ pratyabhijānāti, tasyaitasmād dhetor nityatvaṃ yuktam iti/ karaṇacaitanyābhyupagame tu cetanasvarūpaṃ vacanīyaṃ nānirdiṣṭasvarūpam ātmāntaraṃ śakyam astīti pratipattum/ jñānaṃ ced buddher antaḥkaraṇasyābhyupagamyate cetanasyedānīṃ kiṃ svarūpaṃ ko dharmaḥ kiṃ tattvam? jñānena ca buddhau vartamānenāyaṃ cetanaḥ kiṃ karotīti?
cetayate iti cet na, jñānād arthāntaravacanam — puruṣaś cetayate buddhir jānātīti nedaṃ jñānād arthāntaram ucyate, cetayate jānīte buddhyate paśyati upalabhate ity eko 'yam artha iti/ buddhir jñpayatīti cet addhā — jānīte puruṣo buddhir jñāpayatīti satyam etat/ evaṃ cābhyupagame jñānaṃ puruṣasyeti siddhaṃ bhavati na buddher antaḥkaraṇasyeti/
children.translated_text: For it is the conscious being who recognizes a previously known object — for this being, permanence is justified on this ground. But if consciousness is attributed to the instrument [buddhi], then the nature of the conscious [puruṣa] must be specified; for one cannot ascertain that another <s>ātman</s> (self) of unspecified nature exists. If cognition is attributed to <s>buddhi</s>, the inner instrument, then what is the nature, what is the property, what is the essence of the conscious being? And what does this conscious being do when cognition resides in <s>buddhi</s>? If [you say] 'it is conscious' — no, for that would be stating something other than cognition. 'The <s>puruṣa</s> is conscious, <s>buddhi</s> knows' — this does not state something other than cognition; 'is conscious,' 'knows,' 'cognizes,' 'sees,' 'apprehends' — this is one and the same meaning. If [you say] '<s>buddhi</s> causes to know' — indeed, 'the <s>puruṣa</s> knows, <s>buddhi</s> causes to know' — this is true. And with such an admission, it becomes established that cognition belongs to the <s>puruṣa</s>, not to <s>buddhi</s> the inner instrument.

children.text:
pratipuruṣaṃ ca śabdāntaravyavasthāpratijñāne pratiṣedhahetuvacanam/ yaś ca pratijānīte — kaścit puruṣaś cetayate, kaścid buddhyate, kaścid upalabhate, kaścit paśyatīti; puruṣāntarāṇi khalv imāni cetano boddhopalabdhā draṣṭeti naikasyaite dharmā iti atra kaḥ pratiṣedhahetur iti?
arthasyābheda iti cet samānam/ abhinnārthā ete śabdā iti tatra vyavasthānupapattir ity evaṃ cen manyase, samānaṃ bhavati — puruṣaś cetayate buddhir jānīte ity atrāpy artho na bhidyate tatrobhayoś cetanatvād anyataralopa iti/ yadi punar budhyate 'nayeti bodhanaṃ buddhiḥ mana evocyate tac ca nityam,
children.translated_text: And the statement of the reason for refuting the thesis that different terms are established for each <s>puruṣa</s>. And one who claims — 'one <s>puruṣa</s> is conscious, another cognizes, another apprehends, another sees; these are indeed different puruṣas — the conscious one, the cognizer, the apprehender, the seer — these are not properties of a single one' — what is the reason for refuting this? If [you say] 'because of the non-difference of meaning' — the same [applies to your position]. If you think that the untenable arrangement [of different terms] is because these words have undifferentiated meaning, then the same applies: in 'the <s>puruṣa</s> is conscious' and '<s>buddhi</s> knows,' the meaning is not different either — since both would be conscious, one of the two should be eliminated. But if <s>buddhi</s> means 'that by which one understands' — namely, the means of understanding — that is just <s>manas</s> (mind), and that is permanent,

children.text: astv etad evam, na tu manaso viṣayapratyabhijñānān nityatvam/ dṛṣṭaṃ hi karaṇabhede jñātur ekatvāt pratyabhijñānaṃ `savyadṛṣṭasyetareṇa pratyabhijñānād' iti/
children.translated_text: let this be so; but the permanence of <s>manas</s> does not follow from the recognition of objects. For it is observed that recognition occurs due to the unity of the knower even when the instrument is different — 'from the recognition of what was seen by one [eye] by the other.'

children.text: cakṣurvat pradīpavac ca; pradīpāntaradṛṣṭasya pradīpāntareṇa pratyabhijñānam iti/ tasmāj jñātur ayaṃ nityatve hetur iti//3//
children.translated_text: Like the eye, and like a lamp: what was seen by one lamp is recognized by another lamp. Therefore, this [recognition] is a reason for the permanence of the knower. // 3 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 4

children.text: yac ca manyate buddher avasthitāyā yathāviṣayaṃ vṛttayo jñānāni niścaranti vṛttiś ca vṛttimato nānyeti, tac ca —
children.translated_text: And the view that from the persisting <s>buddhi</s>, cognitions — modifications [of buddhi] — proceed according to their objects, and that a modification is not different from that which has modifications — this too [is refuted]:
No, because of the non-grasping of [all objects] simultaneously. // 3.2.4 //

children.text: vṛttivṛttimator ananyatve vṛttimato 'vasthānād vṛttīnām avasthānam iti yānīmāni viṣayagrahaṇāni tāny avatiṣṭanta iti yugapad viṣayāṇāṃ grahaṇaṃ prasajyata iti//4//
children.translated_text: If the modification is not different from that which has modifications, then due to the persistence of that which has modifications, the modifications too would persist — and thus the grasping of objects, being [always present], would result in the simultaneous grasping of objects. // 4 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
And in the absence of recognition, the consequence of destruction. // 3.2.5 //

children.text: atīte ca pratyabhijñāne vṛttimān apy atīta ity antaḥkaraṇasya vināśaḥ prasajyate, viparyaye ca nānātvam iti//5//
children.translated_text: And when recognition has passed, that which has modifications has also passed — thus the consequence would be the destruction of the inner instrument; and in the converse case, [the consequence would be] multiplicity. // 5 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 6

children.text: avibhu caikaṃ manaḥ paryāyeṇendriyaiḥ saṃyujyata iti —
children.translated_text: And the single, non-pervading <s>manas</s> (mind) conjoins with the sense-organs in succession —
Because of its successive functioning, grasping is non-simultaneous. // 3.2.6 //
[This applies to] sense-organs and objects, and the modification and that which has modifications are different.
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 7
And non-recognition is due to engagement with another object. // 3.2.7 //

children.text: apratyabhijñānam anupalabdhiḥ/ anupalabdhiś ca kasyācid arthasya viṣayāntaravyāsakte manasy upapadyate vṛttivṛttimator nānātvāt, ekatve hi anarthako vyāsaṅga iti//7//
children.translated_text: Non-recognition is non-apprehension. And the non-apprehension of some object is tenable when the mind is engaged with another object, because the modification and that which has modifications are different. For if they were identical, the engagement [with another object] would be purposeless. // 7 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
And if the inner instrument were pervading, its conjunction with the sense-organs in succession [is challenged] —
No, because of the absence of motion. // 3.2.8 //

children.text: prāptānīndriyāṇy antaḥkaraṇeneti prāptyarthasya gamanasyābhāvaḥ/ tatra kramavṛttitvābhāvād ayugapad grahaṇānupapattir iti/
children.translated_text: [If the inner instrument were all-pervading,] the sense-organs would already be reached by the inner instrument — hence there would be an absence of movement for the purpose of reaching [them]. And in that case, because of the absence of successive functioning, the non-simultaneous grasping [of objects] would be untenable.

children.text: gatyabhāvāc ca pratiṣiddhaṃ vibhuno 'ntaḥkaraṇasyāyugapadgrahaṇaṃ na liṅgāntareṇānumīyate iti/ yathā cakṣuṣo gatiḥ pratiṣiddhā sannikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭayos tulyakālagrahaṇāt pāṇicandramasor vyavadhānena pratīghāte so'numīyata iti so 'yaṃ nāntaḥ karaṇe vivādo na tasya nityatve/
children.translated_text: And since motion is impossible, the non-simultaneous apprehension of the all-pervading inner instrument is not inferred by any other <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark). Just as motion of the eye is refuted because near and distant objects are grasped at the same time — as for the hand and the moon, obstruction by an intervening object is inferred — so this dispute is not about the inner instrument nor about its eternality.

children.text: siddhaṃ hi mano 'ntaḥkaraṇaṃ nityaṃ ceti/ kva tarhi vivādaḥ? tasya vibhutve, tac ca pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ pratiṣiddham iti/ ekaṃ cāntaḥkaraṇaṃ nānā caitā jñānātmakā vṛttayaḥ, cakṣurvijñānaṃ ghrāṇavijñānaṃ rūpavijñānaṃ gandhavijñānam/ etac ca vṛttivṛttimator ekatve 'nupapannam iti/ puruṣo jānīte nāntaḥkaraṇam iti/ etena viṣayāntaravyāsaṅgaḥ pratyuktaḥ/ viṣayāntaragrahaṇalakṣaṇo viṣayāntaravyāsaṅgaḥ puruṣasya nāntaḥkaraṇasyeti, kenacid indriyeṇa sannidhiḥ kenacid asannidhir ity ayaṃ tu vyāsaṅgo 'nujñāyate manasa iti//8//
children.translated_text: For it is established that <s>manas</s> (mind) is the inner instrument and is eternal. Where then is the dispute? About its all-pervasiveness — and that is refuted because it is not apprehended by any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). The inner instrument is one, but these cognitive functions are many and of the nature of cognition: visual cognition, olfactory cognition, form-cognition, smell-cognition. And this is impossible if the function and the possessor of the function are identical. It is the <s>puruṣa</s> (self) who knows, not the inner instrument. By this, the objection of engagement with another object is answered: engagement with another object, characterized by the grasping of another object, belongs to the <s>puruṣa</s>, not to the inner instrument. But this kind of engagement — proximity to one sense-organ and non-proximity to another — is conceded as belonging to <s>manas</s>. // 8 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 9

children.text: ekam antaḥkaraṇaṃ nānā vṛttaya iti/ saty abhede vṛtter idam ucyate —
children.translated_text: The inner instrument is one, but the functions are many. Given that there is no difference [in the substance], this is said about the function —
Just as in the case of a crystal, the false apprehension of difference [applies to] the false apprehension of difference in that [cognition]. // 3.2.9 //

children.text: tasyāṃ vṛttau nānātvābhimānaḥ, yathā dravyāntaropahite sphaṭike anyatvābhimāno nīlo lohita iti; evaṃ viṣayāntaropadhānād iti/
children.translated_text: The false apprehension of multiplicity in that function is like the false apprehension of difference in a crystal affected by another substance — 'it is blue,' 'it is red'; similarly, due to the imposition of different objects.

children.text: na hetvabhāvāt/ sphaṭikānyatvābhimānavad ayaṃ jñāneṣu nānātvābhimāno gauṇo na punar gandhādyanyatvābhimānavad iti hetur nāsti hetvabhāvād anupapanna iti/ samāno hetvabhāva iti cet na jñānānāṃ krameṇopajanāpāyadarśanāt — krameṇa hīndriyārtheṣu jñānāny upajāyante cāpayanti ceti dṛśyate/
children.translated_text: No, because of the absence of a reason. The claim that this apprehension of multiplicity in cognitions is figurative, like the false apprehension of difference in a crystal, and not like the apprehension of difference in smell and other [qualities] — for this there is no reason; due to the absence of a reason, it is untenable. If one says the absence of a reason is the same [in both cases] — no, because cognitions are observed to arise and perish in succession;

children.text: tasmād gandhādyanyatvābhimānavad ayaṃ jñāneṣu nānātvābhimāna iti//9//
children.translated_text: for it is observed that cognitions arise and perish successively with respect to sense-objects. Therefore, this apprehension of multiplicity in cognitions is like the apprehension of difference in smell and other qualities. // 9 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 10

children.text: sphaṭikānyatvābhimānavad ity etad amṛṣyamāṇaḥ kṣaṇikavādy āha —
children.translated_text: Not accepting the crystal analogy, the proponent of momentariness says —
Even in a crystal, because of the successive origination [of different instances], and because of the momentariness of particulars, [the analogy] is without basis. // 3.2.10 //

children.text: sphaṭikasyābhedenāvasthitasyopadhānabhedān nānātvābhimāna ity ayam avidyamānahetukaḥ pakṣaḥ/ kasmāt? sphaṭike 'py aparāparotpatteḥ/ sphaṭike 'pi anyā vyaktaya utpadyante anyā nirudhyanta iti/ katham? kṣaṇikatvād vyaktīnām/ kṣaṇaś cālpīyān kālaḥ kṣaṇasthitikāḥ kṣaṇikāḥ/ kathaṃ punar gamyate kṣaṇikā vyaktaya iti? upacayāpacayaprabandhadarśanāc charīrādiṣu/ paktinirvṛttasyāhārarasasya śarīre rudhirādibhāvenopacayo 'pacayaś ca prabandhena pravarttate/ upacayād vyaktīnām utpādaḥ, apacayād vyaktinirodhaḥ/ evaṃ ca saty avayavapariṇāmabhedena vṛddhiḥ śarīrasya kālāntare gṛhyate iti so 'yaṃ vyaktiviśeṣadharmo vyaktimātre veditavya iti//10//
children.translated_text: The position that there is an apprehension of multiplicity in a crystal that persists without difference due to differences in what is superimposed — this is a position without a [valid] reason. Why? Because even in a crystal, different particulars (<s>vyakti</s>) arise and different ones cease. How? Because of the momentariness of particulars. A <s>kṣaṇa</s> (moment) is the smallest unit of time; what lasts for a moment is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>). But how is it known that particulars are momentary? From observing the continuous process of growth and decay in bodies and such things. The nutriment-essence of food, produced by digestion, continuously undergoes growth in the body in the form of blood and the like, and decay. From growth comes the origination of particulars; from decay comes the cessation of particulars. And when this is so, the growth of the body is grasped at a later time through the difference in the transformation of its parts — this property of particular instances should be understood as belonging to all particulars. // 10 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
Because there is no restricting reason, [there should be] acceptance as observed. // 3.2.11 //

children.text: sarvāsu vyaktiṣu upacayāpacayaprabandhaḥ śarīravad iti nāyaṃ niyamaḥ/ kasmāt? hetvabhāvāt/ nātra pratyakṣam anumānaṃ vā pratipādakam astīti/ tasmād yathādarśanam abhyanujñā/ yatra yatropacayāpacayaprabandho dṛśyate, tatra tatra vyaktīnām aparāparotpattir upacayāpacayaprabandhadarśanenābhyanujñāyate,
children.translated_text: That there is a continuous process of growth and decay in all particulars, as in bodies — this restriction does not hold. Why? Because of the absence of a reason. Neither perception nor inference establishes this. Therefore, acceptance should be as observed.

children.text: yathā śarīrādiṣu/ yatra yatra na dṛśyate tatra tatra pratyākhyāyate yathā grāvaprabhṛtiṣu/ sphaṭike 'py upacayāpacayaprabandho na dṛśyate, tasmād ayuktaṃ sphaṭike 'py aparāprotpattir iti/ yathā cārkasya kaṭukimnā sarvadravyāṇāṃ kaṭukimānām āpādayet tādṛg etad iti//11//
children.translated_text: Wherever a continuous process of growth and decay is observed, there the successive origination of particulars is accepted on the basis of observing the process of growth and decay, as in bodies and the like. Wherever it is not observed, there it is rejected, as in stones and such things. In a crystal too, no continuous process of growth and decay is observed; therefore, it is improper to assert successive origination even in a crystal. Just as one should not attribute the bitterness of the <s>arka</s> (sun-plant) to all substances — such is this argument. // 11 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 12

children.text: yaś cāśeṣanirodhenāpūrvotpādaṃ niranvayaṃ dravyasantāne kṣaṇikatāṃ manyate tasyaitat —
children.translated_text: And for one who holds that momentariness consists in complete cessation and novel origination without continuity in the stream of substance, the following applies —
Because a cause of origination and destruction is perceived. // 3.2.12 //

children.text: utpattikāraṇaṃ tāvad upalabhyate avayavopacayo valmīkādīnām, vināśakāraṇaṃ copalabhyate ghaṭādīnām avayavavibhāgaḥ/
children.translated_text: A cause of origination is indeed perceived: the accretion of parts in ant-hills and the like. And a cause of destruction is perceived: the separation of parts in pots and the like.

children.text: yasya tv anapacitāvayavaṃ nirudhyate anupacitāvayavaṃ cotpadyate tasyāśeṣanirodhe niranvaye vāpūrvotpāde na kāraṇam ubhayatrāpy upalabhyate iti//12//
children.translated_text: But for one who holds that something whose parts have not diminished ceases, and something whose parts have not accreted arises — in complete cessation without continuity, or in novel origination, no cause is perceived in either case. // 12 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
That is tenable, like the non-perception of a cause for the destruction of milk, and like the origination of curd. // 3.2.13 //

children.text: yathānupalabhyamānaṃ kṣīravināśakāraṇaṃ dadhyutpattikāraṇaṃ cābhyanujñāyate tathā sphaṭike parāparāsu vyaktiṣu vināśakāraṇam utpādakāraṇaṃ cābhyanujñeyam iti//13//
children.translated_text: Just as the cause of the destruction of milk and the cause of the origination of curd are accepted even though not perceived, so too in the crystal, the cause of destruction and the cause of origination in the successive particulars should be accepted. // 13 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 14
There is no non-perception, because [the cause] is grasped through an inferential mark. // 3.2.14 //

children.text: kṣīravināśaliṅgaṃ kṣīravināśakāraṇaṃ dadhyutpattiliṅgaṃ dadhyutpattikāraṇaṃ ca gṛhyate 'to nānupalabdhiḥ, viparyayas tu sphaṭikādiṣu dravyeṣu aparāparotpattau vyaktīnāṃ na liṅgam astīty anutpattir eveti//14//
children.translated_text: The cause of the destruction of milk is grasped through the inferential mark of milk's destruction, and the cause of the origination of curd is grasped through the inferential mark of curd's origination — therefore there is no non-perception. The opposite holds in the case of crystals and other substances: there is no inferential mark for the successive origination of particulars — hence there is simply non-origination. // 14 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
Here someone offers a defense —
No, because [there is merely] transformation of milk and the manifestation of different qualities. // 3.2.15 //

children.text:
payasaḥ pariṇāmo na vināśa ity eka āha/ pariṇāmaś cāvasthitasya dravyasya pūrvadharmanivṛttau dharmāntarotpattir iti/
guṇāntaraprādurbhāva ity apara āha/ satā dravyasya pūrvaguṇanivṛttau guṇāntaram utpadyata iti/ sa khalv ekapakṣībhāva iva//15//
children.translated_text: One says that there is transformation of milk, not destruction. Transformation is the arising of a different property upon the cessation of a prior property in a substance that persists. Another says there is a manifestation of different qualities — in an existing substance, upon the cessation of prior qualities, a different quality arises. This is indeed as if taking one side. // 15 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 16
But here is the refutation —
The observation that a different substance arises from a different configuration is the inference of the cessation of the prior substance. // 3.2.16 //

children.text: saṃmūrchanalakṣaṇād avayavavyūhād dravyāntare dadhni utpanne gṛhyamāṇe pūrvaṃ payodravyam avayavavibhāgebhyo nivṛttam ity anumīyate, yathā mṛdavayavānāṃ vyūhāntarād dravyāntare sthālyām utpannāyāṃ pūrvaṃ mṛtpiṇḍadravyaṃ mṛdavayavavibhāgebhyo nivarttate iti/ mṛdvac cāvayavānvayaḥ payodadhnor nāśeṣanirodhe niranvayo dravyāntarotpādo ghaṭata iti//16//
children.translated_text: When a different substance, curd, is observed to have arisen from a configuration of parts characterized by coagulation, it is inferred that the prior substance, milk, has ceased due to the separation of its parts — just as when a different substance, a pot, arises from a different configuration of clay-parts, the prior substance, the clay-lump, ceases due to the separation of clay-parts. And as with clay, there is a continuity of parts in milk and curd — the origination of a different substance is not complete cessation without continuity. // 16 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 17

children.text: abhyanujñāya ca niṣkāraṇaṃ kṣīravināśaṃ dadhyutpādaṃ ca pratiṣedha ucyate —
children.translated_text: Having conceded that the destruction of milk and the origination of curd are without a [perceived] cause, the refutation is stated —
Because in some cases the cause of destruction is not perceived and in some cases it is perceived, [the conclusion] is inconclusive. // 3.2.17 //

children.text: kṣīradadhivan niṣkāraṇau vināśotpādau sphaṭikavyaktīnām iti nāyam ekānta iti/ kasmāt? hetvabhāvāt/ nātra hetur asti akāraṇau vināśotpādau sphaṭikādivyaktīnāṃ kṣīradadhivat, na punar yathā vināśakāraṇabhāvāt kumbhasya vināśa utpattikāraṇabhāvāc cotpattiḥ evaṃ sphaṭikādivyaktīnāṃ vināśotpattikāraṇabhāvād vināśotpattibhāva iti/
children.translated_text: The claim that destruction and origination are without cause for the particulars of a crystal, just as for milk and curd — this is not conclusive. Why? Because of the absence of a reason. There is no reason here to establish that destruction and origination of particulars of crystals and the like are without cause, like [those of] milk and curd; and not in the way that destruction of a pot occurs due to the presence of a cause of destruction and origination occurs due to the presence of a cause of origination — so too the destruction and origination of particulars of crystals and the like would occur due to the presence of causes of destruction and origination.

children.text:
niradhiṣṭhānaṃ ca dṛṣṭāntavacanam/ gṛhyamāṇayor vināśotpādayoḥ sphaṭikādiṣu syād ayam āśrayavān dṛṣṭāntaḥ kṣīravināśakāraṇānupalabdhivad dadhyutpattivac ceti, tau tu na gṛhyete/ tasmān niradhiṣṭhāno 'yaṃ dṛṣṭānta iti/
abhyanujñāya ca sphaṭikasyotpādavināśau yo 'tra sādhakas tasyābhyanujñānād apratiṣedhaḥ/ kumbhavan na niṣkāraṇau vināśotpādau sphaṭikādīnām ity anujñeyo 'yaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ pratiṣeddham aśakyatvāt/ kṣīradadhivat tu niṣkāraṇau vināśotpādāv iti śakyo 'yaṃ pratiṣeddhuṃ kāraṇato vināśotpattidarśanāt/ kṣīradadhnor vināśotpattī paśyatā tatkāraṇam anumeyaṃ kāryaliṅgaṃ hi kāraṇam iti//17//
children.translated_text: And the citing of the example has no basis. If destruction and origination were observed in crystals and the like, this example would have a basis — 'like the non-perception of the cause of milk's destruction and like the origination of curd' — but those two are not observed. Therefore this example has no basis. And having conceded destruction and origination in a crystal, the one who establishes this — because of his concession, there is no refutation. One should concede this example — that destruction and origination of crystals and the like are not without cause, like a pot — since it cannot be refuted. But the claim that destruction and origination are without cause, like [those of] milk and curd, can be refuted, because destruction and origination are observed to have causes. One who observes the destruction and origination of milk and curd should infer their cause, for the effect is the inferential mark of the cause. // 17 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 18

children.text: upapannam anityā buddhir iti/ idaṃ tu cintyate kasyeyaṃ buddhir ātmeindriyamano 'rthānāṃ guṇa iti/ prasiddho 'pi khalv ayam arthaḥ parīkaṣāśeṣaṃ pravarttayāmīti prakriyate/ so 'yaṃ buddhau sannikarṣotpatteḥ saṃśayaḥ viśeṣasyāgrahaṇād iti/ tatrāyaṃ viśeṣaḥ
children.translated_text: It is established that cognition is non-eternal. But this is to be considered: of what is this cognition a quality — of the <s>ātman</s> (self), the sense-organs, or <s>manas</s> (mind) and objects? Though this matter is well-known, it is taken up in order to complete the examination. Here then is the doubt, arising from the contact [of each with cognition], due to the non-apprehension of a distinguishing feature. The distinguishing feature here is —
It is not [a quality] of the sense-organs or the objects, because cognition persists even when they are destroyed. // 3.2.18 //

children.text: nendriyāṇām vā guṇo jñānaṃ teṣāṃ vināśo 'pi jñānasya bhāvāt/ bhavati khalv idam indriye 'rthe ca vinaṣṭe jñānam adrākṣam iti/ na ca jñātari vinaṣthe jñānaṃ bhavitum arhati/ anyat khalu vai tad indriyārthasannikarṣajaṃ jñānaṃ yad indriyārthavināśe na bhavati/
children.translated_text: Cognition is not a quality of the sense-organs, because cognition exists even when they are destroyed. For there is cognition even when the sense-organ and the object have perished — 'I saw [it].' And cognition cannot exist when the knower has perished. That cognition which arises from the contact of sense-organ and object is indeed something different — it does not exist when the sense-organ and object are destroyed.

children.text: idam anyad ātmamanaḥsannikarṣajam, tasya yukto bhāva iti/smṛtiḥ khalv iyam adrākṣam iti pūrvadṛṣṭaviṣayā/ na ca vijñātari naṣṭe pūrvopalabdheḥ smaraṇaṃ yuktam, na cānyadṛṣṭam anyaḥ smarati/ na ca manasi jñātary abhyupagamyamāne śakyam indriyārthayor jñātṛtvaṃ pratipādayitum//18//
children.translated_text: This other [cognition] arises from the contact of <s>ātman</s> (self) and <s>manas</s> (mind), and its existence is appropriate. This [cognition] 'I saw' is indeed memory, having a previously seen object as its content. And memory of a previous experience is not appropriate when the knower has perished, nor does one person remember what another has seen.
