And when <s>manas</s> is accepted as the knower, it is not possible to establish that the sense-organs and objects are knowers. // 18 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 19
Let cognition then be a quality of <s>manas</s> —
And because of the non-apprehension of simultaneous objects of knowledge, it is not [a quality] of <s>manas</s>. // 3.2.19 //

children.text: yugapaj jñeyānupalabdhir antaḥkaraṇasya liṅgam, tatra yugapaj jṇeyānupalabdhyā yad anumīyate antaḥkaraṇam, na tasya guṇo jñānam/ kasya tarhi? jñasya vaśitvāt/
children.translated_text: The non-apprehension of simultaneous objects of knowledge is the mark of the inner instrument. The inner instrument that is inferred from the non-simultaneous apprehension of objects of knowledge — cognition is not a quality of that. Of what then? Of the knower, because of his mastery.

children.text: vaśī jñātā vaśyaṃ karaṇam, jñānaguṇatve ca karaṇabhāvanivṛttiḥ/ ghrāṇādisādhanasya ca jñātur gandhādijñānabhāvād anumīyate antaḥkaraṇasādhanasya sukhādijñānaṃ smṛtiś ceti/ tatra yaj jñānaguṇaṃ manaḥ sa ātmā, yat tu sukhādyupalabdhisādhanam antaḥkaraṇaṃ manas tad iti saṃjñābhedamātraṃ nārthabheda iti/
children.translated_text: The knower is the master, the instrument is what is mastered; and if cognition were a quality [of <s>manas</s>], it would lose its status as an instrument. And since the knower who employs the instrument of smell and the like has cognition of smell and other [objects], it is inferred that the knower who employs the inner instrument as instrument has cognition of pleasure and the like, as well as memory. Thus, if <s>manas</s> is that which has cognition as its quality, that is the <s>ātman</s>; and the inner instrument that is the means of apprehending pleasure and the like is <s>manas</s> — this is merely a difference of designation, not a difference of meaning.

children.text: yugapaj jñeyopalabdheś ca yogina iti vā cārthaḥ/ yogī khalu ṛddhau prādurbhūtāyāṃ vikaraṇadharmā nirmāya sendriyāṇi śarīrāntarāṇi teṣu yugapaj jñeyāny upalabhate/ tac caitad vibhau jñātary upapadyate nāṇau manasīti/ vibhutve vā manaso jñānasya nātmaguṇatvapratiṣedhaḥ/ vibhu ca manastadantaḥkaraṇabhūtam iti tasya sarvendriyair yugapat saṃyogād yugapaj jñānāny utpadyerann iti//19//
children.translated_text: Or the meaning is: and because of the <s>yogin</s>'s simultaneous apprehension of objects of knowledge. For a <s>yogin</s>, when supernatural power has manifested, being free of the limitation of instruments, creates other bodies with sense-organs and simultaneously apprehends objects of knowledge in them. And this is tenable for an all-pervading knower, not for an atomic <s>manas</s>. Or even if <s>manas</s> is all-pervading, there is no negation of cognition being a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. If <s>manas</s> is all-pervading and is the inner instrument, then from its simultaneous conjunction with all sense-organs, simultaneous cognitions would arise. // 19 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 20
Even if [cognition is] a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, the same [objection applies]. // 3.2.20 //

children.text: vibhur ātmā sarvendriyaiḥ saṃyukta iti yugapaj jñānotpattiprasaṅga iti//20//
children.translated_text: The <s>ātman</s> is all-pervading and conjoined with all sense-organs — hence the absurd consequence of simultaneous cognitions arising [would apply here too]. // 20 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
Because of the absence of contact of <s>manas</s> with the sense-organs, that [simultaneous cognition] does not arise. // 3.2.21 //

children.text: gandhādyupalabdher indriyārthasannikarṣavad indriyamanaḥsannikarṣo 'pi kāraṇam, tasya cāyaugapadyam aṇutvān manasaḥ/ ayaugapadyād anutpattir yugapaj jñānānām ātmaguṇatve 'pīti//21//
children.translated_text: Just as the contact of sense-organ and object is a cause of the apprehension of odor and the like, so too the contact of sense-organ and <s>manas</s> (mind) is a cause; and its non-simultaneity is due to the atomic nature of <s>manas</s>. Because of non-simultaneity, cognitions do not arise simultaneously, even though they are qualities of the <s>ātman</s> (self). //21//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 22
But if cognition of odor and the like were to arise merely from the contact of <s>ātman</s>, sense-organ, and object?
No, because no cause of [non-simultaneous] origination is indicated. // 3.2.22 //

children.text: ātmendriyasannikarṣamātrād gandhādijñānam utpadyate iti, nātrotpattikāraṇam apadiśyate yenaitat pratipadyemahīti//22//
children.translated_text: If cognition of odor and the like arises merely from the contact of <s>ātman</s> and sense-organ, then no cause of origination [that would prevent simultaneity] is being indicated here, by which we could understand this. //22//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 23
And because no cause of destruction is perceived, if they persist, the consequence would be their eternality. // 3.2.23 //
'Even if [cognitions] are qualities of the <s>ātman</s>, it is the same [objection]' —

children.text: ity etad anena samuccīyate/ dvividho hi guṇanāśahetuḥ, guṇānām āśrayābhāvo virodhī ca guṇaḥ/ nityatvād ātmano 'nupapannaḥ pūrvaḥ, virodhī ca buddher guṇo na gṛhyate — tasmād ātmaguṇatve sati buddher nityatvaprasaṅgaḥ//23//
children.translated_text: this is what is added by this [sūtra]. For the cause of the destruction of a quality is twofold: the destruction of the substratum of the qualities, or an opposing quality. The former is inapplicable because of the eternality of the <s>ātman</s>; and no quality opposing <s>buddhi</s> (cognition) is apprehended. Therefore, if cognition is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, the consequence would be that cognition is eternal. //23//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
Because cognition is apprehended as non-eternal, its destruction is by another cognition, like sound. // 3.2.24 //

children.text: anityā buddhir iti sarvaśarīriṇāṃ pratyātmavedanīyam etat/ gṛhyate ca buddhisantānaḥ tatra buddher buddhyantaraṃ virodhī guṇa ity anumīyate yathā śabdasantāne śabdaḥ śabdāntaravirodhīti//24//
children.translated_text: That cognition is non-eternal — this is something to be known by every embodied being in their own experience. And the continuity of cognitions is apprehended; in that [continuity], it is inferred that a subsequent cognition is the opposing quality [that destroys] the preceding cognition — just as in the continuity of sounds, a [subsequent] sound is opposed to the preceding one. //24//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 25

children.text: asaṅkhyeyeṣu jñānakāriteṣu saṃskāreṣu smṛtihetuṣv ātmasamaveteṣv ātmamanasoś ca sannikarṣe samāne smṛtihetau sati na kāraṇasyāyaugapadyam astīti yugapat smṛtayaḥ prādurbhaveyuḥ yadi buddhir ātmaguṇaḥ syād iti/ tatra kaścit sannikarṣasyāyaugapadyam upapādayiṣyann āha —
children.translated_text: When there are innumerable <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) produced by cognitions, which are the causes of memory, and which are inherent in the <s>ātman</s>, and when the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is the same as the cause of memory — since there is no non-simultaneity of the cause, memories should arise simultaneously, if cognition were a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. In this regard, someone wishing to establish the non-simultaneity of the contact says —
<s>Manas</s> makes contact with the regions of the <s>ātman</s> in which cognition inheres; from this arises memory; therefore there is no simultaneous arising. // 3.2.25 //

children.text: jñānasādhanaḥ saṃskāro jñānam ity ucyate jñānasaṃskṛtair ātmapradeśaiḥ paryāyeṇa manaḥ sannikṛṣyate/ ātmamanaḥsannikarṣāt smṛtayo 'pi paryāyeṇa bhavantīti//25//
children.translated_text: The <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression), being the means of cognition, is called 'cognition'; <s>manas</s> makes contact successively with the regions of the <s>ātman</s> imprinted by cognitions. From the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, memories too arise successively. //25//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 26
No, because <s>manas</s> operates within the body. // 3.2.26 //

children.text: sadehasyātmano manasā saṃyogo vipacyamānakarmāśayasahito jīvanam iṣyate/ tatrāsya prāk prāyaṇād antaḥśarīre vartamānasya manasaḥ śarīrād bahirjñānasaṃskṛtair ātmapradeśaiḥ saṃyogo nopapadyata iti//26//
children.translated_text: The conjunction of <s>manas</s> with the <s>ātman</s> of one who possesses a body, together with the ripening store of <s>karma</s>, is accepted as constituting life. In that case, for <s>manas</s>, which prior to death operates within the body, conjunction with the regions of the <s>ātman</s> imprinted by cognitions that are outside the body is untenable. //26//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
Because it is what is to be proved, it is not a valid reason. // 3.2.27 //

children.text: vipacyamānakarmāśayamātraṃ jīvanam, evaṃ ca sati sādhyam antaḥśarīravṛttitvaṃ manasa iti//27//
children.translated_text: That life consists merely in the ripening store of <s>karma</s> — if so, then the claim that <s>manas</s> operates within the body is what is to be proved. //27//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
Because the maintenance of the body while remembering is tenable, there is no refutation. // 3.2.28 //

children.text: susmūrṣayā khalv ayaṃ manaḥ praṇidadhānaś cirād api kaṃcid arthaṃ smarati, smarataś ca śarīradhāraṇaṃ dṛśyate/ ātmamanaḥsannikarṣajaś ca prayatno dvividhaḥ — dhārakaḥ prerakaś ca, niḥsṛte ca śarīrād bahir manāsi dhārakasya prayatnasyābhāvād gurutvāt patanaṃ syāt śarīrasya smarata iti//28//0
children.translated_text: One who concentrates his <s>manas</s> with the desire to remember eventually recalls some object, and while remembering, the maintenance of the body is observed. And the effort arising from the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is twofold — sustaining (<s>dhāraka</s>) and impelling (<s>preraka</s>). If <s>manas</s> were to go outside the body, due to the absence of sustaining effort and due to the heaviness [of the body], the body of one who is remembering would fall. //28//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 29
No, because of the swiftness of <s>manas</s>. // 3.2.29 //

children.text: āśugati manaḥ tasya bahiḥśarīrātmapradeśena jñānasaṃskṛtena sannikarṣaḥ, pratyāgatasya ca prayatnotpādanam ubhayaṃ yujyata iti/ utpādya vā dhārakaṃ prayatnaṃ śarīrān niḥsaraṇaṃ manasaḥ, atas tatropapannaṃ dhāraṇam iti//29//
children.translated_text: <s>Manas</s> is swift; its contact with a region of the <s>ātman</s> outside the body that is imprinted by cognition, and its generation of effort upon returning — both are possible. Alternatively, having generated the sustaining effort, <s>manas</s> may then leave the body; hence the maintenance [of the body] there is tenable. //29//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
No, because the time of remembering is not fixed. // 3.2.30 //

children.text:
kiñcit kṣipraṃ smaryate kiñcic cireṇa/ yadā cireṇa, tadā susmūrṣayā manasi dhāryamāṇe cintāprabandhe sati kasyacid arthasya liṅgabhūtasya cintanam ārādhitaṃ smṛtihetur bhavati/ tatraitac ciraniścarite manasi nopapadyata iti/
śarīrasaṃyogānapekṣaś cātmamanaḥsaṃyogo na smṛtihetuḥ śarīrasya bhogāyatanatvāt/
children.translated_text:
Some things are remembered quickly, others after a long time. When [it takes] a long time, with <s>manas</s> being held by the desire to remember, and with a continuous stream of thought, the thinking about some object that serves as a mark becomes perfected and becomes the cause of memory. In that case, this is untenable if <s>manas</s> has long departed [from the body].
And the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> without dependence on conjunction with the body is not the cause of memory, because the body is the locus of experience.

children.text: upabhogāyatanaṃ puruṣasya jñātuḥ śarīraṃ na tato niścaritasya manasa ātmasaṃyogamātraṃ jñānasukhādīnām utpattau kalpate, kḷptau vā śarīravaiyarthyam iti//30//
children.translated_text: The body is the locus of experience for the knower, the <s>puruṣa</s> (person); the mere conjunction of <s>manas</s>, having departed from it, with the <s>ātman</s> cannot account for the arising of cognition, pleasure, and the like. And if it could, the body would be purposeless. //30//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 31
And because [the theory cannot explain] the specific conjunction through the impulsion by the <s>ātman</s>, by chance, or by the sentience [of <s>manas</s>]. // 3.2.31 //

children.text: ātmapreraṇena vā manaso bahiḥ śarīrāt saṃyogaviśeṣaḥ syāt, yadṛcchayā vā, ākasmikatayā jñatayā vā manasaḥ? sarvathā cānupapattiḥ/ katham? smartavyatvāt, icchātaḥ smaraṇāj jñānāsambhavāc ca/ yadi tāvad ātmā amuṣyārthasya smṛtihetuḥ saṃskāraḥ amuṣminn ātmadeśe samavetas tena manaḥ saṃyujyatām iti manaḥ prerayati tadā smṛta evāsāv artho bhavati na smartavyaḥ/ na cātmapratyakṣa ātmapradeśaḥ saṃskāro vā, tatrānupapannātmapratyakṣeṇa saṃvittir iti/ susmūrṣayā cāyaṃ manaḥ praṇidadhānaś cirād api kañcid arthaṃ smarati nākasmāt, jñatvaṃ ca manaso nāsti jñānapratiṣedhād iti//31//
children.translated_text: Would the specific conjunction of <s>manas</s> outside the body be through impulsion by the <s>ātman</s>, by chance — i.e., accidentally — or by the sentience of <s>manas</s>? In every case, it is untenable. How? Because [the object] must be [first] remembered [to direct manas to its location], because remembering is by volition, and because cognition is impossible [for manas itself]. If the <s>ātman</s> were to impel <s>manas</s> — 'let <s>manas</s> be conjoined with that region of the <s>ātman</s> where the impression, the cause of memory of that object, inheres' — then that object would already be remembered, not something yet to be remembered. And the regions of the <s>ātman</s> and the <s>saṃskāras</s> are not directly perceived by the <s>ātman</s>; therefore, awareness through direct perception of the <s>ātman</s> — which is untenable — cannot [guide this process]. And one who concentrates his <s>manas</s> with the desire to remember eventually recalls some object — not by accident. And <s>manas</s> does not possess sentience, because cognition has been denied [for it]. //31//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 32
And this —
[Is] the same as the specific conjunction [required to explain] the pain in the foot of one whose <s>manas</s> is absorbed [elsewhere]. // 3.2.32 //

children.text:
yadā khalv ayaṃ vyāsaktamanāḥ kvacid deśe śarkarayā kaṇṭakena vā pādavyathanam āpnoti tadā ātmamanaḥ saṃyogaviśeṣa eṣitavyaḥ, dṛṣṭaṃ hi duḥkhaṃ duḥkhavedanaṃ ceti/ tatrāyaṃ samānaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ yadṛcchayā tu na viśeṣo nākasmikī kriyā nākasmikaḥ saṃyoga iti/
karmādṛṣṭam upabhogārthaṃ kriyāhetur iti cet samānam/ karmādṛṣṭaṃ puruṣasthaṃ puruṣopabhogārthaṃ manasi kriyāhetuḥ evaṃ duḥkhaṃ duḥkhasaṃvedanaṃ ca sidhyatīty evaṃ cen manyase, samānam — smṛtihetāv api saṃyogaviśeṣo bhavitum arhati/ tatra yad uktam

children.translated_text: 'because [the theory cannot explain] the specific conjunction through the impulsion by the <s>ātman</s>, by chance, or by the sentience [of manas]'

children.text: ity ayam apratiṣedha iti/ pūrvas tu pratiṣedho
children.translated_text: — this is not a [valid] refutation. But the earlier refutation —
'because <s>manas</s> operates within the body'

When one whose <s>manas</s> is absorbed somewhere steps on a pebble or thorn and experiences pain in the foot, a specific conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> must be sought — for suffering and the awareness of suffering are observed. In this regard, the same refutation applies. Nor does the specific [conjunction come about] by chance — for there is no accidental action and no accidental conjunction.
If [one says] <s>karma-adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit/demerit), which is for the purpose of experience, is the cause of the action [of manas] — [the reply is:] it is the same. If you think that <s>karma-adṛṣṭa</s>, residing in the person and intended for the person's experience, is the cause of action in <s>manas</s>, and that thus both suffering and the awareness of suffering are established — then it is the same: a specific conjunction should be possible also for the cause of memory. In that case, the statement
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 33

children.text: kaḥ khalv idānīṃ kāraṇayaugapadyasadbhāve yugapad asmaraṇasya hetur iti?
children.translated_text: What then, when the causal conditions are simultaneously present, is the reason for not remembering simultaneously?
Because attention (<s>praṇidhāna</s>), cognition of marks (<s>liṅga</s>), and the like do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous remembering. // 3.2.33 //

children.text: yathā khalv ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣaḥ saṃskāraś ca smṛtihetur evaṃ praṇidhānaṃ liṅgādijñānāni tāni ca na yugapadbhavanti tatkṛtā smṛtīnāṃ yugapad anutpattir iti/ pratibhavat tu praṇidhānādyanapekṣe smārte yaugapadyaprasaṅgaḥ/ yat khalv idaṃ prātibham iva jñānaṃ praṇidhānādyanapekṣaṃ smārttam utpadyate kadācit tasya yugapadutpattiprasaṅgo hetvabhāvāt/ sataḥ smṛtihetor asaṃvedanāt prātibhena samānābhimānaḥ/ bahvarthaviṣaye vai cintāprabandhe kaścid evārthaḥ kasyacit smṛtihetuḥ,
children.translated_text: Just as the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> and the <s>saṃskāra</s> are the causes of memory, so too are attention, cognition of marks, and the like; and these do not arise simultaneously — hence the non-simultaneous arising of memories caused by them. But with regard to spontaneous (<s>prātibha</s>) memory that does not depend on attention and the like, there would be the consequence of simultaneity. For that memory-based cognition which sometimes arises like spontaneous knowledge, without depending on attention and the like — there would be the consequence of simultaneous arising, due to the absence of a [restricting] reason. [This is explained:] Because the cause of memory exists but is not ascertained [by the rememberer], there is the impression of similarity with spontaneous [knowledge]. Indeed, in a stream of thought about many objects, some particular object becomes the cause of the memory of some other object;

children.text:
tasyānucintanāt tasya smṛtir bhavati/ na cāyaṃ smartā sarvaṃ smṛtihetuṃ saṃvedayate evaṃ me smṛtir utpanneti/ asaṃvedanāt prātibham iva jñānam idaṃ smārtam iti abhimanyate, na tv asti praṇidhānādyanapekṣaṃ smārtam iti/
prātibhe katham iti cet puruṣakarmaviśeṣād upabhogavan niyamaḥ/ prātibham idānīṃ jñānaṃ yugapat kasmān notpadyate? yathopabhogārthaṃ karma yugapadupabhogaṃ na karoti evaṃ puruṣakarmaviśeṣaḥ pratibhāhetur na yugapad anekaṃ prātibhaṃ jñānam utpādayati/
hetvabhāvād ayuktam iti cet, na karaṇasya pratyayaparyāye sāmarthyāt/
children.translated_text:
from continuously thinking about that, the memory of that [other object] arises. And this rememberer does not ascertain every cause of memory as 'thus has my memory arisen.' Because of this non-ascertainment, one regards this memory-based cognition as if it were spontaneous knowledge — but there is in fact no memory-based cognition that is independent of attention and the like.
If [one asks] how about spontaneous [knowledge] — by the specific <s>karma</s> of the person, the regularity is like that of experience. Why then does spontaneous knowledge not arise simultaneously? Just as <s>karma</s> for the purpose of experience does not cause simultaneous experience, so too the specific <s>karma</s> of a person, being the cause of intuition, does not produce multiple spontaneous cognitions simultaneously.
If [one says] this is unreasonable because of the absence of a reason — no, because of the capacity of the instrument in the sequence of cognitions.
'The regularity is like that of experience' —

children.text: ity asti dṛṣṭānto hetur nāstīti cen manyase? na, karaṇasya pratyayaparyāye sāmarthyāt/ naikasmin jñeye yugapad anekaṃ jñānam utpadyate, na cānekasmin/ tad idaṃ dṛṣṭena pratyayaparyāyeṇānumeyaṃ karaṇasāmarthyam itthambhūtam iti na jñātuḥ vikaraṇadharmaṇo dehanānātve pratyayayaugapadyād iti/
children.translated_text: if you think: there is an example but no reason? No, because of the capacity of the instrument in the sequence of cognitions. Not multiple cognitions arise simultaneously regarding one object of knowledge, nor regarding many. This capacity of the instrument, being of such a nature, is to be inferred from the observed sequence of cognitions — [and this holds] not [just] because of the non-simultaneity of cognition in the different bodies of the knower who lacks the instruments [to cognize simultaneously].

children.text: ayaṃ ca dvitīyaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, avasthitaśarīrasya cānekajñānasamavāyād ekapradeśe yugapad anekārthasmaraṇaṃ syāt/ kvacid deśe 'vasthitaśarīrasya jñātur indriyārthaprabandhena jñānam anekam ekasminn ātmapradeśe samavaiti/ tena yadā manaḥ saṃyujyate tadā jñātapūrvasyānekasya yugapat smaraṇaṃ prasajyate pradeśasaṃyogaparyāyābhāvād iti/ ātmapradeśānām adravyāntaratvād ekārthasamavāyasyāviśeṣe sati smṛtiyaugapadyapratiṣedhānupapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: And this is a second refutation: since for a knower whose body is stationary, many cognitions inhere in one region [of the ātman], there should be the simultaneous remembering of many objects at one location. For a knower whose body is stationed at some location, many cognitions inhere in one region of the <s>ātman</s> through the stream of sense-objects. When <s>manas</s> conjoins with that [region], the simultaneous remembering of many previously known [objects] would follow, because there is no sequence of conjunction with [different] regions. Since the regions of the <s>ātman</s> are not distinct substances, and since there is no distinction in the inherence of one object [per region], the refutation of the simultaneity of memories is untenable.

children.text: śabdasantāne tu śrotrādhiṣṭhānapratyāsattyā śabdaśravaṇavat saṃskārapratyāsattyā manasaḥ smṛtyutpatter na yugapad utpattiprasaṅgaḥ/ pūrva eva tu pratiṣedho nānekajñānasamavāyād ekapradeśe yugapat smṛtiprasaṅga iti//33//
children.translated_text: But in the continuity of sounds, just as hearing a sound depends on proximity to the substrate of the ear, so too the arising of memory from <s>manas</s> depends on proximity to the <s>saṃskāra</s> — hence there is no consequence of simultaneous arising. But the earlier refutation stands: there is no consequence of simultaneous memory from the inherence of many cognitions in one region. //33//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 34

children.text: puruṣadharmo jñānam antaḥkaraṇasyecchādveṣaprayatnasukhaduḥkhāni dharmā iti kasyacid darśanam, tat pratiṣidhyate —
children.translated_text: The view of some is that cognition is a property of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person), while desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and suffering are properties of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). This is refuted —
Because desire and aversion are the reasons for undertaking and ceasing, [they belong to] the knower. // 3.2.34 //

children.text: ayaṃ khalu jānāti tāvad idaṃ me sukhasādhanam idaṃ me duḥkhasādhanam iti jñātvā svasya sukhasādhanam āptum icchati, duḥkhasādhanaṃ hātum icchati, prāptīcchāprayuktasyāsya sukhasādhanāvāptaye samīhāviśeṣa ārambhaḥ, jihāsāprayuktasya duḥkhasādhanaparivarjanaṃ nivṛttiḥ, evaṃ jñānecchāprayatnadveṣasukhaduḥkhānām ekenābhisambandhaḥ/ ekakartṛkatvaṃ jñānecchāpravṛttīnāṃ samānāśrayatvaṃ ca/ tasmāj jñasyecchādveṣaprayatnasukhaduḥkhāni dharmā nācetanasyeti/ ārambhanivṛttyoś ca pratyagātmani dṛṣṭatvāt paratrānumānaṃ veditavyam iti//34//
children.translated_text: This [being] first knows: 'this is a means to my pleasure, this is a means to my suffering.' Having known, he desires to obtain what is a means to his own pleasure, and desires to abandon what is a means to suffering. For one impelled by the desire to obtain, the specific exertion for acquiring the means to pleasure is undertaking (<s>ārambha</s>); for one impelled by the desire to avoid, the abandoning of the means to suffering is cessation (<s>nivṛtti</s>). Thus, cognition, desire, effort, aversion, pleasure, and suffering are connected in one [entity]. The agency of cognition, desire, and activity is one, and the substratum is the same. Therefore, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and suffering are properties of the knower, not of something non-sentient. And since undertaking and ceasing are observed in one's own self, inference regarding others is to be understood. //34//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 35
Here, the proponent of consciousness arising from the elements (<s>bhūtacaitanyavādin</s>) says —
Because [bodies made of] earth and the like bear those marks [of desire and aversion], the denial [of consciousness in them is refuted]. // 3.2.35 //

children.text: ārambhanivṛttiliṅgāv icchādveṣāv iti yasyārambhanivṛttī tasyecchādveṣau tasya jñānam iti prāptaṃ pārthivāpy ataijasavāyavīyānāṃ śarīrāṇām ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣajñānair yoga iti caitanyam//35//
children.translated_text: Desire and aversion are marked by undertaking and ceasing. One who has undertaking and ceasing has desire and aversion; one who has desire and aversion has cognition — this follows. Since undertaking and ceasing are observed even in bodies made of earth, water, fire, and air, they are endowed with desire, aversion, and cognition — hence [they possess] consciousness. //35//
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 36
Because undertaking and ceasing are observed in axes and the like. // 3.2.36 //

children.text: śarīre caitanyanivṛttiḥ/ ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣajñānair yoga iti prāptaṃ paraśvādeḥ karaṇasyārambhanivṛttidarśanāc caitanyam iti/ atha śarīrasyecchādibhir yogaḥ, paraśvādes tu karaṇasyārambhanivṛttī vyabhicarataḥ, na tarhy ayaṃ hetuḥ pārthivāpy ataijasavāyavīyānāṃ śarīrāṇām ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣajñānair yoga iti/
children.translated_text: The cessation of consciousness in the body [is argued]. Since the arising and cessation of the instrument, namely the axe and the like, is observed, the connection [of the body] with desire, aversion, and cognition is established — thus, from the observed arising and cessation of such instruments, consciousness [would follow]. But if the body has a connection with desire and the like, while the arising and cessation of the instrument, the axe and the like, deviate [from this rule], then this is not a valid reason — for from the observed arising and cessation of earthy, non-fiery, and airy bodies too, the connection with desire, aversion, and cognition [would follow].

children.text:
ayaṃ tarhy anyo 'rthaḥ — talliṅgatvād icchādveṣayoḥ pārthivādyeṣv apratiṣedhaḥ/ pṛthivyādīnāṃ bhūtānām ārambhas tāvat trasasthāvaraśarīreṣu tadavayavavyūhaliṅgaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣaḥ loṣṭādiṣu ca liṅgābhāvāt pravṛttiviśeṣābhāvo nivṛttiḥ/ ārambhanivṛttiliṅgāv icchādveṣāv iti pārthivādyeṣv aṇuṣu taddarśanād icchādveṣayogas tadyogāj jñānayoga iti siddhaṃ bhūtacaitanyam iti/
kumbhādiṣv anupalabdher ahetuḥ/ kumbhādimṛdavayavānāṃ vyūhaliṅgaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣa ārambhaḥ, sikatādiṣu pravṛttiviśeṣābhāvo nivṛttiḥ/ na ca mṛtsikatānām ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣaprayatnajñānair yogaḥ/ tasmāt talliṅgatvād icchādveṣayor ity ahetur iti//36//
children.translated_text: Here then is a different meaning — because they are marks of that [consciousness], desire and aversion are not denied in earthy and other [elements]. The activity of the earthy and other elements, characterized by the arrangement of their parts, is observed as arising in the bodies of mobile and immobile beings — and the absence of such activity in clods of earth and the like, due to the absence of marks, is cessation. Since desire and aversion are the marks of arising and cessation, and since these are observed in the earthy and other atoms, the connection with desire and aversion — and from that, the connection with cognition — is established; thus consciousness of the elements is proved. [Reply:] This is not a valid reason, because it is not observed in pots and the like. The arising of clay-particles in pots and the like is an activity characterized by arrangement of parts; in sand and the like, the absence of such activity is cessation. Yet from the observed arising and cessation of clay and sand, there is no connection with desire, aversion, effort, and cognition. Therefore, 'because they are marks of that, desire and aversion [are not denied in earthy elements]' is not a valid reason. // 36 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
But regularity and irregularity are what distinguish them. // 3.2.37 //

children.text: tayor icchādveṣayor niyamāniyamau viśeṣakau bhedakau/ jñasyecchādveṣanimitte pravṛttinivṛttī na svāśraye/
children.translated_text: Regularity and irregularity are what distinguish — differentiate — those desire and aversion. The arising and cessation caused by the desire and aversion of a knower do not [occur] in his own substratum;

children.text:
kiṃ tarhi? prayojyāśraye/ tatra prayujyamāneṣu bhūteṣu pravṛttinivṛttī staḥ na sarveṣv ity aniyamopapattiḥ/
yasya tu jñatvād bhūtānām icchādveṣanimitte ārambhanivṛttī svāśraye tasya niyamaḥ syāt, yathā bhūtānāṃ guṇāntaranimittā pravṛttir guṇapratibandhāc ca nivṛttir bhūtamātre bhavati niyamena, evaṃ bhūtamātre jñānecchādveṣanimitte pravṛttinivṛttī svāśraye syātām, na tu bhavataḥ tasmāt prayojakāśritā jñānecchādveṣaprayatnāḥ, prayojyāśraye tu pravṛttinivṛttīti siddham/
children.translated_text: rather, [they occur] in the substratum of what is impelled. Among the elements being impelled, arising and cessation occur not in all of them — hence the irregularity is explained. But if, because the elements are knowers, the arising and cessation caused by desire and aversion were in their own substratum, there would be regularity — just as the activity of elements caused by other qualities, and their cessation due to the obstruction of qualities, occurs regularly in all elements. Similarly, the arising and cessation caused by cognition, desire, and aversion would occur in one's own substratum in all elements — but this does not happen. Therefore cognition, desire, aversion, and effort belong to the impeller, while arising and cessation [occur] in the substratum of what is impelled — this is established.

children.text: ekaśarīre tu jñātṛbahutvaṃ niranumānam/ bhūtacaitanikasyaikaśarīre bahūni bhūtāni jñānecchādveṣaprayatnaguṇānīti jñātṛbahutvaṃ prāptam/ om iti bruvataḥ pramāṇaṃ nāsti, yathā nānāśarīreṣu nānā jñātāro buddhyādiguṇavyavasthānāt, evam ekaśarīre 'pi buddhyādivyavasthānumānaṃ syāj jñātṛbahutvasyeti/
children.translated_text: However, the multiplicity of knowers in a single body is without inference. For one who holds that elements are conscious, there are many elements in a single body possessing the qualities of cognition, desire, aversion, and effort — hence a multiplicity of knowers would follow. One who asserts this has no proof; just as in different bodies there are different knowers because of the fixed correspondence of qualities like cognition, so too in a single body, one could infer a multiplicity of knowers from the fixed correspondence of cognition and the like.

children.text:
dṛṣṭaś ca anyaguṇanimittaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣo bhūtānāṃ so 'numānam anyatrāpi/ dṛṣṭaḥ karaṇalakṣaṇeṣu bhūteṣu paraśvādiṣu upādānalakṣaṇeṣu ca mṛtprabhṛtiṣv anyaguṇanimittaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣaḥ/ so 'numānam anyatrāpi trasasthāvaraśarīreṣu/ tadavayavavyūhaliṅgaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣo bhūtānām anyaguṇanimitta iti/ sa ca guṇaḥ prayatnasamānāśrayaḥ saṃskāro dharmādharmasamākhyātaḥ sarvārthaḥ puruṣārthārādhanāya prayojako bhūtānāṃ prayatnavad iti/
ātmāstitvahetubhir ātmanityatvahetubhiś ca bhūtacaitanyapratiṣedhaḥ kṛto veditavyaḥ/
children.translated_text: And an activity of elements caused by a different quality is observed — that serves as an inference for other cases too. In elements characterized as instruments, such as axes and the like, and in elements characterized as material causes, such as clay and the rest, an activity caused by a different quality is observed. That serves as an inference for other cases too — in the bodies of mobile and immobile beings. The activity of elements, marked by the arrangement of their parts, is caused by a different quality. And that quality, which shares the same substratum as effort, is the <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional tendency) called <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), which serves all purposes and impels the elements to serve the purposes of the <s>puruṣa</s> (self), just as effort does. The refutation of consciousness of elements should be understood as accomplished by the reasons for the existence of the <s>ātman</s> (self) and the reasons for the eternality of the <s>ātman</s>.
'Because cognition persists even when the sense-organ and its object are destroyed' —

children.text: iti ca samānaḥ pratiṣedha iti/ kriyāmātraṃ kriyoparamamātraṃ cārambhanivṛttī ity abhipretyoktam
children.translated_text: this refutation too is the same. It is stated with the understanding that arising and cessation are merely activity and the cessation of activity:
'Because they are marks of that, desire and aversion are not denied in earthy and other [elements].'

children.text: / anyathā tv ime ārambhanivṛttī ākhyāte, na ca tathāvidhe pṛthivyādiṣu dṛśyete/ tasmād ayuktam
children.translated_text: But arising and cessation have been described differently [here], and such [arising and cessation] are not observed in earth and the like. Therefore it is untenable [to say]:
'Because they are marks of that, desire and aversion are not denied in earthy and other [elements].'
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 38
The refutation applies equally to elements, sense-organs, and <s>manas</s> (mind); <s>manas</s> is merely cited as an example.

children.text: yathoktahetutvāt pāratantryād akṛtābhyāgamāc ca na manasaḥ // 3.2.38 //
children.translated_text: Because of the reasons already stated, because of dependence, and because of the unwanted consequence of reaping what one has not sown — [consciousness does] not [belong to] <s>manas</s> (mind). // 3.2.38 //
'Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, suffering, and cognition are the marks of the <s>ātman</s> (self)' —

children.text:
ity ataḥ prabhṛti yathoktaṃ saṅgṛhyate, tena bhūtendriyamanasāṃ caitanyapratiṣedhaḥ/
pāratantryāt — paratantrāṇi bhūtendriyamanāṃsi dhāraṇapreraṇavyūhanakriyāsu prayatnavaśāt pravarttante, caitanye punaḥ svatantrāṇi syur iti/
children.translated_text: from this point onward, what has been stated is summarized, and by that, the consciousness of elements, sense-organs, and <s>manas</s> is refuted. Because of dependence — elements, sense-organs, and <s>manas</s> are dependent; they function in the activities of sustaining, impelling, and arranging under the control of effort. But if they were conscious, they would be independent.
And because of the unwanted consequence of reaping what one has not sown —
'Activity is the initiation of speech, mind, and body' —

children.text: iti caitanye bhūtendriyamanasāṃ parakṛtaṃ karma puruṣeṇopabhujyata iti syāt, acaitanye tu tatsādhanasya svakṛtakarmaphalopabhogaḥ puruṣasyety upapadyata iti//38//
children.translated_text: if elements, sense-organs, and <s>manas</s> were conscious, then <s>karma</s> (action) performed by another would be experienced by the <s>puruṣa</s> (self). But if they are not conscious, the <s>puruṣa</s>'s experience of the fruits of <s>karma</s> done by himself through his own instruments is tenable. // 38 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 39
Now, this is the summary of what has been established —
By elimination, and because the reasons already stated are valid. // 3.2.39 //

children.text: ātmaguṇo jñānam iti prakṛtam/ pariśeṣo nāma

children.translated_text: 'When there is a general negation and the application [of the negation] does not hold in a remaining case, there is certainty regarding that remainder.'

children.text:
/ bhūtendriyamanasāṃ pratiṣedhe dravyāntaraṃ na prasajyate śiṣyate cātmā tasya guṇo jñānam iti jñāyate/
yathoktahetūpapatteś ceti
children.translated_text: When elements, sense-organs, and <s>manas</s> are eliminated [as substrata of cognition], no other substance is applicable; the <s>ātman</s> remains, and cognition is known as its quality. 'And because the reasons already stated are valid' —
'Because there is the grasping of one and the same object through sight and touch' —

children.text:
ityevamādīnām ātmapratipattihetūnām apratiṣedhād iti/ pariśeṣajñāpanārthaṃ prakṛtasthāpanādijñānārthaṃ ca yathoktahetūpapattivacanam iti/
atha vā upapatteś ceti hetvantaram evedam/ nityaḥ khalv ayam ātmā, yasmād ekasmin śarīre dharmaṃ caritvā kāyasya bhedāt svarge deveṣūpapadyate, adharmaṃ caritvā dehabhedāt narakeṣūpapadyata iti/ upapattiḥ śarīrāntaraprāptilakṣaṇā, sā sati sattve nitye cāśrayavatī, buddhiprabandhamātre tu nirātmake nirāśrayā nopapadyata iti/ ekasattvādhiṣṭhānaś cānekaśarīrayogaḥ saṃsāra upapadyate, śarīraprabandhocchedaś cāpavargo muktir ity upapadyate/ buddhisantatimātre tv ekasattvānupapatter na kaścid dīrgham adhvānaṃ sandhāvati na kaścic charīraprabandhād vimucyata iti saṃsārāpavargānupapattir iti/ buddhisantatimātre ca sattvabhedāt sarvam idaṃ prāṇivyavahārajātam apratisaṃhitam avyāvṛttam apariniṣṭhaṃ ca syāt,
children.translated_text: and so forth: because the reasons for establishing the <s>ātman</s> are not refuted. The statement 'because the reasons already stated are valid' serves both to make known the elimination and to establish the thesis under discussion, etc. Alternatively, 'because of valid [reasoning]' is itself an additional reason. For this <s>ātman</s> is indeed eternal: having practiced <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) in one body, upon the destruction of that body, it is reborn among the gods in heaven; having practiced <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness), upon the destruction of that body, it is reborn in the hells. <s>Upapatti</s> (rebirth), characterized by the attainment of another body, is tenable when there is an existing, eternal substratum; but in a mere succession of cognitions without a self, being without a substratum, it is not tenable. And <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly bondage), as the connection of a single being with many bodies, is tenable; and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), as the cutting off of the succession of bodies — freedom — is tenable. But in a mere succession of cognitions, since a single being cannot be established, no one traverses the long road [of transmigration], and no one is freed from the succession of bodies — hence <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>apavarga</s> would be untenable. And in a mere succession of cognitions, due to the difference of [momentary] existences, all this activity of living beings would be without continuity, without distinction, and without conclusion.
The topic is: cognition is a quality of the <s>ātman</s> (self). Elimination means:

children.text: tataḥ smaraṇābhāvāt nānyadṛṣṭam anyaḥ smaratīti/ smaraṇaṃ ca khalu pūrvajñātasya samānena jñātrā grahaṇam ajñāsiṣam amum arthaṃ jñeyam iti/ so .yam eko jñātā pūrvajñātam arthaṃ gṛhṇāti tac cāsya grahaṇaṃ smaraṇam iti, tad buddhiprabandhamātre nirātmake nopapadyate//39//
children.translated_text: Furthermore, due to the absence of memory, one does not remember what was seen by another. Memory is indeed the grasping by the same knower of what was previously known — 'I did not know this object; it is to be known.' This one knower grasps a previously known object, and that grasping of his is memory — and that is not tenable in a mere succession of cognitions without a self. // 39 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 40
But memory belongs to the <s>ātman</s> (self), because of its nature as a knower. // 3.2.40 //

children.text: upapadyata iti/ ātmana eva smaraṇaṃ na buddhisantatimātrasyeti/ tuśabdo 'vadhāraṇe/ katham? jñasvabhāvatvāt/ jña iti asya svabhāvaḥ svo dharmaḥ/ ayaṃ khalu jñāsyati jānāti ajñāsīd iti trikālaviṣayeṇānekena jñānena sambadhyate,
children.translated_text: [Memory] is tenable [only for the <s>ātman</s>]. Memory belongs to the <s>ātman</s> alone, not to a mere succession of cognitions. The word 'but' is for emphasis. How? Because of its nature as a knower. 'Knower' is its own nature, its own property. This [self] is connected with multiple cognitions pertaining to the three times — 'he will know,' 'he knows,' 'he knew';

children.text: tac cāsya trikālaviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ pratyātmavedanīyaṃ jñāsyāmi jānāmi ajñāsiṣam iti varttate, tad yasyāyaṃ svo dharmas tasya smaraṇaṃ na buddhiprabandhamātrasya nirātmakasyeti//40//
children.translated_text: and this cognition of his pertaining to the three times proceeds as individually experienced — 'I will know,' 'I know,' 'I knew.' That of which this is the own property — to that belongs memory, not to a mere succession of cognitions without a self. // 40 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 41

children.text: smṛtihetūnām ayaugapadyād yugapad asmaraṇam ity uktam/ atha kebhyaḥ smṛtir utpadyata iti? smṛtiḥ khalu —
children.translated_text: It has been stated that due to the non-simultaneity of the causes of memory, there is no simultaneous remembering. Now, from what causes does memory arise? Memory indeed [arises from] —

Attention, binding [association], repetition, mark, distinguishing characteristic, similarity, ownership, substratum-dependent relation, sequence, separation, common effect, opposition, eminence, attainment, intervention, pleasure, suffering, desire, aversion, fear, need, action, passion, <s>dharma</s> (merit), and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — from these [memory arises]. // 3.2.41 //

children.text: susmūrṣayā manaso dhāraṇaṃ praṇidhānaṃ susmūrṣitaliṅgacintanaṃ cārthasmṛtikāraṇam/ nibandhaḥ khalv ekagranthopayamo 'rthānām, ekagranthopayatāḥ khalv arthā anyonyasmṛtihetava ānupūrvyeṇetarathā vā bhavantīti/
children.translated_text: Attention is the fixing of the mind with the desire to remember, and the contemplation of the mark of what one wishes to remember — this is the cause of recollecting the object. Binding is the linking together of objects in a single group; objects linked in a single group become causes of each other's memory, whether in sequence or otherwise.

children.text:
dhāraṇaśāstrakṛto vā prajñāteṣu vastuṣu smartavyānām upanikṣepo nibandha iti/
abhyāsas tu samāne viṣaye jñānānām abhyāvṛttiḥ, abhyāsajanitaḥ saṃskāra ātmaguṇo 'bhyāsaśabdenocyate, sa ca smṛtihetuḥ samāna iti/
liṅgaṃ punaḥ saṃyogi samavāyy ekārthasamavāyi virodhi ceti/ yathā dhūmo 'gneḥ, gor viṣāṇam, pāṇiḥ pādasya, rūpaṃ sparśasya abhūtaṃ bhūtasyeti/
lakṣaṇaṃ paśvavayavasthaṃ gotrasya smṛtihetuḥ, vidānām idaṃ gargāṇām idam iti/ sādṛśyaṃ citragataṃ pratirūpakaṃ devadattasyetyevamādi/ parigrahāt svena vā svāmī svāminā vā svaṃ smaryate/ āśrayād grāmaṇyā tadadhīnaṃ saṃsmarati/ āśritāt tadadhīnena grāmaṇyam iti/ sambandhād antevāsinā yuktaṃ guruṃ smarati, ṛtvijā yājyam iti/
children.translated_text: Or, binding is the depositing of things to be remembered among known entities through the technique of a memory-system. Repetition is the recurrence of cognitions regarding the same object; the <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional imprint), a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, generated by repetition, is denoted by the word 'repetition,' and it too is a cause of memory — the same [principle applies]. A mark is something conjoined, something inherent, something co-inherent with the same thing, or something opposed. For example: smoke [is the mark] of fire; a horn of a cow; the hand of a foot; form of touch; what has not occurred of what has occurred. A distinguishing characteristic — a mark on the limbs of an animal is the cause of remembering its lineage: 'this [mark] belongs to the <s>Vidā</s> family, that to the <s>Garga</s> family.' Similarity — a portrait or likeness recalls <s>Devadatta</s>, and so forth. From ownership, by one's own property the owner is remembered, or by the owner the property. From the substratum, the village headman remembers what is dependent on him. From what is dependent, the one dependent on him [remembers] the headman. From relation, a student remembers his teacher with whom he is associated; a priest remembers his patron.

children.text: ānantaryād iti karaṇīyeṣv artheṣu/ viyogād yena viyujyate tadviyogapratisaṃvedī bhṛśaṃ smarati/ ekakāryāt kartrantaradarśanāt kartrantare smṛtiḥ/ virodhāt, vijigīṣamāṇayor anyataradarśanād anyataraḥ smaryate/ atiśayād yenātiśaya utpāditaḥ/ prāpteḥ yato 'nena kiṃcit prāptam āptavyaṃ vā bhavati tam abhīkṣṇaṃ smarati/ vyavadhānāt kośādibhir asiprabhṛtīni smaryante/
children.translated_text: From sequence — in matters to be done. From separation, one who is separated intensely remembers the one from whom he is separated, experiencing the pain of separation. From a common effect, seeing one agent [of a common task] reminds one of the other agent. From opposition, when two rivals [are involved], seeing one reminds one of the other. From eminence — by one who has produced an extraordinary [impression]. From attainment, one who has obtained or will obtain something from someone remembers that person frequently. From intervention — by sheaths and the like, swords and the like are remembered.

children.text: sukhaduḥkhābhyāṃ taddhetuḥ smaryate/ icchādveṣābhyāṃ yam icchati yaṃ ca dveṣṭi taṃ smarati/ bhayād yato bibheti/ arthitvād yenārthī bhojanenācchādanena vā/ kriyayā rathena rathakāraṃ smarati/ rāgād yasyāṃ striyāṃ rakto bhavati tām abhīkṣṇaṃ smarati/ dharmāj jātyantarasmaraṇam iha cādhītaśrutāvadhāraṇam iti/ adharmāt prāganubhūtaduḥkhasādhanaṃ smarati/ na caiteṣu nimitteṣu yugapat saṃvedanāni bhavantīti yugapad asmaraṇam iti/ nidarśanaṃ cedaṃ smṛtihetūnāṃ na parisaṅkhyānam iti//41//
children.translated_text: From pleasure and suffering, their cause is remembered. From desire and aversion, one remembers the one whom one desires or hates. From fear — that which one fears. From need — that from which one needs food or clothing. From action — by a chariot, one remembers the chariot-maker. From passion — the woman to whom one is attached, one remembers her constantly. From <s>dharma</s> (merit) — the remembering of previous births, and in this life the retention of what has been studied and heard. From <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — one remembers the means of suffering experienced previously. And since the experiences [of these causes] do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous remembering. This is an illustration of the causes of memory, not an exhaustive enumeration. // 41 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 42

children.text: anityāyāṃ ca buddhāv utpannāpavargitvāt kālāntarāvāsthānāc ca anityānāṃ saṃśayaḥ kim utpatpannāpavargiṇī buddhiḥ śabdavat āhosvit kālāntarāvasthāyinī kumbhavad iti/ utpannāpavargiṇīti pakṣaḥ parigṛhyate/kasmāt?
children.translated_text: Since cognition is impermanent, [there is] doubt: does cognition perish once it has arisen, like a sound; or does it persist for a period of time, like a pot? Because it arises and then ceases, and because it persists for a period of time — among impermanent things, the doubt is: which of these two applies to cognition? The position that it perishes once arisen is accepted. Why?
Because an action is grasped as non-persisting. // 3.2.42 //

children.text: karmaṇo 'navasthāyino grahaṇād iti/ kṣiptasyeṣor āpatanāt kriyāsantāno gṛhyate, pratyarthaniyamāc ca buddhīnāṃ kriyāsantānavad buddhisantānoupapattir iti/ avasthitagrahaṇe ca vyavadhīyamānasya pratyakśanivṛtteḥ/ avasthite ca kumbhe gṛhyamāṇe santānenaiva buddhir vartate prāg vyavadhānāt tena vyavahite pratyakṣaṃ jñānaṃ nivartate,
children.translated_text: Because a non-persisting action is grasped — from the flight of a shot arrow, a continuum of action is grasped; and since cognitions are restricted to their respective objects, the occurrence of a cognition-continuum like an action-continuum is tenable. And when a persisting object is grasped, if it becomes obstructed, direct perception ceases — when a persisting pot is being perceived, the cognition proceeds through a continuum until obstruction; when it is obstructed, perceptual cognition ceases.

children.text:
kālāntarāvasthāne tu buddher dṛśyavyavadhāne 'pi pratyakṣam avatiṣṭheteti/
smṛtiś cāliṅgaṃ buddhyavasthāne saṃskārasya buddhijasya smṛtihetutvāt/ yaś ca manyeta avatiṣṭhate buddhiḥ dṛṣṭā hi buddhiviṣaye smṛtiḥ sā ca buddhāv anityāyāṃ kāraṇābhāvān na syād iti/ tad idam aliṅgam/ kasmāt? buddhijo hi saṃskāro guṇāntaraṃ smṛtihetur na buddhir iti/
children.translated_text: But if cognition persists over time, then even when the visible object is obstructed, perception would continue. And memory is not a logical mark for the persistence of cognition, because the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) born of cognition is the cause of memory. And whoever thinks 'cognition persists — for memory is observed regarding the object of cognition, and if cognition were non-eternal, memory would not arise due to the absence of its cause' — this is a non-reason. Why? Because the <s>saṃskāra</s> born of cognition is a different quality that serves as the cause of memory, not cognition itself.

children.text: hetvabhāvād ayuktam iti cet? buddhyavasthānāt pratyakṣatve smṛtyabhāvaḥ/yāvad avatiṣṭhate buddhis tāvad asau boddhavyārthiḥ pratyakṣaḥ pratyskṣe ca smṛtir anupapanna iti//42//
children.translated_text: If it be objected that this is unjustified because the cause [of memory] is absent — if cognition persists, then since it remains present, there would be [ongoing] perception, and memory would not arise. For as long as cognition persists, one seeks the object to be known through direct perception, and memory is untenable in the presence of direct perception. // 42 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 43
The grasping of the object to be known is indistinct because of the non-persistence [of cognition], like the indistinct grasping of form during a flash of lightning. // 3.2.43 //

children.text: yady utpannāpavargiṇī buddhiḥ prāptam avyaktaṃ boddhavyasya grahaṇam, yathā vidyutsampāte vaidyutasya prakāśasyānavasthānād avyaktaṃ rūpagrahaṇam iti; vyaktaṃ tu dravyāṇāṃ grahaṇaṃ tasmād ayuktam etad iti//43//
children.translated_text: If cognition arises and perishes, then the grasping of the object to be known would be indistinct, just as during a flash of lightning, due to the non-persistence of the lightning's light, the grasping of form is indistinct. But the grasping of substances is actually distinct; therefore this [view that cognition is momentary] is unjustified. // 43 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 44
By adducing the reason, the very thing to be refuted is conceded. // 3.2.44 //

children.text: utapannāpavargiṇī buddhir iti pratiṣeddhavyaṃ tad eva abhyanujñāyate vidyutsampāte rūpāvyaktagrahaṇavad iti/
children.translated_text: 'Cognition arises and perishes' — this is what was to be refuted, and this very thing is conceded by 'like the indistinct grasping of form during a flash of lightning.'

children.text: yatrāvyaktagrahaṇaṃ tatrotpannāpavargiṇī buddhir iti/ grahaṇahetuvikalpād grahaṇavikalpo na buddhivikalpāt/ yad idaṃ kvacid avyaktaṃ kvacid vyaktaṃ grahaṇam ayaṃ vikalpo grahaṇahetuvikalpāt yatrānavasthito grahaṇahetuḥ tatrāvyaktaṃ grahaṇam yatra avasthitas tatra vyaktam, na tu buddher avasthānānavasthānābhyām iti/ kasmāt? arthagrhaṇaṃ hi buddhiḥ yat tadarthagrahaṇam avyaktaṃ vyaktaṃ vā buddhiḥ sā iti/ viśeṣāgrahaṇe ca sāmānyagrahaṇamātram avyaktagrahaṇaṃ tatra viṣayāntare buddhyanatarānutpattir nimittābhāvāt/ yatra samānadharmayuktaś ca dharmī gṛhyate viśeṣadharmayuktaś ca tad vyaktam grahaṇam, yatra tu viśeṣe 'gṛhyamāṇe sāmānyagrahaṇamātraṃ tad avyaktaṃ grahaṇam/ samānadharmayogāc ca viśiṣthadharmayogo viṣayāntaram, tatra yad grahaṇaṃ na bhavati tad grahaṇanimittābhāvād na buddher anavasthānād iti/
children.translated_text: Where there is indistinct grasping, there cognition arises and perishes. The variation in grasping arises from the variation in the cause of grasping, not from variation in cognition. This variation — that grasping is sometimes indistinct and sometimes distinct — is due to the variation in the cause of grasping: where the cause of grasping is non-persisting, there grasping is indistinct; where it is persisting, there it is distinct; but it is not due to the persistence or non-persistence of cognition. Why? Because cognition is the grasping of an object — whatever that object-grasping is, whether indistinct or distinct, that is cognition. And when particular features are not grasped and there is mere grasping of the general, that is indistinct grasping — there, another cognition of a different object does not arise, due to the absence of a cause. Where the <s>dharmin</s> (subject) is grasped as possessing both common and specific qualities, that is distinct grasping; but where, with specific features not being grasped, there is merely the grasping of the general — that is indistinct grasping. And since the possession of specific qualities is a different object from the possession of common qualities, the non-arising of grasping there is due to the absence of the cause of grasping, not due to the non-persistence of cognition.

children.text:
yathāviṣayaṃ ca grahaṇaṃ vyaktam eva pratyarthaniyatatvāc ca buddhīnām/ sāmānyaviṣayaṃ ca grahaṇaṃ svaviṣayaṃ prati vyaktaṃ viśeṣaviṣayaṃ ca grahaṇaṃ svaviṣayaṃ prati vyaktaṃ pratyarthaniyatā hi buddhayaḥ, tad idam avyaktagrahaṇaṃ deśitaṃ kva viṣaye buddhyanavasthānakāritaṃ syyad iti?
dharmiṇas tu dharmabhede buddhinānātvasya bhāvābhāvābhyāṃ tadupapattiḥ/dharmiṇaḥ khalv arthasya samānāś ca dharmā viśiṣṭāś ca, teṣu pratyarthaniyatā nānābuddayaḥ, tā ubhayo yadi dharmiṇi vartante tadā vyakataṃ grahaṇaṃ dharmiṇam abhipretya/ yadā tu sāmānyagrahaṇamātraṃ tadāvyaktaṃ grahaṇam iti/ evaṃ dharmiṇam abhipretya vyaktāvyakatayor grahaṇayor upapattir iti//44//
children.translated_text: And grasping, as it relates to its object, is always distinct, since cognitions are restricted to their respective objects. Grasping of the general is distinct with respect to its own object, and grasping of the particular is distinct with respect to its own object — for cognitions are restricted to their respective objects. So where has this indistinct grasping been shown to be caused by the non-persistence of cognition? The tenability of [distinct and indistinct grasping] is rather through the presence and absence of a difference in qualities of the <s>dharmin</s> (subject). Indeed, the qualities of a subject-object are both common and specific; the various cognitions are restricted to their respective objects; when both [types of cognitions] occur regarding the subject, the grasping is distinct with respect to the subject. But when there is mere grasping of the general, the grasping is indistinct. Thus, with respect to the subject, the tenability of both distinct and indistinct grasping is established. // 44 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 45

children.text: na cedam avyaktaṃ grahaṇaṃ budder boddhavyasya vānavasthāyitvād upapadyate iti/ idaṃ hi —
children.translated_text: And this indistinct grasping is not tenable as being due to the non-persistence of either cognition or the object to be known. For —
The grasping [of objects illuminated by lamp-flame] is not like that, as it is like the grasping that is manifested by a continuum of lamp-flames. // 3.2.45 //

children.text: anavasthāyitve 'pi buddhes teṣāṃ grahaṇaṃ vyaktaṃ pratipattavyam/ katham? pradīpārciḥsantatyabhivyaktagrahaṇavat/ pradīpārciṣāṃ santatyā vartamānānāṃ grahaṇānavasthānaṃ grāhyānavasthānaṃ ca pratyarthaniyatatvād buddhīnāṃ yāvanti pradīpārcīṃṣi tāvatyo buddaya iti/ dṛśyate cātra vyaktaṃ pradīpārciṣām grahaṇam iti//45//
children.translated_text: Even though cognition does not persist, the grasping of those [objects] should be understood as distinct. How? Like the grasping manifested by a continuum of lamp-flames. The non-persistence of the grasping by the continuum of existing lamp-flames and the non-persistence of the graspable — since cognitions are restricted to their respective objects, there are as many cognitions as there are lamp-flames. And the grasping of the lamp-flames is observed to be distinct. // 45 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 46

children.text: cetanā śarīraguṇaḥ sati śarīre bhāvād asati ca abhāvād iti
children.translated_text: '<s>Cetanā</s> (consciousness) is a quality of the body, because it exists when the body exists and is absent when the body is absent' — regarding this —
There is doubt, because both one's own and another's qualities are observed in a substance. // 3.2.46 //

children.text: sāṃśayikaḥ sati bhāvaḥ, svaguṇo 'psu dravatvam upalabhyate, paraguṇaś coṣṇatā, tenāyaṃ saṃśayaḥ kiṃ śarīraguṇaś cetanā śarīre gṛhyata atha dravyāntaraguṇa iti//46//
children.translated_text: The statement 'it exists when [the body] exists' is doubtful. In water, fluidity — its own quality — is observed, and heat — the quality of another substance — is also observed. Hence this doubt: is <s>cetanā</s> (consciousness) a quality of the body perceived in the body, or is it the quality of another substance? // 46 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 47
<s>Cetanā</s> (consciousness) is not a quality of the body. Why?
Because form and the like exist as long as the substance exists. // 3.2.47 //

children.text: na rūpādihīnaṃ śarīraṃ gṛhyate cetanāhīnan tu gṛhyate yathoṣṇatāhīnā āpaḥ, tasmān na śarīraguṇaś cetaneti/
children.translated_text: A body devoid of form and the like is not perceived, but a body devoid of consciousness is perceived — just as water devoid of heat is perceived. Therefore <s>cetanā</s> is not a quality of the body.

children.text:
saṃskāravad iti ced na kāraṇānucchedāt/ yathāvidhe dravye saṃskāraḥ tathāvidha evoparamo na, tatra kāraṇocchedād atyantaṃ saṃskārānupapattir bhavati/ yathāvidhe śarīre cetanā gṛhyate tathāvidhe evātyantoparamaś cetanāyā gṛhyate/ tasmāt saṃskāravad ity asamaḥ samādhiḥ/
athāpi śarīrasthaṃ cetanotpattikāraṇaṃ syāt? dravyāntarasthaṃ vā? ubhayasthaṃ vā? tan na, niyamahetvabhāvāt/ śarīrasthena kadācic cetanotpadyate kadācin neti niyame hetur nāstīti/ dravyāntarasthena ca śarīra eva cetanotpadyate na loṣṭādiṣv ity atra na niyame hetur astīti/ ubhayasthasya nimittatve śarīrasamānajātīyadravye cetanā notpadyate śarīra eva cotpadyate iti niyame hetur nāstīti//47//
children.translated_text: If it is objected that it is like a <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) — no, because in that case the cause is not destroyed. The <s>saṃskāra</s> ceases in the very type of substance in which it exists; there, due to the destruction of its cause, the <s>saṃskāra</s> becomes completely untenable. Consciousness is perceived in a certain type of body, and its complete cessation is perceived in that very type of body. Therefore the analogy with <s>saṃskāra</s> is an inappropriate parallel. Moreover, could the cause of the production of consciousness be located in the body? Or in another substance? Or in both? None of these, because there is no reason for the restriction. There is no reason why consciousness is sometimes produced by something in the body and sometimes not. There is no reason why consciousness is produced only in the body and not in clods of earth and the like, by something in another substance. And if the cause is in both, there is no reason why consciousness is not produced in substances of the same kind as the body, and is produced only in the body. // 47 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 48

children.text: yac ca manyeta sati śyāmādiguṇe dravye śyāmādyuparamo dṛṣṭaḥ evaṃ cetanoparamaḥ syād iti —
children.translated_text: And if one thinks that just as the cessation of dark color and other qualities is observed in a substance that possesses them, so too the cessation of consciousness would occur —
No, because another quality is produced through transformation by heat. // 3.2.48 //

children.text: nātyantaṃ rūpoparamo dravyasya, śyāme rūpe nivṛtte pākajaṃ guṇāntaraṃ raktaṃ rūpam utpadyate, śarīre tu cetanāmātroparamo 'tyantam iti//48//
children.translated_text: The cessation of form in a substance is not complete — when dark form ceases, another form, red, produced by heat-transformation arises. But in the body, the cessation of consciousness alone is total and complete. // 48 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 49
Moreover —
Because of the establishment of an opposing [quality], there is no refutation of heat-transformed [qualities]. // 3.2.49 //

children.text: yāvatsu dravyeṣu pūrvaguṇapratidvandvisiddhis tāvatsu pākajotpattir dṛśyate pūrvaguṇaiḥ saha pākajānām avasthānasyāgrahaṇāt/ na ca śarīre cetanāpratidvandvisiddhau sahānavasthāyi guṇāntaraṃ gṛhyate yenānumīyeta tena cetanāyā virodhaḥ/ tasmād apratiṣiddhā cetanā yāvac charīraṃ varteta, na tu vartate, tasmān na śarīraguṇaś cetanā iti//49//
children.translated_text: In those substances in which the establishment of a quality opposing the prior quality is observed, in those the production of a heat-transformed quality is seen — because the coexistence of the prior quality with the heat-transformed one is not observed. But when consciousness ceases in the body, no other quality that is incompatible [with consciousness] and cannot coexist with it is perceived, by which the opposition of that [quality] with consciousness could be inferred. Therefore consciousness is unrefuted — it should persist as long as the body persists. But it does not persist; therefore consciousness is not a quality of the body. // 49 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 50
And for this further reason, <s>cetanā</s> (consciousness) is not a quality of the body —
Because it would pervade the [entire] body. // 3.2.50 //

children.text: śarīraṃ śarīrāvayavāś ca sarve cetanotpattyā vyāptā iti na kvacid anutpattiś cetanāyāḥ, śarīravac charīrāvayavāś cetanā iti prāptaṃ cetanabahutvam/ tatra yathā pratiśarīraṃ cetanabahutve sukhaduḥkhajñānānāṃ vyavasthā liṅgam evam ekaśarīre 'pi syāt, na tu bhavati, tasmān na śarīraguṇaś cetaneti//50//
children.translated_text: The body and all the parts of the body are pervaded by the production of consciousness — so there would be no part where consciousness does not arise. Body-parts, like the body itself, would possess consciousness, and the consequence would be a multiplicity of conscious entities. In that case, just as when there are multiple conscious entities — one per body — the orderly arrangement of pleasure, pain, and cognition is the evidence, so too this [orderly arrangement] should exist within a single body. But it does not; therefore consciousness is not a quality of the body. // 50 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 51

children.text: yad uktaṃ na kvacic charīrāvayave cetanāyā anutpattir iti sā —
children.translated_text: What was said — that there is no part of the body where consciousness does not arise — that is —
Not so, because it is not perceived in hair, nails, and the like. // 3.2.51 //

children.text: keśeṣu nakhādiṣu cānutpattiś cetanāyā iti anupapannaṃ śarīravyāpitvam iti//51//
children.translated_text: Since consciousness does not arise in hair, nails, and the like, the claim that it pervades the body is untenable. // 51 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 52
Because the body extends only to the skin, there is no applicability to hair, nails, and the like. // 3.2.52 //

children.text: indriyāśrayatvaṃ śarīralakṣaṇam, tvakparyantaṃ jīvamanaḥsukhaduḥkhasaṃvittyāyatanabhūtaṃ śarīram, tasmān na keśādiṣu cetanotpadyate/ arthakāritas tu śarīropanibandhaḥ keśādīnām iti//52//
children.translated_text: The defining characteristic of the body is being the seat of the sense-organs. The body extends to the skin and is the locus for the experience of life, mind, pleasure, and pain. Therefore consciousness does not arise in hair and the like. But hair and the like are connected to the body for a functional purpose. // 52 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 53
And for this further reason, <s>cetanā</s> is not a quality of the body —
Because of dissimilarity with the qualities of the body. // 3.2.53 //

children.text: dvividhaḥ śarīraguṇaḥ — apratyakṣaś ca gurutvam, indriyagrāhyaś ca rūpādiḥ, vidhāntaraṃ tu cetanā, nāpratyakṣā saṃvedyatvāt, nendriyagrāhyā manoviṣayatvāt/ tasmād dravyāntaraguṇa iti//53//
children.translated_text: The qualities of the body are of two kinds: imperceptible, such as gravity, and sense-perceptible, such as form and the like. But <s>cetanā</s> (consciousness) is of a different type — it is not imperceptible, because it is experienced; it is not sense-perceptible, because it is an object of the mind. Therefore it is the quality of another substance. // 53 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 54
Not so, because form and the like are also dissimilar from one another. // 3.2.54 //

children.text: yathā itaretaravidharmāṇo rūpādayo na śarīraguṇatvaṃ jahaty evaṃ rūpādivaidharmyāc cetanā śarīraguṇatvaṃ na hāsyatīti//54//
children.translated_text: Just as form and the like, though dissimilar from one another, do not cease to be qualities of the body, so too consciousness, despite being dissimilar from form and the like, should not cease to be a quality of the body. // 54 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 55
Because form and the like are sense-perceptible, there is no refutation [of their being body-qualities]. // 3.2.55 //

children.text:
apratyaksatvāc ceti/ yathetaretaravidharmāṇo rūpādayo na dvaividhyam ativartante tathā rūpādivaidharmyāc cetanā na dvaividhyam ativarteta yadi śarīraguṇaḥ syād iti/ ativarttate tu, tasmān na śarīraguṇa iti/
bhūtendriyamanasāṃ jñānapratiṣedhāt siddhe saty ārambho viśeṣajñāpanārthaḥ, bahudhā parīkṣyamāṇaṃ tattvaṃ suniścitataraṃ bhavatīti//55//
children.translated_text: And because [consciousness] is imperceptible — just as form and the like, though dissimilar from one another, do not go beyond the twofold classification [of body-qualities], so too consciousness, being dissimilar from form and the like, should not go beyond the twofold classification if it were a quality of the body. But it does go beyond it; therefore it is not a quality of the body. Since knowledge has been negated of the elements, sense-organs, and mind, the undertaking [of this discussion], given that [the existence of the self] is already established, is for the purpose of detailed knowledge — for truth that is examined in many ways becomes more firmly established. // 55 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 56

children.text: parīkṣitā buddhiḥ, manasa idānīṃ parīkṣākramaḥ/ tat kiṃ pratiśarīram ekam anekam iti vicāre —
children.translated_text: Cognition has been examined. Now comes the turn of examining the mind. In the inquiry as to whether there is one mind per body or many —
The mind is one, because of the non-simultaneity of cognitions. // 3.2.56 //

children.text: asti khalu vai jñānāyaugapadyam ekaikasyendriyasya yathāviṣayam, karaṇasyaikapratyayanirvṛttau sāmarthyāt, na tadekatve manaso liṅgam/ yat tu khalv idam indriyāntarāṇāṃ viṣayāntareṣu jñānāyaugapadyam iti tal liṅgam/ kasmāt? sambhavati khalu vai bahuṣu manaḥsv indriyamanaḥsaṃyogayaugapadyam iti jñānayaugapadyaṃ syāt, na tu bhavati/ tasmād viṣaye pratyayaparyāyād ekaṃ manaḥ//56//
children.translated_text: There is indeed non-simultaneity of cognitions of each individual sense-organ with respect to its own object, due to the capacity of the instrument in producing one cognition at a time — but this is not a mark of the oneness of mind. Rather, it is the non-simultaneity of cognitions of different sense-organs regarding different objects that serves as the logical mark. Why? Because if there were many minds, then due to the simultaneity of the conjunction of the sense-organs with [their respective] minds, there would be simultaneity of cognitions. But this does not occur. Therefore, from the successive occurrence of cognitions regarding objects, the mind is one. // 56 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 57
Not so, because simultaneous multiple activities are perceived. // 3.2.57 //

children.text: ayaṃ khalv adhyāpako 'dhīte vrajati kamaṇḍaluṃ dhārayati panthānaṃ paśyati śṛṇoty āraṇyajān śabdān bibhyad vyālaliṅgāni bubhutsate smarati ca gantavyaṃ sthānīyam iti/ kramasyāgrahaṇād yugapad etāḥ kriyā iti prāptaṃ manaso bahutvam iti//57//
children.translated_text: Consider this teacher: he recites, he walks, he holds a water-vessel, he looks at the road, he hears the sounds of wild animals, being afraid he examines the signs of predators, and he remembers the destination he must reach. Since no sequence is perceived [among these], these activities are simultaneous, and hence the multiplicity of mind is established. // 57 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 58
The perception of those [as simultaneous] is like the appearance of a firebrand-circle — due to the rapid movement [of the mind]. // 3.2.58 //

children.text: āśusañcārād alātasya bhramato vidyamānaḥ kramo na gṛhyate/ kramasyāgrahaṇād avicchedabuddhyā cakravad buddhir bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: Due to the rapid movement of a whirling firebrand, the sequence that exists is not grasped. Because the sequence is not grasped, there arises a cognition as of a circle, due to the notion of uninterruptedness.

children.text:
tathā buddhīnāṃ kriyāṇāṃ cāśuvṛttitvād vidyamānaḥ kramo na gṛhyate kramasyāgrahaṇād yugapat kriyā bhavanntīty abhimāno bhavati/
kiṃ punaḥ kramasyāgrahaṇād yugapat kriyābhimānaḥ, atha yugapadbhāvād eva yugapadanekakriyopalabdhir iti nātra viśeṣapratipatteḥ kāraṇam ucyata iti/ uktam indriyāntarāṇāṃ viṣayāntareṣu paryāyeṇa buddhayo bhavantīti tac cāpratyākhyeyam ātmapratyakṣatvāt/ athāpi dṛṣṭaśrutān arthān cintayataḥ krameṇa buddhayo vartante na yugapad anenānumātavyam iti/ varṇapadavākyabuddhīnāṃ tadarthabuddhīnāṃ cāśuvṛttitvāt kramasyāgrahaṇam/ katham? vākyastheṣu khalu varṇeṣūccaratsu prativarṇaṃ tāvac chravaṇaṃ bhavati, śrutaṃ varṇam ekam anekaṃ vā padabhāvena sa pratisandhatte, pratisandhāya padaṃ vyavasyati, padavyavasāyena smṛtyā padārthaṃ pratipadyate, padasamūhapratisandhānāc ca vākyaṃ vyavasyati, sambaddhāṃś ca padārthān gṛhītvā vākyārthaṃ pratipadyate/ na cāsāṃ krameṇa vartamānānāṃ buddhīnām āśuvṛttitvāt kramo gṛhyate, tad etad anumānam anyatra buddhikriyāyaugapadyābhimānasyeti/ na cāsti muktasaṃśayā yugapad utpattir buddhīnāṃ yayā manasāṃ bahutvam ekaśarīre 'numīyeta iti//58//
children.translated_text: Similarly, because cognitions and actions are of rapid occurrence, the sequence that exists is not grasped; because the sequence is not grasped, there arises the false impression that actions occur simultaneously. Is it that the impression of simultaneity arises from non-grasping of sequence, or is it that the apprehension of multiple simultaneous actions is due to actual simultaneity? No ground for the determination of a distinction is stated here. It has been said that cognitions of the other sense-organs with respect to their different objects arise in succession — and that cannot be denied, since it is self-evident through introspection. Moreover, one should infer from this: when one thinks about objects seen and heard, cognitions proceed in sequence, not simultaneously. The non-grasping of sequence is due to the rapid occurrence of cognitions of phonemes, words, sentences, and their meanings. How? When the phonemes in a sentence are being uttered, hearing occurs for each phoneme; one connects the heard phoneme — one or many — into a word-form; having connected it, one determines the word; through the determination of the word, one apprehends its meaning through memory; through the connection of a group of words, one determines the sentence; and having grasped the connected word-meanings, one apprehends the sentence-meaning. And because these cognitions, which proceed in sequence, are of rapid occurrence, the sequence is not grasped. This is the inference that the impression of simultaneity of cognitive activities is [erroneous]. And there is no doubt-free simultaneous origination of cognitions from which the plurality of minds in a single body could be inferred. // 58 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 59
And because of the aforementioned reason, [the mind] is atomic. // 3.2.59 //

children.text: aṇu mana ekaṃ ceti dharmasamuccayo jñānāyaugapadyāt/ mahattve manasaḥ sarvendriyasaṃyogād yugapad viṣayagrahaṇaṃ syād iti//59//
children.translated_text: That the mind is atomic and one — this is a collection of properties [inferred] from the non-simultaneity of cognitions. If the mind were large, there would be simultaneous grasping of objects due to conjunction with all the sense-organs. // 59 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 60

children.text:
manasaḥ khalu bhoḥ sendriyasya śarīre vṛttilābho nānyatra śarīrāt/ jñātuś ca puruṣasya śarīrāyatanā buddhyādayo viṣayopabhogo jihāsitahānam īpsitāvāptiś ca sarve ca śarīrāśrayā vyavahārāḥ/ tatra khalu vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ — kim ayaṃ puruṣakarmanimittaḥ śarīrasarga āhosvid bhūtamātrād akarmanimitta iti/ śrūyate khalv atra vipratipattir iti/
tatredaṃ tattvam —
children.translated_text: Now, the mind, being endowed with sense-organs, obtains its activity in the body, not outside the body. And for the knowing <s>puruṣa</s> (person/self), intellect and the rest, the enjoyment of objects, the abandonment of what is desired to be abandoned, the attainment of what is desired to be attained, and all transactions that depend on the body, are based on the body. Now, concerning this, due to conflicting views, there is doubt: Is this creation of the body occasioned by the <s>karma</s> (action) of the <s>puruṣa</s>, or does it arise from the elements alone without any occasion of <s>karma</s>? Indeed, conflicting views on this are heard. The truth of the matter is:
Its origination is from the connection with the fruit of what was done previously. // 3.2.60 //

children.text: pūrvaśarīre yā pravṛttir vāgbuddhiśarīrārambhalakṣaṇā tat pūrvakṛtaṃ karmoktam, tasya phalaṃ tajjanitau dharmādharmau/
children.translated_text: The activity in the previous body, characterized by the initiation of speech, mind, and body — that is called the previously performed <s>karma</s>; its fruit is the <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) produced by it.

children.text: tatphalasyānubandha ātmasamavetasyāvasthānam, tena prayuktebhyo bhūebyas tasyotpattiḥ śarīrasya, na svatantrebhya iti/ yad adhiṣṭhāno 'yam ātmā 'yam aham iti manyamāno yatrābhiyukto yatropabhogatṛṣṇayā viṣayānupalabhamāno dharmādharmau saṃskaroti tad asya śarīram, tena saṃskāreṇa dharmādharmalakṣaṇena bhūtasahite patite 'smin śarīra uttaraṃ niṣpadyate, niṣpannasya cāsya pūrvaśarīravat puruṣārthakriyā, puruṣasya ca pūrvaśarīravat pravṛttir iti karmāpekṣebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ śarīrasarge saty etad upapadyata iti/
children.translated_text: The connection with the fruit is its abiding as inherent in the <s>ātman</s> (self); by that [connection], directed from elements, the body originates — not from independent [elements]. That of which this <s>ātman</s> is the presiding entity, thinking "this is I," where being engaged, and apprehending objects through the craving for enjoyment, he produces <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — that is his body. Through that impression characterized by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, when this body falls along with the elements, a subsequent [body] is produced; and of this newly produced [body], there is the functioning for the person's purpose just as in the previous body; and the person's activity is as in the previous body. When the creation of the body is from elements that depend on <s>karma</s>, all this is tenable.

children.text: dṛṣṭā ca puruṣaguṇena prayatnena prayuktebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ puruṣārthkriyāsamarthānāṃ dravyāṇāṃ rathaprabhṛtīnām utpattiḥ/ tathānumātavyaṃ śarīram api puruṣārthakriyāsamartham utpadyamānaṃ puruṣasya guṇāntarāpekṣebhyo bhūtebhya utpadyata iti//60//
children.translated_text: And it is observed that from elements directed by effort — a quality of the <s>puruṣa</s> — objects such as chariots and the like, which are capable of serving the person's purpose, are produced. Similarly, one should infer that the body too, being capable of serving the person's purpose, when being produced, is produced from elements that depend on a different quality of the <s>puruṣa</s>. // 60 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 61
Here the materialist (<s>nāstika</s>) says:
Just as material forms are taken up from the elements, so too this [body] is taken up [from the elements]. // 3.2.61 //

children.text: yathā karmanirapekṣebhyo bhūtebhyo nirvṛttā mūrtayaḥ sikatāśarkarāpāṣāṇagairikāñjanaprabhṛtayaḥ puruṣārthakāritvād upādīyante tathā karmanirapekṣebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ śarīram utpannaṃ puruṣārthakāritvād upādīyate iti//61//
children.translated_text: Just as material forms such as sand, gravel, rocks, red chalk, antimony, and the like, produced from elements without dependence on <s>karma</s>, are taken up because they serve human purposes, so too the body, produced from elements without dependence on <s>karma</s>, is taken up because it serves human purposes. // 61 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 62
No, because it is equivalent to what is to be proved. // 3.2.62 //

children.text: yathā śarīrotpattir akarmanimittā sādhyā tathā sikatāśarkarāpāṣāṇagairikāñjanaprabhṛtīnām apy akarmanimittaḥ sargaḥ sādhyaḥ sādhyasamatvād asādhanam iti

children.translated_text: "Just as material forms are taken up from the elements"
— this also needs to be proved. // 62 //

Just as the origination of the body without <s>karma</s> as its occasion is what needs to be proved, so too the creation of sand, gravel, rocks, red chalk, antimony, and the like without <s>karma</s> as its occasion needs to be proved. Being equivalent to what is to be proved, it is not a proof.
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 63
Because the mother and father are the occasion of origination, [the body is not produced from elements alone]. // 3.2.63 //

children.text: viṣamaś cāyam upanyāsaḥ/ kasmāt? nirbījā imā mūrtaya utpadyante bījapūrvikā tu śarīrotpattiḥ/ mātāpitṛśabdena lohitaretasī bījabhūte gṛhyete/ tatra sattvasya garbhavāsānubhavanīyaṃ karma pitroś ca putraphalānubhavanīye karmaṇī mātur garbhāśraye śarīrotpattiṃ bhūtebhyaḥ prayojayantīty upapannaṃ bījānuvidhānam iti//63//
children.translated_text: And this comparison is unequal. Why? These material forms are produced without a seed, but the origination of a body is preceded by a seed. By the words "mother and father," the blood and semen, which are the seeds, are meant. There, the <s>karma</s> of the being that is to be experienced during its stay in the womb, and the <s>karmas</s> of the parents that are to be experienced as the fruit of having a child, impel the origination of the body from elements in the mother's womb. Thus the dependence on the seed is tenable. // 63 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 64
Likewise of food. // 3.2.64 //

children.text: utpattinimittatvād iti prakṛtam/ bhuktaṃ pītam āhāraḥ tasya paktinirvṛttaṃ rasadravyaṃ mātṛśarīre copacīyate bīje garbhāśayasthe bījasamānapākam, mātrayā copacayo bīje yāvad vyūhasamarthaḥ sañcaya iti/ sañcitaṃ ca kalalārbudamāṃsapeśīkaṇḍarāśiraḥpāṇyādinā ca vyūhenendriyādhiṣṭhānabhedena vyuhyate, vyūhe ca garbhanāḍyāvatāritaṃ rasadravyam upacīyate yāvat prasavasamartham iti/ na cāyam annapānasya sthālyādigatasya kalpata iti/ etasmāt kāraṇāt karmanimittatvaṃ śarīrasya vijñāyata iti//64//
children.translated_text: "Because of being the occasion of origination" is the continuing topic. Food is what is eaten and drunk; the nutrient substance produced from its digestion accumulates in the mother's body and in the seed residing in the womb with the same rate of transformation as the seed, and the accumulation in the seed by degrees continues until there is a sufficient collection for the formation [of the body]. And the accumulated [matter] is organized through the formation of <s>kalala</s> (embryonic fluid), <s>arbuda</s> (embryonic knot), flesh, sinew, tendon, head, hands, etc., differentiated into the substrates of the sense-organs.
