And in the organized [body], the nutrient substance channeled through the umbilical cord accumulates until [the fetus] is capable of birth. And this [process] is not possible for food and drink placed in a pot and the like. For this reason, it is known that the body is occasioned by <s>karma</s>. // 64 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 65
And because of the absence of regularity in [the conditions for] obtaining [a body]. // 3.2.65 //

children.text: na sarvo dampatyoḥ saṃyogo garbhādhānahetur dṛśyate tatrāsati karmaṇi na bhavati sati ca bhavatīty anupapanno niyamābhāva iti/ karmanirapekṣeṣu bhūteṣu śarīrotpattihetuṣu niyamaḥ syāt na hy atra kāraṇābhāva iti//65//
children.translated_text: Not every union of husband and wife is observed to be the cause of conception. In the absence of <s>karma</s>, it does not occur; when <s>karma</s> is present, it does occur — so the absence of regularity is untenable. If elements that are independent of <s>karma</s> were the cause of bodily origination, there would be regularity, since there would be no absence of cause. // 65 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 66
Moreover —
Just as <s>karma</s> is the occasion of bodily origination, so too it is the occasion of the origination of [the self's] conjunction [with the body]. // 3.2.66 //

children.text: yathā khalv idaṃ śarīraṃ dhātuprāṇasaṃvāhinīnāṃ nāḍīnāṃ śukrāntānāṃ dhātūnāṃ ca snāyutvagasthiśirāpeśīkalalakaṇḍarāṇāṃ ca śirobāhūdarāṇāṃ sakthnāṃ ca koṣṭhagānāṃ vātapittakaphānāṃ ca mukhahṛdayāmāśayapakvāśayādhaḥsrotasāṃ ca paramaduḥkhasampādanīyena sanniveśena vyūhanam aśakyaṃ pṛthivyādibhiḥ karmanirapekṣair utpādayitum iti karmanimittā śarīrotpattir iti vijñāyate; evaṃ ca pratyātmaniyatasya nimittasyābhāvān niratiśayair ātmabhiḥ sambandhāt sarvātmanāṃ ca samānaiḥ pṛthivyādibhir utpāditaṃ śarīraṃ pṛthivyādigatasya ca niyamahetor abhāvāt sarvātmanāṃ sukhaduḥkhasaṃvittyāyatanaṃ samānaṃ prāptam/ yat tu pratyātmaṃ vyavatiṣṭhate tatra śarīrotpattinimittaṃ karma vyavashtāhetur iti vijñāyate/ paripacyamāno hi pratyātmaniyataḥ karmāśayo yasminn ātmani vartate tasyaivopabhogāyatanaṃ śarīram utpādya vyavasthāpayati/ tad evaṃ

children.translated_text: just as <s>karma</s> is the occasion of bodily origination, so too it is the occasion of conjunction [with the body]

children.text: iti vijñāyate/ pratyātmavyavasthānaṃ tu śarīrasyātmanā saṃyogaṃ pracakṣmaha iti//66//
children.translated_text: — this is known. And the specific determination of each body with its <s>ātman</s> — that is what we call the conjunction of the body with the <s>ātman</s>. // 66 //

Indeed, this body — with its channels that carry bodily constituents and vital airs ending in semen, its constituents of sinew, skin, bone, veins, flesh, embryonic fluid, and tendon, its parts of head, arms, abdomen, and thighs, its internal cavities of wind, bile, and phlegm, and its passages of mouth, heart, stomach, intestine, and lower apertures — with an arrangement that requires extreme precision to produce, cannot be produced by elements such as earth and the like independently of <s>karma</s>. Thus it is known that bodily origination is occasioned by <s>karma</s>. And since, in the absence of a cause specific to each <s>ātman</s>, due to there being no superior and inferior among <s>ātmans</s> by virtue of their being unlimited, and due to the sameness of elements such as earth, etc., and due to the absence of a cause of regularity pertaining to the elements, the body of all <s>ātmans</s> would turn out to be the same as a locus for the experience of pleasure and pain. But what is specific to each <s>ātman</s> — it is known that <s>karma</s>, the occasion of bodily origination, is the cause of the specific determination. For the <s>karmāśaya</s> (store of <s>karma</s>), specific to each <s>ātman</s>, ripening in whichever <s>ātman</s> it resides, produces and establishes the body as the locus of experience for that very [<s>ātman</s>]. Thus
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 67
By this, the [objection regarding] absence of regularity has been answered. // 3.2.67 //

children.text: yo .yam akarmanimitte śarīrasarge saty aniyama ity ucyate, ayaṃ

children.translated_text: — "just as <s>karma</s> is the occasion of bodily origination, so too it is the occasion of the origination of conjunction" —
has been answered by this.
This absence of regularity that is asserted when bodily creation is not occasioned by <s>karma</s>, this

children.text: kas tāvad ayaṃ niyamaḥ? yathaikasyātmanaḥ śarīraṃ tathā sarveṣām iti niyamaḥ/ anyasyānyathānyasyānyathety aniyamo bhedo vyāvṛttir viśeṣa iti/
children.translated_text: What, then, is this regularity? The regularity is that the body of all <s>ātmans</s> would be the same. That one's is one way and another's is another way — this irregularity is difference, distinction, specificity.

children.text:
dṛṣṭā ca janmavyāvṛttir uccābhijano nikṛṣṭābhijana iti, praśastaṃ nindatam iti, vyādhibahulam arogam iti, samagraṃ vikalam iti, pīḍābahulaṃ sukhabahulam iti, puruṣātiśayalakṣaṇopapannaṃ viparītam iti, praśastalakṣaṇaṃ ninditalakṣaṇam iti, paṭvindriyaṃ mṛḍvindriyam iti/ sūkṣmaś ca bhedo 'parimeyaḥ/ so 'yam janmabhedaḥ pratyātmaniyatāt karmabhedād upapadyate, asati karmabhede pratyātmaniyate niratiśayatvād ātmanāṃ samānatvāc ca pṛthivyādīnāṃ pṛthivyādigatasya niyamahetor ahbāvāt sarvaṃ sarvātmanāṃ prasajyeta, na tv idam itthambhūtaṃ janma/ tasmān nākarmanittā śarīrotpattir iti/
upapannaś ca tadviyogaḥ karmakṣayopapatteḥ/ karmanimitte śarīrasarge tena śarīreṇātmano viyoga upapannaḥ/ kasmāt? karmakṣayopapatteḥ/ upapadyate khalu karmakṣayaḥ samyagdarśanāt prakṣīṇe mohe vītarāgaḥ punarbhavahetukarma kāyavāṅmanobhir na karotīty uttarasyānupacayaḥ pūrvopacitasya vipākapratisaṃvedanāt prakṣayaḥ/ evaṃ prasavahetor abhāvāt patire 'smin śarīre punaḥ śarīrāntarānupapatter apratisandhiḥ/ akarmanimitte tu śarīrasarge bhūtakṣayānupapattes tadviyogānupapattir iti//67//
children.translated_text: And there is observed a differentiation at birth: one is of high birth, another of low birth; one is praiseworthy, another is blameworthy; one is prone to disease, another is healthy; one is whole, another is deficient; one has much suffering, another has much happiness; one is endowed with marks of human excellence, another is the opposite; one has auspicious marks, another has inauspicious marks; one has keen senses, another has dull senses. And the differentiation is subtle and immeasurable. This differentiation at birth is tenable on account of the differentiation of <s>karma</s> specific to each <s>ātman</s>; in the absence of differentiation of <s>karma</s> specific to each <s>ātman</s>, since there is no superiority or inferiority among <s>ātmans</s>, and since the elements such as earth and the like are the same, and since there is no cause of regularity pertaining to the elements, everything would turn out to be the same for all <s>ātmans</s> — but such-and-such a birth does not [so occur]. Therefore, bodily origination is not without <s>karma</s> as its occasion. And the separation from it (the body) is tenable because of the tenability of the exhaustion of <s>karma</s>. When bodily creation is occasioned by <s>karma</s>, the separation of the <s>ātman</s> from that body is tenable. Why? Because of the tenability of the exhaustion of <s>karma</s>. Indeed, the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> is tenable: through right knowledge (<s>samyagdarśana</s>), when delusion is destroyed, one becomes free from attachment and does not produce through body, speech, and mind any <s>karma</s> that is the cause of rebirth — thus there is no accumulation of future [<s>karma</s>]; and through experiencing the ripening of previously accumulated [<s>karma</s>], there is exhaustion. Thus, due to the absence of a cause of production, when this body falls, there is no further production of another body — hence no re-linking. But if bodily creation were not occasioned by <s>karma</s>, since the elements cannot be exhausted, the separation from the body would be untenable. // 67 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 68

children.text: tad adṛṣṭakāritam iti cet punas tatprasaṅgo 'pavarge // 3.2.68 //
children.translated_text: If it be said that this [body] is produced by the unseen [destiny], then there would be the recurrence of that [body] even in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 3.2.68 //

children.text: adarśanaṃ khalv adṛṣṭam ity ucyata adṛṣṭakāritā bhūtebhyaḥ śarīrotpattiḥ/ na jātv anutpanne śarīre draṣṭā nirāyatano dṛśyaṃ paśyati/ tac cāsya dṛśyaṃ dvividhaṃ viṣayaś ca nānātvaṃ cāvyaktātmanaḥ, tadarthaḥ śarīrasargaḥ/ tasminn avasite caritārthāni bhūtāni na śarīram utpādayantīty upapannaḥ śarīraviyoga ity evaṃ cen manyase,

children.translated_text: there would be the recurrence of that [body] even in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation)

children.text: — punaḥ śarīrotpattiḥ prasajyata iti/ yā cānutpanne śarīre darśanānutpattir adarśanābhimatā yā cāpavarge śarīranivṛttau darśanānutpattir adarśanabhūtā naitayor adarśanayoḥ kvacid viśeṣa ity adarśanasyānivṛtter apavarge punaḥ śarīrotpattiprasaṅga iti/
children.translated_text: — the production of a body would again follow. For the non-arising of seeing when no body has been produced, which is considered to be "non-seeing," and the non-arising of seeing upon the cessation of the body in <s>apavarga</s>, which constitutes "non-seeing" — there is no difference between these two cases of non-seeing. Therefore, since non-seeing is not eliminated, the production of a body would again follow even in <s>apavarga</s>.

Non-seeing is indeed called the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>); [the argument is that] bodily origination from elements is caused by the unseen. Never does the seer, when a body has not been produced, see the visible without a bodily basis. And this visible [world] is of two kinds for him — objects and the diversity of the unmanifest <s>ātman</s>; the creation of the body serves that purpose. When that [purpose] has been accomplished, the elements, having fulfilled their purpose, do not produce a body — thus the separation from the body is tenable. If you think so,

children.text: caritārthatā viśeṣa iti cet na karaṇākaraṇayor ārambhadarśanāt/ caritārthāni bhūtāni darśanāvasānān na śarīrāntaram ārabhanta ity ayaṃ viśeṣa evaṃ ced ucyate; na, karaṇākaraṇayor ārambhadarśanāt — caritārthānāṃ bhūtānāṃ viṣayopalabdhikaraṇāt punaḥ punaḥ śarīrārambho dṛśyate prakṛtipuruṣayor nānātvadarśanasyākaraṇān nirarthakaḥ śarīrārambhaḥ punaḥ punar dṛśyate/ tasmād akarmanimittāyāṃ bhūtasṛṣṭau na darśanārthā śarīrotpattir yuktā, yuktā tu karmanimitte sarge darśanārthā śarīrotpattiḥ/ karmavipākasaṃvedanaṃ darśanam iti/
children.translated_text: If it be said that the distinguishing feature is that the purpose has been fulfilled — no, because the commencement (of a new body) is observed in both cases, whether the purpose has been fulfilled or not. 'The elements, having fulfilled their purpose, do not commence another body after the cessation of seeing' — if this is what is meant by the distinguishing feature, then no, because the commencement (of a new body) is observed in both cases: again and again the commencement of a body is observed for the elements whose purpose has been fulfilled through producing the instrument of object-apprehension; and again and again the commencement of a body is observed to be purposeless because of the non-fulfillment of the purpose of perceiving the difference between <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (person). Therefore, in a creation of elements that is not caused by <s>karma</s>, the production of a body for the purpose of seeing is not tenable; but in a creation caused by <s>karma</s>, the production of a body for the purpose of seeing is tenable. 'Seeing' here means the experience of the ripening of <s>karma</s>.

children.text:
tad adṛṣṭakāritam iti cet? kasyacid darśanam adṛṣṭaṃ nāma paramāṇūnāṃ guṇaviśeṣaḥ kriyāhetus tena preritāḥ paramāṇavaḥ sammūrcchitāḥ śarīram utpādayantīti tan manaḥ samāviśati svaguṇenādṛṣṭena preritaṃ samanaske śarīre draṣṭur upalabdhir bhavatīti/
etasmin vai darśane guṇānucchedāt punas tatprasaṅgo 'pavarge/ apavarge śarīrotpattiḥ paramāṇuguṇasyādṛṣṭasyānucchedyatvād iti//68//
children.translated_text: If it be said that this is caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (the unseen force)? Someone's view is that <s>adṛṣṭa</s> is a special quality of atoms that causes motion; impelled by this, atoms aggregate and produce a body — and then <s>manas</s> (mind) enters it, impelled by its own quality <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, and in a body possessed of <s>manas</s>, the apprehension of the seer occurs. But in this view, since the quality (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) is not destroyed, the same consequence would follow in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) — namely, the production of a body would occur even in liberation, since the quality <s>adṛṣṭa</s> of the atoms is indestructible. // 3.2.68 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 69
And because <s>manas</s> is caused by <s>karma</s>, the conjunction cannot be severed. // 3.2.69 //

children.text: manoguṇenādṛṣṭena samāveśite manasi saṃyogavyucchedo na syāt, tac ca kiṃkṛtaṃ śarīrād apasarpaṇaṃ manasa iti? karmāśayakṣaye tu karmāśayāntarād vipacyamānād apasarpaṇopapattir iti/ adṛṣṭād evāpasarpaṇam iti cet — yo 'dṛṣṭaḥ śarīropasarpaṇahetuḥ sa evāpasarpaṇahetur apīti? na, ekasya jīvanaprāyaṇahetutvānupapatteḥ — evaṃ ca saty ekam adṛṣṭaṃ jīvanaprāyaṇayor hetur iti prāptam, naitad upapadyate//69//
children.translated_text: If <s>manas</s> is installed (in the body) by the quality <s>adṛṣṭa</s> of <s>manas</s>, the severing of the conjunction would not occur — then what would cause the departure of <s>manas</s> from the body? But when the store of <s>karma</s> is exhausted, the departure is tenable because another store of <s>karma</s> is ripening. If it be said that the departure too is caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> alone — that the same <s>adṛṣṭa</s> that is the cause of approach to the body is also the cause of departure — no, because it is untenable for one and the same thing to be the cause of both living and dying. For if so, the consequence would be that a single <s>adṛṣṭa</s> is the cause of both living and dying — and this is untenable. // 3.2.69 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 70
And the consequence of eternality (of the body), because death would be untenable. // 3.2.70 //

children.text: vipākasaṃvedanāt karmāśayakṣaye śarīrapātaḥ prāyaṇam, karmāśayāntarāc ca punarjanma/ bhūtamātrāt tu karmanirapekṣāc charīrotpattau kasya kṣayāc charīrapātaḥ prāyaṇam iti? prāyaṇānupapatteḥ khalu vai nityatvaprasaṅgaṃ vidmaḥ/ yādṛcchike tu prāyaṇe prāyaṇabhedānupapattir iti//70//
children.translated_text: Death (<s>prāyaṇa</s>) is the fall of the body upon the exhaustion of the store of <s>karma</s> through the experience of its ripening, and rebirth is from another store of <s>karma</s>. But if the body is produced from mere elements without regard to <s>karma</s>, through the exhaustion of what would the fall of the body — death — occur? Indeed, from the untenability of death, we know the consequence of eternality (of the body). And if death were accidental, the difference in (types of) death would be untenable. // 3.2.70 //

children.text: punas tatprasaṅgo 'pavarga ity etat samādhitsur āha —
children.translated_text: Wishing to address the consequence that 'the same would follow in liberation,' he says —
This would be like the eternality of the blackness of an atom. // 3.2.71 //

children.text: yathāṇoḥ śyāmatā nityā agnisaṃyogena pratiṣiddhā na punar utpadyata evam adṛṣṭakāritaṃ śarīram apavarge punar notpadyata iti// 71 //
children.translated_text: Just as the eternal blackness of an atom, once counteracted by contact with fire, does not arise again — so too the body caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> would not arise again in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 3.2.71 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 72
No, because of the consequence of accepting what is unestablished. // 3.2.72 //

children.text:
nāyam asti dṛṣṭāntaḥ/ kasmāt? akṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅgāt/ akṛtaṃ pramāṇato 'nupapannam, tasyābhyāgamo 'bhyupapattir vyavasāyaḥ, etacchraddadhānena pramāṇato ṇupapannaṃ mantavyam/ tasmān nāyaṃ dṛṣṭānto na pratyakṣaṃ na cānumānaṃ kiṃcid ucyata iti/ tad idaṃ dṛṣṭāntasya sādhyasamatvam abhidhīyata iti/
atha vā nākṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅgāt/ aṇuśyāmatādṛṣṭāntenākarmanimittāṃ śarīrotpattiṃ samādadhānasyākṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅgaḥ/ akṛte sukhaduḥkhahetau karmaṇi puruṣasya sukhaṃ duḥkham abhyāgacchatīti prasajyeta/ om iti bruvataḥ pratyakṣānumānāgamavirodhaḥ/
children.translated_text: This is not a valid example. Why? Because of the consequence of accepting what is unestablished (<s>akṛtābhyāgama</s>). 'Unestablished' means untenable on the basis of any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge); its 'acceptance' (<s>abhyāgama</s>) is its endorsement, its assertion. One who accepts this must hold what is untenable on the basis of any <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore this is not a valid example — neither perception nor inference nor anything else is adduced (in its support). This amounts to saying that the example is equivalent to what is to be proved (<s>sādhyasama</s>). Alternatively: no, because of the consequence of accepting what is unproduced (<s>akṛtābhyāgama</s>). For one who, using the example of the blackness of an atom, establishes a non-<s>karma</s>-caused production of the body, the consequence is: the acceptance of the unproduced — that pleasure and pain would come to a person without having been caused by (prior) action. If one says 'yes' to this, it contradicts perception, inference, and scripture.

children.text:
pratyakṣavirodhas tāvat — bhinnam idaṃ sukhaduḥkhaṃ pratyātmavedanīyatvāt pratyakṣaṃ sarvaśarīriṇām/ ko bhedaḥ? tīvraṃ mandaṃ ciram āśu nānāprakāram ekaprakāram ity evam ādir viśeṣaḥ/ na cāsti pratyātmaniyataḥ sukhaduḥkhahetuviśeṣaḥ, na cāsati hetuviśeṣe phalaviśeṣo dṛśyate/ karmanimitte tu sukhaduḥkhayoge karmaṇāṃ tīvramandatopapatteḥ karmasañcayānāṃ cotkarṣāpakarṣabhāvāt nānāvidhaikavidhabhāvāc ca karmaṇāṃ sukhaduḥkhabhedopapattiḥ/ so 'yaṃ hetubhedābhāvād dṛṣṭaḥ sukhaduḥkhabhedo na syād iti pratyakṣavirodhaḥ/
tathānumānavirodhaḥ — dṛṣṭaṃ hi puruṣaguṇavyavasthānāt sukhaduḥkhavyavasthānam/ yaḥ khalu cetanāvān sādhananirvartanīyaṃ sukhaṃ buddhvā tad īpsan sādhanāvāptaye prayatate sa sukhena yujyate na viparītaḥ/ yaś ca sādhananirvartanīyaṃ duḥkhaṃ buddhvā taj jihāsuḥ sādhanaparivarjanāya yatate sa ca duḥkhena tyajyate na viparītaḥ/ asti cedaṃ yatnam antareṇa cetanānāṃ sukhaduḥkhavyavasthānaṃ tenāpi cetanaguṇāntaravyavasthākṛtena bhavitavyam ity anumānam/
children.translated_text: First, the contradiction with perception — this pleasure and pain is differentiated, and being experienced individually, it is perceptible to all embodied beings. What is the differentiation? There are distinctions such as: intense and mild, long and brief, manifold and uniform, and so forth. And there is no cause-distinction specific to each person that would account for the pleasure-and-pain distinction; and without a cause-distinction, a result-distinction is not observed. But if the conjunction with pleasure and pain is caused by <s>karma</s>, then the distinction in pleasure and pain is tenable because actions are intense and mild, and because accumulations of <s>karma</s> vary in degree, and because actions are manifold and uniform. Thus, the observed distinction in pleasure and pain would not exist without a cause-distinction — this is the contradiction with perception. Likewise, the contradiction with inference — for it is observed that the arrangement of pleasure and pain is due to the arrangement of human qualities. One who is conscious, having cognized the pleasure that is to be accomplished by certain means, and desiring that, strives to acquire those means — he is conjoined with pleasure, not the opposite. And one who is conscious, having cognized the pain that is to be accomplished by certain means, and wishing to avoid it, strives to shun those means — he too is freed from pain, not the opposite. And if this arrangement of pleasure and pain for conscious beings exists even without effort, then it must be due to some other quality of the conscious being — this is the inference.

children.text:
tad etad akarmanimitte sukhaduḥkhayoge virudhyata iti/ tac ca guṇāntaram asaṃvedyatvād adṛṣṭaṃ vipākakālāniyamāc cāvyavasthitam/ buddhyādayas tu saṃvedyāś cāpavargiṇaś ceti/
athāgamavirodhaḥ — bahu khalv idam ārṣam ṛṣīṇām upadeśajātam anuṣṭhānaparivarjanāśrayam, upadeśaphalaṃ ca śarīriṇāṃ varṇāśramavibhāgeṇānuṣṭhānalakṣaṇā pravṛttiḥ, parivarjanalakṣaṇā nivṛttiḥ/ tac cobhayam etasyāṃ dṛṣṭau
children.translated_text: This contradicts the position that the conjunction with pleasure and pain is not caused by <s>karma</s>. And that other quality, being imperceptible, is <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (the unseen), and being indeterminate regarding the time of its ripening, it is unstable. But <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) and the rest are both perceptible and subject to cessation in <s>apavarga</s>. And the contradiction with scripture — abundant indeed is this body of teaching of the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages), based on observance and abstention; and the fruit of this teaching for embodied beings is activity characterized by observance, according to the divisions of <s>varṇa</s> (social class) and <s>āśrama</s> (life-stage), and cessation characterized by abstention. And both of these, according to this view —

children.text: nāsti karma sucaritaṃ duścaritaṃ vā? karmanimittaḥ puruṣāṇāṃ sukhaduḥkhayogaḥ
children.translated_text: 'There is no action, well-performed or ill-performed; the conjunction of persons with pleasure and pain is not caused by <s>karma</s>' —

children.text: iti virudhyate/ seyaṃ pāpiṣṭhānāṃ mithyādṛṣṭiḥ — akarmanimittā śarīrasṛṣṭir akarmanimittaḥ sukhaduḥkhayoga iti//72//
children.translated_text: are contradicted. This is the sinful wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>) of the wicked — that the creation of the body is not caused by <s>karma</s>, and that the conjunction with pleasure and pain is not caused by <s>karma</s>. // 3.2.72 //
Chapter 3, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 73

children.text:
iti śrīvātsyāyanīye nyāyabhāṣye tṛtīyādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam// 2 //
samāptaś cāyaṃ tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ// 3 //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second section of the third chapter in <s>Vātsyāyana</s>'s <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>. // 2 // And thus the third chapter is complete. // 3 //
The <s>Nyāyadarśana</s>. Now the first section of the fourth chapter.
Chapter 4
Chapter 4, Section 1
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 1

children.text: manaso 'nantaraṃ pravṛttiḥ parīkṣitavyā/ tatra khalu yāvad dharmādharmāśrayaśarīrādi parīkṣitam, sarvā sā pravṛtteḥ parīkṣety āha —
children.translated_text: After <s>manas</s> (mind), <s>pravṛtti</s> (activity) is to be examined. In this regard, all that has been examined — including the body and the rest, which are the substrates of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — all of that is an examination of <s>pravṛtti</s>. Therefore he says —
<s>Pravṛtti</s> (activity) is as previously stated. // 4.1.1 //
It has been examined accordingly. // 4.1.1 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 2

children.text: pravṛttyanantarās tarhi doṣāḥ parīkṣyantām ity ata āha —
children.translated_text: Since <s>doṣas</s> (faults) come immediately after <s>pravṛtti</s>, let them be examined — therefore he says:
Likewise, the <s>doṣas</s> (faults). // 4.1.2 //

children.text: parīkṣitā iti/ buddhisamānāśrayatvād ātmaguṇāḥ, pravṛttihetutvāt punarbhavapratisandhānasāmarthyāc ca saṃsārahetavaḥ, saṃsārasyānāditvād anādinā prabandhena pravartante, mithyājñānanivṛttis tattvajñānāt tannivṛttau rāgadveṣaprabandhocchyede 'pavarga iti/ prādurbhāvatirodhānadharmakā ityevamādyuktam doṣāṇām iti//2//
children.translated_text: Have been examined. Being qualities of the <s>ātman</s> (self), having the same substrate as <s>buddhi</s> (intellect); being the cause of <s>pravṛtti</s> (activity) and having the capacity to forge the link to rebirth, they are the causes of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence); since <s>saṃsāra</s> is beginningless, they operate in a beginningless succession. The cessation of false knowledge comes from <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality); upon its cessation, when the succession of <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) is cut off, there is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). It has been said that they have the character of appearing and disappearing, and so forth regarding the <s>doṣas</s>. // 4.1.2 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 3

children.text: pravartanālakṣaṇā doṣā ity uktam, tathā ceme mānerṣyāsūyāvicikitsāmatsarādayaḥ, te kasmān nopasaṅkhyāyante ity ata āha —
children.translated_text: It has been said that the <s>doṣas</s> are characterized by incitement to activity. Then what about pride (<s>māna</s>), jealousy (<s>īrṣyā</s>), envy (<s>asūyā</s>), suspicion (<s>vicikitsā</s>), covetousness (<s>matsara</s>), and the rest — why are they not separately enumerated? Therefore he says:
The triad of those (<s>doṣas</s>) consists of <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion), because these are mutually distinct categories. // 4.1.3 //

children.text: teṣāṃ doṣāṇāṃ trayo rāśayas trayaḥ pakṣāḥ/ rāgapakṣaḥ — kāmo matsaraḥ spṛhā tṛṣṇā lobha iti/ dveṣapakṣaḥ — krodha īrṣyā asūyā droho 'marṣa iti/ mohapakṣo
children.translated_text: Of these faults, there are three groups, three classes. The <s>rāga</s>-class: desire (<s>kāma</s>), covetousness (<s>matsara</s>), longing (<s>spṛhā</s>), craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), and greed (<s>lobha</s>). The <s>dveṣa</s>-class: anger (<s>krodha</s>), jealousy (<s>īrṣyā</s>), envy (<s>asūyā</s>), malice (<s>droha</s>), and resentment (<s>amarṣa</s>). The <s>moha</s>-class:

children.text: mithyājñānaṃ vicikitsā mānaḥ pramāda iti/ trairāśyān nopasaṅkhyāyante iti/ lakṣaṇasya tarhy abhedāt tritvam anupapannam? nānupapannam, rāgadveṣamohārthāntarabhāvāt;
children.translated_text: false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>), suspicion (<s>vicikitsā</s>), pride (<s>māna</s>), and heedlessness (<s>pramāda</s>). Because of the triad, they are not separately enumerated. But if the defining characteristics are not different, how is the threefold division tenable? It is tenable, because <s>rāga</s>, <s>dveṣa</s>, and <s>moha</s> are mutually distinct categories;

children.text: āsaktilakṣaṇo rāgaḥ, amarṣalakṣaṇo dveṣaḥ, mithyāpratipattilakṣaṇo moha iti/ etat pratyātmavedanīyaṃ sarvaśarīriṇām — vijānāty ayaṃ śarīrī rāgam utpannam
children.translated_text: <s>rāga</s> is characterized by clinging, <s>dveṣa</s> is characterized by resentment, <s>moha</s> is characterized by false apprehension. This is experienced individually by all embodied beings — the embodied being recognizes that attachment has arisen:
'There is in me, in my inner self, the nature of <s>rāga</s>'
— and also recognizes dispassion:
'There is not in me, in my inner self, the nature of <s>rāga</s>'

children.text: iti/ evam itarayor apīti/ mānerṣyāsūyāprabhṛtayas tu trairāśyam anupatitā iti nopasaṅkhyāyante//3//
children.translated_text: — and likewise for the other two. But pride, jealousy, envy, and the rest, having fallen within the triad, are not separately enumerated. // 4.1.3 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 4
Not so, because they have a single antidote. // 4.1.4 //

children.text: nārthāntaraṃ rāgādayaḥ/ kasmāt? ekapratyanīkabhāvāt — tattvajñānaṃ samyaṅmatir āryaprajñā sambodha ity ekam idaṃ pratyanīkaṃ trayāṇām iti//4//
children.translated_text: <s>Rāga</s> and the rest are not distinct categories. Why? Because they have a single antidote — <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality), right understanding, noble wisdom, enlightenment — this one thing is the antidote of all three. // 4.1.4 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
Not a reason, because of deviation. // 4.1.5 //

children.text: ekapratyanīkāḥ pṛthivyāṃ śyāmādayo 'gnisaṃyogenaikena, ekayonayaś ca pākajā iti//5//
children.translated_text: In the case of earth, blackness and the rest (qualities) have a single antidote — contact with fire — and they are of a single origin, being produced by baking; (yet they are distinct). // 4.1.5 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 6
And if there is indeed a distinction of categories —
Among them, <s>moha</s> (delusion) is the worst, because the other two do not arise in one who is not deluded. // 4.1.6 //

children.text: mohaḥ pāpaḥ, pāpataro vā dvāv abhipretyoktam/ kasmāt? nāmūḍhasyetarotpatteḥ —
children.translated_text: <s>Moha</s> is sinful, or rather the most sinful of the two (others) — this is stated with reference to both. Why? Because the other two do not arise in one who is not deluded —

children.text: amūḍhasya rāgadveṣā notpadyante mūḍhasya tu yathāsaṅkalpam utpattiḥ, viṣayeṣu rañjanīyāḥ saṅkalpā rāgahetavaḥ, kopanīyāḥ saṅkalpā dveṣahetavaḥ, ubhaye ca saṅkalpā na mithyāpratipattilakṣaṇatvān mohād anye, tāv imau mohayonī rāgadveṣāv iti/ tattvajñānāc ca mohanivṛttau rāgadveṣānutpattir ity ekapratyanīkabhāvopapattiḥ/ evaṃ ca kṛtvā tattvajñānād
children.translated_text: <s>rāga</s> and <s>dveṣa</s> do not arise in one who is not deluded, but in one who is deluded, they arise according to his imaginings. Imaginings that find objects attractive are the causes of <s>rāga</s>; imaginings that find objects irritating are the causes of <s>dveṣa</s>; and both types of imagining, being characterized by false apprehension, are not different from <s>moha</s>. Thus <s>rāga</s> and <s>dveṣa</s> are born of <s>moha</s>. And from the cessation of <s>moha</s> through <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality), <s>rāga</s> and <s>dveṣa</s> do not arise — and thus the tenability of a single antidote is established. And by doing so, from <s>tattvajñāna</s>,

through the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, faults, and false knowledge — each subsequent one ceasing from the cessation of its antecedent — <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) is attained.
This has been explained. // 4.1.6 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 7
Then it follows —
The faults are a distinct category because of the cause-and-effect relationship. // 4.1.7 //

children.text: anyad dhi nimittam anyac ca naimittikam iti doṣanimittatvād adoṣo moha iti//7//
children.translated_text: The cause is one thing and the effect is another — therefore, since <s>moha</s> is the cause of the faults (i.e., <s>rāga</s> and <s>dveṣa</s>), <s>moha</s> is not itself a fault but something different. // 4.1.7 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
No, because <s>moha</s> is included within the defining characteristic of a fault. // 4.1.8 //

children.text: pravarttanālakṣaṇā doṣā ity anena doṣalakṣaṇenāvarudhyate doṣeṣu moha iti//8//
children.translated_text: <s>Moha</s> is included among the faults by the defining characteristic: 'faults are characterized by incitement to activity.' // 4.1.8 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 9
And because the cause-and-effect relationship among things of the same class is not refuted. // 4.1.9 //

children.text: dravyāṇāṃ guṇānāṃ vānekavidhavikalpo nimittanaimittikabhāve tulyajātīyānāṃ dṛṣṭa iti//9//
children.translated_text: The manifold differentiation of substances and qualities in the cause-and-effect relationship among things of the same class is observed. // 4.1.9 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 10

children.text: doṣānantaraṃ pretyabhāvaḥ, tasyāsiddhir ātmano nityatvāt — na khalu nityaṃ kiṃcij jāyate mriyate vā iti janmamaraṇayor nityatvād ātmano 'nupapattiḥ, ubhayaṃ ca pretyabhāva iti tatrāyaṃ siddhānuvādaḥ —
children.translated_text: After the faults, <s>pretyabhāva</s> (rebirth) — its non-establishment would follow from the eternality of the <s>ātman</s>: since nothing eternal is born or dies, birth and death are untenable for the eternal <s>ātman</s>; and both (birth and death) constitute <s>pretyabhāva</s>. To this, this established position is restated —
<s>Pretyabhāva</s> (rebirth) is established because of the eternality of the <s>ātman</s>. // 4.1.10 //

children.text: nityo 'yam ātmā praiti pūrvaśarīraṃ jahāti mriyate iti, pretya ca pūrvaśarīraṃ hitvā
children.translated_text: This <s>ātman</s> is eternal — it departs, i.e., it abandons the previous body, i.e., it dies; and having departed, having abandoned the previous body,

children.text: bhavati jāyate śarīrāntaram upādatta iti/ tac caitad ubhayaṃ
children.translated_text: it comes into being, i.e., it is born, i.e., it takes up another body. And both of these —
re-birth after death is <s>pretyabhāva</s>.

children.text: ity atroktaṃ pūrvaśarīraṃ hitvā śarīrāntaropādānaṃ pretyabhāvaḥ iti tac caitannityatve sambhavatīti/ yasya tu sattvotpādaḥ sattvanirodhaḥ pretyabhāvaḥ tasya kṛtahānam akṛtābhyāgamaś ca doṣaḥ/ ucchedahetuvāde ṛṣyupadeśāś cānarthakā iti//10//
children.translated_text: Here it has been stated that <s>pretyabhāva</s> (afterlife existence) is the abandoning of the previous body and the taking up of another body, and this is possible when consciousness is permanent. But for one who holds that <s>pretyabhāva</s> is the origination and cessation of a being, there is the fault of loss of what was done and the occurrence of what was not done. And on the doctrine that postulates annihilation, the teachings of the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages) would be purposeless. // 10 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
If it is asked, how does origination occur? —
The manifest arises from the manifest, because of the authority of perception. // 4.1.11 //

children.text: kena prakāreṇa kiṃdharmakāt kāraṇād vyaktaṃ śarīrādy utpadyata iti? vyaktād bhūtasamākhyātāt pṛthivyāditaḥ paramasūkṣmān nityād vyaktaṃ śarīrendriyaviṣayopakaraṇādhāraṃ prajñātaṃ dravyam utpadyate/ vyaktaṃ ca khalv indriyagrāhyaṃ tatsāmānyāt kāraṇam api vyaktam/ kiṃ sāmānyam? rūpādiguṇayogaḥ rūpādiguṇayuktebhyaḥ pṛthivyādibhyo nityebhyo rūpādiguṇayuktaṃ śarīrādy utpadyate/
children.translated_text: By what manner, from a cause of what nature, does the manifest — body and the rest — originate? From the manifest, designated as elements — from the earth and the rest, which are supremely subtle and eternal — there originates the manifest substance that is known as body, sense organs, objects, instruments, and substratum. The manifest is indeed perceptible to the senses, and by that commonality, the cause too is manifest. What is the commonality? The possession of qualities such as color and the rest — from earth and the rest, which are eternal and possess qualities such as color, there originates the body and the rest, which possess qualities such as color.

children.text: pratyakṣaprāmāṇyāt — dṛṣṭo hi rūpādiguṇayuktebhyo mṛtprabhṛtibhyas tathābhūtasya dravyasyotpādaḥ, tena cādṛṣṭasyānumānam iti/ rūpādīnām anvayadarśanāt prakṛtivikārayoḥ, pṛthivyādīnāṃ nityānām atīndriyāṇāṃ kāraṇabhāvo 'numīyata iti//11//
children.translated_text: Because of the authority of perception — for the origination of such a substance from things possessing qualities such as color, like clay and the like, is observed; and by that, what is unobserved is inferred. From the observation of the continuity of color and the rest between material cause and modification, the causal status of the eternal, supersensible earth and the rest is inferred. // 11 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 12
Because a pot is not produced from a pot. // 4.1.12 //

children.text: idam api pratyakṣam — na khalu vyaktād ghaṭād vyakto ghaṭa utpadyamāno dṛśyate iti, vyaktād vyaktasyānutpattidarśanān na vyaktaṃ kāraṇam iti//12//
children.translated_text: This too is a matter of perception — a manifest pot is not seen being produced from a manifest pot. Since the non-production of a manifest thing from a manifest thing is observed, the manifest is not the cause. // 12 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
The production of a pot from the manifest is not refuted. // 4.1.13 //

children.text: na brūmaḥ sarvaṃ sarvasya kāraṇam iti, kin tu yad utpadyate vyaktaṃ dravyaṃ tat tathābhūtād evotpadyate iti/ vyaktaṃ ca tanmṛddravyaṃ kapālasaṃjñakaṃ yato ghaṭa utpadyate/ na caitannihnuvānaḥ kvacid abhyanujñāṃ labdhum arhatīti/ tad etat tattvam//13//
children.translated_text: We do not say that everything is the cause of everything. Rather, whatever manifest substance is produced, it is produced from something of the same kind. And the manifest clay-substance designated as potsherds is that from which a pot is produced. One who denies this does not deserve to gain acceptance anywhere. This is the truth of the matter. // 13 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 14
Hereafter, the views of the disputants are presented —
Existence arises from non-existence, because something comes into being only by destroying (its cause). // 4.1.14 //

children.text: asataḥ sad utpadyate ity ayaṃ pakṣaḥ/ kasmāt? upamṛdya prādurbhāvāt/ upamṛdya bījam aṅkura utpadyate nānupamṛdya, na ced vījopamardo 'ṅkurakāraṇam anupamarde 'pi bījasyāṅkurotpattiḥ syād iti//14//
children.translated_text: The thesis is: the existent arises from the non-existent. Why? Because something comes into being by destroying (its cause). A sprout arises by destroying the seed, not without destroying it. If the destruction of the seed were not the cause of the sprout, then even without the destruction of the seed, the sprout would arise. // 14 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
To this it is replied —
This usage is inapplicable because of self-contradiction. // 4.1.15 //

children.text: upamṛdya prādurbhāvād ity ayuktaḥ prayogo vyāghātāt/ yad upamṛdnāti na tad upamṛdya prādurbhavitum arhati vidyamānatvāt/ yac ca prādurbhavati na tenāprādurbhūtenāvidyamānenopamarda iti//15//
children.translated_text: The expression 'coming into being by destroying' is unjustified because of self-contradiction. That which destroys does not deserve to come into being by destroying, because it (already) exists. And that which comes into being — by that, which has not come into being and does not exist, there is no destruction. // 15 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 16
Because causal terms are used with reference to the past and future. // 4.1.16 //

children.text: atīte cānāgate cāvidyamāne kārakaśabdāḥ prayujyante/ putro janiṣyate, janiṣyamāṇaṃ putram abhinandati, putrasya janiṣyamāṇasya nāma karoti, abhūt kumbhaḥ, bhinnaṃ kumbham anuśocati, bhinnasya kumbhasya kapālāni, ajātāḥ putrāḥ pitaraṃ tāpayantīti bahulaṃ bhāktāḥ prayogā dṛśyante/ kā punar iyaṃ bhaktiḥ? ānantaryaṃ bhaktiḥ, ānantaryasāmarthyād upamṛdya prādurbhāvārthaḥ, prādurbhaviṣyann aṅkura upamṛdnātīti bhāktaṃ kartṛtvam iti//16//
children.translated_text: Causal terms are used with reference to what is past and future, which do not (presently) exist. 'A son will be born,' 'he rejoices at the son about to be born,' 'he names the son about to be born'; 'the pot existed,' 'he mourns the broken pot,' 'the potsherds of the broken pot'; 'unborn sons torment the father' — such figurative usages are abundantly observed. What then is this figuration? Figuration is (based on) temporal contiguity; by the capacity of contiguity, it conveys the meaning of 'coming into being by destroying' — 'the sprout that is about to come into being destroys' — this is figurative agency. // 16 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 17
Not so, because nothing is produced from what has been destroyed. // 4.1.17 //

children.text: na vinaṣṭād bījād aṅkura utpadyate iti tasmān nābhāvād bhāvotpattir iti//17//
children.translated_text: A sprout is not produced from a destroyed seed; therefore, existence does not arise from non-existence. // 17 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 18
There is no refutation, because of the indication of sequence. // 4.1.18 //

children.text: upamardaprādurbhāvayoḥ paurvāparyaniyamaḥ kramaḥ, sa khalv abhāvād bhāvotpatter hetur nirdiśyate; sa ca na pratiṣidhyate iti/ vyāhatavyūhānām avayavānāṃ pūrvavyūhanivṛttau vyūhāntarād dravyaniṣpattir nābhāvāt/ bījāvayavāḥ kutaścin nimittāt prādurbhūtakriyāḥ pūrvavyūhaṃ jahati vyūhāntaraṃ cāpadyante vyūhāntarād aṅkura utpadyate/ dṛśyante khalu avayavās tatsaṃyogāś cāṅkurotpattihetavaḥ/ na cānivṛtte pūrvavyūhe bījāvayavānāṃ śakyaṃ vyūhāntareṇa bhavitum ity upamardaprādurbhāvayoḥ paurvāparyaniyamaḥ kramaḥ,
children.translated_text: Sequence is the fixed order of priority and posteriority between destruction and coming-into-being, and it is adduced as the reason for the arising of existence from non-existence; and that is not refuted. The production of a substance from a different arrangement of parts whose (previous) arrangement has been disrupted, upon the cessation of the prior arrangement, is not from non-existence. The parts of the seed, their activity having arisen from some cause, abandon their prior arrangement and assume another arrangement; from that other arrangement, the sprout is produced. Indeed, the parts and their conjunctions are seen to be the causes of the sprout's production. And without the cessation of the prior arrangement of the seed's parts, another arrangement cannot come about — hence the fixed order of priority and posteriority between destruction and coming-into-being constitutes sequence.

children.text: tasmān nābhāvād bhāvotpattir iti/ na cānyad bījāvayavebhyo 'ṅkurotpattikāraṇam ity upapadyte bījopādānaniyama iti//18//
children.translated_text: Therefore, existence does not arise from non-existence. And no cause of the sprout's production other than the parts of the seed is tenable — hence the restriction to the seed as material cause. // 18 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 19
Now another says —
<s>Īśvara</s> (God) is the cause, because the actions of men are seen to be fruitless. // 4.1.19 //

children.text: puruṣo 'yaṃ samīhamāno nāvaśyaṃ samīhāphalaṃ prāpnoti tenānumīyate parādhīnaṃ puruṣasya karmaphalārādhanam iti, yadadhīnaṃ sa īśvaraḥ/ tasmād īśvaraḥ kāraṇam iti//19//
children.translated_text: This person, though striving, does not necessarily obtain the fruit of his striving; from this it is inferred that the attainment of the fruit of man's action depends on another; that on which it depends is <s>Īśvara</s>. Therefore <s>Īśvara</s> is the cause. // 19 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 20
Not so, because without human effort there is no production of fruit. // 4.1.20 //

children.text: īśvarādhīnā cet phalaniṣpattiḥ syād api tarhi puruṣasya samīhām antareṇa phalaṃ niṣpadyeteti//20//
children.translated_text: If the production of fruit depended on <s>Īśvara</s>, then fruit would be produced even without the person's effort. // 20 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
This is a non-reason, because (the fruit) is caused by Him. // 4.1.21 //

children.text: puruṣakāram īśvaro 'nugṛhṇāti, phalāya puruṣasya yatamānasyeśvaraḥ phalaṃ sampādayatīti/ yadā na sampādayati tadā puruṣakarmāphalaṃ bhavatīti/ tasmād īśvara

children.translated_text: being the causer (of the fruit), is a non-reason —

children.text:
puruṣakarmābhāve phalāniṣpatter iti/
guṇaviśiṣṭam ātmāntaram īśvaraḥ/ tasya ātmakalpāt kalpāntarānupapattiḥ, adharmamithyājñānapramādahānyā dharmajñānasamādhisampadā ca viśiṣṭam ātmāntaram īśvaraḥ,
children.translated_text: because without human effort there is no production of fruit. <s>Īśvara</s> is another self distinguished by (superior) qualities. For Him, since He is of the nature of a self, no other nature is tenable; distinguished by the absence of <s>adharma</s> (demerit), false knowledge, negligence, and loss, and by the possession of <s>dharma</s> (merit), knowledge, <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), and accomplishment — He is another self, <s>Īśvara</s>.

<s>Īśvara</s> favors human effort; for one who strives toward a fruit, <s>Īśvara</s> brings about the fruit. When He does not bring it about, then human action becomes fruitless. Therefore, <s>Īśvara</s>

children.text: tasya ca dharmasamādhiphalam aṇimādyaṣṭavidham aiśvaryam/ saṅkalpānuvidhāyī cāsya dharmaḥ pratyātmavṛttīn dharmādharmasañcayān pṛthivyādīni ca bhūtāni pravartayati/ evaṃ ca svakṛtābhyāgamasyālopena nirmāṇaprākāmyam īśvarasya svakṛtakarmaphalaṃ veditavyam/ āptakalpaś cāyam — yathā pitāpatyānāṃ tathā pitṛbhūta īśvaro bhūtānām/ na cātmakalpād anyaḥ kalpaḥ sambhavati/ na tāvad asya buddhiṃ vinā kaścid dharmo liṅgabhūtaḥ śakya upapādayitum/ āgamāc ca draṣṭā boddhā
children.translated_text: And His sovereignty is of eight kinds, beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness), which is the fruit of <s>dharma</s> and <s>samādhi</s>. And His <s>dharma</s>, which follows His will, sets in motion the streams of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> of individual selves and the elements such as earth and the rest. Thus, without the loss of what He Himself has accomplished, the creative freedom of <s>Īśvara</s> should be understood as the fruit of His own <s>karma</s>. And He is like an authoritative teacher — just as a father is to his children, so is <s>Īśvara</s>, being a progenitor, to all beings. No other nature than that of a self is possible for Him. First, without cognition, no attribute of His that serves as a mark can be established. And from scripture, He is a seer, a knower,
omniscient —

children.text: īśvara iti/ buddhyādibhiś cātmaliṅgair nirupākhyam īśvaraṃ pratyakṣānumānāgamaviṣayātītaṃ kaḥ śakta upapādayitum/
children.translated_text: <s>Īśvara</s>. And who is able to establish an <s>Īśvara</s> that is indescribable and beyond the scope of perception, inference, and scripture, by means of the marks of the self such as cognition and the rest?

children.text: svakṛtābhyāgamalopena ca pravartamānasyāsya yad uktaṃ pratiṣedhajātam akarmanimitte śarīrasarge tat sarvaṃ prasajyate iti//21//
children.translated_text: And for One who operates without the loss of what He Himself has accomplished, all the objections that were stated regarding the creation of bodies without <s>karma</s> as the cause apply equally. // 21 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 22
Now another says —
Things arise without a cause, as seen from the sharpness of thorns and the like. // 4.1.22 //
The origination of bodies and the rest is without a cause. Why? As seen from the sharpness of thorns and the like. The

children.text: taikṣṇyam, parvatadhātūnāṃ citratā, grāvṇāṃ ślakṣṇatā, nirnimittaṃ ca upādānavac ca dṛṣṭaṃ tathā śarīrādisargo .pīti//22//
children.translated_text: sharpness of thorns, the variegated colors of mountain minerals, the smoothness of stones — these are seen to be without a cause yet possessing a material substratum; similarly, the creation of bodies and the rest is also (without a cause). // 22 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 23
Not from the absence of a cause, because the absence-of-cause itself has a cause. // 4.1.23 //

children.text: animittato bhāvotpattir ity ucyate yataś cotpadyate tannimittam/ animittasya nimittatvān nānimittā bhāvotpattir iti//23//
children.translated_text: It is said that things arise without a cause; but that from which something arises is its cause. Since the absence-of-cause itself is a cause, the arising of things is not without a cause. // 23 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
There is no refutation, because cause and absence-of-cause are different things. // 4.1.24 //

children.text: anyad dhi nimittam anyac ca nimittapratyākhyānam, na ca pratyākhyānam eva pratyākhyeyaṃ
children.translated_text: A cause is one thing and the denial of a cause is another; the denial itself does not become what is denied,

children.text: yathānudakaḥ kamaṇḍalur iti nodakapratiṣedha udakaṃ bhavatīti/ sa khalv ayaṃ vādo 'karmanimittaḥ śarīrādisarga ity etasmān na bhidyate, abhedāt tatpratiṣedhenaiva pratiṣiddho veditavya iti//24//
children.translated_text: just as a waterless water-vessel — the negation of water does not become water. This argument — that the creation of bodies and the rest is without <s>karma</s> as a cause — is not different from the previous one; being non-different, it should be understood as refuted by the refutation of the former. // 24 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 25
Others, however, maintain —
Everything is impermanent, because everything has the nature of origination and destruction. // 4.1.25 //

children.text: kim anityaṃ nāma? yasya kadācid bhāvas tad anityam/ utpattidharmakam anutpannaṃ nāsti vināśadharmakaṃ ca vinaṣṭaṃ nāsti/ kiṃ punaḥ sarvam? bhautikaṃ ca śarīrādi
children.translated_text: What does 'impermanent' mean? That which exists only sometimes is impermanent. What has the nature of origination does not exist when unoriginated; and what has the nature of destruction does not exist when destroyed. What then is 'everything'? Both the material — body and the rest —

children.text: abhautikaṃ ca buddhyādi, tad ubhayam utpattivināśadharmakaṃ vijñāyate, tasmāt tat sarvam anityam iti//25//
children.translated_text: and the non-material — cognition and the rest; both are known to have the nature of origination and destruction; therefore all of that is impermanent. // 25 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 26
Not so, because of the impermanence of impermanence itself. // 4.1.26 //

children.text: yadi tāvat sarvasyānityatā nityā, tannityatvān na sarvam anityam/ athānityā tasyām avidyamānāyāṃ sarvaṃ nityam iti//26//
children.translated_text: If the impermanence of everything is permanent, then since that is permanent, not everything is impermanent. If it is impermanent, then when it does not exist, everything is permanent. // 26 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
The impermanence of that (impermanence) is like fire perishing along with what is to be burnt. // 4.1.27 //

children.text: tasyā anityatāyā apy anityatvam/ katham? yathā agnir dāhyaṃ vināśyānuvinaśyati evaṃ sarvasyānityatā sarvaṃ vināśyānuvinaśyatīti//27//
children.translated_text: That impermanence too is impermanent. How? Just as fire perishes along with what is to be burnt, so the impermanence of everything perishes along with everything that is to be destroyed. // 27 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
The permanent is not refuted, because things are established in accordance with how they are apprehended. // 4.1.28 //

children.text: ayaṃ khalu vādo nityaṃ pratyācaṣṭe, nityasya ca pratyākhyānam anupapannam/ kasmāt? yathopalabdhi vyavasthānāt/ yasyotpattivināśadharmakatvam upalabhyate pramāṇatas tad anityam,
children.translated_text: This argument indeed denies the permanent; but the denial of the permanent is untenable. Why? Because things are established in accordance with how they are apprehended. That whose nature of origination and destruction is apprehended through <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) is impermanent;

children.text: yasya nopalabhyate tadviparītam/ na ca paramasūkṣmāṇāṃ bhūtānām ākāśakāladigātmamanasāṃ tadguṇānāṃ ca keṣāñcit sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyānāṃ cotpattivināśadharmakatvaṃ pramāṇata upalabhyate, tasmān nityāny etānīti//28//
children.translated_text: that whose (nature of origination and destruction) is not apprehended is the opposite. And the nature of origination and destruction is not apprehended through <s>pramāṇas</s> for the supremely subtle elements, <s>ākāśa</s> (space), <s>kāla</s> (time), <s>dik</s> (direction), <s>ātman</s> (self), <s>manas</s> (mind), some of their qualities, and some of the universals, particulars, and inherence relations. Therefore these are permanent. // 28 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 29
This is another extreme view —
Everything is permanent, because the five elements are permanent. // 4.1.29 //

children.text: bhūtamātram idaṃ sarvaṃ tāni ca nityāni bhūtocchedānupapatter iti//29//
children.translated_text: All this is nothing but elements, and they are permanent, because the destruction of elements is untenable. // 29 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
Not so, because the causes of origination and destruction are apprehended. // 4.1.30 //

children.text: utpattikāraṇaṃ copalabhyate vināśakāraṇaṃ ca, tat sarvanityatve vyāhanyate iti//30//
children.translated_text: Both the cause of origination and the cause of destruction are apprehended; this contradicts the view that everything is permanent. // 30 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 31
There is no refutation, because (origination and destruction) are subsumed under the definition of elements. // 4.1.31 //

children.text: yasyotpattivināśakāraṇam upalabhyate iti manyase, na tad bhūtalakṣaṇahīnam arthāntaraṃ gṛhyate, bhūtalakṣaṇāvarodhād bhūtamātram idam ity ukto 'yaṃ pratiṣedha iti//31//
children.translated_text: What you consider to be that whose cause of origination and destruction is apprehended — that is not grasped as something different, lacking the defining characteristics of elements; because it is subsumed under the definition of elements, all this is nothing but elements — this is the stated refutation. // 31 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 32
Not so, because the origination and its cause are apprehended. // 4.1.32 //

children.text:
kāraṇasamānaguṇasyotpattiḥ kāraṇaṃ copalabhyate/ na caitad ubhayaṃ nityaviṣayam, na cotpattitatkāraṇopalabdhiḥ śakyā pratyākhyātum, na cāviṣayā kācid upalabdhiḥ/ upalabdhisāmarthyāt kāraṇena samānaguṇaṃ kāryam utpadyate ity anumīyate, sa khalūpalabdher viṣaya iti/ evaṃ ca tallakṣaṇāvarodhopapattir iti/
utpattivināśakāraṇaprayuktasya jñātuḥ prayatno dṛṣṭa iti/ prasiddhaś cāvayavī taddharmā/ utpattivināśadharmā cāvayavī siddha iti/
children.translated_text: There is origination of that which has qualities similar to the cause, and the cause is perceived. Neither of these two pertains to eternal things, nor can the perception of origination and its cause be denied, nor is any perception without an object. From the capacity of perception, it is inferred that an effect having qualities similar to the cause is produced — that indeed is the object of perception. Thus the inclusion under that definition is established. The effort of a knower prompted by origination, destruction, and causation is observed. And the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) possessing those properties is well-known. Thus the composite whole possessing the properties of origination and destruction is established.

children.text:
śabdakarmabuddhyādīnāṃ cāvyāptiḥ/ pañcabhūtanityatvāt tallakṣaṇāvarodhāc cety anena śabdakarmabuddhisukhaduḥkhecchādveṣaprayatnāś ca na vyāptāḥ tasmād anekāntaḥ/
svapnaviṣayābhimānavan mithyopalabdhir iti cet bhūtopalabdhau tulyam/ yathā svapne viṣayābhimāna evam utpattikāraṇābhimāna iti/ evaṃ caitad bhūtopalabdhau tulyaṃ pṛthivyādyupalabdhir api svapnaviṣayābhimānavat prasajyate/
children.translated_text: And there is non-pervasion with respect to <s>śabda</s> (sound), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>buddhi</s> (cognition), and so forth. Because only the five elements are eternal and because of the inclusion under that definition, <s>śabda</s>, <s>karma</s>, <s>buddhi</s>, <s>sukha</s> (pleasure), <s>duḥkha</s> (pain), <s>icchā</s> (desire), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>prayatna</s> (effort) are not covered; therefore it is a non-exclusive thesis (<s>anekānta</s>). If one objects that perception is false, like the imagined objects in a dream — the same applies to the perception of elements. Just as in a dream there is merely the imagination of objects, so too there would be merely the imagination of origination and causation. And this equally applies to the perception of elements: the perception of earth and so forth would also be subject to the same objection of being like imagined dream-objects.

children.text: pṛthivyādyabhāve sarvavyavahāravilopa iti cet tad itaratra samānam — utpattivināśakāraṇopalabdhiviṣayasyāpy abhāve sarvavyavahāravilopa iti, so 'yaṃ nityānām atīndriyatvād aviṣayatvāc cotpattivināśayoḥ svapnaviṣayābhimānavad ity ahetur iti//32//
children.translated_text: If one says that in the absence of earth and so forth all practical activity would cease — the same applies to the other side: in the absence of the objects of perception of origination, destruction, and causation too, all practical activity would cease. Thus this argument — that eternal things, being beyond the senses and origination and destruction being without objects, are like imagined dream-objects — is a non-reason (<s>ahetu</s>). //32//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 33

children.text: avasthitasyopādānasya dharmamātraṃ nivartate dharmamātram upajāyate sa khalūtpattivināśayor viṣayaḥ/
children.translated_text: Of a persisting substrate (<s>upādāna</s>), only a property ceases and only a property arises — that is the object of origination and destruction.

children.text: yac copajāyate tat prāg apy upajananād asti, yac ca nivartate tan nivṛttam apy astīti, evaṃ ca sarvasya nityatvam iti?
children.translated_text: And that which arises existed even before its arising, and that which ceases continues to exist even after its cessation — thus everything is eternal?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.33: Not so, because determination would be impossible.

children.text: ayam upajanaḥ iyaṃ nivṛttir iti vyavasthā nopapadyate, upajātanivṛttayor vidyamānatvāt/ ayaṃ dharma upajāto 'yaṃ nivṛtta iti sadbhāvāviśeṣād avyavasthā, idānīm upajananivṛttī nedānīm iti kālavyavasthā nopapadyate sarvadā vidyamānatvāt asya dharmasyopajananivṛttī nāsyeti vyavasthānupapattiḥ,
children.translated_text: The determination 'this is origination, this is cessation' would be impossible, since both the arisen and the ceased would be existent. Because there is no distinction in existence between 'this property has arisen' and 'this has ceased,' there would be indeterminacy. The temporal determination — 'origination and cessation occur now, not now' — would be impossible because of always being existent. The determination that 'origination and cessation belong to this property but not to that' would be impossible,

children.text: ubhyor aviśeṣāt/ anāgato 'tīta iti ca kālavyavasthānupapattiḥ, vartamānasya sadbhāvalakṣaṇatvāt/ avidyamānasyātmalābha upajano vidyamānasyātmahānaṃ nivṛttir ity etasmin sati naite doṣāḥ/ tasmād yad uktaṃ prāg apy upajanād asti nivṛttaṃ cāsti tad ayuktam iti//33//
children.translated_text: because there is no distinction between the two. And the temporal determination of 'future' and 'past' would be impossible, since the present is defined by existence. When there is the understanding that origination is the self-attainment of what was non-existent and cessation is the self-loss of what was existent, then these defects do not arise. Therefore what was said — that something exists even before its arising and continues to exist after cessation — is untenable. //33//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 34
Here is another extreme view —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.34: Everything is separate, because of the separateness of the defining characteristics of entities.

children.text: sarvaṃ nānā na kaścid eko bhāvo vidyate/ kasmāt? bhāvalakṣaṇapṛthaktvāt — bhāvasya lakṣaṇam abhidhānam, yena lakṣyate bhāvaḥ sa samākhyāśabdaḥ, tasya pṛthagviṣayatvāt/
children.translated_text: Everything is diverse; no single entity exists. Why? Because of the separateness of the defining characteristics of entities — the defining characteristic of an entity is its designation (<s>abhidhāna</s>), that by which the entity is characterized is the naming word (<s>samākhyā-śabda</s>), and because that has separate objects.

children.text: sarvo bhāvasamākhyāśabdaḥ samūhavācī, kumbha iti saṃjñāśabdo gandharasarūpasparśasamūhe budhnapārśvagrīvādisamūhe ca varttate, nidarśanamātraṃ cedam iti//34//
children.translated_text: Every naming word for an entity denotes an aggregate (<s>samūha</s>). The designation '<s>kumbha</s>' (pot) applies to the aggregate of smell, taste, form, and touch, as well as to the aggregate of bottom, sides, neck, and so forth. And this is merely an illustration. //34//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 35
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.35: Not so, because a single entity is constituted from multiple defining characteristics.

children.text: anekavidhalakṣaṇair iti madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ/ gandhādibhiś ca guṇair budhnādibhiś cāvayavaiḥ sambaddha eko bhāvo niṣpadyate, guṇavyatiriktaṃ ca dravyam avayavātiriktaś cāvayavīti/ vibhaktanyāyaṃ caitad ubhayam iti//35//
children.translated_text: 'By characteristics of multiple kinds' — this is a compound with elision of the middle term. A single entity is constituted from being connected with qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) such as smell and so forth, and with parts (<s>avayava</s>) such as bottom and so forth. And <s>dravya</s> (substance) is distinct from <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is distinct from the parts (<s>avayava</s>). And both of these have been established through separate reasoning. //35//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 36
Moreover —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.36: Because of the fixedness of designation, the denial itself is untenable.

children.text:
na kaścid eko bhāva ity ayuktaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ kasmāt? lakṣaṇavyavasthānād eva/ yad iha lakṣaṇaṃ bhāvasya saṃjñāśabdabhūtaṃ tad ekasmin vyavasthitam, yaṃ kumbham adrākṣaṃ taṃ spṛśāmi yam evāsprākṣaṃ taṃ paśyāmīti nāṇusamūho gṛhyate iti/ aṇusamūhe cāgṛhyamāṇe yad gṛhyate tad ekam eveti/
athāpy etad anūktam nāsty eko bhāvo yasmāt samudāyaḥ, ekānupapatter nāsty eva samūhaḥ — nāsty eko bhāvo yasmāt samūhe bhāvaśabdaprayogaḥ;ekasya cānupapatteḥ
children.translated_text: The denial that 'no single entity exists' is untenable. Why? Precisely because of the fixedness of designation. The defining characteristic of an entity, being a designation-word, is fixed in a single thing — 'the pot I saw is the same I touch, the very one I touched is the one I see' — thus it is not an aggregate of atoms that is apprehended. And when an aggregate of atoms is not apprehended, what is apprehended is a single entity. Furthermore, even this has been stated: 'there is no single entity because it is an aggregate' — since a single thing is impossible, the aggregate itself does not exist — 'there is no single entity because the word for entity is used for the aggregate'; and since a single thing is impossible,

children.text: samūho nopapadyate ekasamuccayo hi samūha iti/ vyāhatatvād anupapannaṃ — nāsty eko bhāva iti yasya pratiṣedhaḥ pratijñāyate, samūhe bhāvaśabdaprayogād iti hetuṃ bruvatā sa evābhyanujñāyate, ekasamuccayo hi samūha iti/ samūhe bhāvaśabdaprayogād iti ca samūham āśritya pratyekaṃ samūhipratiṣedho nāsty eko bhāva iti/ so 'yam ubhayato vyāghātād yatkiñcanavāda iti//36//
children.translated_text: an aggregate is impossible, for an aggregate is a collection of single things. This is untenable due to self-contradiction: one who asserts the denial 'there is no single entity' and then states the reason 'because the word for entity is used for the aggregate' thereby admits the very thing denied, since an aggregate is a collection of single things. And 'because the word for entity is used for the aggregate' — relying on the aggregate, one denies each individual member: 'there is no single entity.' This is mere arbitrary assertion (<s>yatkiñcanavāda</s>) because of contradiction on both sides. //36//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
Here is another extreme view —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.37: Everything is non-existent (<s>abhāva</s>), because of the established mutual non-existence among entities.

children.text: yāvad bhāvajātaṃ tat sarvam abhāvaḥ/ kasmāt? bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddheḥ/

children.translated_text: A cow is non-existent as a horse,
a cow is non-horse,
a horse is non-existent as a cow, a horse is non-cow —

children.text: ity asatpratyayasya pratiṣedhasya ca bhāvaśabdena sāmānādhikaraṇyāt sarvam abhāva iti//37//
children.translated_text: thus, because the cognition of non-existence and the negation are co-referential with the word for entity (<s>bhāva-śabda</s>), everything is <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence). //37//
Whatever class of entities there is, all of it is non-existence. Why? Because of the established mutual non-existence among entities.
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 38

children.text: pratijñāvākye padayoḥ pratijñāhetvoś ca vyāghātād ayuktam/ anekasyāśeṣatā sarvaśabdasyārtho, bhāvapratiṣedhaś cābhāvaśabdasyārthaḥ/ pūrvaṃ sopākhyam uttaraṃ nirupākhyaṃ tatra
children.translated_text: This is untenable because of the contradiction in the words of the thesis, and the contradiction between the thesis and the reason. The meaning of the word 'sarva' (all) is a plurality without remainder, and the meaning of the word '<s>abhāva</s>' is the negation of <s>bhāva</s> (existence). The former has designation (<s>sopākhya</s>), the latter is without designation (<s>nirupākhya</s>) — in that case,

children.text:
samupākhyāyamānaṃ kathaṃ nirupākhyam abhāvaḥ syād iti? na jātv abhāvo nirupākhyo 'nekatayāśeṣatayā śakyaḥ pratijñātum iti/ sarvam etad abhāva iti cet — yad idaṃ sarvam iti manyase tadabhāva iti? evaṃ cet anivṛtto vyāghātaḥ, anekam aśeṣaṃ ceti nābhāve pratyayena śakyaṃ bhavitum/ asti cāyaṃ pratyayaḥ sarvam iti, tasmān nābhāva iti/
pratijñāhetvoś ca vyāghātaḥ — sarvam abhāva iti bhāvapratiṣedhaḥ pratijñā, bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddher iti hetuḥ/ bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvam anujñāyāśritya ca itaretarābhāvasiddhyā sarvam abhāva ity ucyate/ yadi sarvam abhāvo bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddher iti nopapadyate/ atha bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddhiḥ, sarvam abhāva iti nopapadyate/
children.translated_text: how can that which is being designated be <s>abhāva</s>, which is without designation? <s>Abhāva</s>, being without designation, can never be asserted as a plurality without remainder. If one says 'all this is <s>abhāva</s>' — do you mean that what you consider to be 'all' is non-existent? If so, the contradiction is not resolved, for the cognition 'all' as a plurality without remainder cannot pertain to non-existence. Yet this cognition 'all' does exist; therefore it is not <s>abhāva</s>. And there is contradiction between the thesis and the reason: 'everything is <s>abhāva</s>' — the negation of <s>bhāva</s> — is the thesis; 'because of the established mutual non-existence among entities' is the reason. Having admitted mutual non-existence among entities and relying upon it, one says 'everything is <s>abhāva</s>' through that mutual non-existence. If everything were <s>abhāva</s>, the statement 'because of the established mutual non-existence among entities' would be impossible. But if mutual non-existence among entities is established, then 'everything is <s>abhāva</s>' is impossible.
And the connection with the <s>sūtra</s> is as follows:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.38: Not so, because entities are established through their own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>).

children.text: na sarvam abhāvaḥ/ kasmāt? svena bhāvena sadbhāvād bhāvānām/ svena dharmeṇa bhāvā bhavantīti pratijñāyate/ kaś ca svo dharmo bhāvānām? dravyaguṇakarmaṇāṃ sadādisāmānyam, dravyāṇāṃ kriyāvad ityevamādiviśeṣaḥ, sparśaparyantāḥ pṛthivyā iti ca; pratyekaṃ cānanto bhedaḥ/ sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyānāṃ ca viśiṣṭā dharmā gṛhyante/
children.translated_text: Not everything is <s>abhāva</s>. Why? Because entities exist by their own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>). It is maintained that entities exist by their own properties. And what is the own property of entities? For <s>dravya</s> (substance), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and <s>karma</s> (action), the universals (<s>sāmānya</s>) beginning with existence (<s>sat</s>); for substances, the particulars (<s>viśeṣa</s>) such as 'possessing action' and so forth; and for earth, those ending with touch; and individually the distinctions are endless. And for <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), distinctive properties are apprehended.

children.text:
so 'yam abhāvasya nirupākhyatvāt sampratyāyako 'rthabhedo na syāt? asti tv ayam, tasmān na sarvam abhāva iti/
atha vā na svabhāvasiddher bhāvānām iti svarūpasiddher iti/ gaur iti prayujyamāne śabde jātiviśiṣṭaṃ dravyaṃ gṛhyate, nābhāvamātram/ yadi ca sarvam abhāvaḥ gaur ity abhāvaḥ pratīyeta, gośabdena cābhāva ucyeta/ yasmāt tu gośabdaprayoge dravyaviśeṣaḥ pratīyate nābhāvas tasmād ayuktam iti/
atha vā na svabhāvasiddher iti/ asan gaur aśvātmaneti gavātmanā kasmān nocyate? avacanād gavātmanā gaur astīti svabhāvasiddhiḥ, anaśvo 'śva iti vā gaur agaur iti vā kasmān nocyate? avacanāt svena rūpeṇa vidyamānatā dravyasyeti vijñāyate/
children.translated_text: Since <s>abhāva</s> is without designation (<s>nirupākhya</s>), could there be no communicable difference of meaning? But there is such difference; therefore not everything is <s>abhāva</s>. Alternatively, 'because entities are established through their own nature' means established through their own form (<s>svarūpa</s>). When the word 'cow' is used, a substance qualified by the universal (<s>jāti</s>) is apprehended, not mere non-existence. If everything were <s>abhāva</s>, upon hearing 'cow' one would cognize non-existence, and by the word 'cow' non-existence would be denoted. But since upon the use of the word 'cow' a particular substance is cognized, not non-existence, therefore this view is untenable. Alternatively, 'because of establishment through own nature': 'a cow is non-existent as a horse' — why is it not said 'as a cow'? Because it is not said, there is establishment of own nature — 'a cow exists as a cow.' And why is it not said 'a horse is non-horse' or 'a cow is non-cow'? Because it is not said, it is understood that a substance exists by its own form.

children.text: avyatirekapratiṣedhe ca bhāvena asatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇyam bhāve saṃyogādisambandho vyatirekaḥ/ atra avyatirekaḥ abhedākhyasambandhaḥ tatpratiṣedhe sadā ca asatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇyam, yathā na santi kuṇḍe badarāṇīti/ asan gaur aśvātmanā anaśvo gaur iti ca gavāśvayor avyatirekaḥ pratiṣidhyate gavāśvayor ekatvaṃ nāstīti/ tasmin pratiṣidhyamāne bhāvena gavā sāmānādhikaraṇyam asatpratyayasya asan gaur aśvātmaneti, yathā na santi kuṇḍe badarāṇīti kuṇḍe badarasaṃyoge pratiṣidhyamāne sadbhir asatpratyayasya sāmānādhikaraṇyam iti//38//
children.translated_text: And regarding the co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with the entity when non-differentiation is negated: in <s>bhāva</s> (entity), the relation of conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and so forth is differentiation (<s>vyatireka</s>). Here, non-differentiation is the relation called identity (<s>abheda</s>). When that is negated, the cognition of non-existence is always co-referential, as in 'there are no <s>badara</s> (jujubes) in the pot.' 'A cow is non-existent as a horse, a cow is non-horse' — what is negated is the non-differentiation of cow and horse, meaning the identity of cow and horse does not exist. When that is negated, the co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with the entity, the cow, is like 'there are no jujubes in the pot' — when the conjunction of jujubes in the pot is negated, the cognition of non-existence is co-referential with the existing things. //38//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 39
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.39: There is no establishment through own nature, because of relativity (<s>āpekṣikatva</s>).

children.text: apekṣākṛtam āpekṣikam/ hrasvāpekṣākṛtaṃ dīrghaṃ dīrghāpekṣākṛtaṃ hrasvam, na svenātmanāvasthitaṃ kiñcit/ kasmāt? apekṣāsāmarthyāt/ tasmān na svabhāvasiddhir bhāvānām iti//39//
children.translated_text: That which is produced by relation (<s>apekṣā</s>) is relative (<s>āpekṣika</s>). Long is produced by relation to short, and short is produced by relation to long — nothing is established by its own nature. Why? Because of the capacity of mutual relation. Therefore there is no establishment through own nature of entities. //39//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 40
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.40: This is untenable because of self-contradiction.

children.text: yadi hrasvāpekṣākṛtaṃ dīrghaṃ hrasvam anāpekṣikam/ kim idānīm apekṣya hrasvam iti gṛhyate? atha dīrghāpekṣākṛtaṃ hrasvam, dīrgham anāpekṣikam? evam itaretarāśrayayor ekābhāve anyatarābhāvād ubhayābhāva iti apekṣāvyavasthānupapannā/
children.translated_text: If long is produced by relation to short, then short would be non-relative. On what basis then is it apprehended as short? But if short is produced by relation to long, then long would be non-relative. Thus, since each depends on the other, in the absence of one the other would be absent, and both would be absent — so the determination of relativity is impossible.

children.text: svabhāvasiddhāv asatyāṃ samayoḥ parimaṇḍalayor vā dravyayor āpekṣike dīrghatvahrasvatve kasmān na bhavataḥ? apekṣāyām anapekṣāyāṃ ca dravyayor abhedaḥ/ yāvatī dravye apekṣamāṇe tāvatī evānapekṣamāṇe nānyataratra bhedaḥ/ āpekṣikatve tu saty anyataratra viśeṣopajanaḥ syād iti/
children.translated_text: If establishment through own nature does not hold, why do relative length and shortness not apply to two equal or spherical substances? There is no difference in the substances whether related or unrelated — the substance is the same whether in relation or not, with no distinction in either case. But if relativity held, there should be the arising of a distinguishing feature in one of the two.

children.text: kim apekṣāsāmarthyam iti cet? dvayor grahaṇe 'tiśayagrahaṇopapattiḥ/ dve dravye paśyann ekatra vidyamānam atiśayaṃ gṛhṇāti tad dīrgham iti vyavasyati, yac ca hīnaṃ gṛhṇāti tad dhrasvam iti vyavasyatīti/ etac cāpekṣāsāmarthyam iti//40//
children.translated_text: If one asks what the capacity of relativity is: when two things are perceived, the apprehension of superiority is possible. Seeing two substances, one apprehends the superiority present in one and determines it to be long, and apprehends the inferiority and determines it to be short. This is the capacity of relativity. //40//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 41
Now these are the fixed-number doctrines (<s>saṅkhyaikāntavāda</s>) — Everything is one, because there is no distinction in existence (<s>sat</s>).

children.text: sarvaṃ dvedhā nityānityabhedāt/ sarvaṃ tredhā jñātā jñānaṃ jñeyam iti/ sarvaṃ caturddhā pramātā pramāṇaṃ prameyaṃ pramitir iti/ evaṃ yathāsambhavam anye 'pīti/ tatra parīkṣā —
children.translated_text: Everything is twofold, because of the division into eternal and non-eternal. Everything is threefold: knower, knowledge, and the knowable. Everything is fourfold: the cognizer (<s>pramātā</s>), the means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>), the object of cognition (<s>prameya</s>), and the resultant cognition (<s>pramiti</s>). And similarly others as applicable. Regarding these, the examination:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.41: The fixed-number doctrines (<s>saṅkhyaikānta</s>) are not established, because of the impossibility and possibility of the reason.

children.text: yadi sādhyasādhanayor nānātvam, ekānto na siddhyati vyatirekāt/ atha
children.translated_text: If there is difference between what is to be established (<s>sādhya</s>) and the means of establishment (<s>sādhana</s>), the doctrine of oneness is not established, because of the distinction. But if

children.text: sādhyasādhanayor abhedaḥ? evam apy ekānto na sidhyati sādhanābhāvāt, na hi hetum antareṇa kasyacit siddhir iti//41//
children.translated_text: there is no difference between <s>sādhya</s> and <s>sādhana</s>? Even so, the doctrine of oneness is not established, because of the absence of the means of proof — for without a reason, nothing whatsoever can be established. //41//
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 42
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.42: Not so, because of the relation of cause and part.

children.text: na saṅkhyaikāntānām asiddhiḥ kasmāt? kāraṇasyāvayavabhāvāt/ avayavaḥ kaścit sādhanabhūta ity avyatirekaḥ/ evaṃ dvaitādīnām apīti//42//
children.translated_text: There is no failure of the numerical absolutisms. Why? Because the cause has the nature of a component. A certain component constitutes the means of proof — hence there is no distinction [between them]. The same applies to dualism and the rest. // 42 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 43
Because of being without parts, [the reason is] inconclusive. // 4.1.43 //

children.text: kāraṇasyāvayavabhāvād ity ahetuḥ/ kasmāt? sarvam ekam ity anapavargeṇa pratijñāya kasyacid ekatvam ucyate, tatra vyapavṛkto 'vayavaḥ sādhanabhūto nopapadyate/ evaṃ dvaitādiṣv apīti/
children.translated_text: 'Because the cause has the nature of a component' — this is inconclusive. Why? Because having asserted without exception that everything is one, oneness is predicated of something, and in that case a separated component serving as a means of proof is untenable. The same applies to dualism and the rest.

children.text: te khalv ime saṅkhyaikāntā yadi viśeṣakāritasyārthabhedavistārasya pratyākhyānena varttante, pratyakṣānumānāgamavirodhān mithyāvādā bhavanti/ athābhyanujñānena varttante? samānadharmakārito 'rthasaṃgraho viśeṣakāritaś cārthabheda iti evam ekāntatvaṃ jahatīti/ te khalv ete tattvajñānapravivekārtham ekāntāḥ parīkṣitā iti//43//
children.translated_text: Now, if these numerical absolutists maintain their position by rejecting the diversity of things produced by specific differences, they become proponents of falsehood, since they contradict perception, inference, and scripture. But if they maintain their position by accepting [that diversity]? [Then:] the collection of things produced by common properties and the differentiation of things produced by specific properties — thus they abandon their absolutism. These absolutisms have been examined for the purpose of discerning the knowledge of reality. // 43 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 44
After [the discussion of the self's] post-mortem existence, [comes] the fruit [of action]. Regarding that —
There is doubt whether the fruit is produced immediately or at a later time. // 4.1.44 //

children.text: pacati dogdhīti sadyaḥ phalamodanapayasī, karṣati vapatīti kālāntare phalaṃ
children.translated_text: 'He cooks,' 'he milks' — the fruit, food and milk, [is produced] immediately. 'He plows,' 'he sows' — the fruit at a later time

children.text: śasyādhigama iti/ asti ceyaṃ kriyā agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāma iti etasyāḥ
children.translated_text: is the obtaining of grain. And there is this action: 'one who desires heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s>' — regarding the fruit of this,

children.text: phale saṃśayaḥ/ na sadyaḥ kālāntaropabhogyatvāt / svargaḥ phalaṃ śrūyate, tac ca bhinne 'smin dehabhedād utpadyate iti/ na sadyaḥ grāmādikāmānāmü@ārambhaphalam iti//44//
children.translated_text: there is doubt. [The fruit] is not [produced] immediately, because it is to be enjoyed at a later time. Heaven is declared as the fruit, and that arises after this [body] is separated, after the destruction of the body. [The fruit] is not [produced] immediately, as in the case of the fruit of undertaking [actions] for those who desire a village and the like. // 44 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 45
There is no production at a later time, because the cause has perished. // 4.1.45 //

children.text: dhvastāyāṃ pravṛttau pravṛtteḥ phalaṃ na kāraṇam antareṇotpattum arhati, na khalu vai vinaṣṭāt kāraṇāt kiñcid utpadyate iti//45//
children.translated_text: When the activity has ceased, the fruit of the activity cannot arise without a cause. For indeed nothing arises from a cause that has perished. // 45 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 46
Like the fruit of a tree, it would [arise] prior to [the cause's] destruction. // 4.1.46 //

children.text: yathā phalārthinā vṛkṣamūle sekādi parikarma kriyate, tasmiṃś ca pradhvaste pṛthivīdhātur abdhātunā saṃgṛhīta āntareṇa tejasā pacyamāno rasadravyaṃ nirvartayati, sa dravyabhūto raso vṛkṣānugataḥ pākaviśiṣṭo vyūhaviśeṣeṇa sanniviśamānaḥ parṇādi phalaṃ nirvartayati, evaṃ pariṣekādi karma cārthavat/ na ca vinaṣṭāt phalaniṣpattiḥ/ tathā pravṛttyā saṃskāro dharmādharmalakṣaṇo janyate, sa jāto nimittāntarānugṛhītaḥ kālāntare phalaṃ niṣpādayatīti/ uktañ caitat

children.translated_text: its arising is due to the connection with the fruit of what was previously done
