Just as one who desires fruit performs watering and other cultivation at the root of a tree, and when that [water] has perished, the earth element, combined with the water element, being cooked by the inner fire, produces the substance of sap; that sap, having become a substance, following the tree, ripened through specific cooking, settling in a particular arrangement, produces leaves and then fruit — thus the watering and other work is meaningful. And the fruit does not arise from what has perished. Similarly, from activity a <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) characterized as <s>dharma</s> (merit) or <s>adharma</s> (demerit) is generated; that, once generated, being supported by other conditions, produces fruit at a later time. And this has been stated:
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 47
Now, this which is being produced prior to [full] production —

children.text: nāsan na san na sadasat sadasator vaidharmyāt // 4.1.47 //
children.translated_text: It is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the dissimilarity between the existent and the non-existent. // 4.1.47 //

children.text: prāṅ niṣpatter niṣpattidharmakaṃ nāsat, upādānaniyamāt/ kasyacid utpattaye kiñcid upādeyaṃ na sarvaṃ sarvasyety asadbhāve niyamo nopapadyate iti/ na sat, prāṅ utpatter vidyamānasyotpattir anupapanneti/ na, sadasat sadasator vaidharmyāt
children.translated_text: Prior to production, [the effect] is not non-existent while possessing the property of being produced, because of the restriction of material cause. Something specific is required for the production of something specific, not everything for everything — this restriction is untenable if [the effect] were non-existent. It is not existent, because the production of what already exists prior to its production is untenable. It is not both existent and non-existent, because of the dissimilarity of the existent and the non-existent —

children.text: sad ity arthābhyanujñā, asad iti arthapratiṣedhaḥ, etayor vyāghāto vaidharmyaṃ vyāghātād avyatirekānupapattir iti//47//
children.translated_text: 'existent' is the acceptance of a thing; 'non-existent' is the denial of a thing. Their contradiction is the dissimilarity; from the contradiction, the impossibility of non-distinction [between them]. // 47 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 48

children.text: prāg utpatter utpattidharmakam asad ity addhā/ kasmāat?
children.translated_text: Prior to production, [the effect] possessing the property of being produced is indeed non-existent. Why?
Because origination and destruction are observed. // 4.1.48 //

children.text: yat punaruktaṃ prāg utpatteḥ kāryaṃ nāsad upādānaniyamād iti—
children.translated_text: As for what was further said — 'prior to production, the effect is not non-existent, because of the restriction of material cause' —
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 49
That [restriction] is established by the intellect, and [the effect prior to production] is non-existent. // 4.1.49 //

children.text: idam asyotpattaye samarthaṃ na sarvam iti prāg utpatter niyatakāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ buddhyā
children.translated_text: 'This is capable of producing this, not everything [can produce it]' — prior to production, the effect's having a determinate cause is established

children.text: siddham utpattiniyamadarśanāt/ tasmād upādānaniyamasyopapattiḥ sati tu kārye prāg utpatter utpattir eva nāstīti//49//
children.translated_text: by the intellect, from the observation of the regularity of production. Therefore the restriction of material cause is accounted for; but when the effect [already] exists prior to production, production itself does not exist. // 49 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 50
The [analogy with] the production of tree-fruit is inconclusive, because of the difference in substratum. // 4.1.50 //

children.text: mūlasekādi parikarma phalaṃ cobhayaṃ vṛkṣāśrayam, karma ceha śarīre, phalaṃ cāmutra ity āśrayavyatirekād ahetur iti//50//
children.translated_text: Both the watering and other cultivation at the root and the fruit are based on the tree as their substratum, but here the action is in this body while the fruit is in the other [life] — because of the difference in substratum, [the reason] is inconclusive. // 50 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 51
No refutation, because pleasure resides in the self. // 4.1.51 //

children.text: prītir ātmapratyakṣatvād ātmāśrayā, tadāśrayam eva karma dharmasaṃjñitam, dharmasyātmaguṇatvāt tasmād āśrayavyatirekānupapattir iti//51//
children.translated_text: Pleasure resides in the self, since it is directly experienced by the self. Action designated as <s>dharma</s> (merit) also has the self as its substratum, because <s>dharma</s> is an attribute of the self. Therefore the impossibility of difference in substratum [is established]. // 51 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 52
Not so, because the fruit is indicated as sons, cattle, wives, possessions, gold, food, and the like. // 4.1.52 //
'One who desires a village should sacrifice,'
'one who desires a son should sacrifice'

children.text: ti tatra yad uktaṃ prītiḥ phalam ity etad ayuktam iti//52//
children.translated_text: — in these cases, the statement that pleasure is the fruit is untenable. // 52 //
Sons and the like are indicated as the fruit, not pleasure.
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 53
Because the fruit, [which is] pleasure, is produced from connection with those, they are figuratively called 'fruit.' // 4.1.53 //

children.text: putrādisambandhāt phalaṃ prītilakṣaṇam utpadyate iti putrādiṣu phalavadupacāraḥ, yathānne prāṇaśabdo

children.translated_text: 'food indeed is life (<s>prāṇa</s>).'

The fruit characterized as pleasure is produced from connection with sons and the like; hence the figurative usage of 'fruit' for sons and the like — just as the word 'life' (<s>prāṇa</s>) is used for food:
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 54
After the topic of suffering, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) has been enumerated. And it was stated:
'Suffering is characterized by affliction.'

children.text:
iti/ tat kim idaṃ pratyātmavedanīyasya sarvajantupratyakṣasya sukhasya pratyākhyānam, āhosvid anyaḥ kalpa iti?
anya ity āha/ katham? na vai sarvalokasākṣikaṃ sukhaṃ śakyaṃ pratyākhyātum/ ayaṃ tu janmamaraṇaprabandhānubhavanimittād duḥkhān nirviṇṇasya duḥkhaṃ jihāsato duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanopadeśo duḥkhahānārtha iti/
children.translated_text: Now, is this a rejection of pleasure, which is experienced by each individual self and is directly perceived by all beings, or is it some other interpretation? It is another interpretation, he says. How? Indeed, pleasure witnessed by the whole world cannot be rejected. But this is instruction in cultivating the perception of suffering, for the purpose of abandoning suffering, for one who is disgusted with suffering due to the experience of the cycle of birth and death, and who desires to abandon suffering.

children.text: kayā yuktyā? sarve khalu sattvanikāyāḥ sarvāṇy utpattisthānāni sarvaḥ punarbhavo bādhanānuṣakto duḥkhasāhacaryād bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham ity uktam ṛṣibhiḥ, duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanam upadiśyate atra ca hetur upādīyate—
children.translated_text: By what reasoning? Indeed, all classes of beings, all places of birth, all forms of rebirth are attended by affliction — because of the association with suffering, it was said by the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages) that suffering is characterized by affliction. The cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught, and here the reason is adduced —
Birth is indeed suffering, because of the connection with various afflictions. // 4.1.54 //

children.text: janma jāyate iti śarīrendriyabuddhayaḥ śarīrādīnāṃ ca saṃsthānaviśiṣṭānāṃ prādurbhāva utpattiḥ/ vividhā ca bādhanā, hīnā madhyamā utkṛṣṭā ceti/ utkṛṣṭā nārakiṇām, tiraścāṃ tu madhyamā, manuṣyāṇāṃ tu hīnā, devānāṃ hīnatarā vītarāgāṇāṃ ca/ evaṃ sarvam utpattisthānaṃ vividhabādhanānuṣaktaṃ paśyataḥ sukhe tatsādhaneṣu ca śarīrendriyabuddhiṣu duḥkhasaṃjñā vyavatiṣṭhate/
children.translated_text: Birth — 'one is born' — refers to the body, sense organs, and intellect; the manifestation of body and the rest in their specific configurations is 'arising' (<s>utpatti</s>). And affliction is of various kinds: low, middling, and intense. Intense for hell-beings, middling for animals, low for humans, and even lower for gods and those free from passion. Thus, for one who sees every place of birth as attended by various afflictions, the perception of suffering becomes established regarding pleasure and its means — the body, sense organs, and intellect.

children.text: duḥkhasaṃjñāvyavasthānāt sarvalokeṣv anabhiratisaṃjñā bhavati/ anabhiratisaṃjñām upāsīnasya sarvalokaviṣayā tṛṣṇā vicchidyate, tṛṣṇāprahāṇāt sarvaduḥkhād vimucyate iti/ yathā viṣayogāt payo viṣam iti budhyamāno nopādatte, anupādadāno maraṇaduḥkhaṃ nāpnoti//54//
children.translated_text: From the establishment of the perception of suffering, the perception of dissatisfaction with all worlds arises. For one who cultivates the perception of dissatisfaction, craving directed toward all worlds is cut off; from the abandonment of craving, one is liberated from all suffering. Just as one who understands, due to the admixture of poison, that milk is poison, does not partake of it, and by not partaking does not incur the suffering of death. // 54 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 55

children.text: duḥkhoddeśas tu na sukhasya pratyākhyānam, kasmāt?
children.translated_text: However, the exposition of suffering is not a rejection of pleasure. Why?
Because pleasure is produced in the intervals. // 4.1.55 //

children.text: na khalv ayaṃ duḥkhoddeśaḥ sukhasya pratyākhyānam/ kasmāt, sukhasyāntarālaniṣpatteḥ/ niṣpadyate khalu bādhanāntarāleṣu sukhaṃ pratyātmavedanīyaṃ śarīriṇām, tad aśakyaṃ pratyākhyātum iti//55//
children.translated_text: This exposition of suffering is indeed not a rejection of pleasure. Why? Because pleasure is produced in the intervals. Pleasure, which is experienced by each individual self, is indeed produced for embodied beings in the intervals between afflictions — that cannot be rejected. // 55 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 56
Even so —
Because of the non-cessation of affliction, there is no refutation [of the suffering doctrine] due to the flaw of seeking, for one who experiences [pleasure]. // 4.1.56 //

children.text: sukhasya, duḥkhoddeśeneti prakaraṇāt paryeṣaṇaṃ prārthanā viṣayārjanatṛṣṇā, paryeṣaṇasya doṣo yad ayaṃ vedayamānaḥ prārthayate tac cāsya prārthitaṃ na sampadyate, sampadya vā vipadyate, nyūnaṃ vā sampadyate, bahupratyanīkaṃ vā sampadyate iti etasmāt paryeṣaṇadoṣān nānāvidho mānasaḥ santāpo bhavati evaṃ vedayataḥ paryeṣaṇadoṣād bādhanāyā anivṛttiḥ/ bādhanānivṛtter duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanam upadiśyate / anena kāraṇena duḥkhaṃ janma na tu sukhasyābhāvād iti/
children.translated_text: Of pleasure — from the context 'with the exposition of suffering' — seeking is desire, the craving for acquiring objects. The flaw of seeking is this: that one who experiences [pleasure] desires, and what he desires is either not obtained, or once obtained is lost, or is obtained in diminished measure, or is obtained amid much opposition. From this flaw of seeking, various mental torments arise. Thus, for one who experiences, because of the flaw of seeking, affliction does not cease. Because affliction does not cease, the cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught. For this reason, birth is suffering — not because of the absence of pleasure.
And moreover, this has been said elsewhere —

children.text:
kāmaṃ kāmayamānasya yadā kāmaḥ samṛdhyati/
athainam aparaḥ kāmaḥ kṣipram eva prabādhate//
children.translated_text: 'When the desire of one who desires is fulfilled, then another desire quickly afflicts him.'

children.text: api ced udanemi samantād bhūmim imāṃ labhate sagavāśvām/ na sa tena dhanena dhanaiṣī tṛpyati kin nu sukhaṃ dhanakāme//
children.translated_text: 'Even if one conquers this entire earth with its cows and horses on all sides, the wealth-seeker is not satisfied by that wealth — what pleasure then is there for one who craves wealth?'
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 57
And because of the misconception of pleasure in what is a variety of suffering. // 4.1.57 //

children.text: duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanopadeśaḥ kriyate/ ayaṃ khalu sukhasaṃvedane vyavasthitaḥ sukhaṃ paramapuruṣārthaṃ manyate, na sukhād anyan niḥśreyasam asti sukhe prāpte caritārthaḥ kṛtakaraṇīyo bhavati/ mithyāsaṅkalpāt sukhe tatsādhaneṣu ca viṣayeṣu saṃrajyate, saṃraktaḥ sukhāya ghaṭate, ghaṭamānasyāsya janmajarāvyādhiprāyaṇāniṣṭasaṃyogeṣṭaviyogaprārthitānupapattinimittam anekavidhaṃ yāvad duḥkham utpadyate, taṃ duḥkhavikalpaṃ sukham ity abhimanyate/ sukhāṅgabhūtaṃ dukham, na duḥkham anāsādya śakyaṃ sukham avāptum, tādarthyāt sukham evedam iti sukhasaṃjñopahataprajño jāyasva ceti saṃdhāvatīti saṃsāraṃ
children.translated_text: The instruction in cultivating the perception of suffering is given. This person, established in the experience of pleasure, considers pleasure to be the supreme human aim — 'there is no higher good other than pleasure; having obtained pleasure, one has accomplished one's purpose.' Due to false conception, he is attached to pleasure and to the objects that are its means; being attached, he strives for pleasure; and as he strives, manifold suffering arises for him, occasioned by birth, old age, disease, death, association with the undesired, separation from the desired, and the failure to obtain what is sought. He misconceives this variety of suffering as pleasure: 'suffering is a component of pleasure; one cannot obtain pleasure without encountering suffering; since it serves that purpose, this is pleasure itself.' Thus, with his wisdom impaired by the perception of pleasure, he rushes toward 'be born!' — the cycle of existence —

children.text:
nātivarttate/ tad asyāḥ sukhasaṃjñāyāḥ pratipakṣo duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanam upadiśyate, *duḥkhānuṣaṅgād (corr.; duḥkhānusaṅgād, ed.) duḥkhaṃ janmeti, na sukhasyābhāvāt/
yady evaṃ kasmād duḥkhaṃ janmeti nocyate? so 'yam evaṃ vācye yad evam āha duḥkham eva janmeti tena sukhābhāvaṃ jñāpayatīti janma vinigrahārthīyo vai khalv ayam evaśabdaḥ/ katham? na duḥkhaṃ janma svarūpataḥ, kiṃ tu duḥkhopacārāt; evaṃ sukham apīti etad anenaiva nirvarttyate na tu duḥkham eva janmeti//57//
children.translated_text: and does not transcend it. Against this perception of pleasure, the cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught — birth is suffering because of the association with suffering, not because of the absence of pleasure. If this is so, why is it not said [simply] 'birth is suffering'? When one who should speak thus says 'birth is suffering indeed (<s>eva</s>),' by that he indicates the absence of pleasure — the word <s>eva</s> (indeed) here has the sense of exclusion applied to birth. How? Birth is not suffering by its own nature, but through the figurative extension of suffering; and pleasure similarly — this is established by that very [word <s>eva</s>]; it is not that 'birth is suffering only.' // 57 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, Sūtra 58
After the exposition of suffering [comes] <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). It is refuted —
There is no <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), because of the connection with debts, afflictions, and activity. // 4.1.58 //

children.text: jāyamāno ha vai brāhmaṇas tribhir ṛṇair ṛṇavān jāyate, brahmacaryeṇa ṛṣibhyo yajñena devebhyaḥ prajayā pitṛbhya
children.translated_text: 'A <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, being born, is born with three debts: by <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibate studentship) to the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages), by sacrifice to the gods, by offspring to the fathers.'

children.text: iti ṛṇāni, teṣām anubandhaḥ svakarmabhiḥ sambandhaḥ, karmasambandhavacanāt
children.translated_text: These are the debts; their connection is through one's own ritual actions, since the text speaks of the connection with ritual:

children.text: jarāmaryaṃ vā etat satraṃ yad agnihotraṃ darśapūrṇam āsau ca
children.translated_text: 'The <s>agnihotra</s> is a <s>sattra</s> (sacrificial session) [lasting] to old age or death, as are the new-moon and full-moon [sacrifices] and those [others].'

children.text: jarayā ha vā eṣa tasmāt satrād vimucyate mṛtyunā ha vā
children.translated_text: 'From that <s>sattra</s> one is freed either by old age or by death.'

children.text: iti *ṛṇānubandhād (corr.; ṛṇānuvandhād, ed.) apavargānuṣṭhānakālo nāstīty apavargābhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: Because of the connection with debts, there is no time for the practice leading to <s>apavarga</s> — hence the non-existence of <s>apavarga</s>.
Because of the connection with debts, there is no liberation —

children.text:
kleśānubandhān nāsty apavargaḥ kleśānubaddha evāyaṃ mriyate, kleśānubaddhaś ca jāyate nāsya kleśānubandhavicchedo gṛhyate/
pravṛttyanubandhān nāsty apavargaḥ—janmaprabhṛty ayaṃ yāvat prāyaṇaṃ vāgbuddhiśarīrārambheṇāvimukto gṛhyate, tatra yad uktaṃ
children.translated_text: There is no <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) because of the bondage of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) — this person dies bound by afflictions and is born bound by afflictions; no cessation of the bondage of afflictions is observed. There is no <s>apavarga</s> because of the bondage of activity — from birth until death, this person is observed as never free from the engagement of speech, mind, and body. Regarding what was stated —
from the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, faults, and false knowledge, the cessation of what immediately follows leads to <s>apavarga</s> (liberation)
— that is untenable. // 58 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 59

children.text: atrābhidhīyate/ yat tāvad ṛṇānubandhād iti ṛṇair iva ṛṇair iti—
children.translated_text: Here it is stated. First, regarding 'because of the bondage of debts' — 'by debts, as if by debts' —
Because the primary meaning of the word does not apply, it is a figurative usage; and because reproach and praise are applicable. // 4.1.59 //

children.text: ṛṇair iti nāyaṃ pradhānaśabdaḥ/ yatra khalv ekaḥ pratyādeyaṃ dadāti, dvitīyaś ca pratideyaṃ gṛhṇāti tatrāsya dṛṣṭatvāt pradhānam ṛṇaśabdaḥ/ na caitad ihopapadyate, pradhānaśabdānupapatteḥ, guṇaśabdenāyam anuvāda ṛṇair iva ṛṇair iti/
children.translated_text: 'By debts' — this is not a primary usage of the word. Where one person gives what is to be repaid and another receives what is to be given back — there, since it is directly observed, the word 'debt' has its primary meaning. But that does not apply here, since the primary meaning does not apply; this is a figurative usage — 'by debts, as if by debts.'

children.text: prayuktopamaṃ caitad yathāgnir māṇavaka iti—anyatra dṛṣṭaś cāyam ṛṇaśabda iha prayujyate, yathāgniśabdo māṇavake/ kathaṃ guṇaśabdenānuvādaḥ? nindāpraśaṃsopapatteḥ/ karmalope ṛṇīva ṛṇādānān nindyate, karmānuṣṭhāne ca ṛṇīva ṛṇadānāt praśasyate sa evopamārtha iti/
children.translated_text: And this is a simile employed in usage, like 'he is fire, the boy' — the word 'debt,' seen elsewhere, is applied here, just as the word 'fire' is applied to a boy. How is it a figurative usage? Because reproach and praise are applicable. One who neglects his ritual duties is reproached as if he were a debtor taking on debt; one who performs his duties is praised as if he were a debtor repaying debt — this is the purpose of the simile.

children.text: jāyamāna iti guṇaśabdo viparyaye 'nadhikārāt/ jāyamāno ha vai brāhmaṇa iti ca guṇaśabdo gṛhasthaḥ sampadyamāno jāyamāna iti; yadāyaṃ gṛhastho jāyate tadā karmabhir adhikriyate mātṛto jāyamānasyānadhikārāt/ yadā tu mātṛto jāyate kumāro na tadā karmabhir adhikriyate arthinaḥ śaktasya cādhikārāt/ arthinaḥ karmabhir adhikāraḥ karmavidhau kāmasaṃyogas mṛteḥ
children.translated_text: 'Being born' is a figurative expression, because in the literal sense there would be no qualification. 'The <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> being born' — this is a figurative expression meaning 'the householder coming into being'; when this householder is 'born,' then he is qualified for ritual duties, because the one literally being born from the mother has no qualification. When the child is literally born from the mother, he is not then qualified for ritual duties, since qualification belongs to one who desires and is capable. Qualification for ritual duties requires the conjunction of desire with the ritual prescription —
'One who desires heaven should perform the <s>agnihotra</s> (fire sacrifice)'

children.text: ity evamādi/ śaktasya ca (3*) pravṛttisambhavāt śaktasya karmabhir adhikāraḥ pravṛttisambhavāt/ (4*) śaktaḥ khalu vihite karmaṇi pravarttate netara iti/ ubhayābhāvas tu pradhānaśabdārthe/ mātṛto jāyamāne kumāre ubhayam arthitā śaktiś ca na bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: — and so forth. And the qualification of the capable for ritual duties is because of the possibility of undertaking action — for only the capable person engages in a prescribed ritual, not the other. But both are absent in the literal meaning — in the child literally being born from the mother, neither desire nor capability exists.

children.text:
na bhidyate ca laukikād vākyād vaidikaṃ vākyaṃ prekṣāpūrvakāripuruṣapraṇītatvena/ tatra laukikas tāvad aparīkṣako 'pi na *jātamātraṃ (corr.; jātaprātraṃ, ed.) kumārakam evaṃ brūyād adhīṣva yajasva brahmacaryaṃ careti/ kuta evam ṛṣir upapannānavadyavādī upadeśārthena prayukta upadiśati? na khalu vai narttako 'ndheṣu pravarttate na gāyako badhireṣv iti/
upadiṣṭārthavijñānaṃ copadeśaviṣayaḥ/ yaś copadiṣṭam arthaṃ vijānāti taṃ praty upadeśaḥ kriyate, na caitad asti jāyamānakumāraka iti/ gārhasthyaliṅgaṃ ca mantrabrāhmaṇaṃ karma abhivadati/ yac ca mantrabrāhmaṇaṃ karma abhivadati tat patnīsambandhādinā gārhasthyaliṅgenopapannam, tasmād gṛhastho 'yaṃ jāyamāno 'bhidhīyate iti/
arthitvasya cāvipariṇāme jarāmaryavādopapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: And a Vedic statement does not differ from a worldly statement in being composed by persons who act with deliberation. Even an uncritical worldly person would not say to a just-born infant: 'Study! Sacrifice! Practice celibacy!' How much less would a sage — one who speaks aptly and flawlessly, employed for the purpose of instruction — teach thus? For a dancer does not perform for the blind, nor a singer for the deaf. And the domain of instruction is the understanding of the instructed meaning. Instruction is given to one who understands the meaning instructed, and this does not apply to a newborn infant. And the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s> texts prescribe ritual actions marked by the householder state. What the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s> prescribe as ritual action is accompanied by signs of the householder state such as the connection with a wife; therefore this 'being born' refers to the householder. And when the desire for results does not change —

children.text: yāvac cāsya phalenārthitvaṃ na vipariṇamate na nivartate tāvad anena karmānuṣṭheyam ity upapadyate jarāmaryavādas taṃ pratīti/ jarayā ha vety āyuṣasü@turīyasya caturthasya pravrajyāyuktasya vacanaṃ
children.translated_text: as long as one's desire for the result does not change or cease, one must perform the ritual — thus the <s>jarāmarya</s> doctrine (lifelong ritualism) is applicable to such a person. 'By old age indeed' — this is the statement regarding the fourth quarter of life, which is suited for renunciation.

children.text: jarayā ha vā eṣa etasmād vimucyate
children.translated_text: 'By old age indeed one is released from this'

children.text: iti/ āyuṣas turīyaṃ caturthaṃ pravrajyāyuktaṃ jarety ucyate, tatra hi pravrajyā vidhīyate; atyantajarāsaṃyoge jarayā ha vety anarthakam/
children.translated_text: — the fourth quarter of life, suited for renunciation, is called 'old age'; for renunciation is prescribed therein. If there were an absolute connection with old age, the statement 'by old age indeed' would be meaningless.
'The incapable one is released'

children.text: ity etad api nopapadyate, svayam aśaktasya bāhyāṃ śaktim āha—
children.translated_text: — this too is untenable, for scripture itself provides external capability for one who is personally incapable:

children.text: antevāsī vā juhuyād brahmaṇā sa parikrītaḥ, kṣīrahotā vā jahuyād dhanena sa parikrīta
children.translated_text: 'Or a pupil may offer the oblation — he is purchased by <s>brahman</s> (sacred knowledge); or a <s>kṣīrahotṛ</s> (milk-oblation priest) may offer — he is purchased by wealth'
— thus.

children.text: athāpi vihitaṃ vānūdyeta kāmād vārthaḥ parikalpyeta? vihitānuvacanaṃ nyāyyam iti/ ṛṇavān ivāsvatantro gṛhasthaḥ karmasu pravarttate ity upapannaṃ vākyasya
children.translated_text: Moreover, is it a restatement of what is prescribed, or is the meaning constructed from desire? A restatement of the prescribed is proper. The householder, like a debtor not independent, engages in ritual duties — this is the established meaning of the statement.

children.text:
sāmarthyam/ phalasya hi sādhanāni prayatnaviṣayo na phalam, tāni sampannāni phalāya kalpante/ vihitaṃ ca jāyamānam, vidhīyate ca jāyamānam, tena yaḥ sambaddhyate so 'yaṃ jāyamāna iti/
pratyakṣavidhānābhāvād iti cen na, pratiṣedhasyāpi pratyakṣavidhānābhāvād iti/ pratyakṣato vidhīyate *gārhasthyaṃ (corr.; gārhathyaṃ, ed.) brāhmaṇena, yadi cāśramāntaram abhaviṣyat tad api vyadhāsyata
children.translated_text: For the means to the result are the domain of effort, not the result itself; those means, when accomplished, conduce to the result. And 'being born' is what is prescribed; one who is connected with this prescription is the one called 'being born.' If it be objected that there is no direct Vedic prescription [of the householder state] — no, because the negation too lacks direct Vedic prescription.

children.text:
pratyakṣataḥ, pratyakṣavidhānābhāvān nāsty āśramāntaram iti/ na, pratiṣedhasyāpi pratyakṣto vidhānābhāvāt/ na pratiṣedho 'pi vai brāhmaṇena pratyakṣato vidhīyate — na santy āśramāntarāṇi eka eva gṛhasthāśrama iti pratiṣedhasya pratyakṣato 'śravaṇād ayuktam etad iti/
adhikārāc ca vidhānaṃ vidyāntaravat/ yathā śāstrāntarāṇi sve sve 'dhikāre pratyakṣato vidhāyakāni nārthāntarābhāvād evam idaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gṛhasthaśāstraṃ sve 'dhikāre pratyakṣato vidhāyakaṃ nāśramāntarāṇām abhāvād iti/
children.translated_text: The householder state is directly prescribed for the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>; if there were another <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life), that too would have been prescribed directly. Since there is no direct prescription, there is no other <s>āśrama</s> — no, because the negation too is not directly prescribed. No negation is directly prescribed by the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text — since the statement 'there are no other <s>āśramas</s>, the householder is the only <s>āśrama</s>' is not heard directly, this is untenable. And the prescription is based on the domain of authority, like other branches of knowledge. Just as other <s>śāstras</s> (treatises) prescribe directly within their own domain of authority and this does not mean other things do not exist — so too this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text, being the treatise of the householder, prescribes directly within its own domain, and this does not mean other <s>āśramas</s> do not exist.

children.text: ṛgbrāhmaṇaṃ cāpavargābhidhāyy abhidhīyate/ ṛcaś ca brāhmaṇāni cāpavargābhivādīni bhavanti/ ṛcaś ca tāvat —
children.translated_text: And the <s>Ṛc</s> (verses) and <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> texts that declare <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) are cited. Both the <s>Ṛc</s> verses and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> texts speak of liberation. First, the <s>Ṛc</s> verses:

children.text: karmabhir mṛtyum ṛṣayo niṣeduḥ prajāvanto draviṇam icchamānāḥ/ athāpare ṛṣayo manīṣiṇaḥ paraṃ karmabhyo 'mṛtatvam ānaśuḥ//
children.translated_text: The sages who desired progeny and wealth warded off death through ritual actions; but other sages, the wise ones, attained immortality beyond ritual actions.

children.text: na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaike amṛtatvam ānaśuḥ/ pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate yad yatayo viśanti//
children.translated_text: Not by ritual action, not by progeny, not by wealth — some attained immortality through renunciation alone. That which is beyond heaven, hidden in the cave — that shines forth, which the ascetics enter.

children.text: vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam ādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt/ tam eva viditvātimṛtyum eti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate 'yanāya//
children.translated_text: I know this great <s>Puruṣa</s> (Person), sun-colored, beyond darkness. Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for going.
Now the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> texts:

children.text: trayo dharmaskandhāḥ —yajño 'dhyayanaṃ dānam iti prathamas tapa eva dvitīyo brahmacāry ācāryakulavāsīti tṛtīyo 'tyantam ātmānam ācāryakule 'vasādayan sarve evaite puṇyalokā bhavanti brahmasaṃstho 'mṛtatvam eti/
children.translated_text: There are three branches of <s>dharma</s> (duty): sacrifice, study, and giving — this is the first. Austerity alone is the second. The celibate student dwelling in the teacher's house is the third. One who permanently establishes himself in the teacher's house — all these attain worlds of merit; one established in <s>Brahman</s> attains immortality.

children.text: etam eva pravrājino lokam icchantaḥ pravrajantīti
children.translated_text: It is desiring this very world that renunciants renounce.

children.text:
atho khalv āhuḥ kāmamaya evāyaṃ puruṣa iti sa yathākāmo bhavati tatkratur bhavati yatkratur bhavati tat karma kurute yat karma kurute tad abhisaṃpadyate/''
iti karmabhiḥ saṃsaraṇam uktvā prakṛtam anyad upadiśanti
children.translated_text: And so they say: this person is indeed made of desire. As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the action he performs; as is the action he performs, so does he attain. Having thus described transmigration through actions, they teach something different regarding the essential matter:

children.text: iti nu kāmayamāno 'thākāmayamāno yo 'kāmo niṣkāma ātmakāma āptakāmo bhavati na tasya prāṇā utkrāmanti ihaiva samavalīyante brahmaiva san brahmāpy etīti
children.translated_text: Now, whether desiring or not desiring — one who is without desire, who is free from desire, whose desire is the Self, whose desires are fulfilled — his vital breaths do not depart; right here they are dissolved. Being <s>Brahman</s>, he goes to <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text:
/
tatra yad uktam ṛṇānubandhād apavargābhāva ity etad ayuktam iti/
children.translated_text: Therefore, the statement that there is no <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) because of the bondage of debts — that is untenable.
'Those four paths, the paths of the gods'
— and from the Vedic teaching of the four <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life), the doctrine of a single <s>āśrama</s> is untenable. // 59 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 60

children.text: jarāmaryaṃ vā etat satraṃ yad agnihotram. darśapūrṇam āsau ceti
children.translated_text: 'The <s>agnihotra</s> is the <s>jarāmarya</s> (lifelong) <s>satra</s> (sacrificial session). And so are the <s>darśapūrṇamāsa</s> (new and full moon sacrifices)'
— how?
If this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text is for those who desire results —
Because of the consignment [of fires] to the self, there is no prohibition. // 4.1.60 //

children.text: prājāpatyām iṣṭaṃ nirūpya tasyāṃ sarvavedasaṃ hutvā ātmany agnīn samāropya brāhmaṇaḥ pravrajed
children.translated_text: 'Having performed the <s>Prājāpatya</s> sacrifice, having offered therein the essence of all <s>Vedas</s>, and having consigned the fires to the self, the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> should renounce'

children.text:
iti *śrūyate (corr.; śrūyate, ed.)/ tena vijānīmaḥ prajāvittalokaiṣaṇābhyo vyutthitasya nivṛtte phalārthitve samāropaṇaṃ vidhīyate iti/
evaṃ ca brāhmaṇāni
children.translated_text: — thus it is heard. From this we understand that the consignment is prescribed for one who has turned away from the desires for progeny, wealth, and worlds, and whose desire for results has ceased.

children.text: so 'nyad vratam upākariṣyamāṇo yājñavalkyo maitreyīm iti hovāca pravrajiṣyan vā are aham asmāt sthānād asmi hanta te 'nayā kātyāyanyā sahāntaṃ karavāṇīti/ athāpy uktānuśāsanāsi maitreyi etāvad are khalv amṛtatvam iti hoktvā yājñavalkyaḥ pravavrājeti
children.translated_text: And thus the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> texts: 'He who was about to undertake another vow — <s>Yājñavalkya</s> said to <s>Maitreyī</s>: "I am about to go forth from this place; come, let me make a settlement between you and <s>Kātyāyanī</s>." And then, having instructed her, [he said to] <s>Maitreyī</s>: "This much indeed, dear, is immortality" — having said this, <s>Yājñavalkya</s> went forth.'
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 61
And because of the untenable consequence of the <s>pātracaya</s> (accumulation of vessels) being the end, there would be no result. // 4.1.61 //

children.text: jarāmarye ca karmaṇy aviśeṣeṇa kalpyamāne sarvasya pātracayāntāni karmāṇīti prasajyate, tatraiṣaṇāvyutthānaṃ na śrūyeta/

etad dha sma vai tat pūrve brāhmaṇā anūcānā vidvāṃsaḥ prajāṃ na kāmayante kiṃ prajayā kariṣyāmo yeṣāṃ no 'yam ātmāyaṃ loka iti te ha sma putraiṣaṇāyāś ca vittaiṣaṇāyāś ca lokaiṣaṇāyāś ca vyutthāyātha bhikṣācaryaṃ carantīti
children.translated_text: 'Thus indeed those ancient <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, learned and wise, did not desire progeny, thinking: What shall we do with progeny, we whose Self is this world? Having turned away from the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they wandered as mendicants.'

children.text: / eṣaṇābhyaś ca vyutthitasya pātracayāntāni karmāṇi nopapadyante iti nāviśeṣeṇa karttuḥ prayojakaṃ phalaṃ bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: And for one who has turned away from desires, rituals ending with the accumulation of vessels are untenable — therefore the result does not indiscriminately motivate the performer.

If the <s>jarāmarya</s> (lifelong ritualism) is conceived without distinction, it would follow that all rituals end with the accumulation of vessels, and the turning away from desires would not be heard.

children.text: cāturāśramyavidhānāc cetihāsapurāṇadharmaśāstreṣv aikāśramyānupapattiḥ/ tad apramāṇam iti ced na, pramāṇena prāmāṇyābhyanujñānāt — pramāṇena khalu brāhmaṇenetihāsapurāṇasya prāmāṇyam abhyanujñāyate
children.translated_text: And from the Vedic prescription of the four <s>āśramas</s> in the <s>Itihāsas</s>, <s>Purāṇas</s>, and <s>Dharmaśāstras</s>, the doctrine of a single <s>āśrama</s> is untenable. If one says these are not authoritative — no, because their authority is acknowledged by an authoritative source. The <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text itself acknowledges the authority of <s>Itihāsa</s> and <s>Purāṇa</s>:

children.text: te vā khalv ete atharvāṅgirasa etad itihāsapurāṇam abhyavadann itihāsapurāṇaṃ pañcamaṃ vedānāṃ veda iti
children.translated_text: 'These are indeed the <s>Atharvāṅgirasas</s>; this is the <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s>; the <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s> is the fifth <s>Veda</s> among the <s>Vedas</s>.'

children.text: / tasmād ayuktam etadaprāmāṇyam iti/ aprāmāṇye ca dharmaśāstrasya prāṇabhṛtāṃ vyavahāralopāl lokocchedaprasaṅgaḥ/
children.translated_text: Therefore it is untenable to deny their authority. And if the <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> lacked authority, the destruction of the social order of living beings would follow from the collapse of practical conduct.

children.text:
draṣṭṛpravaktṛsāmāṇyāc cāprāmānyānupapattiḥ/ ye eva mantrabrāhmaṇasya draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca, te khalv itihāsapurāṇasya dharmaśāstrasya ceti/
viṣayavyavasthānāc ca yathāviṣayaṃ prāmāṇyam/ anyo mantrabrāhmaṇasya viṣayo 'nyac cetihāsapurāṇadharmaśāstrāṇām iti/ yajño mantrabrāhmaṇasya, lokavṛttam itihāsapurāṇasya, lokavyavahāravyavasthānaṃ dharmaśāstrasya viṣayaḥ/ tatraikena na sarvaṃ vyavasthāpyate iti yathāviṣayam etāni pramāṇānīndriyādivad iti//61//
children.translated_text: And from the commonality of seers and promulgators, the denial of authority is untenable — for the very same persons who are the seers and promulgators of the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s> are also those of the <s>Itihāsa</s>, <s>Purāṇa</s>, and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>. And each is authoritative in its own domain according to the differentiation of subject matter. The subject matter of the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is one thing, and that of <s>Itihāsa</s>, <s>Purāṇa</s>, and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> is another. Sacrifice is the domain of the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s>; worldly affairs are the domain of the <s>Itihāsa</s> and <s>Purāṇa</s>; the regulation of worldly conduct is the domain of the <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>. One alone does not determine everything — each is authoritative in its own domain, like the sense organs and the like. // 61 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 62
As for the objection that there is no cessation of the bondage of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) —
In dreamless sleep, since there is an absence of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) when dreams are not seen, [there is] <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 4.1.62 //

children.text: yathā suṣuptasya khalu svapnādarśane rāgānubandhaḥ sukhaduḥkhānubandhaś ca vicchidyate tathāpavarge 'pīti/ etac ca brahmavido muktasyātmano rūpam udāharantīti//62//
children.translated_text: Just as in dreamless sleep without dreams, the bondage of desire and the bondage of pleasure and pain are severed — so too in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). And those who know <s>Brahman</s> cite this as the form of the liberated self. // 62 //
Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 63
As for the objection regarding the bondage of activity —
There is no activity for one whose <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) are diminished, for the purpose of reconnection. // 4.1.63 //

children.text:
prakṣīṇeṣu rāgadveṣamoheṣu pravṛttir na pratisandhānāya/ pratisandhis tu pūrvajanmanivṛttau punarjanma, tac cādṛṣṭakāritam, tasyāṃ prahīṇāyāṃ pūrvajanmābhāve janmāntarābhāvo 'pratisandhānam apavargaḥ/
karmavaiphalyaprasaṅga iti ced na, karmavipākapratisaṃvedanasyāpratyākhyānāt/ pūrvajanmanivṛttau punarjanma na bhavatīty ucyate, na tu karmavipākapratisaṃvedanaṃ pratyākhyāyate, sarvāṇi pūrvakarmāṇi hy ante janmani pipacyanta iti//63//
children.translated_text:
When <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion) are exhausted, activity does not lead to renewed connection. Renewed connection (<s>pratisandhi</s>) is rebirth upon the cessation of a former life, and that is caused by the unseen force (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>); when that has been abandoned, in the absence of a former life, the absence of another birth — non-reconnection — is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation).
If one objects that this entails the fruitlessness of <s>karma</s> — no, because the experiencing of the ripening of <s>karma</s> is not denied. It is said that when the former life ceases, rebirth does not occur, but the experiencing of the ripening of <s>karma</s> is not denied — for all previous <s>karmas</s> ripen in the final birth.
[Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 64]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.64: No, because the continuity of afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) is natural.

children.text: nopapadyate kleśānubandhavicchedaḥ, kasmāt? kleśasantateḥ svābhāvikatvāt/ anādir iyaṃ kleśasantatiḥ, na cānādiḥ śakya ucchetum iti//64//
children.translated_text: The severance of the bond of afflictions is not possible. Why? Because the continuity of afflictions is natural. This continuity of afflictions is beginningless, and what is beginningless cannot be cut off.
[Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 65]
Here someone offers a counter-argument —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.65: Just as non-existence prior to origination is impermanent, so too there is impermanence even in what is natural.

children.text: yathānādiḥ prāg utpatter abhāva utpannena bhāvena nivartyate, evaṃ svābhāvikī kleśasantatir anityeti//65//
children.translated_text: Just as the beginningless non-existence prior to origination is terminated by the originated entity, so too the natural continuity of afflictions is impermanent.
[Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 66]
Another says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.66: Or like the impermanence of the blackness of an atom.

children.text: yathānādir aṇuśyāmatā atha cāgnisaṃyogād anityā, tathā kleśasantatir apīti/ sataḥ khalu dharmo nityatvam anityatvaṃ ca, tattvaṃ bhāve abhāve bhāktam iti/ anādir aṇuśyāmateti hetvabhāvād ayuktam/ anutpattidharmakam anityam iti nātra hetur astīti//66//
children.translated_text: Just as the beginningless blackness of an atom is impermanent due to contact with fire, so too the continuity of afflictions. Permanence and impermanence are indeed properties of what exists; reality pertains to existence, while figurative usage pertains to non-existence. The statement 'the blackness of an atom is beginningless' is inappropriate because there is no reason — there is no reason here to say that what is not subject to origination is impermanent.
[Chapter 4, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 67]
But this is the proper resolution —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.67: No, and because <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the rest have <s>saṅkalpa</s> (volition) as their cause.

children.text: karmanimittatvād itaretaranimittatvāc ceti samuccayaḥ/ mithyāsaṅkalpebhyo rañjanīyakopanīyamohanīyebhyo rāgadveṣamohā utpadyante, karma ca sattvanikāyanirvartakaṃ naiyamikān rāgadveṣamohān nirvarttayati, niyamadarśanāt/ dṛśyate hi kaścit sattvanikāyo rāgabahulaḥ kaścid dveṣabahulaḥ kaścin mohabahula iti/ itaretaranimittā ca rāgādīnām utpattiḥ/ mūḍho rajyati mūḍhaḥ kupyati rakto muhyati kupito muhyati/
children.translated_text: This is to be taken together with: 'because they have <s>karma</s> as their cause, and because they have each other as their cause.' <s>Rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion) arise from false volitions (<s>mithyāsaṅkalpa</s>) — those pertaining to what is attractive, what provokes anger, and what is deluding. And <s>karma</s>, which produces types of beings, produces the regular attachment, aversion, and delusion — as is seen from observation of regularity. For it is observed that a certain class of beings is dominated by attachment, another by aversion, and another by delusion. And the origination of attachment and the rest has each other as its cause: the deluded one becomes attached, the deluded one becomes angry, the attached one becomes deluded, the angry one becomes deluded.

children.text: sarvamithyāsaṅkalpānāṃ tattvajñānād anutpattiḥ kāraṇānutpātau ca kāryānutpatter iti rāgādīnām atyantam anutpattir iti/ anādiś ca kleśasantatir ity ayuktam, sarve ime khalv ādhyātmikā bhāvā anādinā prabandhena pravarttante śarīrādayaḥ, na jātv atra kaścid anutpannapūrvaḥ prathamata utpadyate 'nyatra tattvajñānāt/ na caivaṃ saty anutpattidharmakaṃ kiñcid avyayadharmakaṃ pratijñāyate iti/ karma ca sattvanikāyanirvartakaṃ tattvajñānakṛtān mithyāsaṅkalpavighātān na rāgādyutpattinimittaṃ bhavati, sukhaduḥkhasaṃvittiḥ phalaṃ tu bhavatīti//67//
children.translated_text: Through <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality), all false volitions cease to arise; and when the cause does not arise, the effect does not arise — therefore attachment and the rest permanently cease to arise. And the claim that the continuity of afflictions is beginningless is untenable — for all these internal states, including the body and the rest, operate in a beginningless succession; no entity in this succession ever arises for the first time except through knowledge of reality. And even so, it is not thereby maintained that anything is not subject to origination or not subject to change. And <s>karma</s> that produces types of beings, when false volitions are destroyed through knowledge of reality, does not become the cause of the arising of attachment and the rest — but the experience of pleasure and pain does remain as its fruit.
Now the second section of the fourth chapter.
[Chapter 4, Section 2]
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 1]

children.text: kiṃ nu khalu bhoḥ yāvanto viṣayās tāvatsu pratyekaṃ tattvajñānam utpadyate, atha kvacid utpadyata iti/ kaś cātra viśeṣaḥ? na tāvad ekaikatra yāvad viṣayam utpadyate jñeyānām ānantyāt/ nāpi kvacid utpadyate, yatra notpadyate tatrānivṛtto moha iti mohaśeṣaprasaṅgaḥ/ na cānyaviṣayeṇa tattvajñānenānyaviṣayo mohaḥ śakyaḥ pratiṣeddhum iti/
children.translated_text: Does knowledge of reality arise in every single object, or only in some? And what is the difference here? It does not arise in each and every object up to the totality of objects, because of the infinity of knowable things. Nor does it arise in only some, because where it does not arise, delusion remains unremoved — and thus the consequence of residual delusion follows. And the delusion pertaining to one object cannot be removed by knowledge of reality pertaining to another object.

children.text:
mithyājñānaṃ vai khalu moho na tattvajñānasyānutpattimātram/ tac ca mithyājñānaṃ yatra viṣaye pravartamānaṃ saṃsārabījaṃ bhavati sa viṣayas tattvato jñeya iti/
kiṃ punas tan mithyājñānam? anātmany ātmagrahaḥ, aham asmīti moho 'haṅkāra iti/ anātmānaṃ khalv aham asmīti paśyato dṛṣṭir ahaṅkāra iti/ kiṃ punas tadarthajātaṃ yadviṣayo 'haṅkāraḥ? śarīrendriyamanovedanābuddhayaḥ/ kathaṃ tadviṣayo 'haṅkāraḥ saṃsārabījaṃ bhavati?
children.translated_text:
False knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>) is indeed delusion — not merely the non-arising of knowledge of reality. And that false knowledge, operating with respect to whatever object becomes the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), that object must be known as it truly is.
What then is that false knowledge? It is the apprehension of the self in what is not the self — the delusion 'I am this,' the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense). One who sees what is not the self as 'I am this' — that view is <s>ahaṅkāra</s>. What then is the class of objects with respect to which the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> operates? Body, sense organs, <s>manas</s> (mind), sensations, and intellect. How does the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> operating with respect to these become the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s>?

children.text:
ayaṃ khalu śarīrādyarthajātam aham asmīti vyavasitaḥ taducchedenātmocchedaṃ manyamāno 'nucchedatṛṣṇāpariplutaḥ punaḥ punas tad upādatte, tad upādadāno janmamaraṇāya yatate, tenāviyogān nātyantaṃ duḥkhād vimucyata iti/ yas tu duḥkhaṃ duḥkhāyatanaṃ duḥkhānuṣaktaṃ sukhaṃ ca sarvam idaṃ duḥkham iti paśyati sa duḥkhaṃ parijānati/ parijñātaṃ ca duḥkhaṃ prahīṇaṃ bhavaty anupādānāt saviṣānnavat/ evaṃ doṣān karma ca duḥkhahetur iti paśyati/ na cāprahīṇeṣu doṣeṣu duḥkhaprabandhocchedena śakyaṃ bhavitum iti doṣān jahāti, prahīṇeṣu ca doṣeṣu na pravṛttiḥ pratisandhānāyety uktam/
pretyabhāvaphaladuḥkhāni ca jñeyāni vyavasthāpayati karma ca doṣāṃś ca praheyān/ apavargo 'dhigantavyas tasyādhigamopāyas tattvajñānam/ evaṃ catasṛbhir vidhābhiḥ prameyaṃ vibhaktam āsevamānasyābhyasyato bhāvayataḥ samyagdarśanaṃ yathābhūtāvabodhas tattvajñānam utpadyate/
evaṃ ca —
children.translated_text:
One who has determined 'I am this' with respect to the body and the rest, thinking that the destruction of these would be the destruction of the self, being overwhelmed by the craving for non-destruction, repeatedly takes them up; taking them up, one strives toward birth and death; and because of non-separation from them, one is never completely freed from suffering. But one who sees that suffering, the abode of suffering, pleasure that is accompanied by suffering — all this is suffering — such a one fully comprehends suffering. And suffering that is fully comprehended becomes abandoned because one no longer takes it up, like food mixed with poison. Similarly, one sees that <s>doṣas</s> (defects) and <s>karma</s> (action) are the cause of suffering. And without the abandonment of defects, one cannot sever the continuity of suffering — therefore one abandons the defects; and when defects are abandoned, there is no activity leading to renewed connection, as has been stated.
And one should know suffering, the fruits of rebirth, and their causes, and one establishes that <s>karma</s> and <s>doṣas</s> are to be abandoned. <s>Apavarga</s> (liberation) is to be attained, and the means of attaining it is <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality). Thus, for one who pursues, practices, and cultivates the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) divided in these four ways, right vision — understanding of things as they are — that is, <s>tattvajñāna</s>, arises.
And thus —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.1: Through knowledge of reality regarding the causes of <s>doṣas</s> (defects), the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense) ceases.

children.text: śarīrādiduḥkhāntaṃ prameyaṃ doṣanimittaṃ tadviṣayatvān mithyājñānasya/ tad idaṃ tattvajñānaṃ tadviṣayam utpannam ahaṅkāraṃ nivartayati samānaviṣaye tayor virodhāt/ evaṃ tattvajñānād
children.translated_text: The <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), beginning with the body and ending with suffering, is the cause of <s>doṣas</s> because false knowledge has it as its object. This <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality), having arisen with respect to that same object, removes the <s>ahaṅkāra</s>, because of the opposition between the two when they have the same object. Thus, through knowledge of reality —
through the successive cessation of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, each one ceasing upon the cessation of the next, there is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation).

children.text: iti/ sa cāyaṃ śāstrārthasaṃgraho 'nūdyate nāpūrvo vidhīyate iti//1//
children.translated_text: And this is a recapitulation of the summary of the teaching of the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise), not a new injunction.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 2]
But the order of contemplation (<s>prasaṅkhyāna</s>) is as follows —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.2: The causes of <s>doṣas</s> (defects) are the objects such as form and the rest, which are produced by <s>saṅkalpa</s> (volition).

children.text: kāmaviṣayā indriyārthā iti rūpādaya ucyante/ te mithyā saṅkalpyamānā rāgadveṣamohān pravartayanti, tān pūrvaṃ prasañcakṣīta/ tāṃś ca prasañcakṣāṇasya rūpādiviṣayo mithyāsaṅkalpo nivartate/ tannivṛttāv adhyātmaṃ śarīrādi prasañcakṣīta/ tatprasaṅkhyānād adhyātmaviṣayo 'haṅkāro nivartate/
children.translated_text: The objects of desire, the objects of the senses, are called form and the rest. When falsely conceived through volition, they give rise to <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion) — one should first contemplate these. And for one who contemplates these, the false volition regarding form and the rest ceases. Upon its cessation, one should contemplate the internal — the body and the rest. Through that contemplation, the <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense) directed toward internal objects ceases.

children.text: so 'yam adhyātmaṃ bahiś ca viviktacitto viharan mukta ity ucyate//2//
children.translated_text: One who thus dwells with a mind detached both internally and externally is said to be liberated (<s>mukta</s>).
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 3]

children.text: ataḥ paraṃ kācit saṃjñā heyā kācid bhāvayitavyety upadiśyate, nāthanirākaraṇam arthopādānaṃ vā/ katham iti? —
children.translated_text: Hereafter, some concepts (<s>saṃjñā</s>) are to be abandoned and some to be cultivated — this is taught, not the rejection of objects nor the adoption of objects. How?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.3: But the cause of those [defects] is the identification with the composite (<s>avayavin</s>).

children.text: teṣāṃ doṣāṇāṃ nimittaṃ tv avayavyabhimānaḥ/ sā ca khalu strīsaṃjñā sapariṣkārā puruṣasya, puruṣasaṃjñā ca striyāḥ sapariṣkārā nimittasaṃjñā anuvyañjanasaṃjñā ca/
children.translated_text: The cause of those <s>doṣas</s> (defects) is the identification with the composite. That is: the concept 'woman,' with its adornments, for a man; and the concept 'man,' with its adornments, for a woman — the concept based on features (<s>nimitta</s>) and the concept based on secondary marks (<s>anuvyañjana</s>).

children.text: nimittasaṃjñā — rasanāśrotram, dantoṣṭham, cakṣurnāsikam/ anuvyañjanasaṃjñā — itthaṃ daṇḍā ittham oṣṭhāv iti/ seyaṃ saṃjñā kāmaṃ vardhayati tadanuṣaktāṃś ca doṣān vivarjanīyān, varjanaṃ tv asyāḥ/ bhedenāvayavasaṃjñā — keśalomamāṃsaśoṇitāsthisnāyuśirākaphapittoccārādisaṃjñā;
children.translated_text: The concept based on features: nose and ear, teeth and lips, eyes and nose. The concept based on secondary marks: 'the staff is of such a kind, the lips are of such a kind.' This conceptualization increases desire (<s>kāma</s>) and the defects associated with it, which are to be abandoned — and the abandonment is of this concept. The concept through analysis into parts is the concept of constituents — hair, body-hair, flesh, blood, bone, sinew, vein, phlegm, bile, excrement, and so forth;

children.text:
tām aśubhasaṃjñety ācakṣate/ tām asya bhāvayataḥ kāmarāgaḥ prahīyate/
saty eva ca dvividhe viṣaye kācit saṃjñā bhāvanīyā kācit parivarjanīyety upadiśyate, yathā viṣasampṛkte 'nne 'nnasaṃjñopādānāya viṣasaṃjñā prahāṇāyeti//3//
children.translated_text:
this is called the concept of impurity (<s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s>). When one cultivates it, sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>) is abandoned.
And given that the object is indeed twofold, the instruction is that one concept is to be cultivated and another to be abandoned — just as, in the case of food mixed with poison, the concept 'food' leads to taking it up, while the concept 'poison' leads to its abandonment.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 4]
Now, for one who would refute the object, the refutation of the composite (<s>avayavin</s>) is established —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.4: Doubt arises from the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance.

children.text: sadasator upalambhād vidyā dvividhā, sadasator anupalambhād avidyāpi dvividhā/ upalambhyamāne 'vayavini vidyādvaividhyāt saṃśayaḥ, anupalabhyamāne cāvidyādvaividhyāt saṃśayaḥ/ so 'yam avayavī *yad upalabhyate (following ṭhakur, yady apalabhyate ṛinsen) athāpi nopalabhyate na kathañcana saṃśayān mucyata iti//4//
children.translated_text: Knowledge is twofold, from the apprehension of what exists and what does not exist; ignorance too is twofold, from the non-apprehension of what exists and what does not exist. When the composite is apprehended, doubt arises from the twofold nature of knowledge; when it is not apprehended, doubt arises from the twofold nature of ignorance. Thus this composite, whether apprehended or not apprehended, is never free from doubt.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 5]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.5: There is no doubt regarding it, because of the established validity of the previously stated reasons.

children.text: tasminn anupapannaḥ saṃśayaḥ/ kasmāt? pūrvoktahetūnām apratiṣedhād asti dravyāntarārambha iti//5//
children.translated_text: Doubt regarding it is untenable. Why? Because the previously stated reasons have not been refuted — the origination of a new substance is established.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 6]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.6: And because of the impossibility of function, there is no doubt.

children.text: vṛttyanupapatter api tarhi saṃśayānupapattir nāsty avayavīti//6//
children.translated_text: Because of the impossibility of function, doubt is untenable — therefore the composite does not not exist.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 7]
He analyzes this —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.7: The non-existence of the composite follows because the parts do not exist in the whole or in a part of it.

children.text: ekaiko 'vayavo na tāvat kṛtsne 'vayavini vartate, tayoḥ parimāṇabhedād avayavāntarasambandhābhāvaprasaṅgāc ca/ nāpy avayavyekadeśena, na hy asyānye avayavā ekadeśabhūtāḥ santīti//7//
children.translated_text: A single part does not exist in the entire composite, because of the difference in magnitude between them and because of the consequence that connection with other parts would be absent. Nor does the composite exist in a part, for it has no other parts that constitute a portion of it.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 8]
But if the composite exists precisely in its parts —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.8: The non-existence of the composite follows because of non-existence in those [parts].

children.text: na tāvat pratyavayavaṃ vartate, tayoḥ parimāṇabhedād dravyasya caikadravyatvaprasaṅgāt/ nāpy ekadeśaiḥ sarveṣu anyāvayavābhāvāt/ tad evaṃ na yuktaḥ saṃśayo nāsty avayavīti//
children.translated_text: It does not exist in each part individually, because of the difference in magnitude and because of the consequence that the substance would be identical with a single substance. Nor does it exist in all parts through portions, because of the absence of other parts. Thus, doubt is not tenable — the composite does not not exist.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 9]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.9: And because of non-existence apart from the parts.

children.text: avayavyabhāva iti vartate/ na cāyaṃ pṛthag avayavebhyo vartate agrahaṇāt nityatvaprasaṅgāc ca/ tasmān nāsty avayavīti//
children.translated_text: 'The non-existence of the composite' is to be supplied. It does not exist apart from its parts, because it is not apprehended [separately] and because of the consequence of permanence. Therefore, the composite does not exist.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 10]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.10: And the parts are not the composite.

children.text: na cāvayavānāṃ dharmo 'vayavī/ kasmāt? dharmamātrasya dharmibhir avayavaiḥ pūrvavat sambandhānupapatteḥ/ pṛthak cāvayavebhyo dharmibhyo dharmasyāgrahaṇād iti samānam//10//
children.translated_text: The composite is not a property of the parts. Why? Because, as before, the relationship of a mere property with its property-bearers — the parts — is untenable. And because a property is not apprehended apart from its property-bearers, the parts — this is the same argument.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 11]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.11: The question is improper because, in what is one, there is no division, and hence the use of the term 'division' is untenable.

children.text: kiṃ pratyavayavaṃ kṛtsno 'vayavī vartate athaikadeśeneti nopapadyate praśnaḥ/ kasmāt? ekasmin bhedābhāvād bhedaśabdaprayogānupapatteḥ/ kṛtsnam ity anekasyāśeṣābhidhānam, ekadeśa iti nānātve kasyacid abhidhānam/ tāv imau kṛtsnaikadeśaśabdau bhedaviṣayau naikasminn avayaviny uapapadyete bhedābhāvād iti//11//
children.translated_text: 'Does the composite exist in each part as a whole or in a portion?' — this question is not tenable. Why? Because in what is one, there is no division, and hence the use of the term 'division' is untenable. 'Whole' (<s>kṛtsna</s>) is the designation of the entirety of something manifold; 'portion' (<s>ekadeśa</s>) is the designation of some among what is manifold. These two terms 'whole' and 'portion,' pertaining to division, are not applicable to the single composite, because of the absence of division.
[Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 12]
The argument 'it does not exist by a portion because of the absence of other parts' is not valid —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.2.12: This is not a valid reason, because of non-existence even when other parts are present.

children.text: avayavāntarābhāvād iti/ yady api ekadeśo 'vayavāntarabhūtaḥ syāt tathāpy avayave 'vayavāntaraṃ vartate nāvayavīti anyo 'vayavīti/
children.translated_text: 'Because of the absence of sub-parts' — even if a part were a sub-part, still the sub-part exists in the part, not in the whole — hence the whole is something different.

children.text:
anyāvayavabhāve 'py avṛtter avayavino naikadeśena vṛttir anyāvayavābhāvād ity ahetuḥ/
vṛttiḥ katham iti cet? ekasyānekatrāśrayāśritasambandhalakṣaṇā prāptiḥ/ āśrayāśritabhāvaḥ katham iti cet? yasya yato 'nyatrātmalābhānupapattiḥ sa āśrayaḥ/ na kāraṇadravyebhyo 'nyatra kāryadravyam ātmānaṃ labhate viparyayas tu kāraṇadravyeṣv iti/
nityeṣu katham iti cet, anityeṣu darśanāt siddham, nityeṣu dravyeṣu katham āśrayāśrayibhāva iti cet? anityeṣu dravyaguṇeṣu darśanād āśrayāśritabhāvasya nityeṣu siddhir iti/
children.translated_text:
Even when there is a different part, because the whole does not inhere [in the part] through one portion of the part due to the absence of another part — this is not a valid reason.
How [does] inherence [work], if one asks? It is the relation characterized by the connection of substrate and dependent, where one [entity] resides in many [substrates]. How [does] the substrate-dependent relation [work], if one asks? That from which something cannot obtain its existence elsewhere — that is the substrate. The effect-substance does not obtain itself elsewhere than in the cause-substances, but the converse [holds] for the cause-substances.
If one asks how [this applies] to eternal [substances] — it is established from observation in non-eternal ones. If one asks how the substrate-dependent relation applies to eternal substances — it is established from the observation of this relation in non-eternal substances and qualities.

children.text: tasmād avayavyabhimānaḥ pratiṣidhyate niḥśreyasakāmasya, nāvayavī, yathā rūpādiṣu mithyāsaṅkalpo na rūpādaya iti//12//
children.translated_text: Therefore, the conception of a whole is denied for one who desires the highest good — [it is denied that] the whole [truly exists as conceived], just as the false conception regarding form and the like [is denied] — not that form and the like [themselves do not exist]. // 12 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 13

children.text: sarvāgrahaṇam avayavyasiddher iti pratyavasthito 'py etad āha —
children.translated_text: Although one who holds that the non-establishment of the whole [entails] the non-grasping of everything has been refuted, he still says —
The apprehension of that [whole] is like the apprehension of a mass of hairs by one suffering from <s>timira</s> (an eye disease). // 4.2.13 //

children.text: yathaikaikaḥ keśas taimirikeṇa nopalabhyate keśasamūhas tūpalabhyate, tathaikaiko 'ṇur nopalabhyate aṇusañcayas tūpalabhyate, tad idam aṇusamūhaviṣayaṃ grahaṇam iti//13//
children.translated_text: Just as individual hairs are not perceived by one with <s>timira</s> but a mass of hairs is perceived, so too individual atoms are not perceived but an aggregate of atoms is perceived — thus this grasping has an aggregate of atoms as its object. // 13 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 14

children.text: svaviṣayān atikrameṇendiryasya paṭumandabhāvād viṣayagrahaṇasya tathābhāavo nāviṣaye pravṛttiḥ // 4.2.14 //
children.translated_text: Because the sharpness and dullness of a sense organ [vary] with regard to its own objects, object-grasping has corresponding [variation] — it is not engagement with what is not its object. // 4.2.14 //

children.text: yathāviṣayam indriyāṇāṃ paṭumandabhāvād viṣayagrahaṇānāṃ paṭumandabhāvo bhavati/ cakṣuḥ khalu prakṛṣyamāṇaṃ nāviṣayaṃ gandhaṃ gṛhṇāti, nikṛṣyamāṇaṃ ca na svaviṣayāt pracyavate/ so 'yaṃ taimirikaḥ kaścic cakṣur viṣayaṃkeśaṃ na gṛhṇāti, kaścid gṛhṇāti keśasamūham/
children.translated_text: According to the objects, the sharpness and dullness of the sense organs produce corresponding sharpness and dullness in object-grasping. The eye, even when enhanced, does not grasp smell, which is not its object; and when diminished, it does not deviate from its own object. So this person with <s>timira</s> does not perceive individual hairs, which are objects of the eye; while another perceives a mass of hairs.

children.text:
ubhayaṃ hy ataimimirikeṇa caks.uṣā gṛhyate/ paramāṇavas tv atīndriyā indriyāviṣayabhūtā na kenacid indriyeṇa gṛhyante, samuditās tu gṛhyante, ity aviṣaye pravṛttir indriyasya prasajyeta/ na jātv arthāntaram aṇubhyo gṛhyata iti/ te khalv ime paramāṇavaḥ sannihitā gṛhyamāṇā atīndriyatvaṃ jahati, viyuktāś cāgṛhyamāṇā indriyaviṣayatvaṃ na labhanta iti/ so 'yaṃ dravyāntarānutpattāv atimahān vyāghāta ity upapadyate dravyāantaram yad grahaṇasya viṣaya iti/
sañcayamātraṃ viṣaya iti cen na, sañcayasya saṃyogabhāvāt tasya cātīndriyasyāgrahaṇād ayuktam/ sañcayaḥ khalv anekasya saṃyogaḥ, sa ca gṛhyamāṇāśrayo gṛhyate nātīndriyāśrayaḥ, bhavati hīdam anena saṃyuktam iti/ tasmād yuktam etad iti/
children.translated_text:
Both are grasped by the eye of one without <s>timira</s>. But atoms are beyond the senses — they are not within the domain of any sense organ and are not grasped by any sense organ; yet their aggregates are grasped — and so the engagement of a sense organ with what is not its object would follow. It is not the case that something other than atoms is ever grasped. These atoms, when proximate and being grasped, would abandon their supersensory nature; and when separated and not being grasped, they would not attain the status of sense-objects. This constitutes a very great contradiction when no other substance is produced — hence it is tenable that there is another substance which is the object of grasping.
If [one says] the mere aggregate is the object — no, because an aggregate is a conjunction, and since that [conjunction] is supersensory, its grasping is untenable. An aggregate is indeed the conjunction of many [things], and conjunction is grasped when its substrate is grasped, not when the substrate is supersensory — for 'this is conjoined with that' [requires perceptible substrates]. Therefore this is tenable.

children.text: gṛhyamāṇasya cendriyeṇa viṣayasyāvaraṇādyanupalabdhikāraṇam upalabhyate/ tasmān nendriyadaurbalyād anupalabdhir aṇūnām, yathā nendriyadaurbalyāc cakṣuṣānupalabdhir gandhādīnām iti//14//
children.translated_text: And for what is grasped by a sense organ as its object, the cause of non-apprehension — such as obstruction — is observed. Therefore, the non-apprehension of atoms is not due to the weakness of the sense organ, just as the non-apprehension of smell and the like by the eye is not due to the weakness of the sense organ. // 14 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
And thus the consequence of parts and wholes [would continue] until dissolution. // 4.2.15 //

children.text: yaḥ khalv avayavino 'vayaveṣu vṛttipratiṣedhād abhāvaḥ so 'yam avayavasyāvayaveṣu prasajyamānaḥ sarvapralayāya vā kalpeta, niravayavād vā paramāṇuto nivarteta/ ubhayathā copalabdhiviṣayasyābhāvaḥ, tadabhāvād upalabhyabhāvaḥ/ upalabhyāśrayaś cāyaṃ vṛttipratiṣedhaḥ, sa āśrayaṃ vyāghnan ātmaghātāya kalpata iti//15//
children.translated_text: The denial of the existence of a whole — based on the denial of its inherence in the parts — when applied to the parts themselves in their sub-parts, would lead either to universal dissolution, or would terminate at the partless atom. In both cases, the object of apprehension would be non-existent; and from that non-existence, the apprehended would be non-existent. This denial of inherence depends on something apprehended [as its basis], and in destroying its own basis, it leads to self-destruction. // 15 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 16
Moreover —
There is no [universal] dissolution, because of the existence of the atom. // 4.2.16 //

children.text: avayavavibhāgam āśritya vṛttipratiṣedhād abhāvaḥ prasajyamāno niravayavāt paramāṇor nivartate na sarvapralayāya kalpate, niravayavatvaṃ tu paramāṇor vibhāgair alpataraprasaṅgasya yato nālpīyas tatrāvasthānāt/ loṣṭasya khalu pravibhajyamānāvayavasyālpataram alpatamam uttaram uttaraṃ bhavati/ sa cāyam alpataraprasaṅgaḥ yasmān nālpataram asti yaḥ paramo 'lpas tatra nivartate, yataś ca nālpīyo 'sti taṃ parama'nuṃ pracakṣmahe iti//16\\
children.translated_text: The non-existence entailed by the denial of inherence, proceeding through the division of parts, terminates at the partless atom and does not lead to universal dissolution; and the partlessness of the atom is due to the fact that the progression toward ever smaller [entities] stops where nothing smaller exists. When a clod of earth is being divided into parts, each subsequent [part] becomes progressively smaller. And this progression toward the smaller terminates at that beyond which nothing smaller exists — that ultimate smallest, that we call the <s>paramāṇu</s> (ultimate atom). // 16 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 17
Or [there would be] what is beyond fragmentation. // 4.2.17 //
Because of the instability of the division of parts, and because of the innumerability of substances, fragmentation would never cease. // 17 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 18

children.text: athedānīm ānupalambhikaḥ sarvaṃ nāstīti manyamāna āha —
children.translated_text: Now, one who holds the non-apprehension [view] — thinking 'everything is non-existent' — says:
Because of the interpenetration by <s>ākāśa</s> (space), the untenability of that [atom]. // 4.2.18 //

children.text: tasyāṇor niravayavasya nityasyānupapattiḥ/ kasmāt? ākāśavyatibhedāt/ antar bahiś cāṇur ākāśena samāviṣṭo vyatibhinnaḥ, vyatibhedāt sāvayavaḥ, sāvayavatvād anitya iti//18//
children.translated_text: That atom — partless and eternal — is untenable. Why? Because of interpenetration by <s>ākāśa</s>. The atom is pervaded and interpenetrated by <s>ākāśa</s> both inside and outside; due to interpenetration it has parts; due to having parts it is non-eternal. // 18 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 19
Or [there would follow] the non-omnipresence of <s>ākāśa</s>. // 4.2.19 //

children.text: athaitan neṣyate — paramāṇor antar nāsty ākāśam ity asarvagatatvaṃ prasajyata iti//19//
children.translated_text: If this is not accepted — that there is no <s>ākāśa</s> inside the atom — then the consequence of non-omnipresence [of <s>ākāśa</s>] follows. // 19 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 20

children.text: antar bahiś ca kāryadravyasya kāraṇāntaravacanād akārye tadabhāvaḥ // 4.2.20 //
children.translated_text: The designation of 'inside' and 'outside' applies to effect-substances due to the mention of other causes — in the non-effect, that [designation] is absent. // 4.2.20 //
'Inside'
refers to a cause that is covered by other causes.
'Outside'

children.text: iti ca vyavadhāyakam avyavahitaṃ kāraṇam evocyate/ tad etat kāryadravyasya sambhavati, nāṇor akāryatvāt/ akārye hi paramāṇāv antar bahir ity asyābhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: refers to a cause that is the intervening one, not intervened. This applies to effect-substances, not to the atom, since it is not an effect. For in the atom, which is not an effect, the [distinction of] 'inside' and 'outside' does not exist.

children.text: yatra cāsya bhāvo 'nukāryaṃ tat, na paramāṇuḥ, yato hi nālpataram asti sa paramāṇur iti//20//
children.translated_text: And that in which this [distinction] exists is a subsequent effect, not the atom — for that beyond which nothing smaller exists is the atom. // 20 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
And [<s>ākāśa</s> is] omnipresent because of sound, conjunction, and pervasion. // 4.2.21 //

children.text: yatra kvacid utpannāḥ śabdā vibhavanty ākāśe — tadāśrayā bhavanti, manobhiḥ paramāṇubhis tatkāryaiś ca saṃyogā vibhavanty ākāśe, nāsaṃyuktam ākāśena kiñcin mūrtadravyam upalabhyate, tasmān nāsarvagatam iti//21//
children.translated_text: Sounds produced anywhere abide in <s>ākāśa</s> — they have it as their substrate; conjunctions of minds, atoms, and their effects abide in <s>ākāśa</s>; no corporeal substance is ever found without conjunction with <s>ākāśa</s>. Therefore it is not non-omnipresent. // 21 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 22
Non-displacement, non-resistance, and omnipresence are the properties of <s>ākāśa</s>. // 4.2.22 //

children.text: saṃsarpatā pratighātinā dravyeṇa na vyuhyate, yathā kāṣṭhenodakam/ kasmāt? niravayavatvāt/ sarpac ca pratighāti na viṣṭambhāti — nāsya kriyāhetuṃ guṇaṃ pratibadhnāti/
children.translated_text: It is not displaced by a moving, impinging substance — as water [is displaced] by wood. Why? Because it is partless. And a moving, impinging [substance] does not encounter resistance — it does not obstruct its quality that is the cause of motion.

children.text:
kasmāt? asparśatvāt/ viparyaye hi viṣṭambho dṛṣṭa iti sa bhavān sāvayave sparśavati dravye dṛṣṭaṃ dharmaṃ viparīte nāśāṅkitum arhati/
aṇvavayavasyāṇutaratvaprasaṅgād anukāryapratiṣedhaḥ/ sāvayavatve cāṇor aṇvavayavo 'nutara iti prasajyate/ kasmāt? kāryakāraṇadravyayoḥ parimāṇabhedadarśanāt/ tasmād aṇvavayavasyāṇutaratvam, yas tu sāvayavo 'nukāryaṃ tad iti/ tasmād anukāryam idaṃ pratiṣidhyata iti/
kāraṇavibhāgāc ca kāryasyānityatvam, nākāśavyatibhedāt/ loṣṭasyāvayavavibhāgād anityatvam, nākāśasamāveṣād iti//22//
children.translated_text:
Why? Because [<s>ākāśa</s>] is intangible. For in the contrary case, resistance is observed — and that you have observed in substances that have parts and possess touch. You should not suspect the same property in what is opposite.
From the consequence that a sub-part of an atom would be yet smaller, the denial of an atomic effect [follows]. If the atom had parts, then a sub-part of the atom would be smaller than the atom. Why? Because a difference in magnitude is observed between cause-substances and effect-substances. Therefore the sub-part of an atom would be smaller; and that which has parts is an atomic effect — thus. Therefore, this atomic effect is what is being denied.
And from the separation of causes comes the non-eternality of the effect — not from the interpenetration by <s>ākāśa</s>. The non-eternality of a clod of earth is from the separation of its parts, not from the penetration of <s>ākāśa</s>. // 22 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 23
And from the tenability of spatial configuration for corporeal [substances], the existence of parts [is established]. // 4.2.23 //

children.text: paricchinnānāṃ hi sparśavatāṃ saṃsthānaṃ trikoṇaṃ caturasraṃ samaṃ parimaṇḍalam ity upapadyate, yat tat saṃsthānaṃ so 'vayavasanniveṣaḥ, parimaṇḍalāś cāṇavas tasmāt sāvayavā iti//23//
children.translated_text: For delimited tangible substances, spatial configuration is tenable — triangular, quadrilateral, even, or spherical. That spatial configuration is the arrangement of parts. And since atoms are spherical, they therefore have parts. // 23 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
And because of the tenability of conjunction. // 4.2.24 //

children.text:
madhye sann aṇuḥ pūrvāparābhyām aṇubhyām saṃyuktas tayor vyavadhānaṃ kurute/ vyavadhānenānumīyate pūrvabhāgena pūrveṇāṇunā saṃyujyate, parabhāgena pareṇāṇunā saṃyujyate, yau tau pūrvāparau bhāgau tāv asyāvayavau, evaṃ sarvataḥ saṃyujyamānasya sarvato bhāgā avayavā iti/
yat tāvan

children.translated_text: As for the [argument that] 'from the tenability of spatial configuration for corporeal substances, the existence of parts [is established]' —

children.text: iti? atroktam/ kim uktam? vibhāge 'lpataraprasaṅgasya yato nālpīyas tatra nivṛtter aṇavayavasya cāṇutaratvaprasaṅgād aṇukāryapratiṣedha iti/
children.translated_text: this has been addressed. What was said? In division, the progression toward the smaller terminates where nothing smaller exists; and from the consequence that a sub-part of an atom would be smaller, the denial of an atomic effect [follows].

An atom situated in the middle, being conjoined with the preceding and following atoms, creates an intervening space between them. From this intervening space it is inferred: it is conjoined with the preceding atom by its front portion and with the following atom by its rear portion; these front and rear portions are its parts. Thus, for something conjoined on all sides, the portions on all sides are parts.

children.text: yat punar etat saṃyogopapatteś ceti? sparśavattvād vyavadhānam āśrayasya cāvyāptyā bhāgabhaktiḥ/ uktaṃ cātra sparśavān aṇuḥ sparśavator aṇvoḥ pratighātād vyavadhāyako na sāvayavatvāt/ sparśavattvāc ca vyavadhāne saty aṇusaṃyogo nāśrayaṃ vyāpnotīti bhāgabhaktir bhavati bhāgavānn ivāyam iti/ uktaṃ cātra vibhāge 'lpataraprasaṅgasya yato nālpīyas tatrāvasthānāt tadavayavasya cāṇutaratvaprasaṅgād aṇukāryapratiṣedha iti//24//
children.translated_text: And as for 'because of the tenability of conjunction' — because [the atom] possesses touch, there is intervening [between other atoms]; and due to the non-pervasion of the substrate, there is the attribution of portions. And it has been stated here: the atom, possessing touch, creates an intervening space due to the resistance of the two tangible atoms — not because it has parts. And because it possesses touch, when there is intervening, the conjunction of atoms does not pervade the substrate — hence the attribution of portions occurs, as if it had portions. And it has been stated here: in division, the progression toward the smaller terminates where nothing smaller exists; and from the consequence that a sub-part of the atom would be smaller, the denial of an atomic effect [follows]. // 24 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 25

children.text: mūrtimatāṃ ca saṃsthānopapatteḥ saṃyogopapatteś ca paramāṇūnāṃ sāvayavatvam iti hetvoḥ —
children.translated_text: For both reasons — 'from the tenability of spatial configuration for corporeal substances, the existence of parts' and 'from the tenability of conjunction, the atoms have parts' —
Because they lead to an infinite regress, and because the infinite regress is untenable, there is no refutation [of partlessness]. // 4.2.25 //

children.text: yāvan mūrtimad yāvac ca saṃyujyate tat sarvaṃ sāvayavam ity anavasthākāriṇāv imau hetū, sā cānavasthā nopapadyate/ satyām anavasthāyāṃ satyau hetū syātām, tasmād apratiṣedho 'yaṃ niravayavatvasyeti/
children.translated_text: Whatever is corporeal and whatever is conjoined — all of that would have parts. These two reasons lead to an infinite regress, and that infinite regress is untenable. If the infinite regress were tenable, the reasons would hold; therefore this is not a refutation of partlessness.

children.text: vibhāgasya ca vibhajyamānahānir nopapadyate tasmāt pralayāntatā nopapadyata iti/
children.translated_text: And in division, the loss of what is being divided is untenable — therefore it does not end in [universal] dissolution.

children.text: anavasthāyāṃ ca pratyadhikaraṇaṃ dravyāvayavānām ānantyāt parimāṇabhedānāṃ gurutvasya cāgraḥaṇam samānaparimāṇatvaṃ cāvayavāvayavinoḥ paramaṇvavayavibhāgād ūrdhvam iti//25//
children.translated_text: And in an infinite regress, for each substrate, due to the infinity of the substance-parts, there would be non-grasping of differences in magnitude and of heaviness, and there would be equality of magnitude between the part and the whole, from the atom-part division onward. // 25 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 26

children.text: yad idaṃ bhavān buddhīr āśritya buddhiviṣayāḥ santīti manyate mithyābuddhaya etāḥ, yadi hi tattvabuddhayaḥ syur buddhyā vivecane yāthātmyaṃ buddhiviṣayāṇām upalabhyeta —
children.translated_text: Now this person who relies on cognitions and thinks 'the objects of cognition exist' — these cognitions are false. For if they were cognitions of reality, then through analytical cognition the true nature of the objects of cognition would be apprehended —

children.text: buddhyā vivecanāt tu bhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhis tantvapakarṣaṇe paṭasadbhāvānupalabdhivat tadanupalabdhiḥ // 4.2.26 //
children.translated_text: But from the non-apprehension of the true nature of things through analytical cognition — like the non-apprehension of the existence of cloth when threads are removed — there is the non-apprehension of that [true nature]. // 4.2.26 //

children.text: yathāyaṃ tantur ayaṃ tantur iti pratyekaṃ tantuṣu vivicyamāneṣu nārthāntaraṃ kiñcid upalabhyate — yat paṭabuddher viṣayaḥ syāt, yāthātmyānupalabdher asati viṣaye paṭabuddhir bhavantī mithyābuddhir bhavati, evaṃ sarvatreti// 26 //
children.translated_text: Just as when threads are analyzed individually — 'this thread, this thread' — nothing else is apprehended that would be the object of the cognition 'cloth'; from the non-apprehension of the true nature, the cloth-cognition, having no [real] object, becomes a false cognition. The same applies everywhere. // 26 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
Because it is self-contradictory, it is not a valid reason. // 4.2.27 //
