children.text: yadi buddhyā vivecanaṃ bhāvānāṃ na sarvabhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhiḥ/ atha sarvabhāvānāṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhir na buddhyā vivecanam/ bhāvānāṃ buddhyā vivecanaṃ yāthātmyānupalabdhiś ceti vyāhanyate/
children.translated_text: If there is analytical cognition of things, there is no non-apprehension of the true nature of all things. If there is non-apprehension of the true nature of all things, there is no analytical cognition. Analytical cognition of things and the non-apprehension of the true nature — these are mutually contradictory.
As it has been stated —
'And thus the consequence of parts and wholes [would continue] until dissolution.'
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
Because [the effect] has that [cause] as its substrate, there is non-separate apprehension. // 4.2.28 //

children.text: kāryadravyaṃ kāraṇadravyāśritaṃ tat kāraṇebhyaḥ pṛthaṅ nopalabhyate, viparyaye pṛthaggrahaṇāt,
children.translated_text: The effect-substance, being dependent on the cause-substance, is not apprehended separately from its causes; in the converse case, [where there is no substrate-dependent relation,] there is separate apprehension.

children.text: yatrāśrayāśritabhāvo nāsti tatra pṛthaggrahaṇam iti/ buddhyā vivecanāt tu bhāvānāṃ pṛthaggrahaṇam atīndriyeṣv aṇuṣu, yad indriyeṇa gṛhyate tad etayā buddhyā vivicyamānam anyad iti// 28 //
children.translated_text: Where there is no substrate-dependent relation, there is separate apprehension. But through intellectual discrimination, there is separate apprehension of entities even in the case of super-sensible atoms; what is grasped by the senses, when discriminated by the intellect, [is apprehended as] different. // 28 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 29
And because the comprehension of objects is from <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge). // 4.2.29 //

children.text: buddhyā vivecanād bhāvānāṃ yāthātmyopalabdhiḥ, yad asti yathā ca yan nāsti yathā ca tat sarvaṃ pramāṇata upalabdhyā sidhyati, yā ca pramāṇata upaloabdhis tad buddhyā vivecanaṃ bhāvānām, tena sarvaśāstrāṇi sarvakarmāṇi sarve ca śarīriṇāṃ vyavahārā vyāptāḥ/ parīkṣamāṇo hi buddhyādhyavasyatīdam astīdaṃ nāstīti tatra na sarvabhāvānupapattiḥ// 29 //
children.translated_text: Through intellectual discrimination comes the apprehension of the true nature of entities — whatever exists, however it exists, whatever does not exist, and however it does not exist — all this is established through apprehension by means of <s>pramāṇas</s>. And that apprehension through <s>pramāṇas</s> is the intellectual discrimination of entities; by this, all <s>śāstras</s> (sciences), all actions, and all transactions of embodied beings are encompassed. For one who examines, the intellect ascertains 'this exists, this does not exist' — and in this, there is no inapplicability to all entities. // 29 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
From the inapplicability and applicability of <s>pramāṇas</s>. // 4.2.30 //

children.text: evaṃ ca sati sarvaṃ nāstīti nopapadyate, kasmāt? pramāṇānupapattyupapattibhyām/ yadi sarvaṃ nāstīti pramāṇam upapadyate, sarvaṃ nāstīti etad vyāhanyate/ atha pramāṇaṃ nopapadyate, sarvaṃ nāstīty asya kathaṃ siddhiḥ? atha pramāṇam antareṇa siddhiḥ, sarvam astīty asya kathaṃ na siddhiḥ?// 30 //
children.translated_text: This being so, 'everything is non-existent' is untenable. Why? From the inapplicability and applicability of <s>pramāṇas</s>. If a <s>pramāṇa</s> is applicable to [the proposition] 'everything is non-existent,' then 'everything is non-existent' is self-contradictory. But if no <s>pramāṇa</s> is applicable, how is 'everything is non-existent' established? And if it is established without a <s>pramāṇa</s>, how is 'everything exists' not [equally] established? // 30 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 31
This conviction about <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) is like the conviction about dream-objects. // 4.2.31 //

children.text: yathā svapne na viṣayāḥ santy atha cābhimāno bhavati, evaṃ na pramāṇāni prameyāṇi ca santy atha ca pramāṇaprameyābhimāno bhavati// 31 //
children.translated_text: Just as in a dream there are no [real] objects and yet conviction arises, so too <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s> do not exist, yet the conviction about <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s> arises. // 31 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 32
Or like illusion, a mirage-city, or a mirage. // 4.2.32 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 33
This is not established, because of the absence of a reason. // 4.2.33 //

children.text: svapnānte viṣayābhimānavat pramāṇaprameyābhimāno na punar jāgaritānte viṣayopalabdhivad ity atra hetur nāsti/ hetvabhāvād asiddhiḥ/ svapnānte cāsanto viṣayā upalabhyanta ity atrāpi hetvabhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: [The analogy holds:] 'the conviction about <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s> is like the conviction about dream-objects at the end of a dream' — but not 'like the apprehension of objects at the end of the waking state.' There is no reason here. Because of the absence of a reason, it is not established. And in the claim that 'non-existent objects are apprehended at the end of a dream' — here too there is no reason.

children.text: pratibodhe 'nupalambhād iti cet? pratibodhaviṣayopalambhād apratiṣedhaḥ/ yadi pratibodhe ṇupalambhāt svapne viṣayā na santīti, tarhi ya ime pratibuddhena viṣayā upalabhyanta upalambhāt santīti/ viparyaye hi hetusāmarthyam/ upalambhāt sadbhāve saty anupalambhād abhāvaḥ siddhyati, ubhayathā tv abhāve nānupalambhasya sāmarthyam asti, yathā pradīpasyābhāvād rūpasyādarśanam iti, tatra bhāvenābhāvaḥ samarthyata iti/
children.translated_text: If [one says] 'because of non-apprehension upon waking' — [the reply is:] because of the apprehension of objects upon waking, there is no refutation. If objects in a dream do not exist because of non-apprehension upon waking, then the objects apprehended by one who is awake exist because of [their] apprehension. For the force of a reason [operates in] the converse [as well]. When existence is established from apprehension, absence can be established from non-apprehension; but when absence [is claimed] in both cases, non-apprehension has no force — just as the non-seeing of form is due to the absence of a lamp, where absence is established by [positive] existence.

children.text: svapnāntavikalpe ca hetuvacanam/ svapnaviṣayābhimānavad iti bruvatā svapnāntavikalpe hetur vācyaḥ/ kaścit svapno bhayopasaṃhitaḥ, kaścit pramodopasaṃhitaḥ, kaścid ubhayaviparītaḥ, kadācit svapnam eva na paśyatīti/ nimittavatas tu svapnaviṣayābhimānasya nimittavikalpād vikalpopapattiḥ// 33 //
children.translated_text: And the reason must be stated for the variations within the dream-state. One who says 'like the conviction about dream-objects' must state the reason for the variations within dreams. Some dreams are accompanied by fear, some by delight, some by the opposite of both, and sometimes one does not dream at all. But since the conviction about dream-objects has a cause, the variation is tenable because of the variation in causes. // 33 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 34
And the conviction about dream-objects is like memory and imagination. // 4.2.34 //

children.text: pūrvopalabdhaviṣayaḥ/ yathā smṛtiś ca saṅkalpaś ca pūrvopalabdhaviṣayau na tasya pratyākhyānāya kalpete tathā svapne viṣayagrahaṇaṃ pūrvopalabdhaviṣayaṃ na tasya pratyākhyānāya kalpata iti/
children.translated_text: [It is] concerned with previously apprehended objects. Just as memory and imagination, being concerned with previously apprehended objects, are not devised for the denial of those [objects], so too the apprehension of objects in dreams, being concerned with previously apprehended objects, is not devised for the denial of those [objects].

children.text: evaṃ dṛṣṭaviṣayaś ca svapnānto jāgaritāntena/ yaḥ suptaḥ svapnaṃ paśyati sa eva jāgrat svapnadarśanāni pratisandhatta idam adrākṣam iti/ tatra jāgradbuddhivṛttivaśāt svapnaviṣayābhimāno mithyeti vyavasāyaḥ/ sati ca pratisandhāne yā jāgrato buddhivṛttis tadvaśād ayaṃ vyavasāyaḥ svapnaviṣayābhimāno mithyeti/
children.translated_text: Thus the dream-state, having objects that were seen [in waking], [is connected] with the waking state. The one who slept and saw a dream is the very same one who, upon waking, connects the dream-experiences: 'I saw this.' Therein, it is by the force of the waking state's cognitive functioning that the determination arises: 'the conviction about dream-objects is false.' And when there is such a connection, it is by the force of the waking state's cognitive functioning that this determination [is made]: 'the conviction about dream-objects is false.'

children.text:
ubhayāviśeṣe tu sādhanānarthakyam/ yasya svapnāntajāgaritāntayor aviśeṣas tasya svapnaviṣayābhimānavad iti sādhanam anarthakaṃ tadāśrayapratyākhyānāt/
atasmiṃs tad iti ca vyavasāyaḥ pradhānāśrayaḥ/ apuruṣe sthāṇau puruṣa iti vyavasāyaḥ, sa pradhānāśrayaḥ, na khalu puruṣe 'nupalabdhe puruṣa ity apuruṣe vyavasāyo bhavati, evaṃ svapnaviṣayasya vyavasāyo hastinam adrākṣaṃ parvatam adrākṣam iti pradhānāśrayo bhavitum arhati// 34 //
children.translated_text: But when the two are not distinguished, the proof is pointless. For one who sees no distinction between the dream-state and the waking state, the proof 'like the conviction about dream-objects' is pointless, because the very basis [of the analogy] is rejected. And the determination 'what is not there is [taken as] that' has a real substrate. The determination 'this is a person' regarding a [mere] post, which is not a person — that has a real substrate. For it is certainly not the case that when the person is not apprehended, the determination 'this is a person' arises regarding a non-person. Likewise, the determination regarding dream-objects — 'I saw an elephant, I saw a mountain' — ought to have a real substrate. // 34 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 35
This being so —
The destruction of false apprehension [comes] from the knowledge of reality, like the annihilation of the conviction about dream-objects upon waking. // 4.2.35 //

children.text:
sthāṇau pruṣo 'yam iti vyavasāyo mithyopalabdhiḥ atasmiṃs tad iti jñānam, sthāṇau sthāṇur iti vyavasāyas tattvajñānam/ tattvajjānena ca mithyopalabdhir nivartyate, nārthaḥ sthāṇupuruṣasāmānyalakṣaṇaḥ/ yathā pratibodhe yā jñānavṛttis tayā svapnaviṣayābhimāno nivartyate nārtho viṣayasāmānyalakṣaṇaḥ, tathā māyāgandharvanagaramṛgatṛṣṇikāṇām api yā buddhayo 'tasmiṃs tad iti vyavasāyās tatrāpy anenaiva kalpena mithyopalabdhivināśas tattvajñānān nārthapratiṣedha iti/
upādānavac ca māyādiṣu mithyājñānam/ prajñāpanīyasarūpaṃ ca dravyam upādāya sādhanavān aparasya mithyādhyavasāyaṃ karoti sā māyā, nīhāraprabhṛtīnāṃ nagarasarūpasanniveśe dūrān nagarabuddhir utpadyate viparyaye tadabhāvāt, sūryamarīciṣu bhaumenoṣmaṇā saṃsṛṣṭeṣu spandamāneṣūdakabuddhir bhavati sāmānyagrahaṇāt, antikasthasya viparyaye tadabhāvāt/
children.translated_text: The determination 'this post is a person' is a false apprehension — a cognition of 'that' in what is 'not that.' The determination 'the post is a post' is the knowledge of reality. And by the knowledge of reality, false apprehension is removed — not the object characterized by the common features of post and person. Just as upon waking, the cognitive functioning [of the waking state] removes the conviction about dream-objects — not the object characterized by the common features of [real and dream] objects — so too with illusion, mirage-cities, and mirages: the cognitions that are determinations of 'that' in what is 'not that' — there too, by this very procedure, the destruction of false apprehension [comes] from the knowledge of reality, not the denial of the object. And in illusions and the like, false cognition depends on a material basis. An illusionist, having taken a substance that resembles what is to be presented, produces in another a false determination — that is <s>māyā</s> (illusion). From the configuration of mist and the like that resembles a city, the cognition 'this is a city' arises for one at a distance, and in the converse [when near], it is absent. In sun-rays mixed with heat rising from the ground, flickering, the cognition 'this is water' arises from the grasping of a common feature, but not for one nearby — in the converse, it is absent.

children.text: kvacit kadācit kasyacic ca bhāvān nānimittaṃ mithyājñānam/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca buddhidvaitaṃ māyāprayoktuḥ parasya ca, dūrānikasthayor gandharvanagaramṛgatṛṣṇikāsu, suputapratibuddhayoś ca svapnaviṣaye/ tad etat sarvasyābhāve nirupākhyatāyāṃ nirātmakatve nopapadyata iti// 35 //
children.translated_text: False cognition is not without cause — it arises for some person, at some place, at some time. And the duality of cognition is observed: of the illusionist and of the other [person], of one far and one near regarding mirage-cities and mirages, and of one asleep and one awake regarding dream-objects. This cannot be accounted for if everything is non-existent, devoid of designation, devoid of a self. // 35 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 36
And because the cause and the existence of <s>buddhi</s> (cognition) are thus apprehended. // 4.2.36 //

children.text: mithyābuddheś cārthavad apratiṣedhaḥ/ kasmāt? nimittopalambhāt, sadbhāvopalambhāc ca/ upalabhyate hi mithyābuddhinimittaṃ mithyābuddhiś ca pratyātmam utpannā gṛhyate saṃvedyatvāt, tasmān mithyābuddhir apy astīti// 36 //
children.translated_text: And false cognition, like [real] objects, is not to be denied. Why? Because its cause is apprehended, and its existence is apprehended. For the cause of false cognition is apprehended, and the false cognition itself, having arisen in one's own self, is grasped because it is experienceable. Therefore, false cognition too exists. // 36 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
And because of the distinction between the real substrate and the superimposed [element], the duality of false cognition is tenable. // 4.2.37 //

children.text: tattvaṃ sthāṇur iti, pradhānaṃ puruṣa iti/ tattvapradhānayor alopād bhedāt sthāṇau puruṣa iti mithyābuddhir utpadyate sāmānyagrahaṇāt/ evaṃ patākāyāṃ balāketi, loṣṭe kapota iti na tu samāne viṣaye mithyābuddhīnāṃ samāveśaḥ sāmānyagrahaṇavyavasthānāt/ yasya tu nirātmakaṃ nirupākhyaṃ sarvaṃ tasya samāveśaḥ prasajyate/
children.translated_text: The real substrate (<s>tattva</s>) is the post; the superimposed element (<s>pradhāna</s>) is the person. False cognition — 'this post is a person' — arises from the non-elimination and distinction of the real substrate and the superimposed element, due to the grasping of a common feature. Similarly, 'that banner is a crane,' 'that clod is a pigeon' — but false cognitions do not converge on the same object, because of the fixed arrangement of grasping common features. But for one for whom everything is without a self and without designation, [such false] convergence would follow.

children.text: gandhādau ca prameye gandhādibuddayo mithyābhimatās tattvapradhānayoḥ sāmānyagrahaṇasya cābhāvāt tattvabuddhaya eva bhavanti/ tasmād ayuktam etat — pramāṇaprameyabuddhayo mithyeti// 37 //
children.translated_text: And in the case of knowable [objects] such as odor and the like, cognitions of odor and the like, though considered false, are in fact cognitions of reality, because of the absence of a common feature between the real substrate and the superimposed element. Therefore, this is untenable — that cognitions of <s>pramāṇas</s> and <s>prameyas</s> are false. // 37 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 38

children.text: doṣanimittānāṃ tattvajñānād ahaṅkāranivṛttir ity uktam/ atha kathaṃ tattvajñānam utpadyata iti?
children.translated_text: It has been said that from the knowledge of reality, there is the cessation of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-sense), which is caused by defects. Now, how does the knowledge of reality arise?
From the practice of a special form of <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption). // 4.2.38 //

children.text: sa tu pratyāhṛtasyendriyebhyo manaso dhārakeṇa prayatnena dhāryamāṇasyātmanā saṃyogas tattvabubhutsāviśiṣṭaḥ/
children.translated_text: That [<s>samādhi</s>] is the conjunction of the <s>ātman</s> with <s>manas</s> — when <s>manas</s> has been withdrawn from the sense-organs and is held by the sustaining effort — [this conjunction being] characterized by the desire to know reality.

children.text: sati hi tasminn indriyārtheṣu buddhayo notpadyante, tadabhyāsavaśāt tattvabuddhir utpadyate// 38 //
children.translated_text: For when this [samādhi] exists, cognitions regarding sense-objects do not arise; and through the practice of this, the cognition of reality arises. // 38 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 39

children.text: sati hi tasminn indriyārtheṣu buddhayo notpadyanta
children.translated_text: 'when this [samādhi] exists, cognitions regarding sense-objects do not arise'
— this [is challenged]:
What was said —
No, because of the predominance of particular objects. // 4.2.39 //

children.text: anicchato 'pi buddhyutpatter naitad yuktam/ kasmāt? arthaviśeṣaprābalyāt/ abubhutsamānasyāpi buddhyutpattir dṛṣṭā yathā stanayitnuśabdaprabhṛtiṣu; tatra samādhiviśeṣo nopapadyate// 39 //
children.translated_text: Because cognition arises even for one who does not desire it, this is not tenable. Why? Because of the predominance of particular objects. The arising of cognition is observed even for one who does not wish [it], as in the case of the sound of thunder and the like; there, the special [state of] <s>samādhi</s> is untenable. // 39 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 40
And because of the impulsion by hunger and the like. // 4.2.40 //

children.text: kṣutpipāsābhyāṃ śītoṣṇābhyāṃ vyādhibhiś cānicchato 'pi buddhayaḥ pravartante tasmād aikāgryānupapattir iti// 40 //
children.translated_text: Cognitions arise even for one who does not desire [them], impelled by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and diseases. Therefore, one-pointedness is untenable. // 40 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 41

children.text: astv etat samādhiṃ vihāya vyutthānaṃ vyutthānanimittaṃ samādhipratyanīkaṃ ca, sati tv etasmin —
children.translated_text: Let there be, besides <s>samādhi</s>, distraction, the cause of distraction, and what is opposed to <s>samādhi</s>; but when this [samādhi] exists —
The arising of that [knowledge of reality] is due to the continuation of the fruit of previously performed [actions]. // 4.2.41 //

children.text: pūrvakṛto janmāntaropacitas tattvajñānahetur dharmapravivekaḥ phalānubandho *yogābhyāsasāmarthyaṃ (corr.; gogābhyāsa-, ed.), niṣphale hy abhyāse nābhyāsam ādriyeran/ dṛṣṭaṃ hi laukikeṣu karmasv abhyāsasāmarthyam// 41 //
children.translated_text: The previously performed, accumulated across births, cause of the knowledge of reality is the discrimination of <s>dharma</s>; the continuation of the fruit is the capacity [gained from] the practice of <s>yoga</s> — for if practice were fruitless, one would not value the practice. And the capacity of practice is observed in worldly activities. // 41 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 42
And for the purpose of avoiding what is opposed [to samādhi] —
The instruction to practice <s>yoga</s> in forests, caves, sandbanks, and the like. // 4.2.42 //

children.text: yogābhyāsajanito dharmo janmāntare 'py anuvartate/ pracayakāṣṭhāgate tattvajñānahetau dharme prakṛṣṭāyāṃ samādhibhāvanāyāṃ tattvajñānam utpadyata iti/ dṛṣṭaś ca samādhinārthaviśeṣaprābalyābhibhavaḥ
nāham etad aśrauṣaṃ nāham etad ajñāsiṣam anyatra me mano 'bhūd
children.translated_text: 'I did not hear that, I did not know that — my mind was elsewhere'
— so says the ordinary person. // 42 //

The <s>dharma</s> produced by the practice of <s>yoga</s> continues even in another birth. When the cause of the knowledge of reality — the <s>dharma</s> — has reached the stage of accumulation, and when the cultivation of <s>samādhi</s> is perfected, the knowledge of reality arises. And it is observed that through <s>samādhi</s>, the predominance of particular objects is overcome —
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 43
If it is conceded that cognition arises even for one who does not desire it, due to the predominance of particular objects —
The same consequence [would apply] even in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 4.2.43 //
Even for one who is liberated, cognitions would arise due to the force of external objects. // 43 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 44
No, because [the arising of cognition] is inevitable when [the body] has been produced. // 4.2.44 //

children.text: karmavaśān niṣpanne śarīre ceṣṭendriyārthāśraye nimittabhāvād avaśyambhāvī buddhīnām utpādaḥ/ na ca prabalo 'pi san bāhyo ṛtha ātmano buddhyutpāde samartho bhavati tasyendriyeṇa saṃyogād buddhyutpāde sāmarthyaṃ dṛṣṭam iti// 44 //
children.translated_text: When the body, which is the seat of effort, sense-organs, and objects, has been produced through the force of <s>karma</s>, the arising of cognitions is inevitable due to the causal conditions [being present]. But even a powerful external object is not capable of producing cognition in the <s>ātman</s> [by itself] — for the capacity to produce cognition is observed [to depend on] its conjunction with a sense-organ. // 44 //
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 45
And the absence of that [body] in <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). // 4.2.45 //

children.text: tasya buddhinimittāśrayasya śarīrendriyasya dharmādharmābhāvād abhāvo 'pavarge/ tatra yad uktam

children.translated_text: 'the same consequence [would apply] even in liberation'

children.text: iti, tad ayuktam/ tasmāt sarvaduḥkhavimokṣo 'pavargaḥ/ yasmāt sarvaduḥkhabījaṃ sarvaduḥkhāyatanaṃ cāpavarge vicchidyate tasmāt sarveṇa duḥkhena vimuktir apavargaḥ/ na nirbījaṃ nirāyatanaṃ ca duḥkham utpadyata iti// 45 //
children.translated_text: — that is improper. Therefore, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) is the release from all suffering. Since in <s>apavarga</s> both the seed of all suffering and the locus of all suffering are severed, <s>apavarga</s> is the release from all suffering. For suffering does not arise when it is without seed and without locus. //45//

The absence in <s>apavarga</s> of that body and sense-organs, which are the substrate of the cause of cognition, is due to the absence of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. Regarding this, what was said —
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 46
For that purpose, self-refinement through restraint (<s>yama</s>) and observance (<s>niyama</s>), and through the methods of inner knowledge from <s>Yoga</s>. // 4.2.46 //

children.text: tasyāpavargasyādhigamāya yamaniyamābhyām ātmasaṃskāraḥ/ yamaḥ samānam āśramiṇāṃ dharmasādhanam, niyamas tu viśiṣṭam/ ātmasaṃskāraḥ punar adharmahānaṃ dharmopacayaś ca/ yogaśāstrāc cādhyātmavidhiḥ pratipattavyaḥ/ sa punas tapaḥ prāṇāyāmaḥ pratyāhāro dhyānaṃ dhāraṇeti/ indriyaviṣayeṣu prasaṃkhyānābhyāso rāgadveṣaprahāṇārthaḥ/ upāyas tu yogācāravidhānam iti// 46 //
children.translated_text: For the attainment of that <s>apavarga</s>, there is self-refinement through <s>yama</s> (restraint) and <s>niyama</s> (observance). <s>Yama</s> is the common means of <s>dharma</s> for all stages of life (<s>āśramins</s>); <s>niyama</s> is the specific [means]. Self-refinement (<s>ātmasaṃskāra</s>) is the abandonment of <s>adharma</s> and the accumulation of <s>dharma</s>. And the inner discipline (<s>adhyātmavidhi</s>) is to be learned from the <s>Yogaśāstra</s>. That consists of <s>tapas</s> (austerity), <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal of the senses), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration). The practice of discernment (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>) with respect to sense-objects is for the purpose of abandoning attachment and aversion. And the method is the system of <s>Yoga</s> practice. //46//
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 47
The study and practice of knowledge, and discussion with those versed in it. // 4.2.47 //

children.text: tadartham iti prakṛtam/ jñāyate 'neneti jñānam ātmavidyāśāstraṃ tasya grahaṇam adhyayanadhāraṇe, abhyāsaḥ satatakriyādhyayanaśravaṇacintanāni/ tadvidyaiś ca saha saṃvāda iti prajñāparipākārtham, paripākas tu saṃśayacchedanam avijñātārthabodho 'dhyavasitābhyanujñānam iti/ samayāvādaḥ saṃvādaḥ// 47 //
children.translated_text: 'For that purpose' continues from before. 'Knowledge' is that by which one knows — the treatise on self-knowledge (<s>ātmavidyā</s>); its 'study' is learning and retention; 'practice' is continuous activity — study, hearing, and reflection. 'Discussion with those versed in it' is for the purpose of the maturation of wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>); and maturation is the cutting of doubt, the understanding of what was not understood, and the confirmation of what has been determined. An agreed-upon discussion is <s>saṃvāda</s>. //47//
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 48

children.text: tadvidyaiś ca saha saṃvāda ity avibhaktārthaṃ vacanaṃ vibhajyate —
children.translated_text: The statement 'discussion with those versed in it,' whose meaning is undivided, is now divided —
One should approach that [discussion] with pupils, teachers, fellow students, and those who seek the highest good, who are free from envy. // 4.2.48 //
The meaning of this is conveyed by the mere recitation [of the sūtra]. //48//
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 49

children.text: yadi ca manyeta pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahaḥ pratikūlaḥ parasyeti —
children.translated_text: And if one thinks that the opponent is averse to the acceptance of thesis and counter-thesis —
Or even one who lacks a counter-thesis, when there is a purpose to be served, [one should approach]. // 4.2.49 //

children.text: tam abhyupeyād iti vartate/ parataḥ prajñām upāditsamānas tattvabubhutsāprakāśanena svapakṣam anavasthāpayan svadarśanaṃ pariśodhayed iti/ anyonyapratyanīkāni ca prāvādukānāṃ darśanāni// 49 //
children.translated_text: 'One should approach' continues. Desiring wisdom from another, by revealing one's desire for truth and without fixing one's own position, one should examine one's own view. And the views of debaters are mutually opposed. //49//
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 50
And some, through attachment to their own position, overstep proper reasoning; in that regard —
<s>Jalpa</s> (sophistic debate) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive criticism) serve to protect the determination of truth, like the fencing of thorny branches to protect a sprouting seed. // 4.2.50 //

children.text: anutpannatattvajñānānām aprahīṇadoṣāṇāṃ tadarthaṃ ghaṭamānānām etad iti// 50 //
children.translated_text: This is for those whose knowledge of truth has not yet arisen, whose defects have not been removed, and who are striving for that purpose. //50//
Chapter 4, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 51
And when one is being disdained by the opponent through displays of learning and the like —
Contentious discourse with those two [jalpa and vitaṇḍā]. // 4.2.51 //

children.text: vigṛhyeti vijigīṣayā, na tattvabubhutsayeti/ tad etad vidyāpālārthaṃ na lābhapūjākhyātyartham iti// 51 //
children.translated_text: 'Contentiously' means with the desire to win, not with the desire to know the truth. This is for the protection of learning, not for the sake of gain, honor, or fame. //51//
Thus ends the fourth chapter in <s>Vātsyāyana</s>'s <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>. //4//

[corr.; p.1200, ed.]
<s>Nyāyadarśana</s>
Now begins the first section of the fifth chapter.
Chapter 5
Chapter 5, Section 1
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 1
because of the variety of alternatives, the futile rejoinders (<s>jāti</s>) are many' —

children.text: iti saṅkṣepeṇaoktam, tad vistareṇa vibhajyate — tāḥ khalv imā jātayaḥ sthāpanāhetau prayukte caturviṃśatiḥ pratiṣedhahetavaḥ/
children.translated_text: this was stated in brief; it is now divided in detail. These futile rejoinders are twenty-four counter-reasons when the establishing reason has been employed:
'The objection through similarity and dissimilarity —

Similarity, dissimilarity, superiority, inferiority, the describable, the indescribable, alternative, the to-be-proved, obtaining, non-obtaining, consequence, counter-example, non-origination, doubt, subject-matter, non-reason, presumption, non-distinction, the applicable, perception, non-perception, the non-eternal, the eternal, and the effect. // 5.1.1 //

children.text: sādharmyeṇa pratyavasthānam aviśiṣyamāṇaṃ sthāpanāhetutaḥ sādharmyasamaḥ/ aviśeṣaṃ tatra tatrodāhariṣyāmaḥ/ evaṃ vaidharmyasamaprabhṛtayo 'pi nirvaktavyāḥ//1//
children.translated_text: An objection through similarity that is undistinguished from the establishing reason is <s>sādharmyasamaḥ</s> (the balancing of similarity). We shall illustrate the absence of distinction in each case. In the same way, <s>vaidharmyasama</s> and the rest are to be explained. //1//
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 2
The definition is —

When there is subsumption through similarity and dissimilarity, because of the applicability of the reversal of that property — [these are] the <s>sādharmya</s> and <s>vaidharmya</s> balancings. // 5.1.2 //

children.text: sādharmyeṇopasaṃhāre sādhyadharmaviparyayopapatteḥ sādharmyeṇaiva pratyavasthānam aviśiṣyamāṇaṃ sthāpanāhetutaḥ sādharmyasamaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ nidarśanam kriyāvān ātmā, dravyasya kriyāhetuguṇayogāt/ dravyaṃ loṣṭaḥ kriyāhetuguṇayuktaḥ kriyāvān, tathā cātmā, tasmāt kriyāvān iti/ evam upasaṃhṛte paraḥ sādharmyeṇaiva pratyavatiṣṭhate niṣkriya ātmā vibhuno dravyasya niṣkriyatvād, vibhu cākāśaṃ niṣkriyaṃ ca, tathā cātmā, tasmān niṣkriya iti/
children.translated_text: When there is subsumption through similarity, and the reversal of the property to be proved is applicable, the objection through similarity alone — undistinguished from the establishing reason — is the <s>sādharmyasama</s> counter-argument. For example: The <s>ātman</s> possesses action, because a substance is endowed with a quality that causes action. The substance, a clod of earth, is endowed with a quality that causes action and possesses action; so too the <s>ātman</s>; therefore, it possesses action. When this subsumption is made, the opponent objects through similarity itself: The <s>ātman</s> is without action, because an all-pervading substance is without action — space is all-pervading and without action; so too the <s>ātman</s>; therefore, it is without action.

children.text:
na cāsti viśeṣahetuḥ kriyāvatsādharmyāt kriyāvatā bhavitavyam, na punar akriyasādharmyād niṣkriyeṇeti/ viśeṣahetvabhāvāt sādharmyasamaḥ pratiṣedho bhavati/
atha vaidharmyasamaḥ — kriyāhetuguṇayukto loṣṭaḥ paricchinno dṛṣṭo na ca tathātmā, tasmān na loṣṭavat kriyāvān iti/ na cāsti viśeṣahetuḥ kriyāvatsādharmyāt kriyāvatā bhavitavyaṃ na punaḥ kriyāvadvaidharmyād akriyeṇeti, viśeṣahetvabhāvād vaidharmyasamaḥ/
vaidharmyeṇa copasaṃhāraḥ — niṣkriya ātmā vibhutvāt, kriyāvad dravyam avibhu dṛṣṭaṃ yathā loṣṭaḥ, na ca tathātmā, tasmān niṣkriya iti/ vaidharmyeṇa pratyavasthānam — niṣkriyaṃ dravyam ākāśaṃ kriyāhetuguṇarahitaṃ dṛṣṭam, na ca tathātmā, tasmān na niṣkriya iti/ na cāsti viśeṣahetuḥ kriyāvadvaidharmyān niṣkriyeṇa bhavitavyaṃ na punar akriyavaidharmyāt kriyāvateti viśeṣahetvabhāvād vaidharmyasamaḥ/
children.translated_text:
And there is no distinguishing reason [to establish that] from similarity with what possesses action it must possess action, but not from similarity with what lacks action it must lack action. Due to the absence of a distinguishing reason, the counter-argument is <s>sādharmyasama</s>.
Now, <s>vaidharmyasama</s>: A clod of earth, endowed with a quality that causes action, is seen to be delimited; but the <s>ātman</s> is not like that; therefore, the <s>ātman</s> is not possessed of action like a clod. And there is no distinguishing reason [to establish that] from similarity with what possesses action it must possess action, but not from dissimilarity with what possesses action it must be without action — due to the absence of a distinguishing reason, this is <s>vaidharmyasama</s>.
And subsumption through dissimilarity [for the proponent]: The <s>ātman</s> is without action because of being all-pervading; a substance possessing action is observed to be non-all-pervading, like a clod; but the <s>ātman</s> is not like that; therefore, it is without action. The objection through dissimilarity: Space, a substance without action, is observed to lack the quality that causes action; but the <s>ātman</s> is not like that; therefore, it is not without action. And there is no distinguishing reason [to establish that] from dissimilarity with what possesses action it must lack action, but not from dissimilarity with what lacks action it must possess action — due to the absence of a distinguishing reason, this is <s>vaidharmyasama</s>.

children.text: atha sādharmyasamaḥ — kriyāvān loṣṭaḥ kriyāhetuguṇayukto dṛṣṭaḥ, tathā cātmā, tasmāt kriyāvān iti/ na cāsti viśeṣahetuḥ kriyāvadvaidharmyān niṣkriyo na punaḥ kriyāvatsādharmyāt kriyāvān iti viśeṣahetvabhāvāt sādharmyasamaḥ//
children.translated_text: Now, <s>sādharmyasama</s> [in this case]: A clod of earth, possessing action, is observed to be endowed with a quality that causes action; so too the <s>ātman</s>; therefore, it possesses action. And there is no distinguishing reason [to establish that] from dissimilarity with what possesses action it must lack action, but not from similarity with what possesses action it must possess action — due to the absence of a distinguishing reason, this is <s>sādharmyasama</s>. //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 3
The response to these —
Just as a cow is established as a cow by cowness (<s>gotva</s>), so is that [property to be proved] established. // 5.1.3 //

children.text: sādharmyamātreṇa vaidharmyamātreṇa ca sādhyasādhane pratijñāyamāne syād avyavasthā,
children.translated_text: When establishing and disproving are asserted through mere similarity and mere dissimilarity, there would be instability [of any thesis];

children.text: sā tu dharmaviśeṣe nopapadyate, gosādharmyād gotvāj jātiviśeṣād gauḥ sidhyati, na tu sāsnādisambandhāt/ aśvādivaidharmyād gotvād eva gauḥ sidhyati, na guṇādibhedāt/ tac caitat kṛtavyākhyānam avayavaprakaraṇe/ pramāṇānām abhisambandhāc caikārthakāritvaṃ samānaṃ vākya iti/ hetvābhāsāśrayā khalv iyam avyavastheti//
children.translated_text: but that does not arise with a specific property. A cow is established as a cow through similarity with cows, by <s>gotva</s> (cowness) — a specific universal — not through the relation with dewlap and the like. A cow is established as a cow through dissimilarity with horses and the like, by <s>gotva</s> itself, not through difference in qualities and the like. And this has been explained in the section on the components [of inference]. And through the connection of the means of valid knowledge, the statement that has a single purpose is the same. This instability indeed rests on fallacious reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>). //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 4

Because of the alternative regarding the property in the probandum and the example, and because both are to be proved — the balancings of superiority, inferiority, the describable, the indescribable, alternative, and the to-be-proved. // 5.1.4 //

children.text:
dṛṣṭāntadharmaṃ sādhye samāsañjayata utkarṣasamaḥ/ yadi kriyāhetuguṇayogāl loṣṭavat kriyāvān ātmā, loṣṭavad eva sparśavān api prāpnoti/ atha na sparśavān, loṣṭavat kriyāvān api na prāpnoti, viparyaye vā viśeṣo vaktavya iti/
sādhye dharmābhāvaṃ dṛṣṭāntāt prasañjayato 'pakarṣasamaḥ/ loṣṭaḥ khalu kriyāvān avibhur dṛṣṭaḥ,
children.translated_text:
One who attributes a property of the example to the probandum raises the <s>utkarṣasama</s> (balancing of superiority): 'If the <s>ātman</s> possesses action like a clod because of being endowed with a quality that causes action, then it should also be endowed with touch like a clod. If it is not endowed with touch, then it should not possess action like a clod either — or the distinguishing reason in the opposite case should be stated.'
One who attributes the absence of a property in the probandum from the example raises the <s>apakarṣasama</s> (balancing of inferiority): 'A clod, possessing action, is observed to be non-all-pervading;

children.text:
kāmam ātmāpi kriyāvān avibhur astu, viparyaye vā viśeṣo vaktavya iti/
khyāpanīyo varṇyo viparyayād avarṇyaḥ/ tāv etau sādhyadṛṣṭāntadharmau viparyasyato varṇyāvarṇyasamau bhavataḥ/
sādhanadharmayukte dṛṣṭānte dharmāntaravikalpāt sādhyadharmavikalpaṃ prasañjayato vikalpasamaḥ/ kriyāhetuguṇayuktaṃ kiñcid guru yathā loṣṭaḥ, kiṃcil laghu yathā vāyuḥ, evaṃ kriyāhetuguṇayuktaṃ kiñcit kriyāvat syāt yathā loṣṭaḥ, kiñcid akriyaṃ yathātmā, viśeṣo vā vācya iti/
hetvādyavayavasāmarthyayogī dharmaḥ sādhyaḥ, taṃ dṛṣṭānte prasañjayataḥ sādhyasamaḥ/ yadi yathā loṣṭas tathātmā, prāptas tarhi yathātmā tathā loṣṭa iti/ sādhyaś cāyam ātmā kriyāvān iti kāmaṃ loṣṭo 'pi sādhyaḥ/ atha naivam, na tarhi yathā loṣṭaḥ tathātmā//4//
children.translated_text:
let the <s>ātman</s> too, possessing action, be non-all-pervading — or the distinguishing reason in the opposite case should be stated.'
What is to be revealed is <s>varṇya</s> (describable); its opposite is <s>avarṇya</s> (indescribable). One who reverses the properties of the probandum and example raises <s>varṇyāvarṇyasama</s> (balancing of the describable and indescribable).
One who, from the alternative of another property in the example that possesses the proving property, attributes an alternative of the property to be proved, raises the <s>vikalpasama</s> (balancing of alternative): 'Some things endowed with the quality that causes action are heavy, like a clod; some are light, like wind. Likewise, some things endowed with the quality that causes action may possess action, like a clod, and some may be without action, like the <s>ātman</s> — or the distinguishing reason should be stated.'
The property that possesses the capacity of the components of reason and the rest is the <s>sādhya</s> (to be proved); one who attributes that to the example raises the <s>sādhyasama</s> (balancing of the to-be-proved): 'If the <s>ātman</s> is like a clod, then a clod too should be like the <s>ātman</s>. And if the <s>ātman</s> is to be proved as possessing action, then let the clod too be to be proved. If not, then the <s>ātman</s> is not like a clod.' //4//
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
The response to these —
Because the subsumption is established through partial similarity, there is no refutation from dissimilarity. // 5.1.5 //

children.text: alabhyaḥ siddhasya nihnavaḥ/ siddhaṃ ca kiñcitsādharmyād upamānaṃ yathā gaus tathā gavaya iti/
children.translated_text: The denial of what is established is impossible to obtain. And the analogy is established through partial similarity: 'as is a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox).'

children.text: tatra na labhyo gogavayayor dharmavikalpaś codayitum/ evaṃ sādhake dharme dṛṣṭāntādisāmarthyayukte na labhyaḥ sādhyadṛṣṭāntayor dharmavikalpād vaidharmyāt pratiṣedho vaktum iti//5//
children.translated_text: In that case, the alternative of properties between cow and <s>gavaya</s> cannot be raised as an objection. Similarly, when the proving property is endowed with the capacity of the example and the rest, it is impossible to assert a refutation through the alternative of properties or dissimilarity between the probandum and example. //5//
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 6
And because the example is tenable through the extension of what is to be proved. // 5.1.6 //

children.text: yatra laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ buddhisāmyaṃ tenāviparīto 'rtho 'tidiśyate prajñāpanārtham/ evaṃ sādhyātideśād dṛṣṭānte upapadyamāne sādhyatvam anupapannam iti//6//
children.translated_text: Where there is an agreement of understanding between ordinary people and examiners, an uncontradicted meaning is extended for the purpose of making [something] known. Thus, when the example is tenable through the extension of what is to be proved, the claim that it is [itself] to be proved is untenable. //6//
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 7

children.text: prāpya sādhyam aprāpya vā hetoḥ prāptyāviśiṣṭatvād aprāptyāsādhakatvāc ca prāptyaprāptisamau // 5.1.7 //
children.translated_text: Whether the reason reaches or does not reach the probandum — because of the non-distinctness of reaching, [it is] non-probative; and because of the non-probativeness of not reaching — [these are] the balancings of reaching and not reaching. // 5.1.7 //

children.text:
hetuḥ prāpya vā sādhyaṃ sādhayed aprāpya vā? na tāvat prāpya prāptyām aviśiṣṭatvād asādhakaḥ/ dvayor vidyamānayoḥ prāptau satyāṃ kiṃ kasya sādhakaṃ sādhyaṃ vā?
aprāpya sādhakaṃ na bhavati, nāprāptaḥ pradīpaḥ prakāśayatīti/ prāptyā pratyavasthānaṃ prāptisamaḥ, aprāptyā pratyavasthānam aprāptisamaḥ//7//
children.translated_text:
Does the reason prove the probandum by reaching it or by not reaching it? If by reaching — then since reaching involves no distinction, it is non-probative. When both exist and reaching obtains between them, what proves what, and what is to be proved?
If by not reaching — it is not probative, for an unreached lamp does not illuminate. The objection through reaching is <s>prāptisama</s>; the objection through non-reaching is <s>aprāptisama</s>. //7//
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
The response to these —
Because of the observation of the production of pots and the like, and because of the efficacy in affliction at a distance — there is no refutation. // 5.1.8 //

children.text: ubhayathā khalv ayuktaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ kartṛkaraṇādhikaraṇāni prāpya mṛdaṃ ghaṭādikāryaṃ niṣpādayanti, abhicārāc ca pīḍane sati dṛṣṭam aprāpya sādhakatvam iti//8//
children.translated_text: In both ways the refutation is improper: the agent, instrument, and locus, reaching the clay, produce effects like pots and the like; and it is observed that in afflicting [through black magic], there is efficacy without reaching. //8//
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 9

children.text: dṛṣṭāntasya kāraṇānapadeśāt pratyavasthānāc ca pratidṛṣṭāntena prasaṅgapratidṛṣṭāntasamau // 5.1.9 //
children.translated_text: Because of the non-indication of the cause of the example, and because of the objection [through a counter-example] — the balancings of consequence and counter-example. // 5.1.9 //

children.text: sādhanasyāpi sādhanaṃ vaktavyam iti prasaṅgena pratyavasthānaṃ prasaṅgasamaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ kriyāhetuguṇayogī kriyāvān loṣṭa iti hetur nāpadiśyate, na ca hetum antereṇa siddhir astīti/
children.translated_text: The <s>prasaṅgasama</s> (balancing of consequence) is the counter-argument that 'a proof must also be given for the proof itself': A clod possesses action because of being endowed with a quality that causes action — but the reason [for the example itself] is not indicated, and without a reason there is no establishment.

children.text: pratidṛṣṭāntena pratyavasthānaṃ pratidṛṣṭāntasamaḥ/ kriyāvān ātmā kriyāhetuguṇayogād loṣṭavad ity ukte pratidṛṣṭānta upādīyate — kriyāhetuguṇayuktam ākāśaṃ niṣkriyaṃ dṛṣṭam iti/ kaḥ punar ākāśasya kriyāhetuguṇaḥ? vāyunā saṃyogaḥ saṃskārāpekṣaḥ, vāyuvanaspatisaṃyogavad iti//9//
children.translated_text: <s>Pratidṛṣṭāntasama</s> (the counter-example equal) is a rejoinder through a counter-example. 'The <s>ātman</s> (self) possesses activity because it possesses qualities that are causes of activity, like a clod of earth' — when this is stated, a counter-example is adduced: '<s>Ākāśa</s> (space), though possessing qualities that are causes of activity, is observed to be without activity.' What then is the activity-causing quality of <s>ākāśa</s>? Conjunction with wind, which depends on <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression), like the conjunction of wind and trees. // 9 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 10
The answer to both of these —
The removal of those [objections] is like the removal of the absurdity of taking a lamp. // 5.1.10 //

children.text: idaṃ tāvad ayaṃ pṛṣṭo vaktum arhati, atha ke pradīpam upādadate, kimarthaṃ veti? didṛkṣamāṇā dṛśyadarśanārtham iti/ atha pradīpaṃ didṛkṣamāṇāḥ pradīpāntaraṃ kasmān nopādadate? antareṇāpi pradīpāntaraṃ dṛśyate pradīpaḥ, tatra pradīpadarśanārthaṃ pradīpopādānaṃ nirarthakam/ atha dṛṣṭāntaḥ kimartham ucyata iti? aprajñātasya jñāpanārtham iti/ atha dṛṣṭānte kāraṇāpadeśaḥ kimarthaṃ deśyate? yadi prajñāpanārtham, prajñāto dṛṣṭāntaḥ/ sa khalu
laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ yasminn arthe buddhisāmyaṃ sa dṛṣṭānta
children.translated_text: 'that with regard to which there is agreement of understanding among ordinary people and inquirers — that is an example.'

children.text: iti/ tatprajñāpanārthaḥ kāraṇāpadeśo nirarthaka iti prasaṅgasamasyottaram//10//
children.translated_text: Therefore the statement of a reason for the purpose of making it known is purposeless — this is the answer to the <s>prasaṅgasama</s> (absurdity-equal). // 10 //

The person asked this should answer: who takes up a lamp, and for what purpose? Those who wish to see take it up for the purpose of seeing visible things. Then why do those who wish to see not take up another lamp [to see the first lamp]? Because the lamp is seen even without another lamp; therefore, taking up a lamp for the purpose of seeing a lamp is purposeless. Then for what purpose is an example stated? For the purpose of making known what is not known. Then for what purpose is the statement of a reason in the example taught? If for the purpose of making known — [but] the example is already known. For indeed,
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
Now the answer to the <s>pratidṛṣṭāntasama</s> (counter-example equal) —
If the counter-example serves as a reason, the example is not a non-reason. // 5.1.11 //

children.text: pratidṛṣṭāntaṃ bruvatā na viśeṣahetur apadiśyate, — anena prakāreṇa pratidṛṣṭānataḥ sādhako na dṛṣṭānta iti/ evaṃ pratidṛṣṭāntahetutve nāhetur dṛṣṭānta ity upapadyate/ sa ca katham ahetur na syāt? yady apratiṣiddhaḥ sādhakaḥ syād iti//11//
children.translated_text: The one who states a counter-example does not adduce a specific reason — [he merely argues] that in this manner, through a counter-example, the example is not probative. Thus, if the counter-example serves as a reason, then 'the example is not a non-reason' is tenable. And how would the example not be a non-reason? If it were unrefuted, it would be probative. // 11 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 12
<s>Anutpattisama</s> (the non-origination equal) — because of the absence of the cause prior to origination. // 5.1.12 //

children.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad ity ukte apara āha — prāgutpatter anutpanne śabde prayatnānantarīyakatvam anityatvakāraṇaṃ nāsti, tadabhāvāt nityatvaṃ prāptam, nityasya cotpattir nāsti/ anutpattyā pratyavasthānam anutpattisamaḥ//12//
children.translated_text: 'Sound is non-eternal because it invariably follows effort, like a pot' — when this is stated, another says: prior to origination, when sound has not yet originated, its invariable following of effort — the cause of non-eternality — does not exist; from its absence, eternality follows; and what is eternal has no origination. This rejoinder through non-origination is the <s>anutpattisama</s>. // 12 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
The answer to this —
There is no refutation of the cause, because the cause is applicable to what has originated as such. // 5.1.13 //

children.text: tathābhāvād utpannasyeti/ utpannaḥ khalv ayaṃ śabda iti bhavati/ prāgutapatteḥ śabda eva nāsti, utpannasya śabdabhāvāc chabdasya sataḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvam anityatvakāraṇam upapadyate, kāraṇopapatter ayukto 'yaṃ doṣaḥ

children.translated_text: 'because of the absence of the cause prior to origination.'

'As such' means: of what has originated. For indeed, this sound has come into being. Prior to origination, sound itself does not exist; since sound exists as something that has originated, the invariable following of effort — the cause of non-eternality — is applicable. Because the cause is applicable, this fault is unjustified —
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 14
<s>Saṃśayasama</s> (the doubt-equal) — because of the similarity with both eternal and non-eternal, since sense-perceptibility is common to both the universal and the example. // 5.1.14 //

children.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad ity ukte hetau saṃśayena pratyavatiṣṭate — sati prayatnānantarīyakatve asty evāsya nityena sāmānyena sādharmyam aindriyakatvam, asti ca ghaṭenānityena, ato nityānityasādharmyād anivṛttiḥ saṃśaya iti//14//
children.translated_text: 'Sound is non-eternal because it invariably follows effort, like a pot' — when this is stated, one objects to the reason through doubt: given the invariable following of effort, there is indeed similarity with something eternal — namely sense-perceptibility — and also with the pot which is non-eternal. Therefore, from the similarity with both eternal and non-eternal, the non-resolution is doubt. // 14 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
The answer to this —

children.text: sādharmyāt saṃśaye na saṃśayo vaidharmyād ubhayathā vā saṃśaye 'tyantasaṃśayaprasaṅgo nityatvānabhyupagamāc ca sāmānysyāpratiṣedhaḥ // 5.1.15 //
children.translated_text: When there is doubt from similarity, there is no doubt from dissimilarity; or if there is doubt from both, then the absurd consequence of endless doubt follows; and since the eternality of the universal is not accepted, there is no refutation of [its similarity with sound]. // 5.1.15 //

children.text: viśeṣād vaidharmyād avadhāryamāṇe 'rthe puruṣa iti, na sthāṇupuruṣasādharmyāt saṃśayo 'vakāśaṃ labhate/ evaṃ vaidharmyād viśeṣāt prayatnānantarīyakatvād avadhāryamāṇe śabdasyānityatve nityānityasādharmyāt saṃśayo 'vakāśaṃ na labhate/ yadi vai labhate, tataḥ sthāṇupuruṣasādharmyānucchedād atyantaṃ saṃśayaḥ syāt/ gṛhyamāṇe ca viśeṣe nityaṃ sādharmyaṃ saṃśayahetur iti nābhyupagamyate/ na hi gṛhyamāṇe puruṣasya viśeṣe sthāṇupuruṣasādharmyaṃ saṃśayahetur bhavati//15//
children.translated_text: When an object is being determined through dissimilarity — through a distinguishing feature — as 'it is a man,' the doubt arising from the similarity of a post and a man does not find scope. Likewise, when the non-eternality of sound is being determined through the distinguishing feature of invariably following effort, the doubt arising from similarity with both eternal and non-eternal does not find scope. If indeed it does find scope, then since the similarity of post and man is never eliminated, there would be endless doubt. And when a distinguishing feature is being grasped, the perpetual similarity as a cause of doubt is not accepted. For when the distinguishing feature of a man is being grasped, the similarity of post and man does not serve as a cause of doubt. // 15 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 16
<s>Prakaraṇasama</s> (the topic-equal) — because of the establishment of the procedure from similarity with both. // 5.1.16 //

children.text: ubhayena nityena cānityena ca sādharmyāt pakṣapratipakṣayoḥ pravṛttiḥ prakriyā/ anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad ity ekaḥ pakṣaṃ pravarttayati, dvitīyaś ca nityasādharmyāt pratipakṣaṃ pravarttayati — nityaḥ śabdaḥ śrāvaṇatvāt śabdatvavad iti/ evaṃ ca sati prayatnānantarīyakatvād iti hetur anityasādharmyeṇa ucyamāno na prakaraṇam ativarttate, prakaraṇānativṛtter nirṇayānativartanam/ samānaṃ caitan nityasādharmyeṇocyamāṇe hetau/ tad idaṃ prakaraṇānativṛttyā pratyavasthānaṃ prakaraṇasamaḥ/ samānaṃ caitad vaidharmye 'pi, ubhayavaidharmyāt prakriyāsiddheḥ prakaraṇasama iti//16//
children.translated_text: From the similarity with both — the eternal and the non-eternal — the procedure is the operation of both thesis and counter-thesis. 'Sound is non-eternal because it invariably follows effort, like a pot' — one person advances the thesis; and a second advances the counter-thesis from similarity with the eternal: 'Sound is eternal because it is audible, like sound-ness.' In this case, the reason 'because it invariably follows effort,' being stated on the basis of similarity with the non-eternal, does not go beyond the topic; and from not going beyond the topic follows the impossibility of determination. The same applies when the reason is stated on the basis of similarity with the eternal. This rejoinder through not going beyond the topic is the <s>prakaraṇasama</s>. The same applies in the case of dissimilarity too — the <s>prakaraṇasama</s> arises because of the establishment of the procedure from dissimilarity with both. // 16 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 17
The answer to this —
The refutation is untenable because the establishment of the topic [follows] from the counter-thesis, and because the counter-thesis is tenable. // 5.1.17 //

children.text: ubhayasādharmyāt prakriyāsiddhiṃ bruvatā pratipakṣāt prakriyāsiddhir uktā bhavati/ yady ubhayasādharmyam, tatra ekataraḥ pratipakṣa ity evaṃ saty upapannaḥ pratipakṣo bhavati/ pratipakṣopapatter anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, yadi pratipakṣopapattiḥ pratiṣedho nopapadyate, atha pratiṣedhopapattiḥ pratipakṣo nopapadyate, pratipakṣopapattiḥ pratiṣedhopapattiś ceti vipratiṣiddham iti/ tattvānavadhāraṇāc ca prakriyāsiddhir viparyaye prakaraṇāvasānāt, tattvāvadhāraṇe hy avasitaṃ prakaraṇaṃ bhavatīti//17//
children.translated_text: By saying that the procedure is established from similarity with both, one has in fact stated that the procedure is established from the counter-thesis. If there is similarity with both, then one of them is the counter-thesis — and in that case, the counter-thesis becomes tenable. Because the counter-thesis is tenable, the refutation is untenable; if the counter-thesis is tenable, the refutation is untenable; but if the refutation is tenable, the counter-thesis is untenable — the counter-thesis being tenable and the refutation being tenable are contradictory. And from the failure to determine the truth, the procedure is established [as remaining unresolved] — for only when the truth is determined does the topic reach its conclusion. // 17 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 18
<s>Ahetusama</s> (the non-reason equal) — because the reason is unestablished in all three times. // 5.1.18 //

children.text: hetuḥ sādhanam, tat sādhyāt pūrvaṃ paścāt saha vā bhavet/ yadi pūrvaṃ sādhanam, asati sādhye kasya sādhanam? atha paścād, asati sādhane kasyedaṃ sādhyam? atha yugapat sādhyasādane, dvayor vidyamānayoḥ kiṃ kasya sādhanaṃ kiṃ kasya sādhyam iti hetur ahetunā na viśiṣyate/ ahetunā sādharmyāt pratyavasthānam ahetusamaḥ//18//
children.translated_text: The reason is the means of proof. It may exist before, after, or simultaneously with what is to be proved. If the means of proof exists before — when what is to be proved does not yet exist, what does it prove? If it exists after — when the means of proof does not yet exist, of what is this the probandum? If the means of proof and the probandum exist simultaneously — when both exist, which is the means and which is the probandum? Thus the reason is not different from a non-reason. The rejoinder through similarity with a non-reason is the <s>ahetusama</s>. // 18 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 19
The answer to this —
There is no non-establishment in all three times, because what is to be proved is established from the reason. // 5.1.19 //

children.text: na traikālyāsiddhiḥ/ kasmāt? hetutaḥ sādhyasiddheḥ/ nirvartanīyasya nirvṛttir vijñeyasya vijñānam ubhayaṃ kāraṇato dṛśyate, so 'yaṃ mahān pratyakṣaviṣaya udāharaṇam iti/ yat tu khalūktam asati sādhye kasya sādhanam iti? yat tu nirvatyate yac ca vijñāpyate tasyeti//19//
children.translated_text: There is no non-establishment in all three times. Why? Because what is to be proved is established from the reason. The production of what is to be produced and the knowledge of what is to be known — both are seen from a cause; this is a great matter within the scope of direct perception, and serves as illustration. As for the objection 'when what is to be proved does not exist, what does the means prove?' — [the answer is:] that which is being produced and that which is being made known. // 19 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 20
And because the refutation [itself] is untenable, what was to be refuted remains unrefuted. // 5.1.20 //

children.text: pūrvaṃ paścād yugapad vā pratiṣedha iti nopapadyate, pratiṣedhānupapatteḥ sthāpanāhetuḥ siddha iti//20//
children.translated_text: The refutation — whether [applied] before, after, or simultaneously — is untenable. Because the refutation is untenable, the reason for establishing [the thesis] is established. // 20 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
<s>Arthāpattisama</s> (the presumption-equal) — because of the establishment of the counter-thesis through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). // 5.1.21 //

children.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad iti sthāpite pakṣe arthāpattyā pratipakṣaṃ sādhayato 'rthāpattisamaḥ/ yadi prayatnānantarīyakatvād anityasādharmyād anityaḥ śabda iti, arthād āpadyate nityasādharmyān nitya iti, asti cāsya nityena sādharmyam asparśatvam iti//21//
children.translated_text: When the thesis 'Sound is non-eternal because it invariably follows effort, like a pot' is established, the <s>arthāpattisama</s> arises for one who establishes the counter-thesis through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). If sound is non-eternal because of its similarity with the non-eternal through invariably following effort, then it follows by implication that it is eternal because of its similarity with the eternal — and it does have a similarity with the eternal, namely intangibility. // 21 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 22
The answer to this —

children.text: anuktasyārthāpatteḥ pakṣahāner upapattir anuktatvād anaikānatikatvāc cārthāpatteḥ // 5.1.22 //
children.translated_text: Because what is implied is unstated, the tenability of the abandonment of the thesis [follows] from its being unstated; and because the <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is inconclusive. // 5.1.22 //

children.text: anupapādya sāmarthyam anuktam arthād āpadyate iti bruvataḥ pakṣahāner upapattir anuktatvāt, anityapakṣasiddhāv arthād āpannaṃ nityapakṣasya hānir iti/ anaikānatikatvāc cārthāpatteḥ/
children.translated_text: For one who says 'what is not demonstrated but merely implied through capacity follows by implication,' the tenability of the abandonment of the [original] thesis follows from its being unstated — the establishment of the non-eternality thesis means that the eternality thesis that 'follows by implication' is abandoned. And because the <s>arthāpatti</s> is inconclusive —

children.text: ubhayapakṣasamā ceyam arthāpattiḥ/ yadi nityasādharmyād asparśatvād ākāśavac ca nityaḥ śabdaḥ arthād āpannam anityasādharmyāt prayatnānantarīyakatvād anitya iti/ na ceyaṃ viparyayamātrād ekāntenārthāpattiḥ/ na khalu vai ghaṇasya grāvṇaḥ patanam ity arthād āpadyate — dravāṇām apāṃ patanābhāva iti//22//
children.translated_text: this <s>arthāpatti</s> applies equally to both theses. If sound is eternal because of its similarity with the eternal — intangibility — like <s>ākāśa</s> (space), then by implication it is non-eternal because of its similarity with the non-eternal — invariably following effort. And this <s>arthāpatti</s> is not conclusive merely from the reverse. For it does not follow by implication from 'a heavy stone falls' that 'liquid water does not fall.' // 22 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 23
<s>Aviśeṣasama</s> (the non-difference equal) — because of the absurd consequence of universal non-difference, from the applicability of one property, since existence applies to all. // 5.1.23 //

children.text: eko dharmaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvaṃ śabdaghaṭayor upapadyata ity aviśeṣe ubhayor anityatve,
children.translated_text: One property — invariably following effort — applies to both sound and pot; from this non-difference, both being non-eternal,

children.text: sarvasyāviśeṣaḥ prasajyate/ katham? sadbhāvopapatteḥ/ eko dharmaḥ sadbhāvaḥ sarvasyopapadyate, sadbhāvopapatteḥ sarvāviśeṣaprasaṅgāt pratyavasthānam aviśeṣasamaḥ//23//
children.translated_text: the non-difference of everything would follow. How? Because existence applies [to everything]. One property — existence — applies to everything; the rejoinder through the absurd consequence of universal non-difference from the applicability of existence is the <s>aviśeṣasama</s>. // 23 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
The answer to this —
There is no refutation, because that property applies in some cases and does not apply in others. // 5.1.24 //

children.text:
yathā sādhyadṛṣṭāntayor ekadharmasya prayatnānantarīyakatvasyopapatter anityatvaṃ dharmāntaram aviśeṣaḥ, naivaṃ sarvabhāvānāṃ sadbhāvopapattinimittaṃ dharmāntaram asti, yena aviśeṣaḥ syāt/
atha matam anityatvam eva dharmānataraṃ sadbhāvopapattinimittaṃ bhāvānāṃ sarvatra syād iti, evaṃ khalu vai kalpyamāne anityāḥ sarve bhāvāḥ sadbhāvopapatter iti pakṣaḥ prāpnoti/ tatra pratijñārthavyatiriktam anyad udāharaṇaṃ nāsti, anudāharaṇaś ca hetur nāstīti/ pratijñaiekadeśasya codāharaṇatvam anupapannam,
children.translated_text: Just as the non-eternality is a further property [that arises] from the non-difference of one property — invariably following effort — applying to both the probandum and the example, there is no such further property for all things arising from the applicability of existence that would produce non-difference. And if one thinks that non-eternality itself is the further property that, arising from the applicability of existence, would apply to all things everywhere, then when postulated thus, the thesis 'all things are non-eternal because of the applicability of existence' is arrived at. In that case, there is no other example apart from what is asserted in the thesis, and a reason without an example is not [a valid reason]. And it is untenable that a part of the thesis serve as an example,

children.text: na hi sādhyam udāharaṇaṃ bhavati/ sataś ca nityānityabhāvāt anityatvānupapattiḥ/ tasmāt sadbhāvopapatteḥ sarvāviśeṣaprasaṅga iti nirabhidheyam etad vākyam iti/ sarvabhāvānāṃ sadbhāvopapatter anityatvam iti bruvatā 'nujñātaṃ śabdasyānityatvam, tatrānupapannaḥ pratiṣedha iti//24//
children.translated_text: for what is to be proved cannot be an example. And since what exists can be either eternal or non-eternal, the applicability of non-eternality [to everything] is untenable. Therefore, 'the absurd consequence of universal non-difference from the applicability of existence' — this statement is meaningless. And by saying that all things are non-eternal because of the applicability of existence, the non-eternality of sound has been conceded; therefore the refutation [of sound's non-eternality] is untenable. // 24 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 25
<s>Upapattisama</s> (the tenability-equal) — because of the tenability of causes for both. // 5.1.25 //

children.text: yady anityatvakāraṇam upapadyate śabdasyety anityaḥ śabdo nityatvakāraṇam apy upapadyate 'syāsparśatvam iti nityatvam apy upapadyate/ ubhayasyānityatvasya nityatvasya ca kāraṇopapattyā pratyavasthānam upapattisamaḥ//
children.translated_text: If the cause of non-eternality applies to sound, and thus sound is non-eternal, the cause of eternality also applies to it — namely intangibility — and thus eternality also follows. The rejoinder through the tenability of the causes of both non-eternality and eternality is the <s>upapattisama</s>.
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 26
The answer to this —
There is no refutation, because the cause of tenability has been conceded. // 5.1.26 //

children.text: ubhayakāraṇopapatter iti bruvatā nānityatvakāraṇopapatter anityatvaṃ pratiṣidhyate, yadi pratiṣidhyate nobhayakāraṇopapattiḥ syāt/ ubhayakāraṇopapattivacanād anityatvakāraṇopapattir abhyanujñāyate, abhyanujñānād anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/
children.translated_text: By saying 'because both kinds of causes are tenable,' the impermanence that follows from the tenability of the cause of impermanence is not denied — for if it were denied, there would be no tenability of both kinds of causes. By the statement 'because both kinds of causes are tenable,' the tenability of the cause of impermanence is conceded; and from that concession, the denial is untenable.

children.text: vyāghātāt pratiṣedha iti cet, samāno vyāghātaḥ/ ekasya nityatvānityatvaprasaṅgaṃ vyāhataṃ bruvatoktaṃ pratiṣedha iti cet? svapakṣaparapakṣayoḥ samāno vyāghātaḥ, sa ca naikatarasya sādhaka iti//26//
children.translated_text: If one says 'the denial follows from contradiction' — the contradiction is equal [on both sides]. If it be said that the denial follows because asserting both permanence and impermanence of one thing is contradictory, [the reply is:] the contradiction is equal in one's own position and the opponent's position, and it does not establish either one. // 26 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 27
<s>Upalabdhisama</s> (the fallacy of counter-observation): because the property to be proved is observed even in the absence of the stated cause. // 5.1.27 //
Even in the absence of the stated cause of impermanence, namely being subsequent to effort, the impermanence of sound produced from the breaking of tree-branches by the force of wind is observed.
A counter-position through the observation of the property to be proved even in the absence of the stated means of proof — this is <s>upalabdhisama</s> (the fallacy of counter-observation). // 27 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 28
The reply to this —
Because the property is tenable even from another cause, there is no refutation. // 5.1.28 //

children.text: prayatnānantarīyakatvād iti bruvatā kāraṇata utpattir abhidhīyate, na kāryasya kāraṇaniyamaḥ/ yadi ca kāraṇāntarād apy utpadyamānasya śabdasya tad anityatvam upapadyate, kim atra pratiṣidhyata iti//28//
children.translated_text: By saying 'because of being subsequent to effort,' origination from a cause is being stated, not a restriction of the effect to [only] that cause. And if the impermanence of sound is tenable even when produced from another cause, what is being refuted here? // 28 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 29

children.text: na prāg uccāraṇād vidyamānasya śabdasyānupalabdhiḥ, kasmāt ? āvaraṇāadyanupalabdheḥ/ yathā vidyamānasyodakāder arthasyāvaraṇāder anupalabdhiḥ naivaṃ śabdasyāgrahaṇakāraṇenāvaraṇādinānupalabdhiḥ/ gṛhyeta caitad asyāgrahaṇakāraṇam udakādivat, na gṛhyate/ tasmād udakādiviparītaḥ śabdo 'nupalabhyamāna iti/
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Sound, which exists prior to utterance, is not apprehended. Why? Because of the non-apprehension of an obstruction and the like. Just as existing water and such objects are not apprehended due to obstruction and the like, so too sound is not apprehended due to some cause of non-apprehension such as obstruction. And this cause of non-apprehension should be grasped, as with water and the like — but it is not grasped. Therefore sound, being unapprehended, is unlike water and the like.

<s>Anupalabdhisama</s> (the fallacy of non-apprehension): because from the non-apprehension of that [obstruction], when the non-existence is established, the opposite [i.e., existence of obstruction] becomes tenable. // 5.1.29 //

children.text: teṣām āvaraṇādīnām anupalabdhir nopalabhyate/ anupalambhān nāstīty abhāvo 'syāḥ sidhyati/ abhāvasiddhau hetvabhāvāt tadviparītam astitvam āvaraṇādīnām avadhāryate/ tadviparītopapatter yatpratijñātaṃ
na prāg uccāraṇād vidyamānasya śabdasyānupalabdhir ity
children.translated_text: 'Sound, which exists prior to utterance, is not apprehended' —
this is not established. This reason —
'because of the non-apprehension of obstruction and the like' —

children.text: ity āvaraṇādiṣu cāvaraṇādyanupalabdhau ca samayānupalabdhyā pratyavasthito 'nupalabdhisamo bhavati//29//
children.translated_text: is countered by the equal non-apprehension of both the obstructions and the non-apprehension of obstructions; thus it becomes an <s>anupalabdhisama</s> (fallacy of non-apprehension). // 29 //

The non-apprehension of those obstructions and the like is not observed. From this non-observation, the non-existence of this [obstruction] is established. When the non-existence is established, due to the absence of the reason, the opposite — the existence of obstructions and the like — is determined. Because of the tenability of the opposite, the thesis —
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 30
The reply to this —
It is not a valid reason, because non-apprehension is essentially the same as non-observation. // 5.1.30 //

children.text: āvaraṇādyanupalabdhir nāsti, anupalambhād ity ahetuḥ/ kasmāt? anupalambhātmakatvād anupalabdheḥ/ upalambhābhāvamātratvād anupalabdheḥ/ yad asti tad upalabdher viṣayaḥ, upalabdhyā tad astīti pratijñāyate/ yan nāsti tad anupalabdher viṣayaḥ, anupalabhyamānaṃ nāstīti pratijñāyate/ so 'yam āvaraṇādyanupalabheḥ anupalambha upalabdhyabhāve 'nupalabdhau svaviṣaye pravarttamāno na svaviṣayaṃ pratiṣedhati/
children.translated_text: 'The non-apprehension of obstruction and the like does not exist, because of non-observation' — this is not a valid reason. Why? Because non-apprehension is essentially non-observation. Non-apprehension is nothing but the absence of apprehension. What exists is the object of apprehension — by apprehension it is asserted that it exists. What does not exist is the object of non-apprehension — what is not apprehended is asserted as not existing. This non-observation of the non-apprehension of obstruction and the like, operating in its own domain — the absence of apprehension, which is non-apprehension — does not negate its own domain.

children.text: apratiṣiddhā cāvaraṇādyanupalabdhir hetutvāya kalpate/ āvaraṇādīni tu vidyamānatvād upalabdher viṣayāḥ, teṣām upalabdhyā bhavitavyam/ yat tāni nopalabhyante, tad upalabdheḥ svaviṣayapratipādikāyā abhāvād anupalambhād anupalabdher viṣayo gamyate — na santy āvaraṇādīni śabdasyāgrahaṇakāraṇānīti/ anupalambhāt tv anupalabhiḥ sidhyati, viṣayaḥ sa tasyeti//30//
children.translated_text: And non-apprehension of obstruction and the like, not being negated, serves as a reason. But obstructions and the like, since they exist, are objects of apprehension; their apprehension should [be expected]. The fact that they are not apprehended indicates — from the absence of apprehension, which would indicate its own object — the domain of non-apprehension is understood: that there are no obstructions and the like as causes of non-grasping of sound. But non-apprehension is indeed established from non-observation — that is its domain. // 30 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 31
And because of the internal awareness of the presence and absence of varieties of cognition. // 5.1.31 //

children.text: ahetur iti varttate/ śarīre śarīre jñānavikalpānāṃ bhāvābhāvau saṃvedanīyau/ asti me saṃśayajñānaṃ nāsti me saṃśayajñānam iti/ evaṃ pratyakṣānumānāgamasmṛtijñāneṣu/ seyam āvaraṇāadyanupalabdhir upalabdhyabhāvaḥ svasaṃvedyaḥ — nāsti me śabdasyāvaraṇādyupalabdhir iti nopalabhyante śabdasyāgrahaṇakāraṇāny āvaraṇādīnīti/ tatra yad uktaṃ tad anupalabdher anupalambhād abhāvasiddhir iti, etan nopapadyate//31//
children.translated_text: The topic continues: it is not a valid reason. In each body, the presence and absence of varieties of cognition are to be experienced [internally]. 'I have the cognition of doubt' — 'I do not have the cognition of doubt.' Similarly with perception, inference, scripture, and memory-cognitions. This non-apprehension of obstruction and the like — the absence of apprehension — is self-known: 'I do not have the apprehension of any obstruction of sound'; therefore, obstructions and the like as causes of non-grasping of sound are not apprehended. In that case, what was said — 'from the non-observation of the non-apprehension, non-existence is established' — that is untenable. // 31 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 32

<s>Anityasama</s> (the fallacy of equal impermanence): because from similarity with an impermanent thing, the tenability of having the same property leads to the unwanted consequence of everything being impermanent. // 5.1.32 //

children.text: anityena ghaṭena sādharmyād anityaḥ śabda iti bruvato 'sti ghaṭenānityena sarvabhāvānāṃ sādharmyam iti sarvasyānityatvam aniṣṭaṃ sampadyate/ so 'yam anityatvena pratyavasthānād anityasama iti//32//
children.translated_text: When one says 'sound is impermanent because of similarity with the impermanent pot,' there is a similarity of all things with the impermanent pot — hence the unintended conclusion that everything is impermanent follows. This is <s>anityasama</s>, a counter-position through [alleged] impermanence. // 32 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 33
The reply to this —
Because [the property] is not established from [mere] similarity, the refutation is not established — because of the similarity [of the refutation] with what is to be refuted. // 5.1.33 //

children.text: pratijñādyavayavayuktaṃ vākyaṃ pakṣanivartakaṃ pratipakṣalakṣaṇaṃ pratiṣedhaḥ/ tasya pakṣeṇa pratiṣedhyena sādharmyaṃ pratijñādiyogaḥ/ tad yady anityasādharmyād anityatvasyāsiddhiḥ, sādharmyād asiddheḥ pratiṣedhasyāpy asiddhiḥ, pratiṣedhyena sādharmyād iti//33//
children.translated_text: A refutation is a counter-thesis, characterized as having the components of thesis and the like, that overturns a position. Its similarity with the position to be refuted is its sharing of the components — thesis and the like. If impermanence is not established from mere similarity with an impermanent thing, then by the same [reasoning], the refutation too is not established — because of its similarity with what is to be refuted. // 33 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 34

children.text: dṛṣṭānte ca sādhyasādhanabhāvena prajñātasya dharmasya hetutvāt tasya cobhayathābhāvān nāviśeṣaḥ // 5.1.34 //
children.translated_text: And because in the example, the property known in the relation of probandum and probans is the reason, and because that [property] exists in both ways, there is no non-distinction. // 5.1.34 //

children.text: dṛṣṭānte yaḥ khalu dharmaḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvena prajñāyate, sa hetutvenābhidhīyate/ sa cobhayathā bhavati,
children.translated_text: In the example, the property that is known in the relation of probandum and probans is cited as the reason. And that exists in both ways —

children.text: — kenacit samānaḥ, kutaścid viśiṣṭaḥ/ sāmānyāt sādharmyaṃ viśeṣāc ca vaidharmyam/ evaṃ sādharmyaviśeṣo hetuḥ, nāviśeṣeṇa sādharmyamātraṃ vaidharmyamātraṃ vā/ sādharmyamātraṃ vaidharmyamātraṃ cāśritya bhavān āha —
children.translated_text: similar to something in some respect, distinct from something in another respect. From the commonality comes similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>), and from the distinction comes dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>). Thus the specific similarity is the reason, not mere undifferentiated similarity or mere dissimilarity. Relying on mere similarity or mere dissimilarity, you say —
'Because from similarity with the impermanent, the tenability of having the same property leads to the unwanted consequence of everything being impermanent — <s>anityasama</s>' —

children.text: iti, etad ayuktam iti/ aviśeṣasamapratiṣedhe ca yad uktaṃ tad api veditavyam//34//
children.translated_text: this is untenable. And what was said regarding the refutation of <s>aviśeṣasama</s> (the fallacy of non-distinction) should also be understood here. // 34 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 35
<s>Nityasama</s> (the fallacy of equal permanence): because from the permanence of impermanence, or the tenability of permanence if impermanence [itself is] impermanent. // 5.1.35 //

children.text: anityaḥ śabda iti pratijñāyate/ tad anityatvaṃ kiṃ śabde nityam athānityam? yadi tāvat sarvadā bhavati? dharmasya sadā bhāvād dharmiṇo 'pi sadā bhāva iti nityaḥ śabda iti/ atha na sarvadā bhavati? anityatvasyābhāvān nityaḥ śabdaḥ/ evaṃ nityatvena pratyavasthānān nityasamaḥ//35//
children.translated_text: It is asserted: 'Sound is impermanent.' Is that impermanence permanent in sound, or impermanent? If it is always present — since a property always exists, the property-bearer also always exists; hence sound is permanent. If it is not always present — since impermanence is absent, sound is permanent. Thus, by the counter-position through permanence, this is <s>nityasama</s>. // 35 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 36
The reply to this —
Since impermanence permanently characterizes what is to be refuted, the refutation is untenable because of the tenability of impermanence of [that which is] impermanent. // 5.1.36 //

children.text: pratiṣedhye śabde nityam anityatvasya bhāvād ity ucyamāne 'nujñātaṃ śabdasyānityatvam, anityatvopapatteś ca

children.translated_text: 'sound is not impermanent' —

children.text: iti pratiṣedho nopapadyate/ atha nābhyupagamyate, nityam anityatvasya bhāvād iti hetur na bhavatīti hetvabhāvāt pratiṣedhānupapattir iti/
children.translated_text: this refutation is untenable. If it is not conceded, then 'because impermanence is permanently present' does not serve as a reason, and from the absence of the reason, the refutation is untenable.
When it is said 'impermanence permanently characterizes sound, which is to be refuted,' the impermanence of sound is [thereby] conceded; and from the tenability of impermanence,

children.text: utapannasya nirodhād abhāvaḥ śabdasyānityatvam, tatra paripraśnānupapattiḥ/ yo 'yaṃ paripraśnaḥ — tad anityatvaṃ kiṃ śabde sarvadā bhavati atha neti, ayam anupapannaḥ/ kasmāt? utpannasya yo nirodhād abhāvaḥ śabdasya tad anityatvam; evaṃ ca saty adhikaraṇādheyavibhāgo vyāghātān nāstīti/ nityānityatvavirodhāc ca/ nityatvam anityatvaṃ ca ekasya dharmiṇo dharmāv iti virudhyete, na sambhavataḥ/
children.translated_text: The impermanence of sound is the non-existence [of sound] through the cessation of what has arisen; in that case, the cross-questioning is inapplicable. The question 'Is that impermanence always present in sound or not?' is inapplicable. Why? Because the impermanence of sound is the non-existence of sound through the cessation of what has arisen; and this being so, a distinction between the locus and what is located in it is contradictory and does not exist. And because permanence and impermanence are contradictory — permanence and impermanence as properties of one and the same property-bearer are contradictory and cannot coexist.

children.text: tatra yad uktaṃ — nityam anityatvasya bhāvān nitya eva, tad avartamānārtham uktam iti//36//
children.translated_text: Therefore, what was said — 'because impermanence is permanently present, it is permanent' — that was stated about something that does not obtain. // 36 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 37
<s>Kāryasama</s> (the fallacy of equal effect): because the effect of effort is of more than one kind. // 5.1.37 //

children.text: prayatnānantarīyakatvād anityaḥ śabda iti/ yasya prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaḥ tat khalv abhūtvā bhavati, yathā ghaṭādikāryam; anityam iti ca bhūtvā na bhavatīty etad vijñāyate/
children.translated_text: 'Sound is impermanent because of being subsequent to effort.' That which comes into existence subsequent to effort — that indeed comes into being having not existed before, like the effect of a pot and the like; and 'impermanent' is understood as: having come into being, it ceases to be.

children.text: evam avasthite prayatnakāryānekatvād iti pratiṣedha ucyate/ prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaś ca dṛṣṭo ghaṭādīnām, vyavadhānāpohāc cābhivyaktir vyavahitānām/ tat kiṃ prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaḥ śabdasyāho 'bhivyaktir iti viśeṣo nāsti/ kāryāviśeṣeṇa pratyavasthānam kāryasamaḥ//37//
children.translated_text: Given this situation, the counter-position 'because the effect of effort is of more than one kind' is stated. The coming into existence subsequent to effort is observed in pots and the like; and the manifestation of things previously obstructed [is observed] through the removal of obstruction.
