So is the coming into being of sound subsequent to effort its origination, or its manifestation? There is no distinction. A counter-position through the non-distinction of the effect — this is <s>kāryasama</s>. // 37 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 38
The reply to this —
If the effect is different [i.e., manifestation], effort is not the cause [of origination], because a cause of non-apprehension is tenable. // 5.1.38 //

children.text: sati kāryānyatve anupalabdhikāraṇopapatteḥ prayatnasyāhetutvaṃ śabdasyābhivyaktau/ yatra prayatnānantaram abhivyaktis tatrānupalabdhikāraṇaṃ vyavadhānam upapadyate, vyavadhānāpohāc ca prayatnānantarabhāvino 'rthasyopalabdhilakṣaṇā 'bhivyaktir bhavatīti,
children.translated_text: Given the difference of the effect [i.e., if it is manifestation rather than origination], effort is not the cause of the manifestation of sound, because a cause of non-apprehension [i.e., obstruction] is tenable. Where manifestation occurs subsequent to effort, a cause of non-apprehension, namely obstruction, is tenable; and through the removal of that obstruction, the manifestation — characterized as the apprehension — of the object that was subsequent to effort occurs.

children.text: na tu śabdasyānupalabdhikāraṇaṃ kiñcid upapadyate, yasya prayatnānantaram apohāc chabdasyopalabhilakṣaṇā 'bhivyaktir bhavatīti, tasmād utpadyate śabdo nābhivyajyate iti//38//
children.translated_text: But for sound, no cause of non-apprehension is tenable, through whose removal by effort the manifestation — characterized as apprehension — of sound would occur. Therefore, sound is produced, not manifested. // 38 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 39

children.text: hetoś ced anaikāntikatvam upapadyate anaikātikatvād asādhakaḥ syād iti/ yadi cānaikāntikatvād asādhakatvam —
children.translated_text: If it is argued that the inconclusive nature of the reason is tenable, then it would be non-probative because of its inconclusive nature. But if non-probativeness follows from inconclusiveness —
The same defect applies to the refutation as well. // 5.1.39 //

children.text: pratiṣedho 'py anaikāntikaḥ, kiñcit pratiṣedhati kiñcin neti anaikāntikatvād asādhaka iti/ atha vā śabdasyānityatvapakṣe prayatnānantaram utpādo nābhivyaktir iti viśeṣahetvabhāvaḥ, nityatvapakṣe 'pi prayatnānantaram abhivyaktir notpāda iti viśeṣahetvabhāvaḥ/ so 'yam ubhayapakṣasamo viśeṣahetvabhāva ity ubhayam apy anaikātikam iti//39//
children.translated_text: The refutation too is inconclusive — it refutes some things and not others — hence it is non-probative because of its inconclusiveness. Alternatively: in the position that sound is impermanent, the absence of a specific reason [to determine] whether the effect subsequent to effort is origination or manifestation; in the position of permanence too, the absence of a specific reason [to determine] whether it is manifestation and not origination. This absence of a specific reason is equal in both positions — hence both are inconclusive. // 39 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 40
The same applies everywhere. // 5.1.40 //

children.text: sarveṣu sādharmyaprabhṛtiṣu pratiṣedhahetuṣu yatra yatrāviśeṣo dṛśyate tatrobhayoḥ pakṣayoḥ samaḥ prasajyata iti//40//
children.translated_text: In all the counter-reasons beginning with similarity, wherever non-distinction is seen, [the defect] applies equally to both positions. // 40 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 41
In the counter-refutation of the refutation, the defect is the same as the defect of the refutation. // 5.1.41 //

children.text: yo 'yaṃ pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣo 'naikāntikatvam āpadyate so 'yaṃ pratiṣedhasya vipratiṣedhe 'pi samānaḥ/
children.translated_text: The same inconclusiveness that attaches to the refutation attaches equally to the counter-refutation of the refutation.

children.text: tatrānityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād iti sādhanavādinaḥ sthāpanā prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ/
children.translated_text: In this context, 'sound is impermanent because of being subsequent to effort' — the establishment by the proponent — is the first position.
'Because the effect of effort is of more than one kind' — <s>kāryasama</s>

children.text: iti dūṣaṇavādinaḥ pratiṣedhahetunā dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ/ sa ca pratiṣedha ity ucyate/ tasyāsya pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa iti tṛtīyaḥ pakṣaḥ vipratiṣedha ucyate/ tasmin pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣo 'naikāntikatvaṃ caturthaḥ pakṣaḥ//41//
children.translated_text: Thus, by the refutation-reason of the objector, the second position is established. And that is called <s>pratiṣedha</s> (refutation). The third position is called <s>vipratiṣedha</s> (counter-refutation), meaning that even in his refutation, the same fault applies. In his refutation and counter-refutation too, the same fault of inconclusiveness constitutes the fourth position. // 41 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 42

children.text: pratiṣedhaṃ sadoṣam abhyupetya pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe samāno doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā // 5.1.42 //
children.translated_text: Having accepted the refutation as faulty, the consequence of the same fault in the counter-refutation constitutes <s>matānujñā</s> (admission of one's position). // 5.1.42 //

children.text: pratiṣedhaṃ dvitīyaṃ pakṣaṃ sadoṣam abhyupetya taduddhāram akṛtvānujñāya pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe tṛtīyapakṣe samānam anaikāntikatvam iti samānaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ prasañjayato dūṣaṇavādino matānujñā prasajyata iti pañcamaḥ pakṣaḥ//42//
children.translated_text: Having accepted the second position — the refutation — as faulty, without removing that (fault), and granting it, when the objector imputes the same fault of inconclusiveness to the third position — the counter-refutation — and thus imputes the same defect, the consequence is <s>matānujñā</s> (admission of one's position) for the objector: this is the fifth position. // 42 //
Chapter 5, Section 1, <s>Sūtra</s> 43

When one who, with regard to a fault characterizing his own thesis, without removing it, applies a tenable fault to the opponent's thesis in adducing the reason, the same fault (arises) due to acceptance of the opponent's thesis-fault. // 5.1.43 //

children.text: sthāpanāpakṣe prayatnakāryānekatvād iti doṣaḥ sthāpanāhetuvādinaḥ svapakṣalakṣaṇo bhavati/ kasmāt? svapakṣasamutthatvāt/ so 'yaṃ svapakṣalakṣaṇaṃ doṣam apekṣamāṇo 'nuddhṛtyānujñāya pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa ity upapadyamānaṃ doṣaṃ parapakṣe upasaṃharati/ itthaṃ cānaikāntikaḥ pratiṣedha iti hetuṃ nirdiśati/ tatra svapakṣalakṣaṇāpekṣayopapadyamānadoṣopasaṃhāre hetunirdeśe ca saty anena parapakṣadoṣo 'bhyupagato bhavati/ kathaṃ kṛtvā? yaḥ pareṇa prayatnakāryānekatvād ityādinānaikāntikadoṣa uktaḥ, tam anuddhṛtya pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa ity āha/ evaṃ sthāpanāṃ sadoṣām abhyupetya pratiṣedhe 'pi samānaṃ doṣaṃ prasañjayataḥ parapakṣābhyupagamāt samāno doṣo bhavati/
children.translated_text: In the establishment-thesis, the fault 'because the effects of effort are many' characterizes the thesis of the proponent of the establishment-reason. Why? Because it arises from his own thesis. This one, with regard to a fault characterizing his own thesis, without removing it and granting it, applies a tenable fault to the opponent's thesis saying 'the same fault exists in the refutation too,' and adduces the reason: 'thus the refutation is inconclusive.' Therein, when the tenable fault is applied to the opponent's thesis with regard to one's own thesis-fault, and when the reason is adduced, the opponent's thesis-fault has been accepted by him. How so? The fault of inconclusiveness stated by the opponent through 'because the effects of effort are many' and so forth — without removing it, he says 'the same fault exists in the refutation too.' Thus, having accepted the establishment as faulty, when he imputes the same fault to the refutation, due to acceptance of the opponent's thesis, the same fault arises.

children.text:
yathā parasya pratiṣedhaṃ sadoṣam abhyupetya pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā prasajyata iti, tathāsyāpi sthāpanāṃ sadoṣām abhyupetya pratiṣedhe 'pi samānaṃ doṣaṃ prasañjayato matānujñā prasajyata iti/ sa khalv ayaṃ ṣaṣṭhaḥ pakṣaḥ/
tatra khalu sthāpanāhetuvādinaḥ prathamatṛtīyapañcamapakṣāḥ, pratiṣedhahetuvādinaḥ dvitīyacaturthaṣaṣṭhapakṣāḥ/ teṣāṃ sādhvasādhutāyāṃ mīmāṃsyamānāyāṃ caturthaṣaṣṭhayor arthāviśeṣāt punaruktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ/ caturthapakṣe samānadoṣatvaṃ parasyocyate --
children.translated_text: Just as for the other party, having accepted the refutation as faulty, the consequence of the same fault in the counter-refutation constitutes <s>matānujñā</s> (admission) — so too for this one, having accepted the establishment as faulty, when he imputes the same fault to the refutation, <s>matānujñā</s> follows. This indeed is the sixth position. Now, the first, third, and fifth positions belong to the proponent of the establishment-reason, and the second, fourth, and sixth positions belong to the proponent of the refutation-reason. When examining the validity and invalidity of these, the fourth and sixth positions involve the fault of repetition due to no difference in meaning. In the fourth position, the same-fault-ness of the opponent is stated —
'In the counter-refutation, a fault like the refutation-fault' —
thus. In the sixth too,
'Due to acceptance of the opponent's thesis-fault, the same fault' —

children.text: iti samānadoṣatvam evocyate, nārthaviśeṣaḥ kaścid asti/ samānas tṛṭīyapañcamayoḥ punaruktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, tṛṭīyapakṣe 'pi
children.translated_text: thus, same-fault-ness alone is stated, and there is no difference in meaning. Similarly, the third and fifth positions involve the fault of repetition — in the third position too,
'the same fault exists in the refutation too' —
thus, sameness is accepted. In the fifth position too,
'the consequence of the same fault in the counter-refutation' —

children.text:
'bhyupagamyate, nārthaviśeṣaḥ kaścid ucyata iti/ tatra pañcamaṣaṣṭhapakṣayor arthāviśeṣāt punaruktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, tṛtīyacaturthayor matānujñā, prathamadvitīyayor viśeṣahetvabhāva iti ṣaṭpakṣyām ubhayor asiddhiḥ/
kadā ṣaṭpakṣī? yadā
children.translated_text: is accepted, and no difference in meaning is stated. Further, the fifth and sixth positions involve the fault of repetition due to no difference in meaning; the third and fourth involve <s>matānujñā</s> (admission); the first and second lack a distinguishing reason — thus, in the six-position scheme, both sides fail to establish (their thesis). When does the six-position scheme arise? When
'the same fault exists in the refutation too' —

children.text: ity evaṃ pravarttate/ tadobhayoḥ pakṣayor asiddhiḥ/ yadā tu
children.translated_text: such a procedure is adopted, then both theses fail. But when
'in the case of the effect being different, effort is not the cause, because a reason for non-apprehension is tenable' —
through this, the third position is justified,
then, due to the statement of a distinguishing reason —
'sound attains its existence immediately after effort, and is not a manifestation' —

children.text: iti siddhaḥ prathamapakṣo na ṣaṭpakṣī pravartata iti//43//
children.translated_text: the first position is established, and the six-position scheme does not arise. // 43 //
Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter in the venerable <s>Vātsyāyana</s>'s <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>.

children.text:
nyāyadarśanam
pañcamādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam
vipratipattyapratipattyor vikalpān nigrahasthānabahutvam iti saṅkṣepeṇoktam, tad idānīṃ vibhajanīyam/ nigrahasthānāni khalu parājayavastūny aparādhādhikaraṇāni prāyeṇa pratijñādyavayavāśrayāṇi tattvavādinam atattvavādinaṃ cābhisaṃplavante/
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyadarśana</s>, fifth chapter, second section. It was stated in summary that the multiplicity of <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) arises from the varieties of misunderstanding and non-understanding; that is now to be classified. <s>Nigrahasthānas</s> are indeed grounds of defeat, domains of fault; they generally rest upon the members (of a syllogism) such as the thesis and the rest, and apply to both the speaker of truth and the speaker of untruth.
Chapter 5, Section 2
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 1
Their classification —

children.text: pratijñāhāniḥ pratijñāntaraṃ pratijñāvirodhaḥ pratijñāsannyāso hetvantaram arthāntaraṃ nirarthakam avijñātārtham apārthakam aprāptakālaṃ nyūnam adhikaṃ punaruktam ananubhāṣaṇam ajñānam apratibhā vikṣepo matānujñā paryanuyojyopekṣaṇaṃ niranuyojyānuyogo 'pasiddhānto hetvābhāsāś ca nigrahasthānāni // 5.2.1 //
children.translated_text: The <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) are: <s>pratijñāhāni</s> (abandoning the thesis), <s>pratijñāntara</s> (shifting the thesis), <s>pratijñāvirodha</s> (contradicting the thesis), <s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s> (renouncing the thesis), <s>hetvantara</s> (shifting the reason), <s>arthāntara</s> (irrelevance), <s>nirarthaka</s> (meaninglessness), <s>avijñātārtha</s> (unintelligible meaning), <s>apārthaka</s> (incoherence), <s>aprāptakāla</s> (untimeliness), <s>nyūna</s> (deficiency), <s>adhika</s> (excess), <s>punarukta</s> (repetition), <s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (failure to respond), <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance), <s>apratibhā</s> (lack of resourcefulness), <s>vikṣepa</s> (evasion), <s>matānujñā</s> (admission of the opponent's position), <s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s> (overlooking what is censurable), <s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s> (censuring what is not censurable), <s>apasiddhānta</s> (deviation from one's doctrine), and <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons). // 5.2.1 //
These are classified into twenty-two kinds and are now defined —
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 2
Admitting in one's own example the property of the counter-example is <s>pratijñāhāni</s> (abandoning the thesis). // 5.2.2 //

children.text: sādhyadharmapratyanīkena dharmeṇa pratyavasthite pratidraṣṭāntadharmaṃ svadṛṣṭānte 'bhyanujānan pratijñāṃ jahātīti pratjñāhāniḥ/ nidarśanam —

children.translated_text: 'Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses, like a pot' —

children.text: ity kṛte apara āha -- dṛṣṭam aindriyakatvaṃ sāmānye nitye, kasmān na tathā śabda iti pratyavasthite idam āha —
children.translated_text: when this is stated, another says: 'Perceptibility is observed in the universal, which is permanent; why should sound not be likewise?' — to this counter-argument, he replies:

When the opponent counters with a property opposed to the property to be proved, one who admits the property of the counter-example in one's own example abandons the thesis — this is <s>pratijñāhāni</s>. Illustration —

children.text: yady aindriyakaṃ sāmānyaṃ nityaṃ kāmaṃ ghaṭo nityo 'stv iti/
children.translated_text: 'If the universal, being perceptible, is permanent, then let the pot too be permanent.'

children.text: sa khalv ayaṃ sādhakasya dṛṣṭāntasya nityatvaṃ prasañjayan nigamanāntam eva pakṣaṃ jahāti, pakṣaṃ jahatpratijñāṃ jahātīty ucyate, pratijñāśrayatvāt pakṣasyeti//2//
children.translated_text: This person, by imputing permanence to his own example (the pot), abandons the thesis up to its conclusion; in abandoning the thesis, he is said to abandon the <s>pratijñā</s> (proposition), because the thesis is the basis of the proposition. // 2 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 3
When the asserted meaning is refuted, the indication of a different meaning due to differentiation of properties is <s>pratijñāntara</s> (shifting the thesis). // 5.2.3 //
'Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses, like a pot' —

children.text: ity ukte yo 'sya pratiṣedhaḥ pratidṛṣṭāntena hetuvyabhicāraḥ — sāmānyam aindriyakaṃ nityam iti, tasmiṃś ca pratijñātārthapratiṣedhe,
children.translated_text: when this is stated, the refutation of it is the deviation of the reason through the counter-example — 'the universal is perceptible yet permanent.' When the asserted meaning is thus refuted,
'due to differentiation of properties' —

children.text: iti dṛṣṭāntapratidṛṣṭāntayoḥ sādharmyayoge dharmabhedāt sāmānyam aindriyakaṃ sarvagatam aindriyakas tv asarvagato ghaṭa iti dharmavikalpāt,
children.translated_text: that is, when the example and counter-example share a common property, a difference of properties (exists): the universal is perceptible and all-pervading, but the pot, being perceptible, is not all-pervading — due to this differentiation of properties,
'the indication of a different meaning' —

children.text: iti sādhyasiddhyartham/ katham? yathā ghaṭo 'sarvagata evaṃ śabdo 'py asarvagato ghaṭavad evānitya iti/
children.translated_text: is for the purpose of establishing what is to be proved. How? 'Just as the pot is not all-pervading, so sound too is not all-pervading; like the pot, it is impermanent.'
The asserted meaning is:

children.text: tatrānityaḥ śabda iti pūrvā pratijñā, asarvagata iti dvitīyā pratijñā pratijñāntaram/ tat kathaṃ nigrahasthām iti? na pratijñāyāḥ sādhanaṃ pratijñāntaram, kiṃ tu hetudṛṣṭāntau sādhanaṃ pratijñāyāḥ, tad etad asādhanopādānam anarthakam iti/ ānarthakyān nigrahasthānam iti//3//
children.translated_text: Here, 'sound is impermanent' is the first thesis, and 'not all-pervading' is the second thesis — a different thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>). How is this a point of defeat? A different thesis is not the proof of the (original) thesis; rather, the reason and example are the proof of the thesis. This adoption of a non-proof is meaningless. Due to meaninglessness, it is a point of defeat. // 3 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 4
The contradiction between thesis and reason is <s>pratijñāvirodha</s> (contradicting the thesis). // 5.2.4 //
'Because nothing different from color and the rest is apprehended' —
this is the reason.
'Substance is different from qualities' — this is the thesis.

children.text: so 'yaṃ pratijñāhetvor virodhaḥ/ katham? yadi guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam, rūpādibhyo 'rthāntarasyānupalabdhir nopapadyate/ atha rūpādibhyo 'rthāntarasyānupalabdhiḥ, guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam iti nopapadyate/
children.translated_text: This is the contradiction between thesis and reason. How? If substance is different from qualities, then the non-apprehension of something different from color and the rest is not tenable. If there is non-apprehension of something different from color and the rest, then 'substance is different from qualities' is not tenable.

children.text: guṇavyatiriktaṃ ca dravyaṃ rūpādibhyaś cārthāntarasyānupalabdhir iti virudhyate — vyāhanyate na sambhavatīti//4//
children.translated_text: 'Substance is different from qualities' and 'nothing different from color and the rest is apprehended' — these are contradictory: they are mutually destructive and cannot coexist. // 4 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 5
The withdrawal of the asserted meaning when the thesis is refuted is <s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s> (renouncing the thesis). // 5.2.5 //

children.text: anityaḥ śabda aindriyakatvād ity ukte paro brūyāt sāmānyam aindriyakaṃ na cānityam,
children.translated_text: When it is stated 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses,' the opponent might say: 'the universal is perceptible yet not impermanent;

children.text: evaṃ śabdo 'py aindriyako na cānitya iti/ evaṃ pratiṣiddhe pakṣe yadi brūyāt —
children.translated_text: similarly, sound too, though perceptible, is not impermanent.' When the thesis is thus refuted, if one were to say —
'Who ever said that sound is impermanent?' —
this denial of the asserted meaning is <s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s> (renouncing the thesis). // 5 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 6

children.text: aviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣam icchato hetvantaram // 5.2.6 //
children.translated_text: When a generally stated reason is refuted, wishing to specify constitutes <s>hetvantara</s> (shifting the reason). // 5.2.6 //

children.text: nidarśanam — ekaprakṛtīdaṃ vyaktam iti pratijñā/ kasmād dhetoḥ? ekaprakṛtīnāṃ vikārāṇāṃ parimāṇāt/ mṛtpūrvakāṇāṃ śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ parimāṇam, yāvān prakṛter vyūho bhavati tāvān vikāra iti/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca prativikāraṃ parimāṇam/ asti cedaṃ parimāṇam prativyaktaṃ tadekaprakṛtīnāṃ vikārāṇāṃ parimāṇāt paśyāmo vyaktam idam ekaprakṛtīti/
children.translated_text: Illustration — 'This manifest (world) has a single material cause' is the thesis. For what reason? 'Because of the measure of modifications having a single material cause.' The measure of things such as pots and the rest, which have clay as their prior (material), is observed — the modification is as extensive as the arrangement of the material cause. And a measure is observed for each modification. This measure exists for each manifest thing; therefore, from the measure of modifications having a single material cause, we see that this manifest (world) has a single material cause.

children.text: asya vyabhicāreṇa pratyavasthānaṃ — nānāprakṛtīnām ekaprakṛtīnāṃ ca vikārāṇāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ parimāṇam iti/ evaṃ pratyavasthite āha — ekaprakṛtisamanvaye sati śarāvādivikārāṇāṃ parimāṇadarśanāt/ sukhaduḥkhamohasamanvitaṃ hīdaṃ vyaktaṃ parimitaṃ gṛhyate, — tatra prakṛtyantararūpasamanvayābhāve saty ekaprakṛtitvam iti/ tad idam aviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣaṃ bruvato hetvantaraṃ bhavati/ sati ca hetvantarabhāve pūrvasya hetor asādhakatvān nigrahasthānam/ hetvantaravacane sati yadi hetvarthanidarśano dṛṣṭānta upādīyate,
children.translated_text: The counter-argument through deviation — 'the measure of modifications is observed both for those having many material causes and for those having a single material cause.' When thus countered, he says: 'because of the observation of measure in modifications such as pots and the rest when there is the concomitance of a single material cause.' For this manifest (world) is apprehended as measured, accompanied by pleasure, pain, and delusion — and in the absence of concomitance with the form of another material cause, there is single-material-cause-ness. Now this, when the generally stated reason is refuted and one states a specification, constitutes <s>hetvantara</s> (shifting the reason). And when there is shifting of the reason, due to the non-probative nature of the former reason, it is a point of defeat. If, when stating the different reason, an example illustrating the meaning of the reason is adduced,

children.text: nedaṃ vyaktam ekaprakṛti bhavati, prakṛtyantaropādānāt/ atha nopādīyate, dṛṣṭānte hetvarthasyānidarśitasya sādhakabhāvānupapatter ānarthakyād dhetor anivṛttaṃ nigrahasthānam iti//6//
children.translated_text: 'this manifest (world) does not have a single material cause, because another material cause is adduced' — (then the thesis itself falls). But if (an example) is not adduced, due to the non-probative nature of the reason whose meaning has not been illustrated in an example, because of its meaninglessness, the point of defeat from the (original) reason is not averted. // 6 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 7
A meaning unconnected with the matter under discussion is <s>arthāntara</s> (irrelevance). // 5.2.7 //

children.text: yathoktalakṣaṇe pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahe (corr.; pakṣapatipakṣa-, ed.) hetutaḥ sādhyasiddhau prakṛtāyāṃ brūyāt — nityaḥ śabdo 'sparśatvād iti hetuḥ/ hetur nāma hinoter dhātos tuni pratyaye kṛdantaṃ padam/ padaṃ ca nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ/ abhidheyasya kriyāntarayogād viśiṣyamāṇarūpaḥ śabdo

children.translated_text: noun.

children.text: / kriyākārakasamudāyaḥ kārakasaṅkhyāviśiṣṭakriyākālayogābhidhāyākhyātam, dhātvarthamātraṃ ca kālābhidhānaviśiṣṭam/ prayogeṣv arthād abhidyamānārūpā nipātāḥ/
children.translated_text: A verb is the expression of the combination of action and agent-factors, denoting the connection of action with time as distinguished by the number of agents; and also that which denotes merely the meaning of a root as distinguished by the expression of time. Particles are those whose forms are expressed incidentally in usage.

When, in the acceptance of thesis and counter-thesis as described, the establishment of what is to be proved from the reason is the matter at hand, one might say: 'Sound is permanent because it is intangible' — this is the reason. 'Reason' (<s>hetu</s>) is a word formed by the suffix 'tun' from the root 'hi' (to impel), a <s>kṛdanta</s> (primary derivative) word. Words are of four kinds: nouns (<s>nāman</s>), verbs (<s>ākhyāta</s>), prefixes (<s>upasarga</s>), and particles (<s>nipāta</s>). A word whose form is distinguished by the connection of the thing denoted with another action is a

children.text: upasṛjyamānāḥ kriyāvadyotakā upasargā ity evamādi/ tadarthāntaraṃ veditavyam iti//7//
children.translated_text: Prefixes are those that illuminate an action by being attached to it — and so forth. This should be understood as <s>arthāntara</s> (irrelevance). // 7 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 8
<s>Nirarthaka</s> (meaninglessness) is like the enumeration of phonemes in sequence. // 5.2.8 //

children.text: yathā 'nityaḥ śabdaḥ — kacaṭatapāḥ, javagaḍadaśatvāt, jhabhañ ghaḍhadhaṣavad iti —-
children.translated_text: For example: 'Sound is permanent — ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa; because of ja, va, ga, ḍa, da, śa-ness; like jha, bha, ña, gha, ḍha, dha, ṣa' —

children.text: evamprakāraṃ nirarthakam/ abhidhānābhidheyabhāvānupapattau arthagater abhāvād varṇā eva krameṇa nirdiśyanta iti//8//
children.translated_text: of this kind is <s>nirarthaka</s> (meaninglessness). When the relation of expression and expressed meaning is untenable, since there is no apprehension of meaning, phonemes alone are enumerated in sequence. // 8 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 9

children.text: pariṣatprativādibhyāṃ trir abhihitam apy avijñātam avijñātārtham // 5.2.9 //
children.translated_text: That which, even though stated three times to the assembly and the opponent, remains not understood, is <s>avijñātārtha</s> (unintelligible meaning). // 5.2.9 //

children.text: yad vākyaṃ pariṣadā prativādinā ca trir abhihitam api na vijñāyate śliṣṭaśabdam apratītaprayogam atidrutoccaritam ity evamādinā kāraṇena,
children.translated_text: When a statement, even though uttered three times by the assembly and the opponent, is not understood — due to slurred words, unfamiliar usage, excessively rapid utterance, and such reasons —

children.text: tadavijñātam avijñātārtham asāmarthyasaṃvaraṇāya prayuktam iti nigrahasthānam iti//9//
children.translated_text: that is <s>avijñāta</s> (the unintelligible), whose meaning is not understood, employed to conceal one's incompetence — this is a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat). // 9 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 10
That whose meaning is disconnected due to the impossibility of sequence is pointless. // 5.2.10 //

children.text: yatrānekasya padasya vākyasya vā paurvāparyeṇānvayayogo nāstīty asambaddhārthatvagṛhyate, tat samudāyārthasyāpāyād apārthakam/ yathā — daśa dāḍimāni, ṣaḍ apūpāḥ;
children.translated_text: Where the sequential connection of multiple words or sentences is not tenable and the meaning is grasped as disconnected — that, due to the loss of the collective meaning, is pointless. For example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes;

children.text: kuṇḍam, ajājinam, palalapiṇḍaḥ, atha raurukam etad, kumāryāḥ pāyaṃ tasyāḥ pitā 'pratiśīna iti//10//
children.translated_text: a pot, a deerskin, a ball of straw, now this is a <s>raurava</s> deer, the girl's drink, her father is <s>apratiśīna</s>." // 10 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 11
A statement with transposition of the members is untimely (<s>aprāptakāla</s>). // 5.2.11 //

children.text: pratijñādīnām avayavānāṃ yathālakṣaṇam arthavaśāt kramaḥ, tatrāvayavaviparyāsena vacanam aprāaptakālam asambaddhārthaṃ nigrahasthānam iti//11//
children.translated_text: The sequence of the members — thesis and the rest — is determined by their defining characteristics and by the requirement of meaning. A statement with transposition of those members is untimely, with disconnected meaning, and is a <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (point of defeat). // 11 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 12
That which is deficient (<s>hīna</s>), lacking any one of the members, is <s>nyūna</s> (the deficient). // 5.2.12 //

children.text: pratijñādīnām avayavānām anyatamenāpy avayavena hīnaṃ nyūnaṃ nigrahasthānam, sādhanābhāve sādhyāsiddhir iti//12//
children.translated_text: That which is deficient by lacking any one of the members — thesis and the rest — is a <s>nigrahasthāna</s>, because in the absence of the means of proof, what is to be proved remains unestablished. // 12 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 13
That which has an excess of reason or example is <s>adhika</s> (the redundant). // 5.2.13 //

children.text: ekena kṛtatvād anyatarasyānarthakyam iti, tad etan niyamābhupagame veditavyam iti//13//
children.translated_text: Since one [reason or example] suffices, the other is purposeless. But this should be understood as applying when a restriction [to a single reason or example] is accepted. // 13 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 14
The repetition of word or meaning is <s>punarukta</s> (tautology), except in the case of restatement. // 5.2.14 //

children.text:
anyatrānuvādāt śabdapunaruktam arthapunaruktaṃ vā, nityaḥ śabdo nityaḥ śabda iti śabdapunaruktam/ arthapunaruktam — anityaḥ śabdo nirodhadharmako dhvanir iti/
anuvāde tv apunaruktaṃ śabdābhyāsād arthaviśeṣopapatteḥ/ yathā hetvapadeśāt pratijñāyāḥ punar vacanaṃ nigamanam iti//14//
children.translated_text: Except in the case of restatement — verbal tautology or tautology of meaning: "sound is eternal, sound is eternal" is verbal tautology. Tautology of meaning: "sound is non-eternal, subject to cessation, a reverberation." But in restatement, there is no tautology, because a special meaning is obtained from the repetition of words. For example, the restatement of the thesis after the adduction of the reason constitutes the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>). // 14 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 15
Restating in one's own words what has [already] been arrived at from the meaning is [also <s>punarukta</s>]. // 5.2.15 //

children.text: punaruktam iti prakṛtam/ nidarśanam — utpattidharmakatvād anityam ity uktvā arthād āpannasya yo 'bhidhāyakaḥ śabdas tena svaśabdena brūyād anutpattidharmakaṃ nityam iti,
children.translated_text: Tautology is the continuing topic. Illustration: having said "it is non-eternal because it has the nature of origination," if one then restates in one's own words what has been arrived at from the meaning — "what does not have the nature of origination is eternal" —

children.text: tac ca punarukataṃ veditavyam/ arthasampratyayārthe śabdaprayoge pratītaḥ so 'rtho 'rthāpttyeti//15//
children.translated_text: that should be understood as tautology. When a word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, and that meaning is already understood, [restating it] is arrival at the meaning (<s>arthāpatti</s>). // 15 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 16

children.text: vijñātasya pariṣadā, trir abhihitasyāpy apratyuccāraṇam ananubhāṣaṇam // 5.2.16 //
children.translated_text: The failure to repeat what has been understood by the assembly, even though stated three times, is <s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (failure to repeat). // 5.2.16 //

children.text: vijñātasya vākyārthasya pariṣadā, prativādinā trir abhihitasya yad apratyauccāraṇaṃ tad ananubhāṣaṇaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam iti/ apratyuccārayan kimāśrayaṃ parapakṣapratiṣedhaṃ brūyāt//16//
children.translated_text: When the meaning of a statement has been understood by the assembly but, even though stated three times by the opponent, one fails to repeat it — that is the <s>nigrahasthāna</s> called <s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (failure to repeat). For on what basis would one who fails to repeat [the opponent's statement] state the refutation of the opponent's thesis? // 16 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 17
And what is not understood is <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance). // 5.2.17 //

children.text: vijñātārthasya pariṣadā, prativādinā trir abhihitasya yad avijñātaṃ tad ajñānaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam iti/ ayaṃ khalv avijñāya kasya pratiṣedhaṃ brūyād iti//17//
children.translated_text: When the meaning of a statement has been understood by the assembly but, even though stated three times by the opponent, one has not understood it — that is the <s>nigrahasthāna</s> called <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance). For what would this person, having failed to understand, be able to refute? // 17 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 18
The failure to conceive of a reply is <s>apratibhā</s> (want of wit). // 5.2.18 //

children.text: parapakṣapratiṣedha uttaram, tad yadā na pratipadyate tadā nigṛhīto bhavati//18//
children.translated_text: A reply is the refutation of the opponent's thesis; when one fails to conceive of it, then one is defeated. // 18 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 19
The interruption of the debate due to involvement in other business is <s>vikṣepa</s> (evasion). // 5.2.19 //

children.text: yatra kartavyaṃ vyāsajya kathāṃ vyavacchinatti — idaṃ me karaṇīyaṃ vidyate, tasmin avasite paścāt kathayāmīti, vikṣepo nāma nigrahasthānam/ ekanigrahāvasānāyāṃ kathāyāṃ svayam eva kathāntaraṃ pratipadyata iti//19//
children.translated_text: When one, citing other business, interrupts the debate — "I have something to do; when that is concluded, I shall debate afterward" — that is the <s>nigrahasthāna</s> called <s>vikṣepa</s> (evasion). In a debate that ends with the defeat of one side, he himself moves on to another debate. // 19 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 20
<s>Matānujñā</s> (admitting the opponent's view) is when, due to accepting a fault in one's own thesis, one imputes a fault to the opponent's thesis. // 5.2.20 //

children.text: yaḥ pareṇa coditaṃ doṣaṃ svapakṣe 'bhyupagamyānuddhṛtya vadati — bhavatpakṣe 'pi samāno doṣa iti,
children.translated_text: When one, having accepted a fault pointed out by the opponent in one's own thesis, without removing it says — "there is the same fault in your thesis as well" —

children.text: sa svapakṣe doṣābhyupagamāt parapakṣe doṣaṃ prasañjayan paramatam anujānātīti matānujñāṃ nāma nigrahasthānam āpadyata iti//20//
children.translated_text: he, by accepting the fault in his own thesis while imputing a fault to the opponent's thesis, concedes the opponent's view, and thus falls into the <s>nigrahasthāna</s> called <s>matānujñā</s> (admitting the opponent's view). // 20 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 21
<s>Paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s> (overlooking the censurable) is the failure to censure one who has arrived at a point of defeat. // 5.2.21 //

children.text: paryanuyojyo nāma nigrahopapattyā codanīyaḥ, tasyopekṣaṇaṃ nigrahasthānaṃ prāpto 'sīty ananuyogaḥ/ etac ca kasya parājaya ity anuyuktayā pariṣadā vacanīyam, na khalu nigrahaṃ prāptaḥ svakaupīnaṃ vivṛṇuyād iti//21//
children.translated_text: The censurable (<s>paryanuyojya</s>) is one who should be challenged because a point of defeat applies to him. The overlooking of such a person is the non-challenging — "you have arrived at a point of defeat." And this should be stated by the assembly when challenged [to identify] whose defeat it is; for one who has arrived at a point of defeat should not expose his own deficiency. // 21 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 22
<s>Niranuyojyānuyoga</s> (censuring the non-censurable) is the imputation of a point of defeat where there is none. // 5.2.22 //

children.text: nigrahasthālakṣaṇasya mithyādhyavasāyād anigrahasthāne nigṛhīto 'sīti paraṃ bruvan niranuyojyānuyojgān nigṛhīto veditavya iti//22//
children.translated_text: Due to a false determination regarding the defining characteristics of a point of defeat, one who says to the opponent "you are defeated" where there is no point of defeat should be understood as defeated by [the fallacy of] censuring the non-censurable. // 22 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 23
<s>Apasiddhānta</s> (abandoning a tenet) is involving oneself in a debate through inconsistency after having accepted a <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine). // 5.2.23 //

children.text: kasyacid arthasya tathābhāvaṃ pratijñāya pratijñātārthaviparyayād aniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayato 'pasiddhānto veditavyaḥ/ yathā na sad ātmānaṃ jahāti, na sato vināśo, nāsad ātmānaṃ labhate, nāsad utpadyata iti siddhāntam abhyupetya svapakṣaṃ vyavasthāpayati — ekaprakṛtīdaṃ vyaktaṃ vikārāṇām anvayadarśanāt/ mṛdanvitānāṃ śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭam ekaprakṛtitvam, tathā cāyaṃ vyaktabhedaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohānvito dṛśyate/ tasmāt samanvayadarśanāt sukhādibhir ekaprakṛtīdaṃ viśvam iti/ evam uktavān anuyujyate — atha pratṛtir vikāra iti kathaṃ lakṣitavyam iti/ yasyāvasthitasya dharmāntaranivṛttau dharmāntaraṃ pravartate, sā prakṛtiḥ/ yad dharmāntaraṃ pravartate nivartate vā sa vikāra iti/ so 'yaṃ pratijñātārthaviparyāsād aniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayati/ pratijñātaṃ khalv anena — nāsad āvirbhavati,
children.translated_text: Having asserted the existence of a certain matter, one who then involves oneself in a debate through inconsistency — by contradicting the asserted matter — should be understood as guilty of <s>apasiddhānta</s>. For example: having accepted the <s>siddhānta</s> — "What exists does not lose its nature; there is no destruction of what exists; what does not exist does not gain a nature; what does not exist does not originate" — one establishes one's own thesis: "This manifest [world] has a single material cause, because of the observed continuity of modifications. The single-material-cause nature of earthen pots, etc., which are pervaded by clay, is observed; similarly, this differentiation of the manifest [world] is observed as pervaded by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Therefore, from the observation of continuity, this universe has a single material cause through pleasure and the rest." Having so stated, one is challenged: "Now, how is one to distinguish <s>prakṛti</s> (primal matter) and <s>vikāra</s> (modification)?" That whose properties change into different properties while it remains stable — that is <s>prakṛti</s>. The different property that arises or ceases — that is <s>vikāra</s>. This person involves himself in a debate through inconsistency by contradicting the asserted matter. For he has asserted: "What does not exist does not come into being,

children.text: na sat tirobhavatīti/ sadasatoś ca tirobhāvāvirbhāvam antareṇa na kasyacit pravṛttiḥ pravṛttyuparamaś ca bhavati/ mṛdi khalv avasthitāyāṃ bhaviṣyati śarāvādilakṣaṇaṃ dharmāntaram iti pravṛttir bhavati, abhūd iti ca pravṛttyuparamaḥ/ tad etad mṛddharmāṇām api na syāt/ evaṃ pratyavasthito yadi sataś cātmahānam asataś cātmalābham abhyupaiti, tad asyāpasiddhānato nigrahasthānaṃ bhavati/ atha nābhyupaiti, pakṣo 'sya na sidhyati//23//
children.translated_text: and what exists does not cease to be." But without the cessation and emergence of what exists and does not exist, there can be no arising or ceasing of anything. When clay remains stable, a different property in the form of a pot, etc., will arise — that is the arising; and "it was not" — that is the cessation. But that should not apply even to the properties of clay. When thus confronted, if he accepts the loss of nature by what exists and the gaining of nature by what does not exist, then his <s>apasiddhānta</s> becomes a point of defeat. But if he does not accept it, his thesis fails. // 23 //
Chapter 5, Section 2, <s>Sūtra</s> 24
And the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons) are as previously described. // 5.2.24 //

children.text: hetvābhāsāś ca nigrahasthānāni/ kiṃ punar lakṣaṇāntarayogād hetvābhāsā nigrahasthānatvam āpannāḥ yathā pramāṇāni prameyatvam ity ata āha — yathoktā iti/ hetvābhāsalakṣaṇenaiva nigrahasthānabhāva iti/
children.translated_text: The <s>hetvābhāsas</s> are also <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat). Have the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> then become <s>nigrahasthānas</s> by possessing another defining characteristic — as the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) are also <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge)? Therefore he says "as previously described" — they are <s>nigrahasthānas</s> by the very defining characteristic of <s>hetvābhāsas</s>.

children.text:
ta ime pramāṇādayaḥ padārthā uddiṣṭā lakṣitāḥ parīkṣitāś ceti//24//
yo 'kṣapādam ṛṣiṃ nyāyaḥ pratyabhād vadatāṃ varam/
tasya vātsyāyana idaṃ bhāṣyajātam avartayat//
iti śrīvātsyāyanīye nyāyabhāṣye pañcamo 'dhyāyaḥ/
children.translated_text:
Thus these categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> have been enumerated, defined, and examined. // 24 //
The <s>Nyāya</s> [system] that illuminated <s>Akṣapāda</s>, the foremost among speakers, the sage —
<s>Vātsyāyana</s> composed this body of commentary upon it.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the glorious <s>Vātsyāyanīya Nyāyabhāṣya</s>.
